p.seg: Preface to the "Shìlèi Fù"
During the Chúnhuà reign period,
Academician Wú Shù presented his work "Shìlèi Fù" in one hundred chapters to the court.
Emperor Tàizōng praised its excellence and comprehensiveness,
and thus ordered it to be annotated,
promoting Wú Shù to the position of a Water Department official.
Now, examining this book,
it employs parallel prose in four- and six-character lines,
with concise language and comprehensive content,
drawing from the classics, histories, and the works of the hundred schools,
as well as biographies and accounts from beyond the orthodox tradition,
leaving nothing unrepresented.
Compared to Lǐ Qiáo's single-topic poems or Dīng Jìngōng's "Qīngjīn Jí",
the effort invested in this work is immeasurably greater.
As time has passed,
it has become rare in the world.
Supervisor Zhèng Gōng of Xíngyáng, upon receiving his appointment to the eastern region of Zhè,
had not been in office for long
before he restored all neglected affairs.
In his leisure time, he gathered various books,
studying and pondering them deeply,
finding pleasure in them after his official duties.
Thus, using the fine edition of "Shìlèi Fù" from his collection, he had it carved onto printing blocks,
to benefit scholars in their textual studies and examinations,
and also instructed Biān Dūndé to record the origins of this work on the right.
Biān Dūndé has carefully observed that the composition of regulated verse based on the four tones
originated in the Qí and Liáng dynasties and flourished in the Suí and Táng dynasties,
and is now used as a step in the selection of officials.
Its matching of words and arrangement of content,
with its meticulous rules and structures,
is sufficient to suppress the spirit of the world's heroes.
As for its origins and various schools,
anything that contributes to parallelism and rhyme
should not be withheld and left untransmitted.
Although Wú Shù's work is broad and profound in its intent,
and aims to benefit future generations,
without Zhèng Gōng, its teachings could not have been widely disseminated,
allowing scholars to study and appreciate it.
On the twenty-third day of the midsummer month in the Bǐngyín year of the Shàoxīng reign period,
Right Assistant for Meritorious Service, specially appointed to supervise the Nányuè Temple in Tánzhōu, Biān Dūndé respectfully writes this preface.
Memorial on the Presentation of the Annotated "Shìlèi Fù"
To the right,
your subject previously presented the one hundred poems of the "Yīzì Tí Fù" he had composed,
and upon reflection, feeling their crude and burdensome nature,
was filled with anxiety and concern,
when I suddenly received your imperial instruction,
commanding me to add annotations.
I humbly submit that works of categorized knowledge
have been passed down in considerable numbers,
but lacking clear organization,
they are generally difficult to memorize.
Now, synthesizing them into poetic form,
makes them brilliantly accessible.
However, since the references are extensive,
annotations are essential.
Considering the reach of your sagely wisdom,
how can my shallow learning suffice?
Now, under each line,
I have provided explanations of the references,
indicating the sources
and the books from which they originate,
so that scholars may know their origins.
Moreover, the essence of categorized collections
lies in being easily understood;
thus, I have included explanations
without exhaustive citation,
but where omission is impossible,
they are fully retained.
All works of prognostication and apocrypha,
as well as Xiè Chéng's "Hòu Hàn Shū",
Zhāng Fán's "Hàn Jì", "Xù Hàn Shū", and "Dìxì Pǔ",
Xú Zhěng's "Cháng Lì", "Xuánzhōng Jì", "Wùlǐ Lùn", and the like,
though now lost or scattered,
have been traditionally used by authors,
and I could not bear to discard them,
so I have also preserved them.
The previously presented twenty volumes,
with added annotations,
have expanded in size,
and are now extended to thirty volumes,
titled "Shìlèi Fù".
Lacking Zhāng Huá's breadth of knowledge,
I am honored to have this presented to you;
unable to match Lù Jiǎ's literary achievements,
how dare I expect praise?
I have merely poured out my humble thoughts,
hardly worthy of your imperial mind.
I humbly beg Your Majesty the Emperor,
to condescend to acknowledge my modest abilities,
and grant your sagely perusal.
If your grace, like heaven and earth,
does not overlook even the lowly straw dog,
then the diligence of my writing brush
may perhaps shine faintly on the margins of silk and paper.
I presume to trouble your imperial presence,
filled with trepidation and deep reverence.
Heaven
In the beginning of the Tàichū era,
the dark and yellow were merged together.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
Tàiyì is
when qi has not yet been seen.
Tàichū is
the beginning of qi.
Chén Sīwáng Cáo Zhí’s *Wèi Dé Lùn* says:
In ancient times during Tàichū,
the dark and yellow were merged together.
When the one qi first separated,
the tangible was born from the intangible.
Pān Yuè’s *Xī Zhēng Fù* says:
Transforming the one qi, it distinguishes the three powers.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
That which has form
is born from that which has no form.
Thus, the earth settled below as the turbid yīn,
Xú Zhěng’s *Sānwǔ Lì* says:
The clear yang became heaven,
the turbid yīn became earth.
Heaven was above, light and clear.
The *Yì Qián Záodù* says:
The light and clear rose upward to become heaven;
the heavy and turbid sank downward to become earth.
This is the essence of the multitude of yang,
the *Chūnqiū Shuōtící* says:
Heaven,
the essence of the multitude of yang,
combines to form Tàiyī,
and divides into different names.
Accumulated qi formed it.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
Heaven
is merely accumulated qi.
The sun, moon, and stars
are also the luminous brilliance of qi.
Vast and boundless, dark and expansive,
it cannot be given form,
the *Huáinánzǐ* says:
In the time before heaven and earth existed,
there was a vast, boundless chaos,
with no knowledge of its gate,
dark and expansive, see below,
Duke Qí looked up and observed.
Note:
Zhāng Héng’s *Língxiàn Fù* says:
Before Tàisù,
there was silence and profound darkness,
it could not be given form.
Vast and boundless, misty and chaotic,
none knew its end.
The *Dìxì Pǔ* says:
When heaven and earth first arose,
it was vast, boundless, misty, and chaotic.
Note:
Míng,
pronounced mò dǐng fǎn.
Xìng,
pronounced hú dǐng fǎn.
Its qi is bright and vast,
the *Ěryǎ* says:
Summer is called Hàotiān.
The note states:
This refers to its qi being bright and vast.
Its body is vaulted and lofty.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
Qiōngcāng,
is the blue sky.
The note states:
The form of heaven is vaulted and lofty,
its color is azure,
hence it is named thus.
Observing the patterns to discern seasonal changes,
the *Yì* says:
Observe the celestial patterns,
to discern seasonal changes.
Displaying images to reveal good and bad fortune.
The *Yì* says:
Heaven displays images,
revealing good and bad fortune.
The sage takes them as a model.
Great is the creative origin of Qián,
from which all things derive their beginning.
From the *Yì*.
Establishing the celestial pole at the Bǎodǒu,
Huán Tán’s *Xīn Lùn* says:
The learned Yáng Zǐyún, based on the theories of many Confucian scholars,
considered heaven to constantly rotate leftward,
with the sun, moon, and stars following it east and west.
He then depicted their forms and movements,
correlating them with the four seasons, calendar calculations, dusk and dawn, day and night,
intending to establish rules for the world,
to pass down methods to later generations.
I challenged him, saying:
"During the spring and autumn equinoxes, day and night should be equal.
At dawn, the sun rises in Mǎo,
due east;
at dusk, the sun sets in Yǒu,
due west.
Now, if we observe based on people across the world,
this is the human Mǎo and Yǒu,
not the celestial Mǎo and Yǒu.
The celestial Mǎo and Yǒu
should be at the North Star.
The North Star
is the celestial pivot.
The pivot
is the axis of heaven.
It is like a canopy having a Bǎodǒu.
Although the canopy rotates, the Bǎodǒu does not move.
Heaven also rotates in a circle,
but the North Star is always constant,
showing it is the center of heaven.
Looking up at it,
it is also in the north,
not directly above people.
Yet during the spring and autumn equinoxes,
the sun's rising and setting are south of the Dipper,
as if the canopy rotates.
Then the northern path is far,
the southern path is near.
How then can the lengths of day and night
be equal?"
Zǐyún had no way to resolve this.
Later, when I was reporting matters with Zǐyún,
we sat in the corridor of the White Tiger Hall.
Because it was cold,
we turned our backs to the sun to warm them.
After a while,
the sunlight left our backs,
and they were no longer warmed.
I then showed Zǐyún and said:
"If heaven rotates like a canopy and the sun moves westward,
its light and shadow should shine along this corridor and gradually move eastward.
Could this instead correspond to the methods of the Húntiān school?"
Zǐyún immediately destroyed what he had made.
Thus, the Confucian view that heaven rotates leftward
is incorrect.
Verifying the sun and stars through the ant on the millstone.
The *Lùnhéng* says:
The gate of heaven is in the northwest.
Also,
the sun, moon, and stars follow heaven westward,
moving slower than heaven.
It is like an ant walking on a millstone:
the ant moves slowly,
the millstone turns quickly;
though their movements differ internally,
externally they still rotate together.
Its motion
turns like a wheel hub;
the *Húntiānyí* says:
Heaven and earth each stand by riding on qi,
floating while carrying water.
The sun, moon, and stars revolve below the earth,
so half of the twenty-eight constellations are hidden.
Heaven rotates
like the motion of a wheel hub.
Its speed
flows like a crossbow bolt.
The *Lùnhéng* says:
Heaven moves 365 degrees,
totaling 730,000 lǐ.
Its movement is very swift,
with nothing to verify it,
perhaps similar to the motion of a potter's wheel or the flight of a crossbow bolt?
Half covers the earth above,
half resides below the earth.
Wáng Fān’s *Húntiān Shuō* says:
The complete circle of heaven is 365 and 145/589 degrees.
East, west, south, and north,
turning and extending within the same circle,
half covers the earth above,
half is below the earth,
so half of the twenty-eight lodgings are hidden.
Measuring it with an instrument,
what is visible is always about 182 degrees and a fraction,
thus it is known that half covers the earth above,
half is below the earth.
Some say it is like an egg containing a yolk,
Yáo Xìn’s *Xīntiān Lùn* says:
If heaven wraps around the earth
like an egg containing a yolk,
what does the earth rely on to stand and be stable?
The *Húntiānyí* says:
Heaven is like a chicken egg,
earth is like the yolk in the center,
residing within heaven.
Heaven is large, earth is small,
and there is water inside and out.
Or like a box pressing down on water.
Yú Bǐng’s *Qióngtiān Lùn* says:
The form of heaven is vaulted and lofty,
like a bamboo hat covering the surface of the earth,
floating above the primordial qi.
It is like a box covering and pressing down on water without sinking,
because qi fills it inside.
The sun revolves around the celestial pole,
It sets in the west and returns to the east,
not entering beneath the earth.
The "Square Heaven" theory was already seen in Wáng Chōng,
Hè Dàoyǎng's "Record of the Celestial Sphere" says:
In recent times there have been four theories:
the first is called "Square Heaven,"
initiated by Wáng Chōng;
the second is called "Canopy Heaven,"
originated by Yáo Xìn;
the third is called "Vaulted Heaven,"
heard of from Yú Bǐng.
All are conjectures and baseless talk,
not worth considering.
Only the matter of the celestial sphere,
has evidence and is beyond doubt.
The "Peaceful Heaven" theory was also heard of from Yú Xǐ.
"The Astronomical Record" says:
The ancients spoke of three forms of heaven and earth:
the first is the celestial sphere,
the second is the canopy heaven,
the third is the expansive night.
The theory of the expansive night,
has never been seen.
Later, Yú Bǐng wrote "On Vaulted Heaven,"
Yú Xǐ wrote "On Peaceful Heaven,"
Yáo Xìn wrote "On Dawn Heaven."
Luò Xiàhóng verified it at the center of the earth,
"The Biographies of Elders of Yìdū" says:
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Luò Xiàhóng was well-versed in astronomy,
at the center of the earth he rotated the celestial sphere,
to determine the seasons.
Gěng Xún measured it within a chamber.
"The Book of Suì" says:
Gěng Xún saw his old friend Gāo Zhìbǎo serving as an astronomer in the Imperial Observatory,
Xún studied astronomy and mathematics under him.
Xún conceived and created an armillary sphere,
not relying on human power,
but using water to turn it,
placed in a dark room,
externally observing the celestial seasons,
matching as perfectly as tally and token.
Vast and profound,
"The Rites" says:
The way of heaven and earth,
is broad and deep.
Bright and revolving,
"The Book of Songs" says:
Bright is that Milky Way,
revolving in the heavens.
Elms are called distinct,
"Ancient Yuefu Poetry" says:
What is there in the heavens?
Distinctly planted are white elms.
The net's theory is vast.
"Lǎozǐ" says:
Heaven's net is vast,
sparse yet nothing escapes.
Snow and frost descend, wind and rain spread,
all are teachings,
"The Rites" says:
Heaven has four seasons,
wind, rain, frost, and dew,
all are teachings.
The four seasons proceed and all things flourish,
what more need be said!
"The Analects" says:
What does Heaven say!
The four seasons proceed,
the hundred things are born.
Admirable is that which holds the yang,
"The Rites" says:
Heaven holds yang,
suspending the sun and stars.
Rooted in affinity with the above.
"The Book of Changes" says:
That which is rooted in heaven is close to the above.
Manifesting ceaselessness and moving with strength,
"The Rites" says:
That which manifests ceaselessness,
is heaven.
"The Book of Changes" says:
Heaven moves with strength.
Arraying the three lights to form images.
"The Book of Changes" says:
In heaven they form images,
on earth they take shape.
Suppressing the high reveals the way of drawing a bow,
"Lǎozǐ" says:
Is not the way of heaven like drawing a bow?
The high is suppressed,
the low is raised.
Looking down recognizes the shape of an overturned bowl.
"Discourses Weighed in the Balance" says:
Heaven is level and no different from earth,
like the shape of an overturned bowl.
As for dark shadows reflecting like jade discs,
myriad stars strung like pearls,
"The Hooked Destiny Decisive" says:
Stars clustered like strung pearls,
shining like linked jade discs.
Investigating the theory of expansive night,
"Bàopǔzǐ" says:
The book of expansive night is lost,
but Qiè Méng recorded the teachings passed down by his master on expansive night, saying:
Heaven has absolutely no substance,
looking up to observe it,
it is high and boundless,
like looking from afar at Huángshān, all appears green,
looking down into a thousand-ren valley appears dark black,
the azure and dark colors are not its substance.
Sun, moon, and stars float in the empty sky,
their movements and stillness are all accumulated qi.
Therefore, the seven luminaries sometimes stay, sometimes wander,
retrograde, direct, hidden, or visible without constancy,
because they have no root or attachment,
hence each is different.
Therefore, the celestial pole always remains in its place,
the Northern Dipper does not set in the west with the other stars.
The seven luminaries all move eastward,
the sun moves one degree,
the moon moves thirteen degrees,
slow or fast according to their nature,
if they were attached to the celestial body,
this would not be so.
Studying the book of the Zhou Gnomon.
Yáng Quán's "Discourse on the Principles of Things" says:
The Confucians established the celestial sphere,
to emulate the form of heaven,
like a chariot wheel.
The Zhou Gnomon established the canopy heaven,
saying celestial qi moves along the edges,
like a millstone.
Shēn Xū spoke of it with utmost subtlety,
"The Zuǒzhuàn" says:
There was a comet at the Great Star,
reaching west to the Milky Way.
Shēn Xū said:
"The broom star is to sweep away the old and establish the new.
Heavenly affairs often manifest signs,
now it sweeps away the fire,
when fire appears it must spread,
will the feudal lords have fire disasters!"
Bí Zào discussed it with abundance.
"The Zuǒzhuàn" says:
A disaster in Chén,
Zhèng's Bí Zào said:
"In five years,
Chén will be re-established.
Established for twenty-five years and then perish."
Zǐchǎn asked the reason,
he replied:
"Chén,
belongs to water.
Water,
is the consort of fire.
And Chǔ is its minister.
Now fire appears and sets fire to Chén,
expelling Chǔ and establishing Chén.
Consort with five completing it,
hence five years.
The year five reaches the Quail Fire,
and then Chén finally perishes,
Chǔ conquers and possesses it,
this is the way of heaven.
Hence twenty-five years."
Also heard of the nine fields as names,
"The Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ" says:
Heaven has nine fields.
What are the nine fields?
The central is called Jūn Tiān,
the eastern is called Cāng Tiān,
the northeast is called Biàn Tiān,
the northern is called Xuán Tiān,
the northwest is called Yōu Tiān,
the western is called Hào Tiān,
the southwest is called Zhū Tiān,
the southern is called Yán Tiān,
the southeast is called Yáng Tiān.
The ten aspects are the principles,
"The Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals" says:
Heaven has ten aspects;
heaven is one aspect,
earth is one aspect,
yang is one aspect,
yin is one aspect,
water is one aspect,
earth is one aspect,
man is one aspect,
metal is one aspect,
wood is one aspect,
fire is one aspect,
altogether ten aspects.
Heaven also has the qi of joy and anger,
the heart of sorrow and joy,
corresponding to man.
Combining by category,
heaven and man are one.
Spring's joyful qi gives birth,
autumn's angry qi kills,
The music of summer nurtures with its qi,
the sorrow of winter stores with its qi.
These four,
are possessed alike by Heaven and humanity.
They are the ancestors of the myriad things.
The Lǐ Tǒng says:
Heaven and Earth,
are born from the primordial qi,
the ancestors of the myriad things.
They employ the four seasons as officials.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The four seasons,
are the officials of Heaven;
the sun and moon,
are the envoys of Heaven;
the stars and constellations,
are the schedule of Heaven;
rainbows and comets,
are the wrath of Heaven.
They startled the State of Zhèng with a second dawn,
The Jí Zhǒng Jìnián says:
In the first year of King Yì,
Heaven dawned twice upon Zhèng.
They awakened Duke Huán of Qí to look up and see.
The Shuōyuàn says:
Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What does a king value?"
He replied:
"He values Heaven."
Duke Huán looked up at Heaven,
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"What is called Heaven,
does not refer to the vast, boundless sky.
Those who stand above the people,
should take the common people as their Heaven."
Cháng Hóng defied it and his support crumbled,
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Nǚ Shūkuān said:
"Zhōu's Cháng Hóng and Qí's Gāo Zhāng,
will both not escape misfortune.
Cháng Hóng defies Heaven,
Master Gāo defies the people.
What Heaven destroys,
cannot be supported;
what the multitude does,
cannot be opposed."
Mùzǐ dreamed of it pressing down upon him.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Initially,
Mùzǐ left the Shūsūn clan,
went to Qí,
married a woman from the Guó clan,
and bore Mèng Bǐng and Zhòng Rén.
He dreamed Heaven was pressing down on him,
and he could not withstand it.
Looking back, he saw a man,
with a black face and hunched back,
deep-set eyes and a snout-like mouth,
who called out to him:
"Niú,
help me."
Then he overcame it.
As for Huángdì's canopy model,
Zhuānxū's armillary sphere,
Liú's Lì Zhèng Wèn Yuē Shuō states:
Zhuānxū created the armillary sphere,
Huángdì made the canopy model,
both taking Heaven's image as a canopy.
It can be measured with a gnomon,
The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn says:
On the day of the winter solstice,
erect an eight-foot gnomon,
at midday observe its shadow,
if the shadow matches the measurement,
the year will be bountiful and people harmonious.
Otherwise, the year will be harsh and people confused.
Who can view it through a tube?
The Hànshū, Dōngfāng Shuò's Dá Nàn says:
Viewing Heaven through a tube,
measuring the sea with a ladle,
how can one examine its patterns,
and comprehend its principles!
The Way is enduring and one hears of the Lǐ,
The Lǐ says:
The Way of Heaven and Earth,
is vast,
is thick,
is high,
is bright,
is enduring,
is lasting.
The steps are difficult and one sees it in the Shī.
The Shī says:
Heaven's steps are difficult,
this man is not worthy.
Since it dwells on high and governs below,
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
Heaven (tiān) means the summit,
dwelling high and ordering below,
it is the warp for humanity.
It is also constantly upright and without partiality.
The Shēnzǐ says:
The Way of Heaven is without partiality,
therefore it is constantly upright;
the Way of Heaven is constantly upright,
therefore it is clear and bright.
We have discussed the image of the covering hat,
the matter is detailed in the note on "using a box to press water."
How could we know the time when the sky leans on a pestle?
The Hétú Tǐng Zuǒ Fǔ says:
A hundred generations later,
the earth will be higher than Heaven,
with no wind or rain,
no cold or heat,
the people will again eat earth,
all will know their mothers,
but not their fathers.
Thus,
a thousand years later,
Heaven can lean on a pestle,
roaring and rumbling,
none know its beginning or end.
Benevolence was already exemplified by Fàngxūn,
The Dàdài Lǐ says:
Fàngxūn,
his benevolence was like Heaven,
his wisdom was like a spirit,
approaching him was like the sun,
gazing at him was like clouds.
His height was still comparable to Zhòngní.
The Lúnyǔ says:
Zhòngní,
is like Heaven, one cannot ascend to him by steps.
He grants the people the seasons,
The Shū says:
Then he commanded Xī and Hé,
to reverently follow the vast Heaven,
to calculate and observe the sun, moon, and stars,
and respectfully grant the people the seasons.
He rectifies with the jade sphere.
The Shū says:
Observe the jade sphere and jade balance,
to regulate the seven governors.
Táng Yáo's command to Xī and Hé,
The Shū says:
Then he commanded Xī and Hé,
to reverently follow the vast Heaven.
Gāoxīn's appointment of Zhòng and Lí to oversee.
The Wényào Gōu says:
Gāoxīn received the mandate, Zhòng and Lí expounded on astronomy.
Therefore, the king wears the dragon robe to symbolize it,
The Lǐ says:
On the day of sacrifice,
the king wears the dragon robe to symbolize Heaven.
He burns firewood and sacrifices to it.
The Lǐ says:
Burning firewood on the great altar,
is sacrificing to Heaven.
The southern suburb is the position of yang,
The Lǐ says:
Sacrificing to Heaven in the southern suburb,
is the principle of approaching yang.
The ceremony of serving as father at the round mound,
The Chūnqiū Gǎnjīngfú says:
The ruler of men,
takes Heaven as father,
Earth as mother,
the sun as elder brother,
the moon as elder sister.
The note says:
He serves Heaven as father at the round mound,
Earth as mother at the square marsh,
the sun as elder brother at the eastern suburb,
the moon as elder sister at the western suburb.
With disasters and anomalies, it sends down warnings,
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
Why does Heaven have calamities and changes?
To warn and admonish the ruler,
awaken him to his faults,
desiring to make him repent, be cautious, and reflect.
Is it truly mysterious and distant and difficult to know?
The Jìnshū says:
When Zhāng Huá was Minister of Works,
the star of the central platform split,
his youngest son Wěi urged Huá to resign.
Huá did not comply,
saying:
"The Way of Heaven is mysterious and distant,
one can only cultivate virtue to respond to it.
It is better to wait quietly,
and await Heaven's mandate."
Therefore, its virtue manifests as clear and bright,
The Lǐ says:
Clear and bright symbolizes Heaven.
Its Way is called gentle overcoming,
The Shū says:
The deep and hidden overcome with firmness,
the lofty and bright overcome with gentleness.
Gaze upon the vast primordial qi,
The Lǐ‧Zhōngyōng says:
Deep, deep as the abyss,
vast, vast as the heavens.
I gaze up at the true color of the azure sky.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Is the azure of the heavens
its true color?
Or is it because it is so distant and we look at it
that it appears without limit?"
It is deficient in the southeast.
The *Chǔcí·Tiānwèn* says:
"Where do the eight pillars stand?
Why is the southeast deficient?"
The commentary states:
"It is said that heaven has eight mountains as pillars,
where do they all stand?
The southeast is insufficient;
who could have caused this lack?"
It is profound in the northwest.
The *Tàixuán Jīng* says:
"Heaven takes the unseen as mysterious,
earth takes the formless as mysterious,
man takes the heart and mind as mysterious.
Heaven's profundity lies in the northwest,
where essence is nurtured and transformed;
earth's profundity lies in the Yellow Springs,
where the soul and spirit are hidden;
man's profundity lies in thought and reflection,
containing the utmost essence."
The celestial street points to Bì and Mǎo.
The *Hànshū* says:
"In the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
there was a lunar halo
encircling Shēn and Bì sevenfold.
The divination stated:
'Between Bì and Mǎo
lies the Celestial Street.
North of the street are the Hú people,
south of the street is the Central Kingdom.'"
Later, the siege of Píngchéng indeed occurred.
The palace is called Yíngshì.
The *Hànshū* says:
"Yíngshì is the ancestral temple,
also called the detached palace."
Heaven is difficult to trust and inconstant.
The *Shū* says:
"Heaven is difficult to trust,
and fate is inconstant."
It shows no partiality but supports virtue.
The *Shū* says:
"August Heaven shows no partiality;
it supports only the virtuous."
It constantly diminishes the full and increases the humble.
The *Yì* says:
"The way of Heaven is to diminish the full and increase the humble."
It often accomplishes things through non-action.
The *Lǐ* says:
"Through non-action, things are accomplished;
this is the way of Heaven."
Zōu Yǎn once discoursed on it.
The *Wǔjīng Tōngyì* says:
"Zōu Yǎn spoke grandly on heavenly matters,
and was called 'Discourser Yǎn.'"
The Bǎozhāng official holds this duty.
The *Zhōulǐ* states that the Bǎozhāng official is in charge of heavenly stars,
recording the changes of stars, the sun, and the moon,
and observing the transformations of the world.
The raining of grain was seen during Shénnóng's time.
The *Zhōushū* says:
"During Shénnóng's time,
heaven rained grain,
and Shénnóng plowed and planted it."
The descent of seeds is also heard of regarding Hòujì.
The *Shī* says:
"Heaven bestowed fine seeds,
both black millet and double-grained millet."
The *Kǒngcóngzǐ* says:
"King Wèi asked Zǐ Shùn:
'I have heard that in ancient times, Heaven miraculously favored Hòujì,
bestowing fine grain upon him,
and thus Zhōu flourished.'"
Gònggōng struck the mountain and broke the pillar.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
"Gònggōng contended with Zhuānxū for the throne,
and in anger struck Mount Bùzhōu,
breaking the pillar of heaven
and severing the cords of earth.
Thus, heaven tilted to the northwest,
and the sun, moon, and stars moved there;
earth became insufficient in the southeast,
and all rivers and waters flowed there."
Nǚwā mended the gap and smelted stones.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
"Heaven and earth are also things;
things have deficiencies.
Thus, in ancient times, Nǚwā selected five-colored stones to mend the gaps."
Qín Mì once presented arguments in a debate.
The *Shǔzhì* says:
"Wú envoy Zhāng Wēn came on a visit.
Qín Mì was twelve years old
and was seated with Zhūgě Liàng.
Wēn asked:
'Who is this?'
Liàng replied:
'A scholar.'
Wēn asked:
'Does heaven have a head?'
Mì said:
'Yes.
The *Shī* says, "It turned its gaze westward."
If heaven had no head,
how could it turn its gaze?'
Wēn asked again:
'Does it have ears?'
Mì said:
'Yes.
The *Shī* says, "The crane cries in the nine marshes,
its voice is heard by heaven."
If it had no ears,
how could it hear?'
'Does heaven have feet?'
Mì said:
'Yes.
The *Shī* says, "Heaven's steps are difficult."
If it had no feet,
how could it step?'
'Does heaven have a surname?'
Mì said:
'Yes.'
'What surname?'
Mì said:
'The surname Liú.'
'How do you know?'
Mì said:
'Its son's surname is Liú,
so I know it.'"
Wēn greatly respected him.
Péi Kǎi also demonstrated keen insight.
The *Jìnshū* says:
"When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he divined the number of generations his dynasty would last.
Drawing a lot, he obtained the number one.
All the ministers turned pale.
The official Péi Kǎi stepped forward and said:
'Heaven obtains oneness and becomes clear;
the feudal lords and kings obtain oneness and become the standard of the world.'
The emperor was greatly pleased."
As for the greatness within the realm,
the *Lǎozǐ* says:
"Within the realm, there are four great things:
the Dào is great,
heaven is great,
earth is great,
and the king is also great."
Obtaining oneness, it becomes clear.
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
"Heaven obtains oneness and becomes clear;
if heaven lacked clarity,
it would fear splitting apart."
Establish the eight-foot circular instrument.
Cài Yōng's *Tiānwénzhì* says:
"Those who speak of the celestial sphere have three schools:
the first is the Zhōubǐ;
the second is the Xuānyè;
the third is the Húntiān.
The Xuānyè school
has no surviving masters or methods.
The Zhōubǐ techniques and calculations are preserved,
but when tested against celestial phenomena,
they often fail to match,
so the official historians do not use them.
Only the Húntiān school closely captures the truth.
The bronze instrument used by the official historians at the observation platform today
follows this method.
Establishing an eight-foot circular instrument,
it embodies the images of heaven and earth,
corrects the ecliptic,
and tracks the five planets.
Precise, profound, and subtle,
it is an unchanging principle for a hundred generations."
Recognize the nine names of the Tàixuán.
The *Tàixuán Jīng* says:
"The nine heavens:
the first is Zhōngtiān;
the second is Xiàntiān;
the third is Shùntiān;
the fourth is Gēngtiān;
the fifth is Zuìtiān;
the sixth is Kuòtiān;
the seventh is Xiántiān;
the eighth is Chéntiān;
the ninth is Chéngtiān."
The creation was heard of from Táo Jǐng.
The *Liángshū* says:
"Táo Hóngjǐng once made a celestial sphere model,
about three feet high,
with earth at the center,
heaven rotating while earth remained still,
driven by mechanisms,
all in harmony with the heavens."
Its marvels were perhaps spoken of by Zhāng Héng.
Zhāng Héng's "Armillary Sphere" states:
The celestial equator is a horizontal belt,
the belly of heaven,
ninety-one and five-nineteenths degrees from the celestial pole.
The ecliptic is an oblique belt,
its belly extends beyond the celestial equator,
with twenty-four degrees on each side, inside and out.
Therefore, at the summer solstice, it is sixty-seven degrees and more from the pole,
and at the winter solstice, it is one hundred and fifteen degrees from the pole,
also more.
Thus, where the ecliptic obliquely intersects the celestial equator,
that is the distance from the pole at the autumn and spring equinoxes.
Now, at this spring equinox, it is ninety degrees from the pole,
and at the autumn equinox, it is ninety-one degrees and a little less.
This follows the method of measuring the distance from the pole using the sundial shadow in the Xià calendar,
taken as the standard.
"The Yìxī Daily Records" states:
In the fourteenth year,
the Chancellor memorialized, saying:
Recently, upon pacifying Cháng'ān,
we obtained the armillary sphere and gnomon made by Zhāng Héng,
treasures from successive dynasties.
We respectfully send them forth,
to be returned to the imperial treasury.
Rotating, one recognizes the shape of a pellet.
Wáng Fán's "Discourse on the Celestial Sphere" states:
The old theory of the forms of heaven and earth
is like that of a bird's egg,
with heaven enveloping earth on the outside,
just as the shell wraps the yolk,
all around like a pellet,
hence called the celestial sphere.
This means its form is perfectly round.
Covering all, one sees the shape of a tilted canopy.
"The Astronomical Records" states:
Heaven is like a tilted carriage canopy,
high in the south and low in the north.
As for its movement through the six qì,
"The Zuǒzhuàn" states:
Heaven has six qì,
which descend to produce the five flavors.
The commentary states:
The six qì
refer to yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
Supported by the eight pillars,
"The Chǔcí: Heavenly Questions" states:
The circle has nine layers,
who measured and planned it?
What achievement is this?
Who first created it?
Where are the cords and ties fastened?
Where is the celestial pole added?
Where do the eight pillars meet?
Why is the southeast deficient?
The commentary states:
Guǎn
means to turn.
Wéi
means the guiding ropes.
"Where do the eight pillars meet?"
means heaven has eight mountains as pillars,
and where do they all stand?
Having warned Jìn and opened up Wèi,
"The Zuǒzhuàn" states:
Heaven is perhaps greatly warning Jìn.
It also states:
The Marquis of Jìn granted Bì Wàn Wèi.
Bǔ Yǎn said:
"Bì Wàn's descendants will surely become great.
Wàn
is a number of fullness;
Wèi
is a great name.
Beginning the reward with this,
Heaven has opened it for him."
Also, it gave Táng to and conferred upon Chǔ.
"The Shǐjì" states:
Shū Yú's mother dreamed that Heaven said to King Wǔ:
"I command you to bear a son named Yú,
and I give him Táng."
When the child was born,
there was the character "Yú" on his palm,
so he was thus named.
"The Zuǒzhuàn" states:
Gōngsūn Guīfù met the ruler of Chǔ in Sòng,
and the people of Sòng reported the emergency to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn wished to rescue them,
but Bó Zōng said:
"It cannot be done.
Heaven is currently conferring [favor] upon Chǔ,
we cannot contend with it.
Even with Jìn's strength,
can we defy Heaven?"
Therefore, one should reverently comply,
"The Shū" states:
Then he commanded Xī and Hé,
to reverently comply with the vast Heaven.
How can one be frivolous and idle?
"The Shī" states:
Revere Heaven's anger,
and dare not be frivolous and idle.
Transmitting Yú Bǐng's profound insight,
one sees "the image of the bamboo hat."
Bowing to Yáo Xìn's refined thought.
Yáo Xìn's "Discourse on the Inclined Heaven" states:
At the winter solstice, the pole is extremely low,
heaven's motion is near the south,
therefore the sun is far from people,
and the Dipper is near to people.
The northern celestial qì arrives,
hence it is icy cold.
At the summer solstice, the pole rises high,
heaven's motion is near the north,
therefore the Dipper is far from people,
and the sun is near to people.
The southern celestial qì arrives,
hence it is steaming hot.
When the pole is high,
the path of the sun through the earth is shallow,
therefore the night is short;
heaven is high above the earth,
therefore the day is long.
When the pole is low,
the path of the sun through the earth is deep,
therefore the night is long;
heaven is close to the earth below,
therefore the day is short.
Thus, the motion of heaven
in winter follows the celestial sphere model,
and in summer follows the canopy model.
As for Wū Xián calling at the gate,
Yáng Zǐyún's "Rhapsody on Gānquán" states:
Selecting Wū Xián to call at the imperial gate,
opening the heavenly court to receive the multitude of spirits.
Commentary:
This means ordering the shaman to call at the heavenly gate.
Master Táo striking the gate,
"The Garden of Marvels" states:
Táo Kǎn dreamed of flying and soaring up to heaven.
The heavenly gate had nine layers,
he had entered eight of them,
but could not enter the remaining one.
He beat against heaven with his wings,
one wing broke,
and he awoke in fright and fell down,
with swelling and pain in his left armpit.
Afterwards, his authority indeed overshadowed his lord,
and he harbored the ambition to spy and emulate [the throne].
Each time he recalled the omen of the broken wing,
he restrained his heart and stopped.
"The Shī" speaks of the Milky Way,
"The Shī" states:
Vast is that Milky Way,
shining and revolving in the sky.
The pillar is known as Kūnlún.
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Classic of Divine Marvels" states:
Kūnlún has a bronze pillar,
so high it reaches heaven,
called the pillar of heaven.
Hearing of King Tāng looking up and licking it,
and the tale of Empress Dèng who once touched it.
"The Book of the Later Hàn" states:
Empress Dèng, the Héxī Empress,
once dreamed of touching heaven.
The heavenly body was vast and azure,
smooth like malt sugar,
with shapes like stalactites,
and she looked up to sip and drink it.
She inquired of a dream interpreter,
and the interpreter said:
"Yáo dreamed of climbing up to heaven,
and Tāng dreamed of reaching heaven and licking it.
These are both omens preceding sage rulers,
auspicious beyond words."
Tracing Gěng's decline to Yángzǐ,
Yángzǐ's "Model Sayings" states:
Someone asked about the celestial sphere,
and he said:
"Luò Xiàhóng constructed it,
Xiānyú Wàngrén measured it,
and Prefect Gěng modeled it."
He was asked about the canopy heaven,
and said:
"The canopy!
The canopy!
It is not nearly [accurate]."
The commentary states:
Jī
means near.
Unifying the celestial sphere and canopy for Líng'ēn.
Confucian scholars discussing heaven
each adhered to the two theories of the celestial sphere and the canopy.
Discussing the canopy did not match the celestial sphere,
discussing the celestial sphere did not match the canopy.
Cuī Líng'ēn established a theory,
making the celestial sphere and canopy into one.
Having recognized the leftward rotation,
"The Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall" states:
Heaven rotates leftward,
and earth revolves rightward.
Just as the ruler and minister, yin and yang, face each other.
It is also said to revolve and return.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
The Way of Heaven is round,
the Way of Earth is square,
and it is by this that the sage establishes the world.
The roundness of Heaven
means that the essence and qi are perfectly connected,
revolving and returning without obstruction,
hence it is called round.
The squareness of Earth
means that the myriad things have different forms,
each with its own distinct duties,
and cannot substitute for one another,
hence it is called square.
The ruler holds the round, while the minister occupies the square;
if round and square do not change, the state will prosper.
It has been heard that insufficiency leads to splitting;
Jīng Fáng’s *Yì Zhuàn* says:
When the earth trembles,
it is because yin is excessive.
When the sky splits,
it is because yang is insufficient.
Often, one must stoop even under a high canopy.
The *Shī* says:
Though the sky is said to be high,
one dares not but stoop.
The discourse of Sīzhēn is subtle and profound.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
In Wú, there was Gě Dào,
styled Sīzhēn,
who modified the celestial sphere,
placing the earth at the center,
and using a mechanism to rotate it,
so that the heavens turned while the earth remained still.
The words of Dàoyǎng are intricate and detailed.
Hè Dàoyǎng’s *Húntiān Jì* says:
In the past, there were three theories about the structure of the heavens:
the first is the celestial sphere,
whose origins are unknown.
The *Shū* states, “The jade sphere and jade balance
were used to regulate the seven celestial bodies,”
which refers to the celestial sphere.
The second is Xuānyè,
the method of the Xià and Yīn dynasties.
The third is Zhōubì,
recorded by the Zhōu people and said to have been transmitted by the Duke of Zhōu.
Some say it passes between two lands.
Yáo Xìn’s *Xīntiān Lùn* says:
The theory of two lands
holds that the lower land is the root of the upper land.
Heaven moves northward between the two lands.
Some say it connects to the Flying Valley.
Yú Xǐ’s *Āntiān Lùn* says:
An ancient saying goes:
The sun and moon travel through the Flying Valley,
meaning they are within the earth,
but it is not heard that the stars also flow through the earth.
Moreover,
the Flying Valley is a single path—
how could it accommodate all this?
Also, the valley contains water,
while the sun is the essence of fire.
Ice and charcoal cannot share the same vessel—
would this not harm the brightness of the sun?
These are all mere conjectures—
how could they be seen or heard with the eyes and ears?
The sun,
is substantial,
symbolizing the ruler who ascends the throne to govern.
The Shuōwén states:
The sun,
is substantial,
never waning.
It also symbolizes the ruler.
Thus, celestial images are suspended and made manifest.
The Yì says:
Celestial images are suspended and made manifest,
none greater than the sun and moon.
It is the essence of utmost yang.
Liú Xiàng's Hóngfàn Zhuàn states:
The sun
is the great standard of illumination,
the great measure of light and shadow,
the essence of all yang,
the image of all that is noble.
The Shīzǐ states:
The sun has five colors,
the essence of utmost yang,
symbolizing the ruler's virtue.
Brilliant is the appearance of flowing pearls.
The Yì Cāntóngqì states:
The sun is flowing pearls, together with the azure dragon.
A note says:
The sun is yang,
its essence is flowing pearls.
The azure dragon
is the lesser yang of the east.
Gleaming is the form of conjoined jade discs.
The Yì Kūnlíng Tú states:
When supreme virtue sprouts,
the sun and moon are like conjoined jade discs.
Bright and shining, it first emerges.
The Shī says:
Will it rain, will it rain?
Bright and shining, the sun emerges.
Radiant and glowing, it first rises.
Jiǎ Yì's writings state:
King Wén of Zhōu asked Yùzǐ:
"May I ask, when a gentleman is about to assume his office,
how should he be towards his people?"
He replied:
"When a gentleman is about to assume his office,
towards his people,
he should be radiant and glowing like the sun at its first emergence;
once he has assumed his office,
towards his people,
he should be warm and bright like the sun at its zenith;
once he has left his office,
towards his people,
he should be dim and obscure like the sun after it has set.
Therefore, when a gentleman is about to assume office and is radiant,
it means his righteousness is heard first;
once he has assumed office and is warm and bright,
the people preserve their blessings;
once he has left office and is dim,
the people lose his teachings."
King Wén said:
"I accept this instruction."
Hàn,
pronounced hàn.
Sometimes it casts its light upon the city of Qióngsāng.
The Shīzǐ states:
Shǎohào, the Jīntiān clan,
had his city at Qióngsāng.
The sun with five colors
mutually illuminated Qióngsāng.
Sometimes its light sinks into the city of Bùyè.
Xiè Dàokāng's Qídì Jì states:
In Qí there was the city of Bùyè.
It is said that in ancient times there was a sun
that shone at night upon the eastern border.
Therefore, the Lái clan built this city
and named it Bùyè (No-Night).
It is said to have a crown,
and also to embrace earrings.
The Zázhàn Shū states:
A solar crown is like a half halo.
By rule, there should be a crown above the sun.
If there are also two earrings,
it is especially auspicious.
Its divine name is Yùyí.
The Qīshèng Jì states:
Yùhuá with red patterns
resides together with the sun.
Jíelín with yellow patterns
resides together with the moon.
Both are the essences of the sun and moon.
Also, the Huángtíng Jīng states:
Yùyí and Jíelín are good at protecting each other.
A note says:
Yùyí and Jíelín
are the spirits of the sun and moon.
Fire is transmitted by the yang mirror.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
When the yang mirror faces the sun, it ignites fire.
A note says:
The yang mirror
is a lens.
Polish and rub it until hot,
then place it facing the sun,
bring mugwort near it,
and fire is produced.
Its course is singular.
The Fànzǐ Jìrán states:
The sun travels across the sky,
one degree per day,
completing a cycle and starting anew,
circling endlessly.
In heaven there is no second.
The Lǐ states:
Heaven has no two suns,
the land has no two kings.
Sometimes the crouching crow is seen.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
In the sun there is a crouching crow.
A note says:
Cūn
means foot.
It refers to the three-legged crow.
Sometimes the character 'wáng' (king) is written.
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
During the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
the character 'wáng' appeared within the sun.
It sets and then rests.
The Yìshì Zhuàn states:
In the time of Yáo,
an old man struck the ground and sang:
"At sunrise I work,
at sunset I rest.
I dig a well to drink,
I plow the fields to eat.
What has the emperor's power to do with me!"
At midday, it is the market.
The Yì states:
At midday is the market,
gathering the people of all under heaven,
assembling the goods of all under heaven.
It ascends Xiánchí and displays its splendor,
halting the six dragons and resting the reins.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
The sun emerges from Yánggǔ,
bathes in Xiánchí,
brushes against Fúsāng—
this is dawn;
ascending above Fúsāng,
then it begins to travel—
this is called the first light;
reaching Qǔ'ē,
this is called morning brightness;
arriving at Zēngquán,
this is called early meal;
stopping at Sāngyě,
this is called late meal;
reaching Héngyáng,
this is called mid-morning;
facing Kūnwú,
this is called high noon;
resting at Niǎocì,
this is called minor return;
reaching Bēigǔ,
this is called afternoon;
turning at Nǚjì,
this is called major shift;
passing Yúquán,
this is called high dusk;
halting at Liánshí,
this is called lower dusk;
then stopping Xīhé,
then resting the six dragons—
this is called suspending the chariot;
approaching Yúquán,
this is called dusk;
sinking into Ménggǔ,
this is called settled darkness.
The sun sets at Yānzī,
passes Xìliǔ,
enters the land of Yúquán,
and dims at the shore of Ménggǔ.
The sun hangs in the west,
its shadow upon the treetops—
this is called Sāngyú.
A note says:
Fúsāng
is the eastern wilderness.
The first light
is when it is about to become bright.
Qǔ'ē
is a mountain valley.
Zēngquán
means layered springs.
At early meal time,
it is in the eastern region with abundant water,
hence called Zēngquán.
Kūnwú
is a southern hill.
Niǎo Cì is a mountain in the southwest.
Bēi Gǔ is a great ravine in the southwest.
Nǚ Jì is a shaded land in the west.
Lián is pronounced làn.
Lián Shí is a mountain in the northwest.
Liù Chī refers to the six dragons.
The sun rides in a chariot,
drawn by six dragons,
with Xīhé as the charioteer,
who drives it to Yúquán and then turns back.
Yānzī is pronounced yān zī,
also called Luòtáng Mountain.
Xìliǔ is a wilderness in the west.
Méng Gǔ is the water of Méng Sì.
Dressed in black court robes to pay homage,
the Rites state:
"Dressed in black court robes, pay homage to the sun outside the eastern gate."
Sacrifices are held in the eastern suburbs.
The "Monthly Ordinances" of the Rites state:
In the second month's middle solar term,
sacrifice to the sun in the eastern suburbs.
Overseeing the ten atmospheric phenomena in the Office of Divination,
the "Spring Offices" section of the Rites of Zhōu states:
The Office of Divination oversees the methods of the ten atmospheric phenomena,
to observe auspicious and inauspicious signs,
and distinguish good and bad omens.
The first is jìn,
the second is méng,
the third is juān,
the fourth is jiān,
the fifth is àn,
the sixth is méng,
the seventh is mí,
the eighth is xù,
the ninth is jī,
the tenth is xiǎng.
The commentary states:
Auspicious and inauspicious signs are indicators of good and evil.
Huī refers to the light and vapor of the sun.
Jìn is when yin and yang vapors intermingle.
Méng is like a red sparrow.
Juān refers to the vapor beside the sun,
reflecting light from all sides like a halo.
Jiān is when clouds and vapor approach the sun.
Àn is solar and lunar eclipses.
Méng is when the sun and moon are dim and lack light.
Mí is when a white rainbow fills the sky.
Xù is when clouds are orderly,
like mountains above the sun.
Jī is rising vapor.
Xiǎng is radiant light.
Dreaming of the sun dividing into three for Emperor Wèi.
The Tán Sǒu states:
When Emperor Wén of Wèi was still a prince,
he dreamed the sun fell to the ground,
splitting into three parts.
He obtained one part and placed it in his bosom.
At midsummer, it reaches its longest with the Fire Star.
The Book of Documents states:
"The day is longest when the Fire Star appears,
marking midsummer."
The commentary states:
Yǒng means long,
referring to the summer solstice day.
Huǒ is the central star of the Azure Dragon constellation;
mentioning the central star allows the visibility of all seven stars to be inferred.
Also, in late winter, it reaches the end of its course.
The "Monthly Ordinances" of the Rites state:
In late winter,
the sun reaches the end of its course,
and the moon reaches the end of its cycle.
Only hearing the drumming of earthen jars by the very aged,
the Yì Jīng states:
"At sunset,
if one does not drum earthen jars and sing,
then the lament of the very aged is inauspicious."
How can one see the strong man who overturns the sun chariot?
Lǐ Yóu's "Nine-Bend Song" states:
"As the year grows late and the sun already slants,
how can I find a strong man to overturn the sun chariot?"
Praising Huáng Wǎn's quick response,
the Book of the Later Hàn states:
Huáng Wǎn's grandfather Huáng Qióng was the governor of Wèi Commandery.
At that time, there was a solar eclipse,
but it was not visible in the capital.
Qióng reported the circumstances of the eclipse.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict asking about the extent of the eclipse,
but Qióng could not answer for a long time.
Wǎn was six years old at the time,
and standing beside him, he said to Qióng:
"The remainder of the eclipsed sun
is like the beginning of the moon."
Qióng then used his words to reply to the edict.
Admiring Jìn Míngdì's childhood wisdom.
Liú Zhāo's "Biographies of Young Children" states:
Jìn Míngdì, personal name Shào,
was the son of Yuándì.
When Yuándì first governed Yángzhōu,
the Central Plains were in chaos and turmoil.
Someone came from Cháng'ān,
and the Emperor asked for news of Luòyáng,
shedding tears.
The Emperor (Míngdì) was several years old at the time and asked why,
and was told the reason for crossing east.
Then he asked the Emperor (Míngdì):
"In your opinion, which is farther, Cháng'ān or the sun?"
He replied:
"I have never heard of anyone coming from the side of the sun,
only of people coming from Cháng'ān,
so obviously it can be known."
The Emperor (Yuándì) thought this remarkable.
The next day,
he gathered his ministers for a banquet
and recounted this answer.
Míngdì then said he thought the sun was closer.
The Emperor (Yuándì) changed expression and asked:
"Why does this differ from what you said yesterday?"
He replied:
"I raise my head and do not see Cháng'ān,
I only see the sun,
so I know it is closer."
The Emperor (Yuándì) was greatly pleased.
Sometimes red birds flanking it bring admonition,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
In the sixth year of Duke Āi,
in Chǔ there were clouds like many red birds,
flanking the sun and flying for three days.
The King of Chǔ sent someone to ask the Grand Historian of Zhōu.
He said:
"It concerns the king's person.
If you perform the yíng sacrifice,
it can be transferred to the Prime Minister or the Minister of War."
The king said:
"Transferring a disease of the heart and belly to the limbs,
what good is that?"
The king did not perform the sacrifice and died.
Confucius said:
"It is fitting that King Zhāo did not lose his state!"
Sometimes a white rainbow piercing it causes astonishment.
The Strategies of the Warring States states:
When Niè Zhèng assassinated the Prime Minister of Hán,
and Jīng Kē assassinated the King of Qín,
in both cases a white rainbow pierced the sun.
Then observe its five colors,
the Yì Zhuàn states:
When a sage king is above, the sun is bright,
and all five colors are present.
Also, the "Lǐ Dǒu Wēi Yí" states:
When truly peaceful and prosperous, the sun appears in five colors.
Enjoy the double radiance,
Cuī Bào's "Ancient and Modern Commentary" states:
When Hàn Míngdì was crown prince,
musicians composed four stanzas of song lyrics.
The first, called "The Sun's Double Radiance," says:
"The virtue of the Son of Heaven
is as bright as the sun."
The crown prince's virtue is compared to it,
hence it is called "double."
Facing Kūnwú and overlooking Niǎo Cì,
entering Xìliǔ and emerging from Fúsāng.
Kūnwú and Niǎo Cì
are explained in the note for "ascending Xiánchí and displaying splendor."
Wáng Chōng's "Discourses Weighed in the Balance" states:
The sun rises from Fúsāng
and sets in Xìliǔ.
Fúsāng is a land in the east.
Xìliǔ is a wilderness in the west.
For learning, hear Shī Kuàng's analogy,
the Shuō Yuàn states:
Shī Kuàng replied to Duke Píng of Jìn:
"Those who study in youth
are like the light of the rising sun;
those who study in adulthood,
Like the light of the midday sun,
those who study in old age
are like those who hold a candle's light."
Entering the bosom was an auspicious sign for Hàn Wǔdì.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Emperor Jǐng of Hàn's consort, Lady Wáng, was pregnant
and dreamed of the sun entering her bosom,
and thus gave birth to Emperor Wǔ.
Comparing fear and affection to Zhào Cuī and Zhào Dùn,
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Fèng Shū asked Jiǎ Jì:
"Which is more worthy, Zhào Cuī or Zhào Dùn?"
He replied:
"Zhào Cuī
is like the sun in winter.
Zhào Dùn,
is like the sun in summer."
The commentary states:
The winter sun is lovely,
the summer sun is fearsome.
Recognizing the rise and fall in Xià and Shāng.
Wáng Chōng's Lùnhéng states:
When Jié was without virtue,
two suns shone together;
the one in the east would rise,
the one in the west would perish.
Fèi Chāng asked Féng Yí:
"Which is Yīn?
Which is Xià?"
Féng Yí said:
"West,
is Xià;
East,
is Yīn."
Thereupon,
Fèi Chāng moved his clan to join Yīn.
As for Chángliú reflecting the light,
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
On Chángliú Mountain,
the god White Emperor Shàohào dwells.
This deity
presides over the reflection of light.
The commentary states:
When the sun sets in the west,
its light reflects eastward,
meaning he observes it.
Dūguǎng has no shadow,
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Dūguǎng,
is where the many emperors ascend and descend,
at midday there is no shadow,
for it is the center of heaven and earth.
The commentary says:
Dūguǎng,
is the name of a southern mountain.
At midday,
directly there is no shadow,
thus it is called the earth's center.
Gazing at Yínbīn for the eastern emergence,
The Book of Documents states:
Respectfully guide out the sun,
orderly manage the eastern works,
at midday the Star Bird is seen,
to mark the mid-spring.
The commentary says:
Yīn,
means to correct.
Passing Yúquán and declining westward.
See the note on "Xiánchí's outstanding beauty."
Looking up at the enduring light,
The Book of Changes states:
The sun and moon attain heaven,
and thus can shine enduringly.
Observing their attachment to heaven,
The Book of Changes states:
The sun and moon attach to heaven.
The same shadow is heard of for ten thousand lǐ,
The Book of Hàn states:
Lǐ Xún submitted a memorial saying:
"The sun,
is the chief of all yang,
its radiance illuminates,
ten thousand lǐ share the same shadow,
it is the symbol of the ruler.
Thus when the sun is about to dawn,
a clear wind arises,
and all yin lie hidden."
Its circumference is also said to be three thousand.
Xú Zhěng's Chánglì states:
The sun's diameter is a thousand lǐ,
its circumference three thousand lǐ,
it is seven thousand lǐ below heaven.
Then it rises over Míngxīng Mountain with splendid light,
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
Míngxīng Mountain,
is where the sun and moon emerge.
Approaching Yānzī and its light ceases,
See the note on "Xiánchí's outstanding beauty."
Holding it aloft was seen by Zhòngní,
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
When Confucius was besieged in Chén and Cài,
Tàigōng Rén condoled him,
saying:
"Your intention is to use wisdom to startle the foolish,
cultivate yourself to illuminate the corrupt,
shining brightly as if carrying the sun and moon while walking,
thus you cannot avoid this."
Holding it up was also transmitted by Chéng Lì.
The Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wèi states:
Chéng Lì dreamed of ascending Mount Tài and holding up the sun.
Lì reported it to Tàizǔ,
Tàizǔ then added "sun" (日) above "stand" (立).
Thus he changed his name to "Yù".
Qín Shǐhuáng crossed the sea,
wishing to observe its eastern emergence;
The Sān Qí Lüè states:
Qín Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge on the sea,
wishing to cross the sea to see where the sun rises.
A deity drove the stones,
they moved not fast enough,
the deity whipped them,
and they all bled.
To this day the stone bridge is still reddish.
King Mù of Zhōu drove his steeds,
wishing to see its western entry.
The Lièzǐ states:
King Mù drove a team of eight steeds,
westward to see where the sun sets.
Then its drying light is radiant,
The Shuōwén states:
The sun's movement is radiant.
Pronounced yì zhī qiē.
Observing the shadow's measure, slow and long,
The Book of Songs states:
The spring day is long and slow,
picking white southernwood, abundant and lush.
It is the symbol of ruler, father, husband, and elder brother,
Liú Xiàng's Hóngfàn Zhuàn states:
The sun,
is of the category of ruler, father, husband, elder brother,
the response of the Central States.
Measuring the appropriateness of cold, heat, yin, and wind.
The Rites of Zhōu: Office of Earth states:
The Grand Minister of Education uses the method of the earth gnomon to measure the land's depth,
correct the sun's shadow to seek the earth's center.
If the sun is south, the shadow is short,
there is much heat;
if the sun is north, the shadow is long,
there is much cold;
if the sun is east, the shadow is evening,
there is much wind;
if the sun is west, the shadow is morning,
there is much yin.
The shadow at the solstice,
is one foot five inches,
this is called the earth's center,
where heaven and earth conjoin.
How could one see melting metal and scorching stone?
The Chǔcí states:
Ten suns emerged together,
melting metal, scorching stone.
Only observe the erected gnomon and set out the jade tablet.
The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn states:
On the day of the winter solstice,
erect an eight-foot gnomon,
at midday observe its shadow,
if the shadow matches the measure,
the year is good and people harmonious,
otherwise the year is bad and people confused.
Setting out the jade tablet,
already seen in the note on "measuring cold, heat, yin, wind."
If then yang affairs are not attained,
it is reproached and seen in this,
The Book of Rites: Meaning of the Marriage Ceremony states:
If male instruction is not cultivated,
yang affairs are not attained,
reproach appears in heaven,
and the sun is eclipsed.
Commoners run,
village officers gallop.
The Book of Documents states:
Then in the last month of autumn, at the new moon,
the celestial bodies did not gather in the room.
Blind musicians beat drums,
village officers galloped,
commoners ran.
Beating drums and using silk,
The Zuǒ Zhuàn:
In the seventeenth year of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ,
there was a solar eclipse,
prayer-officers requested the use of silk,
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"When there is a solar eclipse,
the Son of Heaven does not feast,
beats drums at the altar of soil;
feudal lords use silk at the altar of soil,
beat drums at the court."
Striking the watchman's clapper and winding silk,
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn states:
On the first day of the sixth month, Xīnwèi,
There was an eclipse of the sun,
and red silk cords were wound around the altar of the soil.
Some say this was to coerce it,
some say it was because they feared the darkness would violate it,
so they wound it around the altar of the soil.
The altar of the soil is the lord of the land;
the eclipse of the sun
is the essence of the land.
It ascends to spread over the heavens and violates the sun,
therefore red silk cords are wound around it,
to assist the yang and suppress the yin.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn says:
The Son of Heaven rescues the sun,
setting up five banners,
arraying five weapons and five drums;
the feudal lords set up three banners,
arraying three weapons and three drums;
the grand masters strike the gates,
the officers strike the watchman's clappers—all sounds
are affairs of yang.
To suppress the yin qi.
Together they suppress the yin and assist the yang,
as already seen in the annotation on "striking the clappers and winding the silk."
Finally, when it is corrected, they look up to it.
The Analects says:
The faults of a gentleman
are like eclipses of the sun and moon.
What harm do they do to their brightness?
When he errs,
all men see it;
when he corrects himself,
all men look up to him.
From this we know it is the essence of fire qi.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The accumulated qi of yang produces fire,
the essence of fire qi is the sun.
The mother of yang virtue,
the Chūnqiū Nèishì says:
The sun
is the mother of yang virtue.
It is called Yàolíng and also named Dàmíng,
the Guǎngyǎ says:
The sun's name is Yàolíng,
another name is Zhūmíng,
another name is Dōngjūn,
another name is Dàmíng,
another name is Yángniǎo.
It illuminates the four directions and looks down upon the earth below.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì says:
The sun god is of five colors,
brightly illuminating the four directions.
The Shī says:
The sun rises in the east,
shining upon the earth below.
Eclipses occur because of the fighting of unicorns,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
When unicorns fight, then the sun and moon are eclipsed.
The annotation says:
The qílín,
a one-horned beast,
therefore corresponds with the sun.
Its movement is like the pace of a fine steed.
Wáng Chōng's Lùnhéng says:
The sun travels a thousand lǐ by day,
and a thousand lǐ by night,
a fine steed also travels a thousand lǐ by day.
Thus the sun's movement, whether slow or fast,
is similar to the pace of a fine steed.
The brandishing of a spear was seen with Lǔyáng,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
Duke Lǔyáng was fighting with Hán,
the battle was fierce as the sun was setting,
he seized his spear and brandished it,
and the sun for him turned back three shè.
The discarding of a staff is again heard of with Kuāfù.
The Shānhǎijīng says:
Kuāfù chased the sun,
grew thirsty,
drank from the Hé and Wèi rivers but it was not enough,
went north to drink from the great marsh,
before reaching it,
died of thirst on the way,
discarded his staff,
which transformed into the Dèng forest.
Yì once shot at it,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
In the time of Yáo,
ten suns appeared together,
scorching the plants and trees.
Yáo ordered Yì to shoot at the ten suns from below,
hitting nine of them,
the crows all died,
shedding their feathers and wings.
Xī once served as its charioteer.
The Guǎngyǎ says:
The sun's charioteer is called "Xīhé".
Some speak of it being at the zenith twice,
the Hànshū says:
In the time of Emperor Wén,
Xīnyuán Píng presented a report saying:
"The sun will be at the zenith twice,
I have divined and know this."
After a short while,
the sun indeed was at the zenith twice,
so he changed the seventeenth year to be the first year of the later era.
Some speak of it being at high noon,
the Zuǎnyào says:
Sunlight is called jǐng,
the sun's shadow is called guǐ,
the sun's vapor is called xiàn,
the sun just risen is called xù,
the sun at dawn is called xī,
the sun's warmth is called xù,
at noon it is called tíng,
in the wèi hour it is called dié,
when the sun is late it is called gàn,
when the sun is about to set it is called bómù.
Admiring the sunflower's leaning dependence,
the Zhuàn says:
Bào Qiān had his feet cut off by the Marquis of Qí,
Zhòngní heard of it,
and said:
"Bào Zhuāngzǐ's wisdom does not reach that of the sunflower,
the sunflower can still protect its feet."
Annotation:
The sunflower leans its leaves towards the sun,
to shade its own roots.
Pān Yuè's "Xiánjū Fù" says:
The ránghé relies on shade,
the shíhuò turns towards the sun.
Lamenting the lateness of the mulberry and elm.
Liú Xiūxuán's "Nǐgǔshī" says:
I wish the faint light of dusk would descend,
and shine upon me at the time of the mulberry and elm.
As for emerging from Sūmén,
the Shānhǎijīng says:
Sūmén,
is where the sun and moon emerge.
Ascending to Wēnyuán,
the Shānhǎijīng says:
The sun bathes in the valley of Wēnyuán,
ascends upon the Fúsāng,
one sun has just arrived,
another sun is just emerging,
all are carried by crows.
Annotation:
Wēnyuán,
is also called Yánggǔ.
One sun has just arrived,
another sun is just emerging,
meaning they meet and replace each other.
In the sun there is a three-legged crow,
therefore it says "carried by crows".
Suddenly delighted to part the clouds,
Xú Gàn's Zhōnglùn says:
King Wén met Lord Jiāng on the north bank of the Wèi,
like parting the clouds to see the bright sun.
Again pleased to bask in the sun.
The Lièzǐ says:
In Sòng there was a farmer basking in the sun in the fields,
finding it delightful,
unaware of things like grand mansions and silk wadding,
said to his wife:
"I will present the warmth of this sun I am basking in,
to my lord,
and shall surely receive a great reward."
Zhāng Zhòng's reply to Hàn Míng's question,
the Hòuhànshū says:
Zhāng Zhòng, styled Zhòngdǔ,
in the time of Emperor Míng,
was recommended as Xiàolián.
The Emperor said:
"What commandery's petty official are you?"
He replied:
"Your servant is an official from Rìnán."
The Emperor said:
"A person from Rìnán commandery,
should look north to see the sun."
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that in Yànmén one does not see piled-up geese forming a gate;
in Jīnchéng commandery one does not see accumulated gold forming the commandery.
Although your servant resides in Rìnán,
I have never looked north to see the sun."
Xuānfǔ was bested by the words of a child.
The Lièzǐ says:
Confucius was traveling in the morning,
and saw two small children arguing and fighting.
Confucius asked them the reason.
One child said:
"I think when the sun first rises it is closer to people,
and at midday it is farther from people."
The other child said:
"I think when the sun first rises it is far,
and at midday it is near."
He said:
"How do you know this?"
One child said:
"When the sun first rises,
it is like a large chariot wheel,
and at midday,
It is as small as a dish's lid.
Is this not because the distant appears small,
while the near appears large?"
One child said:
"When the sun first rises,
it is cool and refreshing,
but when it reaches midday,
it feels like dipping into boiling water.
Is this not because the near is hot,
while the distant is cool?"
Confucius could not decide.
The two children laughed and said:
"Qiū,
who said you were knowledgeable?"
As for bathing in Gānquán,
the Shānhǎijīng says:
Beyond the southeastern sea,
between Gānquán,
there is the country of Xīhé.
There is a woman named Xīhé,
the wife of Dì Jùn.
She gave birth to ten suns,
often bathing them in Gānquán.
Guō Pú notes:
Xīhé could give birth to suns,
so the suns are the children of Xīhé.
Yáo therefore established the office of Xīhé,
to oversee the four seasons.
Emerging from Yánggǔ,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
The sun rises from Yánggǔ,
and bathes in Xiánchí.
Having already cast its light upon Rìguān,
Yìng Shào's Hànguānyí says:
The southeast of Tàishān is called "Rìguān",
where the sun is seen at cockcrow.
It also shares its splendor with Ruòmù.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Ruòmù is west of Jiànmù,
at its tip are ten suns,
their radiance illuminates the earth.
As for reaching Dānxué,
entering Tàiméng,
the Ěryǎ says:
Jù,
south of Qízhōu,
where the sun is carried is Dānxué.
East to where the sun rises is Tàipíng,
west to where the sun sets is Tàiméng.
The note says:
Jù,
means to depart.
Qí,
means center.
Tàiméng,
is Měngsì.
Turning back to Nǚjì and greatly shifting,
passing Líshí and descending to chōng.
All seen in the note for "ascending Xiánchí and excelling in beauty".
These are all instances where the light is not at its peak,
unlike the kingly way being at its zenith.
The Yángzǐ Fǎyán says:
The way of the sage,
is it not like the sun at midday?
If not reaching it, it is not yet;
if exceeding it, it declines.
A tax of one-tenth,
is the standard for the world.
Moon
Only that lunar spirit,
Xiè Zhuāng’s “Rhapsody on the Moon” says:
The sun with its yang virtue,
The moon with its yin spirit.
On the fifteenth it wanes, and on the fifteenth it waxes full.
The “Rites” says:
Heaven holds yang,
and suspends the sun and stars;
Earth holds yin,
and is perforated with mountains and rivers.
It disseminates the five phases through the four seasons,
and after harmony is achieved, the moon is born.
Therefore, on the fifteenth it waxes full,
and on the fifteenth it wanes.
Flowing with pure radiance, serene as ice,
Xiè Zhuāng’s “Rhapsody on the Moon” says:
Continuous galleries gleam like frosty silk,
surrounding steps are still as ice.
Deep and cold light congeals like snow.
Xiè Zhuāng’s “Rhapsody on the Moon” says:
The gentle earth congeals like snow.
The gazing hare ascends its essence and flees by night;
The “Chǔcí‧Tiānwèn” says:
How does the night light obtain,
that it dies and yet is reborn?
What benefit is there,
that the gazing hare is in its belly?
The toad glows with splendor, startling the night.
The “Wǔjīng Tōngyì” says:
Why are there a hare and a toad in the moon?
The moon
is yin;
the toad,
is yang.
And together with the hare they shine,
for yin is attached to yang.
The “Chūnqiū Kǒngyǎn Tú” says:
The toad
is the essence of the moon.
It accommodates the transplanted immortal cassia tree;
Yú Xǐ’s “Āntiān Lùn” says:
Common legend says there is an immortal and a cassia tree in the moon;
now observe its first growth:
one sees the immortal’s feet gradually taking form,
and the cassia tree grows afterward.
It looks up to the heavenly stars and aids their brightness.
Sūn’s “Ruìyìng Shū” says:
The propitious star
is the essence of heaven,
shaped like a half-moon,
born on the last and first days of the month,
aiding the moon to shine.
When the ruler is not partial to individuals, it appears.
Jīng,
pronounced jīng.
Suddenly delighting in its first birth,
The “Shū” says:
The first birth of light.
It also says:
The first birth of the dark side.
The commentary says:
Zāi
means beginning.
Shēngmíng,
is the third day.
Shēngpò,
is after the fifteenth day.
Again rejoicing in the first light,
The “Shī Tuīzāi Dù” says:
On the third day the moon forms its dark side,
on the eighth day it forms its light.
The toad’s body is complete,
the burrow-nose first sprouts.
Sòng Jūn’s commentary says:
Xué
means jué.
Juébí
is the hare.
After eight days the light is complete,
after three months the season is formed.
The “Báihǔ Tōng” says:
Why does the moon wax and wane?
It attributes its merit to the sun.
On the third day it forms its dark side,
on the eighth day it forms its light.
The “Rites” says:
The moon on the third day forms its dark side,
in three months it forms the season.
Lǚ Qí shot it and divined the surname;
The “Zuǒzhuàn” says:
When Chǔ and Jìn were about to fight,
the Marquis of Jìn dreamed that Lǚ Qí shot and hit the moon,
then retreated into the mud.
Divining it, it was said:
The surname Jī,
is the sun.
A different surname,
is the moon,
it must be the King of Chǔ.
When the battle came,
he shot King Gōng in the eye,
and Lǚ Qí died in it.
Kàn Zé dreamed of it and saw his name.
The “Huìjī Xiānxián Zhuàn” says:
When Kàn Zé was thirteen,
he dreamed his name shone brightly in the moon.
As for the western suburb’s pit altar,
The “Rites” says:
Sacrifice to the sun on an altar,
sacrifice to the moon in a pit,
to distinguish the dark and the bright,
to regulate the high and the low.
The autumn equinox evening sacrifice,
The “Rites” says:
On the day of the autumn equinox,
sacrifice to the evening moon in the western suburbs.
Its category is in water,
thus it corresponds to the tides;
The “Bàopǔzǐ” says:
The essence of the moon produces water,
therefore when the moon is full, the tides are great.
Its principle lies in yin,
thus it accords with ritual.
The “Rites” says:
The moon on the third day forms its dark side;
in three months it forms the season.
Therefore there are three deferrals,
in establishing a state one must establish three ministers and three guests,
the foundation of governance and teaching,
the great standard of ritual.
The commentary says:
Speaking of ritual,
it is yin.
The great numbers take their model from the moon.
It takes its image from the queen and consorts,
The “Hànshū” says:
Lǐ Xún submitted a memorial saying:
“The moon
is the chief of all yin,
the image of the queen, consorts, great ministers, and feudal lords.”
It observes the principle of the ministers and officers,
The “Shū” says:
The ministers and officers are like the moon.
Therefore it is considered the envoy of heaven above,
The “Huáinánzǐ” says:
The moon
is the envoy of heaven.
The elder sister of the ruler.
The “Chūnqiū Gǎnjīng Fú” says:
The ruler,
is brother to the sun,
elder sister to the moon.
Gazing at the auspicious glow in double halos,
Cuī Bào’s “Gǔjīn Zhù” says:
Emperor Míng of Hàn composed four stanzas of “Songs for the Crown Prince’s Musicians,”
to praise the crown prince’s virtue.
The first is called “The Sun’s Double Radiance”;
the second, “The Moon’s Double Halo”;
the third, “The Stars’ Double Brilliance”;
the fourth, “The Sea’s Double Moisture.”
Sharing the clear light over a thousand miles.
Xiè Zhuāng’s “Rhapsody on the Moon” says:
Separated by a thousand miles, yet sharing the bright moon.
Then there is roaming in the flying canopies of the Western Garden,
Cáo Zǐjiàn’s “Poem on a Public Feast” says:
In the clear night we roam the Western Garden,
flying canopies pursuing one another.
The bright moon clarifies the scene,
the constellations arrayed unevenly.
Galloping with the elegant words of the eastern border.
Xiè Zhuāng’s “Rhapsody on the Moon” says:
Drawing brush and advancing tablet,
he commanded Zhòngxuān,
saying:
“Draw forth your secret thoughts,
gallop with your elegant words.”
Zhòngxuān knelt and said:
“Your servant from the eastern border, obscure and lowly,
grew up among hills and fences.”
Huìjī loved the scene in the courtyard,
The “Jìnshū” says:
Huìjī Prince Dàozǐ,
sitting at night in the courtyard,
the moonlight flawless,
sighed, considering it excellent.
Xiè Chóng said casually:
“I think it would be better with a few clouds as embellishment.”
Dàozǐ said:
“Your mind is not pure,
and you wish to defile the great clarity?”
Lù Jī gathered the radiance in the hall.
Lù Jī’s poem says:
Resting peacefully in the northern hall,
the bright moon enters my window.
Shining, it leaves abundant radiance,
gathering it, it does not fill the hand.
The round light resembles a fan,
Bān Jiéyú’s poem says:
Cut to make a joined-happiness fan,
perfectly round like the bright moon.
The moon's pure form resembles a jade tablet.
Jiāng Wéntōng's "Rhapsody on Parting" says:
Autumn dew is like pearls,
the autumn moon is like a jade tablet.
It shares waxing and waning with clams and crabs,
its fullness and waning are equal to pearls and tortoises.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
Clams, crabs, pearls, and tortoises
wax and wane with the moon.
When the halo formed, the Hàn siege was not yet lifted.
The "Hàn Shū" says:
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
the moon was haloed,
encircling the constellations Shēn and Bì sevenfold.
The prognostication said:
"Between Bì and Mǎo,
lies the Celestial Street.
North of the street,
are the barbarians;
south of the street,
is the Central Kingdom.
Mǎo represents the Xiōngnú,
Shēn represents Zhào,
Bì represents the border troops."
That year,
Emperor Gāozǔ personally led his army to Píngchéng,
was besieged by Mòdú,
and was only relieved after seven days.
When its shadow was full, the enemy cavalry first arrived.
The "Hàn Shū ‧ Xiōngnú Biography" says:
The Xiōngnú always timed their actions by the moon,
attacking when it was full and strong,
and withdrawing their troops when it waned.
As for the moon wearing earrings and a crown as an auspicious sign,
the "Jīngzhōu Divinations" says:
If the moon has earrings and wears a crown,
within a hundred days,
the ruler will have great joy.
The crescent moon shows humility.
Xiè Zhuāng's "Rhapsody on the Moon" says:
The crescent moon shows humility.
The "Shuōwén" says:
Fěi,
is the name for when the moon is not yet full.
Pò,
is when the moon first begins to show its faint light.
Following a long month, it is the second day;
following a short month, it is the third day.
It is the principle of Earth.
The "Chūnqiū Gǎnjīngfú" says:
The moon is
the essence of yīn,
the principle of Earth.
It is the ancestor of yīn.
Huángfǔ Mì's "Niánlì" says:
The moon is
the ancestor of all yīn.
It bestowed an auspicious omen upon the Hàn house.
The "Hàn Shū" says:
The mother of Empress Yuán,
dreamed the moon entered her bosom and then gave birth to the Empress.
It conveyed an auspicious dream to the Wú palace.
The "Sōushénjì" says:
Sūn Jiān's wife, while pregnant with Quán,
dreamed the moon entered her bosom.
She told Jiān:
"When I was previously pregnant with Cè,
I dreamed the moon entered my bosom;
now I have dreamed of the moon again."
Jiān said:
"Our descendants will prosper."
Seeing claws and fangs portends calamity.
The "Chūnqiū Kǎoyìyǒu" says:
When feudal lords plot rebellion,
then the moon grows claws and fangs;
when the empress's clan monopolizes power,
then the sun and moon shine together.
Seeing the moon lingering (cè nì) portends misfortune.
The "Shàngshū Dàzhuàn" says:
At the end of the month, if the moon appears in the west,
it is called tiǎo;
at the beginning of the month, if the moon appears in the east,
it is called cè nì.
The commentary says:
Tiǎo,
means swift.
Swift and unimpeded,
describes rapid movement.
Cè nì,
describes slow movement.
Observe its pure light flowing across the sky.
Xiè Zhuāng's "Rhapsody on the Moon" says:
White dew fills the air,
the pure moon flows across the sky.
Its square radiance enters the household.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's poem "Chanting on the Moon" says:
The moon's splendor approaches the quiet night,
the quiet night extinguishes the dusty air.
Square radiance finally enters the household,
a round shadow comes through a crack.
If a woman's submission is perhaps not cultivated,
The "Lǐjì ‧ Hūnyì" says:
If male instruction is not cultivated,
yang affairs are not properly ordered,
and this appears in the heavens,
the sun undergoes an eclipse;
if female submission is not cultivated,
yin affairs are not properly ordered,
and this appears in the heavens,
the moon undergoes an eclipse.
The queen beats drums for it.
The "Jīngzhōu Divinations" says:
During a lunar eclipse,
the queen herself beats the drum three times.
The palace ladies, various attendants, and palace women beat clappers to rescue it.
Some say:
All the palace women beat clappers.
Regarding the matter, there is only Xú Rú's explanation.
The "Shìshuō" says:
Xú Rúzǐ,
at nine years old,
was once playing under the moonlight.
Someone said to him:
"If there were nothing in the moon,
it should be extremely bright."
Xú said:
"Not so.
It is like a person's eye having a pupil.
Without it,
why would it not be dark?"
The cave appears in Yáng Xióng's rhapsody.
Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on the Tall Poplars" says:
In the west, it presses upon the moon's cave;
in the east, it shakes the sun's domain.
The commentary states:
Kū,
is where the moon emerges and enters.
It spreads its shadow across the mountain passes.
Wáng Bāo's poem "Moon over the Passes" says:
The moon shines on the passes at night,
a sorrowful hue illuminates the lonely fortress.
Its half-shape resembles the Hàn battle array,
its full shadow pursues the Hú soldiers.
It enters the corridors and galleries, accumulating pure whiteness.
Xiè Huìlián's "Rhapsody on Lamenting the Dawn Moon" says:
The courtyard steps are like a mirror's reflection,
the corridors and galleries are clear and pure.
What drives it?
Wàngshū, or Xiān'ē.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
The moon,
also named Yèguāng.
The moon's charioteer is called "Wàngshū",
also called "Xiān'ē".
It hangs down gentle, clear radiance.
The "Rhapsody on the Moon" says:
It bestows gentle, clear radiance.
It plays with majestic golden waves.
The "Hàn Shū" says:
