The moon, majestic with golden waves,
describes its radiant appearance.
We hear of Nǚ Dí, who was moved by essence.
The "Dùnjiǎ Kāishāntú",
explained by Róng Shì, says:
Nǚ Dí drew water one evening at the foot of Shíniǔ Mountain.
In the spring water, she obtained a moon essence like a chicken egg.
She cherished it and held it in her mouth,
swallowed it unconsciously,
and thus became pregnant.
After fourteen months, she gave birth to Xià Yǔ.
We hear the tale of Cháng'é who stole the elixir.
Wáng Chōng's "Lùnhéng" says:
Yì requested the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ.
Yì's wife, Cháng'é,
stole it and fled to the moon,
taking refuge there,
becoming the toad.
Bright, it adorns the heavens.
The "Yìjīng" says:
The sun and moon adorn the heavens.
Clearly, it departs from Bì.
The "Shījīng" says:
When the moon departs from Bì,
it causes pouring rain.
It corresponds to fish brains without error.
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
The moon is
the ancestor of all yīn.
When the moon is damaged, fish brains perish.
Verified by the steps' míng grass, it never errs.
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" says:
In Yáo's time, there was grass that grew flanking the steps.
On the first day of each month, it produced one pod.
By the middle of the month, it produced fifteen pods.
After the sixteenth day,
one pod fell each day,
until by month's end they were all gone.
If the month was short,
one pod remained.
Rulers used this to observe the calendar.
Only a ruler of great virtue,
is born in response to harmonious qi.
It is considered an auspicious sign of Yáo,
named Míngjiá.
Also called Língjiá,
also called Ruìcǎo.
There is also drawing reed ash to create a halo with a gap,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Drawing reed ash, the moon's halo is incomplete.
Xǔ Shèn's annotation says:
The moon's halo,
using reed ash to form a ring,
leaving a gap on one side,
then the moon's halo will also be incomplete above.
Holding the yīn suì, moisture flows.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
When the fāngzhū sees the moon,
it moistens and becomes water.
Gāo Yòu's annotation says:
Fāngzhū,
is the yīn suì, a large clam.
Rub it thoroughly until hot and face it toward the moon,
then water is produced.
Xǔ Shèn's annotation says:
Zhū,
means pearl.
Fāng,
means stone.
Using a copper plate to receive it,
several shēng of water descend.
The pounding heard from the white rabbit,
Fù Xuán's "Imitating Tiānwèn" says:
What is there in the moon?
A white rabbit pounding medicine.
The panting seen from the Wú ox.
The Fēngsútōng says:
The Wú ox sees the moon and pants.
It suffers from the sun,
seeing the moon, it pants in fear.
At first glance, it resembles moth eyebrows,
from afar, startles like a jade hook.
Bào Zhāo's "Watching the Moon" poem says:
First seen at the southeast tower,
delicate like a jade hook.
Finally shining on the northwest steps,
graceful like moth eyebrows.
Moth eyebrows obscure the pearl lattice,
the jade hook reflects in the ornate window.
On the fifteenth and sixteenth nights,
a thousand miles away, I am with you.
Night shifts as the stars and Milky Way set,
lingering in the courtyard and doorway.
Should we not present the zither and extinguish the splendid candles,
to admire the pure essence in its tranquility?
The "Yuè Fù" says:
Leave the candlelit chamber,
approach the moonlit hall,
fine wine is offered,
the zither is presented.
It also says:
Ascend the pure essence in its tranquility.
Xiè Língyùn's "Yuàn Xiǎo Yuè Fù" says:
Lying in the secluded chamber, what joy is there?
Extinguish the splendid candles and admire the moon of the season.
Stars
The essence of all things
ascends to become the arrayed stars,
from the Shuōwén.
They are also called the image of the common people;
the Shàngshū says:
"The common people are like stars."
They are also the finest part of the primordial qi.
The Sānwǔ Lì says:
"Stars are
the finest part of the primordial qi."
In Liáng and Pèi, the rise of Lord Cáo was seen.
The Wèi Zhì says:
During the reign of Emperor Huán,
a yellow star appeared in the division corresponding to Chǔ and Sòng.
Yīn Kuí said:
"Fifty years from now,
a true man shall rise between Liáng and Pèi,
and his momentum will be unstoppable."
Fifty years later,
Lord Cáo defeated Yuán Shào,
and none in the world could oppose him.
The constellation Dōngjǐng recognized the rise of the Han ancestor.
The Hànshū says:
When Gāozǔ first entered the passes,
the five planets gathered at Dōngjǐng.
Dōngjǐng corresponds to the Qín region.
Recognize the bóyuē and chánchēng;
the Ěryǎ says:
"A shooting star is called bóyuē,
a comet is called chánchēng."
The commentary states:
"Bóyuē
is a meteor.
A comet is also called bèi,
meaning its shape is bushy like a broom."
Gaze upon Yáoguāng and Yùshéng.
Zhāng Píngzǐ's "Xījīng Fù" says:
"Ascending the flying tower to gaze afar,
I behold Yáoguāng and Yùshéng."
Commentary:
"Yáoguāng
is the seventh star of the Northern Dipper.
Yùshéng
are the two stars north of Yùhéng."
Songs have praised the double brilliance;
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù says:
When Emperor Míng of Han was crown prince,
he ordered musicians to compose a song poem saying, 'The stars shine doubly bright.'
The crown prince was compared in virtue,
hence the term 'double.'
Records often speak of the night's brightness.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"When the constant stars are not seen,
it is called night brightness."
Look at that one pulling the cart;
the Shī says:
"Bright is that Altair,
yet it does not pull the cart."
Recognize these three stars at the door.
The Shī says:
"What night is this night,
with three stars at the door?"
Chén and Shēn already govern Shāng and Jìn;
the Zuǒzhuàn says:
In ancient times, Gāoxīnshì had two sons,
the elder named Èbó,
the younger named Shíchén.
They could not get along,
daily seeking weapons,
to attack each other.
The later emperor disapproved,
and moved Èbó to Shāngqiū,
to govern Chén.
The Shāng people followed him,
hence Chén is the star of Shāng.
He moved Shíchén to Dàxià,
to govern Shēn.
The Táng people followed him,
hence Shēn is the star of Jìn.
Jī and Bì further presage wind and rain.
The Shàngshū says:
"Some stars favor wind,
some stars favor rain."
Commentary:
"The Jī star favors wind,
the Bì star favors rain."
For Zhāng Huá, it once split;
the Jìnshū says:
When Zhāng Huá was Minister of Works,
the star of the Middle Platform split.
His youngest son, Wěi, urged Huá to resign.
Huá said:
"The Way of Heaven is profound and distant;
one should wait quietly."
Soon after, he was executed by King Lún of Zhào.
Moved by Zhònggōng, they once gathered.
The Yìyuàn says:
Chén Zhònggōng went with his sons and nephews to visit Xún Jìhé and his sons.
At that time, virtuous stars gathered.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"Within five hundred lǐ, worthy men are gathering."
When Dìng is in the center,
they build the Chǔ palace,
from the Shī.
The commentary says:
"Dìng
is Yíngshì."
The lodgings and departures do not err;
the Lǐ says:
"The lodgings and departures do not err,
and the order is not lost."
Three and five are in the east.
The Shī says:
"Dim are those small stars,
three and five in the east."
Zǐ Wéi recognized the virtue of the Duke of Sòng.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
Mars remained in the Heart constellation.
The duke summoned Zǐ Wéi to inquire.
Zǐ Wéi said:
"The calamity falls upon the ruler,
but it can be transferred to the minister."
The duke said:
"The minister governs the state."
He said:
"It can be transferred to the people."
The duke said:
"If the people die,
for whom shall I be ruler?"
He said:
"It can be transferred to the harvest."
The duke said:
"If the harvest fails,
people will starve and die."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"You have spoken three supremely virtuous words;
Heaven will surely reward you thrice."
That night,
Mars retreated three lunar lodgings.
Shǐ Mò knew the misfortune of the state of Wú.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
In the thirty-second year of Duke Zhāo,
Wú attacked Yuè.
Shǐ Mò said:
"Within forty years,
will Yuè not possess Wú?"
Yuè gained the year's influence, and Wú attacked it,
so it was sure to suffer misfortune.
For Xuānyuán, a great lightning encircled the pivot;
the Shìjì says:
At the end of Shénnóngshì's reign,
Shǎohàoshì married Fùbǎo.
She saw a great lightning flash encircling the Northern Dipper,
with the pivot star shining over the suburbs.
Fùbǎo was moved,
conceived for twenty months,
and gave birth to the Yellow Emperor at Shòuqiū.
For the White Emperor, a rainbow flowed at Huázhǔ.
The Hétú says:
A great star like a rainbow
descended and flowed at Huázhǔ.
Nǚjié was moved by the thought,
and gave birth to the White Emperor.
As for observing the brilliance,
the Shī says:
"You rise and look at the night;
the morning star is brilliant."
Gaze upon those dim ones,
already noted above.
Startled by Yán Guāng sharing a bed;
the Hòuhànshū says:
Yán Guāng,
courtesy name Zǐlíng,
was a friend of Guāngwǔ.
Later, when Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he forgot him.
Guāng resented the emperor.
At that time,
the Grand Astrologer said:
"There is a guest star in heaven resenting the emperor."
The emperor said:
"Could it be my old friend Yán Zǐlíng?"
He immediately ordered him summoned.
At night, he shared a bed with Zǐlíng.
Guāng placed his feet on the emperor's abdomen.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"A guest star encroaches upon the imperial seat."
Guāng withdrew his feet,
and the guest star soon retreated.
Laughing at Dài Kuí seeking death.
Sūn's Jìnyáng Qiū says:
Xiè Fū of Kuàijī,
courtesy name Qìngxù,
lived in seclusion on Mount Ruòyē.
The moon encroached upon the Shàowēi star.
Shàowēi,
also called the recluse star.
At that time, Dài Kuí's fame surpassed Fū's,
and people were worried for him.
Shortly thereafter, Fǔ died,
so the scholars of Kuàijī ridiculed Kuí:
"The lofty gentleman of Wúzhōng,
sought death but could not obtain it."
Xīfū pointed at them and incurred guilt,
The Book of Hàn says:
Marquis Yílíng Xīfū Gōng,
was dismissed from office and returned to his fief.
He had no mansion,
and lodged in a hilltop pavilion.
Villains, thinking the marquis's household was wealthy,
often kept watch at night.
Jiǎ Huì taught Gōng a method to curse thieves,
using a branch pointing southeast from a mulberry tree as a dagger,
drawing the Big Dipper upon it,
Gōng himself let down his hair,
stood in the courtyard,
faced the Big Dipper,
and holding the dagger, pointed and cursed the thieves.
Someone submitted a memorial saying Gōng harbored resentment,
observed the stars and constellations,
watched for the emperor's fortune or misfortune,
and together with a sorcerer, performed curses.
Thereupon,
he died in prison.
Wūmǎ wore them and brought order.
The Family Sayings of Confucius says:
Wūmǎ Qī was magistrate of Shànfù,
wearing the stars, he went out and returned to govern the people.
As for the Southern Winnower drawing in its tongue,
The Book of Songs says:
In the south is the Winnower,
drawing in its tongue.
The Northern Dipper ladles the broth,
The Book of Songs says:
In the north is the Dipper,
but it cannot ladle wine or broth.
Towards dawn, they still appear scattered and distinct,
An ancient poem says:
Both ends slender, the new moon is born,
Half black, half white, the pupil of the eye.
Fluttering and bustling, the rooster first crows,
Scattered and distinct, the stars towards dawn.
Surrounding the North, they are often seen shining brightly.
The Analects says:
To govern by virtue,
is like the North Star,
which stays in its place,
while all the other stars revolve around it.
The Book of Songs says:
The bright star shines brilliantly.
Riding the tail already startled Fù Yuè,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
The Way can be transmitted but not possessed,
possessed but not seen.
Fù Yuè attained it,
and became minister to Wǔ Dīng,
encompassing all under heaven,
riding the eastern cord,
straddling the Winnower and Tail,
and was ranked among the constellations.
Whipping the horse, he was further seen as Wáng Liáng.
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
The four stars in the center are called the Celestial Team,
beside them is a star called Wáng Liáng.
When Wáng Liáng whips his horse,
chariots and cavalry fill the wilds.
As for their radiance linking like jade discs,
their brilliance stringing like pearls,
The Hooked Destiny Decision says:
Stars strung together like threaded pearls;
shining resplendent like linked jade discs.
The Western March is Mǎo,
The Ěryǎ says:
The Western March,
is Mǎo.
The commentary says:
A lodge of the west,
also named Banner-Head.
The Northern March is Xū.
The Ěryǎ says:
The Northern March's Xū,
is Xū.
Assisting the night's brightness is the Celestial Essence,
Master Sūn's Illustrations of Auspicious Responses says:
The Auspicious Star,
is the Celestial Essence.
Its shape is like a half-moon,
born on the last or first day of the lunar month,
assisting the moon to give light.
If the ruler shows no partiality to individuals, it appears.
Circling the center is the Imperial Chariot.
The Celestial Officials Star Divination says:
The Big Dipper is the Imperial Chariot,
circling the center.
The Big Dipper is the throat and tongue of the Celestial Officials,
The Book of the Later Hàn says:
Lǐ Gù replied to the edict:
"Your Majesty has the Imperial Secretariat,
just as Heaven has the Big Dipper.
The Big Dipper,
is the throat and tongue of Heaven;
the Imperial Secretariat,
is the throat and tongue of Your Majesty.
It measures and regulates the primordial breath,
operates to balance the four seasons.
It issues and receives the royal commands,
it is what is called the minister who controls the breath."
The Eastern Wall is the emperor's library of charts and books.
The Classic of Stars says:
The Eastern Wall,
is the secret repository of the Son of Heaven's charts and books.
If it is bright, then charts and books are gathered,
the Way and its techniques are practiced,
petty men retreat,
and gentlemen enter.
If it is not so,
the Son of Heaven favors martial prowess,
belittles literary scholars,
worthy men hide,
and the wicked and crooked advance.
As for being brilliantly scattered like brocade,
Yǔ Chǎn's poem says:
The dark scene is like a reflected jade disc,
the myriad stars are like scattered brocade.
Sparkling like linked cowries.
The Ancient Discourses on Anomalies says:
Looking up, the shape of heaven is like a carriage canopy,
the many stars strung together like linked cowries.
Zhōu Téng knew in advance he would not go out,
The Biographies of Exemplary Men of Yùzhāng says:
Zhōu Téng,
styled Shūdá,
served as Censor.
Emperor Huán wished to perform the southern suburban sacrifice,
at daybreak he was about to depart,
Shūdá looked up and said:
"Now in the palace they whip the horses,
but the stars do not move,
how can the emperor go out?"
During the fourth watch,
the crown prince died,
and so it was stopped.
Jīng Fáng himself proclaimed his innocence.
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Hàn says:
Zhōu Chǎng of Wú Commandery studied under Jīng Fáng.
Fáng was slandered by Shí Xiǎn and imprisoned,
he said to Chǎng:
"Forty days after my death,
a guest star will certainly enter the market,
which will be proof of my innocence."
Fáng died,
and it indeed happened as he said.
And as for following the two envoys into Shǔ,
Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Hàn says:
Emperor Hé separately dispatched two envoys,
each to go to the provinces and commanderies to observe and gather folk songs.
The two men were to arrive in the Yì region,
and lodged at the residence of the hostel official Lǐ Hé.
Hé said:
"When you two gentlemen departed the capital,
did you know the court was sending two envoys?"
The envoys asked how he knew,
Hé said:
"Earlier, there were two stars,
heading towards the Yìzhōu division of the heavens."
Observing the five elders roaming the river.
The Apocryphal Treatise on the Analects says:
Zhòngní said:
"I heard that Yáo and Shùn and others roamed Shǒu Mountain,
and observed the river islets.
There were five elders roaming the river,
one elder said:
'The River Chart will come to inform the emperor of the time.'
The second elder said:
'The River Chart will come to inform the emperor of the plan.'
The third elder said:
'The River Chart will come to inform the emperor of the writing.'
The fourth elder said:
'The River Chart will come to inform the emperor of the chart.'
The fifth elder said:
'The River Chart will come to inform the emperor of the tally.'
A dragon held in its mouth a jade case sealed with golden clay and a jade label containing the book,
the five elders flew away as shooting stars,
ascending to enter Mǎo."
The duty lies with the Guardian of the Asterisms,
The Rites of Zhōu:
The Guardian of the Asterisms is in charge of the celestial stars,
to record the changes of the stars, planets, sun, and moon.
He was appointed as Xī Hé.
The Book of Documents says:
Then he appointed Xī and Hé,
reverently to follow the vast heavens,
to calculate and image the sun, moon, and stars,
and respectfully to impart the seasons to the people.
The year then sent down its spirit upon Dōngfāng Shuò,
The Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn says:
The envoy of the Queen Mother of the West arrived,
Dōngfāng Shuò died.
The emperor asked the envoy,
He replied:
"Shuò is the essence of the Wood Emperor,
the Year Star,
which descends to roam among humans,
to observe the world,
and is not Your Majesty's subject."
Mǎo's essence was bestowed upon Xiāo Hé.
The Chūnqiū Zuòzhùqī states:
Xiāo Hé received the Mǎo star at birth.
It is also heard that Zhòu is called Liǔ,
and Zhuó is called Bì.
From the Ěryǎ commentary.
Zhòu,
is the beak of the Vermilion Bird.
The Bì net used to trap rabbits,
is sometimes called Zhuó,
hence named after the star's shape.
Already astonished by the rain-like fall,
Zuǒzhuàn:
In the seventh year of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ,
on the night of Xīnmǎo in the fourth month of summer,
the constant stars were not seen,
and in the middle of the night, stars fell like rain.
Again startled by the falling stones.
Zuǒzhuàn states:
Five stones fell in Sòng,
which were falling stars.
Observing the Celestial Money at Běiluò,
Tiānxiàng Lièxīng Tú states:
The ten stars of Celestial Money are west of Běiluò.
Pointing to the Old Man at the South Pole.
Shǐjì states:
The Old Man star at the South Pole,
when visible, brings peace to the world.
Also, Fáng is the Celestial Quadriga,
Dī is the Celestial Root.
Ěryǎ states:
Celestial Quadriga,
is Fáng.
Celestial Root,
is Dī.
Commentary:
The dragon is the celestial horse,
thus the four stars of Fáng are called Celestial Quadriga;
Jiǎo and Kàng hang down to Dī,
like the root of a tree.
When Dàhuǒ is at the zenith, cold and heat retreat,
Zuǒzhuàn states:
When Huǒ is at the zenith, cold and heat retreat.
Commentary states:
Xīn, in late summer,
culminates at dusk and heat retreats;
in late winter,
culminates at dawn and cold retreats.
When the Dipper's handle points east, heaven and earth are in spring.
Hèguānzǐ states:
When the Dipper's handle points east,
all under heaven experience spring.
Hégǔ is called Qiānniú.
Ěryǎ commentary states:
Now the people of Jīngchǔ call the Qiānniú star Dāngǔ,
Dān means
to carry.
Zhīnǚ is called the Celestial Granddaughter.
Xīngjīng states:
Zhīnǚ,
is the Celestial Granddaughter.
Zǐ Shèn recognized its excess in Xūxiāo.
Zuǒzhuàn states:
Zǐ Shèn said:
"This year, will Sòng and Zhèng not suffer famine?
The year is in Xīngjì,
but excess in Xuánxiāo,
leads to seasonal disasters.
Yīn cannot bear yáng,
the snake rides the dragon.
The dragon,
is the star of Sòng and Zhèng.
Sòng and Zhèng will surely starve.
Xuánxiāo,
is the center of Xū.
Xiāo,
means exhaustion.
Empty and exhausted,
how can they not starve?"
Bǔ Yǎn divined its hidden time.
Zuǒzhuàn states:
The Marquis of Jìn attacked Guó,
and asked Bǔ Yǎn:
"Will I succeed?"
He replied:
"You will conquer it.
A children's rhyme says:
'On the day of Bǐng,
the dragon's tail hides its time.
Tiāncè is dim,
when Huǒ culminates, the army succeeds,
the Duke of Guó will flee.'
Will it be around the ninth and tenth months?"
However, evil cannot overcome virtue,
so why trouble to detail it all?
Wind
The great mass exhales its breath,
which is called wind.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"The great mass exhales its breath,
which is called wind.
It is only when it does not stir,
but when it stirs, all hollows roar angrily."
Yī,
pronounced yī jiè qiē.
It has already broken sprouts and opened husks.
The Xījīng Zá Jì says:
Dǒng Zhòngshū said:
"In an age of great peace,
the wind does not shake the branches,
it merely opens husks and breaks sprouts."
It also nurtures things to accomplish their growth.
The Lǐ Shuō says:
"Wind
means 'to sprout'.
It nurtures things to accomplish their growth,
therefore the eight winds correspond to the eight trigrams."
Recognizing the young maiden in the treetops,
the Wèi Zhì, Biography of Guǎn Lù, says:
Guǎn Lù passed by Ní, the governor of Qīnghé.
At that time there was a great drought.
Lù said:
"There is already a slight breeze from a young maiden in the trees,
and in the branches there are also dark birds singing in harmony.
Rain should arrive."
It indeed happened as he said.
Rejoicing at Zhèng Gōng by the stream.
The Dìlǐ Zhì states:
Shèdì Mountain.
Zhèng Hóng here met an immortal.
When gathering firewood, he often obtained a favorable wind,
which the world called the 'Woodcutter's Wind'.
It went in the morning and returned in the evening,
and is still like this today.
As for singing of its coolness,
the Shī says:
"The north wind is cool."
Speaking of it having a path.
The Shī says:
"The great wind has its path,
greedy men ruin their kind."
Entering the lapel and sleeves, it retains fragrance.
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì says:
In Yíngzhōu, sometimes a fragrant wind arises coolly.
If one spreads one's sleeves to receive it,
then for years it does not fade.
When it touches the skin,
it is necessarily soft and smooth.
Circling among cinnamon and pepper, it stirs the air.
Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind" says:
"It strikes flowers and leaves, stirring the air,
lingering among cinnamon and pepper."
It responds to Guǎngmò to carry out punishments.
The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn says:
At the Winter Solstice,
the Guǎngmò wind arrives,
punishing the guilty,
executing major sentences;
at the Beginning of Spring,
the Tiáo wind arrives,
pardoning minor offenses,
releasing those detained;
at the Spring Equinox,
the Míngshù wind arrives,
rectifying borders,
repairing fields;
at the Beginning of Summer,
the Qīngmíng wind arrives,
presenting worn silks,
paying respects to the feudal lords;
at the Summer Solstice,
the Jǐng wind arrives,
distinguishing great generals,
enfeoffing the meritorious;
at the Beginning of Autumn,
the Liáng wind arrives,
reporting on earthworks,
sacrificing to the four directions;
at the Autumn Equinox,
the Chānghé wind arrives,
removing hanging [instruments],
lutes and zithers are not strung;
at the Beginning of Winter,
the Bùzhōu wind arrives,
repairing palaces and houses,
fortifying border cities.
When the eight winds arrive in their seasons,
then yīn and yáng transform and the Way is accomplished,
and the myriad things are able to be nurtured and grow.
The king should accord with the eight winds,
practice the eight governmental affairs,
corresponding to the eight trigrams.
Then with Míngshù, bestow favors.
The Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yǒu says:
"When the Míngshù wind arrives,
Míngshù welcomes kindness."
The commentary states:
"It is the season of the Spring Equinox.
Shù means the multitude.
Yáng bestows kindness,
welcoming the multitude of things and giving them life."
Await Chānghé to store the multitude of things.
The Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yǒu says:
"When the Chānghé wind arrives, it should be cold,
for Heaven is gathering in."
The commentary states:
"It is the season of the Autumn Equinox.
Chāng means flourishing.
The season flourishes in gathering things,
covering and storing them.
Chāng may be read as dāng."
Observe Bùzhōu to carefully prepare border defenses.
See above.
Empty caves secretly respond,
earthen bags suddenly arise.
Both are seen in Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind".
Furthermore, there is the response to Yǐn Xǐ's divination.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Lǎozǐ was about to leave Zhōu and exit the pass,
to ascend Kūnlún.
The pass official Yǐn Xǐ divined,
the wind was contrary,
he knew a divine person would come passing by.
He then swept the road,
and saw Lǎozǐ.
Lǎozǐ knew Xǐ's destiny was fit to attain the Way,
so he stopped below the pass,
and taught him matters of longevity.
Directed by Gě Xuán's finger.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Gě Xuán was traveling past a spirit temple,
riding in a carriage and did not dismount.
In a moment,
a great wind pursued Xuán,
dust and dirt filled the sky.
Xuán was greatly angered and said:
"Petty evil dares to act thus!"
He immediately raised his hand and pointed at the wind,
and the wind then stopped.
Riding it was heard of in Zōng Què.
The Sòng Shū says:
Zōng Què,
style Yuángàn.
In his youth,
his father, the recluse Zōng Bǐng, asked Què about his aspirations.
He replied:
"I wish to ride the long wind and break the waves for ten thousand lǐ."
Mastering it was also transmitted concerning Lièzǐ.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Lièzǐ mastered the wind,
riding it coolly and skillfully,
for fifteen days and then returned.
Compose a fù on Sòng Yù's Lántái.
Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind" says:
King Xiāng of Chǔ was traveling in the palace of Lántái,
Sòng Yù and Jǐng Chā were in attendance.
The wind came soughing,
and the king then opened his lapel to face it.
Sing of Jīng Kē's Yìshuǐ;
the Shǐjì says:
Jīng Kē entered Qín,
Yān Crown Prince Dān saw him off on the Yìshuǐ.
He sang:
"The wind soughs soughs, oh the Yìshuǐ is cold,
the brave warrior once gone, oh returns no more."
Apply Jìn Wǔdì's liúlí.
The Shì Shuō says:
Mǎn Fèn feared the wind.
He was seated with Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
The north window had a liúlí screen,
actually dense but seeming sparse.
Fèn had a look of cold.
The emperor laughed at Fèn.
He replied:
"Your servant is like a Wú ox,
seeing the moon and panting."
Establish Sòng Míngdì's order officials.
The Sòng Shū says:
Emperor Míng of Sòng was corpulent,
he hated the wind.
In summer he often wore a small leather garment.
He appointed two attendants as Wind Order Officials.
When the wind arose from a direction,
they would immediately first report it.
How in the Southern Sea do sparrows transform?
The Fēngtǔ Jì says:
In the southern regions, in the sixth month there is a southeast long wind,
commonly called the Yellow Sparrow Wind.
At that time sea fish transform into yellow sparrows,
hence the name.
What deity of Hěn Mountain makes the shallots bend?
The Jīngshān Tú says:
Hěnshān County.
Below the mountain there is a stone bed,
beside it grow wild shallots.
When people go to beg for them,
If the gods permit, the wind blows, controlling its measure;
it follows the direction of the grass as it bends and trims it,
not exceeding its bounds.
Clear and cool,
it cures illness and dispels hangovers.
From Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Wind."
Its force startles like a tiger's roar;
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"When a tiger roars, the valley wind arrives."
Commentary:
The tiger,
a yang creature,
is of the same category as the wind.
It also astonishes like the cry of a kite.
The Lǐjì · Qūlǐ says:
"If there is dust ahead,
then display the kite banner."
Commentary:
"When the kite cries, wind is born."
Verify by the magpie's moving nest;
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Magpies know when the year will have much wind,
and leave tall trees to nest on side branches."
Commentary:
"Fú" means
"side."
Recognize when chickens and dogs fall silent.
The Nányuèzhì says:
"In Xī'ān, there are many hurricanes.
A hurricane
possesses the winds of all four directions.
Also called 'fearful wind,'
meaning it inspires terror.
It often arises in the sixth and seventh months;
three days before it arrives,
chickens and dogs become silent because of it.
'Jù'
is pronounced 'jù.'
As for gazing at the bronze bird on the tower,
The Shùzhēngjì says:
"South of the Cháng'ān palace, on the Spirit Tower, there is a bronze wind-measuring bird.
Some say:
This bird moves only when encountering a wind of a thousand lǐ."
Shake the feather-fan jerky in the kitchen.
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
"In the time of Yáo,
meat jerky naturally grew in the kitchen,
thin as a feather fan;
when shaken, it produced wind,
keeping food cold and preventing spoilage,
named 'shà fǔ' (feather-fan jerky)."
It is both the messenger of heaven and earth;
The Hétú Dìtōngjì says:
"Wind is
the messenger of heaven and earth."
It is also the wrath of yīn and yáng.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo says:
"The wrath of yīn and yáng becomes wind."
When it comes, it can sometimes shake bolts;
Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Wind" says:
"It rushes through holes and shakes bolts."
Seeking its place, it often relies on burning feathers.
The Huáinán Wànbìshù says:
"To summon a swift wind,
burn chicken feathers."
Opening the golden casket at dawn;
The Shàngshū · Jīnténg says:
"The Duke of Zhōu resided in the east for two years,
composing a poem to present to the king,
naming it 'Chīxiāo' (Owl).
In autumn,
the harvest was abundant but not yet gathered.
Heaven sent great thunder, lightning, and wind,
and all the grain lay flat.
Great trees were uprooted,
and the people were greatly terrified.
The king and his officials all donned ceremonial caps
and opened the book in the golden casket,
whereupon they found the Duke of Zhōu's request to substitute for King Wǔ.
The king held the book and wept, saying:
'In the past, the Duke labored diligently for the royal house,
but I, a young and ignorant person, did not know of it.
Now Heaven has moved in majesty
to manifest the Duke of Zhōu's virtue.'
The king went out to the suburbs,
and Heaven then sent rain,
the wind reversed,
and the grain all stood up again."
Recognize the gathering of the yuánjū in Lǔ.
The Guóyǔ says:
"A sea bird called yuánjū
alighted outside the eastern gate of the state of Lǔ.
Zāng Wénzhòng had the people of the state sacrifice to it.
Zhǎn Qín said:
'Is this sea bird a sign of disaster this year?
For the birds and beasts of the wide rivers often know to avoid their disasters.'
That year,
the sea had many great winds."
Sometimes summoned by Chīyóu;
The Shǐjì says:
"Chīyóu could summon wind and rain,
and contended with the Yellow Emperor for supremacy.
The Emperor destroyed him in Zhōngjì."
Sometimes stirred by a common woman.
The Shǐjì says:
"A common woman,
a widow of Qí,
cared for her mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law's daughter, coveting the mother's wealth, killed her mother
and accused the widow.
The widow could not clear herself,
and appealed her injustice to Heaven.
Then a great wind assailed the hall of Qí."
The flying chariot first astounded the Jīgōng people;
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
"The Jīgōng people could make flying chariots,
which traveled far with the wind.
In the time of Tāng,
a west wind blew a Jīgōng chariot to Yùzhōu.
Tāng broke the chariot,
not showing it to the people.
Ten years later,
an east wind arrived.
Tāng again made a chariot and sent it as a gift to them,
four myriad lǐ from the Jade Gate."
The curved canopy first originated with King Wǔ of Zhōu.
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù says:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
a great wind broke his canopy.
Tàigōng then fashioned a curved canopy based on the shape of the broken one."
As for calling it 'líhé' (parting and joining);
Lù Jī's Yàolǎn says:
"Lièzǐ rode the wind,
often roaming the eight wildernesses at the beginning of spring,
and returning to the wind cave at the beginning of autumn.
When this wind arrives, plants and trees grow;
when it departs, they wither and fall.
It is called the 'líhé wind.'"
Named 'fénlún' (burning wheel).
The Ěryǎ says:
"The south wind is called the kǎifēng (triumphant wind),
the east wind is called the gǔfēng (valley wind),
the north wind is called the liángfēng (cool wind),
the west wind is called the tàifēng (great wind).
Fénlún is called tuí (collapsing),
fúyáo is called biāo (whirlwind).
Wind with fire is dùn (blazing),
a revolving wind is piāo (whirlwind),
wind at sunrise is bàofēng (violent wind),
rain mixed with wind is mái (dust storm),
wind on a cloudy day is yì (gloomy wind)."
Commentary:
"Tuí:
a violent wind descending from above."
"Biāo:
a violent wind ascending from below."
"Dùn:
dùndùn,
blazing, intense."
"Piāo:
a whirlwind."
The cave is in Yídū.
Shèng Hóngzhī's Jīngzhōu Jì says:
"In Héngshān County, Yídū,
the mountain has a wind cave,
its mouth several chǐ wide,
named 'wind well.'
In summer, wind comes out;
in winter, wind goes in.
When the wind enters or exits,
it blows and cleanses the surroundings.
Passing by in the summer heat,
one feels a chill and thinks of wearing furs."
The gate is passed down from Jiǔzhēn.
The Jiāozhōu Jì says:
"Fēngshān is in Jiǔzhēn commandery.
The wind gate is on the mountain peak,
where there is constant wind."
Startled by the beast encountered at Fǎyù;
The Shānhǎijīng says:
"On Fǎyù mountain there is a beast,
its name is 'shān huī,'
it moves like the wind.
When it appears, there is great wind under heaven."
"Huī"
is pronounced "huī."
Astonished by the person seen at Jūlíng.
The Shānhǎijīng says:
"In the great wilderness,
there is a mountain called 'Jūlíng.'
On the mountain is a person named 'Zhédān,'
residing at the eastern extremity, controlling the entry and exit of wind."
Commentary:
"Zhédān
is a spirit person."
Gently bending the grass;
The Lúnyǔ says:
"The virtue of the gentleman is wind,
the virtue of the petty person is grass.
When wind blows over the grass,
must bend.
Swiftly dispelling dust.
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì" says:
Kūnlún Mountain has winds from all four sides,
and there is also a dust-dispelling wind.
If clothes are soiled with dust,
when the wind arrives,
blowing on the clothes will cleanse them.
It is often heard that it follows things and spreads its breath.
Yáng Quán's "Wùlǐ Lùn" says:
Wind is
the stirring of the disordered breaths of yīn and yáng, which arouses and rises.
When angry, it scatters sand and raises gravel,
uproots houses and topples trees;
when pleased, it does not shake branches or stir grass,
but follows things and spreads its breath.
This is the nature of heaven and earth,
the principle of spontaneity.
It also blinds the eyes and chaps the lips.
Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind" says:
Reaching the lips causes chapping,
entering the eyes causes blindness.
Then, its gentle wafting turns the huì orchid,
"Chǔcí" says:
Bright winds turn the huì orchid, rippling over the lofty lán orchid.
Drifting and blowing on the jujube tree,
"Shījīng":
The gentle wind from the south,
blows on that jujube tree's heart.
Howling angrily through ten thousand apertures,
see above annotation on "the great clod's belched breath."
Retreating flight of six yì birds.
"Zuǒzhuàn" says:
Six yì birds flew backwards,
passing over the capital of Sòng,
due to the wind.
Fan bestowed upon Yuán Hóng,
"Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
Yuán Hóng was governor of the Eastern Commandery,
Xiè Ān took Hóng's hand and bestowed a fan,
Hóng said:
"I shall respectfully uphold and spread benevolent winds,
to comfort those common people."
Clothes blown off Jiǎ Mì.
"Jìnshū" says:
In Jiǎ Mì's home, there were several strange occurrences,
a whirlwind blew his court robe up several hundred feet,
a large snake emerged from his sleeve,
later, disaster indeed befell him.
Warning of cold often appears with the sight of fire,
"Guóyǔ" says:
When fire appears, the clear wind warns of cold.
Responding to categories is sometimes heard with wine overflowing.
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
The mutual response of things and categories,
is mysterious, profound, and subtle,
debate and argument cannot explain it,
thus when the east wind arrives, the wine sinks and overflows.
Annotation:
Wine sediment,
is clear, strained wine.
Rice matter sinks down,
the wood flavor is sour,
sour wind enters the wine,
therefore the vinegar-like sediment boils.
Tiáotiáo, diāodiāo,
"Zhuāngzǐ" says:
The pipes of earth are the myriad apertures,
the whirlwind is the great harmony,
the gentle breeze is the small harmony,
have you alone not heard the tiáotiáo?
The diāodiāo?
Sheep's horn, soaring whirlwind,
see below annotation on "although bearing great wings."
Its ability can only hunt leaves,
"Zhōushēng Lièzǐ" says:
The leaf-hunting wind,
does not correspond to the eight nodes.
Truly does not make branches sing.
"Yántiě Lùn" says:
In times of great peace,
the wind does not make branches sing.
Although bearing great wings,
"Zhuāngzǐ" says:
The péng bird's back is like Tài Mountain,
the péng bird's wings are like clouds hanging from the sky,
it soars on the whirlwind and sheep's horn wind upwards for ninety thousand lǐ.
The annotation says:
If the accumulation of wind is not thick,
then it lacks the strength to bear great wings,
therefore at ninety thousand lǐ, the wind is then below.
Whirlwind, sheep's horn,
are winds.
Now whirlwinds rise like ram's horns.
How can it last all morning?
"Lǎozǐ" says:
A whirlwind does not last all morning.
As for the gentle breeze fanning harmony,
"Shījīng" says:
Gentle valley winds,
bring shade and bring rain.
"Wénxuǎn" poem says:
Spring wind fans a mild warmth.
Tenderly thawing the ice,
"Lǐjì‧Yuèlìng" says:
On the day of the beginning of spring,
the east wind thaws the ice.
When at the great mountain's foot, not getting lost,
"Shūjīng" says:
He was sent into the great mountain's forests,
fierce winds, thunder, and rain, yet he did not get lost.
How could it be shared by common people?
Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind" says:
This is solely the great king's wind,
how could common people obtain and share it?
Yǒuyú arose with the song dispelling resentment,
"Dìwáng Shìjì" says:
Shùn strummed the five-stringed qín,
singing the "Southern Wind" song:
"The fragrance of the southern wind,
can dispel my people's resentment."
Huángdì obtained the dream of blowing dust.
"Qiánfū Lùn" says:
Huángdì dreamed a great wind blew the world's dust and soil,
and obtained Fēng Hòu to make him his minister.
It also comforts people and eases the body,
Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind" says:
It enlightens the ears and eyes,
eases the body and comforts people.
Stirring grass and shaking branches.
See above annotation on "follows things and spreads its breath."
Some sing of Fēng and Pèi for joy,
"Hànshū":
"Gāozǔ passed through Pèi,
striking the zhù and singing himself:
A great wind rises, oh! clouds fly and scatter,
majesty covers the land within the seas, oh! I return to my hometown,
how can I obtain fierce warriors, oh! to guard the four directions."
Some crossed the Fén River and had verses.
Hàn Wǔdì's "Autumn Wind Song" says:
"Autumn wind rises, oh! white clouds fly,
plants and trees yellow and fall, oh! geese return south.
Floating on a tower ship, oh! crossing the Fén River,
traversing the midstream, oh! raising white waves."
Divination was already heard from Shī Kuàng,
"Zuǒzhuàn" says:
Chǔ invaded Zhèng,
heavy rain.
The Chǔ army suffered much from cold,
laborers nearly exhausted.
The Jìn people heard there was a Chǔ army,
Shī Kuàng said:
"No harm,
I repeatedly sang of the north wind,
and also sang of the south wind,
the south wind is not strong."
Dust sometimes disgusted Yuánguī.
"Jìnshū" says:
Yǔ Liàng went out to garrison Jiāngzhōu,
because he was the emperor's maternal uncle,
he internally held court power.
Wáng Dǎo could not bear it,
once encountering the west wind rising,
he would raise a fan to shield himself, saying:
"Yuánguī's dust soils people."
Rushing fierce and how could it bear toppling trees,
"Huángdì Fēngjīng" says:
Harmonious and auspicious,
is heaven's joyful breath;
breaking, lifting, rushing, fierce,
is heaven's angry breath.
"Hànshū" says:
The King of Yān made Jì his capital,
a great wind toppled sixteen trees in the palace,
later the king was executed.
Harmonious and auspicious, it only allows opening one's robe.
"Harmonious and auspicious" already seen in the above annotation.
Sòng Yù's "Fù on Wind" says:
The king then opened his lapels and faced it.
It is because the ruler is sage and the season is compliant,
naturally balanced and harmonious, obtaining appropriateness.
"Shàngshū‧Hóngfàn" says:
Sage, timely winds are compliant.
Cloud
Clouds are
the vapor of rivers and marshes, the gathering of yīn and yáng.
The Shuōwén states:
Clouds are
the breath of mountains and rivers.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
The gathering of yīn and yáng forms clouds.
Then, they arise bleakly,
and rain falls densely.
The Shuōwén states:
Qī means
the rising of rain clouds.
Yǎn means
the appearance of rain clouds.
The Shī states:
Dense and bleak,
the rain falls gently.
Dark and misty, they follow the dragon;
the Yì states:
Clouds follow the dragon.
Drifting and soaring, they reach the pitch pipes.
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shízhōu Jì states:
In the third year of the Tiānhàn era,
the Yuèzhī state offered divine incense,
and the envoy said:
"Our state has a constant omen:
when the east wind enters the pitch pipes,
and does not cease for a hundred days,
and azure clouds reach the pitch pipes,

Therefore, we sought rare treasures and offered divine incense."
Behold the flower-like patterns of Huángdì;
the Shǐjì states:
When Huángdì battled Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,

like golden branches and jade leaves,
hovering above the emperor,
resembling floral patterns,
and thus the huágài canopy was created.
Recognize the dragons and tigers of the Hàn emperor.
The Shǐjì states:
Fàn Zēng advised Xiàng Yǔ:
"I had someone observe Liú Bāng,
and above him were clouds,
all taking the form of dragons and tigers,
displaying five colors.
This is the aura of the Son of Heaven.
Strike quickly and do not miss the opportunity."
Thus, they take their image from Kǎn;
the Yì states:
Kǎn represents clouds.
Observe the judgment of Xū.
The Yì states:
Clouds ascend to the heavens,
Xū: the nobleman feasts and enjoys himself.
Some sang praises in the time of Yú Shùn;
the Shàngshū Dàzhuàn states:
In Shùn's time, the auspicious clouds appeared,
and all the artisans harmonized in song.
Shùn sang:
"Brilliant are the auspicious clouds,
vast and boundless."
Some served as an auspicious sign for Qìngdū.
The Chūnqiū Héchéngtú states:
Yáo's mother, Qìngdū,
was born with divine anomalies,
and yellow clouds often covered her.
The traces of Bái Qǐ and Jì Zǐxùn;
the Sōushénjì states:
When Jì Zǐxùn arrived in Luò,
he met dozens of high officials,
and after he left, white clouds arose.
Fragrance followed the carriage of the Queen Mother of the West.
The Hàn Wǔdì Nèizhuàn states:
The emperor was at the Xúnzhēn Terrace,
on the seventh night of the seventh month,
when he saw the Queen Mother of the West arriving in a purple cloud chariot.
Upon her arrival,
cloud vapors billowed densely,
all turning into fragrant scents.
Emerging from Fúyáng, they gather and disperse;
the Shānhǎijīng states:
Above Fúyáng,
strange clouds emerge.
Departing from Cāngwú, they roll and stretch.
An ancient poem states:
Clouds depart from the Cāngwú wilderness,

As for examining the omen of no rain in the western suburbs,
the Yì states:
Dense clouds bring no rain,
from our western suburbs.
Observe the meaning of morning clouds over the southern mountains.
The Shī states:
Lush and luxuriant,
morning clouds over the southern mountains.
Note:
Huìwèi
describes the appearance of clouds rising.
Covering the precious tripod of Fényīn;
the Hànshū states:
When Emperor Wǔ welcomed the Fényīn tripod to the Gānquán Palace,

Sheltering the recluse of the west.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Fēihòu states:
Observe the west: if there are large clouds of five colors,

Lush and abundant,

Like smoke yet not smoke,
like clouds yet not clouds,
lush and abundant,
serene and towering,
these are called auspicious clouds.
Neither mist nor dust,
Wèi Wǔ's Bīngshū Jiéyào states:
Sūnzǐ speaks of observing cloud auras:
neither clouds nor smoke,
neither dust nor mist,
shaped like birds and beasts,
auspicious for the guest, inauspicious for the host.
Mountainous like grass and thickets,
watery like fish scales.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
Mountain clouds resemble grass and thickets,
water clouds resemble fish scales,
drought clouds resemble smoke and fire,
rain clouds resemble water vapor,
all analogizing their origins to show people.
Also said to be the immortal chariot of the emperor's realm;
the Zhuāngzǐ states:
The Huàfēng man said to Yáo:
"When the world follows the Way,
all things flourish together.
After a thousand years, weary of the world,
you depart and ascend as an immortal,
riding those white clouds,
to reach the emperor's realm."
The beautiful form of Gāotáng;
Sòng Yù's Gāotáng Fù Preface states:
King Xiāng of Chǔ and Sòng Yù were touring the Yúnmèng Terrace,
the Gāotáng Observatory.
Above were cloud vapors,
and in a short while,
they transformed endlessly.
The king asked:
"What vapor is this?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"It is the morning clouds.
Long ago, the former king once toured Gāotáng,
and while napping during the day,
he dreamt of a woman who said:
'I am the daughter of Wūshān,
a visitor to Gāotáng.
Hearing of your tour to Gāotáng,
I wish to share your pillow and mat.'
The king thus favored her.
As she left, she bid farewell:
'I dwell on the sunny side of Wūshān,
amidst the heights and barriers.
At dawn, I am the traveling clouds;
at dusk, the traveling rain.
Morning and evening,
beneath the Yángtái.'
At dawn, he looked,
and it was as she said.
Thus, he erected a temple for her,
named 'Morning Clouds.'"
Phoenixes soar, simurghs glide;
Lù Jī's Fúyún Fù states:
Like layered terraces and lofty observatories,
tiered towers and stacked pavilions,
sometimes like the dense peaks of Zhōngshǒu,
suddenly resembling the vastness of a frontier pass.
Dragons leap, serpents rise,
bears rage, tigers battle,
simurghs glide, phoenixes soar,
wild swans startle and stir.
Dragons stretch, inchworms curl.
Chéng Gōngsuí's Yún Fù states:
Dragons stretch, inchworms curl,
winding and meandering,
continuously like phoenixes in flight,
tigers turning in succession.
For the Zhōu, they were auspicious signs when observing the river;
the Lǐdǒu Wēiyí states:
When King Chéng of Zhōu governed peacefully, he observed the river.

For Yáo, they manifested as auspicious signs when sinking jade discs.
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
When Yáo sank jade discs into the river,
white clouds arose,
and a whirlwind shook and scattered them.
As for fish-washing clouds awaiting rain,
Huáng Zǐfā's Xiàngyǔshū states:
When there are fish-washing clouds in the four directions,
if swift,
rain falls immediately;
if slow,
When rain is scarce, it is hard to arrive.
If clouds over the Jiāng and Hàn rivers move swiftly,

Burning stones to smell their fragrance,

Làn stones are red in color, resembling lungs.

When the smoke rises to the heavens,
it forms fragrant clouds;
when fragrant clouds spread and moisten,

Golden branches and jade leaves,

Embroidered patterns and brocaded designs,

Some are like embroidered patterns and brocaded designs,
faint and subtle,
extending far and wide, soaring into the void,
lightly drifting and floating.
Some appear as flying birds,
others resemble flocks of sheep.
Jīng Fáng's "Yì Fēi Hòu" states:
In general, to predict rain,
if there are black clouds resembling flocks of sheep,
rushing like flying birds,

The Bǎozhāng official verifies the auspicious or inauspicious vapors,
The "Zhōulǐ" states:
The Bǎozhāng official uses the colors of clouds and atmospheric phenomena to distinguish the auspicious or inauspicious vapor signs.
He observes the cloud vapors beside the sun:
blue indicates insects,
white indicates military affairs,
red indicates drought,
black indicates floods,
yellow indicates abundance.
The observation platform records the auspicious signs of opening and closing.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
At each equinox, solstice, opening, and closing,
the cloud phenomena must be recorded.
One then ascends the observation platform,
gazes out, and records them.
Annotation:
Equinox,
refers to the spring and autumn equinoxes.
Solstice,
refers to the winter and summer solstices.
Opening,
refers to the beginning of spring and summer.
Closing,
refers to the beginning of autumn and winter.
There are also ethereal red silks,
and fluttering white swans.
The "Yì Tōng Guà Yàn" states:
At the winter solstice,
yang clouds emerge from the constellation Jī,
resembling the shape of trees.
At the beginning of spring,
qīngyáng clouds emerge from the constellation Fáng,

At the spring equinox,
zhèngyáng clouds emerge from the constellation Zhāng,
resembling accumulated white swans.
At grain rain,
tàiyáng clouds emerge from the constellation Shēn,
resembling a carriage canopy.
At the beginning of summer,
chángyáng clouds emerge from the constellation Zuǐ,

At the summer solstice,
shàoyīn clouds resemble rippling water waves.
At the beginning of autumn,
zhuóyīn clouds emerge,
resembling red silk.
At cold dew,
zhèngyīn clouds emerge,
resembling hat tassels.
At frost descent,
tàiyīn clouds emerge,
above resembling sheep,
below resembling millstones.
Moistening those reeds and thatch,
The "Shījīng" states:
Bright, bright white clouds,
moisten those reeds and thatch.
Behold these pearls and jades.
The "Dìtú" states:
When observing stone vapors resembling floating clouds,
they are the essence of pearls and jades.
When vapor moistens the pillar base,
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
When mountain clouds steam,
the pillar bases become moist.
Rain must wait for the gathering.
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
Guǎng Chéngzǐ said to Huángdì:

The Hàn emperor composed the song of Fēng and Pèi,

Gāozǔ passed through Pèi,

The Queen Mother performed the melody of Yáochí.

The Son of Heaven toasted the Queen Mother of the West at Yáochí,

In Sòng, observed atop a pine,

In the eighth year of the Dàmíng era,

a five-colored cloud appeared atop a pine tree,

In Hàn, recorded from within the fēng sacrifice.

Startled by the shapes resembling forests and trees,

Gazing upon the clear sky, one thinks of Yuè Guǎng,

Seeing the bright sun, one thinks of Lord Jiāng.

Pheasants and hares reflected against the clear azure,

When there are blue-green clouds,

A carriage canopy halts in the distant sky.
Emperor Wén of Wèi wrote in a poem:
In the northwest, there is a floating cloud,

Recording Huángdì's officials,

Huángdì used clouds to designate his officials,

Praising Zhòngróng's capacity.

White clouds as an auspicious sign for Tāng,

When Tāng was about to rise,

Yellow clouds as an auspicious sign for Shùn,
The "Chūnqiū Yǎnkǒngtú" states:

Although lacking the intention to emerge from the mountain crevice,

Zhāng Mèngyáng wrote in a poem:
Flowing water longs for its old shore,

Observing their towering and lofty forms,
densely layered and unevenly arranged,

The clouds of Zhōu are lofty and dense.
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Ode to Clouds" states:
When spreading, they envelop and cover the four seas;

Chaotically darting crimson snakes,

Lightly drifting crimson garments.

Sòng Jūn annotated:
Zhěn
corresponds to the region of Chǔ.
Clouds are the vapor of water.
Ashes are
the vapor of fire.
By scattering ashes in a diagram,
the clouds were thus extinguished.
These phenomena serve to manifest warnings of calamities and anomalies,
admonishing against flaws in governance and decrees.
How could they be merely for reciting Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Autumn Wind" verse
or savoring Tāng Xiū's "Dusk" poem?
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Ode to the Autumn Wind" says:
The autumn wind rises, oh! white clouds fly;

Tāng Xiū's poem says:
At dusk, azure clouds gather;

Now rain is
the harmony of yīn and yáng,

"Rain is

He was placed in the great wilds yet was not lost;

From our lord's fields it reaches our private ones.

When the five policies are without error,

fourth, govern the borders,

When the five policies accord with the season,
spring rain then arrives.
Once every ten days is the period.

It does not break up clods;

It is just enough to wash the branches.

Gentle as dew lying on grass,

Dense like silk threads scattered in the air.

Drinking wine, he was just observed by Yùshū;

In his town,

the Jiāyǔ says:

When clouds first touch the rocks,

It detained the divine chariot of Guàntán;

King Wǔ awoke,

It resembled the beautiful form of Gāotáng.
the Xiāngyáng Chuán says:

Though its moisture does not last a morning,

the Lǎozǐ says:

Then it harnesses Píngyì,
the Guǎngyǎ says:

the Fēngsú Tōng says:

It makes the longing wife in the chamber sigh;

It gathers the Jiāomíng on the water.

is a water bird."
On the Shǔ road, bells dripped with rain;

At Zhōu's outskirts, it washed the weapons;

They drilled the turtle shell,

It played flutes and drums in Liú City.
the Shùyì Jì says:

Heaven has no fierce winds,

They followed this,
and when the army was raised, rain fell.

Moss grows in the hall.

Rejoicing that sweet rain has already flown,

All the hundred grains look up to it.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
When Lǔ's Jì Wǔzǐ went to Jìn,
Fàn Xuānzǐ recited the "Shǔ Miǎo";
Wǔzǐ said:
"A small state looking up to a great state
is like the hundred grains looking up to nourishing rain."
There is also the whipping of stones in a cave;
Shèng Hóngzhī's Jīngzhōu Jì says:
In Héngshān County there is a mountain,
standing alone, steep and precipitous.
To the northwest is a stone cave;
walking about a hundred paces with a torch,
there are two large stones about ten feet apart.
Commonly, one is called the Yang Stone,
and one the Yin Stone.
When flood or drought causes disaster,
whipping the Yin Stone brings rain,
whipping the Yang Stone brings clear weather.
Clouds flying from a saddle;
the Sòng Yǒngchū Shānchuān Jì says:
On Póyáng's Chángshòu Mountain,
shaped like a horse,
white clouds emerge from its saddle,
and by morning there is rain.
Troubling the River Earl's messenger;
the Shényì Jīng says:
On the Western Sea there is a man,
riding a white horse with a red mane,
wearing white clothes and a black cap,
followed by twelve youths,
galloping on the Western Sea as if flying,
named the "River Earl's Messenger."
In whichever state he arrives,
there is torrential rain.
Relying on the Lord of Non-Action.
The Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú says:
In Zhèng there is the Bùmáo Mountain,
upon which dwells the Lord of Non-Action,
who distributes clouds and rain within the Nine Provinces.
Then there is Liàng Fǔ gathering mugwort;
the Hòu Hànshū says:
Liàng Fǔ served in the commandery as a Wǔguān Yuàn.
At that time, there was a great summer drought;
the Grand Administrator personally went out to pray to the mountains and rivers,
but for days nothing descended.
Fǔ then exposed himself in the courtyard,
and passionately swore:
"Fǔ serves as an aide,
unable to offer remonstrance and loyalty,
harmonize yīn and yáng,
causing Heaven and Earth to be blocked,
all things scorched and withered;
the fault lies entirely with Fǔ.
Now I dare to pray and request;
if by midday there is no rain,
I beg to use my body to atone for this offense."
Then he piled firewood and gathered mugwort and thatch to surround himself,
and set a fire to burn himself.
Before midday arrived,
the sky clouded over and darkened,
and in a moment, torrential rain fell.
Dài Fēng piled firewood.
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū says:
Dài Fēng,
styled Píngzhòng,
was promoted to Magistrate of Xīhuá.
That year there was a great drought;
prayers brought no results,
so he piled firewood and sat upon it to burn himself.
When the fire rose, heavy rain fell.
People near and far sighed in admiration;
he was promoted to Chancellor of Zhōngshān.
Floating wheat was already praised regarding Gāo Fèng;
the Hòu Hànshū says:
Gāo Fèng loved learning without rest.
His family was sunning wheat,
and ordered Fèng to guard it from chickens,
giving him a pole.
Fèng held the pole and read;
heavy rain came,
Fèng read on unaware,
holding the pole as before.
His wife returned,
saw the wheat washed away,
and was very angry.
Fèng also showed no shame.
Flowing grain is still told of regarding Mǎi Chén.
The Zōu Zǐ says:
Zhū Mǎi Chén diligently pursued his studies,
unaware of the rain washing away the grain.
Following Jǐngshān's traveling carriage;
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū says:
Bǎilǐ Sōng,
styled Jǐngshān,
served as Governor of Xúzhōu.
The region suffered drought;
wherever Sōng went on inspection,
sweet rain would pour down.
Elders from two counties, Zhùqí and Héxiāng in Dōnghǎi, pleaded:
"We are equally your people;
why are we alone not visited?"
So he turned and went to them,
and rain followed his carriage down.
Folding Línzōng's cornered headscarf.
The Hòu Hànshū says:
Guō Línzōng was traveling between Chén and Liáng,
encountered rain,
and one corner of his headscarf got soaked and drooped.
People of the time then deliberately folded their scarf corners,
calling it the "Línzōng scarf."
Such was the admiration for him.
Also heard is Marquis Wén keeping his promise by going hunting as scheduled;
the Zhànguó Cè says:
Marquis Wén of Wèi scheduled a hunt with a gamekeeper.
On that day it rained;
Marquis Wén was about to go out,
but his attendants advised against it.
The lord said:
"I made an appointment with the gamekeeper;
I cannot break it."
So he went.
Wèi then began to grow strong.
Minister Xiè going out and becoming angry.
The Shì Shuō says:
Grand Tutor Xiè Ān showed neither anger nor joy.
Once, returning from seeing off his elder brother Zhēngxī's burial,
at dusk he encountered rain,
and the drivers were all drunk.
The lord then, from within the carriage,
took the carriage pillar and struck the drivers,
his voice and expression very stern.
Some diligently pray for rain out of concern;
the Gǔliáng Zhuàn says:
In the first month of spring,
recording "no rain"
shows diligence about rain.
In the fourth month of summer,
again recording "no rain"
shows concern about rain.
Some suffer from continuous excessive rain.
The Ěryǎ says:
A sudden rainstorm is called dòng,
a light rain is called màimù.
Long-lasting rain is called yín,
excessive rain is called lín.
Offending the divine turtle of Luófú;
the Luófú Shān Jì says:
The mountain has a Turtle Abyss,
in the abyss is a divine turtle,
with a copper ring through its nose.
If someone defiles this abyss,
rain immediately pours down.
The stone drum of Wǔchāng sounding.
The Wǔchāng Jì says:
West of the city is Shígǔ Mountain,
upon which are three stone drums.
When the drums sound,
Heaven is sure to rain.
Again seen is the Shāngyáng leaping vigorously;
the Jiāyǔ says:
In Qí there was a one-legged bird,
which flew and gathered before the palace hall,
spreading its wings and hopping.
The Marquis of Qí found it strange,
and inquired of Confucius.
Confucius said:
"This bird is called the Shāngyáng.
In the past, children would bend one foot, vigorously shake both arms, and hop,
Moreover, a ballad says:
"Heaven is about to send great rain,
the shāngyáng dances and leaps.
Quickly dredge the ditches and channels,
repair the dikes and embankments."
Indeed, great continuous rain fell,
harming the people of various states,
only Qí was prepared."
Stone swallows take flight,
The Xiāngzhōu Jì says:
On the Línglíng mountain there are stone swallows,
when encountering wind and rain they immediately fly,
then return and settle, becoming stone again.
The jade maiden dons her garment,
Wáng Cǎi's Ānchéng Jì says:
At the Xīchéng ford in Píngxiāng,
there is a Jade Maiden Ridge.
When heaven is about to rain,
five-colored qi always first surges among the rocks,
commonly called 'the jade maiden donning her garment'.
The thunder lord dons his attire.
The Yìlín Biànzhān says:
The thunder lord dons his attire,
rumbling as he travels west.
Continuous rain does not cease,
flowing to become rivers and streams.
Recognizing the bathing boar in the Milky Way,
Huáng Zǐfā's Yǔ Shū says:
When the four directions and the Big Dipper have no clouds,
but only within the River there are three patches of cloud,
connected like a bathing pig,
after three days there will be great rain.
Observing the flock of sheep on the mǎo day.
The Shī Kuàng Zhān says:
On the fifth mǎo day,
if you watch for clouds in the northwest resembling a flock of sheep,
rain will arrive.
Benefiting things makes it divine,
The Shīzǐ says:
When Shénnóng governed the world,
if he desired rain it would arrive.
Five days was 'traveling rain';
ten days was 'grain rain';
fifteen days was 'seasonal rain'.
All things received benefit,
therefore it was called 'divine rain'.
Líng clouds have fragrance.
See the annotation "burning stones to smell fragrance" in the Yún Fù.
Abundant rain is likened to Xuānní's governance of Lǔ,
The Yántiě Lùn says:
Confucius,
was a great sage.
He once occupied a minor position,
governing Lǔ for three months.
Without issuing orders, things were done;
without imposing prohibitions, things ceased.
Abundant like timely rain irrigating all things,
nothing failed to rise and flourish.
Continuous rain is like Fù Yuè's assistance to Shāng.
The Shàngshū·Yuè Mìng says:
If the year sees great drought,
I will use you as continuous rain.
Also, there is Luán Bā spraying wine,
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Luán Bā,
was a man of Shǔ.
He was appointed as a Secretary Gentleman.
During a grand court assembly, he received wine,
but did not drink it,
instead spraying it towards the southwest.
The emperor inquired of Bā,
Bā said:
"My home county, Chéngdū, has a great fire,
I used the wine to make rain to save it."
The emperor sent a post-horse to inquire,
and all reported:
"Rain came from the north,
carrying the smell of wine."
Fán Yīng rinsing water,
The Jìn Shū says:
Fán Yīng lived in seclusion at Hú Mountain.
Once a violent wind arose from the southwest,
Yīng said to his students:
"The fire in Chéngdū city is very fierce."
Thereupon, he took water in his mouth and rinsed it towards the west,
then ordered them to record the date and time.
Later, someone coming from Shǔ said:
"On that day there was a great fire,
clouds arose from the east,
and in a short while, great rain fell,
extinguishing the fire."
Red turtles floating upon the waves,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
If red turtles float upon the waves,
there will certainly be great rain.
Black water-lizards leaping in the water's depths.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Black water-lizards, divine dragons,
dwell hidden in springs.
When rain is about to come, they leap.
When yīn and yáng merge harmoniously, wind is plentiful,
The Xījīng Zájì says:
Dǒng Zhòngshū said:
When the yīn and yáng vapors first steam,
they seem to exist and not exist.
If wind is plentiful, they merge quickly,
therefore rain is great and sparse;
if wind is scant, they merge slowly,
therefore rain is fine and dense.
When the sun and moon are obscured and eclipsed, clouds are fine.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Fēihòu says:
If there are azure clouds,
fine like a shuttle's axis,
obscuring the sun and moon,
within five days it will certainly rain.
Sometimes it falls because of burying exposed bones,
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū says:
Zhōu Chàng,
was by nature benevolent and kind.
He served as Governor of Hénán.
During a summer drought,
long prayers brought no response.
He therefore collected and buried over ten thousand skeletons of travelers who had died beside Luò city.
Timely soaking rain fell immediately.
Sometimes it is brought about by redressing injustices.
The Dōngguān Hàn Jì says:
In the second year of Yǒngchū, third month,
the capital experienced drought.
By the fifth month,
the Empress Dowager Héxī Dèng visited Luòyáng,
inspecting prisons and rectifying injustices.
Before she returned to the palace,
soaking rain poured down heavily.
Examining the Xī's Changes,
one laments the dense clouds over the western suburbs not releasing rain;
The Yì says:
Dense clouds do not release rain,
they come from our western suburbs.
Pondering that classic of the unicorn,
one gazes upon the northern ridge where shelter could be found.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Xiáo has two ridges:
its southern ridge,
is the tomb of Xiàhòu Gāo;
its northern ridge,
is where King Wén took shelter from wind and rain.
Fog
Fog is when
the earth's qi rises but the heavens do not respond.
The *Erya* says:
When the earth's qi rises,
and the heavens do not respond,
it is called fog.
It is dense and moistening.
The *Shiming* says:
Fog (wù)
means to cover (mào).
It is qi that densely covers and envelops things.
In times of darkness and chaos,
it becomes an ominous disaster;
for enlightened kings and sage rulers,
it becomes an auspicious sign.
Moistening,
see the note below for "placed with patterned rhinoceros horn."
In the deep gloom of dawn,
the *Rites* say:
If the ordinances of summer are practiced in midwinter,
then there will be dense, gloomy fog.
The black leopard hides and its patterns become resplendent.
Liú Xiàng's *Biographies of Exemplary Women* says:
When Táo Dázǐ governed Táo for three years,
his reputation did not flourish,
yet his family wealth tripled.
His wife admonished him, saying:
"Your ability is meager, yet your office is high;
this is called inviting harm.
Having no merit, yet your household prospers;
this is called accumulating calamity.
I have heard that on the southern mountains there is a black leopard:
For seven days during fog and rain, it does not come down to eat.
Why is this?
It desires to moisten its fur,
so that its patterns may become splendid.
Therefore, it hides to avoid harm.
Now, sir, you act contrary to this.
Will there not be future troubles?"
The soaring serpent swims and winds its way.
The *Hánzǐ* says:
The flying dragon rides the clouds,
the soaring serpent swims through the fog.
When the clouds cease and the fog disperses,
they are the same as earthworms and ants.
Mǎ Yuán, having been at Làngbó,
the *Book of the Later Hàn* says:
Mǎ Yuán campaigned south against Jiāozhǐ,
beheaded Zhēng Cè,
and then poured wine to reward the army.
Calmly, he said to his officials:
"My younger cousin Shǎoyóu often pitied me for my fervor and great ambitions,
saying:
'A scholar lives but one lifetime;
he should only seek sufficient food and clothing,
ride a simple carriage,
drive a slow horse,
serve as a commandery clerk,
guard the ancestral graves,
and be called a good man by his village—
this is enough.'"
When I was between Làngbó and Xīlǐ,
with the enemy not yet destroyed,
there was mire below and fog above,
poisonous vapors steaming forth.
Looking up, I saw kites fluttering and falling into the water.
Lying there, I thought of Shǎoyóu's words from his lifetime—
how could they be attained!"
Luán Bā was just then returning to Shǔ's capital.
Gě Hóng's *Biographies of Immortals* says:
Luán Bā was a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
On New Year's Day,
a great fog arose,
and those sitting opposite could not see each other.
Bā's whereabouts were lost.
Later, when asked the reason,
it turned out Bā had returned to Chéngdū to bid farewell to relatives and old friends.
Liú Yī, bearing the state seal,
the *Yānshū Lièzǔ Hòujì* says:
In the sixth year of Yuánxǐ,
Jiǎng Gàn dispatched the Palace Attendant Miào Sōng and the Supervisor of the Household of the Crown Prince Liú Yī,
carrying the hereditary seal of state,
to go to Jìn to seek aid.
Yī bore it,
and after traveling several *lǐ*,
yellow fog filled the four directions,
confusing and bewildering them so they could not advance,
and they returned.
Only after changing to the traveling seal
were they able to depart.
Xuānyuán obtaining the great fish.
The *Imperial Century* says:
During the time of the Yellow Emperor,
heaven sent a great fog for three days.
The Emperor was traveling by the Luò River,
when he saw a great fish.
He slaughtered five sacrificial animals to make a libation to it.
Heaven then sent heavy rain,
for seven days and seven nights,
and only after the fish drifted away did he obtain the charts and writings.
The present *Hétú*
is that very text.
It is passed down in the world that "a great fog for three days,
must be followed by heavy rain"—
this began from that time.
As for Zǔhé covering half the sky,
the *Biography of Mr. Lǐ* says:
The gentleman's name was Kuàng,
styled Zǔhé,
a man of Nányáng.
Liú Bèi sent troops to capture the gentleman.
The gentleman raised a fog covering half the sky,
and Bèi's cavalry killed each other.
The gentleman then entered Wú.
Gōngchāo's five *lǐ*,
Xiè Chéng's *Book of the Later Hàn* says:
In Hénán, there was Zhāng Kǎi,
styled Gōngchāo,
fond of Daoist arts.
He lived in Huàyīn,
and could create a fog for five *lǐ*.
At that time, a man from Guānxī, Péi Yōu,
could also create a fog for three *lǐ*.
Observing those groups of cunning ones,
the *Qiántán Jì* says:
When a great fog lasts thirty days,
groups of cunning ones arise.
Superiors and inferiors deceive each other,
with few above and many below,
hence groups of cunning ones arise.
Inferring its hidden scholars.
Jīng Fáng's *Ominous Divinations* says:
When clouds and fog rise from the four directions,
then the times have many hidden scholars.
Observing the divine well of Yōngqiū,
the *Chénliú Customs Record* says:
In Yōngqiū County, there is a shrine,
named the Shrine of the Xià Hòu.
There is a divine well
that can summon fog and hail.
Recognizing the fragrant vapor of Màolíng,
the *Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn* says:
Emperor Wǔ was buried at Màolíng.
The fragrant vapor was extraordinary,
accumulating between the tomb mound and its path,
like a great fog.
Moreover, worrying about excessive yin,
the *Book of Hàn* says:
During the Jiànshǐ era of Emperor Chéng,
yellow fog filled the four directions.
The Emperor inquired,
and Yáng Xìng and others replied:
"It is the qi of excessive yin encroaching upon yang."
Soon, rain was heard to arrive.
The *Imperial Century* says:
A great fog for three days
must be followed by heavy rain.
Before the rain falls,
one must not venture forth.
Huáinán, being exiled, did not return.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
During the Hàn Emperor Wén's time,
King Cháng of Huáinán was exiled to Shǔ for his crimes.
Yuán Àng admonished, saying:
"The King is a man of stern character.
If he encounters fog and dew,
and dies on the journey,
Your Majesty will bear the name of fratricide."
The Emperor did not listen.
Cháng reached Yōng,
and died of illness.
Xióng Míng, not lost, departed far away.
The *Wèi Lüè* says:
Whenever Liú Xióngmíng went out traveling,
he could recognize the path in fog without getting lost.
People of the time therefore said he "could command clouds and fog."
Then there were those who traveled together and drank wine.
The *Records of Diverse Matters* says:
Wáng Ěr, Zhāng Héng, and Mǎ Jūn
once all ventured forth in fog.
One was unharmed,
one fell ill,
and one died.
The unharmed one had drunk wine,
the ill one had eaten,
and the dead one had an empty stomach.
Meeting an immortal guest riding a turtle.
Wáng Liè's *Ānchéng Jì* says:
A man of the county, Xiè Lǐn, was traveling on the road
when he suddenly encountered clouds and fog.
In the fog, there was a person
riding on a turtle.
Lǐn knew it was a divine being,
bowed, and begged to follow him.
The person said:
"You lack the bones of an immortal."
Sighing at the five marquises being enfeoffed.
The *Book of Hàn* says:
The five marquises of the Wáng family
were all enfeoffed on the same day.
On that day, yellow fog filled the four directions.
It recalled the encirclement of Hàn Gāozǔ.
The *Hànshū* states:
When Gāozǔ reached Píngchéng,
he was besieged by the Xiōngnú for seven days.
The sky was filled with great fog,
and the Hàn men came and went,
yet the Hú did not notice.
Later, he escaped the calamity at Píngchéng.
It is likened to a good person.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
Traveling with a good person
is like walking in fog.
Although you are not drenched,
you are subtly moistened.
Placed with a patterned rhinoceros horn.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
The horn of the Tōngtiān rhinoceros
has white lines like threads
running from base to tip.
On nights of heavy fog and dew,
if placed in the central courtyard,
it will never become damp.
In Yídū, ethereal mist drifts.
The *Yídū Shānchuān Jì* states:
On Dān Mountain, when the sky is clear,
fog suddenly rises,
swirling like smoke.
Within two days,
rain is sure to fall.
In Qūjiāng, accumulated white mist hangs faintly.
The *Xiāngzhōu Jì* states:
On Yín Mountain in Qūjiāng County,
white mist often arises.
Some used it to confound Chīyóu's arts.
The *Zhìlín* states:
Huángdì battled Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù.
Chīyóu created a great fog
that lasted three days,
confusing all the soldiers.
Huángdì then ordered Fēnghòu to model the Dipper's mechanism to create a south-pointing chariot,
to distinguish the four directions,
and thus captured Chīyóu.
Some used it to transmit Xuánnǚ's strategies.
The *Huángdì Xuánnǚ Zhànfǎ* states:
Huángdì fought Chīyóu nine times and did not prevail.
Huángdì returned to Tài Mountain,
where for three days and nights fog darkened the sky.
There was a woman,
with a human head and bird form.
Huángdì bowed his head and prostrated twice,
lying prone, not daring to rise.
The woman said:
"I am Xuánnǚ.
What do you wish to ask?"
Huángdì said:
"This humble one wishes to win every battle."
He then obtained the art of warfare.
Recognizing the omen of Xià Jié's impending downfall,
the *Shū Zhōnghòu* states:
When Jié was without virtue,
the earth spewed yellow fog.
Recalling the time when Yī Yǐn had just died.
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
Yī Yǐn died at over a hundred years of age.
For three days, fog filled the sky.
Wò Dīng buried him with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
sacrificed with the Tàiláo offering,
and personally attended the mourning for three years,
to repay his great virtue.
King Wén met Jiāng Gōng and shared his carriage.
The *Zhōnglùn* states:
King Wén encountered Jiāng Gōng on the north bank of the Wèi River,
holding a fishing rod.
When King Wén obtained him,
it was as dazzling as parting clouds to see the bright sun;
as clear as dispersing fog to behold the blue sky.
Wèi Guàn saw Yuè Guǎng and praised him as extraordinary.
The *Jìnshū* states:
Wèi Guàn praised Yuè Guǎng, saying:
"Whenever I see Guǎng,
it is brilliantly clear, like parting clouds and mist to behold the blue sky."
There was also the white trees of Jìngníng.
Fú Hòu's *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
In the first year of the Jìngníng era of Hàn Yuándì,
there was great fog,
and all the trees turned white.
Déyáng Palace obscured the sun.
The *Sòngshū* states:
In the Later Hàn, on the first morning of the first month,
the Son of Heaven attended Déyáng Hall to receive congratulations.
A *shèlì* came from the south,
performing in front of the hall.
It stirred water, transforming it into flatfish,
which leaped and spurted water,
creating clouds that obscured the sun.
The immortal guest of Huáinán.
The *Shénxiān Zhuàn* states:
The King of Huáinán, hearing of men with Daoist arts,
would use humble words and rich gifts to summon them.
Thus, the Eight Lords went to him.
One could sit and summon wind and rain,
or stand and raise clouds and mist.
The marvelous art of Dōnghǎi.
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
Huáng Gōng of Dōnghǎi
could stand and summon clouds and mist,
or sit and create mountains and rivers.
Fierce beasts spewed mist as they came and went.
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shízhōu Jì* states:
During the Tiānhàn era of Hàn Wǔdì,
the Western Hú state presented a fierce beast.
The envoy said:
"This fierce beast is born in Kūnlún,
or born in Xuánpǔ.
It can stand and raise wind and clouds,
spew and spurt fog and dew.
All evils flee from it,
hence it is named 'Fierce Beast'."
Dèng Gōng breathed and dispelled illness.
The *Sūzǐ* states:
Dèng Gōng of Shǔ Commandery
could breathe and create fog.
This is the pervasive encroachment of light fog,
which is the overflowing of rising water vapor.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
Rising water vapor overflows, thus forming fog.
Dew
Dew is
the qi of yin and yang.
The Da Dai Li states:
Dew
is the qi of yin and yang.
When yin qi is abundant, it congeals into frost and snow;
when yang qi is abundant, it disperses as rain and dew.
It is the essence of divine spirits.
The Ruì Yìng Tú states:
Sweet dew
is beautiful dew.
It is the essence of divine spirits,
the benevolent auspice's moisture.
Its congealed form is like fat,
its sweetness like malt sugar.
One name is "grease dew,"
another is "heavenly wine."
It embodies the accumulated purity of Xuānyuán.
The Lǐ Dǒu Wēi Yí states:
When the ruler governs well,
then the essence of Xuānyuán disperses as sweet dew.
It contains the pure essence of Tiānrǔ.
The Liè Xīng Tú states:
The star Tiānrǔ is north of Dǐ,
presiding over sweet dew.
Divination:
When it is bright and moist, then sweet dew descends.
It was received by the immortal palms of the Hàn palaces.
The Hàn Wǔ Gùshì states:
Emperor Wǔ had bronze dew-receiving plates made,
on top were immortal hands holding up jade plates,
to receive dew from beyond the clouds.
Beside them grew nine-stemmed zhī grass,
its stems like golden leaves with red fruit,
glowing at night.
The Emperor praised it.
It was lifted by the golden stems of the Wèi chambers.
The Wèi Zhì states:
Emperor Míng cast dew-receiving plates,
the stems were twelve zhàng long,
bronze dragons coiled around their bases,
erected in the Fānglín Garden,
and sweet dew then descended.
Sometimes it moved even the most filial in Zhàojùn.
The Suí Shū states:
Lǐ Déráo,
a man of Bǎixiāng, Zhàojùn.
He was extremely filial by nature.
Mourning his father's passing,
he wore coarse hempen mourning clothes and went barefoot.
Sweet dew descended on his trees,
white doves nested on his hut.
Sometimes it signaled good governance in Línglíng.
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū states:
Shěn Fēng served as governor of Línglíng.
Within a year of taking office,
sweet dew descended,
greasily moistening the plants and trees.
As for its color rivaling deep red cinnabar,
the Shí Yí Jì states:
On Kūnlún Mountain there is sweet dew.
Looking at it,
its color is like cinnabar,
but when it adheres to wood or stone it appears bright as frost and snow.
Its taste matches spoonfuls of honey.
The Lùn Héng states:
Sweet dew tastes like honey,
an omen of the king's peaceful reign.
Since it is called heavenly wine,
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shén Yì Jīng states:
Beyond the northwest seas,
there is a person two thousand lǐ tall,
the distance between his two feet is one thousand lǐ,
he only drinks five dǒu of heavenly wine daily.
Zhāng Huá said:
"Heavenly wine
is sweet dew."
It is also called yīn liquid.
Cài Yōng's Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù states:
Dew
is yīn liquid.
Dispersing, it becomes dew;
congealing, it becomes frost.
It is gathered from the fāngzhū.
The Huái Nán Zǐ states:
The fāngzhū gathers dew from the moon.
Drinking is heard of on Gūyè.
The Zhuāng Zǐ states:
On Mount Gūyè there are spirit people,
who do not eat the five grains,
but inhale the wind and drink the dew.
It receives the morning fall on magnolia.
The Chǔ Cí states:
At dawn I drink the falling dew on the magnolia,
at dusk I dine on the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums.
It scoops up the five colors of auspicious clouds.
The Dòng Míng Jì states:
Dōngfāng Shuò traveled to the land of auspicious clouds.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn asked him about it.
He said:
"Their custom is to always use cloud-qi to divine matters of fortune, misfortune, suffering, and joy.
For good fortune, clouds fill the room and rise,
five-colored light shines,
settling on plants and trees, all becoming five-colored dew.
The dew tastes sweet."
The Emperor said:
"Can it be obtained?"
Shuò then went east,
returning by evening,
having obtained dark, yellow, and blue dew,
which he placed in a glass vessel and presented to the Emperor.
The Emperor bestowed it upon all his ministers.
Those who tasted the dew,
the old all became young,
the sick all recovered.
Heavy, heavy the dew,
not without sun does it dry,
from the Shī.
How could it adorn the crown?
The Shù Xī Jí states:
Thin ice congealing on a pond
is not a treasure for the ancestral temple;
scattered dew hanging on the forest
is not an ornament for the crown.
Yet it can still be drunk by a turtle.
The Dòng Míng Jì states:
In the second year of Yuánfēng,
the state of Shùguò presented a turtle that could speak.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"Only receive it with osmanthus dew to drink."
Treading with caution and reverence, one encounters ritual.
The Lǐ states:
When spring rain and dew have moistened,
the gentleman treads upon it,
necessarily feeling a heart of caution and reverence.
Walking through drenching dew, one hears the poem.
The Shī states:
Drenching is the dew on the path,
How could I not wish to go before dawn or night?
