But I say the path has much dew.
Note:
The path's dew is abundant,
therefore one does not travel,
metaphorically, ritual is insufficient,
therefore the woman is unwilling to go.
There is also that which congeals like fat,
that which is sweet like malt sugar.
The Jìn Zhōng Xīng Shū states:
When the king
respectfully nurtures the elderly,
then sweet dew descends upon the pines and cypresses;
when he honors the worthy and accommodates the multitude,
then the bamboo and reeds receive it.
Sweet dew
is benevolent moisture.
Its congealed form is like fat,
its beauty is like malt sugar.
It bestows long life on Yáoshān.
The Shān Hǎi Jīng states:
In the wilderness of all fertile lands,
the people of Yáoshān
drink this sweet dew,
and those who are not long-lived live eight hundred years.
It sprinkles sweet liquid on Sānwēi.
The Lǚ Shì Chūn Qiū states:
Yī Yǐn advised Tāng, saying:
"Among the beauties of water,
there is the dew of Sānwēi."
Note:
Sānwēi
is the westernmost state.
As for being collected in a bag,
the Shù Zhēng Jì states:
On the first day of the eighth month, make a five-brightness bag,
gather the dew from the heads of a hundred herbs to wash the eyes,
and the eyes will become clear.
It is taken from beyond the clouds.
The Hàn Wǔ Gùshì states:
The Emperor made golden stems,
holding up jade cups,
to receive dew from beyond the clouds.
Already vast and broad, it increases the sea.
Zhāng Héng's Zòu Shì states:
Flying dust increases mountains,
mist and dew increase the sea.
It also moistens and wets, thereby nourishing grass.
The Chūn Qiū Yuán Mìng Bāo states:
Frost kills trees,
dew moistens grass.
As for covering the reed's deep green,
the Shī states:
The reeds are deep green,
white dew becomes frost.
It falls on the creeping grass, lush and thick.
The Shī states:
In the wilds there is creeping grass,
falling dew lush and thick.
As an auspice, it is heard to be like snow.
The Sòng Shū states:
During Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā era,
Sweet dew frequently descends,
appearing like fine snow.
Due to the cold, it is often seen turning into frost.
The *Shī Hán Shén Wù* states:
When the yang qi ends,
white dew becomes frost.
As for storing it in precious vessels,
the *Shí Yí Jì* states:
The sweet dew of Kūnlún
tastes like maltose.
When the ruler possesses sage virtue, it descends.
To receive it in jade cups,
Cáo Zhí’s *Wèi Dé Lùn* states:
Profound virtue penetrates the obscure,
transforming and ascending like steam.
Sweet dew descends,
thick as honey, congealed as ice.
Seeing the sun, it does not dry;
jade cups are used to receive it.
Offered at the imperial court,
to manifest the auspicious sign of sageliness.
Distant journeys first marvel at the soaring serpent,
the *Shuō Yuàn* states:
The soaring serpent travels through mist and dew,
for a thousand li without stopping.
Nighttime vigilance is still heard from the white crane.
Zhōu Chù’s *Fēngtǔ Jì* states:
The white crane is naturally vigilant;
when dew descends in the eighth month,
flowing on grass and leaves,
it drips with sound, and then it cries out.
Zǐxū foresaw it dampening his clothes,
the *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
Zǐxū admonished the King of Wú,
and the king grew angry.
Zǐxū returned at dusk,
lifting his clothes as he left the palace,
saying:
“Grass and thorns grow in the palace,
mist and dew dampen my clothes.”
Shàorú borrowed the pretext of catching sparrows.
Liú Xiàng’s *Shuō Yuàn* states:
Wú intended to attack Jīng,
and the king decreed:
“Whoever dares to remonstrate shall die.”
Among the retainers was a youth named Shàorú who wished to remonstrate.
Carrying a slingshot in the rear garden,
dew dampened his clothes,
and this continued for three mornings.
The king said:
“Why do you endure such hardship?
Dew dampens your clothes like this.”
He replied:
“In the garden, there is a tree,
on its tip sits a cicada,
the cicada perches high, singing mournfully,
sucking wind and drinking dew,
unaware of the mantis behind it,
bending its legs to seize it;
and the mantis, in turn, is unaware of the yellow sparrow behind it,
stretching its neck to peck at it.
Yet the yellow sparrow is unaware of me holding a slingshot beneath it.
I only aim to catch the yellow sparrow,
unaware that dew has dampened my clothes.
In such a situation,
one covets the immediate gain,
without considering the future calamity.”
The king heard this,
and thus did not attack Jīng.
There is also that which settles on water, pure and white,
as seen above in the note on “color bright as frost.”
Descending to the earth, it displays patterns.
Jiāng Yān’s *Bié Fù* states:
The sun rises in the sky, shining brilliantly,
dew descends to the earth, displaying patterns.
It transmits exquisite flavor from the immortal hills,
the *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
Sweet dew descends on the immortal hills,
and immortals often drink it.
Recognizing the flow of qi at Kūnlún,
Xú Zhěng’s *Cháng Lì* states:
The Big Dipper aligns with the qi flow above Kūnlún.
Note:
In the world, spring and summer bring dew,
autumn and winter bring frost.
As for the Bìlè containing cinnabar,
the *Dòng Míng Jì* states:
The people of Bìlè country,
three cùn tall,
with wings,
skilled in speech and jesting,
are thus named “Yǔguó” (Land of Speech).
They drink cinnabar dew as syrup.
Cinnabar dew refers to
when the sun first rises,
there is dew juice like pearls.
Jiēyú spreads purple,
the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
Among the finest harmonies,
is the dew of Jiēyú.
The dew of Jiēyú,
its color is purple.
It congeals when yang qi ends,
the *Shī Hán Shén Wù* states:
When yang qi ends,
white dew congeals into frost.
It descends in response to the beginning of autumn,
the *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* states:
At the beginning of autumn,
white dew descends.
Singing the “Xiè Lù” song to express sorrow,
the *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
“Xiè Lù” (Dew on the Garlic),
is a funeral song.
Its first stanza says:
“Dew on the garlic,
how easily it dries.
Tomorrow it falls again,
but when will the dead return?”
Feasting the feudal lords with propriety.
The *Shī* states:
“Zhàn Lù” (Heavy Dew),
is when the Son of Heaven feasts the feudal lords.
“Heavy is the dew,
not drying without the sun.”
Praising the abundant falling dew,
containing moisture widely spread.
The *Shī* states:
In the wilds, there are creeping grasses,
the falling dew is abundant.
Frost
The reeds are lush and green,
the white dew turns to frost.
From the Book of Songs.
When things contract,
the Book of Songs says:
In the ninth month, frost descends.
Commentary:
Sù (肃) means
to shrink.
Frost descends and causes all things to contract.
Its meaning relates to death and loss.
The Shìmíng says:
Shuāng (霜, frost)
means sàng (丧, loss).
Its qi is harsh and poisonous,
and all things perish.
The Kǎoyìyóu says:
Shuāng (霜) speaks of wáng (亡, perishing),
the end of things.
The courtyard trees shed their leaves,
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Autumn Stirrings" says:
The courtyard trees shed their leaves and scatter them.
The mulberry leaves turn dark yellow.
The "Ancient Song of Beauty" says:
When autumn frost and white dew descend,
the mulberry leaves turn dark yellow.
It is not fitting for trees to be armored,
the Tángshū says:
When Nìngwáng Xiàn was ill,
it was extremely cold,
and congealed frost encased the trees.
Some believed this was the "spring and autumn rain freezing on trees" mentioned in the classics,
also called "tree armor,"
meaning it resembled armor.
Xiàn sighed and said:
"This is what commoners call 'tree marriage.'
A proverb says, 'When trees marry, high officials fear.'
Am I about to die?"
Xiàn indeed passed away.
Do not be a penned sheep.
The Hòuhànshū says:
After Emperor Guāngwǔ passed away,
Guǎnglíngwáng Jīng sent an anonymous letter to Dōnghǎiwáng Qiáng inciting rebellion, saying:
"Be the autumn frost,
do not be a penned sheep."
Commentary:
Autumn frost
sternly destroys things.
A penned sheep
is controlled by others.
It stirs the sorrow of sensing the season,
the Lǐjì says:
When frost and dew have descended,
a gentleman treading upon them
must feel a sorrowful heart,
not because of the cold itself.
Commentary:
He is moved by thoughts of his parents and the season.
It increases the grief of Zhēngyuè.
The Book of Songs says:
In Zhēngyuè, the frost is thick,
my heart is grieved and wounded.
Commentary:
Zhēngyuè
refers to the fourth month of summer,
the month of true yang.
As for its purity congealing on branches,
Hé Jǐn's "Rhapsody Lamenting an Autumn Night" says:
Frost congeals on the branches, glittering,
dew moistens the leaves, clear and cold.
It scatters and kills the trees,
the Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo says:
Frost serves to kill trees,
dew serves to moisten grass.
Gleaming white,
the Shuōwén says:
Ái (皑)
describes the whiteness of frost and snow.
Severe and harshly poisonous.
Harshly poisonous
has already been seen in the commentary for "its meaning relates to death and loss."
Bóqí, expelled, took up his qin,
the Qíncāo says:
Yǐn Jìfǔ, listening to his later wife's words,
suspected his filial son Bóqí,
and thus expelled him.
Bóqí, at dawn, trod upon frost,
grieving his own innocence,
then took up his qin and played it,
composing the "Treading Frost Melody."
Zōu Yǎn, slandered, wailed bitterly.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Zōu Yǎn served King Huì of Yān with utmost loyalty,
those around him slandered him,
the king imprisoned him,
and he cried out to heaven.
In the fifth month of summer,
heaven sent down frost for him.
Having heard it rises from the earth,
the Wǔjīng Tōngyì says:
Cold qi congeals to form frost,
rising from the earth.
We also know dew congeals.
Cài Yōng's "Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" says:
Dew congeals to form frost.
When the Fáng star appears, fur garments are prepared,
the Guóyǔ says:
When Sì appears, frost falls,
when frost falls, winter furs are prepared.
Commentary:
Sì
is the Fáng star.
The hundred craftsmen rest and glue and lacquer work ceases.
The Lǐjì says:
When frost first descends, the hundred craftsmen rest.
Commentary:
The making of glue and lacquer ceases.
As for the sweet flavor of Qiǎnzhōu,
see the commentary for "the Western Mother presented the flavor of Qiǎnzhōu" in the "Rhapsody on Snow."
Guǎngyán's frost is bluish-green,
the Shíyíjì says:
In the land of Guǎngyán, there is frost,
of a dark bluish-green color.
Wild geese beat their wings and fly south,
the Wǔjīng Gōushěn says:
When heaven sends frost,
trees shed their leaves,
and wild geese fly south.
Hawks and falcons, following the season, begin to strike.
the Gǎnjīngfú says:
Frost
is an emblem of killing and punishment.
In late autumn,
when frost first descends,
hawks and falcons strike.
The ruler, complying with heaven, carries out executions,
to complete the stern power of killing.
Thereupon, winter ordinances are implemented,
the Kǎoyìyóu says:
Frost
is the essence of yin, the ordinance of winter.
The four seasons alternate,
using frost for contraction and storage.
Women's work is completed,
the Jiāyǔ says:
When frost descends, women's work is completed,
and marriages and weddings take place.
It covers the cold silkworms of Yuánqiáo,
the Shíyíjì says:
Yuánqiáo
is a mountain name.
Huánqiū has ice silkworms,
covered with frost and snow,
after which they spin their cocoons.
Their colors are variegated,
woven into patterned brocade,
which does not get soaked in water;
thrown into fire, it does not burn.
In the time of Táng Yáo,
people from the sea presented it to be made into ceremonial robes.
It shakes the great bell of Fēngshān.
the Shānhǎijīng says:
Fēngshān has nine bells,
which sound when frost descends.
We also hear of partridges hiding under leaves,
the Gǔjīn Zhù says:
Partridges often fly towards the sun,
fearing frost and dew,
at night they roost in trees,
with leaves covering their backs.
Kūnlún moves the qi,
see the commentary for "recognizing the movement of qi at Kūnlún" in the "Rhapsody on Dew."
Knowing what the horse's hoof treads upon,
the Zhuāngzǐ says:
A horse's hoof can tread upon frost and snow,
its hair can ward off wind and cold.
Thinking of the hempen sandals once worn.
The Book of Songs says:
Intricately woven hempen sandals,
can be worn to tread frost.
When yin qi first congeals,
the Dàdài Lǐjì says:
When yin qi prevails,
it congeals and becomes frost.
It gradually leads to solid ice.
the Yìjīng says:
Treading on frost, solid ice
means yin begins to congeal.
Gradually proceeding along this path
leads to solid ice.
Sometimes, responding to the season, it damages things,
the Yuánshénqì says:
Frost serves to damage things.
Sometimes, in spring, it causes great injury.
The Lǐjì says:
If in the first month of spring winter ordinances are implemented,
then frost and snow cause great injury.
Commentary:
Zhì (挚)
means injury.
If its spirit is the Qīngnǚ,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
When the three autumn months arrive,
the Qīngnǚ emerges,
descending with snow and frost.
The commentary states:
Qīngnǚ,
a heavenly deity.
The Jade Maiden of the Azure Sky,
presides over snow and frost.
Wēi Lì Hóu Wén,
the Hànshū says:
Sǔn Bǎo served as the Governor of the Capital,
on the day of the Beginning of Autumn,
he appointed Hóu Wén as the Eastern District Inspector to enter for an audience.
He commanded:
"Today, hawks and falcons begin to strike;
we should follow the heavenly qi,
capture the treacherous and wicked,
to carry out the execution of severe frost."
Thus, if it does not kill,
it indicates the failure of governance;
the Kǎoyì Jì says:
When Duke Xī of Lǔ ascended the throne,
frost fell but did not kill the grass,
signifying the ministers' excessive power.
If frost falls in summer,
it reveals a tyrannical ruler.
The Mìnglì Xù says:
When Jié was without virtue,
frost fell in summer.
Therefore,
if the Way and righteousness are upheld,
then the seasonal orders are harmonious,
what more need be said?
Snow
The significance of snow is profound indeed!
It is the coagulation of yin energy,
as stated in the Yuánmìng Bāo:
"Yin energy coagulates to form snow."
It is the essence of the five grains.
As Fàn Shèngzhī's Book states:
"Take snow water and soak silkworm excrement for five or six days,
wait until it dissolves,
knead it by hand,
mix it with grain seeds,
and it can ward off drought,
hence it is said, 'Snow is the essence of the five grains.'"
First, the shadow of uniform clouds spreads;
the Shījīng says:
"The heavens are covered with uniform clouds,
and snow falls thickly."
Soon, six-petaled snowflakes drift down.
As the Hán Shī Wàizhuàn states:
"Among all plants and trees,
most flowers have five petals,
but snowflakes alone have six."
Snowflakes are called yīng,
pronounced yīng.
Xiè Nǚ's comparison to willow catkins rising in the wind:
The Jìnshū records:
Grand Tutor Xiè Ān,
upon seeing a sudden snowfall,
joyfully asked:
"What does the swirling white snow resemble?"
His nephew Hú'ér said:
"It roughly resembles salt scattered in the air."
His niece Dàoyùn said:
"It is not as good as willow catkins rising in the wind."
The courtier's robe adorned with bright flowers:
The Sòngshū records:
During the Dàmíng era,
on New Year's Day,
snowflakes fell in the palace courtyard.
General of the Right Xiè Zhuāng descended the steps,
and snow gathered on his robe, turning it white.
The emperor considered this an auspicious sign,
and all the courtiers composed poems about snowflakes.
As for the Snow Garden created by King Liáng,
Xiè Huìlián's "Snow Rhapsody" states:
King Liáng was displeased,
so he wandered in the Tù Garden.
Suddenly, fine sleet began to fall,
followed by heavy snow.
The king then sang of the north wind from the Wèi poems,
and chanted of the southern mountains from the Zhōu odes.
He handed a writing tablet to Minister Simǎ,
saying:
"Draw upon your secret thoughts,
unleash your fine words,
match the colors and weigh the descriptions,
and compose a rhapsody for me."
The Snow Palace built in the state of Qí:
The Mèngzǐ states:
King Xuān of Qí met Mencius at the Snow Palace.
The king asked:
"Do the virtuous also have such pleasures?"
Mencius replied:
"For a ruler not to share joy with the people
is wrong."
Timely without necessarily sealing the branches:
The Xījīng Zá Jì records:
Dǒng Zhòngshū said:
"In an age of great peace,
snow does not seal the branches,
merely serving to dispel poison and harm."
As an auspicious sign, it is often heard to accumulate a foot deep:
Xiè Huìlián's "Snow Rhapsody" states:
A foot deep brings auspicious signs for a bountiful year,
while a zhang deep indicates calamity from excessive yin virtue.
Jiǎo Āi, impoverished on the road, sharing his clothes:
See the annotation in "Qín Fù" for "pity the poor scholar who went to Chǔ."
Dōngguō, with worn-out shoes, leaving footprints:
The Shǐjì records:
Dōngguō Xiānshēng long awaited an audience at the public carriage station,
impoverished, hungry, and cold.
His shoes had tops but no soles,
so when he walked in the snow,
his feet fully touched the ground.
People on the road laughed at him.
King Wǔ's five chariots and two horsemen:
The Jīn Kuì records:
When King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
he established his capital at Luòyì.
It snowed for over ten days,
accumulating more than a zhang deep.
At dawn on the jiǎzǐ day,
five men arrived in five chariots,
accompanied by two horsemen,
and stopped outside the gate.
The king sent Shàngfǔ to greet the five men,
saying:
"You honor us with your presence,
but we failed to inquire beforehand.
We are now preparing ceremonial robes."
Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ had someone bring out a bowl of porridge,
presented it, and said:
"The former king's ministers are inside,
currently facing the king.
You are cold,
so we offer hot porridge."
Shàngfǔ then informed King Wǔ:
"The guests may be received.
The five chariots and two horsemen
are the gods of the four seas,
along with the Hé Bó and the Rain Master."
The King of Chǔ's kingfisher-feather cloak and leopard-skin shoes:
The Zuǒzhuàn records:
The King of Chǔ encamped at Gānxī.
It was snowing,
and the king wore a leather cap,
a Qín fútáo garment,
a kingfisher-feather cloak,
leopard-skin shoes,
and came out holding a whip.
Annotation:
Qín fútáo
refers to a feather garment bestowed by Qín.
Jiāo Xiān, sleeping exposed, remaining composed:
The Gāoshì Zhuàn records:
Jiāo Xiān,
whose origins were unknown to the world.
When a wildfire burned his hut,
he slept in the open.
When heavy winter snow arrived,
he lay naked without moving.
People thought he was dead,
but upon closer inspection, he was as before.
Yuán Ān, lying loftily indoors without going out:
The Lù Yì Zhuàn records:
Snow piled over a zhang deep.
The magistrate of Luòyáng went out to inspect,
and saw that the commoners' households had all cleared the snow.
Arriving at Yuán Ān's gate,
there were no paths cleared.
Thinking Yuán Ān had died,
he ordered people to clear the snow and enter the house,
where they found Yuán Ān lying stiffly.
When asked why he had not gone out,
Yuán Ān replied:
"With heavy snow,
everyone is hungry.
It is not right to trouble others."
As for Wáng Gōng's crane-feather cloak:
The Jìnshū records:
Wáng Gōng wore a crane-feather cloak
and walked around at night in the snow.
People of the time called him "a man among immortals."
The hemp garments of the state of Cáo:
The Shījīng says:
"Mayflies emerge from their burrows,
their hemp garments white as snow."
Annotation:
Hemp garments
refer to deep robes.
Its beauty is seen in Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's rhapsody:
See the annotation for "Snow Garden created by King Liáng."
Its whiteness resembles the skin of the Gūyè maiden:
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
On the distant Gūyè Mountain,
there dwells a divine being.
Her skin is like ice and snow,
and she is as graceful as a maiden.
The song "Yángchūn" by the Chǔ guest:
See the annotation for "Chǔ's Yángchūn" in "Gē Fù."
King Wén of Zhōu's chant of "coming home":
The Shījīng says:
King Wén sang "Cǎiwēi" to send off the troops.
"When I left here,
willows shed tear.
Now I come back,
snow bends the bough."
Zēngzǐ's melody of Liángshān:
The Qín Cāo records:
Zēngzǐ was plowing at the foot of Tàishān.
He could not return due to the snow.
Longing for his parents,
he composed the "Liángshān Melody."
King Mù's verses of Huángzhú:
The Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn records:
While hunting at Xíngshān,
amid north wind and snow,
there were people frozen to death.
The Son of Heaven composed three stanzas of the "Huángzhú" poem to mourn the people.
Visiting Dài Kuí on a sudden whim:
The Yǔ Lín records:
Wáng Zǐyóu lived in Shānyīn.
During heavy snow,
he opened his room at night and called for wine.
Looking around at the bright whiteness,
he chanted the "Summoning the Recluse" poem.
Suddenly, he remembered Dài Āndào.
Dài Āndào was then in Shàn,
so he took a boat on a whim.
After traveling all night, he arrived,
but turned back upon reaching the door.
Someone asked him about it,
and he replied:
"I came on a whim,
and now that my whim is spent, I return.
Why must I see Dài!"
They postponed the burial of Lord Téng Wén.
The Mèngzǐ says:
When Lord Téng Wén passed away,
a date had been set for his burial.
Heaven sent down heavy snow,
piling up to the height of a cow's eyes.
The ministers requested a postponement,
but the crown prince would not allow it.
Master Huì remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, when King Jì was buried at the foot of Wōshān,
the Luò River's waters eroded his tomb,
exposing the front of his coffin.
King Wén said:
'Our former lord wishes to see his ministers and the people once more.'
So they brought the coffin out and set up a canopy,
and only after three days was he buried.
Now, the crown prince should say, 'Our former lord wishes to remain a little longer to watch over the altars of state,
and therefore has caused this heavy snow.'
Postpone the date and choose another day.
This is the righteousness of King Wén."
The crown prince said:
"Well said."
They marveled at Yúnnán's snow in the fifth month.
The Guǎngzhì says:
In Yúnnán Commandery,
even in the fourth and fifth months, snow still lies pure and white.
At Yīnshān in Dài Commandery,
lingering snow remains in the fifth month,
and snow falls again by the end of the eighth month.
They found it strange that Kōngsāng had snow in all seasons.
The Shānhǎijīng says:
The mountains of Yóushǒu, Bǔchéng, and Kōngsāng
all have snow in both winter and summer.
As for its dark, overcast gloom,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on a Beauty" says:
The time was already the western evening,
dark and overcast, gloomy and dim.
A cool wind blew austerely,
and pure snow drifted down.
The northern wind was fierce.
Wáng Shàozhī's "Separating-and-Joining Poem on Snow" says:
First sleet gathers, then snow falls,
scattering radiant white over eaves and courtyards.
Winding chambers grow cold as the north wind rages,
rivers and land freeze as a hundred sounds cry out.
In the sky, it was first recognized as scattered salt,
see the note on "Xiè Nǚ's willow catkins rising in the wind."
At night, it could still illuminate characters for reading.
The Sòng Qí Jì says:
Sūn Kāng's family was poor,
so he often read by the light reflected from snow.
In the land of Guǎngyán, there was blue rain.
The Shíyíjì says:
The state of Guǎngyán is in Fúsāng.
It often rains blue snow there,
and the color of ice and frost is like dark blue-green.
In the land of Héyīn, there was red cloth.
The Jìncháo Záshì says:
In the seventh year of the Tàikāng era,
red snow fell over two qǐng at Héyīn.
King Zhōu was astonished by the singing at Kūnmíng.
The Shíyíjì says:
King Líng of Zhōu built the Kūnmíng Terrace.
He summoned various masters of esoteric arts.
Two of them arrived in a flying chariot
and ascended to the mat, deeply intoxicated.
At that time, there was a severe drought and the earth cracked.
One of them could summon frost and snow with his singing.
So he drew in his breath with one inhalation,
and clouds arose and snow flew.
The Queen Mother of the West presented the flavor of Qiǎnzhōu.
The Shíyíjì says:
King Mù journeyed east to the valley of Dàqí.
The Queen Mother of the West came
and offered sweet snow from Qiǎnzhōu.
Qiǎnzhōu
is three thousand lǐ from Yùmén.
The land is cold and has much snow.
When the dew settles on trees and stones there,
it all melts and is sweet,
and can be made into fruit.
Note:
𣟵 (qí),
pronounced qí.
嵰 (qiǎn),
pronounced qiǎn (according to the fǎnqiè spelling 'qiū yǎn fǎn').
One has also seen Sū Wǔ holding his ceremonial staff.
The Hànshū says:
Sū Wǔ, holding his ceremonial staff, was sent as an envoy to the Xiōngnú.
The Chányú imprisoned Sū Wǔ in a large cellar,
completely cutting off food and drink.
Heaven sent down snow.
Sū Wǔ lay down, gnawed on snow mixed with felt wool, and swallowed it.
After several days, he did not die.
The Xiōngnú therefore considered him divine.
It made clear that the Hàn woman was innocent.
The Hànshū says:
There was a woman of Hàn
who lived in Dōnghǎi and cared for her mother-in-law.
Her sister-in-law slandered her to the mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law went straight to the Grand Administrator to accuse her, and she was killed.
In the fifth month, snow fell.
It made Yànzǐ realize and bestow kindness.
The Yànzǐ Chūnqiū says:
During the time of Duke Jǐng,
it snowed for three days.
The Duke wore a robe of white fox fur.
Yànzǐ entered.
The Duke said:
"How strange!
It has snowed for three days, yet it is not cold."
Yànzǐ said:
"Wise rulers of old,
when full, knew of others' hunger;
when warm, knew of others' cold."
The Duke said:
"Well said."
He then took off his fur robe
and distributed grain to those suffering from hunger and cold.
It moved the one wearing firewood to bestow favor.
The Sūnzǐ says:
Long ago, the Lord of Wèi sat wearing heavy furs and layered mats.
He saw a man on the road carrying firewood and weeping.
He asked what the reason was.
The man replied:
"Snow is falling and my clothes are thin,
therefore I weep."
Then the Lord of Wèi became alarmed,
and it showed on his face.
He said:
"To be a ruler and not know the people's condition—
who would consider me their ruler?"
Thereupon, he opened the treasury's gold
and brought out the granary's grain
to relieve the poor and destitute.
How could it be limited to hunting on Xíngshān to obtain medicine,
see the note on "King Mù Mǎn's 'Yellow Bamboo'."
or to obtaining a jade horse and calling it an auspicious omen, that is all!
See the note in the "Rhapsody on Jade" on "marveling at the accumulated snow's disappearance."
Thunder
That which stirs the myriad things,
nothing is swifter than thunder.
The Book of Changes says:
"That which stirs the myriad things,
nothing is swifter than thunder."
As for its terrifying approach,
the Book of Changes says:
"The shock comes, terrifying."
The rumbling does not cease;
the Book of Songs says:
"Gloomy and dark is the sky,
rumbling is the thunder."
It thrusts forth the myriad things;
the Shuōwén says:
"The lingering sound of thunder and lightning
is what thrusts forth the myriad things."
It startles a hundred lǐ.
The Book of Changes says:
"It startles a hundred lǐ,
yet the ladle and sacrificial wine are not lost."
It clarifies punishments and rectifies laws;
the Book of Changes says:
"Thunder and lightning: Shìkè.
The ancient kings used this to clarify punishments and rectify laws."
It also alarms the distant and frightens the near.
The Book of Changes says:
"It startles a hundred lǐ,
alarming the distant and frightening the near."
As for naming it the celestial drum,
the Hétú Dì Tōng Jì says:
"Thunder
is the drum of Heaven."
It is governed by the Xuān star;
the Héchéng Tú says:
"The Xuānyuán star
is the spirit governing thunder and rain."
It verifies the foreknowledge of the pheasant's crow;
the Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Lùn says:
"In the first month,
thunder slightly stirs and the pheasant crows."
It knows the morning cry of the jade tiger;
the Hétú says:
"The jade tiger cries at dawn,
it is the sound of thunder."
The noble man uses it to create music and exalt virtue;
the Book of Changes says:
"Thunder emerges from the earth, stirring: Yù.
The ancient kings used this to create music and exalt virtue,
earnestly offering it to the Supreme Deity."
He decides lawsuits and administers punishments;
the Book of Changes says:
"Thunder and lightning both arrive: Fēng.
The noble man uses this to decide lawsuits and administer punishments."
He reveres Heaven's anger,
and even at night he must rise.
The Book of Rites says:
"If a noble man encounters a fierce wind, sudden thunder, or heavy rain,
he must change his demeanor.
Even at night he must rise,
put on his clothes and cap, and sit upright."
Note:
"This is revering Heaven's anger."
Then Heaven and Earth are greatly startled;
the Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Yīn and Yáng err in their courses,
Heaven and Earth are greatly startled,
and then there is thunder and lightning."
Yīn and Yáng press against each other;
the Gǔliáng Zhuàn says:
"Yīn and Yáng press against each other,
are moved and become thunder,
are agitated and become peals of thunder."
Sometimes at night someone pushes a cart;
the Sōushén Jì says:
"Yìxīng man Zhōu Yǒnghé went out to the fields,
at dusk,
a woman by the roadside asked to stay overnight.
After the first watch,
someone called Ā Xiāng, saying:
'The official summons you to push the thunder cart.'
The woman then bid farewell to Zhōu,
saying:
'I have official business and must go.'
Shortly after, there was great thunder.
At dawn,
Zhōu found himself in a strange place,
and upon returning to search,
he only saw a new grave,
with hoofprints at the grave's entrance."
Sometimes it first shakes a bell;
see the note on "first thunder shakes the bell" in the "Spring Rhapsody."
As for being within the earth, it is Fù;
the Book of Changes says:
"Thunder is within the earth:
Fù.
The ancient kings, on the solstice day, closed the passes,
merchants did not travel,
and the ruler did not inspect the regions."
In the marsh, it is Suí;
the Book of Changes says:
"There is thunder in the marsh:
Suí.
The noble man, at dusk,
enters to rest."
He is received into the great mountain forest and is not bewildered;
the Book of Documents, "Shùn Diǎn," says:
"He was received into the great mountain forest,
fierce winds, thunder, and rain did not bewilder him."
On the southern mountain, it rumbles;
the Book of Songs says:
"Rumbling is the thunder,
on the sunny side of the southern mountain."
One only hears that covering sauce is taboo;
the Fēngsú Tōng says:
"Do not cover sauce during thunder,
the common saying is it causes thunder in the belly."
How can one cover the ears and know beforehand?
the Wénzǐ says:
"Sudden thunder leaves no time to cover the ears."
Silently it emits sound;
the Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhì says:
"Ten days after spring,
thunder then emits sound."
With a roaring and urgent force;
the Ěryǎ says:
"Sudden thunder is called tíngní."
The note says:
"The urgent and forceful thunder is the霹靂."
Sometimes it is used to sing Liángzǐ's melody;
the Qíncāo says:
"Chǔ's Gāo Liángzǐ traveled to the marsh of Jiǔgāo,
viewed the terrace by the Jiàn River,
set up nets on Jīng Mountain,
and fished by the winding pool.
A fierce wind, falling hail, thunder, and lightning darkened the sky,
a black crane soared before him,
a white tiger roared behind him,
so he took up the qín and composed the 'Pīlì Yǐn.'"
Sometimes it shatters the Gāoméi stone;
the Jìncháo Záshì says:
"In the seventh year of Yuánkāng,
a霹靂 shattered the Gāoméi stone south of the city.
This foretold Jiǎ Hòu's impending execution.
Gāoméi
is the palace shrine for praying for children.
Jiǎ Hòu was jealous,
intending to kill Mǐnhuái,
so Heaven was angry."
Then there is Cài Shùn circling the grave;
the Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn says:
"Cài Shùn's mother
was afraid of thunder in her lifetime.
After her death,
whenever there was thunder,
Shùn would circle the grave and weep,
saying:
'Shùn is here.'"
Fán Chóng rebuilt a chamber;
the Jīngzhōu Jì says:
"Húyáng County's Fán Chóng,
whose mother feared thunder,
built a stone chamber for his mother to avoid it.
He used patterned stone for the steps and foundations,
which still exist today."
In Kuàijī, it once struck a flock of sheep;
the Lùnhéng says:
"In the summer, sixth month of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
thunder struck five sheep in Yín County, Kuàijī.
What hidden fault did the sheep have to be struck by thunder?
Common belief holds that Heaven takes dragons.
Killing people punishes hidden faults,
which differs in auspiciousness and inauspiciousness from taking dragons,
and is not the true way."
In Línhè, one once observed axe marks;
Mèng Ào's Běizhēng Jì says:
"In Línhè there is a stone,
two zhàng square.
The stone has very fresh磨刀斧 marks,
named 'Thunder God's磨石.'"
Since it is the eldest son,
the Hóngfàn Lùn says:
"Thunder is the eldest son of Heaven and Earth."
It is also compared to the ruler;
the Hóngfàn Lùn says:
"Thunder
is an image of the ruler.
Entering, it can eliminate harm;
emerging, it can promote benefit."
Observing the hexagram statements, one often hears of Shìkè;
see the note above on "clarifying punishments and rectifying laws."
Examining the images also reveals governance;
the Book of Changes says:
"Clouds and thunder: Zhūn.
The noble man uses this to govern."
Strike the drum of eight wildernesses, a thousand lǐ wide;
the Shényì Jīng says:
"In the eight wildernesses there is a stone drum,
its diameter a thousand lǐ.
Strike it,
and its sound is thunder."
Heaven uses this to display the majesty of its joy and anger.
As ministers who withstand and repel calamities.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* states:
The *Wǔxīng Zhàn* says:
Why do thunder and lightning kill people?
Thunder,
is Heaven's minister who repels calamities and withstands assaults.
If the ruler upholds and employs proper measures,
then thunder acts to restrain violent people.
If he abuses his power for personal gain, then thunder and lightning kill people.
There are also those who eat flying fish and feel no fear.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
The flying fish resembles a piglet,
with red patterns and no feathers.
Eating it
wards off weapons,
and one does not fear thunder.
Consuming Jiāróng and feeling no dread;
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
On Bànshí Mountain there is a plant,
named "Jiāróng".
Consuming it,
one does not fear thunderclaps.
Avoiding inauspicious trees and not taking shelter under them;
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
Sheltering under an inauspicious tree,
one will be struck by thunder.
Pointing to a stone chamber and speaking of taking refuge.
Mèng Ào's *Běizhēng Jì* says:
One hundred paces from the southern corner of Língyún Terrace,
there is a white stone chamber,
named the "Thunder-Avoiding Chamber."
As for its formation from accumulated wind,
The *Wùlǐ Lùn* says:
Accumulated wind becomes thunder.
Arising from the Golden Gate,
The *Shī Kuàng Zhàn* says:
Thunder follows metal,
if it arises from the Golden Gate in the first ten-day period [of the month],
the fields will yield a good harvest.
It grieved Wáng Póu, who circled the grave;
The *Jìn Shū* says:
Wáng Póu of the Jin Dynasty, his mother feared thunder.
After his mother passed away,
whenever it thundered,
Póu would circle her grave and say:
"Póu is here."
Praising Zhú Mí, who prostrated on the grave mound.
The *Xiàozǐ Zhuàn* says:
Zhú Mí,
styled Dàolún.
His father, when alive, feared thunder.
Whenever the sky grew overcast,
he would hasten to the grave,
prostrate on the mound and weep.
There was a white rabbit by his side.
Tàichū, with his clothes scorched, remained composed;
The *Shì Shuō* says:
Xiàhóu Xuán once leaned against a pillar reading.
Suddenly there was a torrential downpour,
a thunderbolt shattered the pillar he was leaning against,
his clothes were scorched,
but Xuán's expression did not change,
and he continued reading as before.
Zhūgě, leaning against a pillar, remained unaware.
Cáo Jiāzhī's *Jìn Jì* says:
Zhūgě Dàn was renowned for his lofty spirit.
He once leaned against a pillar reading,
a thunderclap shook his pillar,
yet Dàn remained composed.
It is also said its sound emerges from the earth,
The *Yì* says:
Thunder emerges from the earth, stirring joy.
Its form resembles connected drums,
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
In the fourth year of the Jiànshǐ era of Emperor Chéng,
there were no clouds but there was wind,
heavenly thunder sounded like striking connected drums,
the sound lasted for four or five kè,
rumbling like the continuous sound of carts.
It struck Zīqiū of the Eastern Sea,
The *Hánshī Wàizhuàn* says:
On the Eastern Sea there was a brave warrior,
named "Zīqiū Xīn",
who traveled the world with his courage.
Passing by a divine abyss, he let his horse drink,
and the horse sank.
Xīn removed his court robes,
grasped his sword and entered,
for three days and three nights,
killed two flood dragons and emerged.
The thunder god followed and struck him,
for ten days and ten nights,
blinding his left eye.
It moved the common woman of the Qí terrace.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
In Huái Qí, a common woman was widowed,
and cared for her mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law's daughter killed her own mother,
and falsely accused the common woman.
The woman cried out to heaven in her injustice,
and thunder and lightning struck down upon Duke Jǐng's terrace.
As for shattering Téng Fàng's stone pillow,
The *Yì Yuàn* says:
Téng Fàng, in summer, lay down using a patterned stone pillow.
Thunder struck,
his pillow broke into four pieces.
Those nearby were all terrified,
but Fàng alone remained composed.
It struck Wáng Dǎo's cypress tree.
The *Shì Shuō* says:
Guō Pú once divined for Wáng Dǎo,
saying:
"My lord, you have a thunder calamity.
You should order your carriage to go west for several lǐ,
where you will find a cypress tree.
Cut a piece the length of your height,
take it to your sleeping quarters,
and the disaster can be averted."
Within a few days, thunder indeed struck,
and the cypress tree was shattered to pieces.
Having observed its role in resolution,
The *Yì* says:
Thunder and rain bring resolution.
The nobleman uses this to pardon faults and forgive crimes.
It also says:
Heaven and earth resolve, and thunder and rain occur.
Thunder and rain occur, and all fruits, plants, and trees break open their shells.
Again we hear of stirring joy.
See above.
Its essence was already heard of in the time of the Yellow Emperor;
The *Hétú* says:
The Yellow Emperor arose from the essence of thunder.
The influence of its qi was also transmitted to Zǐlù.
The *Lùn Héng* says:
Zǐlù was born influenced by the essence of thunder,
he upheld strength and loved courage,
personally involved himself in the troubles of Wèi,
and died tying his cap strings.
Whenever Confucius heard the rumble of thunder,
his heart felt sorrowful.
Looking up at the might of a single thunderclap,
one should not forget fear and awe.
The *Huáyáng Guózhì* says:
Lord Cáo once sat together with the former lord Liú,
and leisurely said to the former lord:
"Of the heroes under heaven,
only you, my lord, and Cáo are such.
Men like Běnchū are not worth counting."
The former lord was just then eating,
and dropped his spoon and chopsticks.
At that moment, a great thunderclap resounded.
The former lord said:
"The sage said:
'One must show a changed demeanor at sudden thunder and violent wind.'
This is truly meaningful."
The might of a single thunderclap,
could indeed cause this.
Lord Cáo also regretted his slip of the tongue.
Spring
The spring days are long and drawn out,
picking white southernwood in great abundance.
From the *Book of Songs*.
The commentary states:
"Qíqí"
means slow and gentle.
Enjoying the gentle breeze and the beautiful scenery,
cherishing the fragrant season and the auspicious time.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's *Zuǎnyào* says:
The spring breeze is called the gentle breeze,
the scenery is called beautiful,
the season is called the fragrant season,
the time is called the auspicious time.
Gōumáng and Tàihào.
The *Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances* says:
In the first month,
its sovereign is Tàihào,
its spirit is Gōumáng.
The commentary states:
In ancient times, Tàihào succeeded to Heaven by virtue of wood and became king,
therefore he is the spring sovereign.
Emperor Gāoxīn ruled the world,
and established the five officials of the five phases.
The wood official was called Gōumáng,
he was the wood spirit,
assisting Tàihào.
Riding the trigram Zhèn and holding the compass.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
What are the Five Stars?
The east is wood.
Its sovereign is Tàihào.
Tàihào
was the reign title of Fúxī when he ruled the world,
after death he was entrusted to the eastern sovereign.
His assistant Gōumáng
holds the compass and governs spring.
The *Book of Hàn* says:
Wèi Xiàng submitted a memorial stating:
"Tàihào rides the trigram Zhèn,
holds the compass and governs spring."
The herald follows the road, parading with a wooden bell.
The *Book of Documents* says:
Every year in the first month of spring,
the herald parades on the road with a wooden bell.
The commentary states:
The herald
is an official who proclaims orders.
The wooden bell,
a metal bell with a wooden clapper,
is used to promote culture and education.
The Grand Music Master performs his duty and presents songs.
The *Book of Rites* says:
In the second month,
the Grand Music Master is ordered to present songs to observe the customs of the people.
The time when hibernating insects begin to stir.
The *Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances* says:
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
the east wind thaws the ice.
After five days,
hibernating insects begin to stir.
After five days,
fish rise to the ice.
The time when turtle shells are consecrated.
The *Book of Xià* says:
In the first month of spring, consecrate turtle shells,
for divination before sacrifices.
The commentary states:
Consecration
means killing a sacrificial animal and smearing its blood.
Sometimes the Music Master is ordered to practice dances.
The *Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances* says:
On the first day, the Son of Heaven prays for grain to the Supreme Deity,
and orders the Music Master to practice dances.
The commentary states:
In spring and summer, dances are favored,
therefore they are practiced.
Sometimes prison officials are ordered to decide cases.
The *Xiàojīng Gōumìngjué* says:
Seven days before the Beginning of Spring,
prison officials are ordered to decide lawsuits.
Those guilty should be imprisoned,
those innocent should be released.
Thus, the correct is established in the middle,
and the beginning is set at the start.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
The first month is called the beginning month.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
Set the beginning at the start,
establish the correct in the middle.
Gazing at the green banner being displayed.
The *Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances* says:
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
the Son of Heaven welcomes spring in the eastern suburbs,
riding in a green carriage,
carrying a green banner.
Seeing the Dipper's handle pointing east.
The *Hèguānzǐ* says:
When the Dipper's handle points east,
the whole world is in spring.
The Farmer's Star is upright at dawn,
the fertile soil's veins begin to stir.
The *Discourses of the States* says:
When King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne,
he did not perform the thousand-acre plowing ceremony.
Duke Wén of Guó admonished him, saying:
"In ancient times,
the Grand Historian observed the seasons and inspected the soil,
when the yang energy was full and vigorous,
the earth's energy stirred and rose,
the Farmer's Star was upright at dawn,
and the soil's veins began to move.
Nine days before the time,
the Grand Historian informed the Minister of Agriculture, saying:
'From now until the first auspicious day,
the yang energy will all steam forth,
the fertile soil will begin to stir.'" The commentary states:
The Farmer's Star,
is the constellation Fáng.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
it is centered in the south at dawn.
It is a sign for agricultural activities,
therefore it is called the Farmer's Star.
Gazing at the three-pure clouds.
The *Secret Words for Cultivating Truth and Entering the Way* says:
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
looking north in the clear morning, if there are purple, green, and white clouds,
they are the three-primal, three-pure flying clouds.
Drinking the water of the eight winds.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
In the first month of spring,
the Son of Heaven drinks the water of the eight winds.
The commentary states:
It is the dew collected in a bronze dew basin,
blown by the winds from the eight directions.
It also says:
When the winds from the eight directions arrive, the well is dredged,
and fresh spring water is drawn,
which is drunk in all four seasons,
not only in spring.
Having proclaimed the ordinances for the five seasons.
The *Book of Jìn: Treatise on Rites* says:
Each year, the Grand Historian presents the calendar for the coming year,
and on the Beginning of Spring, reads the ordinances for the five seasons,
with clothing colors each matching their direction.
The Emperor sits on his throne,
the officials from the Imperial Secretariat down take their seats,
after the reading is finished,
a cup of wine is bestowed.
Again, the heart is wounded for a thousand miles.
The *Chǔcí* says:
The eye reaches a thousand miles, wounding the spring heart.
The wind has already thawed the ice,
the fish are just rising to the ice.
See the commentary above under "The time when hibernating insects begin to stir."
The hoopoe descends upon the mulberry trees, soaring and gathering.
The *Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances* says:
In the middle period of the third month,
the hoopoe descends upon the mulberry trees,
and the officials are ordered not to cut down mulberry or paper mulberry trees.
The osprey flaps its wings, chirping and calling.
Zhāng Héng's *Rhapsody on Returning to the Fields* says:
"In the second month, the pleasant season,
the weather is harmonious and the air clear.
The plains and lowlands are lush and dense,
a hundred grasses grow and flourish.
The osprey flaps its wings,
the golden oriole sadly calls.
Neck to neck they soar and glide,
calling 'guān guān' and chirping 'yīng yīng'.
Here I wander free,
to amuse my feelings for a while."
As for the song of bathing in the Yí from the school of Confucius,
the *Analects* says:
Zēng Diǎn said:
"In late spring,
when the spring clothes are ready,
with five or six adults,
and six or seven youths,
to bathe in the Yí River,
enjoy the breeze at the Wǔyú altar,
and return home singing."
The joy of Lǎozǐ ascending the terrace.
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
The multitude are merry and bustling,
as if enjoying a grand sacrifice,
as if ascending a spring terrace.
Knowing that the abundant virtue resides in wood.
The *Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances* says:
Three days before the Beginning of Spring, the Grand Historian
reports to the Son of Heaven:
"On such-and-such a day is the Beginning of Spring,
the abundant virtue resides in wood."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the dukes, ministers, feudal lords, and high officials,
to welcome spring in the eastern suburbs.
Seeing the orderly arrangement of the eastern labors.
The *Book of Documents* says:
Separately ordering Yì Zhòng
to reside at Yúyí,
It is called Yánggǔ,
the orderly commencement of work in the east,
at midday the star Bird is visible,
marking the middle of spring.
Rain moistens the elm seeds,
as stated in the Fàn Shèngzhī Shū:
In the third month,
when the elm seed rain falls,
sorghum can be planted on high, firm soil.
Clouds fly like white swans,
as noted in the Yì Shuō:
In spring, white swan clouds appear.
Once sturgeon are offered and boats are taken,
the Lǐ records:
In the third month’s season,
the Son of Heaven begins to ride in boats,
and offers sturgeon in the ancestral temple.
Also, before thunder sounds, bells are rung.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
In the middle month of spring,
three days before thunder is heard,
bells are rung to announce to the people:
"Thunder is about to sound;
those who do not restrain their conduct,
will bear children with defects,
and surely meet with misfortune."
Not restraining conduct
refers to engaging in marital relations during thunder,
which will cause children to be born mute, lame, foolish, or mad.
As for wearing dark green jade discs,
the Shàngshū Kǎo Língyào says:
In spring, wear dark green jade discs,
and ride dark green horses when going out.
Setting up earthen oxen,
the Xù Hànshū records:
On the day of Lìchūn,
before the fifth mark of the night water-clock,
all officials in the capital wear blue garments,
erect spring banners,
and place earthen oxen and ploughmen outside the gates.
They sacrifice to the household deity,
as the Lǐ states:
In the first month’s season,
they sacrifice to the household deity.
Note:
In spring,
yang energy emerges.
Sacrificing to the household deity follows the yang energy.
Their weapon is the spear.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
In spring,
the weapon is the spear,
sharp and pointed,
resembling the myriad things piercing the earth to grow.
As for the initial bestowal of colored trees,
the Jǐnglóng Wénguǎn Jì records:
In the fourth year of Jǐnglóng, on Lìchūn,
the emperor ordered his attendants to pass from Fānglín Gate through the eastern garden to the guard,
and proceed to Wàngchūn Palace to welcome spring.
Colored flower trees were brought from within,
and each person was given a branch.
Cherries are first offered.
The Shǐjì states:
Emperor Huì of Hàn once went on a spring outing to a detached palace,
and Shūsūn Shēng said:
"In ancient times, fruits were tasted in spring;
now cherries are ripe,
I hope Your Majesty will take them to offer in the ancestral temple."
Thus began the offering of various fruits.
Raising these blue banners,
the Hòu Hànshū says:
On the day of Lìchūn,
all wear blue headbands and banners,
and welcome spring outside the eastern outer wall.
Wearing colored swallows,
the Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì states:
On Lìchūn day,
all cut colored silk into swallows to wear,
and paste the characters 'Yíchūn' (suitable for spring).
Collecting divine water to brew wine,
the Sìshí Zuǎnyào says:
On Lìchūn, store water,
called divine water,
which makes wine that does not spoil.
Using peach blossoms to wash the face,
Yú Shìnán’s Shǐ Lüè records:
The wife of Lú Shìshēn of Northern Qí,
daughter of Cuī Línyì,
was talented and learned.
In spring, she washed her child’s face with peach blossoms,
chanting:
"Take red flowers,
take white snow,
wash the child’s face to make it bright and joyful.
Take white snow,
take red flowers,
wash the child’s face to make it beautiful and splendid.
Take flower red,
take snow white,
wash the child’s face to make it glossy.
Take snow white,
take flower red,
wash the child’s face to make it radiant."
Again, singing the Bīn poems,
the Zhōu Lǐ states:
The Yuèzhāng officer.
In mid-spring,
drums are beaten by day,
and the Bīn poems are sung to welcome the heat.
Dancing the Yúnqiáo,
the Hòu Hànshū says:
During the Yuánshǐ era,
on Lìchūn,
the Green Emperor Gōumáng was sacrificed to in the eastern suburbs,
with chariot banners and garments all blue,
singing Qīngyáng with eight rows of dancers,
performing the Yúnqiáo dance.
The consorts first present seeds for planting,
as the Zhōu Lǐ states:
In mid-spring,
the queen leads the ladies of the six palaces,
to produce seeds for planting and present them to the king.
The eastern palace’s zithers are tuned.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The women of the eastern palace,
wear blue and colored garments,
and play zithers.
Note:
Spring rules the east,
hence they reside in the eastern palace.
Zithers are of wood,
wood grows in spring,
thus they are played.
Also said to correspond to Qīngyáng,
the Ěryǎ states:
Spring is Qīngyáng,
also called Fāshēng (generation).
Energy gradually moves to the eastern path.
The Yì Tōngtǒng Tú says:
In spring, the moon travels the eastern green path,
called Dōnglù (eastern land).
Eating wormwood cakes,
the Xījīng Zá Jì records:
Jiǎ Pèilán said:
"When in the palace,
on the first Chén day of the first month,
we went to the pond to wash,
and ate wormwood cakes to ward off evil."
Drinking congee,
the Qírén Yuè Lìng says:
In the month of Lìchūn,
eating raw vegetables should not be excessive,
only to take the meaning of welcoming the new.
And congee is served,
to guide harmonious energy.
Promote the gentle and good,
Jīng Fáng’s Yì Zhàn says:
In spring, dismiss the greedy and cruel,
promote the gentle and good,
care for the young and orphaned,
relieve the insufficient.
Seek out recluses,
then the myriad things will emerge in accordance with the season,
and grow following the energy.
Remove the shackles.
The Lǐ states:
In the second month’s season,
inspect the prisons,
and remove the shackles.
Again, it is heard that the blue bird governs the opening,
the dark bird governs the division.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Tánzǐ replied to Confucius:
"Shàohào Zhì made birds his teachers and named them,
the Qīngniǎo clan,
governs the opening.
The Xuánniǎo clan,
governs the division."
Note:
Qīngniǎo is the cuckoo,
which sings at Lìchūn,
and stops at Lìxià.
Xuánniǎo,
is the swallow,
which comes at Chūnfēn,
and leaves at Qiūfēn.
The time when the myriad things break their shells,
the Shì Míng says:
Why Jiázhōng in the second month?
Jiá means
armor.
It says the myriad things break their shells,
and species divide.
The hour when essence and splendor knot together.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo says:
Spring is
when the divine light shifts,
and essence and splendor knot together.
Note:
Divine light refers to yin and yang.
Mutual promotion causes the essence of things to coalesce into a bond.
Bond,
means essential.
It can be used to discuss the order of conferring ranks and rewards,
as stated in the Guǎnzǐ:
On the court day in early spring,
the ruler holds court,
discussing ranks and rewards.
It can be used to extend the grace of magnanimity.
In the Hòu Hàn Shū, Láng Yǐ submitted a memorial stating:
"The Gōngyáng Zhuàn says:
In the first year, spring, the king's first month.
What is the first year?
It is the beginning year of the ruler.
What is the first month?
It is the beginning of the year.
The king models himself on heaven's image,
following the sequence of seasons,
should promulgate virtuous edicts,
confer ranks on the worthy and appoint officers,
extend the favor of magnanimity,
and bestow the grace of benevolence and kindness."
The eastern suburbs are just seeing the morning sun,
as stated in the Lǐjì:
On the day of the spring equinox,
sacrifice to the morning sun in the eastern suburbs.
The observatory never forgets to record the clouds.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
At the equinoxes, solstices, openings, and closings,
one must record the clouds and phenomena,
to be prepared.
Then the sun already carries warmth,
as stated in the Shī:
In spring days, it carries warmth.
The time is the beginning of the year,
as stated in the Chǔcí:
At the beginning of the year, spring emerges, and I hurriedly journey south.
One must bury decaying bones and cover skeletons,
as stated in the Lǐ:
In the middle of the first month,
cover skeletons and bury decaying bones.
Also, carry out celebrations and bestow favors.
The Lǐ states:
Welcome spring in the eastern suburbs,
upon returning,
then reward the dukes, ministers, and high officials in court,
order the prime minister to promulgate virtue and harmonious decrees,
carry out celebrations and bestow favors,
reaching down to the myriad people.
Sacrifice to the horse ancestor and worship the high matchmaker,
as stated in the Lǐ:
On the day of the spring equinox, sacrifice to the horse ancestor.
Note:
Sacrifice at the great marsh on a yang day.
Also states:
Worship the high matchmaker.
Note:
In the time of Gāoxīn,
the dark bird left an egg,
Jiǎndí swallowed it and gave birth to Xiè.
Later kings considered it an auspicious sign for matchmaking,
and established its sacrifice.
Present the jūyī and prepare silkworm tools.
The Lǐ states:
In the third month's festival,
the Son of Heaven presents the jūyī to the former emperors.
It is a yellow mulberry garment.
Also,
in the third month, prepare silkworm tools,
the queen and consorts fast and purify themselves,
offer sacrifice to the first silkworm and personally tend mulberries,
to encourage silkworm affairs.
On the first day, pray for grain,
see the note above on "Yuèzhèng practices dance."
In the eastern suburbs, welcome the seasonal qi.
See the note above on "abundant virtue resides in wood."
Nǚyí drums and sings,
as stated in the Huáinánzǐ:
Nǚyí drums and sings,
to regulate heavenly harmony,
to nurture all grains, birds and beasts, grasses and trees.
Note:
Nǚyí,
is the spirit presiding over growth and nourishment in spring and summer.
People hold plows.
The Lùnhéng states:
On the beginning of spring,
make earthen figures of people,
two men and two women,
holding plows and hoes.
Or erect earthen figures of oxen,
following the season and responding to the qi,
to show leading by example.
As for the three beginnings and three origins,
the time is the proper commencement.
The Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn states:
The first month is the duān month,
its first day is the yuán day,
also called the shàng day,
also called the zhèngcháo,
also called the sānyuán,
also called the sānshuò.
Note:
Sānyuán refers to the origins of the year, season, and month.
Sānshuò:
The Xià considered dawn as shuò;
the Yīn considered cockcrow as shuò;
the Zhōu considered midnight as shuò.
The Jìn Xióng Yuǎn Yì states:
On the yuán day, the beginning step,
the start of proper commencement,
people of discernment,
then revere ritual and music,
glorify the sights and sounds.
Present pepper flowers to offer longevity,
Liú Zhēn's wife,
in the first month presented the "Jiāohuā Sòng," stating:
"Vast heaven revolves,
the three dynasties begin.
Qīngyáng scatters radiance,
clear light carries brilliance.
Praising this divine stem,
I gather and present it.
The sage's countenance reflects it,
eternal longevity for ten thousand years."
Pour from the white tiger to discuss affairs.
Zāng Róngxù's Jìn Shū states:
At the yuán assembly, a white tiger wine vessel is set in the hall,
the vessel cover has a white tiger on it.
Those who can offer straightforward advice,
then open the vessel and drink wine,
which is the legacy of Dù Jǔ.
The white tiger signifies no fear or taboo.
Prepare the five-wood decoction,
as stated in the Zá Xiūyǎng Shū:
On the first day of the first month,
take five kinds of wood to boil a decoction for bathing,
it makes people's beard and hair black until old age.
Daoists call qīngmùxiāng the five fragrances,
also called five woods.
Arrange the five pungent flavors.
The Fēngtǔ Jì states:
On yuán day, make a five pungent plate,
the pungency is to stimulate the qi of the five organs.
Dài Píng sat on layered mats and discussed classics,
as stated in the Dōngguān Hàn Jì:
Dài Píng,
style name Cìzhòng,
served as shìzhōng.
On the first morning court congratulations,
all officials gathered.
The emperor ordered the ministers who could explain classics and histories,
to challenge each other.
If one's interpretation was not thorough,
their mat was taken and given to the more thorough one.
Dài Píng thus sat on over fifty layered mats.
Jiāngxià lifted his robe to report auspicious signs.
The Sòng Shū states:
In the fifth year of Xiàowǔ's Dàmíng reign, first month,
morning snow.
Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià used his robe to catch snow,
forming six-petal flowers,
presented as an auspicious sign,
the emperor was very pleased.
Painted chickens and reed ropes are all displayed,
as stated in the Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì:
On yuán day,
first set off bamboo explosions in front of the courtyard,
paste painted chickens on the door,
some also hang chickens on the door,
suspend reed charcoal above it,
plant peach trees beside it,
then ghosts fear it.
The Kuòdìtú states:
On Táodū Mountain, there is a great peach tree,
coiling for three thousand li.
Above it is a golden rooster,
when sunlight shines, it crows.
Below are two spirits:
one named Yù;
one named Lěi.
Both hold reed ropes,
to watch for inauspicious ghosts,
if caught, they kill them.
Cypress wine and peach soup are fully prepared.
The Fēngtǔ Jì states:
On yuán day,
old and young all dress properly,
pay respects in order,
present pepper wine,
drink peach soup and cypress leaf wine.
Release the doves of Hándān,
as stated in the Lièzǐ:
The people of Hándān,
on the first morning of the first month, presented doves to Jiǎnzǐ,
Jiǎnzǐ richly rewarded them.
A guest said:
"The people know you wish to release them,
so they compete to catch and present them,
many die."
If you wish to keep them alive,
it would be better to forbid the people from catching them.
To catch and then release them
does not make up for the kindness with the fault."
They presented the rice of Diāohú.
The "Jìn Qǐjū Zhù" states:
In the fourth year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
the Granary Department memorialized:
"The region of Yángzhōu has presented one shēng of Diāohú rice,
to be offered to the imperial court on New Year's Day."
An edict ordered it to be stopped.
Some would hang a sheep and dismember a chicken.
Péi Xuán's "Xīn Yán" states:
On New Year's Day,
the county officials would kill a sheep,
hang its head on the gate,
and also dismember a chicken to cover it.
Common lore says this was to suppress pestilential vapors.
Xuán asked Fú Jūn of Hénán about this,
who said:
"In this month,
the earth's energy
rises upwards,
and grasses and trees begin to sprout.
Sheep gnaw on all kinds of grass,
and chickens peck at the five grains.
Therefore, they are killed to assist the vital energy."
Some presented treasures and held gifts of introduction.
Zhāng Héng's "Dōngjīng Fù" states:
On the first day of the first month of spring,
the various lords gathered from all sides.
They were all servants of the Emperor,
presenting treasures and holding gifts of introduction.
This is called the 'upper day'.
The "Shū" says:
On the first day of the first month,
he received the mandate at the temple of Wénzǔ.
Annotation:
The 'upper day'
is the first day of the month.
The four seasons begin to commence.
The "Hànshū" says:
The first day of the first month
is the beginning of the year.
The Beginning of Spring
is the start of the four seasons.
On that first day,
they command the soil altar to pray for agricultural auspiciousness.
The "Lǐ" says:
In the second month's solar term,
choose an auspicious day,
and command the people to make offerings at the soil altar.
Annotation:
This is to sacrifice to the soil and grain altars.
Spring activities commence,
so they pray for agricultural auspiciousness.
The auspicious day
is near the Wù day before or after the Spring Equinox.
It is what Gōulóng presided over,
being in charge of water and soil, and indeed excellent.
The "Shǐjì" says:
Gònggōng's son was named Gōulóng.
He was able to level water and soil,
so he was sacrificed to as the soil altar.
The Hàn founder established the Yú altar, and the affair became prominent.
The "Hànshū" says:
After Gāozǔ pacified the realm,
he issued an edict to the Censor,
ordering the establishment of the Yú altar.
In spring,
they used sheep and pigs to sacrifice there.
Chén Píng divided meat, and his virtue shone brightly.
The "Hànshū" states:
Chén Píng was the village altar butcher,
dividing the meat very evenly.
The elders praised him.
Píng said:
"If I were to govern the world,
it would be just like this meat."
Indeed, it is associated with yīn and presides over killing.
The "Shū" says:
Those who obey orders are rewarded before the ancestral altar;
those who disobey orders are executed before the soil altar.
Annotation:
The soil altar presides over yīn,
and yīn presides over killing.
How could it be that cutting down the tree caused its demise?
The "Jìnshū" says:
Sometimes an altar is represented by a tree.
If the tree is cut down, the altar moves;
if a tree is made into an altar,
cutting down the tree causes the altar to perish.
It also uses mounded earth to convey the vital energy.
The "Xiàojīng Wěi" says:
The soil altar
is the lord of the land.
The land is vast,
and cannot be fully sacrificed to,
so mounded earth is made into an altar
to repay its merits.
Conveying the vital energy
is explained in the annotation below.
Repaying the root and returning to the origin,
the "Shǐjì" says:
The soil altar must receive frost, dew, wind, and rain
to convey the vital energy of Heaven and Earth.
The soil altar is how we draw close to the earth.
The earth carries the myriad things.
Heaven displays images, taking materials from the earth,
and taking models from Heaven.
This is how we honor Heaven and draw close to earth.
The soil altar provides the sacrificial grains,
to repay the root and return to the origin.
Some were established for the multitude of surnames.
The "Lǐ" says:
The King establishes an altar for the multitude of surnames called the Great Altar;
the King establishes an altar for himself called the King's Altar.
The feudal lords establish an altar for the hundred surnames called the State Altar;
they establish an altar for themselves called the Lord's Altar.
Great officers and below establish altars called Established Altars.
Sometimes a hundred households jointly establish one.
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" says:
On the altar day,
the four neighbors all gather together,
assembling sacrificial animals and wine for the altar,
and build a hut beneath the altar.
First they sacrifice to the spirits,
and then feast on the sacrificial meat.
Master Zhèng says:
"The altar gatherings established by a hundred households today
are the jointly established altars."
As for the Cold Food Festival,
fires are forbidden and smoke is hidden.
See the annotation below.
There is cockfighting and kickball.
The "Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
During the Cold Food Festival,
in cities there are especially many games of fighting with chicken eggs.
Liú Xiàng's "Bié Lù" says:
Cold Food kickball
was created by the Yellow Emperor,
originally a military exercise.
Some say it originated in the Warring States period.
Assisted by swings.
The "Gǔjīn Yìshù Tú" says:
Cold Food swings
originally were a game of the northern Shānróng people,
to practice lightness and agility.
The paulownia flowers begin to bloom.
The "Lǐ" says:
During the Clear and Bright festival,
the paulownia begins to flower.
The elm fire is about to be kindled.
The "Shí Xùn" says:
In spring, take fire from elm and willow.
In antiquity there were prohibitions by the Fire Officer,
in common custom there are tales of Jiè Tuī.
Lù Huì's "Yèzhōng Jì" says:
The Cold Food fire prohibition
originated with Zǐtuī.
According to the "Zuǒ Zhuàn" and "Shǐjì", there is no event of Jiè Tuī being burned.
The "Zhōu Lǐ" states:
The Fire Officer,
in mid-spring, goes through the state with a wooden clapper to enforce the fire prohibition.
Annotation:
In late spring, they will bring out the fire.
Now, Cold Food, according to the solar terms, is the end of mid-spring,
and Clear and Bright is the beginning of the third month.
Thus, the fire prohibition is probably an old regulation of the Zhōu.
Therefore, Zhōu Jǔ's letter had already been circulated.
The "Hòu Hànshū" says:
Zhōu Jǔ was transferred to be Governor of Bìngzhōu.
In Tàiyuán, an old custom
held that because Jiè Tuī's bones were burned,
there was a prohibition on the Dragon's Taboo.
He then sent a letter to Zǐtuī's temple,
whereupon the public's confusion gradually dissipated.
The annotation states:
The Dragon
is a star,
the position of Wood,
which appears in the east in spring.
The Heart constellation is the great fire.
Fearing the abundance of fire,
they therefore instituted the fire prohibition.
Common legend says Zǐtuī was burned on this day, hence the fire prohibition.
And Wèi Wǔ's order was then promulgated.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's "Míng Fá Lìng" states:
"I have heard that in Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, and Yànmén,
for one hundred and five days after the winter solstice, all fires are prohibited,
said to be for Jiè Tuī.
Moreover, when Zǐxū drowned in the river, there was no event of cutting off water.
Now, in these bitterly cold lands,
the old and young, weak and frail,
will suffer intolerable hardship.
Let it be ordered that people may not observe Cold Food.
If anyone violates this,
the head of the household shall receive six months' penal servitude,
the responsible official one hundred days' penal servitude,
and the magistrate shall forfeit one month's salary."
There is also the beginning of late spring,
Wáng Xīzhī’s “Preface to the Orchid Pavilion” on the third day of the third month says:
In the ninth year of the Yǒnghé era,
at the beginning of late spring,
we gathered at the Orchid Pavilion in Shānyīn,
to perform the purification ritual.
The time for spreading harmony.
Yán Yánnián’s “Preface to the Qu River Poems” says:
At the beginning of the imperial spirits’ awakening,
the time for kings to spread harmony.
Gathering by the flowing waters,
the purification feast is laid out.
The “Treatise on Rituals” in the *Continued Book of the Hàn* says:
On the third day of the third month,
officials all gather to feast by the eastern flowing waters.
Passing by the residence of Píngyáng,
the *Book of Hàn* says:
Princess Píngyáng sought over ten women from good families,
and adorned and kept them at home.
When Emperor Wǔ performed the purification ritual at Bàshàng,
he returned and visited the princess.
The princess presented the beauties she kept,
but the emperor was displeased.
After drinking,
singers were presented,
and the emperor was only pleased with Wèi Zǐfū.
Yìng Shào explains:
“Fú”
means to remove.
This is the purification ritual performed on the third day of the third month.
By the ford of Bóluò,
the *Records of Wèi* says:
Yuán Shào, on the third day of the third month,
held a grand gathering of guests and attendants at Bóluò Ford,
when he heard that troops from Wèi Commandery and bandits from the Black Mountains had together captured Yè City.
Among those seated were guests whose families were in Yè,
and they all turned pale with fear.
Yuán Shào’s expression remained unchanged,
and he did not alter his usual demeanor.
Gathering those like Zhāng and Péi,
the *Discourses on the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove* says:
“Wáng Jì once held a purification feast at Luò River.
The next day, someone asked Jì:
‘What did the guests talk about yesterday?’”
He replied:
“Zhāng Huà excelled at discussing the *Records of the Grand Historian* and the *Book of Hàn*,
and Péi Yìmín recounted past words and deeds,
all eloquently and worth hearing.”
Enjoying these waters of Zhēn and Wěi,
the *Hán Shī Zhāngjù* says:
“The Zhēn and Wěi rivers are overflowing,
men and women are holding orchids.”
Note:
“Jiān”
means orchid.
When peach blossoms fall on the water in the third month,
it is the custom of the state of Zhèng
to perform purification rituals on the third day of the third month to ward off misfortune.
There are also fragrant dishes lightly floating,
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì’s “Preface to the Qu River Poems on the Third Day” says:
The third day of the third month is an auspicious time,
the remaining sprouts reach the soil,
the orioles respond to the rhythm,
and the goddess of spring oversees the season.
Then, feathers are arranged along the steps,
wine cups float on the flowing streams,
feathered cups drift along the currents,
fragrant dishes come and go,
guests are seated in proper order,
and great virtue is displayed with grace.
A calf cart is seen approaching,
the *Continued Records of Searching for the Divine* says:
Lú Chōng was hunting,
saw a deer and shot it,
hitting it,
and chased after it,
unaware of how far he had gone.
Suddenly, he saw a black gate like a mansion,
asked the gatekeeper,
who replied:
“This is the mansion of Prefect Cuī.”
He entered to see the prefect,
who said to Chōng:
“Your late father sought a marriage with my daughter,
so I have welcomed you here.”
After three days of marriage,
he sent Chōng home by carriage.
His mother asked him,
and he recounted everything.
After parting from Cuī,
on the third day of the third month of the fourth year,
while playing by the water,
he saw a calf cart by the water in the distance,
Chōng went and opened the carriage door,
saw Cuī’s daughter with three boys inside,
their affection unchanged.
She handed the child to Chōng,
and gave him a gold bracelet before parting again.
The Duke of Zhōu’s city of Luòyì,
the *Continued Records of Qíxié* says:
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn asked the Imperial Secretary Láng Zhì Yú:
“What is the meaning of the Qu River on the third day of the third month?”
He replied:
“During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Xú Zhào of Píngyuán had three daughters born at the beginning of the third month,
and all three died on the third day.
The whole village considered it an omen,
so they went together to the riverside to wash,
and floated wine cups on the water.
The meaning of the Qu River
originated from this.”
The emperor said:
“If it is as you say,
then it is not a good thing.”
The Imperial Secretary Láng Shù Xī said:
“Zhì Yú is young and inexperienced,
and does not know enough.
Allow me to explain its origin.
Long ago, when the Duke of Zhōu built the city of Luòyì,
he floated wine on the flowing water,
hence the lost poem says:
‘Feathered cups follow the waves.’
Also, King Zhāo of Qín held a banquet by the river bend on the third day of the third month,
when a golden man emerged,
holding a sword from the heart of the water, saying:
‘I grant you control over the western Xià,
and Qín will dominate the feudal lords.’
Thus, this place was established as the Qu River.
Both Hàn dynasties followed this tradition,
and it became a grand gathering.”
The emperor said:
“Good.”
He awarded fifty catties of gold,
and demoted Zhì Yú to the position of magistrate of Yángchéng.
King Zhāo of Qín receiving the sword from the heart of the water.
Already mentioned in the note above.
Some hold orchids and stroll leisurely,
see the note above on “enjoying these waters of Zhēn and Wěi.”
Some sun medicine and ponder deeply.
The *Separate Biography of Xià Tǒng* says:
Tǒng visited Luò.
On the third day of the third month,
princesses and nobles in Luò
all rode in carriages side by side,
and gathered by the southern floating bridge for purification.
Tǒng was in a boat at the time,
sun-drying the medicine he had bought,
sitting steadily without moving.
Jiǎ Chōng saw him from afar,
deeply admired his composure,
and sent someone to ask who the person sitting calmly in the boat was.
He slowly replied:
“Xià Zhòngyù, a commoner from Kuàijī.”
Tǒng’s courtesy name was Zhòngyù.
Tiānyuān is the name of the terrace with piled stones,
Dài Yánzhī’s *Records of the Western Expedition* says:
South of Tiānyuān,
there is a terrace of piled stones,
said to be the place where the emperor sat on the third day of the third month to float wine cups.
Huálín is the embankment called Qiānjīn.
The *Records of Yè* says:
In the Huálín Garden,
on the Qiānjīn Embankment, two bronze dragons were made,
facing each other and spouting water.
Note:
At Tiānyuān Pond,
on the third day of the third month, gatherings were held by the pond for enjoyment.
Clusters of flowers surround the silk-like river as one gazes intently,
the *Book of Sòng* says:
Emperor Wǔ climbed the old terrace of Liú Ān on Bāgōng Mountain on the third day of the third month,
and said while looking:
“The city walls are like a bolt of silk winding around clusters of flowers.”
Flowing orioles fill the branches and change their songs.
Liáng Shěn Yuē’s “Poem for the Third Day” says:
A beautiful day belongs to the third day of the third month,
the fragrance of the year is all here.
Blossoms already cover the trees,
and flowing orioles again fill the branches.
These are all recorded in the seasonal annals,
and thus preserved in the literary collections.
Summer,
means great.
It nurtures all things,
causing them to grow large.
From the Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng.
As for its seasonal name being Zhūmíng,
the Ěryǎ says:
Summer is called Zhūmíng.
Its time is called Chángyíng.
The Ěryǎ says:
Summer is called Chángyíng.
Zhùróng serves as its assistant,
the Lǐ says:
In summer,
its sovereign is Yándì;
its deity is Zhùróng.
Yándì holds the balance.
The Hànshū:
Wèi Xiàng submitted a memorial saying:
"The deity of the south is Yándì,
who rides on Lí and holds the balance, governing summer."
Annotation:
Fire corresponds to ritual,
which harmonizes and levels, hence it is the balance.
Cherries are offered first,
the Lǐ says in the middle of the fourth month,
cherries are first offered at the ancestral temple.
The shrike falls silent.
The Lǐ says:
In the fifth month's solar term,
the shrike falls silent.
Some see the three stars at the door,
the Shī says:
Bound tightly with brambles,
three stars are at the door.
The commentary says:
The Heart Star is at the door,
meaning in the middle of the fifth month,
or the sixth month's solar term.
Some use five colors to ward off weapons.
The Fēngsútōng says:
On the summer solstice,
wear five colors to ward off weapons,
inscribed as Yóuguāng.
Yóuguāng,
is a fierce ghost.
Those who know its name,
will not suffer from warm diseases.
Bitter vegetables bloom and delicate grasses die,
the Lǐ says:
On the day of Xiǎomǎn,
bitter vegetables bloom;
five days later,
delicate grasses die.
Earthworms emerge and king melons grow.
The Lǐ says:
On the day of Lìxià,
mole crickets chirp.
Five days later,
earthworms emerge.
Five days later,
king melons grow.
As for the fourth month being summer,
the fifth month brings intense heat,
from the Shī.
Some hear crickets dwelling in walls,
the Lǐ says:
In the sixth month's solar term,
crickets dwell in walls.
Some see katydids shaking their wings.
The Shī says:
In the sixth month, katydids shake their wings.
Hunting in the western lands and presenting remonstrance,
the Tàigōng Jīnguì says:
Zhòu hunted in the western lands in the sixth month,
mobilizing the people to chase animals.
Someone remonstrated saying:
"Now in the sixth month,
heaven's duty is to cover and bestow,
earth's duty is to nurture and grow,
yet you mobilize the people to chase animals,
leaving the common folk exposed in the wilds.
If the ruler tramples one day's seedlings,
then the people will have no food for a hundred days.
If the Son of Heaven loses the Way,
there will surely be no fortune later."
Zhòu executed him for spreading evil words.
Heaven sent violent wind and rain,
uprooting houses and breaking trees.
Excessive fishing in the Sì River and cutting nets,
the Guóyǔ says:
Lǔ Xuāngōng excessively fished in the Sì River in summer,
Lǐ Gé cut his net and discarded it,
saying:
"In ancient times, when the great cold descended,
and hibernating creatures stirred,
the water officials then prepared nets and traps,
caught famous fish,
gathered river creatures,
and offered them at the ancestral temple,
distributed them among the people,
to help spread the vital energy.
Now the fish are just separating and pregnant,
not allowing the fish to grow,
yet you still cast nets,
this is greed without limit."
The Duke said:
"I was wrong."
Annotation says:
Excessive fishing,
means soaking nets to catch fish.
When cold air descends,
refers to late winter.
Hibernating creatures stir,
refers to early spring.
Water officials,
are fishing masters.
Gū,
is a fishing net.
Liǔ,
is a bamboo trap.
In Tiāndú, even plants and trees dry up,
the Kuòdìtú says:
The country of Tiāndú is extremely hot,
in summer,
plants and trees all dry up.
In Zhūtí, even flying birds cannot pass.
The Yǒngchāngjùn Zhuàn says:
In Zhūtí Commandery, Tángláng Mountain has many poisonous plants,
in the height of summer,
when flying birds pass over,
they cannot leave.
A distinguished guest visited Xiè Ān while fans were waved,
the Shìshuō says:
Xī Jiābīn,
in the hottest month of summer visited Xiè Gōng,
even with fans waving in the wind,
he was still drenched in sweat.
Wáng Gōng met Zhēncháng and spoke in the Wú dialect.
The Shìshuō says:
When Liú Zhēncháng first met Chancellor Wáng,
in the hottest month of summer,
the Chancellor pressed his belly against a chessboard and said:
"How about this coolness?"
People from Wú call cold "qìng",
pronounced as chǔ jìng qiē.
After Liú left,
people asked how his meeting with Wáng Gōng went,
Liú said:
"I saw nothing unusual about him,
except that he spoke in the Wú dialect."
Some restrain desires and cease music and beauty,
the Lǐ says:
