In mid-summer,
yin and yang interact,
life and death separate,
the gentleman fasts and abstains,
ceases music and beauty,
restrains desires.
Some teach chariot and armor skills to observe martial talent.
The Dàdài Lǐ says:
In summer,
they teach soldiers chariot and armor skills.
Soldiers demonstrate skills and strength,
cultivate the four defenses,
strengthen limbs,
test archery, charioteering, and martial talent,
enfeoff seven meritorious men,
to complete summer affairs.
Considering this oppressive heat,
the Lǐ says:
On the day of Dàshǔ,
decaying grass turns into fireflies,
five days later,
the earth becomes damp and oppressively hot.
Truly it is the direction of responsibility.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn says:
What is the south?
It is the direction of responsibility.
The direction of responsibility,
is where things take responsibility.
Why is it called summer?
Summer,
means borrowing.
Borrowing,
means exhaling and nurturing all things,
nourishing them outwardly.
Exhaling and nurturing,
is read as xū shū.
Wú Měng did not drive away mosquitoes,
the Sōushénjì says:
Wú Měng,
was extremely filial by nature.
When he was a child,
sleeping beside his parents,
in summer there were many mosquitoes,
yet he did not wave a fan, fearing the mosquitoes would leave him and bite his parents.
Zǐpíng often sought coolness to avoid the heat.
Sòng Gōng's Xiàozǐ Zhuàn says:
Hé Zǐpíng served his mother with utmost filial piety.
At the age of sixty,
he still possessed the affection of a young child.
In summer, he sought coolness to avoid the heat.
The King of Yuè, thinking of Wú, would hold fire.
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
The King of Yuè, contemplating Wú's revenge,
would hold fire in summer.
Lù Jī, while in Luòyáng, longed for his hometown.
The *Yǔlín* states:
Lù Jī,
during summer in Luòyáng,
suddenly thought of drinking from the bamboo grove in the eastern part of his home,
and said to Liú Bǎo:
"My longing for home grows deeper."
He cherished Jī Kāng's forging furnace.
The *Jìn Shū* states:
Jī Kāng was skillful and fond of forging.
There was a willow tree by his residence,
very lush,
so he channeled water to encircle it.
In the summer months,
he would forge beneath it.
He admired Chē Wǔzǐ's firefly bag.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
Chē Wǔzǐ's family was poor,
and he often lacked oil for reading.
In the summer months,
he would fill a silk bag with dozens of fireflies,
continuing his studies day and night.
He recalled Shī Wén's "flying snow."
See the annotation in the *Qín Fù*: "Shī Wén said clouds float and fish leap."
He remembered Zōu Yǎn's "descending frost."
See the annotation in the *Shuāng Fù*: "Zōu Yǎn, slandered, wept bitterly."
As for the Zōngbó's ritual to avert famine and calamity,
the *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
The Zōngbó, at the summer solstice, summons earth spirits and ghosts,
to avert the state's famine and calamity,
and the people's pestilence and death.
Annotation:
"Guì"
means to remove.
"Mèi,"
pronounced mèi.
King Mù of Zhōu traveled to Huòzé.
The *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* states:
The Son of Heaven rested at Huòzé in the fourth month,
and there he shot birds.
Huòzé
is present-day Huò County in Píngyáng.
"Huò,"
pronounced hù.
Already mentioned in the regulations for horses,
the *Lǐ* states:
In the fifth month's season,
the horse administration is promulgated.
The annotation explains:
The policies and teachings for horse breeding in the twelve stables.
Again, the cuckoo's call is heard.
The *Lǐ* states:
In the fifth month's season,
the cuckoo begins to call.
Fire is already drilled from jujube and apricot trees,
the *Shíxùn* states:
In summer, take fire from jujube and apricot trees.
Weapons also begin with halberds and swords.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
In the first month of summer,
the weapon is the halberd;
in the last month of summer,
the weapon is the sword.
Annotation:
The halberd has branches and a shaft,
symbolizing the spreading of yang energy;
the sword has two edges,
symbolizing the generation of all things.
Then, the long wind fans away the heat.
The *Fēngtǔ Jì* states:
In mid-summer,
the long wind fans away the heat.
During this season, winds often come from the southeast,
commonly called the "yellow sparrow long wind."
Lush trees form continuous shade.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's *Zuǎnyào* states:
Summer grass is called lush grass,
trees are called dense forest.
Lush forests and thick trees.
Lù Jī's *Zuǎnyào* states:
Summer trees are called "continuous shade,"
summer rain is called "continuous rain."
Light fans are presented, and fine linen is worn.
Pān Yuè's *Qiūxìng Fù* states:
Put away the light fan,
remove the fine linen.
Sweet melons float, and crimson plums sink.
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Letter to Wú Zhì* states:
Float sweet melons in clear springs,
sink crimson plums in cold water.
Gé Hóng's encounter with the immortal elder,
often entering the water while drunk;
the *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
Gé Hóng's granduncle, the immortal elder,
whenever heavily drunk,
would enter the bottom of a spring in summer,
staying for about a day before emerging.
This was because he could hold his breath and practice fetal breathing.
Yánlíng's meeting with the noble scholar,
how could he take off his fur robe to retrieve gold?
See the annotation in the *Jīn Fù*: "In summer, there is the propriety of wearing fur robes."
At this time of southern transformation,
the *Shū·Yáo Diǎn* states:
He ordered Xī Shū to reside in the southern border,
to regulate the southern transformation.
Annotation:
means transformation.
It refers to the transformative and nurturing affairs of the south.
This is the time when the dragon appears.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
When the dragon appears, the rain sacrifice is held.
Annotation:
The dragon refers to the stars Horn and Neck.
In the fourth month,
they appear in the east at dusk.
The Son of Heaven drinks the mellow wine.
The *Lǐ* states:
In the middle of the fourth month,
the Son of Heaven drinks the mellow wine,
accompanied by ritual music.
The empress and consorts present silkworm cocoons.
The *Lǐ* states:
In the middle of the fourth month,
when the silkworm work is completed,
the empress and consorts present silkworm cocoons.
The Shǔ chancellor was seen crossing the Lú River.
Zhūgě Liàng's *Chūshī Biǎo* states:
In the fifth month, we crossed the Lú River,
penetrating deep into barren lands.
The ritual general is not heard to wield a fan.
The *Liùtāo* states:
In summer, do not wield a fan;
in winter, do not wear fur robes;
when it rains, do not open an umbrella;
this is called the ritual general.
Again, it is heard that wells are dredged and water is changed.
The *Xù Hànshū·Lǐyí Zhì* states:
At the summer solstice,
dredge wells and change water;
at the winter solstice,
drill for fire and change the fire source,
to ward off warm diseases.
Facing the wind, one fans with a large fan.
The *Lùnhéng* states:
During the height of summer,
face the wind and fan with a large fan;
in the depth of winter,
face the sun and light a stove.
However, heaven never changes its qi for winter or summer,
because cold and heat have their seasons,
and do not change for humans.
Sūn Dēng was at ease in his grass robe.
The *Jìn Shū* states:
Sūn Dēng,
styled Gōnghé.
People found him in an earthen cave on Běishān in Jí County.
In summer, he would weave grass into robes.
Yáng Mào wandered freely on his plank bed.
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hànshū* states:
Yáng Mào,
styled Jìshí,
served as the governor of Dōngjùn.
In summer, he stayed on a single plank bed.
As for the rotting grass turning into fireflies,
see the annotation above for "Considering this humid heat."
Red cords are tied to meat.
The *Xù Hànshū·Lǐyí Zhì* states:
In the middle month of summer,
when yin energy begins to stir,
there is fear that things may not flourish.
The ritual involves tying red cords to meat,
and hanging them on doors.
The Zhà clan's felling of yang trees,
the *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
The Zhà clan,
at the summer solstice, orders the felling of yang trees and burning them;
at the winter solstice, orders the stripping of yin trees and soaking them in water.
Yáng Xīn's practice of wearing a plain silk skirt.
The *Sòng Shū* states:
Yáng Xīn's father, Bùyí,
served as the magistrate of Wúchéng County.
Yáng Xīn was twelve years old at the time.
Wáng Xiànzhī was the governor of Wúxīng
and held him in great affection.
Once, during the summer months, he entered the county office,
and found Yáng Xīn wearing a new plain silk skirt, napping during the day.
Wáng Xiànzhī wrote several scrolls of calligraphy and left.
Yáng Xīn had originally studied calligraphy,
and from then on, he became even more skilled.
It is also heard that the Sù clan lived in nests.
The *Jìn Shū* states:
The Sùshèn state,
also known as Yìlóu,
in summer dwells in nests.
Jiǎ Shēng composed a fu on the owl.
Jiǎ Yì’s “Fu on the Owl” says:
In the year of Dān’è,
in the fourth month, the beginning of summer.
On the Gēngzǐ day as the sun slanted,
an owl alighted in my dwelling.
At the start of summer, clear and mild,
Xiè Língyùn’s poem says:
The beginning of summer is still clear and mild,
and fragrant grasses have not yet withered.
One sees the flourishing transformation of growth.
Sòng Yù’s “Nine Arguments” says:
Gathering the flourishing growth of early summer,
yet then thwarted and sinking into concealment.
The Ice Officer distributes ice.
The “Zhōu Lǐ” says:
The Ice Officer is in charge of ice,
and in summer distributes ice.
The Mountain Forester fells trees.
The “Zhōu Lǐ” says:
The Mountain Forester in midsummer fells the yīn trees,
and in midwinter fells the yáng trees.
Note:
Yīn trees grow on the north side of mountains,
yáng trees grow on the south side of mountains.
In winter, fell yáng trees;
in summer, fell yīn trees;
thus hardness and softness are balanced.
Some take the Mysterious Ice Pills.
The “Bàopǔzǐ” says:
Someone asked about the method to avoid heat.
The reply was:
“On the day of the beginning of summer,
either take Mysterious Ice Pills,
or take Flying Snow Powder,
along with the talismans of Liùrén and Liùguǐ,
then one will not feel hot.
Yòu Bózǐ and Wáng Zhòngdū—these two men,
clad in heavy fur robes,
exposed to the summer sun,
surrounded by ten stoves of fire,
their mouths did not claim heat,
their bodies did not shed sweat.
It is because they used this method.”
Some listen to the tune of Autumn Frost.
The “Shíyí Jì” says:
The Dòngtíng Mountain,
floating on the water,
has beneath it several hundred golden halls,
where the Emperor’s daughter resides.
Throughout the four seasons, the sounds of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo are heard,
reaching to the mountain’s peak.
King Huái of Chǔ gathered a group of talents to compose poems by the water’s edge,
hence it is said the music of Xiāoxiāng and Dòngtíng,
listening to it makes one hard to age;
even “Xiánchí” and “Xiāosháo” cannot compare.
Every season of the four mid-months,
the king would often roam and feast around the mountain,
each raising the qi of the mid-season to create musical movements.
In midsummer, the pitch-tube corresponds to Ruíbīn,
so they composed the “Tune of Bright Dew and Autumn Frost.”
As for Píngshū sweating,
the “Yǔlín” says:
Hé Píngshū had beautiful appearance and was extremely fair,
Emperor Wén of Wèi suspected he used powder.
In summer, he gave him hot soup cakes;
after eating,
he broke into great sweat,
then wiped himself with a red garment,
and his complexion became even more radiant.
Zhòngdū exposed to the sun.
See the note above on “Mysterious Ice Pills.”
Verify the response of the blooming yāo plant to the season.
The “Shī” says:
In the fourth month, the yāo plant blooms.
Note:
It bears fruit without flowering.
Recognize that Ruíbīn corresponds to the pitch-tube.
The “Shìmíng” says:
The pitch-tube of the fifth month is Ruíbīn.
Ruí means
descending.
Bīn means
respect.
It says the yáng qi descends,
the yīn qi reaches its peak,
and the yīn qi begins to show respect to the yáng.
Beasts have already shed their fur.
The “Shū‧Yáodiǎn” says:
The days are long and the star Huǒ is at its zenith,
to mark midsummer.
The people are at ease,
and birds and beasts shed their fur.
Note:
In summer,
the feathers and fur of birds and beasts become sparse and change.
All things bloom and bear fruit.
The “Sùwèn” says:
During the three months of summer,
heaven and earth’s qi intermingle,
and all things bloom and bear fruit.
Sleep late and rise early,
keep the will free from anger;
let the essence flourish into beauty,
allow the qi to be released.
Know the initial arrival of the Lí qi.
The “Yì Tōng Guà Yàn” says:
At the summer solstice,
at midday, red qi emerges straight,
this is the correct qi of Lí.
If it emerges to the right,
half of all things die;
if it emerges to the left,
the land turns barren for a thousand miles.
See the sudden emergence of yáng creatures.
The “Lùnhéng” says:
Tigers appear at certain times,
just as dragons appear at set periods.
Yīn creatures appear in winter,
yáng creatures emerge in summer.
Their emergence responds to the qi,
and the qi moves their kind.
Shēnfá appears in winter,
Xīnwěi appears in summer;
Shēnfá corresponds to the tiger constellation,
Xīnwěi corresponds to the dragon constellation.
The stars appear and creatures are seen,
the qi arrives and the kind moves—
this is the nature of heaven and earth.
Then wear summer clothing.
The “Lǐ” says:
At the mid-season of the fourth month,
the Master first wears summer clothing.
The “Lúnyǔ” says:
In summer, wear fine or coarse hemp garments.
Carry red banners.
The “Lǐ” says:
At the beginning of summer,
the Son of Heaven rides a red carriage,
drives red horses,
carries red banners,
and welcomes summer in the southern suburbs.
When cool, drink from the Míngyì Well.
The “Shòuyáng Jì” says:
South of Míngyì Tower is Míngyì Well,
in summer, there are cool beverages, sweet drinks, rice, silk fans, damask fans, and feather fans.
There are three bathhouses:
the upper for princes, marquises, officials, and clerks;
the middle for gentlemen and scholars;
the lower for the common people.
When cold, wade through the stream of Fán Mountain.
The “Wǔchāng Jì” says:
East of Fán Mountain is a small stream;
in the height of summer,
it is always chillingly cold,
called the Cold Stream.
Clear dew drips with the qi of Kūnlún.
See the note in “The Fu on Dew”: “Moving qi to Kūnlún.”
The summer hù urges the time for plowing and sowing.
Cuī Shí’s “Zhènglùn” says:
The summer hù urges weeding and hoeing; it is also called Qièzhī,
also known as Huògǔ.
As for welcoming the qi in the southern suburbs,
the “Lǐ” says:
The Grand Historian, three days before the beginning of summer,
pays respects to the Son of Heaven,
saying:
“On such-and-such day, summer begins,
the abundant virtue resides in fire.”
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the beginning of summer,
the Son of Heaven personally leads dukes, ministers, feudal lords, and grandees
to welcome summer in the southern suburbs.
At the square mound, sacrifice to the earth.
The “Lǐ” says:
At the summer solstice,
sacrifice to the Imperial Earth Deity at the square mound.
Know that abundant virtue resides in fire.
See the note above.
See the Dipper handle pointing to Sì.
The “Huáinánzǐ” says:
In early summer,
Zhāoyáo points to Sì.
Thereupon, bestow kindness upon the worthy and good.
The “Huáinánzǐ” says:
The summer ordinance states:
Enfeoff the meritorious,
reward the virtuous,
bestow kindness upon the worthy and good,
and relieve the hungry and thirsty.
Confer noble ranks.
The “Huáinánzǐ” says:
When the Jǐngfēng wind arrives,
then confer noble ranks
and reward the meritorious.
To release serious prisoners,
the Book of Rites says:
When the Minor Heat arrives,
serious prisoners are released,
and those lightly imprisoned are set free.
Annotation:
Tǐng means
to be lenient.
To bestow rewards and gifts.
The Book of Rites says:
The Son of Heaven welcomes summer in the southern suburbs,
and upon returning,
he rewards the dukes, ministers, and high officials at court.
Thus, rewards and gifts are bestowed,
and all are delighted.
After raising the tortoise and hunting the jiao-dragon,
the Annals of Lü Buwei say:
In the last month of summer,
the fish masters are ordered to hunt the jiao-dragon and raise the tortoise.
The annotation states:
The jiao-dragon can harm people,
so it is difficult to capture, hence the term "hunt."
The tortoise is divine and can determine good or bad fortune,
and is used in ancestral temples,
so it is revered, hence the term "raise."
Also, to nourish the kidneys and support the lungs.
The Monthly Ordinances for Health Preservation says:
The fourth month is dry,
vital energy is at mǎo,
and death energy is at yǒu.
This month is extremely hot,
do not expose yourself to wind after heavy sweating,
do not expose yourself under the stars,
or else you will contract severe illnesses.
In this month, the liver is prone to illness,
the spirit and energy do not flow smoothly,
fire energy gradually approaches,
and water energy gradually weakens.
Slightly nourish the kidneys and support the lungs,
harmonize stomach energy,
and do not miss the proper timing.
The numerous performances of the palace women of the Southern Palace,
the Huainanzi says:
In the first month of summer,
the palace women of the Southern Palace,
wear red clothes and red ornaments,
and play the yú and shēng.
Annotation:
Fire is born in the south,
so they reside in the Southern Palace.
The yú and shēng,
being hollow, symbolize yang,
hence they are played.
The proud gaze of Fúxī by the northern window.
The Collected Works of Táo Qián says:
Táo Qián often said that in the fifth and sixth months,
lying by the northern window,
when a cool breeze briefly arrives,
he felt like a person from the time of Fúxī.
If one can make zòngzi in accordance with the seasonal customs,
the Records of Local Customs says:
The fifth day of the fifth month is called "Duānwǔ."
Duān means
beginning.
Customarily, it is as important as the Summer Solstice.
Glutinous rice is wrapped in wild rice leaves,
called zòng,
also known as jiǎoshǔ,
symbolizing the unbroken unity of yin and yang.
Colorful silk threads convey the sentiment of gifts.
Comprehensive Meaning of Customs says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
colorful silk threads are tied around the arms,
called "long-life threads,"
also known as "life-prolonging threads,"
"evil-warding ribbons,"
"five-colored threads,"
or "vermilion cords."
There are also items like tiáodá,
woven with various materials,
to be given as gifts.
As an ancient poem says, "Wrapped around the arms are double tiáotuō."
Hanging vermilion cords to decorate doors,
the Book of Later Han, Treatise on Rituals says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
vermilion cords and five-colored peach seals
are used to decorate doors,
to ward off evil energy.
Wearing spiritual talismans to ward off weapons.
The Baopuzi says:
When asked about the method to ward off the five weapons,
the answer is: on the fifth day of the fifth month,
make a red spiritual talisman,
and wear it over the heart.
The tongues of mynah birds are first trimmed,
the Garden of Marvels says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
trim the tongues of mynah birds,
and they can learn human speech.
The horns of toads suddenly grow.
The Baopuzi says:
Toads that live for ten thousand years
have horns on their heads,
and eight red characters under their chins.
If captured at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
dried in the shade for a hundred days,
and their feet used to draw on the ground,
water will immediately flow.
The significance of pickled turtle is recorded,
the Records of Local Customs says:
On Duānwǔ, pickled turtle is eaten.
The turtle,
with bones on the outside and flesh inside,
symbolizes yin within and yang without,
thus it praises the season.
The exquisite craftsmanship of mirror casting.
Supplement to the National History says:
Yángzhōu used to tribute mirrors cast in the heart of the river,
on the fifth day of the fifth month,
cast in the middle of the Yángzǐ River.
Treading on a hundred herbs while roaming afar,
the Records of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
four people together tread on a hundred herbs,
hence the game of "competing with a hundred herbs."
Rowing flying ducks while swiftly traveling.
The Records of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month, dragon boat races are held,
a custom said to commemorate Qū Yuán throwing himself into the Mìluó River,
mourning his death,
so boats are used to rescue him.
The boats are light,
called "flying ducks."
Collecting orchids for bathing,
the Elder Dai's Book of Rites says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
orchids are collected for bathing.
Binding mugwort into human shapes.
The Records of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
mugwort is gathered and shaped into human figures,
hung on doors,
to ward off poisonous energy.
Throwing into the Mìluó River, where chinaberry leaves are present,
the Continued Records of Qíxié says:
Qū Yuán threw himself into the Mìluó River on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and the people of Chǔ mourned him.
On this day,
they stored rice in bamboo tubes,
and threw them into the water as offerings.
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn dynasty,
a man named Ōu Huí from Chángshā
met someone who claimed to be the Sānlǘ Dàfū.
He said to Huí:
"I have seen the offerings, which are very good,
but I fear they will be stolen by jiao-dragons.
You can seal them with chinaberry leaves,
and tie them with five-colored silk threads.
These two things
are what jiao-dragons fear."
Today, people make zòngzi on the fifth day,
and include five-colored threads and chinaberry leaves.
Worshipping at Cāngwú while children's dances are performed.
Xiè Chéng's Book of Later Han says:
Chén Lín served as the governor of Cāngwú,
governing with sincerity,
and guiding people with filial piety and brotherly love.
After Chén Lín was recalled,
the local people worshipped him at the eastern city gate on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and had children in clean clothes dance for him.
The world praises Cáo É's virtue,
the Records of Kuàijī says:
A girl named Cáo É,
from Shàngyú, Kuàijī,
her father was a shaman who could sing and play string instruments.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
he rowed against the waves to welcome the wave god in the county river,
and drowned.
É was fourteen years old,
and she cried along the river,
her voice never ceasing day or night for seven days,
then she threw herself into the river and died.
A few days later,
she emerged holding her father's body.
The custom mentions the name of Jièzǐtuī.
the Records of Yèzhōng says:
In Bīngzhōu, it is customary to say that Jièzǐtuī was burned to death on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and people avoid this day,
so they do not cook food.
This is incorrect.
In the north, on the fifth day of the fifth month,
people prepare their own food to worship gods,
and make five-colored spicy plates to give as gifts,
not for Jièzǐtuī.
the Qíncāo says:
After Jièzǐtuī was burned to death,
Duke Wén of Jìn ordered the people not to light fires on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Tián Wén was celebrated for being born on a high day,
the Records of the Grand Historian says:
Tián Wén was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
The father ordered not to raise him,
but the mother secretly raised him.
When Wén grew up,
he was told the truth.
Wén asked his father:
"Why not raise a child born on the fifth day of the fifth month?"
The father said:
"Such a child reaching the doorway is harmful to the father."
Wén replied:
"Lifespan lies with Heaven,
not with the doorway.
If this were true,
why not raise the doorway higher,
so the child cannot reach it?"
The father considered him wise,
and established him as heir.
Hú Guǎng was revived from a drifting jar.
The Shì Shuō states:
Hú Guǎng originally had the surname Huáng.
Born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
his parents despised him,
placed him in a jar,
and set it adrift on rivers and lakes.
Lord Hú saw a child crying inside the jar,
took him,
and raised him as his own son.
He rose seven times to the highest offices.
As for Zhèn'è and Jì Mài—
the Sòng Shū states:
Wáng Zhèn'è was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His family wanted to abandon him.
His grandfather Měng said:
"Long ago, Lord Mèngcháng was born on this day,
and eventually became chancellor of Qí.
This child will surely bring prosperity to our clan."
Thus he was named Zhèn'è.
The Xiào Zǐ Zhuàn states:
Jì Mài was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His mother abandoned him.
The wife of village man Jì Chún raised him.
At age six,
his birth parents said:
"You are our child."
Mài wept.
Later, from his hired labor earnings,
he always gave to his mother.
As for Wáng Fèng and Xìn Míng—
the Xī Jīng Zá Jì states:
Wáng Fèng was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His father wanted not to raise him.
His uncle said:
"Considering Tián Wén's case,
it is not inauspicious."
Thus he was raised.
The Táng Shū states:
Cuī Xìn Míng was born precisely at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Several unusual birds,
very small in size,
displaying all five colors,
gathered on the courtyard trees,
singing with clear, bright voices.
The Suí dynasty Grand Astrologer divined this,
saying:
"The fifth month corresponds to Fire;
Fire corresponds to Lí;
Lí corresponds to literary brilliance.
Midday is the peak of literary brilliance.
Birds with colorful plumage singing—
this child will certainly possess literary talent,
and his fame will spread throughout the world.
Since the birds were small,
his official rank and fortune will likely not be high."
When he grew up,
he was widely learned with a strong memory,
composing essays as soon as he took up the brush,
but his official career indeed did not reach high rank.
All these were born on this day,
and each left their name for posterity.
As for the Fire Phase fearing Metal,
it lies hidden on Gēng days.
The Lì Jì Shì states:
What is 'hidden'?
It is the day when Metal energy lies concealed.
The four seasons alternate,
each giving birth to the next.
When Lìqiū arrives,
Metal replaces Fire.
Metal fears Fire,
so on Gēng days it must hide.
Gēng represents Metal.
Màn Qiàn cutting and receiving meat—
the Hàn Shū states:
Dōngfāng Shuò was a court gentleman.
On a Fú day,
an edict granted meat to the gentlemen.
Shuò alone drew his sword to cut the meat,
saying:
"On a Fú day, one should return early;
I request to receive the grant."
He then pocketed the meat and left.
The Emperor asked Shuò:
"Granting meat—
you did not wait for the edict's command;
why?"
Ordering him to reprimand himself.
Shuò said:
"Receiving a grant without awaiting the edict's command—
how rude!
Drawing a sword to cut meat—
how bold!
Cutting not too much—
how frugal!
Taking it home for my wife—
how benevolent!"
The Emperor said:
"I ordered you to reprimand yourself,
but instead you praised yourself."
The Zhāng family's offering to Huáng Shí.
See the note "offering at Gǔchéng" in the Shí Fù.
Sheep's milk is said to supply expenses—
the Hàn Guān Yí states:
Where fierce ghosts roam,
thus Fú.
During the Hàn and Wèi dynasties on Fú days,
there were gatherings with wine and food.
Thus the Hàn Shū states:
Yáng Yùn's "Xián Jū" says:
"Raising sheep and selling milk
to supply the expenses of Fú and Là."
In Bā and Shǔ, it is also heard they chose their own Fú days.
The Fēng Sú Tōng states:
In Hànzhōng, Bā, and Shǔ, they chose their own Fú days.
Custom says the land is warm and hot,
plants sprout early and wither late,
the climate differs from the Central Plains.
Since the Yí and Dí tribes lived there,
they were allowed to choose their own Fú days.
Respectfully submitted:
The Hàn Shū states:
Emperor Gāozǔ returned to pacify the Three Qín,
sweeping across the world.
It is because the gentleman relies on fundamentals,
thus he repeatedly bestowed special favor,
allowing them to choose their own Fú.
Jī Hán, distressed by heat, thought of wind—
Jī Hán's preface to the Kùn Rè Fù states:
The three Fú periods have just begun,
the season of autumn's decline has not yet arrived.
A lowly, poor scholar,
living in humble, narrow quarters.
No clear breeze enters the mean alley,
the short eaves provide no added shade.
Under the same sky, cold and heat differ;
in the same world, worry and joy are not the same.
Chéng Xiǎo closed his gate to avoid guests—
Chéng Xiǎo's poem states:
All my life during the three Fú times,
no carts travel on the roads.
Closing the gate, I lie avoiding the heat,
neither going out nor receiving visitors.
I advise all you wise gentlemen,
venturing out in the heat deserves reproach.
Xuán Mó's well just opened—
see the note above "when cold, drink from Míng Yì's well."
Qín Mù's offering first increased—
the Shǐ Jì states:
Qín Mù first established the Fú offering.
In Hé Shuò, there is the heat-avoidance drinking—
the Diǎn Lüè states:
The imperial carriage was at Xǔ.
Guānglù Dàfū Liú Sōng was sent north to oversee Yuán Shào's army.
He daily feasted and drank with Shào's sons and brothers.
Often during the three Fú period,
they drank to extreme drunkenness day and night,
saying:
"To avoid the heat of the season."
Thus in Hé Shuò there is the heat-avoidance drinking.
In Yè, there was the granting of ice—
the Yè Zhōng Jì states:
Shí Jìlóng stored ice at the Bīngjǐng Terrace.
During the three Fú months,
he granted ice to his high officials.
Following the custom of hot noodle soup for the season—
the Jīng Chǔ Suì Shí Jì states:
On the Fú day in the sixth month,
they all make hot noodle soup,
called "avoiding evil."
Offering wheat and melons at the ancestral shrine—
the Sì Mín Yuè Lìng states:
At the start of Fú, offer wheat and melons to ancestors.
These are all practices of the summer season,
thus recorded here to preserve what might be forgotten.
Autumn
The autumn days are bleak and dreary,
All plants wither and decay.
The Book of Songs says:
"The autumn days are bleak and dreary,
All plants wither and decay."
Annotation:
"Decay"
means to sicken.
As the humid heat fades and the clear autumn air arrives,
an ancient poem says:
"The bright sunlight through the window
Shines upon the southern end of my room.
The clear autumn air responds to autumn's arrival,
The humid heat fades with the changing season."
Wild geese come, and swallows return.
The Book of Rites says:
In the eighth month,
on the day of White Dew,
wild geese come;
five days later,
swallows return.
Chanting poems under the moonlight,
one appreciates Yuán Hóng's contentment:
The Book of Jin says:
Yuán Hóng
was orphaned and poor,
earning his living by transporting rent grain.
When Xiè Shàng was stationed at Niúzhǔ,
on an autumn night,
he sailed on the river under the moonlight
and encountered Yuán Hóng reciting poems in a boat.
He sent someone to inquire,
and it turned out to be his composition on history.
Xiè Shàng approached his boat and conversed with him,
staying awake until dawn,
and from then on, Yuán Hóng's fame grew daily.
Longing for home in Wúzhōng,
one admires Zhāng Hàn's foresight.
The New Account of the Tales of the World says:
Zhāng Hàn,
styled Jìyīng,
was appointed as an Eastern Officer under Prince Qí Jiǒng.
While in Luòyáng, he saw the autumn wind rise
and thought of the water shield soup and perch slices of Wúzhōng.
He said:
"Life is about following one's heart's desires;
why should one serve as an official a thousand miles away just to seek fame?"
So he ordered his carriage and returned home.
Soon after, Prince Qí fell from power,
and everyone said he had acted with foresight.
At this time, contraction and storage begin.
The Huainanzi says:
In early autumn, contraction begins;
in mid-autumn, storage begins.
The Chūlóu sacrifice is performed.
The Book of the Later Han says:
Shēntú Jiàn and others
joined with the Imperial Censor Wěi Xiāo
to plan to seize Gēngshǐ during the Chūlóu sacrifice on the day of the Beginning of Autumn.
The Commentary on the Former Han says:
"Chū"
refers to sacrificing animals on the day of the Beginning of Autumn.
The king also hunts animals on this day
to offer sacrifices at the ancestral temple.
In the north of Jìzhōu,
on the first day of the eighth month, food and drink are prepared for the Lóu sacrifice,
a custom called Lóulà.
"Lóu"
is pronounced "lóu."
Its affairs are speech,
its nature is righteousness.
The Commentary on the Monthly Ordinances says:
The "Great Plan" Treatise on the Five Phases says:
The west corresponds to metal,
its nature is righteousness,
its affairs are speech.
Speech is about compliance,
compliance leads to governance.
When the ruler's speech complies with righteousness and harmony,
the divine turtle appears.
The emperor's tribute grain is stored in the divine granary.
The Book of Rites says:
In the ninth month,
the emperor's tribute grain is stored in the divine granary,
with reverence and diligence.
The Director of Music is ordered to practice wind instruments.
The Book of Rites says:
In the eighth month,
the Director of Music is ordered to practice wind instruments.
Annotation:
Wind instruments are favored in autumn and winter,
so they are practiced.
The Fire Official is commanded to enforce fire regulations.
The Rites of Zhou says:
The Fire Official is in charge of fire regulations,
and in late autumn, fires are brought indoors.
Annotation:
In the ninth month, at dusk,
the Heart Star sets in the west,
and people are ordered to bring fires indoors.
"Guàn" is pronounced "guàn."
The "Bīn" poems are sung to welcome the cold air.
The Rites of Zhou says:
The Director of Flutes is in charge of mid-autumn,
beating the earthen drum
and playing the "Bīn" poems
to welcome the cold air.
Annotation:
Welcoming the cold
is to usher in the yin energy of the night.
White dew falls,
and cold cicadas chirp.
The Book of Rites says:
On the day of the Beginning of Autumn,
white dew descends;
five days later,
cold cicadas chirp.
The weaver insect cries sadly.
Bào Zhào of the Song dynasty wrote in "Reply to Tāng Huìxiū":
"Withered mulberry leaves fall easily,
A weary traveler's heart is easily startled.
Why is it so early this year?
Already I hear the weaver insect's cry."
Crickets chirp at night.
The "Nine Arguments" says:
How sorrowful is the autumn air!
Wild geese honk as they fly south,
and pheasants chirp mournfully.
Alone, I stay awake until dawn,
lamenting the crickets' nightly chirping.
Thus, the season of stern execution arrives.
The "Spring and Autumn Essence and Subtlety" says:
Frost kills and destroys,
signifying late autumn.
Frost begins to fall,
and hawks strike.
The ruler follows heaven's will to execute punishments,
to manifest the stern power of autumn.
Efforts focus on harvest.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng wrote in the "Compiled Essentials":
Autumn is called the season of white storage,
also the season of harvest.
Judgments are made and punishments carried out.
The "Great Commentary on the Book of Documents" says:
In autumn, the Son of Heaven orders the Three Dukes and generals
to select soldiers and sharpen weapons
to punish the unjust,
settle lawsuits,
carry out punishments,
and hasten the harvest.
This follows the way of heaven
and assists autumn's killing energy.
Generals are also selected and weapons sharpened.
The Book of Rites says:
The Son of Heaven welcomes autumn in the western suburbs.
Upon returning,
he rewards military commanders and warriors at court,
then orders generals
to select soldiers and sharpen weapons,
training the outstanding and brave.
He entrusts authority to the meritorious
to punish the unjust;
he interrogates and punishes the violent and arrogant,
to clarify good and evil.
At this time, heaven and earth begin to turn stern.
The Book of Rites says:
In the seventh month,
heaven and earth begin to turn stern,
and grain ripens.
Hawks and falcons strike.
The "Origin and Destiny" says:
On the day of the Beginning of Autumn,
hawks and falcons strike.
The Green Maiden descends with frost.
See the annotation "The deity is the Green Maiden" in the "Ode to Frost."
The Fur Official performs his duties.
The Rites of Zhou says:
The Fur Official
presents fine furs in mid-autumn
and functional furs in late autumn.
Seeing one leaf fall, one knows autumn has come.
The Huainanzi says:
When one leaf falls,
one knows autumn is here.
Observe all things bearing fruit.
The Huainanzi says:
Spring energy arises and all plants grow;
when autumn arrives, all fruits ripen.
Its emperor is Shàohào,
its deity is Rùshōu.
From the Book of Rites.
He rides the Dui trigram and holds the square.
The Huainanzi says:
The emperor of the west is Shàohào,
assisted by Rùshōu,
who holds the square to govern autumn.
His deity is Tàibái.
The Xun trigram declines and the Li trigram rests.
The "Discussion on the Rise and Fall of the Five Phases" says:
On the day of the Beginning of Autumn,
Kūn is king, Duì is minister,
Qián is fetus, Kǎn is hidden,
Gěn is death, Zhèn is imprisoned,
Xùn is abandoned, Lí is at rest.
Observe the Dipper’s handle pointing west;
The *Hèguànzǐ* says:
“When the Dipper’s handle points west,
all under heaven it is autumn.”
Recognize the Great Fire star thus descending.
The *Shī* says:
“In the seventh month the Fire star descends.”
Note:
“Liú” means
to go down.
As for taking fire from the oak and evergreen oak,
the *Zōuzǐ* says:
“In autumn, take fire from the oak and evergreen oak.”
Plant the pagoda tree and mulberry tree.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
In the first month of autumn,
the divine maiden of the Western Palace,
white in color and white in adornment,
strikes the white bell,
her weapon is the battle-axe.
The eighth month’s official is the Commandant,
its tree is the mulberry.
The ninth month’s official is the Inspector,
its tree is the pagoda tree.
The Star of Longevity already appears at the South Pole;
The *Lǐ* says:
At the autumn equinox,
offer sacrifices to the Star of Longevity in the southern suburbs.
Note:
The South Pole
is the Old Man star.
The sun’s chariot also travels along the Western Path.
The *Yì Tōngtǒng Tú* says:
“The sun’s path in the west, the white path, is called the Western Path.”
Flocks of birds thereby store up food;
The *Lǐ* says:
“In the eighth month, flocks of birds store up food.”
The Director of Arrows thereby presents arrow quivers.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
The Director of Bows and Arrows,
in mid-autumn presents arrow quivers.
Note:
“Fú” is
a vessel for holding arrows.
Command the Minister of War to drill the troops;
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
“The Grand Minister of War, in mid-autumn, instructs in drilling the troops.”
Order the light carriages to gather customs.
The *Fēngsútōng* says:
The Zhōu and Qín often in the eighth month dispatched envoys in light carriages to gather unusual customs and dialects,
storing them in the secret archives.
As for reverently sending off the setting sun,
The *Shū* says:
“Separately commanded Hé Zhòng,
to dwell in the west,
at the Valley of Dusk.
Reverently send off the setting sun,
orderly regulate the western completion.”
The flourishing virtue resides in Metal.
The *Lǐ* says:
The Grand Historian, three days before the beginning of autumn,
announces to the Son of Heaven:
“On such a day begins autumn,
the flourishing virtue resides in Metal.”
On the day of the beginning of autumn,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the dukes, marquises, and high officials,
to welcome autumn in the western suburbs.
Chanting and whistling in groups,
moved by Lǐ Líng at the frontier;
Hàn Lǐ Líng’s *Letter to Sū Wǔ* says:
“In the deep autumn of the ninth month,
beyond the frontier the grass withers.
Barbarian flutes call back and forth,
herding horses neigh mournfully.
Chanting and whistling in groups,
border sounds arise on all sides.”
Too many to attend to,
wearied Zǐjìng in Shānyīn.
The *Shìshuō* says:
Wáng Zǐjìng said:
“Walking along the road in Shānyīn,
mountains and rivers reflect each other in splendor,
making one feel there is too much to attend to.
If it happens in autumn or winter,
it is especially hard to bear.”
One may repair city walls;
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
The farthest reaches of the west,
the mountain of three colors.
Stone walls and golden chambers,
people who feed on breath,
the land of immortality,
what Shàohào and Rùshōu govern
extends twelve thousand lǐ.
Its command says:
“Examine the application of laws,
punish the guilty.
Repair city walls?
Mend broken dikes.
Guard the ravines and valleys,
secure the gates and alleys.”
One may secure gates and alleys.
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
In autumn,
on the days of Gēng and Xīn,
issue five governmental measures:
First,
prohibit gambling;
second, do not display the blades of the five weapons;
third,
encourage the traveling farmers,
hasten to gather the harvest;
fourth,
repair deficiencies and cracks,
mend walls and fences,
secure gates and alleys;
fifth,
follow the seasons for the five grains.
Hàn Emperor Wǔ dredged divine creatures from the Lín Pond;
The *Shíyíjì* says:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn once in late autumn floated a divine egret boat on the Lín Pond,
using fragrant gold for hooks,
twisted silk threads for lines,
red carp as bait,
hooked a white flood dragon,
and gave it to the Grand Provisioner to make cured fish.
Its flesh was purple, bones blue,
fragrant and delicious beyond compare.
King Mù’s bookworms at Yǔlíng.
The *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* says:
On the jiǎxū day of mid-autumn,
the Son of Heaven traveled east,
stopped at Quèliáng,
and had bookworms at Yǔlíng.
Note:
Refers to airing books to kill bookworms,
hence called “bookworming.”
Gazing at the clouds over the high hill,
secretly connecting to an auspicious dream;
The *Yuánmìngbāo* says:
Yáo was Son of Heaven,
in the last ten days of late autumn,
dreamed the White Emperor bestowed upon him a bird-beaked child.
His mother sought support,
first ascended a high hill.
Above the White Emperor were clouds like a tiger,
moved, she gave birth to Gāoyáo.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
Gāoyáo
had a bird’s beak.
Meeting for chess in the carved chamber,
naturally harmonizing with auspicious signs.
The *Xījīng Zájì* says:
Jiǎ Pèilán said:
“When in the palace,
on the fourth day of the eighth month, we would go out the north door of the carved chamber to the bamboo grove below to play chess.
The winner would have good fortune all year;
the loser would suffer illness all year.”
As for when plants and trees turn yellow and fall,
hibernating insects seal their burrows.
The *Lǐ* says:
At the autumn equinox node,
hibernating insects seal their burrows.
See the divine dragon diving into the abyss;
The *Shuōwén* says:
The dragon,
chief of the scaly creatures,
at the spring equinox ascends to heaven;
at the autumn equinox dives into the abyss.
Recognize the colorful pouch holding dew.
The *Xù Qíxiéjì* says:
Dèng Shào from Hóngnóng,
on the morning of the eighth month entered Huàshān,
saw a youth,
using a five-colored pouch to collect dew from under cypress leaves,
saying:
“Master Chìsōng takes it to brighten the eyes.”
Now on the morning of the eighth month, making bright-eye pouches
imitates this.
As for when the Metal qi is just vigorous,
Bào Zhào’s poem “Autumn Evening” says:
“The Metal qi is just fiercely killing,
the descending sun weakens and wanes.”
The clear wind warns of cold.
The *Guóyǔ* says:
“When the constellation Sì appears, frost falls;
when the Fire star appears, the clear wind warns of cold.”
Severe frost enacts Hóu Wén’s duty;
see the “Frost Rhapsody” note on “Majesty establishes Hóu Wén.”
Flying cicadas alight on Zhū Yì’s cap.
The *Liángshū* says:
When Zhū Yì was appointed Central Secretariat Gentleman,
on an autumn day at the beginning of his appointment,
a flying cicada alighted right on Zhū Yì’s martial cap.
At the time, all said it was an omen of “cicada ear ornaments.”
Dew begins to moisten the garden chrysanthemums,
Xiè Huìlián’s poem “Pounding Clothes” says:
The celestial measure knows no lingering pace,
The sundial’s motion swift as if urged on.
White dew moistens the garden chrysanthemums,
Autumn wind sheds leaves from the courtyard sophora.
The wind has already withered the clustered orchids.
The Wénzǐ says:
The sun and moon wish to shine bright,
But floating clouds cover them;
Clustered orchids wish to flourish,
But the autumn wind withers them.
Then there is the hawk sacrificing birds without error,
The Lǐ says:
In the seventh month,
The hawk then sacrifices birds.
Five days later,
Heaven and earth begin to turn severe.
The jackal sacrifices beasts without fail.
The Lǐ says:
In the ninth month,
The jackal then sacrifices beasts.
The bell of the Western Palace has already been struck,
See the note above on “planting sophora and paper mulberry trees.”
The fire of Xiāoqiū naturally extinguishes.
See the note on “pointing to the blazing heat at Xiāoqiū” in the “Rhapsody on Fire.”
Dew condenses cold and turns bleak and clear,
Pān Yuè’s “Rhapsody on Autumn Stirrings” says:
The moon, hazy and dim, holds its light,
Dew, bleak and clear, condenses cold.
Cicadas, imbued with wind, sound desolate.
Xiè Huìlián’s poem “Longing for Autumn” says:
Desolate, wind-imbued cicadas,
Lonely cries of geese passing through clouds.
As for the reeds, lush and green,
White dew becomes frost;
From the Shī.
Chrysanthemums have yellow blooms,
The Lǐ says:
In the ninth month,
Chrysanthemums have yellow flowers.
Clouds appear like flocks of sheep;
The Yuèlìng Zhānhòu Tú says:
At the beginning of autumn,
The Kūn trigram takes effect.
In the late afternoon,
A cool wind arrives from the southwest,
Yellow clouds like flocks of sheep,
Favorable for millet and grain.
Tree leaves begin to fall slightly,
Xiè Xīyì’s “Rhapsody on the Moon” says:
The Dòngtíng Lake begins to ripple,
Tree leaves begin to fall slightly.
Green grass turns to withered yellow.
Liú Shuò’s poem says:
The vast sky, clear and high,
Autumn air brings the first coolness.
White dew descends in fine droplets,
The bright moon flows with pure light.
Condensed mist drifts over city walls and towers,
A bleak wind enters the chamber.
Red flowers wither and fall first,
Green grass turns to withered yellow.
Fine silk returns to the chest,
Light gauze changes to clothing.
Solemn and clear scenes in the plain season,
Lù Jī’s poem says:
Solemn, solemn plain autumn season,
Deep, deep thick dew congeals.
Following the seasonal order in the white storehouse.
The Ěryǎ says:
Autumn is called the white storehouse.
As for the celestial river’s divine pair,
Seen on the seventh night of the seventh month.
Xiè Huìlián’s poem “The Seventh Night of the Seventh Month” says:
The celestial river has a divine pair,
Through the years and months they accompany each other.
The Ruǎn lane boasts clothes of fine silk and brocade,
The Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn says:
The various Ruǎn were quite adept at managing their households,
Ample in wealth within,
Only Jí in the lane,
Fond of wine but poor.
According to old custom, on the seventh day of the seventh month,
It was customary to air clothes in the sun,
In the courtyards of the various Ruǎn, splendidly displayed,
None were not fine silk and brocade.
Jí’s elder brother’s son Xián,
At the time still wearing his hair in tufts,
Then erected a long pole,
Hung a large cloth apron in the courtyard,
Saying:
“Unable to avoid custom,
I merely follow suit.”
The Wèi palace grieves over the glass brush.
The Fēngtǔ Jì says:
Lù Jī wrote:
While in Píngyuán,
I once inspected the utensils of Lord Cáo,
Five writing knives,
One glass brush.
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the second year of Jīngchū,
Consort Liú said:
“Seeing this makes one feel sorrowful.”
Note:
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi served as Chancellor in Hàn,
He could not have had a consort.
Moreover,
Jīngchū was the reign era of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Knowing this, it must be an object from Emperor Wén’s time,
Placed together with Lord Cáo’s utensils and playthings,
Hence causing confusion.
Some spread curtains of cloud-patterned brocade,
The Hàn Wǔdì Nèizhuàn says:
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
The palace quarters were swept clean,
Curtains of cloud-patterned brocade were spread,
Nine subtle lamps were lit,
After the second watch at night,
The Queen Mother of the West rode a nine-colored dappled dragon up to the hall.
Some tread in dark jade shoes.
The Hàn Wǔdì Nèizhuàn says:
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
The Queen Mother of the West descended,
Emperor Wǔ wore the crown of Tàizhēn’s morning tassels,
Treading in dark jade shoes with phoenix patterns.
Dàowǔ then received auspicious signs at Cānhé,
The Hòu Wèi Shū says:
Emperor Dàowǔ was born at Cānhébēi on the seventh day of the seventh month.
The Hàn Emperor then received auspicious news at Yīlán.
The Hàn Wǔdì Gùshì says:
Emperor Jǐng dreamed that Emperor Gāozǔ said to him:
“Consort Wáng will give birth to a son,
He may be named Zhì.”
In the year Yǐyǒu,
At dawn on the seventh day of the seventh month,
Emperor Wǔ was born in the Yīlán Hall.
The Dòngmíng Jì says:
Emperor Jǐng dreamed of a red pig descending from the clouds to the Chóngfāng Pavilion,
The Emperor awoke and sat in the pavilion,
Indeed saw red vapor like a forest,
Coming to cover the doors and windows,
Then changed the pavilion’s name to Yīlán Hall.
Later, Consort Wáng gave birth to Emperor Wǔ.
According to this, Emperor Wǔ was initially named Zhì.
Playing in the layered city,
The Yúdì Zhì says:
Emperor Qíwǔ built the Layered City Tower,
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Many palace ladies climbed it to thread needles,
The world called it the Needle-Threading Tower.
Fittingly opening the lapel.
The Xījīng Zájì says:
Hàn palace ladies often threaded needles in the Open Lapel Tower on the seventh day of the seventh month.
The Queen Mother of the West then had green birds attending beside her,
The Hàn Wǔ Gùshì says:
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
The Emperor was fasting in the center of the Chénghuá Hall,
Suddenly a bird came from the west and alighted before the hall.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
“This means the Queen Mother of the West wishes to come.”
After a while,
The Queen Mother arrived,
With two green birds attending beside the Queen Mother.
Empress Dòu then had divine light illuminating the room.
The Hòu Hànshū says:
Empress Dòu was bald as a child,
Not regarded by her family,
On the seventh night of the seventh month,
Everyone went to see the Weaving Maid,
Only the Empress was not allowed to go out,
Then divine light illuminated the room,
An auspicious sign for the Empress.
There was also threading needles through seven holes,
The Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì says:
On the seventh night of the seventh month,
Women build colorful towers,
Thread needles through seven holes,
Or use gold, silver, or brass for needles.
Lamps lit with nine subtle lights.
See the note above on “spreading curtains of cloud-patterned brocade.”
Commanding the carriage of five dragons,
The Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Wú Cài Jīng left home when already old,
Upon returning,
Became young and vigorous again,
Beard and hair all black.
He told his family,
Saying on the seventh day of the seventh month,
Lord Wáng would come,
They could prepare several hundred hu of drink for him.
On the appointed day,
Wáng Fāngpíng indeed came,
Riding a feathered carriage,
Driving five dragons.
They heard the sounds of golden drums, pipes, and men and horses.
By the Hundred Sons Pond.
The Xījīng Zájì says:
Consort Qī’s maid Jiǎ Pèilán said:
“While in the palace,
I saw Consort Qī attending Emperor Gāozǔ,
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
by the Baizi Pond,
after performing the music of Yútián,
they tied each other with five-colored threads,
calling it "linked ribbons."
Ascending Shùn Mountain to gaze afar,
the Youyáng Zázǔ states:
Wei's Deputy Director Shōu visited Dài,
on the seventh day of the seventh month,
he ascended Shùn Mountain,
lingered and looked around,
and said to his Registrar Cuī Fǔ:
"I have traveled extensively.
In terms of fertile lands and rivers,
strategic terrain and natural barriers,
no renowned prefecture under heaven
surpasses this place.
I only wonder how Dōngyáng compares."
Composing poetry while attending at Xuánpǔ Garden.
Jìn Pān Ní's poem "Attending the Crown Prince's Banquet at Xuánpǔ Garden on the Seventh Day of the Seventh Month" says:
The autumn wind begins to blow,
the morning fire faintly flows.
The bright summer is sent off,
Shàohào welcomes autumn.
Fine grains flourish in the garden,
fragrant grasses cover the fields.
At this time, our lord,
finds joy and leisure.
Jìn Xuān airing books in haste,
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states:
Wèi Wǔ summoned Gāozǔ,
but Gāozǔ, believing the Hàn dynasty was nearing its end,
did not wish to submit to the Cáo family,
excused himself by claiming paralysis,
unable to rise or move.
Wèi Wǔ sent a trusted clerk in plain clothes to rest under the shade of a tree outside Gāozǔ's gate.
At the time, it was the seventh day of the seventh month,
and Gāozǔ was airing his books.
The clerk secretly observed this.
Returning,
he reported everything.
Wèi Wǔ then sent another summons,
instructing the envoy:
"If he still refuses to move,
you may arrest him."
Gāozǔ, fearing this, accepted the command.
Hǎo Lóng basking his belly leisurely;
the Shì Shuō states:
Hǎo Lóng,
on the seventh day of the seventh month,
saw his neighbors airing their clothes in the sun,
so he lay on his back, exposing his belly,
saying he was airing his books.
Táo Ān riding a dragon far away,
see the note "scatter Táo Ān's smelting" in the "Fu on Fire."
Zǐ Qiáo riding a crane, hard to follow.
See the note "seeing Wáng Qiáo at Gōushì" in the "Fu on Mountains."
As for the auspicious day of Chóngyáng,
it falls on the ninth day.
The Qí Rén Yuè Lìng states:
On Chóngyáng day, one must have cake and wine,
ascend high to gaze afar,
to express autumn sentiments,
picking zhūyú and chrysanthemums to steep in wine.
Dropping Mèng Jiā's hat,
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states:
Mèng Jiā served as Huán Wēn's military advisor.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, Wēn visited Lóng Mountain,
with all his subordinates gathered.
The wind blew off Jiā's hat,
but he did not notice,
and went to the restroom.
Sūn Shèng was present at the time,
and Wēn gave him paper and brush, ordering him to mock Jiā,
placing the writing at Jiā's seat.
When Jiā returned and saw it,
he laughed and requested paper to reply,
without a moment's hesitation.
Transmitting Fèi Chángfáng's method.
The Xù Qíxié Jì states:
Rǔnán Huán Jǐng studied under Fèi Chángfáng.
Chángfáng told him:
"On the ninth day of the ninth month,
your family will face disaster.
Hurry home,
have each family member make a crimson pouch,
fill it with zhūyú and tie it to their arm,
ascend high and drink chrysanthemum wine,
and this calamity can be avoided."
Jǐng returned home
and did as instructed.
When he came back,
he saw the chickens, dogs, cows, and sheep
had all died suddenly.
Drinking wine while ascending high on the ninth day
and wearing zhūyú pouches
originates from this.
White-clad,
Wáng Hóng's delivery,
the Xù Jìnyáng Qiū states:
Táo Qián once had no wine on the ninth day of the ninth month.
By the eastern fence near his house,
he plucked a handful of chrysanthemums from the bushes
and sat beside them.
Before long,
he saw a white-clad person arriving—
it was Wáng Hóng delivering wine.
He then drank to his heart's content.
Yellow chrysanthemums,
Wèi Wén's gift.
Wèi Wéndì's "Letter to Zhōng Yáo on the Ninth Day" states:
In the past, Qū Píng, lamenting his gradual aging,
thought of eating the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums,
to nourish the body and prolong life—
nothing is more precious than this.
I respectfully offer a bundle
to aid in the methods of Péngzǔ.
Ascending the high Biāo Pavilion for enjoyment,
the Nán Qí Shū states:
Gāozǔ ascended the Biāo Pavilion on the ninth day of the ninth month.
The pavilion is on the ridge of Sūnlíng Temple,
commonly called the Ninth Day Terrace.
Pointing to Xìmǎ Terrace as the departure point.
The Nán Qí Shū states:
When Sòng Wǔdì was Duke of Sòng,
in Péngchéng,
on the ninth day of the ninth month, he departed from Xiàng Yǔ's Xìmǎ Terrace.
To this day, this tradition continues,
regarded as an established custom.
The three steps where Shān Jiǎn ascended.
The Xiāngyáng Jì states:
Wàngchǔ Mountain,
formerly called Mǎ'ān Mountain.
When Sòng's Prince Wǔlíng Jùn served as regional inspector,
he renamed it Wàngchǔ Mountain.
Later, when he ascended the throne,
people called it Fèng Ridge.
At its peak are three steps,
where Liú Hóng and Shān Jiǎn feasted and enjoyed the view on the ninth day.
The nine wells where Zhòng Wén roamed.
The Gūshú Jì states:
Ten lǐ south of the county are the Jiǔjǐng Mountains,
where Yīn Zhòngwén composed poetry with Huán on the ninth day at the nine wells.
Indulging in Xiè Língyùn's poetic thoughts,
Xiè Língyùn's poem "On the Ninth Day, Following the Duke of Sòng to Xìmǎ Terrace" says:
Late autumn on the northern frontier is harsh,
migrating geese flee frost and snow.
Admiring Xiè Zhān's poetic brush,
Xiè Zhān's poem "On the Ninth Day, Following the Duke of Sòng to Xìmǎ Terrace" says:
The wind arrives, bestowing cold garments,
frost descends, all labors cease.
In Jìn, they held scriptures to illuminate the Way,
the Jìnyáng Qiū states:
In the third year of Níngkāng,
on the ninth day of the ninth month,
the emperor once lectured on the Xiàojīng,
with Xiè Ān in attendance,
Lù Nà and Biàn Dān reading aloud,
Xiè Shí and Yuán Hóng holding the scriptures,
Chē Yìn and Wáng Wēn selecting passages.
In Qí, they practiced martial arts to respond to auspicious signs.
The Nán Qí Shū states:
In Southern Qí, on the ninth day of the ninth month, they held mounted archery,
some saying autumn's metal energy
calls for martial training,
imitating the Hàn dynasty's Lìqiū rituals.
Such are the grand gatherings of the ninth day,
revealing the traces of former worthies.
The night is excessively hot,
which is not a method for nurturing health."
The Emperor said:
"It is because the night is quiet."
Xiè Gōng sighed and said:
"His Majesty's understanding of principles is no less than that of the late Emperor."
Xīhuá still wore a coarse silk skirt.
The Book of Liáng states:
Rén Fǎng was always poor and upright.
After his death,
his son Xīhuá,
in the winter months, wore a hempen cape and a plain silk skirt.
On the road, he met Liú Xiàobiāo,
who shed tears of pity for him.
Thereupon, he wrote "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn"
to criticize Rén Fǎng's old friends.
There were even those who inquired about the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the coming year.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Tiānfǔ official is in charge of displaying jade in the last month of winter
to divine the good or ill fortune of the coming year.
The annotation says:
To inquire about the correctness of affairs is called zhēn,
meaning to consult the tortoise shell.
They presented the dreams of the officials.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The dream interpreter:
In the last month of winter,
he inquires about the king's dreams,
presents auspicious dreams to the king,
and the king bows and accepts them.
The annotation says:
Pìn means to inquire.
They present the auspicious dreams of the officials to attribute beauty to them.
They ordered the Sīkòu to present the population figures.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The minor Sīkòu, in the first month of winter, sacrifices to the Sīmín star
and presents the population figures to the king.
The king bows and accepts them,
using them to plan the state's expenditures
and to promote or demote officials.
Annotation:
Sīmín is a star,
the horn of Xuānyuán.
They ordered the Sīkōng to discuss land affairs.
The Dà Dài Lǐ states:
The Sīkōng is in charge of winter,
using regulations to manage land affairs.
He surveys the mountains and forests,
marks out the plains and fertile lands,
stores water, establishes markers for irrigation,
and regulates the affairs of the four seasons.
He manages the distances of the land,
assigns the people's labor,
and regulates the people's food.
The year is ending and the time is growing dark.
The "Snow Rhapsody" says:
The year is coming to an end,
the time is growing dark,
the cold wind accumulates,
and sorrowful clouds abound.
The moon reaches the end of its cycle and the sun reaches the end of its course.
The Book of Rites says:
In the twelfth month,
the sun reaches the end of its course,
the moon reaches the end of its cycle,
and the stars complete their circuit in the sky.
The numbers are nearly at their end,
and the year is about to begin anew.
Yán Yánnián shed blood in deciding legal cases.
The Book of Hàn states:
Yán Yánnián was the governor of Hénán.
In the winter months,
he summoned prisoners from the subordinate counties
to gather at the prefectural office,
and blood flowed for several miles.
Hénán called him the Butcher.
Wáng Wēnshū stamped his feet in carrying out his duties.
The Book of Hàn states:
Wáng Wēnshū was the governor of Hénèi.
He memorialized to execute over a thousand powerful and crafty families in the commandery,
the larger ones exterminating their clans,
the smaller ones put to death.
By the end of the twelfth month,
there were no thieves in the commandery, not even a barking dog.
When criminals fled to neighboring commanderies,
he pursued and captured them.
When spring arrived and the executions ceased,
Wáng Wēnshū stamped his feet and sighed:
"Alas,
if only the winter could be extended by one more month,
my work would be sufficient."
The annotation says:
After the beginning of spring,
executions are not carried out,
hence he said this.
Shèng Jí wrote legal documents while weeping.
The Records of Kuàijī states:
Shèng Jí was the Commandant of Justice.
Every winter month,
when prisoners were to be sentenced,
his wife held a candle,
and Shèng Jí held a red brush,
facing each other and weeping.
Yú Jīng sentenced prisoners and shed tears.
The Book of the Later Hàn states:
Yú Xǔ's grandfather, Yú Jīng,
was a prison officer in the commandery and county.
He applied the law fairly and justly,
always seeking leniency and forgiveness.
In the winter months, when he submitted his reports,
he often shed tears as he did so.
He once said:
"Yú Gōng of Dōnghǎi built a high gate for his village,
and his son, Yú Dìngguó, eventually became Chancellor.
I have decided legal cases for sixty years.
Although I am not equal to Yú Gōng,
am I not close?
Why should my descendants not become the Nine Ministers?"
Therefore, he named his grandson Xǔ, with the courtesy name Shēngqīng.
Yú Xǔ rose to the position of Imperial Secretary.
Also,
Fù Xián of the Later Hàn
also shed tears when sentencing prisoners on the winter solstice.
These are the seasonal ordinances that were followed,
yet the practices of leniency and cruelty differed.
As for guarding the passes and bridges and blocking the paths,
The Book of Rites says:
In the tenth month,
order the officials:
Close up and complete winter,
guard the passes and bridges,
and block the paths.
Carefully cover and store, and close the gates.
The Great Commentary of the Book of Documents states:
The Son of Heaven, in winter, orders the Three Dukes
to carefully cover and store,
close the gates,
and secure the borders,
to assist winter in solidifying the earth's storage.
The ice officer cuts ice.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The ice officer is in charge of ice.
In the twelfth month of the regular year,
he orders the cutting of ice,
three times the amount needed.
Annotation:
"The twelfth month of the regular year
refers to the twelfth month of the Xià calendar.
Three times the amount needed
is to account for melting."
The Son of Heaven tastes fish.
The Monthly Ordinances of the Book of Rites states:
In the twelfth month,
on the day of the great cold,
the Son of Heaven personally goes to taste fish.
The annotation says:
The fish is pure and delicious at this time.
The virtue of Zhào Cuī is akin to cherishing the day.
See the annotation in the "Rhapsody on the Sun": "Comparing fear and love to Cuī and Dùn."
The duty of Hé Shū is in Yōudū.
The Book of Documents says:
He further ordered Hé Shū
to reside in the north,
called Yōudū,
to peacefully observe the changes of the north.
The farmers have already completed their tasks.
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
In the tenth month,
the farming tasks are completed,
the five grains are already harvested,
and households prepare their stores.
Scholars diligently study during the remaining days of the year.
The Wèi Lüè states:
Dǒng Yù was fond of learning.
When people came to study with him,
Dǒng Yù said:
"You should first read the book a hundred times,
and its meaning will naturally become clear."
The followers said:
"It is difficult to find leisure time."
Dǒng Yù said:
"You should use the three spare times:
the spare time in winter,
the spare time at night, and the spare time on rainy days."
They laugh at the farmer who basks in the sun.
See the annotation in the "Rhapsody on the Sun": "Returning joyfully to bask in the sun."
They praise the clerk who escorts prisoners.
The Book of the Later Hàn states:
Zhōnglí Yì was appointed as a clerk under the Grand Minister over the Masses, Hóu Bà.
He was ordered to escort prisoners to Hénèi.
At that time, it was cold in winter,
and the prisoners were ill and unable to walk.
Passing through Hóngnóng,
he immediately ordered the subordinate counties to make clothes for the prisoners.
The counties had no choice but to comply.
He submitted a report explaining the situation,
and Zhōnglí Yì also fully reported it to the emperor.
Emperor Guangwu received the memorial and
said to Xiàn Bà:
"The clerk you sent is truly devoted in his intentions!
He is indeed a fine official."

Now the secretariat has neither ancient maps,

each lacking a scale,

Some contain extravagant and absurd words about distant wilderness,

Now the principles for making maps have six:
first is the scale,
used to distinguish the degrees of breadth and length.
Second is zhǔnwàng,
used to correct the relative positions of places.
Third is the road distance,
used to determine the numbers of routes taken.
Fourth is elevation,
fifth is direction and slope,
sixth is winding and straightness,
these three are each determined according to the terrain,
used to compare the numbers of ease and difficulty.
Having images without a scale,
then there is no way to examine the differences of far and near;
having a scale without zhǔnwàng,
even if obtained in one corner,
will surely be lost in other directions;
having zhǔnwàng without road distance,
then applied to lands separated by mountains and seas,
cannot connect;
having road distance without comparing elevation, direction and slope, winding and straightness,
then the numbers of direct paths will surely contradict the reality of far and near,
losing the correctness of zhǔnwàng.
These six, examined together,
therefore even with the separation of high mountains and vast seas,
the remoteness of distant lands and foreign regions,
the reasons for ascent, descent, and winding paths,
all can be raised and determined.

also called Shào Suǒ.
North: Jī Bīng,
also called Wěi Yǔ.
The energies of the Eight Hóng
give rise to cold and heat.
Beyond the Eight Hóng,
there are the Eight Extremes.
The clouds from the Eight Extremes
rain upon all under heaven."
The commentary says:
"Fǎn Hù is in Rìnán,
where doors face north.
The Jiāo Yáo people
are three chǐ tall,
wearing clothes, hats, and belts with swords.
Jīn Qiū
is where gold comes from.
Yī Mù:
its people have one eye.
Wěi Yǔ
is a mountain name;
to its north, the sun is not seen."
The Four Extremes and Four Wilds:
The *Eryǎ* says:
"East to Tài Yuǎn,
west to Bīn Guó,
south to Pú Qiān,
north to Zhù Lì—
these are called the Four Extremes.
Gū Zhú,
Běi Hù,
Xī Wáng Mǔ,
Rì Xià—
these are called the Four Wilds."
They reach as far as Shù Hài could tread
and Dà Zhāng could measure.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
"The Emperor ordered Shù Hài
to pace from the eastern extreme
to the western extreme,
a distance of 510,098,008 paces."
The commentary says:
"Xuǎn
means ten thousand."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"Yǔ sent Dà Zhāng to pace from the eastern extreme to the western extreme,
a distance of 230,000,357 lǐ.
He sent Shù Hài to pace from the northern extreme to the southern extreme,
and it was the same."
How virtuous is that gentle earth!
Xiè Zhuāng's *Rhapsody on the Moon* says:
"The gentle earth congeals like snow,
the round spirit mirrors like water."
How supreme is the mare!
The *Book of Changes* says:
"The origin of Kūn brings prosperity;
it is beneficial for the mare's constancy."
It follows Qián above,
as the *Shìmíng* says:
"Earth is called Kūn.
Kūn
means compliance,
complying with Qián above."
It also draws near to what is below.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"What originates from heaven draws near to what is above;
what originates from earth draws near to what is below."
As for examining the animals and plants of the five soils
and measuring the breadth and length of the Nine Provinces:
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
"The Grand Minister of Education oversees the maps of the land under heaven,
comprehensively knowing the breadth and length of the Nine Provinces' territories.
He distinguishes the living things of the five lands:
First, mountains and forests:
animals suitable are furred,
plants suitable are dark.
Second, rivers and marshes:
animals suitable are scaled,
plants suitable are oily.
Third, hills and mounds:
animals suitable are feathered,
plants suitable are stone-fruited.
Fourth, mounds and plains:
animals suitable are shelled,
plants suitable are podded.
Fifth, plateaus and wetlands:
animals suitable are naked,
plants suitable are clustered."
The commentary says:
"East-west is breadth,
north-south is length."
Duke Huán asked and thus knew the numbers.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"May I hear the numbers of the earth?"
He replied:
"East-west: 26,000 lǐ,
north-south: 26,000 lǐ,
land above water: 8,000 lǐ,
land receiving water: 8,000 lǐ."
Mòzǐ answered and called it benevolent.
The *Mòzǐ* says:
Qínzǐ asked whether heaven or earth is more benevolent.
Mòzǐ said:
"Dí considers earth benevolent.
People clothe from it, eat from it, die on it, and are buried in it,
yet earth never demands virtue in return.
Therefore, I consider earth benevolent."
It is said to be selfless.
The *Book of Rites* says:
Confucius said:
"Serve the three selfless ones
to labor for all under heaven.
Heaven covers selflessly,
earth carries selflessly,
the sun and moon shine selflessly."
It is also said to be established later.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"When the Supreme Ultimate first formed,
the clear and turbid began to separate,
so heaven formed first and earth was established later."
The way of earth is lowly yet ascends.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"The way of earth is lowly, yet it ascends."
Its virtue is square and supremely still.
See the annotation above on "embracing all things and transforming their radiance."
As for establishing the Office of Earth Instruction to announce affairs,
the *Rites of Zhōu* states:
The Earth Instructor is in charge of explaining maps to announce matters concerning the land.
Appointing the Fire Director to oversee this.
The *Records of the Grand Historian: Calendar Treatise* states:
Zhuānxū appointed the Southern Director Zhòng to oversee the heavens and govern the spirits,
and appointed the Fire Director Lí to oversee the earth and govern the people.
Yìng Shào said:
Lí
was an official of the yin.
The number of fire is two.
Two
is the number of earth,
so the Fire Director oversees the earth.
The vastness of the six directions and four extremes,
see the annotation below.
The suitability of the seven surfaces and nine regions.
The *Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng* states:
Heaven has the five phases,
earth has the five sacred mountains.
Heaven has the seven stars,
earth has the seven surfaces.
Heaven has the eight energies,
earth has the eight winds.
Heaven has the nine paths,
earth has the nine provinces.
Heaven has the four dimensions,
earth has the four great rivers.
Zhāng Héng's *Língxiàn Fù* states:
Earth has nine regions of mountains and rivers.
Reaching the boundless wilderness of Wǎnglǎng,
making an appointment with Hànmàn.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
Lú Áo traveled to the Northern Sea,
reaching the summit of Ménggǔ,
he saw a man there,
and spoke to him, saying:
"Only I, Áo, have turned my back on the crowd and left my companions,
exhaustively observing beyond the six directions,
traveling all around the four extremes,
only the northern darkness I have not yet glimpsed.
You might perhaps be able to befriend me, Áo?"
The man sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
You are a man of the central region,
how could you be willing to come this far?
As for me, I have traveled south to the wilderness of Wǎnglǎng,
rested north in the land of deep darkness,
exhausted the west in the realm of obscurity,
opened the light of vastness in the east,
there below is no earth and above is no heaven,
listening, one hears nothing,
looking, one sees no flicker.
You begin your travels here,
yet speak of exhaustive observation,
is that not also far-fetched!
However, you stay here,
I have an appointment with Hànmàn atop the nine layers of heaven."
He raised his arms and straightened his body,
then entered the clouds.
The annotation states:
Lú Áo
was a man of Yān.
Qín Shǐhuáng summoned him to be an Erudite,
sent him to seek immortals and spirits,
but he vanished and never returned.
𥁠
is pronounced quán.
Hànmàn
means unknowable.
Jiǔgāi
means the nine heavens.
As for its formation from accumulated yin,
the *Huángdì Sùwèn* states:
Accumulated yin forms the earth.
Tranquil in attaining the One,
the *Lǎozǐ* states:
Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil,
if earth were not tranquil, it would fear upheaval.
Stirring rivers and seas without leaking,
the *Rites* states:
Now take the earth,
as much as a pinch of soil,
yet in its breadth and thickness,
it bears the sacred mountains without heaviness,
stirs rivers and seas without leaking,
and carries all things.
Rising with Bì and Mǎo and opening to the right.
The *Shīzǐ* states:
Within the eight extremes, there are rulers and elders,
east to west twenty-eight thousand lǐ,
north to south twenty-six thousand lǐ,
therefore it is said, "Heaven stretches left and rises with Qiānniú,
earth opens right and rises with Bì and Mǎo."
Supported by eight pillars,
the *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
Below the earth are eight pillars,
spanning one hundred thousand lǐ,
with three thousand six hundred axles,
mutually restraining each other,
famous mountains and great rivers,
with caves and openings interconnecting.
Divided into nine categories,
the *Chǔcí* states:
The earth's nine categories, how did Yǔ mound them?
Kānghuí, filled with rage,
why did the earth tilt to the southwest?
The annotation states:
Fén
means to divide,
referring to the nine provinces of the land, each of nine grades,
how was Yǔ able to distinguish them.
Kānghuí
is Gònggōng.
Stone as bones and grass as hair,
soil as flesh and rivers as veins.
The *Bówùzhì* states:
Earth uses famous mountains as its assistants,
stone as its bones,
rivers as its veins,
grass and trees as its hair,
soil as its flesh.
Above three chǐ is fertilizer,
below three chǐ is earth.
Established with the method of burial,
the *Rites* states:
Burying at Tàizhé,
is to sacrifice to earth.
Demonstrating the virtue of humility.
The *Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì* states:
Earth compliantly receives moisture,
humble and open.
The annotation says:
Opening the nine cores,
receiving flowing sprinkles and moisture,
this is its humility.
All rivers gather in the southeast,
the *Lièzǐ* states:
The earth is not full in the southeast,
all rivers flow there.
The terrain is also higher in the northwest.
Yáng Quán's *Wùlǐ Lùn* states:
Earth
is the root of heaven.
Its shape
is high in the northwest and low in the southeast,
long east to west,
short north to south.
It extends to the four seas.
Thus,
taking the square earth as a carriage,
deep and firm, strong and overcoming.
Sòng Yù's *Dàyán Fù* states:
Taking the square earth as a carriage,
the round heaven as a canopy.
The *Shū* states:
Deep and firm, strong and overcoming.
Sea
Vast is the numinous sea,
where all rivers gather and flow.
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
Vast is the numinous sea,
ever receiving their flow.
It floats beneath the sky with no shore in sight.
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
Vast and shimmering,
it floats beneath the sky with no shore in sight.
It contains forms yet is empty within.
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
What marvel does it not nurture?
What wonder does it not store?
Boundless are its accumulated waters,
containing forms yet empty within.
It reaches the Celestial Ruins and floats to the Xīmù constellation.
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
To the south it washes the Red Cliffs,
to the north it sprinkles the Celestial Ruins,
to the east it extends to Xīmù,
to the west it brushes against Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu.
Note:
The *Erya* says:
Xīmù is called the Celestial Ford.
It pours against Jiéshí and surges to Zhīfú.
Yáng Shīdào’s “Poem in Response to Gazing at the Sea” says:
Morning mists disperse at Jiéshí,
returning geese soar at Zhīfú.
It is buttressed by Wòjiāo,
The *Xuánzhōng Jì* says:
The strongest thing under heaven
is the Wòjiāo in the Eastern Sea,
into which water pours ceaselessly.
Wòjiāo
is the name of a mountain,
located thirty thousand *lǐ* east of the sea.
It drains through the Wěilǘ.
See the note below under “Yuánjiào and Fānghú.”
The lands of the Black-Toothed and Naked People,
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
Some are pulled along, drifting to the land of the Naked People,
some float leisurely to the realm of the Black-Toothed.
The regions of the Ear-Clasping and the Farthest North.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
The Ear-Clasping Country lies east of the No-Intestines Country,
its people clasp their ears with both hands
and dwell suspended in the sea.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
North of the Farthest North there is a dark sea,
which is the Heavenly Pool.
Yíngzhōu and Péng Island,
The *Bówùzhì* says:
In the vast sea,
there are three divine mountains: Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu.
Yuánjiào and Fānghú.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
East of the Bó Sea there is a great abyss,
named the Guīxū.
Within it are five mountains: Dàiyú, Yuánjiào, Fānghú, Yíngzhōu, and Pénglái.
The note says:
Guīxū is the Wěilǘ.
Where the Kūn transforms into the Péng,
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
In the Northern Dark Sea there is a fish,
whose name is Kūn.
It transforms into a bird,
whose name is Péng.
When the sea moves, it migrates to the Southern Dark Sea.
And where immortals make their dwellings.
The *Bówùzhì* says:
On the sea there are three divine mountains,
with palaces and towers of gold and silver,
where immortals gather.
As for raising the Fúsāng above the azure ford,
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
When the great sun harnesses its steeds at the Golden Pivot’s cave,
the soaring sun dashes forth at the Fúsāng’s ford.
The *Shízhōu Jì* says:
The Fúsāng is planted in the azure ford.
And stirring great waves upon the blue shores.
The *Nányuèzhì* says:
Hǎi’ān County has a small stream
that flows south into the sea.
Gazing to the horizon at the blue shores,
one sees the vast expanse of great waves.
Some ride floating rafts and reach the Dipper,
The *Bówùzhì* says:
An old tale says the Milky Way connects with the sea.
In recent times, a man living by a sea isle
saw a floating raft come and go every eighth month,
never missing its schedule.
This man then built a hut on the raft,
took provisions,
and rode the raft away.
In a daze, he lost track of day and night.
Suddenly he arrived at a place
with walls, houses, and dwellings.
He saw many weaving women inside a room,
and a man leading an ox to the islet to drink.
Startled, the man asked him:
“How did you get here?”
This man in turn asked:
“What place is this?”
The reply was:
“You may go to Shǔ and ask Yán Jūnpíng.”
This man returned
and asked Jūnpíng,
who said:
“On such-and-such a month, a guest star intruded upon the Ox and Dipper.”
That was when this man reached the Milky Way.
Others boil the waves to produce white salt.
The *Qí Shū* says:
Zhāng Róng composed a “Rhapsody on the Sea,”
with ornate and intense language.
