He showed it to General Zhènjūn Xú Kǎizhī,
who said:
“Your rhapsody truly surpasses Xuánxū’s,
but it is a pity you did not mention salt.”
Róng immediately asked for a brush and added:
“Filtering sand to form white,
boiling waves to produce pure salt.
Piled snow in mid-spring,
flying frost on summer roads.”
Lord Jǐng of Qí forgot to return,
The *Shuōyuàn* says:
Lord Jǐng of Qí traveled on the sea and delighted in it,
not returning for six months.
He told his attendants:
“Whoever dares speak of returning first shall die.”
Yán Chù came forward and said:
“Your lordship delights in ruling the sea,
but not in ruling the state.
If someone else were to rule the state,
how could your lordship still delight in this sea?”
So he returned.
On the way, he heard that the people of the state were plotting not to admit him.
The First Emperor of Qín desired to cross it.
The *Sān Qí Lüè* says:
The First Emperor of Qín built a stone bridge on the sea,
wishing to cross and view the place where the sun rises.
A divine being drove the stones,
but they moved too slowly,
so the divine being whipped them,
and they all bled.
To this day, the stone bridge remains reddish.
Zǔ Yíng gazed upon it and composed a poem,
The Northern Qí poet Zǔ Yíng’s “Gazing at the Sea” says:
Ascending high, I face the great abyss,
not knowing how many thousand *lǐ* it spans.
Cloudy isles connect one to another,
wind and waves have no end.
Wáng Càn roamed it and wrote a rhapsody.
Wáng Càn’s “Rhapsody on Roaming the Sea” says:
As for the long isles and separate lands,
they are arrayed like chess pieces, standing like stars.
Cassia and orchids cluster upon them,
coral grows at their bases.
Think of Mùróng crossing the ice,
Wáng Yǐn’s *Jìn Shū* says:
Mùróng Huǎng reported to the throne:
“I personally campaigned in the northern suburbs,
relying from afar on Your Majesty’s heaven-and-earth-like might.
The sea formed frozen ice,
and we traveled over three hundred *lǐ* upon it.
I and the elders said:
‘Since the founding of our state,
there has never been such a thing as seawater freezing.’”
And admire Zhònglián’s refusal of official rank.
The *Shǐjì* says:
Tián Dān massacred Liáochéng
and wished to ennoble Lǚ Zhònglián,
but Zhònglián fled to the sea,
saying:
“I would rather be poor and humble, acting freely according to my will,
than enjoy wealth and honor yet bow to others.”
Then there are Lùhún and Yángchí,
The *Hòu Wèi Shū* says:
The Grand Ancestor campaigned westward
and encamped at Lùhún Sea.
Guō Yìgōng’s *Guǎngzhì* says:
West of Qiāngzhōng there are Tánmí Sea and Yángchí Sea.
Púchāng and Bódī.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
Púchāng Sea,
also called Salt Marsh,
is believed to flow underground
and emerge south at Jīshí,
becoming the river of the Central Kingdom.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Dòu Xiàn campaigned against the Xiōngnú
and reached Bódī Sea.
It is where all valleys gather,
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
The reason rivers and seas can be kings of all valleys
is because they excel at staying low.
And where ten thousand channels converge and return.
Mù Xuánxū’s “Rhapsody on the Sea” says:
Once rivers are guided,
all channels flow together.
Pity the water creatures trapped in the ruts,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Zhōu looked back at the wheel tracks,
and there was a crucian carp.
It said:
"I am a wave servant of the Eastern Sea,
might you, sir, have a dou or sheng of water to keep me alive!"
A fearsome horse blocked the path with it in its mouth.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
If one approaches the depths bearing defilement,
making empty vows and failing in prayers,
then the Sea Child will block the road,
and the horse will block the path with it in its mouth.
Chén Mào drew his sword to calm the waves.
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū says:
Chén Mào once served as Biéjià of Jiāozhǐ.
Formerly, the Inspector did not cross the swelling sea during his circuit.
Inspector Zhōu Chǎng, while crossing the sea, encountered a storm,
and the boat was about to capsize.
Mào drew his sword and cursed the water god,
and the wind immediately ceased.
Bào Jìng boiled stones to relieve hunger.
The Jìn Shū says:
Bào Jìng was the Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi.
Once, while on his circuit,
he entered the sea and encountered a storm.
Being extremely hungry,
he took white stones, boiled and ate them to sustain himself.
He saw the reclusive Jiāng Gōng.
The Gāoshì Zhuàn says:
Jiāng Gōng was summoned ten times by the ducal offices,
and recommended nine times as a man of virtue,
but he did not take up any post.
During the reign of Emperor Líng,
Cáo Jié informed the emperor to summon Gōng.
Gōng concealed himself and fled his fate,
floating on a raft into the sea.
He recognized Confucius who rode a raft.
The Analects says:
The Master said:
"If the Way does not prevail,
I will get upon a raft and float out to sea."
Observe how it controls the clear and draws in the turbid.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
The virtue of the pit repeatedly arrives,
the source of water is deep and vast,
it pours into the hundred rivers,
controls the clear and draws in the turbid,
beginning from a floating cup,
it conveys and transports to the great abyss.
It washes the clouds and drenches the sun.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
Vast and surging, swirling and deep,
it washes the clouds and drenches the sun.
Gaze upon that young sea.
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
On Wúgāo Mountain,
looking south, one sees the Yòu Sea.
Note:
The Yòu Sea
is the Shào Sea.
Observe this morning and evening tide.
Wáng Jiǎnqī's "Stele Inscription of the Head-Shaven Temple" says:
One who scoops from the morning and evening pool
cannot measure its shallowness or depth.
Morning and evening
refers to the pool, the sea.
The golden palace towers aloft.
See the note on "Immortal's dwelling."
The purple stone chamber opens.
The Shízhōu Jì says:
On the Cānghǎi Island there is a purple stone chamber,
the immortal capital of the nine elders.
Marvel at Jīngwèi carrying wood.
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
On Fājiū Mountain,
there is a bird called Jīngwèi.
She was the daughter of Emperor Yán,
who went swimming in the Eastern Sea,
drowned and did not return.
She constantly takes wood and stones from the Western Mountains to fill up the Eastern Sea.
Be startled by Xú Yǎn carrying stones.
The Hàn Shū says:
Zōu Yáng's letter says:
"Shēntú Dí drowned himself in the Yōng River,
Xú Yǎn carried stones into the sea,
being unacceptable to the world."
In times of peace, though waves do not rise,
the Lǐ Dǒu Wēi Yí says:
If the ruler rides on earth and becomes king, then the sea is calm.
The note says:
The sea being calm
means waves do not rise.
The Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn says:
During King Chéng's time,
the Yuèshāng clan, after triple translation, came to court and said:
"For three years, heaven has not sent contrary winds or violent rain,
and the sea has not raised waves.
Must there be a sage in the Central Kingdom?"
When a comet falls, it is said to cause breaches and floods.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
When a comet falls, the Bó Sea breaches.
As for admiring the beauty of paying homage,
the Shū says:
The Jiāng and Hàn rivers pay homage to the sea.
Examine the saying about excelling in lowliness.
See the note on "the gathering of all valleys."
I have glimpsed the mermaid's chamber.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
Then there are heavenly treasures, water monsters, and the chambers of mermaids.
I have often seen mulberry fields.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Má Gū said to Wáng Fāngpíng:
"Since I began serving you,
I have seen the Eastern Sea become mulberry fields three times.
When I recently went to Pénglái,
the water had become shallow,
about half of what it was before.
Could it be about to become hills and land again?"
Zǐ Móu yearned and galloped, longing for the court.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Zhōngshān Prince Móu said to Zhānzǐ:
"Though my body is above the rivers and seas,
my heart remains beneath the palace gates of Wèi.
What should I do about this?"
Zhānzǐ said:
"Value life,
if you value life, you will regard profit lightly."
Zǐ Móu said:
"Though I know this, I cannot overcome it."
Zhānzǐ said:
"If you cannot overcome it yourself, then follow it."
Guǎn Níng, in peril, reflected on his faults.
Zhōu Jǐngshì's Xiàozǐ Zhuàn says:
Guǎn Níng took refuge in Liáodōng.
Once he encountered a storm,
the boatmen were in danger and fear,
all kowtowing and repenting their faults.
Níng reflected on his own transgressions and faults,
recalling that he had once gone to the latrine without wearing a hat,
so he kowtowed towards heaven,
and the wind soon calmed.
There is also the sight of yin fire amidst the waves.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
Yang ice does not melt,
yin fire burns hidden.
Gather stone flowers on the mountain's edge.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
Jade mussels, sea moons,
earth flesh, stone flowers.
Note:
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
Jade mussels
are a type of clam,
pronounced yáo.
The Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Wùzhì says:
Sea moons
are as large as mirrors,
white in color,
perfectly round.
Earth flesh
is pitch black,
as large as a child's arm,
has a belly but no mouth or eyes,
and has thirty feet.
Stone flowers
grow attached to rocks.
Spread the glittering coral.
The Wàiguó Zhuàn says:
Southwest of Dàqín,
in the swelling sea about eight hundred lǐ away,
one reaches the coral isles.
At the bottom of the isles are flat rocks,
upon which coral grows.
People use iron nets to gather it.
Steam the dense clouds and mist.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
Dripping and seeping,
dense and misty clouds.
In rites, sacrifice first to the river.
The Lǐjì says:
When the three kings sacrificed to rivers,
they first sacrificed to the river and then to the sea.
Waves sometimes shake the earth.
The Shīzǐ says:
Seawater completes a cycle every three years,
flowing waves press against each other,
therefore the earth moves.
A ruler models himself on it to achieve greatness.
The Wénzǐ says:
A ruler who excels
models himself on the sea to emulate its greatness,
lowering himself to achieve its vastness.
The hundred rivers learn from it and thus reach it.
The Fǎyán says:
The hundred rivers learn from the sea and reach the sea,
hills and mounds learn from mountains but do not reach the mountains.
Thus we know it overlooks the mountain ranges.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
The mountain ranges are already overlooked,
the hundred rivers secretly flow away.
Drying up the nine provinces,
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
It uproots the five sacred mountains,
And dries up the nine provinces.
It is not that the sea rejects water,
The Wénzǐ says:
The sea does not reject water,
It accumulates the small to become great.
One must accumulate streams.
The Sūnqīngzǐ says:
Without accumulating half-steps,
One cannot reach a thousand miles;
Without accumulating small streams,
One cannot reach the rivers and seas.
Already harnessing giant turtles as bridges,
Jiāng Wéntōng's "Rhapsody on Regret" says:
I shall harness giant turtles and alligators as bridges,
And patrol the right of the sea to escort the sun.
It also spews mirages to form towers.
The Hànshū says:
By the sea, there are mirage vapors that form towers and terraces.
Plucking fragrant trees from the Gathering Mound Isle,
The Shízhōu Jì says:
The Gathering Mound Isle lies in the Western Sea,
There is a great tree similar to the maple,
Its fragrance spreads for hundreds of miles,
Named the Soul-Returning Tree.
Visiting the jade fields on the Ancestral Isle.
The Shízhōu Jì says:
The Ancestral Isle lies in the Eastern Sea,
Its land spans five hundred miles,
Upon it grows the herb of immortality,
Born in jade fields,
The herb resembles wild rice seedlings.
For those already dead,
Covering them with this herb revives them all.
The well frog, confined,
Realizes its sight and hearing are not broad;
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
The turtle of the Eastern Sea said to the frog in the sunken well:
"The sea, a thousand miles distant,
Is insufficient to convey its vastness;
A thousand fathoms high,
Is insufficient to reach its depth.
In the time of Yǔ,
There were nine years of ten floods,
Yet the waters did not increase;
In the time of Tāng,
There were eight years of seven droughts,
Yet the shores did not diminish.
It does not shift with the brief or long,
Nor advance or retreat with the much or little,
This is the great joy of the Eastern Sea."
The River Earl, upon seeing it,
Knew the disparity in size.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
When the autumn floods arrive,
A hundred streams pour into the river,
Between the banks and shores,
Oxen and horses cannot be distinguished.
The River Earl joyfully congratulated himself,
Believing all the beauty under heaven was within him.
Following the current eastward,
He reached the Northern Sea,
Gazing eastward,
He saw no end to the waters,
And sighed toward Ruò.
The Northern Sea Ruò said:
"One cannot speak of the sea to a well frog,
For it is confined to its hollow;
One cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,
For it is bound by its season;
One cannot speak of the Way to a petty scholar,
For he is constrained by his teachings.
Of all waters under heaven,
None is greater than the sea.
Ten thousand rivers flow into it,
Yet one knows not when it will cease and not overflow;
The Wěilǘ drains it,
Yet one knows not when it will stop and not empty.
It does not change with spring or autumn,
Nor know flood or drought.
This surpasses the flow of rivers,
Beyond measure or count."
Sīmǎ Biāo says:
"The Wěilǘ,
Is where water flows out beyond the sea."
River
The virtue of water is profound and enduring.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"Consider the five materials used together,
truly the virtue of water is profound and enduring.
From Mín Mountain, it originates as a trickle."
The Xúnzǐ states:
"The River emerges from Mín Mountain,
its source can fill a cup,
but when it reaches the river's ford,
without a boat,
without avoiding the wind,
one cannot cross."
It gazes upon the brilliance of the Jǐng constellation's network.
The Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng states:
"The land of Mín Mountain
corresponds above to the Jǐng network."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"The essence of Mín sinks its brilliance into the Eastern Well."
It is shaded by the Ox and Maiden constellations, which hang down their rays.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo states:
"The Ox and Maiden are the rivers and lakes,
and the rivers and lakes
are what open the spirits and moisten transformations,
therefore their qi is swift and urgent."
It gathers the Hàn and Sì rivers,
draws in the Jǔ and Zhāng rivers.
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"It gathers the Hàn and Sì,
encompasses the Huái and Xiāng,
swallows up the Yuán and Lǐ,
draws in the Jǔ and Zhāng."
It divides into two sources at Jū and Lái mountains.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"One hundred and thirty li northeast of Mín is Lái Mountain,
from which the River water emerges.
Another fifty li northeast is Jū Mountain,
from which the River water emerges,
and flows eastward into the Great River."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"It divides into two sources at Jū and Lái,
flows into nine branches at Xúnyáng."
It flows into nine branches at Xúnyáng.
The Shuǐ Jīng states:
"The River reaches Xúnyáng,
and divides into nine courses."
Also, the Xúnyáng Jì states:
"The Nine Rivers:
first, the Báiwū River;
second, the Bàng River;
third, the Wūtǔ River;
fourth, the Jiāmí River;
fifth, the Quǎn River;
sixth, the Fú River;
seventh, the Lǐn River;
eighth, the Tí River;
ninth, the Jūn River."
"Torrential are the Jiāng and Hàn,
they regulate the southern states,"
from the Shī.
It stirs swift rapids in the Wū Gorge.
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"It charges through Wū Gorge with swift ferocity,
ascends the river ford and swells its waves."
It drums up great waves at Pénglí.
The Shuǐ Jīng states:
"It meets east at Pénglí,
passes Wúhú,
and is named the Middle River."
Táo Kǎn's gaming pieces were already cast into the waves.
The Jìn Shū states:
Táo Kǎn said to people:
"Great Yǔ was a sage,
yet he cherished every inch of time;
as for ordinary people,
they should cherish every fraction of time."
If his subordinates wasted affairs with games,
he would take their gambling implements,
and cast them all into the river.
Wú Měng's fan once drew upon the water.
The Jìn Shū states:
Wú Měng was around forty years old
when a townsman named Dīng Yì first taught him divine methods.
Returning to Yùzhāng,
the river current was very swift,
yet Měng, without using boat or oar,
drew upon the water with a white feather fan and crossed.
Emperor Wén of Wèi campaigned south and sighed.
The Wèi Zhì states:
Emperor Wén campaigned against Wú,
reached the Cháng Jiāng and sighed:
"Heaven indeed uses this to divide north and south."
Zǔ Dì campaigned north and made an oath.
The Jìn Shū states:
Zǔ Dì crossed the river northward,
and in midstream swore:
"If Dì does not clear the Central Plains and return to cross again,
may he be like this Great River."
Wēn Qiáo burned rhinoceros horn.
The Jìn Shū states:
Wēn Qiáo reached Niúzhǔ Jī,
where it was said the water was deep and unfathomable,
so he burned a rhinoceros horn to illuminate it.
Shortly after,
he saw strange water creatures,
some riding in chariots or on horses.
That night,
he dreamed someone said to him:
"You and I are separated by the paths of darkness and light,
why trouble to illuminate us?"
Qiáo was greatly disturbed,
and not long after died.
Qín Gāo rode a carp.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn states:
Qín Gāo wandered about Jìzhōu
for over two hundred years.
Later, he entered the Dàngshuǐ,
came riding a red carp,
stayed out for a month,
then re-entered the water and left.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River":
"Where the sea-child roams and patrols,
where Qín Gāo displays his divine agility."
Zhāng Yǔ adjudicated lawsuits and the waves cleared.
The Xù Hàn Shū states:
Zhāng Yǔ was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and had to cross the river.
While touring his district,
the locals all said the river had the spirit of Zǐxū,
making it difficult to cross.
Yǔ declared sternly:
"If Zǐxū has any spirit,
knowing my intent is to investigate unjust lawsuits,
how would he endanger me!"
He then rowed across.
Wáng Hóng drew his sword and the wind ceased.
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū states:
Wáng Hóng of Wú Commandery was crossing the Qiántáng River
when he encountered a wind
that nearly capsized his boat.
Hóng drew his sword and struck the water,
cursing Wǔ Zǐxū,
and the wind abated, allowing him to cross.
As for its racing through a hundred valleys,
the Lǎozǐ states:
"The reason the river and sea can be king over a hundred valleys
is because they excel at staying below them."
It guides twin currents.
Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Shǔ Capital" states:
"Girdled by the twin flows of two rivers."
It pours its startling rapids past Báidì.
Yǔ Xìn's poem "Sailing on the River" states:
"The spring river descends from Báidì,
the painted barge heads toward Huángniú."
It winds past the curved banks at Huángniú.
Suí dynasty Xuē Dàohéng's poem "Entering Chēn River" states:
"The journey is not by white horse,
the water's force resembles Huángniú."
Yánghóu drums the waves and gazes arrogantly.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Yángguó's Hóu drowned in water,
his spirit can create great waves."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"Yánghóu conceals his form within great waves."
Bīngyí leans on the waves and lingers leisurely.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"In the river of the utmost depths,
only Bīngyí constantly dwells there.
Bīngyí
has a human face and rides a dragon."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"Bīngyí leans on the waves and gazes arrogantly,
the river goddesses frown with distant gaze."
Bīngyí
is Féngyí.
Admirable was King Mù of Zhōu's shouting at the giant turtles.
The Jìnián states:
"King Mù of Zhōu went east to the Jiǔjiāng,
and shouted at the giant turtles and alligators to form a bridge."
One thinks of King Xiàng's mooring his boat.
The Shǐjì states:
"Xiàng Yǔ wished to cross east over the Wū River.
The Wū River station master moored a boat waiting for him."
As for journeying to the three mountains with a clear silken expanse,
Xiè Xuánhuī's poem "Climbing Three Mountains at Dusk and Gazing Back at the Capital" states:
"The lingering clouds scatter into brocade,
the clear river lies still like a silk ribbon."
Passing Xīlíng, it winds like a girdle.
Yuán Shānsōng's Yídū Jì states:
"Facing the southern bank of Xīlíng is a mountain,
its peak the most beautiful.
Climbing from the south side to the summit,
one looks down upon the great river winding like a girdle,
seeing boats and ships like ducks and geese."
It passes Jīngmén and races afar.
Shèng Hóngzhī's Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"Sixty li upriver from the commandery seat at Xīlíng,
on the southern bank is a mountain,
named Jīngmén;
on the northern bank is a mountain,
named Hǔyá."
The banks face each other,
forming the western pass of Chǔ.
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"Hǔyá stands jagged and precipitous,
Jīngmén towers lofty and vast."
It emerges from Xìnyáng and flows far.
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"It emerges from Xìnyáng and flows far,
pouring into the great abyss and Wòjiāo."
Zāng Róngxù's *History of the Jìn* says:
"Jiànpíng Commandery had a Xìnlíng County.
Xìnyáng
is Xìnlíng."
It irrigates the Five Lakes, vast and boundless.
In the *Records of the Grand Historian*, the Grand Historian says:
"I ascended Gūsū and gazed upon the Five Lakes."
Zhāng Bó's *Record of Wú* says:
"The Five Lakes
are another name for Tài Lake.
They extend over five hundred *lǐ*."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"It pours into the Five Lakes, spreading wide,
irrigates the Three Rivers, surging and rushing."
It gathers the Three Rivers, roaring and turbulent.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"When the Three Rivers were regulated,
Zhènzé was settled."
Kǒng Ānguó says:
"Pénglí divides the river into three,
which enter Zhènzé."
One also hears of Língjūn casting stones in passionate grief,
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"I grieve for Língjūn casting stones,
and sigh for the fisherman's song."
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"Qu Yuán composed the 'Embracing the Sands' rhapsody,
then clasped a stone and threw himself into the Mìluó River to die."
The fisherman plied his oars and lingered along the banks.
The *Songs of Chǔ* says:
"The fisherman's song while rowing goes:
'When the Cānglàng's waters are clear,
I can wash my hat strings;
when the Cānglàng's waters are muddy,
I can wash my feet.'"
One laughs at the failed strategy of sandbags,
The *Record of Wú* says:
"Bù Zhì reported, saying:
'Northern defectors say the north is making many cloth bags,
intending to fill them with sand
to block the Great River.'
The King of Wú said:
'These fellows certainly dare not come.
If it is not as I say,
I will use a thousand oxen to host a feast for you.'
Later, when he heard Lǚ Dài recount Zhì's words,
he laughed and said:
'This river has been thus since creation;
how could it be blocked with bags?'"
One sees sharpness blunted by the boast of throwing whips.
Zāng Róngxù's *History of the Jìn* says:
"Fú Jiān had pacified the northern nine provinces,
and was about to launch a major southern campaign.
Fú Róng and others all remonstrated to stop him,
but he would not listen,
saying:
'With my million troops,
throwing their whips into the river would suffice to cross it.'
When they arrived,
the Féi River was in flood,
and they were defeated by Xiè Xuán and others."
The Chǔ lady displayed integrity on the Jiàntái,
The *Biographies of Immortals* says:
"King Zhāo of Chǔ went on an excursion,
leaving his wife Zhēn Jiāng at the Jiàntái.
The river rose greatly,
and he sent a messenger to fetch the lady.
The messenger forgot to bring the tally.
The lady said:
'The king made a pact with the palace women:
summons must be with a tally.
Now the messenger has no tally;
I dare not go.'
So the messenger returned to fetch the tally.
Before he returned,
the terrace collapsed.
She drowned and died."
The Jiāng woman demonstrated filial piety at the gushing spring.
The *Biographies of Immortals* says:
"The wife of Jiāng Shī of Guǎnghàn
served her mother-in-law with utmost filial piety.
The mother-in-law liked to drink river water,
which was seven *lǐ* from home.
The wife often fetched water upstream at cockcrow.
Once, encountering wind and snow,
she could not fetch water in time,
and Shī reproached and dismissed her.
The wife lodged with a neighbor, spinning and weaving,
to buy delicacies,
which she had the neighbor's mother give to her mother-in-law.
Shī heard of this and brought her back.
Suddenly, a spring gushed forth beside their dwelling,
tasting like river water."
Observe the winding Huángcén,
Shèng Hóngzhī's *Record of Jīngzhōu* says:
"Shǐ'ān Commandery has eastern and northern rivers;
the northern river originates from Línwǔ Huángcén Mountain in Guìyáng;
the eastern river originates from the Dàyǔ Ridge in Nánkāng."
Rushing past Chì'àn,
Shān Qiānzhī's *Record of Nánxú* says:
"The Jīng River,
as in the *Tribute of Yǔ*:
flows northward,
broad and vast for thirty *lǐ*,
opening to a great abyss.
Often on the first and fifteenth days of spring and autumn,
great tides arise,
their sound and force terrifyingly mighty,
an extremely wondrous sight.
The tide, reaching north of the river, strikes Chì'àn,
especially swift and fierce."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"It drums great waves at Chì'àn,
submerging remaining ripples at Cháisāng."
Passing through Yúnmèng, vast and boundless,
The *Book of Documents* says:
"The cloud-covered land of Mèng was made arable."
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"Beside it lie Yúnmèng and Léichí,
Pénglí and Qīngcǎo."
Irrigating Jùqū, expansive and wide,
Guō Jǐngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"Jùqū, Táo, and Gé."
Note:
"All are marsh names.
Táo is pronounced yáo,
Gé is pronounced hé."
Marvel at the weeping pearls of the spring guest,
The "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" says:
"The spring guest, impassioned, weeps pearls."
Recognize the constructed abode of the mermen.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"The spring guest builds a dwelling at the cliff's base,
the mermen construct a lodge in the hanging stream."
As for the names Ruòliǔ and Báiwū,
The *Record of Lǜjiāng* says:
"A branch of the Western River is the Ruòliǔ River,
the water passes through Xúnyáng's Nine Rivers,
one of which is called 'Báiwū'."
Praise the names Jiāmí and Guābù.
The *Water Classic*:
"The Jiāmí River
is one of the Nine Rivers.
The Guābù River is within the boundaries of Liùhé County in Yángzhōu,
where Emperor Wén of Wèi and Emperor Tàiwǔ of Later Wèi once visited."
Moved by Jiàofǔ's loss of the pendant,
The *Biographies of Immortals* says:
"Two river goddesses
were strolling by the riverbank,
when they met Zhèng Jiàofǔ,
and gave him their pendants.
Jiàofǔ took the pendants and left.
After a few dozen steps,
the pendants were gone from his bosom,
and the maidens had vanished."
Think of King Zhāo of Chǔ obtaining the duckweed fruit.
The *Family Sayings of Confucius* says:
"King Zhāo of Chǔ was crossing the river,
when something in the river,
as big as a dou measure,
round and red,
struck the king's boat directly.
The boatman retrieved it.
The king found it very strange,
and sent someone to Lǔ
to ask Confucius.
Confucius said:
'This is a duckweed fruit.
It can be cut open and eaten;
it is auspicious.
Only a hegemon can obtain it.'
When the envoy returned,
the king promptly ate it,
and found it delicious."
Stirring the wrathful spirit of Zǐxū,
The *Discourses Weighed in the Balance* says:
"Confucian texts say Wǔ Zǐxū, resentful of the King of Wú,
drove the waters to create tides.
Now at Qiánfáng in Kuàijī and Dāntú on the river,
all have established shrines to Zǐxū,
hoping to stop his tides."
Trace the hanging stream to Biē Lìng.
The *Annals of the Kings of Shǔ* says:
"King Wàng ruled at Pí under Wèn Mountain for over a hundred years.
In Jīngzhōu, there was a dead man named Biē Lìng,
whose corpse vanished,
floated up the river to Pí, and revived.
King Wàng made him chancellor.
Later, feeling his virtue inferior to Biē Lìng's,
he abdicated and handed the state to him."
I admire Qíxiàng's attainment of the Way,
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
The river god is called Qíxiàng.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
Qíxiàng attained the Way and became a dwelling spirit.
Pitying the spirit envoy who made light of his life.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
Duke Yuán of Sòng dreamed at midnight of a man with disheveled hair peeping through the side gate,
who said:
"I am an envoy of the Clear River on my way to Hé Bó's place,
and the fisherman Yùjū caught me."
Duke Yuán awoke,
summoned a dream interpreter to divine it.
The interpreter said:
"This is a divine turtle."
Duke Yuán obtained it, cut it open, and used it for divination,
performing seventy drillings without a single miscalculation.
Yāolí plotted against Qìngjì and established his fame.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
Yāolí fled,
went to see Prince Qìngjì on the street,
Qìngjì was pleased,
Yāolí said:
"I request to go with the prince to seize the state."
Prince Qìngjì and Yāolí crossed the river together,
Yāolí drew his sword to stab Qìngjì,
Qìngjì seized him and threw him into the river.
He floated up,
and Qìngjì took him and threw him in again,
repeating this three times.
In the end, he said:
"You are a hero of the world,
I am fortunate to have you to make my name."
Yāolí did not die and returned to Wú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn shot a flood dragon, and the scene became clear.
The *Hànshū* states:
In the fifth year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ,
he hunted at Shèngtáng,
and performed sacrifices from afar to Yú Shùn at Jiǔyí.
From Xúnyáng, he personally shot a flood dragon in the river,
and captured it.
Boats stretched for a thousand *lǐ*.
The act of throwing letters was already praised by Guānglù.
Xiāo Fāngděng's *Thirty Kingdoms Spring and Autumn* states:
Guānglùxūn Yīn Xiàn was returning to Yùzhāng,
many nobles entrusted him with their letters,
Yīn Xiàn, upon reaching Bǎnqiáo, threw the letters into the river,
saying:
"Let those that sink sink,
let those that float float.
Yīn Hóngqiáo cannot act as a letter carrier."
The destruction of the jade disc is still heard of in Mièmíng.
The matter is seen in the annotation "Dàntái destroyed the jade disc" in the "Rhapsody on the River."
Some say:
He beheaded a flood dragon in the river.
Gathering all the rivers for a distant view,
I see it in the *Shuǐjīng*.
River
The lower reaches of the Yīhóng River,
the Shìmíng states:
"Hé" means "low,"
as it flows through low-lying areas.
It originates from the remote region of Kūnlún.
The Shānhǎijīng states:
Mount Kūnlún spans ten thousand lǐ in length and breadth,
with green, white, red, and black rivers encircling its base.
Its white waters emerge from the northeast,
bend and flow southeastward,
forming the Zhōngguó River.
The Ěryǎ states:
The river emerges from the base of Kūnlún,
its color white.
Investigating the distant traces of Bówàng,
the Hànshū states:
Zhāng Qiān was sent to Dàxià,
and he traced the source of the river.
Did he see what is called Kūnlún?
Examining the distant traces of King Xià.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
Before Lóngmén was opened,
and before Lǚliáng was breached,
the river emerged from Mèngmén,
overflowing in reverse flow,
and was called the Great Flood.
Yǔ dredged the rivers and channeled the waters,
creating the barrier of Pénglí,
and governed eighteen hundred states.
By the Hàn dynasty, eight of its branches had been lost.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
North of Jùlù,
it divided into nine rivers,
which then converged into one river to enter the sea.
Duke Huán of Qí blocked the nine rivers to expand farmland and settlements.
During the Hàn dynasty, the river breached the Jīndī,
and officials sought to locate the old courses of the nine rivers to reopen them,
but their locations were unknown.
Thus, Bān Gù said:
"From then until the Hàn dynasty,
eight of its branches were lost."
Jiǎ Fù discussed his three strategies.
The Hànshū states:
During the reign of Emperor Āi,
Jiǎ Ràng submitted a memorial stating:
"There are three strategies for managing the river: upper, middle, and lower.
If those living in the path of the water are relocated to avoid it,
and the river is allowed to flow north into the sea,
the flooding will subside on its own within a month,
without exhausting human labor.
Once this achievement is established,
the river will be stabilized and the people secure,
ensuring no disasters for a thousand years.
This is called the upper strategy.
If multiple canals are dug,
allowing people to irrigate their fields,
though not the method of sages,
it is still a technique to remedy disaster.
Now, if stone embankments are built on firm ground,
with water gates to the east and west made of wood and earth,
during droughts, the eastern water gates can be opened to irrigate fields,
and during floods, the western high gates can be opened to divert the river.
This truly enriches the state, secures the people, promotes benefits, and eliminates harm.
This is called the middle strategy.
If the old embankments are merely repaired,
raising low sections and doubling thin ones,
labor and expenses will be endless,
and disasters will recur frequently.
This is the lowest strategy."
Observe its gentle flow,
the Shī states:
"The new terrace is bright,
the river waters flow gently."
Delight in its vastness,
the Shī states:
"The river waters are vast,
flowing northward, swift and lively."
Emerging from the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
it flows into Púchāng.
The Shānhǎijīng states:
The river emerges from Kūnlún and flows east,
submerging underground,
until north of Guīqī Mountain, where it surfaces.
It divides into two sources:
one from the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
and one from Yútián.
They converge again,
and flow east into Púchāng Lake.
Later, the sea was understood as the foundation.
The Lǐ states:
When the three kings sacrificed to rivers,
they always prioritized the river over the sea.
Some are sources,
some are outlets,
and this is called focusing on the foundation.
A single reed was once said to be enough to cross it.
The Shī states:
"Who says the river is wide?
A single reed can cross it."
As for the torrential flow like bamboo arrows,
the Shènzǐ states:
West of the river, below Lóngmén,
its flow is as swift as bamboo arrows.
Stirring the waters of the peach blossoms,
Huán Tán's Xīnlùn states:
Grand Marshal Zhāng Zhòng proposed:
"The river water is turbid,
with six dou of mud in one shí of water.
Yet the people compete to breach the river for irrigation,
causing the river to flow poorly.
By the third month,
when the peach blossom waters arrive, breaches occur,
because the blockage prevents drainage.
The people should be prohibited from diverting the river again."
The mud already fills six dou,
as seen in the note above.
Its bends are also said to span a thousand lǐ.
Yáng Quán's Wùlǐlùn states:
The river has small bends over a hundred lǐ,
and over a thousand lǐ,
one bend and one straight section.
Huángdì's dream of two dragons,
the Hétú states:
Huángdì dreamed of two dragons presenting a map.
He then fasted,
went to the Héluò,
where a fish surfaced with a white map,
which drifted and stopped,
and he knelt to receive it.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's song of Hùzǐ,
the Shǐjì states:
During the Yuánguāng era,
the emperor visited the breach at Hùzǐ,
sacrificed a white horse and jade discs,
and ordered all officials,
from generals down, to carry brushwood to fill the breach.
Bamboo from the Qí Garden was used as stakes.
The emperor lamented the failure of the effort,
and composed the "Hùzǐ Song."
Jiǎn, Jié, Gōupán,
Húsū, Tàishǐ.
The Ěryǎ:
The nine rivers:
Túhài, Tàishǐ, Mǎjiá, Fùfǔ, Húsū, Jiǎn, Jié, Gōupán, Géjīn.
Note:
Túhài and Tàishǐ
are not detailed.
Mǎjiá
is shaped like a horse's cheek.
Fùfǔ
is a place in the water where one can dwell,
shaped like an overturned cauldron.
Húsū:
Dōngguǎn has a Húsū Pavilion.
Jiǎn:
the watercourse is simple and easy.
Jié:
the water is often restrained.
Gōupán:
the water bends like a hook, flowing circuitously.
Géjīn:
the water is often narrow and constrained,
allowing one to cross as a ford,
and traverse horizontally.
As for the perilous rapids of the three gates,
the Shuǐjīng states:
Yǔ cut through Dǐzhù to allow the river to flow,
which is called the three gates.
It is hailed as the essence of the four great rivers.
The Chūnqiū Kǎoyìyǒu states:
The river
is the energy of water,
the essence of the four great rivers,
through which transformation flows.
Thus it is said, "The river moistens a thousand lǐ."
Winding in nine bends before flowing into the sea,
the Huáinánzǐ states:
The river flows in nine bends into the sea, yet its flow never ceases,
because it is supplied by Kūnlún.
Passing a thousand years before clearing once,
the Shíyíjì states:
The Yellow River clears once every thousand years,
a great auspicious sign of a sage.
Lǐ Xiāoyuǎn's Yùnmìnglùn states:
When the Yellow River clears, a sage is born.
Could it cause the affliction of King Zhāo of Chǔ?
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
King Zhāo of Chǔ fell ill,
and divination indicated the river was the cause.
The ministers requested a sacrifice,
but the king said:
"The Jiāng, Hàn, Jǔ, and Zhāng
are the rivers of Chǔ,
the river is not where I incurred offense."
Only the name of Wáng Mǎng is heard.
The Shǐjì·Héqúshū states:
The river's disasters
are especially severe in Zhōngguó.
The Shàngshū guides the river,
from Jīshí to Lóngmén.
Two more channels were dug to divert the river.
Rú Chún's commentary states:
The two channels—
one originated at Bèiqiū,
the other at Xíchuān.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, they were blocked and abandoned,
hence they were commonly called "Wáng Mǎng's River."
Recognize the story of the three men carrying earth.
The *Classic of Filial Piety* says:
There were three men,
all solitary and alone,
who agreed to become father and sons.
The elder then ordered the two younger ones to build a house in the great marsh.
When it was nearly completed,
the father said:
"This is not as good as by the river."
The two said, "Yes."
When the riverside house was almost finished,
the father said:
"Still not as good as in the middle of the river."
The two again filled the river,
but after twenty days, nothing was established.
A scholar passed by
and tied two lumps of earth to throw into the river.
The father went and called to stop him, saying:
"Have you ever seen a river that can be filled?
I'm just watching what you do."
The next day, they saw earth in the river piled over ten feet high.
See the flying stars of the Five Elders.
See the annotation to "The Five Elders Roam the River" in the *Rhapsody on Stars*.
Then there are dwellings of fish scales and purple shells.
The *Chǔcí* says:
A house of fish scales, a hall of dragons;
A tower of purple shells, a palace of pearls.
The commentary states:
This describes the dwelling of the River Earl.
Sacrifices of black raccoon dogs and white foxes.
The *Biography of King Mù of Zhōu* says:
The Son of Heaven hunted in the west
and captured a white fox and a black raccoon dog to sacrifice to the river.
Some use it to make the oath of the cypress boat.
The *Book of Songs* says "Cypress Boat,"
which is Gòng Jiāng's vow to herself.
"That cypress boat drifts,
there in the middle of the river.
With hair bound on both sides,
he is truly my match.
Until death, I vow no other."
Some use it to declare the oath of the belt.
The *Book of Hàn* records:
When Gāozǔ pacified the realm,
he enfeoffed one hundred and forty-three meritorious officials,
vowing:
"Should the Yellow River become a belt,
Mount Tài wear down to a whetstone,
may the state endure forever,
extending to your descendants.
Sealed with the trust of vermilion writing,
reinforced by the covenant of the white horse."
Zhòngní, heading to Zhào, turned his carriage back.
The *Family Sayings of Confucius* says:
Confucius went to Jìn.
Upon reaching the river,
he heard that Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had killed Dòu Míngdú and Shùn Huá.
He then approached the river and sighed, saying:
"How magnificent, vast and boundless!
That I, Qiū, do not cross this—
it is fate."
Zǐgòng hurried forward and asked:
"May I ask what you mean?"
The Master said:
"Dòu Míngdú and Shùn Huá
were worthy grand officers, yet he killed them.
I have heard: 'If one cuts open wombs and kills the young,
then qílín will not come to its suburbs;
if one drains the pond to catch fish,
then jiāolóng will not dwell in its depths;
if one overturns nests and breaks eggs,
then fènghuáng will not soar over its city.'
Why?
A gentleman avoids harming his own kind!"
He then returned.
Fāng Shū left Lǔ and departed far away.
The *Analects* says:
The drummer Fāng Shū entered the river.
The commentary states:
"Entered"
means he resided within the river region.
During the time of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
rites collapsed and music crumbled,
and the musicians all left.
The Marquis of Jìn heeded Bó Zūn's words.
The *Gǔliáng Commentary* says:
Mount Liáng collapsed,
blocking the river for three days without flow.
The ruler of Jìn summoned Bó Zūn.
Bó Zūn encountered a cart-puller and asked him.
The cart-puller said:
"The ruler should personally wear plain white mourning clothes,
lead his ministers in weeping for it,
and then make offerings."
Bó Zūn arrived,
the ruler asked him,
Bó Zūn spoke as advised,
and the river flowed again.
Xuān Huáng heard Fēng Hòu's response.
The *River Chart* says:
Fēng Hòu replied to the Yellow Emperor:
"There are five rivers in all,
all originating from the ruins of Kūnlún."
The white horse was already invoked in the Hàn prayer.
See the annotation above for "Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Song of Hùzǐ."
The yellow dragon was also praised as an auspicious sign for Shùn.
The *Yùndǒushū* says:
Shùn and the feudal lords observed the Hé and Luò rivers.
A yellow dragon emerged bearing a chart,
placed it before the emperor,
then departed into the water and went away.
The commentary states:
means to depart,
pronounced *zhìshì* qiè.
Also pronounced *dì*.
Also heard of its course through Zhāngyè.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* says:
The Yellow River flows east into Púchāng,
runs hidden underground,
emerges at Mount Jīshí,
and flows southeast.
Then it turns east back into the frontier passes,
passes south of Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and Zhāngyè,
and merges with the Táo River.
Channeling that lowland river,
see the annotation above for "only hearing the name of Wáng Mǎng."
To irrigate the upper ridge.
The *Book of Hàn*, "Treatise on Canals" says:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
a man from Qí named Yánnián submitted a memorial stating:
"The river emerges from Kūnlún,
passes through the Central States,
and empties into the Bó Sea.
This is because the terrain is high in the northwest and low in the southeast.
Following the high and low,
we could open a great river at the upper ridge,
lead it out among the Hú people,
and have it flow east into the sea.
If so,
Guāndōng would long be free from floods,
and the northern frontier would not worry about the Xiōngnú.
Once this achievement is accomplished,
it would be a great benefit for ten thousand generations."
The emperor admired his boldness,
but replied:
"Yánnián's plan is very profound.
However, the river was channeled by the Great Yǔ.
When a sage acts,
it connects with the divine and spiritual.
I fear it would be difficult to alter."
Commentary:
"Upper ridge"
means the mountain top.
Connecting to Mount Huà.
Guō Yuánshēng's *Record of a Campaign* says:
Mount Huà and Shǒuyáng were originally one mountain.
The river god Jùlíng split it above,
stepped on it below,
dividing the two mountains to let the river flow through.
The traces of his palm and foot still remain.
In Qín, it was named the Virtuous Water.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
When Qín destroyed the six states,
it considered itself to have received the auspicious sign of the Water Virtue,
and renamed the river "Virtuous Water."
In Hàn, Lóngyuān Palace was built.
The *Book of Hàn* says:
During the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
the river shifted to Dùnqiū.
He dispatched a hundred thousand troops to repair the breached river
and built Lóngyuān Palace.
It cannot be governed by an inch of glue.
The *Master Who Embraces Simplicity* says:
An inch of glue cannot clarify the Yellow River's turbidity;
a foot of water cannot extinguish the fire of Xiāoqiū.
How could a handful of soil fill it?
The *Master Who Embraces Simplicity* says:
A handful of soil cannot fill a breached river;
a liter of water cannot cool a prairie fire.
As for Dàntái destroying the jade disc.
The *Commentary on the Water Classic* says:
Once Dàntái Zǐyǔ,
carrying a jade disc worth a thousand gold, was crossing the river.
Yánghóu stirred the waves,
two jiāo dragons gripped the boat.
Zǐyǔ said:
"I can be sought through righteousness,
but cannot be coerced by force."
He drew his sword and slew the jiāo dragons.
The jiāo died and the waves calmed.
He then threw the jade disc into the river.
Three times he threw it, and each time it leaped back out.
He then destroyed the jade disc and departed,
showing no sign of regret.
Shēntú Dī carried a stone,
as recorded in the *Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*:
Shēntú Dī, disdaining the world,
was about to throw himself into the river.
Cuī Jiā stopped him, saying:
"The sage is
the parent of the people.
Now, for the sake of wetting your feet,
you would not save a drowning man—
is that acceptable?"
Shēntú Dī replied:
"In the past, Jié killed Lóng Páng and Zhòu killed Bǐ Gān,
and they lost the world.
Wú killed Zǐ Xū and Chén killed Xiè Yě,
and their states perished.
It was not that they lacked sages and wise men,
but that they did not employ them."
He then carried the stone and sank into the river.
Marquis Wǔ was pleased while in midstream,
as recorded in the *Shǐ Jì*:
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi sailed down the Western River,
and in midstream,
he turned to Wú Qǐ and said:
"How magnificent!
The solidity of these mountains and rivers
is the treasure of the state of Wèi."
Qǐ replied:
"It lies in virtue, not in natural barriers.
In the past, the Sān Miáo,
with Dòngtíng on the left
and Pénglí on the right,
relied on these barriers,
but they did not cultivate virtue and righteousness,
and Yǔ destroyed them.
The dwelling place of Xià Jié,
with Héjì on the left
and Tàihuá on the right,
Yīquē to its south,
and Yángcháng to its north,
he governed without cultivating benevolence,
and Tāng overthrew him.
The state of Yīn Zhòu,
with Mèngmén on the left
and Tàiháng on the right,
Chángshān to its north,
and the Great River flowing to its south,
he governed without cultivating virtue,
and King Wǔ destroyed him.
From this perspective,
it lies in virtue, not in natural barriers."
Marquis Wǔ said:
"Well said."
The people of Jìn had a "boat transport campaign."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* records:
Jìn suffered a famine,
and requested grain from Qín.
Qín transported millet to Jìn,
continuously from Yōng to Jiàng,
and it was called the "boat transport campaign."
It then corresponded to the Milky Way,
as stated in the *Xiàojīng Yuán Shén Qì*:
The river is
the chief of waters,
corresponding above to the Milky Way.
It breached the Golden Dike,
see the annotation above for "Báimǎ Shēn yú Hàn Dǎo."
It arose from Jīshí and floated past Dǐzhù,
passed Luòruì and reached Dàpī.
The *Shàngshū·Yǔ Gòng* states:
The river was guided from Jīshí,
reaching Lóngmén,
then south to Huáyīn,
and east to Dǐzhù.
Further east, it reached Mèngjīn,
passed east of Luòruì,
and reached Dàpī.
Jǔ Shòu sighed repeatedly by the flowing river,
as recorded in the *Wèi Zhì*:
When Yuán Shào crossed the river,
Jǔ Shòu sighed by the boat, saying:
"Those above are filled with ambition,
those below boast of their achievements.
Vast is the Yellow River—
how can we cross it!"
Gān Mào held an oar, but it was not fitting.
The *Shuō Yuàn* records:
Gān Mào was sent to Qí,
and crossed the river.
The boatman said:
"The river is but a stream—
if you cannot cross it,
how can you persuade kings?"
Gān Mào replied:
"Holding an oar and following the current,
I am not as good as you;
but persuading a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
you are not as good as I."
Observe how he cut through that Lóngmén,
see the annotation above.
It divided at Jùlù,
as recorded in the *Shānhǎi Jīng*:
Present-day Xíngzhōu and Jùlù
spread northward into nine rivers,
which converged into the Nì River and entered the sea.
Laugh at the attempt to block Mèngjīn with handfuls of soil,
as in Zhū Fú's *Letter to Péng Chǒng*:
How can you, with the tiny Yúyáng,
provoke the anger of the Son of Heaven?
This is like a person by the riverbank
trying to block Mèngjīn with handfuls of soil—
it only shows their lack of understanding of measure.
Recognize the taking of bamboo from Qíyuán.
See the annotation above for "Hàn Wǔ Gē Hùzǐ."
King Wǔ of Zhōu waved his hand at Yáng Hóu,
as recorded in the *Huáinánzǐ*:
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu and reached Mèngjīn,
the waves of Yáng Hóu surged against the current,
with fierce winds and darkness,
so that men and horses could not see each other.
Then King Wǔ, holding a yellow battle-axe in his left hand
and a white yak-tail banner in his right,
glared and waved, saying:
"I am here in the world—
who dares harm me!"
Thereupon, the wind ceased and the waves calmed.
Yíng Zhèng received the jade tablet.
The *Hétú Kǎo Líng Yào* records:
King Zhèng of Qín sank a white jade disc into the river,
and a black duke emerged from the river,
saying to Zhèng:
"The Ancestral Dragon has come to bestow the heavenly treasure."
When opened,
inside was a jade tablet one foot two inches long.
Sometimes it flooded four commanderies and caused disaster,
as recorded in the *Hàn Shū*:
During the reign of Emperor Chéng,
the river breached the Golden Dike,
flooding a total of four commanderies.
The River Dike Commissioner Wáng Yánshì blocked it with bamboo baskets,
four zhàng long,
nine wéi in circumference,
filled with small stones,
lowered between two boats.
In thirty-six days,
the river dike was completed.
The era name was changed to Hépíng.
Sometimes it moistened nine lǐ and brought blessings.
Zhāng Fán's *Hàn Jì* records:
Guō Jí was the governor of Yǐngchuān,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ issued an edict, saying:
"A virtuous and capable governor is not far from the imperial city—
the river moistens nine lǐ,
and I hope the capital will also share in its blessings."
It is also said that a fish-man saw Yǔ,
as recorded in the *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù*:
When Yǔ managed the waters,
he observed the river,
and saw a white-faced, tall man
with a fish body,
who emerged and said:
"I am the essence of the river."
He gave Yǔ the *Hétú* and returned to the depths.
The horse diagram was bestowed upon Fúxī.
The *Lǐ* records:
The river produced the horse diagram.
Celebrate the radiant light that filled the four directions,
as stated in the *Shū Zhōng Hòu*:
Radiant light emerged from the river,
and auspicious energy filled the four directions.
Sigh at the difficulty of expecting human longevity.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* records:
A Zhōu poem says:
"Waiting for the river to clear—
how long is a human lifespan?"
Recognize the hidden flow beneath the surface,
see the annotation above for "Jīng yú Zhāngyè."
Marvel at the swift, winding passage of its rapid flow.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
The river, because it winds, can flow far;
mountains, because they slope gradually, can rise high;
the Way, because it is leisurely, can transform.
Gāo Bìng's words were profound,
as recorded in the *Hàn Shū*:
Commandant of Chángshuǐ Gāo Bìng said:
River breaches often occur around Píngyuán and Dōngjùn,
because the terrain is low and the soil loose and poor.
I have heard that when Yǔ managed the river,
he originally left this area empty,
to serve as a bend for the water.
Examining recent breaches of the Qín and Hàn periods in the areas of Cáo and Wèi,
they did not exceed one hundred eighty lǐ.
This area could be left empty,
without building official posts or civilian houses.
Wáng Jǐng's understanding was subtle.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* records:
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
discussions were held on managing the Biàn Canal.
The emperor summoned the man from Lèlàng, Wáng Jǐng, to inquire about the water's form.
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Wáng Jǐng the "Classic of Mountains and Seas," the "Records of Rivers and Canals," and the "Maps of the Tribute of Yǔ."
He mobilized several hundred thousand soldiers,
and ordered Wáng Jǐng, along with the court architect Yèzhě Wáng Wú,
to manage the canal embankments.
They constructed over a thousand lǐ from Xíngyáng to the estuary at Qiānchéng.
Wáng Jǐng assessed the terrain,
cut through mountains and opened up gorges,
fortified strategic points against flooding,
dredged and cleared blockages,
installing a sluice gate every ten lǐ.
The water was thus able to flow and circulate,
eliminating the risk of breaches and leaks.
The following year,
the canal was completed.
The Emperor personally inspected it,
and ordered the commanderies and kingdoms along the river
to appoint officials for river embankments,
following the old system of the Western Capital.
These measures all captured the most effective techniques for managing rivers and canals.
Why, then, did later generations fail to reflect on them?
Mountains
Mountains are
that which disseminate,
disseminating qi and giving birth to the myriad things.
From Shuōwén.
As for its Celestial Grandson and Sunrise Viewing Peak,
Bówùzhì states:
Mount Tài,
also called Celestial Grandson,
meaning it is the grandson of the Celestial Emperor.
It governs the summoning of human souls.
In the east, where the myriad things first take form,
it knows the length of a ruler's life.
Yìng Shào's Hànguānyí states:
To the southeast of Mount Tài is a place called Sunrise Viewing Peak,
where at the first crow of the rooster,
one can see the sun begin to rise.
Zhōngnán and Tàiyī,
Wǔjīng Yàoyì states:
Mount Tàiyī is in Wǔgōng County, Fúfēng,
connected to the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Pénglái and the Nine Qi,
Shízhōujì states:
Outside Pénglái Mountain is a circular sea,
called the Míng Sea,
where even without wind, waves rise a hundred zhang high.
Above it dwells the Nine Qi Elder,
a True Official of the Nine Heavens.
Kūnlún and the Five Colors,
Bówùzhì states:
Kūnlún Mountain stretches ten thousand li in breadth,
a gathering place for divine beings,
producing five-colored clouds and qi,
and five-colored flowing water.
This water flows southeast to become the Hé River of the Central Kingdom.
Tiāntāi and Chìchéng,
Sūn Chuò's "Tiāntāi Fù" states:
"Chìchéng rises with rosy clouds to mark its peak,
waterfalls cascade to define its paths."
Lóngmén and Jīshí.
The Shū states:
"Floating past Jīshí,
one reaches Lóngmén on the western Hé."
Seeking the ultimate Way at Kōngtóng,
Zhuāngzǐ states:
The Yellow Emperor heard that Guǎngchéngzǐ was atop Kōngtóng Mountain,
and went there to inquire about the Way.
Recognizing the divine person at Gūyè.
See the note on "imagining the skin and flesh of Gūyè" in the "Bīng Fù."
Regarding Jiāngláng's one son returning home,
Jùnguózhì states:
Jiāngláng Mountain has three peaks,
each further topped with massive rocks.
In ancient times, three brothers from a family at the mountain's base
transformed here.
During the turmoil of the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn,
a man named Zhàn Mǎn also lived by the mountain.
He had a son serving as an official who could not return home.
Zhàn prayed to the three rocks.
Within ten days,
Zhàn's son, while out on the Luò River,
encountered three youths.
They told him to close his eyes,
enter a carriage,
and in a daze, he knew not where he went.
After a long while, he arrived home.
Regarding the twin youths of Línlǜ who did not eat.
Yán Xiū Nèizhuàn states:
Qiáo Shùn had two sons,
named Zhāng and Ruì.
They served as disciples to the immortal Lú Zǐjī
in the Qīxiá Valley of Lónglǜ Mountain.
They each took one pill of the Flying Dragon medicine,
and for a thousand years felt no hunger.
Thus, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi wrote in a poem:
"On the western mountain are twin youths,
who neither drink nor eat."
Lofty is that southern mountain,
the Shī states:
Lofty is that southern mountain,
its rocks rugged and steep.
Beginning with a single fist-sized stone.
The Lǐ states:
Now, take a mountain:
it begins with the accumulation of fist-sized stones.
When it becomes vast and great,
grasses and trees grow upon it,
birds and beasts dwell within it,
and treasures arise from it.
The offering of placing sacrifices on mounds,
Ěryǎ states:
Sacrificing to mountains is called "guǐ xuán" (placing on mounds).
Pèilín takes precedence.
The Lǐ states:
When the people of Qí were to perform rites at Mount Tài,
they would first perform rites at Pèilín.
Thus, Liáng was the object of sacrifice for Jìn,
Ěryǎ states:
Mount Liáng
was the object of sacrifice for Jìn.
The note says:
It is in Féngyì.
Mín is indeed the source of the Jiāng.
The Shū states:
Mount Mín guides the Jiāng.
Towering is the elegant prominence of the Incense Burner Peak,
Nán Yōngzhōu Jì states:
Mount Wǔdāng,
lofty and precipitous,
resembles a Boshan incense burner.
Mount Lú also has an Incense Burner Peak.
Opposing is the high suspension of Shèdì.
Shuǐjīngzhù states:
In Kuàijī, there is Mount Shèdì,
which from afar looks like an archery target.
The locals use it for divination:
if it appears dark, rice will be expensive.
A proverb says:
"If Shèdì is bright,
a hú (of rice) costs a hundred;
if Shèdì is dark,
a hú costs a thousand."
As for touching the rocks and exhaling clouds,
Shuōyuàn states:
The Five Sacred Peaks can broadly spread clouds and rain,
and can broadly gather clouds and rain.
Touching the rocks, they emerge;
spreading an inch, they merge;
before the morning is high, they rain upon the world.
Containing marshes and disseminating qi,
Chūnqiū Shuōtící states:
The word for mountain (shān) means to disseminate (xuān).
It contains marshes and disseminates qi,
harmonizing with the hundred spirits.
Crowing is the treasure chicken of Chéncāng,
Sān Qín Jì states:
South of Mount Tàibái lies Mount Chéncāng.
On the mountain, there is a stone indistinguishable from a chicken.
When Zhào Gāo set fire to the mountain,
the chicken flew away.
It crows at dawn on the mountaintop,
its sound heard thirty li away.
Some say it is a jade chicken.
Soaring is the white pheasant of Chúnyú.
Wǔlíng Jì states:
Mount Chúnyú is near Mount Báizhì.
Halfway up a sheer ravine, there is a white stone pheasant.
From afar, its head and tail appear about two zhang long.
It stretches its feet and spreads its wings,
as if soaring through the void.
Already imbued with feeling for measuring timber,
Zuǒzhuàn states:
If the mountain has timber,
the craftsman measures it.
Also, the mind wanders in piling baskets of earth,
Lúnyǔ states:
It is like building a mountain:
if one basketful is lacking for completion,
and I stop, I stop.
It is like leveling ground:
though I have only piled one basketful,
if I advance, I advance.
Ascending Wǎnwěi to obtain writings,
Wú Yuè Chūnqiū states:
Yǔ grieved that his father's task remained unaccomplished.
He ascended Mount Héng, sacrificed a white horse, and offered prayers.
He dreamed of a man in crimson embroidered robes,
who called himself the envoy of Xuányí and Cāngshuǐ.
He said to Yǔ:
"If you wish to obtain my mountain writings,
fast and purify at the peak of the Yellow Emperor."
Yǔ then withdrew,
fasted for three days,
ascended Wǎnwěi,
opened the rocks, and obtained writings of gold slips and jade characters,
which detailed the essentials of flood control.
Producing vessel-carts to manifest auspicious signs.
The Lǐ states:
Mountains produce vessel-carts,
rivers produce horse diagrams.
The Yellow Emperor's journey to Jùcí,
Yángchéng Jì states:
The Yellow Emperor ascended Mount Jùcí,
climbed to the top of the Great Embankment,
and received the Divine Mushroom Diagram from the Huánglú童子 (Yellow Reed Youth).
King Xià's ascent to Kuàijì.
Wú Yuè Chūnqiū states:
Yǔ toured Yuè,
held a grand assembly to discuss the way of governing the state,
and renamed Mount Máo as Kuàijì.
As for exploring Yǔ's Cave,
Shuǐjīngzhù states:
East of Mount Kuàijī, there is a cave,
deep and bottomless,
called Yǔ's Cave.
Many eastern travelers explore this cave.
Recording the achievements of Qín.
Shuǐjīngzhù states:
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended Mount Kuàijī,
engraved a stone to record his achievements,
inscribed by Lǐ Sī.
Some mountains are marked by nine peaks,
as recorded in the "Jiǔhuáshān Lù":
"The peaks and ridges have extraordinary forms,
their number being nine,
hence they are called Jiǔzǐ."
Lǐ Bái later renamed them Jiǔhuá.
Some mountains receive ceremonial honors equivalent to the Three Dukes.
The "Lǐ" states:
"The Five Sacred Mountains are honored as the Three Dukes,
the Four Great Rivers are honored as the feudal lords."
We have heard of Xiè Língyùn wearing clogs;
the "Sòng Shū" says:
"Xiè Língyùn loved climbing mountains,
and often wore wooden clogs.
When ascending, he removed the front teeth,
when descending, he removed the rear teeth."
We have also heard of Bó Zōng being consulted about crumbling soil.
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
"Mount Liáng collapsed,
and the Marquis of Jìn summoned Bó Zōng.
Bó Zōng made way for a courier,
saying:
'Make way for the courier!'
The courier said:
'Waiting for me is not as fast as taking a shortcut.'
[Bó Zōng] asked where he was from,
and he replied:
'I am from Jiàng.'
[Bó Zōng] asked about affairs in Jiàng,
and he said:
'Mount Liáng has collapsed,
and they are about to summon Bó Zōng to discuss it.'
[Bó Zōng] asked what should be done,
and he replied:
'The mountain had crumbling soil and collapsed,
what can be done?
The state is master of the mountains and rivers.
Therefore, when mountains collapse and rivers dry up,
the ruler refrains from feasting, wears plain garments, rides in an unadorned carriage, suspends music, leaves his residence,
offers sacrifices to the spirits,
and the scribes recite prayers according to ritual.'"
As for the Wèn being the Celestial Well,
the "Hé Tú" says:
"The land of Mount Wèn forms a well's network,
Heaven uses it to bring prosperity,
the spirits use it to establish blessings,
above it is the Celestial Well."
Qí is the Earth's Breast,
the "Hé Tú" says:
"Mount Qí,
located southeast of Kūnlún, is the Earth's Breast."
The constellation Wéi corresponds to Tóngbó,
the "Hé Tú" says:
"Mount Tóngbó is an earthly cavern,
above it is the star Wéi."
The constellation Bì is connected to Niǎoshǔ.
The "Hé Tú" says:
"Mount Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué,
is the stem of the earth,
above it is the star Yǎnbì."
We praise Wú Xù's observation of Dài,
the "Shǐ Jì" says:
"Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said to his sons:
'I have hidden a precious tally on Mount Cháng.
Whoever goes and obtains it shall be established as my heir.'
The sons all rushed there,
but found nothing.
Wú Xù said:
'Mount Cháng overlooks Dài,
Dài can be taken.'
Jiǎnzǐ said:
'He understands the tally.'
And so he established him."
We admire Zhòngní's regarding Lǔ as small.
The "Mèngzǐ" says:
"Confucius ascended the Eastern Mountain and regarded Lǔ as small;
he ascended Mount Tài and regarded the world as small."
Some mountains resemble caps and headscarves,
the "Xuānchéng Tújīng" says:
"Mount Zé has layered peaks, lofty and steep,
shaped like a cap and headscarf."
Some take the form of drumsticks and drums.
The "Suí Tújīng" says:
"Mount Yān is in Yì County.
On the cliff side there is a stone drum,
over a hundred *zhàng* from the ground.
Looking at it,
it resembles several hundred *dàn* grain bins,
with beams passing through it left and right.
Southeast of the drum is a stone man,
holding a drumstick as if striking it.
It is said among the people,
'When the stone drum of Mount Yān sounds, there will be war.'"
We are moved by the loyal minister who urged his carriage onward,
the "Hàn Shū" says:
"Wáng Yáng was the Inspector of Yì Province.
While on an inspection tour, he reached the Jiǔzhébǎn slope at Qiónglái,
and sighed, saying:
'I have received this body from my ancestors;
how can I repeatedly traverse such peril?'
Later, he resigned due to illness.
When Wáng Zūn became Inspector,
upon reaching that slope,
he asked his subordinate:
'Is this not the path that Wáng Yáng feared?'
Zūn shouted to his driver:
'Drive on!'
Wáng Yáng was a filial son,
Wáng Zūn was a loyal minister."
We recognize the Jade Maiden pounding clothes.
The "Jùn Guó Zhì" says:
"On Mount Líng,
in ancient times, a divine maiden pounded clothes here,
hence it was called Mount Dǎoyī.
On the southernmost cliff of the mountain is a square stone, bright and lustrous,
called the Jade Maiden's Pounding Stone."
Xuánpǔ once detained Mù Mǎn,
the "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"Mount Kūnlún
is 110,000 *lǐ* from the earth.
Above it is a layered city of nine tiers;
if one ascends twice that height,
it is called Lángfēng;
if one descends twice that height,
it is called Xuánpǔ."
The "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" says:
"The Son of Heaven reached the hill of Kūnlún.
On the summer solstice, day Dīngmǎo, he ascended Mount Chūn,
to gaze upon the four wilds.
This is the highest mountain under heaven,
what the former kings called Xuánpǔ."
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"It is truly the level garden of the Emperor."
Shūshǔ once confined Èrfù.
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"Èrfù's minister was named Wēi.
Together with Èrfù, he killed Yàyǔ.
The Emperor then shackled them on Mount Shūshǔ,
fettering his right foot,
binding his hands behind his back,
and tying his hair to a large rock beneath the mountain,
northwest of Kāití.
Note:
During the reign of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
men were sent to excavate in Shàng Commandery.
They uncovered a large rock and found a man,
naked, with disheveled hair, hands bound behind his back,
and one foot shackled.
No one recognized him.
Liú Zǐzhèng, referring to this account,
greatly astonished Emperor Xuān.
People of the time vied to study the 'Shānhǎi Jīng.'"
Then there are solitary stone sails,
as recorded in Xiàhóu Céngxiān's "Zhì":
"Mount Kuàijī has stone sails,
rocks surging forth, standing like walls,
spanning the river and hanging in the air.
Viewed from afar, they are lush and abundant,
resembling unfurled sails."
Also,
the "Wǔlíng Jì" says:
"Mount Shífān,
with perilous rising rocks,
looks like several hundred sails."
Dǐzhù divides the flow.
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" says:
"Regarding Dǐzhù:
When Yǔ controlled the great flood,
he cut through mountains that blocked the water,
thus breaking the mountain to open the river.
The river water divided and flowed around the mountain,
appearing in the water like a pillar,
hence it is called 'Dǐzhù.'"
The Giant Spirit splitting Mount Tàihuà,
Guō Yuánshēng's "Shù Zhēng Jì" says:
"Mount Huà and Mount Shǒuyáng
were originally one mountain.
The river god, the Giant Spirit, split it open
to allow the river to flow through,
hence palm prints remain there."
Gònggōng striking Mount Bùzhōu.
See the annotation for 'Gònggōng breaking the pillar' in the "Tiān Fù."
Qínwàng holds golden tablets and jade books,
where spiritual secrets lie hidden;
the "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" says:
"Mount Qínwàng in Kuàijī is directly south of the province,
the most outstanding among the peaks,
visible upon entering the region.
The 'Wú Yuè Chūnqiū' states:
'The mountain resembles an overturned cauldron or jar,
within the jar are golden tablets and jade books,
the Yellow Emperor's hidden prophecy.'
It also says:
'The books with golden tablets and jade characters,
which Xià Yǔ uncovered,
contained the principles for governing all rivers.'"
Luófú holds jade chambers and gem halls,
where immortals and divine beings roam and play.
The "Rìnán Zhì" says:
"Mount Luófú was originally Mount Pénglái,
A peak contains seventy-two jade chambers and gem-studded rooms.
It is also heard that Yíng Zhèng once drove them,
see the annotation "Qín Huáng Guò Hǎi" in the "Rì Fù".
Yúgōng desired to move them,
the "Lièzǐ" says:
The two mountains Tàiháng and Wángwū,
are seven hundred li square,
and ten thousand rèn high.
The Foolish Old Man of the Northern Mountain,
nearly ninety years old,
lived facing the mountains.
Troubled by the obstruction of the mountains to the north,
and the circuitous routes for coming and going,
he gathered his household to deliberate,
saying:
"I and you shall exhaust our strength to level the perilous heights,
is it acceptable?"
They all agreed in a chorus.
His wife said:
"With your strength,
you cannot even damage the mound of Kuífù.
What can you do about Tàiháng and Wángwū?
Moreover, where will you place the earth and stones?"
They chorused:
"Throw them at the edge of the Bó Sea,
north of Yǐntǔ."
Thereupon, he led three sons and grandsons who could carry loads,
knocking on stones and digging up earth,
and transported them to the edge of the Bó Sea.
The widow of the Jīngchéng family, a neighbor, had a surviving son,
just at the age of losing his baby teeth,
who went to assist them.
When cold and heat exchanged seasons,
they had only made one round trip.
The Wise Old Man of Héqū laughed and stopped him,
saying:
"Extreme indeed,
is your lack of wisdom!
With your remaining years and waning strength,
you cannot even destroy a single hair of the mountain.
What can you do about the earth and stones?"
The Foolish Old Man of the Northern Mountain sighed deeply and said:
"Your mind is not even equal to that of a widow and a weak child.
Though I die,
there will be my sons surviving.
Sons will in turn bear grandsons,
grandsons will in turn bear sons,
grandsons and sons, sons and grandsons,
will be without end or exhaustion.
Yet the mountains do not increase in height,
why worry that they cannot be leveled!"
The Wise Old Man of Héqū had nothing to reply.
The god who handled snakes heard of this,
feared that he would not cease,
and reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor was moved by his sincerity,
commanded the two sons of Kuā'éshì to carry the mountains away,
one placed east of Shuò,
one placed south of Yōng.
Saw Xiū Yáng at Huàyīn,
the "Lièxiān Zhuàn" says:
Xiū Yáng Gōng,
was a man of Shǔ,
in a stone chamber on Huàyīn Mountain,
there was a suspended stone couch,
he lay upon it,
and the stone was completely worn through and sunken.
Saw Wáng Qiáo at Gōushì.
The "Lièxiān Zhuàn" says:
Wáng Qiáo,
was Prince Jìn of King Líng of Zhōu,
fond of playing the shēng to imitate the cry of the phoenix,
he wandered between the Yī and Luò rivers,
Fúqiū Gōng received him and ascended Sōnggāo Mountain.
After more than thirty years,
on the mountain he saw Huán Liáng,
said:
"Tell my family,
on the seventh day of the seventh month await me at the summit of Gōushì Mountain."
On that day,
he indeed rode a white crane and alighted on the mountain peak.
Gazing, they could not reach him,
he raised his hand to bid farewell to the people of the time,
and after several days departed.
Pointed to the palace gate tower distantly connecting to Niútóu,
the "Jìn Shū" says:
Emperor Yuán of Jìn crossed the river and founded the state,
wishing to erect a stone gate tower at the palace gate,
it was undecided.
Wáng Dǎo accompanied him,
the imperial carriage exited Xuānyáng Gate,
then he pointed distantly to the southern peak of Niútóu Mountain as the Heavenly Gate Tower,
Emperor Zhōngzōng followed his suggestion.
Piled armor distantly equaled Xióng'ěr.
The "Dōngguān Hàn Jì" says:
The Chìméi rebels first surrendered,
carts transported armor, helmets, weapons, and crossbows,
piled up equal to Xióng'ěr Mountain.
There is even the Qúnyù Cèfǔ,
the "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" says:
On the day Guǐsì,
arrived at Qúnyù Mountain,
its four sides are straight as a plumb line,
it is what the former kings called the Cèfǔ.
Annotation:
The four sides are straight as a plumb line,
means all are level and straight.
The lower capital of Kūnlún,
the "Sōushén Jì" says:
Kūnlún Mountain,
is the lower capital of the Emperor,
surrounded by mountains of blazing fire.
Dòngtái Qián Huò,
the "Dào Jīng" says:
Below Huò Mountain there is Dòngtái,
two hundred li square,
it is the residence of the Lord of Fate.
Yuánjiào and Fānghú.
The "Lièzǐ" says:
East of the Bó Sea there is a great sea,
within it are mountains:
one called Dàiyú,
two called Yuánjiào,
three called Fānghú,
four called Yíngzhōu,
five called Pénglái.
Upon them, terraces and pavilions contain gold and jade.
Trees of pearl and jade-like stones grow in clusters,
their fruits all have flavor,
eating them grants immortality.
The people are all immortals and sages,
flying and traveling back and forth in a single day and night.
The one who feasted the hundred spirits was Dìtái,
the "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
Gǔzhōng Mountain,
is the place of Dìtái,
where he feasted the hundred spirits.
Now named Zhōng Mountain,
is in Lùhún County.
Welcomed the Four Hoary Ones at Gāochē.
The "Gāoshì Zhuàn" says:
On Gāochē Mountain there are steles and shrines of the Four Hoary Ones,
all erected by Emperor Huì of Hàn.
It is the place where Empress Gāo of Hàn sent Zhāng Liáng to the Southern Mountains to welcome the Four Hoary Ones,
hence named Gāochē Mountain.
And then, gazing at the graceful hanging crane,
the "Línhǎi Jì" says:
West of the commandery is Báihè Mountain,
on the mountain there is a pool with spring water cascading down,
viewed from afar like an inverted white crane,
hence named "Guàhè Spring".
Looking at the winding coiled dragon.
Xú Xuàn's "Shì Wèn" says:
Zhūgě Liàng considered Zhōng Mountain to be a coiled dragon,
which is Jiǎng Mountain.
Heard the clear whistle of Sūmén,
the "Shí Dào Zhì" says:
Sūmén Mountain,
also called Sū Lǐng,
is where Ruǎn Jí saw Sūn Dēng give a long whistle,
and a phoenix gathered at the place where Dēng lived in seclusion,
hence Dēng was called Master Sūmén.
Sought the lost texts of Yǒuyáng.
The "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:
On Xiǎoyǒu Mountain,
within a stone cave there are a thousand volumes of books,
traditionally said to be left by people of Qín who studied here,
hence they remained,
therefore Prince Xiāngdōng of Liáng said:
"Seek the lost texts of Yǒuyáng."
Chanted about lodging and drinking at Gānyán,
Lǐ Gōngxù's "Zhào Jì" says:
Bǎirén County has Gānyán Mountain,
the "Wèi" ode says "lodged at Gān,
drank farewell at Yán" refers to this.
Recorded the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices at Yúntíng.
The "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Mountain,
and the Shàn sacrifice on Liángfǔ.
Annotation:
Yúnyún, Tíngtíng, Sùrán, Hāolǐ, Shèshǒu, Liángfǔ,
are all small mountains below Tài Mountain.
The stone gate tower is below the western cliff.
There is also Lán Yán where cranes cry,
the "Shénjìng Jì" says:
Xíngyáng County has Lán Yán Mountain,
steep and towering a thousand zhàng.
Tradition says:
In the past, a husband and wife lived in seclusion on this mountain for several hundred years,
and transformed into a pair of cranes.
Suddenly one morning,
one crane was harmed by a person,
the other crane yearly often cried mournfully,
to this day the sound echoes through the cliffs and valleys,
no one knows for how many years.
Jīnhuá where sheep were scolded,
see the annotation "Chūpíng Chì Yáng" in the "Shí Fù".
Twice formed, thrice layered,
the "Ěryǎ ‧ Shì Shān" says:
Thrice layered ascending,
Again forming excellence.
Morning sun and evening sun.
The *Erya* says:
The west side of a mountain is called the evening sun,
the east side of a mountain is called the morning sun.
Guìyáng’s talking stones,
the *Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
Guìyáng’s Wànsuì Mountain,
produces the herb of divine longevity and immortal prescriptions,
it is said that consuming it grants immortality.
There is also Huàshí Mountain,
where stones make sounds,
as if people are conversing together.
Wú palace gathering fragrant herbs.
The *Wúdì Jì* says:
Xiāngshān,
the King of Wú sent beauties to gather fragrant herbs on this mountain,
hence it was named accordingly,
thus there is the Fragrant Herb Gathering Path.
Bitterly cold, the Wind Gate howls fiercely,
the *Shuǐjīng Zhù* says:
Běiqū County has Fēngshān,
on which there is a cave like a wheel,
where the wind blows desolately without cease.
Where it strikes directly,
there is almost no living grass,
truly it is the gate of all winds.
Sparkling and brilliant, the fire well emits light.
See the annotation “Observing that luminous terrace” in the *Fu on Fire*.
As for those with stones atop them, they are called jū,
the *Erya* says:
Earth bearing stones is called jū.
The annotation states:
A earthen mountain with stones on top.
Abundant with grass is called hù.
The *Erya·Shì Shān* says:
Abundant with grass and trees is hù,
without grass and trees is qǐ.
Plucking the immortal peach of Tiānzhù,
the *Jùnguó Zhì* says:
On the Tiānzhù Cliff of Língtái Mountain,
there is a peach tree,
five chi tall,
its bark is that of a peach,
its core and flesh resemble cypress.
Zhāng Líng, Wáng Liáng, and Zhào Shēng tested their methods here,
for over four hundred years.
The peach tree remains undecayed to this day,
with a small stele recording it.
Gathering the mica of Huáróng,
the *Jīngnán Zhì* says:
Huáróng’s Fāngtái Mountain,
produces mica,
the local people gather it,
first observing where the clouds emerge,
then digging beneath that spot,
and none fail to obtain a great harvest.
Often there are pieces five or six chi long,
which can be made into screens.
When digging, one must avoid making noise,
otherwise what is obtained will be coarse and inferior.
Seeking Xiè Fū’s purple stones,
Kǒng Língfú’s *Kuàijī Jì* says:
Zhūjì County has Niǎodài Mountain,
on which there are many purple stones,
unknown to the world.
The recluse Xiè Fū,
in his youth began ventures in various mountains,
often moving from place to place,
spending thousands in costs,
nearly exhausting his livelihood,
later traveled to this area,
dreamt the mountain spirit spoke to him,
saying:
“I shall assist you with five hundred thousand.”
In the morning, he saw an unusual stone beneath the host’s bed,
its color very bright and clear,
tried taking it to polish and wipe,
and it was a purple stone.
He then asked where it came from,
the host said:
“It comes from this mountain.”
So he went to dig,
and indeed gained immeasurable profit.
Visiting Huán Wēn’s Báizhù,
the *Xuānchéng Tújīng* says:
Báizhù Mountain was originally called Chǔshān.
Huán Wēn led singing girls to roam this mountain,
and when performing music, favored the *Báizhù Gē*,
hence it was renamed.
Marveling at the terraces and pavilions of the Wāgōng,
the *Nánkāng Jì* says:
Jūnshān,
verdant, beautiful, and vivid,
from afar resembling terraces and pavilions,
is named the Wāgōng.
After wind and rain,
the scenery is clear and tranquil,
and one can distinctly hear the sounds of drums and pipes.
Recognizing the towers and battlements of Chóuchí,
the *Qínzhōu Jì* says:
Chóuchí Mountain was originally called Chóuwéi Mountain.
Its shape resembles an overturned sack,
broad on top covering a hundred qǐng,
with cliffs standing a thousand rèn high,
naturally formed towers and battlements to repel enemies,
evenly distributed and well-proportioned,
soaring several zhàng high,
as if made by human effort.
There are also Wūlóng Báiqí,
the *Xiāngchuān Jì* says:
Rǔchéng County has Wūlóng Báiqí Mountain,
with black stones resembling dragons,
and white stones resembling horses.
Zǐgài Qīngní,
the *Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
Héngshān has three peaks,
one of them named Zǐgài.
The *Jùnguó Zhì* says:
Xīngzhōu’s Qīngní Ridge,
with cliffs ten thousand rèn high,
often covered with clouds and rain,
frequently turning into muddy marshes,
hence it was so named.
Yángcháng Niǎohé,
the *Jùnguó Zhì* says:
Yángcháng Pass is west of Lóngmén.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
Dàhé Mountain and Xiǎohé Mountain,
have a temple to Wáng Zhòng.
Zhòng,
styled Cìzhòng,
during the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
transformed the old script of Cāngjié into the modern clerical script,
which was greatly praised in use.
He was summoned,
but did not come.
The First Emperor was furious,
and sent a caged cart for him.
Cìzhòng transformed into a great bird,
emerged from the cart,
soared high into the sky,
reached Xīmén Mountain,
shed two wing feathers,
hence the name.
Mǎ’ān Niúpí,
the *Jùnguó Zhì* says:
Chēnzhōu’s Mǎlǐng Mountain,
was originally called Niúpí Mountain.
The *Xù Nányuè Zhì* says:
Mǎ’ān Mountain,
