during the time of Qín Shǐhuáng, a diviner observing qi said:
“There is five-colored qi in the Southern Sea.”
So a thousand soldiers were dispatched,
to dig and sever the mountain’s ridges.
Now the mountain’s shape resembles a horse’s saddle,
hence it was so named.
Also, the *Xiāngyáng Jì* says:
Wàngchǔ Mountain,
also called Mǎ’ān Mountain,
was where Liú Hóng and Shān Jiǎn held their Double Ninth festival banquets.
Yuánmén lofty and steep,
the *Yìzhōu Jì* says:
Yuánmén Mountain is in Fú County,
with many gibbons on it.
The mountain has two peaks,
towering erect like a gate.
Yànsài winding and extending,
the *Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
Jǐngshān,
where wild geese flying south and returning north,
consistently pass over it,
people call it Yànsài Mountain.
The immortal old man planting jade,
see the annotation “Old Man Yáng planted it and took a wife” in the *Fu on Jade*.
The resolute woman grinding her hairpin,
the *Suí Tújīng* says:
Mójī Mountain is in Huáiróng County.
Long ago, Zhào Xiāngzǐ killed the King of Dài.
His wife said:
“Dài is already destroyed,
where shall I return?”
So she ground her hairpin on the mountain and killed herself.
The people of Dài named the mountain Mójī Mountain.
Listening to the words of Cài Dàn,
the *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Cài Dàn,
claimed to have been exiled to Kūnlún,
and was asked:
“What is Kūnlún like?”
He replied:
“Heaven does not ask how many li high it is,
but when you look up at it,
it is no more than a dozen li from heaven.”
Making a pact with Ānqī,
the *Lièxiān Zhuàn* says:
Ānqīshēng,
a man of Fùxiāng in Lángyá,
all say he lived a thousand autumns.
Qín Shǐhuáng spoke with him,
He was presented with gold and jade worth tens of millions.
Upon leaving Fùxiāng Pavilion,
he left it all behind,
keeping only a pair of red jade shoes,
and replied:
"In a thousand autumns, seek me beneath Pénglái Mountain."
Witness Zhùróng descending upon the lofty peak,
hear the yuèzhuó calling at Qí Mountain.
The Guóyǔ states:
When the Xià dynasty rose,
Zhùróng descended upon Sōng Mountain;
when the Zhōu dynasty rose,
the yuèzhuó called at Qí Mountain.
Note:
The characters "chóng" and "sōng"
were interchangeable in ancient times.
Again, hear of Mǎ Yuán at Hútóu,
The Wǔlíng Jì states:
Hútóu Mountain lies east of the county,
where Mǎ Yuán excavated a chamber.
Within the chamber was a serpent,
as large as a hundred-hú vessel,
said to be the lingering spirit of Yuán.
Yáng Gōng at Xiànshǒu.
The Shídào Zhì states:
Yáng Hù once ascended Xiàn Mountain with his assistant Zōu Zhàn,
and wept, saying:
"Since the universe began, this mountain has existed.
Throughout the ages, many worthy and accomplished men have climbed here,
gazing into the distance as you and I do now.
All have vanished into obscurity,
and thinking of this fills one with sorrow.
After my death,
my soul shall still ascend this mountain."
Zhàn replied:
"Your virtue crowns the four seas,
your Way matches the sages of old.
Your fine reputation and renown
shall be passed down alongside this mountain.
As for one like me,
it shall be as you say."
Scoop the jade ointment of Shàoshì,
The Hétú states:
Shàoshì Mountain possesses white jade ointment;
consuming it makes one an immortal.
Drink the fine wine of Dòngtíng.
The Bówù Zhì states:
At Jūn Mountain in Dòngtíng,
the two daughters of the Emperor dwell,
called the Xiāng Consorts.
Also, the Jīngzhōu Tújīng states:
Where Xiāng Jūn roamed,
hence it is called Jūn Mountain.
A hidden passage connects it with Wú's Bāo Mountain.
Upon it are several dǒu of fine wine;
those who drink it become deathless.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn fasted for seven days,
then dispatched several dozen men and women to Jūn Mountain,
where they obtained the wine and were about to drink it.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"I recognize this wine;
allow me to inspect it."
Thereupon he drank it all in one go.
The Emperor wished to execute him,
but Shuò said:
"If you kill me and I die,
this proves the wine ineffective.
Since it is effective,
even if you kill me, I shall not die."
So he was pardoned.
Again, gaze upon the morning clouds at Chì'àn,
The Nányǎnzhōu Jì states:
Five lǐ east of Guābù Mountain,
lies Chì'àn Mountain,
facing south over the river.
Luó Jūnzhāng said:
"Chì'àn is like morning clouds."
Guō Jǐngchún's "Jiāng Fù" states:
Surging waves pound at Chì'àn.
Sacrifice to Huáng Shí at Gǔchéng.
See the note "Sacrifice at that Gǔchéng" in the "Shí Fù."
Though Yángqí could be purchased,
The Jīngzhōu Jì states:
At Yángqí Mountain in Shíshǒu County,
nothing is produced,
nothing worth recording.
Originally it belonged to Nánpíng's territory.
Fàn Xuánpíng's record states:
According to ancient tradition,
Hú Bóshǐ, because his county had no mountains,
purchased this mountain to include in the census register.
Could Běimáng ever be leveled?
The Wèi Zhì states:
Emperor Míng wished to level Běimáng,
so that from the terrace one could see Mèngjīn.
Xīn Pí remonstrated:
"Heaven and earth have their nature,
heights high and depths low.
To reverse this now
is contrary to principle,
and moreover wastes human labor,
which the people cannot bear."
The Emperor then desisted.
Chén Yīn thereby established his name,
The Kuàijī Jì states:
At Chén Yīn Mountain,
there once was an expert archer named Chén Yīn.
The King of Yuè sent him to train soldiers in archery outside the capital, where he died,
and was buried there.
The tomb walls were all painted with images of mounted archery,
hence the mountain was named after him.
Zhāng Shèng thereby gained his name.
The Sòng Shū states:
When Zhāng Jìng served as magistrate of Shàn,
he reached Shèng Pavilion, where his son was born,
so he named him Shèng,
style name Sìshān.
Clouds and mist sometimes form palace towers,
Yuán Shānsōng's Hòu Hàn Shū states:
When Emperor Guāngwǔ fēnged Tài Mountain,
clouds and mist formed into palace towers.
Wind and rain once were avoided at Xiáo Ridge.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Duke Mù of Qín
sent Mèng Míng to lead a covert army to attack Zhèng,
and the army departed outside the eastern gate.
Jiǎn Shū's son was among the troops;
weeping, he saw them off,
saying:
"The Jìn will surely intercept our army at Xiáo,
where there are two ridges.
The southern ridge
is the tomb of Xià Hòu Gāo;
the northern ridge
is where King Wén once took shelter from wind and rain.
You will surely die there,
and I shall gather your bones."
Alas! The terrace for ascending to immortality at Shàoshì,
The Shùzhēng Jì states:
Shàoshì Mountain abounds in divine herbs;
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn built a terrace for ascending to immortality there.
The Huáyáng cave at Jūqū.
The Máo Jūn Nèi Zhuàn states:
Máo Mountain,
also called Jūqū Mountain,
was known in Qín times as the Huáyáng cave heaven.
Engraving names at Yānrán,
The Hòu Hàn Shū states:
Dòu Xiàn battled the Chányú at Jīluò Mountain,
and routed them utterly.
Xián then ascended Yānrán Mountain,
carved stone and erected a stele,
ordering Bān Gù to compose an inscription.
Qílián becoming a tomb mound.
The Hàn Shū states:
Huò Qùbìng, as General of Swift Cavalry, attacked the Xiōngnú,
reaching Qílián Mountain,
where he captured thirty thousand heads and prisoners.
When Qùbìng died,
the Emperor mourned him,
mobilized the black-armored troops of the dependent states,
and arrayed the army from Cháng'ān to Màolíng,
constructing a tomb mound shaped like Qílián Mountain.
Some are renowned for their military achievements,
others esteemed by divine immortals.
If passing them brings fever to the body,
traversing them causes headaches,
The Hàn Shū states:
Dù Qīn advised Grand General Wáng Fèng:
"The route to the state of Jìbīn passes over Great Headache Mountain and Lesser Headache Mountain,
and the red earth fever-inducing slopes."
They merely bring affliction to the barbarians,
and offer no benefit to wealth or utility.
Water
That which moistens all things,
nothing moistens like water.
From the *Book of Changes*.
As for admiring the patterned colors in the Suī and Huàn rivers,
the *Shu Yi Ji* says: the Suī and Huàn are two rivers,
whose waves resemble five colors,
having patterned colors,
hence they are called the "Embroidered Waters."
Performing the purification rites by the Zhēn and Wěi rivers,
see the note on "admiring these Zhēn and Wěi" in the "Spring Rhapsody."
Drinking the honey-like water of Xuánzhōu,
the *Long Yu He Tu* says:
Xuánzhōu is in the Northern Sea,
100,000 *li* from the southern shore.
On it grows *zhi* mushrooms by the Xuán stream,
the stream water is like honey,
drinking it leads to long life.
Tasting the sweet-spring-like water of Jìn'ān.
The *Míng Shān Lüè Jì* says:
Monk Quán Dàorén lived on Huò Mountain in Jìn'ān.
One morning when he went out,
he suddenly saw exceptionally white water in the stream,
drinking it was sweet as sweet spring water.
The water flowed very swiftly,
he managed to fetch a little with a vessel,
and offered it to Táo Jìn'ān.
It was no longer suitable for drinking.
Quán lived to be over 130 years old,
and later his end was unknown.
Some speak of it wetting chariots,
the *Book of Songs* says:
"The Qí River flows vast and wide,
wetting the curtains of the chariot."
Note:
"Curtains of the chariot"
refers to a woman's carriage.
Some speak of it soaking the axle.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The Jǐ River is full and overflowing,
yet the full Jǐ does not soak the axle."
Singing of Qū Yuán washing his hat-strings,
the *Chǔ Cí* says:
"When the Cānglàng's waters are clear,
I can wash my hat-strings therein;
when the Cānglàng's waters are muddy,
I can wash my feet therein."
Ashamed of Cháo Fǔ washing his ears.
The *Yì Shì Zhuàn* says:
Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
Yóu fled from it.
Cháo Fǔ heard of this and washed his ears by the pool.
Fán Shù,
styled Zhòngwén,
was just watering his ox,
so he drove it away and returned,
ashamed to let the ox drink from the downstream water where he had washed his ears.
As for drawing from that and pouring into this,
the *Book of Songs* says:
"Draw from that distant runoff,
draw from that and pour into this."
Swimming in it, wading through it.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Where it is deep,
I use a raft or boat;
where it is shallow,
I swim or wade through."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* already speaks of it carrying away filth,
the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"There are the Fén and Kuài rivers to carry away its filth."
The *Book of Songs* also speaks of it delighting in hunger.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The Bì spring, so vast and wide,
can delight one even in hunger."
The hexagram image resides in repeated peril,
the *Book of Changes* says:
"Water arrives repeatedly, symbolizing repeated peril."
Its nature lies in following decline.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
The nature of water
is to follow the terrain as it flows,
descending along decline.
Note:
"Decline"
means low ground.
Deepening the spiritual source at Shūlè,
the *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Gěng Gōng was the Colonel Protector of the Wù-Jǐ region.
Seeing that by Shūlè city there was a stream that could be fortified,
he occupied it.
The Xiōngnú came again to attack.
Gōng dug a well in the city fifteen *zhàng* deep but found no water.
He then sighed, saying:
"In the past, General Èrshī drew his sword and stabbed the mountain, and a spring gushed forth."
Then he straightened his clothes and bowed toward the well.
Thereupon, a swift flow rushed out,
and all exclaimed "Long live!"
He then raised the water to show the enemy,
who thought it divine,
and thus withdrew.
Gushing clear streams at Èrshī.
Already seen in the note above.
As for surrounding mountains and flooding hills,
the *Book of Documents* says:
"The vast floodwaters wreak destruction,
wildly surrounding mountains and flooding hills,
massively reaching to the heavens."
Floating the heavens and bearing the earth,
the *Xuán Zhōng Jì* says:
Of all things under heaven, water is the most abundant,
floating the heavens and bearing the earth,
reaching all heights and depths,
moistening all things.
Full and then advancing,
Yángzǐ's *Fǎ Yán* says:
Someone asked about advancement,
he said:
"Water."
Someone said:
"Is it because it never ceases day or night?"
He said:
"That is so.
Full and then advancing—
is that not water!"
Full yet not needing leveling.
The *Sūn Qīngzǐ* says:
Confucius, upon seeing great waters, would always observe them,
saying:
"Water is yielding and acts without striving, resembling virtue;
its vastness, never bending, resembles the Way;
its rushing into hundred-*ren* valleys without fear resembles courage.
When contained, it levels itself, resembling law;
full, it seeks no leveling, resembling justice;
issuing from its source, it flows eastward, resembling purpose."
Knowing the different names for Jiàn and Guǐ springs,
the *Ěryǎ* says:
"Jiàn springs emerge straight up,
meaning they gush forth;
Wò springs hang forth,
meaning they flow downward;
Guǐ springs emerge from caves,
meaning they issue sideways."
Recognizing the distinct meanings of Fèn and Féi.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"Issuing from different sources but flowing together is called Féi;
Fèn,
gushing greatly from below the tail."
The note says:
"Tail"
means the bottom.
Crossing in winter and spring, it freezes and thaws.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
Water, facing winter,
congeals and becomes ice;
welcoming spring,
thaws and becomes water.
Measuring depth and shallowness to lift garments or wade through.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"Deep, then wade through;
shallow, then lift garments."
"Lift" means lifting one's clothes.
Crossing water with clothes on is called "wading."
As for its flowing, bubbling and boiling,
the *Book of Songs* says:
"Bubbling and boiling, the Jiàn spring."
Its Way is spiritually enduring.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"Considering the five materials used together,
truly the virtue of water is spiritually enduring."
The spring of Tiānqí,
the *Hàn Shū* says:
Qín Shǐ Huáng traveled east to the sea,
sacrificing to the eight spirit generals.
The first was the Lord of Heaven,
sacrificed to at Tiānqí.
The Tiānqí deep spring
lies south of Línzī at the foot of the mountain.
The note says:
Five springs issue forth together.
The broth of Dìtái.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
On Gāoqián Mountain,
there is water upon it,
extremely cold and clear,
it is the broth-water of Dìtái.
Startled by the swift rapids at Yànyù,
the *Kuízhōu Tú Jīng* says:
Yànyù is at the mouth of Qútáng.
In summer, the waters are swift and turbulent,
making passage extremely difficult.
A proverb says:
"When Yànyù is as big as a bundle,
Qútáng cannot be touched.
When Yànyù is as big as a horse,
Qútáng dares not be descended."
Awed by the hanging flow at Lǚliáng.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Confucius observed at Lǚliáng,
where the hanging water was thirty *ren* high,
The frothy torrents flow for forty li,
where giant turtles, alligators, fish, and soft-shelled turtles cannot swim,
yet there is a man swimming in it.
He enters along with the swirling eddies.
He emerges together with the bubbling currents.
Then there is a fragrance surpassing pepper and orchids.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
When Yǔ was regulating the waters and lands,
he lost his way and came to a country.
There was no wind, rain, fog, or dew,
and no birds or beasts were born.
There was a mountain named Hú Lǐng,
on whose summit was an opening,
like a circular ring,
named the Zī Cavity.
Water gushed forth from it,
named the Shén Fèn,
whose fragrance surpassed pepper and orchids,
and whose flavor surpassed fine wine.
Its sharpness could pierce metal and stone.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
Water as a substance,
when struck, leaves no wound;
when shot, suffers no injury;
when chopped, is not severed;
when burned, does not ignite.
Its sharpness can pierce metal and stone,
its merit benefits all under heaven.
The Hé River divides at Jiǎn Jié,
see the annotation "Jiǎn Jié, Gōu Pán" in the *Hé Fù*.
The canal is named Zhèng Bái.
The *Hànshū‧Gōuxùzhì* says:
Zhèng Guó,
a hydraulic engineer from Hán.
Hán wished to exhaust Qín,
to prevent it from campaigning eastward,
so they sent Guó to secretly persuade Qín,
to have them channel the Jīng River,
from the west of Zhōngshān to the mouth of Húkǒu to build a canal,
to irrigate the fields and crops.
As the work proceeded, the deceit was discovered,
and Qín wanted to kill Guó.
Guó said:
"I have prolonged Hán's life by a few years,
but for Qín I have established merit for ten thousand generations."
So it was completed,
named the Zhèng Guó Canal.
Also,
in the second year of the Tàishǐ era of Hàn,
the Grand Master Bái Gōng of Zhào again petitioned to channel the Qín canal,
drawing water from the Jīng River alongside to flow into the Wèi,
named the Bái Canal.
A folk song says:
"Where are the fields?
Chíyáng, Gǔkǒu.
Zhèng Guó in front,
Bái Canal rising behind.
Raising shovels like clouds,
opening channels like rain.
One shí of Jīng River water,
carries several dǒu of mud.
Both irrigating and manuring,
making our millet and grain grow.
Clothing and feeding the capital,
millions of mouths."
Praising the gentleman's way of forming friendships,
The *Lǐ* says:
The gentleman's interactions are like water,
the petty person's interactions are like sweet wine.
The gentleman, through plainness, achieves;
the petty person, through sweetness, ruins.
Lamenting the petty person's drowning in it.
The *Lǐ* says:
The petty person drowns in water,
the gentleman drowns in words.
Ritual manifests as deep springs.
The *Lǐ‧Zhōngyōng* says:
Vast and broad as the heavens,
deep springs as the abyss.
The sacrificial name is Qīng Dí.
The *Lǐ* says:
Water used in sacrifices to the ancestral temple is called Qīng Dí.
Admiring Wén Gōng's unique foresight.
The *Hòuhànshū* says:
Rén Wéngōng,
a man of Bājùn,
served as Zhìzhōng.
At that time, there was a great drought,
he told the Cìshǐ:
"On the first day of the fifth month,
there will be a great flood,
we should prepare in advance."
The Cìshǐ did not listen.
Wéngōng alone stored a large boat,
some among the common people believed Wéngōng,
and made considerable preparations.
When that month arrived,
at midday clouds gathered,
and in a moment rain came.
In the late afternoon,
the Jiān River surged up over ten zhàng,
suddenly destroying houses,
harming several thousand people.
Praising Gōngshā's prior knowledge.
The *Hòuhànshū* says:
Gōngshā Mù diligently studied the arts of river and Luo divination and calendrical calculations.
In the first year of Yǒngshòu,
there was heavy rain and flooding,
and from Sānfǔ eastward, nothing was not swept away or submerged.
Mù forewarned the common people to move to high ground,
thus the people of Hóngnóng alone were spared.
Emerging differently yet flowing together,
see the annotation above for "the difference of the fèn's richness."
It bears boats and also overturns boats.
Yuán Hóng's *Sānguó Míngchén Zàn Xù* says:
Rivers and lakes are what bear boats,
and also what overturn boats.
Benevolence and righteousness are what preserve the self,
and also what destroy the self.
Admiring that supreme goodness,
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
The highest goodness is like water,
water benefits all things and does not contend.
Applauding its utmost softness.
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
Water,
the softest thing under heaven,
overcomes the hardest things under heaven.
Moved by Ruòsī's placement by his seat,
The *Tángshū* says:
Kǒng Ruòsī often said that in official service, reaching Zhōngláng was enough.
When he was promoted to Kùbù Láng,
he placed a stone vessel of still water by his seat on the right,
to signify the meaning of knowing when to stop.
As for Zuǒ Cí's reversing the flow.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Zuǒ Cí used qì to control water,
causing the water to reverse its flow for one or two zhàng.
He controlled water placed in the central courtyard exposed to dew,
and even in great cold it did not freeze.
As for observing those ripples and eddies,
The *Shī* says:
The river water is clear and rippling, yī,
and also clear and swirling, yī.
Riding it downstream and upstream,
The *Shàngshū Zhuàn* says:
Going with the flow downstream is called yán.
The *Shī* annotation:
Going against the flow upstream is called sù.
Moistening below and nourishing secretly,
The *Shū* says:
Water is said to moisten what is below.
Paying homage to the source and racing afar.
The *Shī* says:
Full is that flowing water,
paying homage to the sea.
Lamenting that which passes away is like this,
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
The Master standing by a stream said:
"That which passes away is like this,
never ceasing day or night."
Dwelling in what the multitude dislikes.
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
Water benefits all things and does not contend,
dwelling in what the multitude dislikes,
therefore it is close to the Dào.
Admiring that if not mixed, it is clear;
if not stirred, it is level.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
The nature of water,
if not mixed, it is clear;
if not stirred, it is level.
The five colors cannot but be displayed,
The *Lǐ* says:
Water does not correspond to the five colors,
yet the five colors cannot but be displayed.
All affairs cannot but be accomplished.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
Under heaven, nothing is softer and weaker than water,
ascending to heaven it becomes rain and dew,
descending to earth it becomes moisture and nourishment,
all things cannot but be born,
all affairs cannot but be accomplished.
Recognizing the purple mud of Wǔdū,
The *Lǒngyòu Jì* says:
The purple water of Wǔdū has mud,
its color is purple and sticky,
it is presented as tribute for sealing imperial edicts,
hence imperial decrees have the beauty of purple mud.
Seeing the green snake of Bīn territory.
The *Tángshū* says:
Yáng Cháoshèng was the Cìshǐ of Bīnzhōu,
he memorialized:
"Fāngqú, Hédào, and Mùbō,
are all routes for bandits,
I request to fortify them."
The army encamped at Fāngqú,
there was no water,
the troops were clamorous,
suddenly a green snake descended from a height and stood upright.
Observing its traces,
water follows and flows.
Building embankments to encircle it,
it then becomes a still spring.
In Chéngdū,
it is named after brocade;
the Huáyáng Guózhì states:
west of the city wall in Chéngdū,
was the former Brocade Office.
When brocade workers weave brocade,
washing it in this river makes it bright and vivid,
washing it in other rivers is not as good,
hence the name Brocade Lane City.
From Fánglíng,
it is named after powder.
The Jīngzhōu Jì states:
the powder water of Yáng County,
originates from Fánglíng,
taking its water to make powder,
makes it exceptionally fresh and pure compared to other waters.
There is also the sinking feathers of Fúyú,
the Guǎngzhì states:
the Ruò River is north of Fúyú,
unable to bear even feathers.
Xiāngchéng’s blood transformation.
the Gǔjīn Zhù states:
during the Yánpíng era of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
the water of Hédōng transformed into blood.
In the Yuánchū era,
the water of Xiāngchéng in Yǐngchuān transformed into blood,
and did not flow.
Fàn Yún admired benevolence and never slackened,
the Sháozhōu Tújīng states:
north of the Xiūrén River in Qūjiāng County,
there are the Sānfēng Pavilion and the Wǔdù River.
When Fàn Yún of Qí served as Shǐxīng governor,
arriving at the Xiūrén River,
he scooped and drank from it,
composing a poem that said:
"How rustling are the three maples,
how leisurely the five crossings.
Let us drink the Xiūrén water,
without dipping from any evil stream."
Wú Yǐn drank from the Greed Spring yet remained pure.
the Jìnshū states:
When Wú Yǐnzhī served as governor of Guǎngzhōu,
at Shímén in the prefecture, there was a Greed Spring,
legend says those who drink from it become greedy.
Yǐnzhī scooped and drank from it,
composing a poem that said:
"South of the ridges there is a stream,
named the deep Greed Spring.
If Bóyí and Shūqí drank it,
they would never change their hearts."
Xīnfēng’s water clears when times are peaceful,
the Tángshū states:
the water of the Yīngwǔ Valley in Xīnfēng is clear.
A folk saying goes:
"When the valley water is clear,
the world is at peace."
Línzī’s water dries up when the world is in chaos.
the Shùzhēng Jì states:
at the foot of Niú Mountain in Línzī, there is the Nǚ River,
a Qí proverb says:
"When the world is well-governed, the Nǚ River flows;
when the world is in chaos, the Nǚ River dries up."
During Mùróng’s rise, it dried up for years,
but when Sòng Wǔ campaigned north, it surged with great flow.
Huái becomes Hǔ,
Jiāng becomes Tuó,
Hàn becomes Qián,
Luò becomes Bō.
the Ěryǎ · Shìshuǐ states:
Jǐ becomes Chǔ,
Wèn becomes Chǎn,
Luò becomes Bō,
Hàn becomes Qián,
Huái becomes Hǔ,
Jiāng becomes Tuó,
Guō becomes Xún,
Yǐng becomes Shā,
Rǔ becomes Fén.
Praising Chén Xuān for accepting remonstrance,
Xiè Chéng’s Hòuhànshū states:
during the Jiànwǔ era,
the Luò River overflowed,
reaching the Jīnchéng Gate.
Some wanted to build a dam to block it,
Chén Xuān remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Wáng Zūn rectified himself at the Golden Dike and the water receded,
how much more a sage."
Before his words ended, the water withdrew.
Approving Wáng Shāng for stopping rumors.
the Hànshū states:
during the Jiànshǐ era,
the capital’s people,
for no reason panicked,
saying a great flood was coming.
Emperor Chéng summoned his ministers to discuss,
the Grand General Wáng Fèng,
believed the Empress Dowager, the Emperor, and the rear palace could board boats,
and ordered officials and people to ascend the Cháng’ān city walls to avoid the water.
All ministers followed Fèng’s proposal.
Only Left General Wáng Shāng said:
"Since ancient times, even in lawless states, water has never inundated city walls,
now our sage governance is peaceful,
high and low are at ease,
why would a great flood suddenly arrive in a day?
This must be a rumor,
we should not further alarm the people."
The Emperor then stopped.
After a while,
Cháng’ān gradually calmed,
upon inquiry,
it was indeed a rumor.
Throwing into Shūgū brings spiritual transformation,
the Xuānchéng Jì states:
on Gài Mountain in Línchéng County, there is the Shūgū Spring,
folklore says a Shū family girl was gathering firewood with her father,
the girl sat by the spring,
suddenly she could not be moved,
the father hurriedly informed the family.
By the time they returned,
only a clear spring was seen, deep and still.
The mother said:
"The girl loved music."
So they played stringed music and sang.
The spring surged and flowed,
two carp came to the rhythm.
Sailing on the Cānglàng and singing heartily.
See the note above on "washing the hat tassels."
Some call it the hall’s hollow,
the Zhuāngzǐ states:
If the accumulation of water is not deep,
then it lacks the strength to bear a large boat.
Pour a cup of water into a hollow in the hall,
then a mustard seed can be a boat,
but place a cup there and it will stick,
for the water is shallow and the boat large.
Some call it intermittent spring,
the Ěryǎ · Shìshuǐ states:
A spring,
appearing and disappearing is called Jiān,
one with water and one without is called Jìzhuó.
Jì,
pronounced jì.
Zhuó,
pronounced zhuó.
Discerning the tastes of Zī and Shéng,
the Lièzǐ states:
Báigōng asked Confucius:
"Can one speak subtly with others?"
Confucius did not respond.
Báigōng said:
"What if one throws a stone into water?"
Confucius said:
"A skilled swimmer from Wú could retrieve it."
He said:
"What if one pours water into water?"
Confucius said:
"When Zī and Shéng are mixed,
Yìyá could taste and know."
Báigōng said:
"So one cannot speak subtly with others."
Hearing of the clash of Gǔ and Luò.
the Guóyǔ states:
In the twenty-second year of King Líng of Zhōu,
the Gǔ and Luò rivers clashed,
destroying the royal palace.
The King wanted to block them,
Crown Prince Jìn said:
"Mountains,
are the gathering of earth;
marshes,
are the return of creatures;
rivers,
are the passage of energy;
lakes,
are the accumulation of water.
Heaven and earth take from the high,
and return to the low.
Now, our governance may indeed have flaws,
disturbing the two spirits."
The King eventually blocked them.
The royal house fell into great chaos.
Though pouring into a hundred rivers,
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì’s Hǎi Fù states:
The virtue of Kǎn repeatedly arrives,
the source of water is deep and vast,
pouring into a hundred rivers,
controlling the clear and drawing the turbid.
It originates from a single spoonful.
the Lǐ states:
Now take water,
as little as a spoonful,
yet when it becomes immeasurable,
turtles, alligators, dragons, fish, and turtles are born in it,
and goods and wealth multiply.
Considering that following it is hard to destroy,
the Huáinánzǐ states:
Light can be seen but cannot be grasped,
water can be followed but cannot be destroyed.
It is intimate yet not revered.
The *Book of Rites* says:
"Water, in relation to man,
is intimate yet not revered."
In movement, it accords with the wise.
The *Analects* says:
"The benevolent delight in mountains;
the wise delight in water.
The wise are active;
the benevolent are tranquil."
In tranquility, it matches the sage.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"When water is still, it clearly reflects beard and eyebrows."
If still water is so clear,
how much more so is the tranquil mind of a sage!
Sometimes it soaks that clump of artemisia.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Cold is that spring below,
soaking that clump of artemisia."
Sometimes it cannot float a bundle of firewood.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The rippling waters,
cannot float a bundle of firewood."
Nǚwā's piling of reed ashes.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"In ancient times,
the four pillars were broken,
the nine provinces split apart,
and waters surged wildly without cease.
Thereupon,
Nǚwā piled up reed ashes to stop the floodwaters."
Xià Yǔ's dredging of Lóngmén.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"In antiquity,
water was a calamity for the people.
Yǔ dredged Lóngmén,
leveled the land and waters,
and only then could the people dwell on dry land."
And when gazing upon its limpid flow,
The *Book of Songs* says:
"How limpid and clear it is."
Observing its gushing forth,
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Gushing forth are those spring waters,
also flowing into the Qí."
The names Xuán Bà and Sù Chǎn.
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Western Journey" says:
"The dark Bà, the white Chǎn,
the hot springs and warm valleys."
The auspicious signs of the warm Luò and flourishing Hé.
The *Yi Qian Zao Du* says:
"In response to abundant virtue,
the Luò River first grew warm,
after nine days it turned cold,
and in five days it changed to five colors, dark and yellow."
The *Shang Shu Zhong Hou* says:
"Yáo built an altar by the Hé River,
and the Luò's flourishing appeared first;
the Hé's auspicious energy filled the four directions."
Being near it makes one easily drowned.
The *Book of Rites* says:
"Water is close to man,
and thus easily drowns him."
Playing with it also causes many deaths.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
Zǐchǎn said to Zǐ Tàishū:
"Only the virtuous
can govern the people with leniency.
Next to that, nothing is better than severity.
Fire is fierce;
people see it and fear it,
thus few die by it.
Water is gentle and weak;
people become familiar with it and play with it,
and thus many die by it.
Therefore, leniency is difficult."
Issuing orders is like this.
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
"Establish the state on unshakable ground;
issue orders from the source of flowing water."
A minister's heart is compared to this.
The *Book of Hàn* says:
"Zhào Chāng was sycophantic and flattering.
He memorialized that Shàngshū Zhèng Chóng was in communication with his clan;
suspecting treachery.
The Emperor reprimanded Chóng, saying:
'Your gate is like a marketplace;
how can you wish to restrict and admonish your sovereign?'
He replied:
'Though my gate is like a marketplace,
my heart is like water.'"
The merit of bearing heavy burdens and reaching afar.
The *Shang Shu Da Zhuan* says:
"Without water, there is nothing to level the ten thousand *li*;
without water, there is nothing to connect distant places and bear heavy burdens."
The virtue of stirring the turbid and raising the clear.
The *Shīzǐ* says:
"Water has four virtues:
Cleansing all living things,
flowing through and connecting the myriad things—this is benevolence.
Raising the clear, stirring the turbid,
washing away dregs and filth—this is righteousness.
Soft yet difficult to violate,
weak yet difficult to overcome—this is courage.
Guiding the Jiāng, dredging the Hé,
disliking fullness, flowing to the humble—this is wisdom."
Holding gourd leaves, the spring pools become still.
The *Bówùzhì* says:
"The Pà water of Tíngzhōu
will leak through any vessel of gold, silver, copper, or iron;
only a gourd leaf does not leak."
Uncovering the spinning basket, the waves surge forth.
The *Xù Shù Zhēng Jì* says:
"West of Liángzōu city is Lóngshuǐ.
It is said that a filial daughter-in-law of Qí,
moved the spirits with her sincerity,
causing a spring to well up inside her house.
She secretly covered it with her spinning basket,
thus sparing the labor of drawing water with jars.
Her family grew suspicious.
Once when she was out,
they searched her room
and tried lifting this basket; the spring then surged forth,
flooding the dwelling.
Therefore it was named Lóngshuǐ (Basket Water)."
There is even the case of the sunken village of Kōngsāng.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"A woman of the Yǒushēn clan
was gathering mulberry leaves and found an infant in a hollow mulberry tree,
and presented it.
Her lord ordered a cook to raise him
and investigate the reason.
It was said:
'His mother was by the Yī River.
She once dreamed a spirit told her:
"When the mortar emits water, flee eastward."
The next day the mother looked at the mortar;
sure enough, water came out.
She told her neighbors and fled east ten *li*,
and her former village was entirely submerged by water.
Her body transformed into a hollow mulberry tree.
Therefore he was named Yī Yǐn.'"
And the transformation of Lìyáng's capital.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"In Lìyáng there was an old woman who often practiced benevolence and righteousness.
A passerby told her:
'This place is destined to sink and become a lake.
If you see blood on the east city gate,
then flee to the mountain;
do not look back.'
From then on,
the woman went repeatedly to look at the gate.
The gatekeeper asked her,
and she answered truthfully.
The officer killed a chicken and smeared its blood on the gate.
The next day the woman went early to look;
there was blood on the gate,
so she fled to the mountain.
Lìyáng then sank and became a lake."
A cup floats by the winding bank—
see the annotation "King Zhāo of Qín receiving the water's heart" in the "Spring Rhapsody."
The moon shines upon the fāngzhū.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"When the fāngzhū sees the moon,
it moistens and produces water."
Also,
the *Wàn Bì Shù* says:
"The fāngzhū draws water."
The annotation says:
"The fāngzhū
is shaped like a cup,
without handles.
It is made by combining five minerals,
on the Rénzǐ day of the twelfth month,
at midnight, holding it up to receive the moon,
and water will come."
Chanting Bào Zhāo's nine roads.
Bào Zhào's poem says:
"The nine roads are level like water,
the twin towers seem to float on clouds."
Gazing upon the Mǎ family's flowing carriages.
The *Book of the Later Hàn* says:
"Empress Mǎ, virtuous and enlightened, favored frugality.
She often said:
'Once before, passing by Zhuólóng Gate,
I saw the attendants of my maternal family—
their carriages were like flowing water,
their horses like dragons.
Looking at my own attendants, they are far from comparable.'"
The Luò is suitable for grain and the Wèi for millet—
this is from the text of the *Huáinánzǐ*.
Square waters hold jade and round waters hold pearls.
The *Shīzǐ* says:
"Generally, where water bends squarely, there is jade;
Round pearls are found in deep pools.
Clear waters hold golden sands,
and dragon-deeps contain jade blossoms.
How can one measure the vast sea with a ladle or a calabash?
See the note on "Who can glimpse through a tube" in "Heavenly Endowment."
Diverting a river leaves more than enough for the wave-subjects.
The Zhuangzi says:
He borrowed grain from the Marquis of Jianhé.
The Marquis said:
"I am about to receive the revenues from my fief,
and then I can lend you three hundred gold. Is that acceptable?"
Zhuāng Zhōu replied:
"Yesterday, I saw someone calling out on the road."
Zhuāng Zhōu looked down at the wheel ruts,
and there was a crucian carp inside.
It said:
"I am a subject of the waves of the Eastern Sea.
Could you spare a dipperful of water to keep me alive?"
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
"I am about to travel south to persuade the kings of Wú and Chǔ
to stir up the waters of the Western River and welcome you.
Would that do?"
The fish said:
"All I need is a dipperful of water to stay alive.
But now you speak of this—
you might as well go look for me in the dried-fish market!"
Thus, the beauty of water flowing to moisten things
is not limited to offerings drawn from puddles and ditches.
The Yìjīng says:
Water flows to what is damp;
fire moves toward what is dry.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Vessels of baskets, round baskets, tripods, and cauldrons,
and water from puddles and roadside ditches,
may be offered to ghosts and spirits,
and may be presented to kings and lords.
Stone
The Book of Changes says:
Gen represents the mountain,
and it represents small stones.
From the Book of Changes.
These are the essence of earth,
and the core of qi.
The Treatise on Principles states:
The essence of earth becomes jade and stone,
the core of stone qi.
As for the solitary and lofty appearance,
Laozi says:
Do not wish to be jumbled like jade,
but solitary like stone.
The clear and crystalline quality,
an ancient poem says:
Clear and crystalline, the stone in the water.
Though it cannot be turned,
The Book of Songs says:
My heart is not a stone,
it cannot be turned.
Yet sometimes it crumbles.
The Rites of Zhou says:
Stone sometimes crumbles.
The annotation says:
Crumbling,
means disintegration.
Pronounced lè.
Sīmǎ used it to make an outer coffin,
The Book of Rites says:
Huán Sīmǎ made a stone outer coffin for himself,
but after three years it was still unfinished.
The Master said:
"If it is so wasteful,
death would be better if it came quickly and decayed."
Fán Chóng built with it to make a house.
The Records of Jīngzhōu says:
Fán Chóng's mother feared thunder,
so he built a stone chamber for her to take shelter.
Recognizing the horses and oxen at Liǔgǔ,
The Wei Lüe says:
In Liǔgǔ of Liángzhōu,
stones collapsed without reason,
forming patterns resembling oxen and horses:
an omen that the Sīmǎ clan would gain the empire.
Startling Yuèwáng's shoes and comb.
The Records of Jīngzhōu says:
By the water in Xīng'ān County, there is a flat stone,
on which lies a stone comb and a stone shoe.
Folklore says,
when Yuèwáng crossed the stream,
he took off his shoes and dropped his comb here.
Some take the shape of lotus flowers,
The Records of Famous Mountains says:
At Fúróngzhǔ, there is a towering stone resembling a newly bloomed lotus,
of bluish-white color.
Some stones are named "thunderclap."
The Records of Mysteries says:
Southwest of Yùmén, there is a country,
where there are thousands of thunderclap stones in the mountains,
named "thunderclap stones,"
which diminish with the spring thunder,
and vanish completely by autumn.
Stone,
pronounced zǐlín.
Then there are the five-colored stones that mended the heavens,
see the annotation "Nǚwā mended the breach" in the Ode to Heaven.
The mountain formed from a fistful of stones,
The Book of Rites says:
Now, as for the mountain,
it is formed from many fist-sized stones,
and as it grows vast,
grass and trees grow upon it,
birds and beasts dwell on it,
and treasures arise within it.
Obtaining Dǒng Wēi's sleeping place,
The Autumn of Jìnyáng says:
Dǒng Wēiniǎn fled,
and no one knew where he went.
At his sleeping place,
a stone was found,
along with two poems.
Placed before Zhào Qí's tomb.
The Book of Later Hàn says:
Zhào Qí said:
"After I die,
place a round stone before my tomb,
inscribed: 'In Hàn, there was a recluse,
surnamed Zhào, named Qí,
with aspirations but no opportunity,
such is fate, what can be done?'"
The beauty of the floating chime stones from the Sì River's banks,
The Book of Documents says:
Floating chime stones from the banks of the Sì.
From other mountains, the hardness for polishing jade is heard.
The Book of Songs says:
Stones from other mountains,
can be used to polish jade.
As for worshipping at Gǔchéng,
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
Zhāng Liáng met an old man on the bridge at Xiàpī, who gave him a book,
saying:
"Read this, and you will become the teacher of a king.
Thirteen years later,
meet me at the foot of Gǔchéng Mountain in Jìběi,
the yellow stone is me."
Later, Zhāng Liáng indeed obtained the yellow stone,
treasured it, and worshipped it.
When he died,
he was buried together with the yellow stone,
and sacrifices were offered to it during the summer and winter festivals.
Burned in Dōngjùn.
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
In the twentieth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
a star fell in Dōngjùn,
and upon reaching the ground, it turned to stone.
Someone carved on it: "When Qín Shǐhuáng dies, the land will divide."
Qín Shǐhuáng had all the people near the stone executed,
and the stone was burned and destroyed.
Astonished by the nine colors of Dàqín,
The Wei Lüe says:
In Dàqín, stones form the city walls,
and nine-colored jade stones are produced.
Admiring the Eight Formations at Miǎnyáng.
The Records of Liángzhōu says:
Fifteen lǐ upstream from Miǎnyáng City along the Hàn River,
there is a place garrisoned by Zhūgě Wǔhóu,
south of the Hàn River,
with its back to the mountain and facing the water,
where stones were piled before the gate to form formations.
When the water rose,
it disrupted their arrangement;
when the water receded,
they returned to their original state.
An auspicious dream fulfilled for Gāo Lín,
The Book of Later Hàn says:
Gāo Lín,
courtesy name Jìmín.
Lín's mother once performed ablutions by the banks of the Sì River,
and saw a stone, bright and lustrous,
so she took it home.
That night,
she dreamed of a person who said to her:
"This is the essence of a floating chime stone,
if you treasure it,
you will surely bear a fine son."
Soon after, she became pregnant.
When she gave birth to a son,
she named him Lín.
Recording ominous signs for Liú Yuánjìn.
The Book of Suí says:
The emperor ordered Wáng Shìchōng, the magistrate of Jiāngdū, to attack Liú Yuánjìn.
A great star fell towards Jiāngdū,
but before reaching the ground, it flew south,
brushing against bamboo and trees, making sounds,
and fell in Wúdū.
Liú Yuánjìn was troubled by this,
dug two zhàng into the ground,
and found a stone,
over a zhàng in diameter.
A few days later,
the stone disappeared.
Fàn Wén's knife, transformed from fish,
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
Fàn Wén,
originally a slave from Xījuàn County in Rìnán.
While a slave,
he herded sheep in a stream,
and caught two carp,
intending to eat them secretly.
His master found out and questioned Wén,
Wén lied, saying:
"I brought back a whetstone,
not fish."
The master went to the place where the fish were,
and indeed saw two stones,
which Wén found strange.
The stones contained iron,
so Wén entered the mountains,
used the stones to smelt iron and made two knives,
raised the knives towards a barrier and chanted:
"Carp transformed,
stones forged into knives,
if the barrier is cut and broken by these stones,
then there are divine spirits,
and Wén shall rule this place."
He then struck the stone barrier,
like Lóngyuān and Gānjiàng cutting reeds,
and thus became ruler of that land.
Téng Fàng's pillow, once struck by thunder.
See the annotation "shattering Téng Fàng's stone pillow" in the Ode to Thunder.
There are also stones that ignite when watered,
The Records of Marvels says:
In Yùzhāng, there are stones yellow-white in color and coarse in texture,
which become hot when watered,
and if a tripod is placed on them,
it is sufficient to cook food.
When they cool, water them again.
Léi Huàn asked Zhāng Huá about this,
Huá said:
"These are burning stones."
Boiling it yields salt.
The Records of Huáyáng states:
Wènshān has salt-bearing stones,
boiling them yields salt.
The proof of Tiáozhī turning hair black,
The Records of Dòngmíng states:
During the Yuándǐng era,
the state of Tiáozhī presented a strange stone,
used to blend with the Nine-Cycle Elixir,
when those with white hair rubbed it with this stone,
their hair turned black instantly.
The sharpness of Kūnwú cutting jade.
The Records of Ten Continents states:
Liúzhōu lies in the Western Sea,
upon it is Kūnwú stone,
smelting it produces iron,
forging it into a sword yields a luminous, transparent glow,
like crystal,
cutting jade as if it were mud.
Again, it is heard that tribute included lead and pine,
The Book of Documents states:
Qīngzhōu's tribute consisted of lead, pine, and strange stones.
Collected together with hù arrows,
see the annotation in "Ode to Arrows": "The hù arrows stored in Chén's courtyard."
How could it only ward off charges?
Bào Zhào's "Ode to the Ruined City" states:
Crafting magnetic stones to ward off charges.
It could also knock on catalpa trees.
Lè Zī's Spring and Autumn Annals states:
A man of Qín, Zhèng Róng,
sent as an envoy by the First Emperor,
upon returning to the pass,
saw a plain carriage and white horse atop Huàshān.
Shortly after,
a person from the plain carriage said to Róng:
"I am an envoy of Huàshān,
I wish to entrust a letter to be delivered to Lord Hàochí.
On your way to Xiányáng,
passing Hàochí,
you will see a large catalpa tree,
beneath it is a patterned stone,
take it and knock on the tree,
someone will respond,
then give the letter to them."
Róng did as instructed,
and indeed, someone emerged from the tree,
accepted the letter, and left.
Recognizing the head-flattening of Chénhán,
The Records of Wèi states:
Chénhán lies east of Mǎhán.
When a child is born, a stone is pressed against its head,
to flatten it.
Today, the people of Chénhán all have flattened heads.
Witnessing Sūn Jīng's teeth-sharpening,
The Book of Jìn states:
Sūn Zǐjīng said to Wáng Wǔzǐ:
"One should pillow on the stream and rinse with stones."
Wáng said:
"Stones cannot be rinsed with,
streams cannot be pillowed on."
Sūn said:
"Pillowing on the stream is to cleanse one's ears,
rinsing with stones is to sharpen one's teeth."
Qín Zhèng's harshness caused bloodshed,
see the annotation in "Ode to the Sun": "The Qín Emperor crossing the sea."
Wèi's virtue flourished, and intertwined patterns appeared.
The Records of Lost Histories states:
At the foot of Tàishān, there are intertwined patterned stones,
twelve zhàng high.
At the beginning of Wèi Míngdì's reign,
they gradually seemed to draw closer,
like a pair of watchtowers.
Earth and stone are yin categories,
an omen of Wèi's earth virtue.
Prayers for rain were once made with a mud ox,
The Records of Commanderies and States states:
Guìzhōu has a cave pool,
beneath it lies a stone ox,
when it emerges from the pool, the year will be dry.
The people kill an ox to pray for rain,
mixing blood with mud,
placing it on the stone ox's back,
and after the sacrifice, rain falls.
Unopposed, or described as throwing into water.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Throwing a stone into water,
nothing opposes it.
Xióng Qú shooting a tiger,
The Outer Commentary to the Book of Songs by Hán states:
Chǔ's Xióng Qúzǐ traveled at night,
saw a reclining stone,
mistook it for a crouching tiger,
shot it, and the arrow sank deep.
Looking by daylight,
he realized it was a stone,
and shot it again,
but could not penetrate it.
Chūpíng commanding sheep,
Gě Hóng's Biographies of Immortals states:
Huáng Chūpíng, at age fifteen,
was sent by his family to herd sheep.
A Daoist priest, seeing his goodness and diligence,
took him to Jīnhuá.
He lived in a stone chamber for over forty years,
without missing his family.
His elder brother, Chūqǐ, searched for Chūpíng,
and a Daoist priest led him to the mountain.
After speaking with his brother,
he asked Chūpíng, "Where are the sheep?"
Chūpíng went with his brother to the east of the mountain,
saw white stones,
and commanded them,
whereupon the stones rose and became tens of thousands of sheep.
Hearing dogs bark at night,
The Records of Commanderies and States states:
Sòng Wǔ campaigned north against Nán Yān,
reaching Fèigǒushān,
heard dogs barking at night,
and the next day looked,
seeing stone dogs.
Observing geese flying in autumn.
The Records of Xúnyáng states:
On the summit of Lúshān, there is a pond,
within it are three stone geese,
which fly when frost descends.
The granary of Línchuān,
The Records of Línchuān states:
The stone granary can hold a thousand hú.
When the granary's mouth opens, the year is lean;
when closed, the year is abundant.
The storehouse of Póyáng.
The Records of Póyáng states:
Qiáncāng Stone is in Ráozhōu,
shaped like a granary silo.
Once, a fisherman stayed overnight beneath the stone,
suddenly saw the stone open,
peered inside and saw coins,
filled his boat with them,
hence the name.
Some hung high like the Shǔ mirror,
The Basic Annals of Shǔ states:
A man from Wǔdū transformed into a woman,
of exceptional beauty,
likely the essence of the mountain,
the King of Shǔ married her as his wife.
Not long after, she passed away,
and was buried within the walls of Chéngdū.
There was a stone mirror,
two zhàng in diameter,
five chǐ high.
Some traveled far to Qínliáng.
The Records of Campaigns states:
Qínliáng,
is the name of a collapsed bridge.
Some say:
The First Emperor of Qín traveled east, crossing this water,
ordered all officials and below,
each to throw a stone to fill it,
and soon a bridge was formed.
As for gazing at her husband from the mountain,
A New Account of the Tales of the World states:
On the northern mountain of Wǔchāng, there is a Gazing-at-Husband Stone,
shaped like a standing person.
Tradition says:
In the past, there was a chaste woman,
whose husband went on campaign,
far away to serve the nation's crisis,
she brought her young child to bid farewell at this mountain,
stood gazing and transformed into stone.
The girl transformed at the bedside,
The Records of the Hidden and Visible states:
Yángměi County's minor official Wú Kān,
once saw a five-colored floating stone in a stream,
took it and placed it by his bedside,
and by night,
it transformed into a girl.
Already told of the Qín women,
The Records of Shǔ states:
Zǐtóng County has the Five Women Mountain,
in the past, Qín sent five beauties to Shǔ,
and Shǔ dispatched five strongmen to welcome them.
Upon arriving here,
the five strongmen stamped the ground and shouted loudly,
and the five women all transformed into stone.
Again, it is heard of Qǐ's mother.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Yǔ married a woman of Túshān,
who transformed into stone,
at the foot of Sōngshān,
Yǔ said:
"Return my son."
The stone split open to the north, and Qǐ was born.
Swallowing it was seen with Chōngzōng,
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
Wǔlù Chōngzōng,
studied under Mí Chéngzǐ.
Mí Chéngzǐ once met someone who gave him a patterned stone like an egg,
Chéngzǐ swallowed it,
and became exceptionally intelligent.
Later, Chéngzǐ fell ill,
He spat out this stone and gave it to Chōngzōng.
Chōngzōng swallowed it,
and again became proficient in learning.
The mining of it was also heard of by Shí Hǔ.
Shí Hǔ,
as recorded in the Yèzhōng Jì, said:
"In Gǔchéng Mountain,
there are brightly colored patterned stones in the earth.
Hǔ had them mined
to build palaces and halls."
As for Wáng Jiǎn's delight in the long jump,
the Shǐjì states:
Wáng Jiǎn attacked Jīng.
The Jīng troops repeatedly challenged to battle,
but he never came out.
After a long time,
Jiǎn sent someone to ask if the army was playing games.
The reply was:
"They are throwing stones and competing in the long jump."
Jiǎn said:
"The soldiers are now ready for use."
Gāo Gù was brave in throwing stones at people.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Qí's Gāo Gù entered the Jìn army,
picked up stones and threw them at people.
Whip the yin and yang to respond to prayers,
see the note on "whipping stones in the cave" in the "Rhapsody on Rain."
Sit on the jiā stone to oversee the people.
The Zhōulǐ states:
The Grand Minister of Justice used the jiā stone to pacify the idle people.
Those who were guilty
were made to sit on the jiā stone.
The fèi stone was used to convey the grievances of the poor.
All solitary, elderly, and young people who wished to appeal to the authorities and seek redress
stood on the fèi stone.
Note:
Jiā
means patterned stone.
Fèi
means red stone.
Again, like the child-begging stone at Mǎhú,
the Jùnguó Zhì states:
The child-begging stone is on the southern bank of Mǎhú.
From the belly of the eastern stone emerges a small stone,
and the belly of the western stone holds a small stone.
Therefore, the Bó people beg for children here,
and it is effective,
hence the name.
The grinding stone at Línhè,
the Jīngzhōu Jì states:
In Línhè, there is a blue stone
with marks from grinding knives and axes on it.
In spring and summer, it is clear and clean,
but in autumn and winter, it becomes overgrown and filthy.
It is said to be where the Thunder God sharpens his knife.
The auspicious omen of Chancellor Liáng observing the magpie's transformation,
the Sōushén Jì states:
Zhāng Hào was the chancellor of Liáng.
A bird resembling a mountain magpie
flew into the market.
The market people threw things at it,
and it fell to the ground, transforming into a round stone.
Hào broke it open with a hammer,
and inside found a gold seal
inscribed with the words "Seal of the Marquis of Loyalty and Filial Piety."
The good fortune of Empress Dòu upon hearing the swallow's fall.
The Xījīng Zájì states:
When Empress Dòu was at home,
a white swallow once carried a stone as large as a finger
and dropped it into her spinning basket.
She took the stone and split it into two,
finding inside the inscription "Mother of Heaven and Earth, Empress."
She then joined the two halves,
and they never opened again.
Later, when she became empress,
she often placed it together with the imperial seal in a box,
and it was called the Heavenly Seal.
Some were obtained at Dàogōng's residence.
The Nánshǐ states:
Dào Gài's mountain pond had a strange jiāng stone,
sixteen feet long.
Emperor Liáng Wǔ won it in a bet,
and immediately had it moved and placed in front of the Huálín Yànjū Hall.
For three days while moving the stone,
the entire capital turned out to watch the spectacle.
This is the so-called Dàogōng Stone.
Some were moved by Dàohéng's seat.
The Tángshū states:
Xuē Yuánchāo,
grandson of Dàohéng,
served as a Secretariat Drafter.
In the Secretariat, there was a large flat stone.
Earlier,
when Dàohéng served as Vice Director of the Secretariat,
he often sat on it to draft edicts.
Whenever Yuánchāo saw this stone,
he could not help but shed tears.
Consider that auspiciousness is like being firm as a rock.
The Yì states:
Firm as a rock, not lasting a whole day.
Perseverance brings good fortune.
Inauspiciousness speaks of being trapped.
The Yì states:
Trapped by a stone,
relying on thistles.
Entering his house,
he does not see his wife.
Inauspicious.
Some boil them to make food.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn states:
There was a man named Báishí Shēng
who often boiled white stones for food
and lived near white stones.
Some wash them to mount the carriage.
The Zhōulǐ states:
When the king travels, the mounting stone is washed.
The note says:
The mounting stone
is the stone the king steps on to mount the carriage.
In Línglíng, there are flying swallows.
Gù Kǎizhī's Qǐméng Jì states:
In Línglíng Commandery, there are stone swallows.
When wind and rain come, they fly like real swallows.
The one placed at Jiǔyí covers books.
The Wúyuè Chūnqiū states:
Yǔ consulted the Huángdì Zhōngjīng
and saw what the sages recorded, saying:
"At Jiǔyí Mountain,
to the southeast is called Wǎnwěi.
It is supported by patterned jade
and covered with a flat stone.
The books are on golden slips with jade characters."
Yǔ then fasted for three days
and removed the stone to retrieve the books.
As for Guī Hào carrying it and kowtowing,
Xiè Chéng's Hòuhànshū states:
Guī Hào of Wú Commandery
had a father who served as Prefect of Nán Commandery.
He was imprisoned due to a legal case.
Hào carried a small stone to the gates of the high officials,
and each time he took out the stone and kowtowed,
until blood covered his face.
His father was thus spared.
Zhāng Fēng placed it in a pouch and tied it to his elbow.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Zhāng Fēng, Prefect of Zhuō Commandery,
raised troops in rebellion.
Earlier,
Fēng was fond of occult arts.
A Daoist priest said Fēng would become emperor,
and placed a stone in a five-colored pouch tied to Fēng's elbow,
saying:
"There is a jade seal."
Fēng believed it
and thus rebelled.
After his defeat, when he was to be executed,
he still said:
"There is a jade seal on my elbow."
Some floated and fulfilled prophecies.
The Dānyáng Jì states:
During the Yǒngníng era of Jìn Huìdì,
in Húshú County's lake, there was a large stone
two hundred paces from the shore.
It floated and came ashore.
The common people watched in amazement,
all saying, "The stone has come."
The following year,
Shí Bīng entered Yángzhōu.
Some were used to remove dirt.
The Shānhǎijīng states:
On Qiánlái Mountain,
there are many washing stones.
If used for bathing,
they can scrub away dirt.
Others include the falling star at Gōngtíng,
the Xúnyáng Jì states:
The falling star stone is in Gōngtíng Lake,
with a circumference of over a hundred paces.
The flying clouds of Yuánqiáo,
the Shíyí Jì states:
East of Yuánqiáo Mountain, there are cloud stones,
five hundred li wide,
mottled like brocade.
When struck, piece by piece,
clouds rise densely.
Thus, gold led to the fall of Shǔ.
The Shǔwáng Běnjì states:
Qín Huìwáng wanted to attack Shǔ,
but the road was impassable.
So he carved five stone oxen
and placed gold behind them.
The Shǔ people saw them
and thought the oxen could defecate gold.
The King of Shǔ sent a thousand soldiers
and had five strong men drag the oxen to make a road.
Thus, Qín attacked Shǔ.
Jade hidden makes the mountain glow.
Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on Literature" states:
Water holding pearls makes the river charming;
stones containing jade make the mountain glow.
Amazed at the filial son fetching water,
The Records of Shǔzhōng states:
Wěi Shūtōng,
a man of Bó,
was extremely filial by nature.
His mother required Jiāng River water for every meal,
but the water was deep and difficult to draw.
One day,
a rock emerged from the water for him,
and Shūtōng was thus able to draw water.
Today, there is a rock in the river
called the Filial Son Rock.
Moved by the maiden washing clothes.
The Records of Commanderies and States states:
On Nǚláng Mountain in Liángzhōu,
Zhāng Lǔ's daughter was washing clothes on a rock,
and she then became pregnant,
giving birth to two dragons.
When the maiden died,
as they were preparing for burial,
the hearse suddenly leaped and ascended this mountain,
and she was buried there.
The rock by the water where she washed clothes still exists,
and it is called Nǚláng Mountain.
Questioning Liú Gēn, his defiance grew even fiercer.
The Biographies of Literary Men states:
When Wèi Wén was feasting various literary scholars in the Eastern Palace,
as the wine flowed freely,
he ordered Empress Zhēn to come out and pay respects.
Everyone prostrated themselves,
only Liú Gēn looked up at her.
Tàizǔ heard of this and was furious,
punishing him by sentencing him to hard labor.
Later, Tàizǔ inspected the convicts.
All the convicts showed respect,
but Gēn sat grinding a stone, unmoving.
Tàizǔ asked:
"What is the nature of this stone?"
Gēn replied:
"The stone comes from beneath the cliffs of Jīngshān.
Carving it adds no pattern,
grinding it adds no luster."
Tàizǔ said:
"Its reputation is not undeserved."
Fearing Fèi Chángfáng, his mind remained unshaken.
The Biographies of Immortals states:
Hú Gōng confined Fèi Chángfáng in a stone chamber.
Above his head was a large rock several zhang square,
suspended by a straw rope.
Various snakes gnawed at the rope, about to break it,
but Chángfáng did not move.
Gōng patted him and said:
"You can be taught."
Some used it for the chess pieces of Dìtái.
The Records of the Investigation of Things states:
On the mountain where cattle rested in Táolín, there is a stone
called the chess pieces of Dìtái.
It is of five colors and patterned,
shaped like a quail's egg.
Some used it to prop up the loom of the Milky Way.
The Record of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ states:
Zhāng Qiān was searching for the source of the river
and obtained a stone, which he showed to Dōngfāng Shuò.
Shuò said:
"This is the stone that props up the loom of the Weaving Maiden in heaven."
When Yú Yuàn came,
there was no concealment by light clouds.
The Book of Qí states:
Yú Yuàn was the governor of Jìnpíng.
By the seaside, there was the Yuèwáng Stone,
which was often concealed by clouds and mist.
Tradition says:
"Only a pure and honest governor can see it."
Yuàn went to observe it,
and it was clear and unobstructed, without concealment.
When Chén Zǒng arrived,
he composed a lofty text and prayed.
Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jìn states:
Chén Zǒng was promoted to Palace Attendant Censor.
He was dispatched to Zhōngnán Mountain to pray for rain.
Zǒng first removed the small stone shrines,
keeping only one large stone site and prayed to it.
His prayer text said:
"Lofty great stone,
assisting the mountain, connecting with principle,
containing moisture, emitting moisture,
bestowing grace upon our four seas."
As for the stone speaking in Jìn,
it is heard from old traditions.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
A stone spoke in Jìn at Wèi Yú.
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng:
"Why did the stone speak?"
He replied:
"Stones cannot speak.
Perhaps something was relying on it.
If not,
the people's hearing was mistaken.
Moreover, I have also heard it said:
'When actions are not timely,
resentment and slander stir among the people,
then things that do not speak will speak.'"
The meteorites falling in Sòng are seen in earlier records.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Five meteorites fell in Sòng; they were falling stars.
Marveling at the jade maiden closing the door.
The Records of Yìzhōu states:
On Lóngpán Mountain, there is a stone.
In its center are a door and door leaves,
as if closed by a person.
Tradition says it is the Jade Maiden's Chamber.
Wondering at the Inspector rolling up his sleeves.
Liú Yìqìng's Records of the Hidden and Visible states:
On the border between Yídū and Jiànpíng commanderies,
there are five or six peaks
rising unevenly one after another.
On them are strange rocks
resembling two human figures
rolling up their sleeves facing each other.
Commonly said to be the inspectors of the two commanderies disputing the border here.
Carving at Kūnmíng to display the marvelous.
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
Hàn Wǔ raised fish in the Kūnmíng Pond.
They often flew away.
Later, a stone was carved into a whale
and placed in the water,
and the fish then no longer flew away.
Whenever there was thunder and rain,
the whale would often roar.
Striking at Línpíng to record the extraordinary.
See the annotation in the "Ode to the Drum": "Hearing the stone struck at Línpíng."
Carrying it on the back is seen with Shēntú.
The Master Xún states:
"Carrying a stone and throwing oneself into the river
is a difficult act,
but Shēntú Dí was capable of it."
Holding it in the beak is also heard of with Jīngwèi.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
On Fājiū Mountain,
there is a bird shaped like a crow,
with a patterned head, white beak, and red feet,
named Jīngwèi.
Its call is its own name.
The daughter of Yándì roamed the Eastern Sea,
drowned and did not return.
She constantly took wood and stones from the Western Mountains to fill the sea.
Annotation:
Fājiū Mountain
is in Zhǎngzǐ County, Shàngdǎng.
Such is the extraordinary form of hardness and moisture,
also where beautiful names gather.
Well
The significance of the well is indeed profound!
As for the plain rope and cold water,
an ancient song says:
"In the rear garden, a well is dug with a silver frame,
A golden vase with a plain rope draws cold water."
Warm in winter and cool in summer.
The *Fēngtǔ Jì* says:
"A spiritual well is called warm in winter and cool in summer,
it is a stone well."
Beyond the mundane world, jade railings are heard of;
the annotation to the *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"The Kūnlún Ruins lie in the northwest,
the lower capital of the Emperor,
ten thousand rèn high,
with nine wells on its face,
using jade as railings."
In the garden, a silver frame is suddenly recognized.
See above.
The office of the "Well-Rope Bearer" is established in the palace;
the *Zhōulǐ* says:
"The Well-Rope Bearer is in charge of carrying the rope,
to command the army's wells."
Annotation:
"When a well is dug for the army,
the rope is hung above it,
so the soldiers know."
The village chief entrusts the auspicious sign of the new well.
The *Hànshū* says:
"When Wáng Mǎng was regent,
Liú Jīng reported:
'Xīn Dāng, the village chief of Línzī County in Qí Commandery, repeatedly dreamed of a person saying:
am a heavenly envoy.
The regent emperor shall become the true emperor.
If you do not believe me,
there shall be a new well in this village."'
The village chief rose and looked in the village,
and there was a new well,
reaching a hundred feet into the ground.'"
Then there is Bào Lù hanging a whip;
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìnshū* says:
"Bào Lù of Shàngdǎng had many misfortunes and deaths in his household,
Chúnyú Zhì divined for him,
saying:
'Your dwelling is inauspicious.
You should go directly to the market gate,
where there will be a person selling a new horsewhip.
Buy it and return,
hang it on the large tree northeast of your house,
and within three years you shall suddenly gain wealth.'
Lù followed the advice and went to the market,
obtained the horsewhip,
and hung it.
After three years,
tens of thousands of coins were found in the well,
and thus his livelihood expanded,
and his household was also free from misfortune."
Chén Zūn threw the linchpin.
The *Hànshū* says:
"Chén Zūn was fond of drink,
and whenever he hosted guests,
he would take the linchpins and throw them into the well,
so even if there was an urgent matter,
they could not leave."
Though it is said that taking does not diminish it,
Lǐ Yóu's *Jǐng Míng* says:
"Taking much does not diminish it,
taking little does not overflow it.
If one upholds the law thus,
how could there be any evil or deviation?"
Yet it is also said that the sweet well dries up first.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Straight trees are felled first,
sweet wells dry up first."
The Court Minister first obtained cinnabar.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"My late grandfather, the Court Minister,
in his youth served as magistrate of Línyuán,
and said that in this county, the Liào family had long-lived generations,
suspecting their well water was unusually red,
so he tried digging around the well,
and found tens of hú of cinnabar buried by ancient people.
The Court Minister's name was Xuán."
Yú Shùn fled through a side tunnel.
The *Shǐjì* says:
"Gǔsǒu made Shùn dig a well,
and the old man and Xiàng together threw earth to fill the well,
but Shùn made a tunnel and escaped from the side."
As for Bó Yì having already created it,
the *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"When Bó Yì made wells,
dragons ascended to the dark clouds,
and spirits dwelled in Kūnlún."
Annotation:
"Dragons feared harm,
so they ascended to the clouds and departed,
dwelling their spirits in Kūnlún."
Shénnóng had already been born.
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
"In Zhòngshān of Suí Commandery, there is a cave,
tradition says:
'Shénnóng was born here,
and the land has nine wells.'
It is said that after Shénnóng was born,
the nine wells opened by themselves."
The image remains though the settlement changes,
the *Yì* says:
"The settlement changes, but the well does not change."
Annotation:
"Its virtue lies in not changing."
The principle is seen in the broken vase.
The *Yì* says:
"Almost reaching but not yet drawing from the well,
breaking the vase,
is inauspicious."
Worried about them filling in the wells and leveling the stoves,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Chǔ and Jìn fought at Yānlíng.
Bó Zhōulí attended behind the king.
The king looked at the Jìn army and said:
'They are very noisy,
and dust is rising.'
'Why?'
He said:
'They are about to fill the wells and level the stoves to form ranks.'"
Narrow indeed is viewing stars.
The *Shīzǐ* says:
"Viewing stars from a well,
one sees only a few stars;
viewing from a hilltop,
one sees them as they first appear.
It is not that one's vision improves,
but the situation makes it so."
The Zhèng army once saw trees felled.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Chǔ and Chén's armies attacked Zhèng,
along Chén's path,
wells were filled and trees felled."
In the Jìn dynasty, a dragon's appearance was once heard of.
The *Jìnshū* says:
"A dragon appeared in the well of the armory,
Emperor Wǔ personally observed it,
with a joyful expression,
all officials congratulated him,
but Liú Yì alone had a dissenting opinion."
Some mocked Zǐyáng's pettiness,
the *Hòuhànshū* says:
"Wěi Xiāo sent Mǎ Yuán to observe Gōngsūn Shù in Shǔ.
Yuán and Shù were old acquaintances,
and Yuán thought they would shake hands as in the past,
but Shù arranged a grand guard of honor to receive Yuán.
Yuán said:
'Gōngsūn does not spit out his food and run to welcome a scholar of the state,
but instead fusses over appearances.'
Returning, he said to Xiāo:
'Zǐyáng is just a frog at the bottom of a well.'"
Some saved Wèi Téng from punishment.
The *Kuàijī Diǎnlù* says:
"Sūn Cè's merit official Wèi Téng,
having offended, was to be punished,
and was about to be killed.
Lady Wú, his mother, leaned against the large well and said to Cè:
'You have newly established yourself in Jiāngnán,
and your affairs are not yet settled.
Merit Official Wèi has served you with full loyalty and advice.
If you kill him today,
people will rebel against you tomorrow.
I cannot bear to see disaster befall you,
so I shall first throw myself into this well.'
Cè was greatly alarmed,
and hastily released Téng."
As for the *Yì*'s words "do not cover it,"
the *Yì* says:
"The top six,
the well is drawn from but not covered,
there is sincerity, great auspiciousness."
Annotation:
"Not monopolizing what one has,
not privatizing its benefits,
thus it is said 'do not cover.'"
Zhòngní spoke of benevolence in it.
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
"Zǎi Wǒ asked:
'If a benevolent person is told, "There is benevolence in the well,"
should he follow it?'
The Master said:
'A gentleman may go to it,
but not be trapped in it;
he may be deceived,
but not be deluded.'"
Gěng Gōng of Shūlè's bowing,
see the annotation to "deep spiritual source in Shūlè" in the *Water Rhapsody*.
The spirit of Empress Xī of the Liáng dynasty.
The *Liángshū* says:
"Emperor Gāozǔ's Empress Xī was jealous by nature,
and after her death,
she transformed into a dragon,
entered the well of the rear palace,
and communicated with the emperor through dreams.
Sometimes she appeared in form,"
Its radiance shines brilliantly.
When the emperor's health was unwell,
a dragon would stir the water, causing it to surge and churn.
Thus, at the well, clothes and various delicacies were offered in sacrifice to it,
which is why the emperor ultimately did not establish an empress.
The discovery of a sheep startled Jìzǐ.
The Guóyǔ states:
Jì Huánzǐ dug a well,
and found an earthen jar,
inside which was a sheep.
He sent someone to ask Zhòngní,
who replied:
"The monsters of wood and stone are Kuí and Wǎngliǎng;
the monsters of water are dragons and Wǎngxiàng;
the monster of earth is called Fényáng."
Also, the Hán Shī Wàizhuàn states:
Lǔ Āigōng dug a well and obtained an earthen sheep.
The duke was frightened.
Confucius heard of this,
went to see the duke, and said:
"I have heard that the essence of water becomes jade,
and the essence of earth becomes sheep.
This sheep's liver must be earth."
They killed the sheep and examined it,
and indeed it was so.
The phrase "obtaining a person" alarmed the ruler of Sòng.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
There was a man named Dīng in Sòng,
whose household had no well and had to fetch water from outside,
often requiring one person to stay out for this purpose.
When he dug a well,
he told people:
"I dug a well and obtained a person."
This was reported to the ruler of Sòng.
The ruler sent someone to inquire,
and Dīng replied:
"I obtained the service of one person,
not that I found a person in the well."
Then there is the inscription obtained by Guàn Yīng.
The Xúnyáng Jì states:
Pénchéng
was built by Guàn Yīng.
When Sūn Quán passed by this city,
he personally marked a spot for a well,
and ordered people to dig there.
They obtained an old "Well Inscription" which said:
"Opened by Yǐngyáng Hóu,
it will be blocked after three hundred years.
Less than a hundred years later,
it will be opened by one who responds to destiny."
Quán was delighted and considered it an auspicious sign for himself.
The well was very deep;
when there were wind and waves on the great river,
this well would also stir.
Solving Bào Zhào's riddle.
Bào Zhào's "Well Riddle" says:
One eight four eight,
a flying spring looks upward to flow.
The explanation says:
One eight four eight,
is five eights.
Five eights are forty,
which is the character "jǐng" (well).
Some can produce fog and hail.
The Chénliú Fēngsú Jì states:
In Yōngqiū County, at the temple of Xiàhòu, there is a divine well
that can produce fog and hail.
Some can secretly dispel epidemics.
The Guìyáng Lièxiān Zhuàn states:
Sū Dān told his mother:
"There will be guests coming to meet,
Dān will ascend to immortality,
and will be unable to provide for you.
This year there is an epidemic,
but drinking the water from this well
can keep one free from illness.
Selling this water is better than providing for you."
Watering oxen reveals Chúnyú's virtue.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
At Chúnyú Gōng's home,
the well was by the gate.
Neighbor children watered their oxen there,
and Gōng disliked the impurity,
so he placed many vessels by the well.
Setting out vessels demonstrates Guǎn Níng's righteousness.
The Gāoshì Zhuàn states:
In the settlement where Guǎn Níng lived,
when men and women gathered to draw water, it was chaotic,
with disputes and noise at the well.
Níng was troubled by this,
so he bought many vessels,
placed them by the well,
and drew water to await them.
Drinking the sweetness of the Míngyì well,
see the annotation in the "Xià Fù": "When cold, drink from the Míngyì well."
Observing the aura above the Zhēnguān well.
The Wú Zhì states:
When Sūn Jiān campaigned against Dǒng Zhuó and entered Luòyáng,
he encamped south of the city.
He saw five-colored vapor above the Zhēnguān well,
sent someone into the well,
and obtained the Imperial Seal.
At Tàijí, there is a Lùlú Bóshān well.
Dài Yánzhī's Xīzhēng Jì states:
On the Tàijí Hall, there is a well
with a Bóshān-style pulley,
intertwined dragons bearing a mountain above the well,
and also a golden lion beneath the dragons.
At Jiǔlóng, there is a toad holding water.
The Wèi Lüè states:
Before the Jiǔlóng Hall of Emperor Míng, there was a jade well,
with a toad holding and receiving [water],
and a divine dragon spouting water.
There is also the Yánjiān Tiānshuǐ well.
The Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū states:
The land of Lǒng was short on salt,
only the Tiānshuǐ well was constantly boiled,
to supply the prefecture's needs,
and bestowed upon the soldiers and Qiāng people.
The Línqióng well blazes with fire.
See the annotation in the "Huǒ Fù": "the well of Línqióng."
Some, upon looking into it, give birth.
The Hòu Hànshū states:
Elders of Dōngwòjū said:
"In the women's kingdom in the sea, there is a divine well;
looking into it causes one to give birth."
Some, upon digging it, obtain copper.
See the annotation in the "Qián Fù": "Páng Qiàn digs a well."
It can be used for drawing water,
fulfilling the image of the third nine line.
The Yì Jīng, "Jǐng Guà" states:
The third nine line,
the well is cleansed but not drunk from,
causing sorrow in my heart.
It can be used for drawing water;
if the king is enlightened, all will receive his blessing.
To dig and drink from it,
who knows the merits of Yáo and Shùn?
The Yìshì Zhuàn states:
During Yáo's time,
an old man struck the ground and sang:
"At sunrise I work,
at sunset I rest.
I dig a well and drink from it,
I plow the fields and eat from them.
What has the emperor's power to do with me!"
As for the Northern Dipper and the dog lying in wait,
the Yōumíng Lù states:
There was an old woman Wáng,
a person from the time of Wú.
During the Huánglóng era,
at age nine, she fell ill and died.
From morning till evening she revived,
and said:
"I saw an old woman taking me flying,
and saw the lord of the Northern Dipper had a dog as big as a lion,
with deep-set eyes,
lying in wait at the well railing,
and was told this is the heavenly duke's dog."
The dragon emerging from the east wing,
the Liángzhōu Jì states:
The Mùróng clan,
in the second year of Xiánníng,
at night saw a dragon emerge from the well in the east wing,
travel before the great hall and coil up to lie down.
In the morning, its scales, armor, and footprints were seen,
and there were still damp spots.
The Huálín well paved with jade.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
In the Huálín Garden, there is an ancient well,
entirely made of Mín jade,
with a mouth carved from stone,
the workmanship precise and exquisite.
The Língyún Terrace and throwing stones.
Zhū Chāoshí, in a letter to his elder brother, said:
On the Língyún Terrace, there is a marvelous well,
appearing deep and serene when gazed upon.
If one throws a stone into it,
it takes a long time before the sound is heard.
Inquiring about the ancient structure of Jīnyōng.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
Nánzhèng,
within the great city there is a small city,
encircled by the Jīnyōng rampart,
with seventy wells,
all built by Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
Peering into the hidden chamber of Jiānglíng.
The Jīngzhōu Jì states:
In Jiānglíng County, there is a Tiānjǐng Terrace,
facing east toward the Tiānjǐng well.
The well's circumference is about two lǐ,
and within it is a hidden chamber.
When people occasionally see it,
there will be military conflict.
Yùlín has the name Sīmìng well.
The Guǎngzhōu Jì states:
In Yùlín Commandery, there is an ancient well,
named the Sīmìng well.
Yùzhāng has traces of Hóngyá.
The Yùzhāng Jì states:
At Xiànyuán Mountain, there is a Hóng Well,
where a flying stream cascades down,
its depth unfathomable.
It is traditionally said to be the "Well of Master Hóngyá."
It was once heard that it formed without being dug,
as the *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"A làng well
forms without being dug.
How could it be filled in to make farmland?"
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"To tear down a gate for firewood,
or fill a well to make farmland,
though there may be small gains, the loss is great."
The story of carrying a jar is told at Hànyīn:
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Zǐgòng passed by Hànyīn,
and saw a man preparing a garden plot,
digging a tunnel to reach the well,
carrying a jar out to water it.
Zǐgòng said:
"There is a device here,
heavy at the back, light at the front,
that draws water like pumping,
called a jiégāo.
It can irrigate a hundred plots in a day,
with little effort and great results.
Do you not want it?"
The gardener said:
"Where there is mechanical work, there must be a mechanical heart.
If a mechanical heart resides in the chest,
then the Way cannot be upheld."
Watering chives was also heard of from Dèng Xī.
The *Shuō Yuàn* says:
In Wèi, there were five senior officials,
who all carried jars into the well,
came out and watered chives,
spending a whole day on just one plot.
Dèng Xī passed by,
got off his carriage and taught them,
saying:
"Make a device heavy at the back,
light at the front,
called a jiégāo.
You can water chives all day,
a hundred plots without tiring."
The bird's nest on Huà Mountain was seen:
The *Yì Yuàn* says:
On Huà Mountain in Lánlíng, there is a well,
where a bird nests,
with golden wings and black color,
whose appearance foretells great floods.
The well cannot be peered into;
those who peer into it die within a year.
Strange was the water overflowing at Běigōng.
The *Hànshū* says:
At Emperor Chéng's Běigōng,
