the well water overflowed.
Testing with Gé's chicken feathers:
Gé Hóng's prescription says:
Deep wells often have poisonous air.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, test by dropping chicken feathers into the well.
If the feathers sink straight down,
there is no poison;
if they swirl around the edges,
do not enter.
The grub-eaten fruit at Yǔlíng was obtained.
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
Chén Zhòngzǐ lived at Yǔlíng.
There was a plum tree by the well,
eaten by grubs.
He crawled to eat it,
swallowed three times,
and only then could his ears hear,
his eyes see.
Also heard of crying with a straw rope:
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
The King of Chǔ attacked Xiāo.
Xiāo's minister Huán Wúshè spoke to Chǔ's Shēn Shūzhǎn:
"Look for me in the dry well and get me out."
Zhǎn said:
"If you make a straw rope,
cry by the well, and it will be done."
The next day,
Xiāo fell,
Shēn Shū looked at the well,
and the straw rope was there.
He called out and got him out.
Cold is that spring.
The *Yì* says:
The well is cold, the spring water is drinkable.
Some set a method to cast wine:
The *Máojūn Nèizhuàn* says:
To refine elixir,
first purify and fast for a hundred days,
then seal the earthen pot.
On the fasting day,
first cast five hú of clear wine into flowing water.
If there is no flowing water,
then into a well.
Some display skill to fly coins.
See the annotation "The immortal elder is summoned" in the *Qián Fù*.
Then examine that there are no birds:
The *Yì* says:
Muddy well, undrinkable,
an old well has no birds.
Consider this shooting of minnows:
The *Yì* says:
In the well valley, shooting minnows,
the jar is broken and leaks.
Yuèzhī's gushing wine spring:
The *Hànshū* says:
Emperor Wǔ established Jiǔquán Commandery,
where there was well water in the commandery,
white in color,
with the scent of wine,
hence the name.
Shàoshì's transmission of mica:
The *Sōnggāo Jì* says:
On Shàoshì Mountain, there is a mica well.
Whenever frogs rest:
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
A frog in a sunken well said to a sea turtle:
"I leap about on the well's rim,
rest in the broken brick's edge,
none can match me."
Once spied on sparrows nursing:
Fù Xuán's poem says:
Swallows nest by the hill city's side,
sparrows nurse in an empty well.
Dwelling not attached to dragons or phoenixes,
often fearing snakes and insects.
Some speak of the bronze man covering the spring:
The *Nánkāng Jì* says:
At Pángù Mountain in Yúdū,
on its peak there is a well,
guarded by a large bronze man.
Every fifty years it gushes once,
water rising tens of zhàng high,
and the bronze man always covers it with his hand.
Some say a golden man holds a pestle:
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
In Héngyáng, Yìyáng County has a flat ridge,
on the ridge are several hundred golden wells,
the deep ones unfathomable.
Tradition says a golden man struck the ground with a pestle,
and a well would form.
It is thought that people of old dug them to mine gold,
hence called "golden wells."
Marvel at the withered plum's destruction:
An ancient poem says:
Plant a peach by the dew-covered well,
a plum tree grows beside the peach.
Insects come to eat the peach roots,
the plum tree withers in the peach's place.
See the twin paulownias' luxuriance:
Emperor Míng of Wèi's "Měnghǔ Xíng" says:
Twin paulownias grow in an empty well,
their branches and leaves intertwine.
The flowing spring soaks their roots,
dark clouds moisten their boughs.
Such are the merits of the golden well,
too numerous to fully recount.
Ice
The Book of Changes says:
Treading on frost, it begins to congeal;
gradually following its course,
it reaches solid ice.
The Book of Changes says:
Treading on frost, solid ice,
is when yin begins to congeal.
Gradually following its course,
it reaches solid ice.
Then it is stored in the ice cellar;
The Máo Shī, "Qī Yuè," says:
On the third day of the month, it is stored in the ice cellar.
It is brought out at the morning appearance;
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Shēn Fēng said:
"In ancient times, when the sun was in the northern constellation, ice was stored;
when the sun was in the western constellation, it was brought out at the morning appearance.
When storing it,
a black bull and black millet
were offered to Sī Hán;
when bringing it out,
peachwood bows and thornwood arrows
were used to ward off disasters."
Note:
In the eleventh month,
the sun is in the constellations Xū and Wēi;
at the spring equinox,
the star Kuí appears in the east at dawn.
Chōngchōng, chiseling away,
see the Shī.
Towering, it accumulates.
The Chǔ Cì says:
O soul, return!
The north is no place to linger.
Layered ice towers high,
flying snow stretches for a thousand miles.
Transparently clear as a jade pot,
Bào Zhào's poem says:
Straight as a vermilion silk cord,
clear as ice in a jade pot.
Imagine the skin of the Gūshè goddess.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
On the distant Gūshè Mountain, there is a divine being,
with skin like ice and snow,
graceful as a maiden.
As for melting with the east wind,
the Lǐjì says:
On the day of Lìchūn,
the east wind thaws the ice.
When the sun is in the northern constellation, it is stored.
See above,
note to "brought out at the morning appearance."
Wáng Xiáng sought fish and saw them lying there;
the Jìn Shū says:
Wáng Xiáng served his stepmother with filial devotion.
In winter, his mother longed for carp,
so Wáng Xiáng removed his clothes and knocked on the ice;
the ice cracked,
and two carp leaped out.
Zǐ Féng dug a pit and made a bed.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
The King of Chǔ sent Wěi Zǐ Féng to be Lìngyǐn,
but he declined due to illness.
In the heat of summer, he dug a pit, placed ice in it, and slept on a bed over it.
Wrapped in multiple layers of silk and fur,
he ate little and lay still.
The King of Chǔ sent a physician to examine him,
who reported:
"He is extremely thin,
but his vital energy remains unaffected."
Six feet thick in the land of the Hú and Mò,
the Hàn Shū:
Cháo Cuò submitted a memorial saying:
"In the land of the Hú and Mò,
the water's surface is three inches thick,
and the ice is six feet thick."
Five hú given for the funeral in Rǔnán;
the Bā Wáng Gùshì says:
When the Prince of Rǔnán was buried,
an edict granted five hú of ice.
The icehouse was beside the Xuānyáng Gate;
Lù Jī's Luòyáng Jì says:
The icehouse was inside the Xuānyáng Gate,
where the Son of Heaven used it to bestow ice upon princes, dukes, and officials.
A well was dug beside the Yúntái Terrace.
Dài Yánzhī's Xī Zhēng Jì says:
The Língyún Terrace had an ice well;
Dài Yánzhī took some away in the sixth month,
and after a day, it remained solid.
As for Zǐ Shèn's divination,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
In spring, there was no ice,
and Zǐ Shèn said:
"This year, Sòng and Zhèng will suffer famine!
Yin cannot overcome yang."
The ice master is in charge.
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
The ice master oversees ice,
providing ice vessels for sacrifices,
ice for guests,
and ice for the Yí Pán in grand funerals.
Doubts often arise from the fox listening;
the Shù Zhēng Jì says:
The fox listens to the ice;
if the river makes no sound,
the fox proceeds.
In response to the season, fish are heard rising.
The Lǐ says:
Ten days after Lìchūn,
fish rise to the ice.
From the beginning of winter, it starts to form;
by midwinter, it grows stronger.
The Lǐ says:
In the first month of winter,
water begins to freeze,
and the ground begins to harden.
In the second month of winter,
the ice grows stronger.
Think of Mùróng's crossing the sea,
relying on divine power;
the Jìn Shū says:
Mùróng Huàng submitted a memorial saying:
"On the thirteenth day of the first month, I personally led an expedition against Guō Yuǎn;
borrowing Your Majesty's heavenly and earthly might,
the officers and soldiers exhausted their efforts,
their sincerity moved the spirits,
and the sea froze over,
allowing us to travel over three hundred lǐ."
Recall the Huángjīn crossing the river,
soon hearing of their defeat.
The Hòu Hàn Shū says:
The Huángjīn rebels rose in force;
the Governor of Qīngzhōu, Jiāo Hé, fearing the bandits would cross the river on ice,
had many ice-breaking pellets made and thrown into the river,
causing the rebel forces to collapse.
Thus, without polishing, it shines bright;
the Bàopǔzǐ says:
The five jades need no dyeing to be hard;
cold ice needs no polishing to be bright.
Facing the sun, it can ignite.
the Bówùzhì says:
Carve ice into a round shape,
hold it up to the sun,
and place mugwort in its shadow to produce fire.
Meeting a strong wind, it seals itself;
the Shù Zhēng Jì says:
In the north, when it is extremely cold and rain falls,
a strong wind blows, preventing it from flowing,
so it freezes solid,
forming ice several feet thick.
Under the bright sun, it is hard to remain intact.
the Wèizǐ says:
To govern a perilous state
and unruly people
is like thin ice under the bright sun,
or dry grass meeting a fierce fire.
Wáng Chōng's theory of one foot,
the Lùn Héng says:
If you light a torch,
or boil a pot of water,
it will not heat up all day.
Place a foot of ice
in the kitchen,
and it will not grow cold all night.
Dōngmén's words on five inches.
the Yànzǐ says:
Duke Jǐng attacked Lǔ
and captured Dōngmén Wúzé,
asking him:
"How are the harvests in Lǔ?"
He replied:
"When yin does not congeal yang,
and the ice is five inches thick,
it indicates a balanced cold and warmth.
Balanced cold and warmth mean orderly governance;
orderly governance leads to abundant harvests.
I ask you to treat Lǔ with courtesy to quell resentment."
Yǔ Shòu's rhapsody on the cold well,
Yǔ Shòu's "Bīng Jǐng Fù" says:
I once lived near the southern city,
where there was an ice well.
In the height of summer,
I would bring friends,
ascend and wander about,
lingering and pacing,
feeling the chill of the cold,
and thus composed the "Hán Jǐng Fù."
Mǎ Biāo's ode to the long river.
Sīmǎ Biāo's poem says:
Fiercely, the dark whirlwind rises,
brilliantly, the heavy frost congeals.
A strong wind swirls white snow,
the long river stimulates the ice.
Test it with the theory of the bottle,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
Seeing a leaf fall,
one knows the year is nearing its end;
observing the ice in a bottle,
one knows the cold of the world.
This is using the near to discuss the far.
Reciting this "Seventh Month" chapter.
See the note above on "stored in the ice-house."
As for chopping through that accumulated snow,
The *Chǔcí* says:
Cassia oars and orchid rudder,
chopping ice through piled snow.
Born of cold water,
The *Xúnzǐ* says:
Ice is born of water,
yet is colder than water.
Thinking of vengeance, he often held it to his bosom,
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* says:
The King of Yuè, dwelling on avenging the grudge against Wú,
in winter's cold would embrace ice,
in summer's heat would grasp fire.
Bearing a heavy burden, how could he tread on ice?
The book of Dèng Xī says:
An enlightened ruler governs the people,
as if riding a galloping horse without reins,
treading on ice while bearing a heavy load.
Once melted, men and women begin to unite,
The *Fēngsútōng* says:
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
The matchmaker, for men of thirty,
and women of twenty,
when the ice melts and the wild geese cry,
then they unite.
As it thaws, farming and sericulture both commence.
The *Jiāyǔ* says:
When frost descends, women's work is completed,
and marriages take place.
When ice melts, farming and sericulture begin,
and wedding ceremonies diminish.
The well marveled at the cold of Lángyé,
The *Xù Hànshū* says:
In the sixth year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
winter was extremely cold,
in Běihǎi, Dōnglái, and Lángyé,
the ice in wells was over a foot thick.
The river astonished with the strangeness of the Hūtuó.
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* says:
Emperor Guāngwǔ, evading Wáng Láng's troops from Hándān,
went south to Fēng.
An official from Qūyáng reported:
"The Hūtuó River has floating ice,
there are no boats, it cannot be crossed."
All those around were terrified.
The Emperor ordered Wáng Bà to go ahead and inspect it,
and it was indeed so.
Wáng Bà, thinking that reporting the truth would alarm the crowd,
instead reported:
"The ice is solid, it can be crossed."
The Emperor laughed heartily and said:
"It was indeed a false report."
By the time they reached the river,
the ice had already frozen over,
the Emperor then crossed,
before a few chariots had finished,
the ice gave way.
Although not a treasure for the ancestral temple,
The collected works of Shù Xī say:
Thin ice congealing on the pond,
is not a treasure for the ancestral temple;
dew-drops hanging like pearls,
are not ornaments for the ceremonial crown.
One must gather plain jade from layered mountains,
pluck round pearls from deep streams.
Truly given as a gift to the assembled ministers.
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
The Ice Officer distributes ice in summer.
The commentary says:
Bestowed upon the ministers.
Opened in mid-spring,
just as leeks are offered and lambs presented;
The *Shī* says:
On the fourth day, early,
present the lamb, offer the leek.
This refers to opening the ice.
Sacrificing to Sīhán,
one must use peachwood bows and thornwood arrows.
See the note above on "emerging at morning audience."
Fire
Fire, in relation to humans,
is respected but not intimate,
as stated in the Lǐjì.
Its issuance and containment are observed through celestial phenomena;
nèi (containment),
pronounced nà.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"In ancient times, the Fire Official,
sometimes took from the Heart constellation,
sometimes took from the Beak constellation to issue and contain fire.
Therefore, the Beak is the Quail Fire,
and the Heart is the Great Fire."
Also, the Zhōulǐ states:
"The Si Guǎn official oversees the governance and commands of fire.
In late spring, fire is issued,
and the people all follow it;
in late autumn, fire is contained,
and the people do likewise."
The internal and external aspects are also seen in the family.
The Yìjīng says:
"Wind comes forth from fire,
the family."
Wáng Tōng said:
"It means internal clarity and external order."
The Sī Xuǎn official performs his duties,
then obtains it from the yang mirror;
the Zhōulǐ says:
"The Sī Xuǎn official of the autumn ministry,
is in charge of using the fire mirror,
to obtain fire from the sun."
Zhuāng Zhōu wrote a discourse,
sometimes speaking of the pointing to firewood.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"When the pointing is exhausted, it becomes firewood,
but the fire is transmitted.
The former fire is not the latter fire,
thus it is the firewood that transmits the fire."
Observe that Flaming Terrace,
the Jùnguózhì says:
"West of Liánhún Prefecture's Yáohuǒ Mountain,
there is a fire well,
so deep the bottom cannot be seen.
Fiery air rises upward,
often like faint lightning.
If one ignites grass with it,
then smoke billows and fire bursts forth,
hence it is named Flaming Terrace."
Obtaining it from the burning stone,
the Shíyíjì says:
"During the era of Qín Shǐhuáng,
there were people from Wǎnqú who rode in snail boats,
sailed the Black Water,
and reached the Yōng region.
The First Emperor spoke with them about the time when heaven and earth first opened,
and they understood it as if they had personally witnessed it.
They also said:
'In our country,
it is ninety thousand lǐ from the Xiánchí, where the sun sets,
a place where the sun and moon do not shine.
Ten thousand years are considered day,
and ten thousand years are considered night.
During the day, the sky suddenly splits open in the middle,
several hundred zhàng wide.
After ten thousand years, it closes again,
and that constitutes one day.
At night, they polish burning stones to substitute for sunlight.
These stones come from Rán Mountain.
Their soil and stones all emit light.
If one drills or chops them, fire emerges,
as large as a millet grain,
illuminating the entire room.'"
If not restrained, it will burn itself out;
the Zuǒzhuàn says:
"War is like fire;
if not restrained, it will burn itself out."
Also, when disaster erupts, it will certainly overcome.
The Yīnfújīng says:
"Fire is born from wood;
when disaster erupts, it will certainly overcome."
Often seen burning harmony,
the Zhuāngzǐ says:
"When benefit and harm rub against each other,
much fire is generated,
and the masses burn harmony."
I have heard of things being dried.
The Yìjīng says:
"Nothing dries the myriad things more than fire."
Purifying Guǎn Zhòng at the Qí border,
the Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
"Duke Huán of Qí sent someone to inform Lǔ:
'Guǎn Yíwú
is my enemy;
I wish to capture him alive.'
The ruler of Lǔ agreed,
then had his eyes glued shut,
placed him in a box,
and sent him to the Qí border.
Duke Huán had him welcomed with a court carriage,
and purified him with Guàn fire."
Following Wáng Mǎng to the Xuānshì Hall,
the Hànshū says:
"Hàn troops besieged Wáng Mǎng in the city.
Youths like Fáng Zhū and Zhāng Yú burned the workshop gate,
shouting:
'Rebel traitor Wáng Mǎng,
why do you not surrender?'
The fire reached the side courtyards.
Mǎng took refuge in the Xuānshì front hall,
and the fire followed him there."
As for the shepherd boy burning the Qín tomb,
the Sānfǔ Huángtú says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng was buried at Líshān.
Within six years, it was excavated by Xiàng Jí.
A shepherd boy was herding sheep,
and a sheep fell into the tomb.
He lit a fire to search for the sheep,
and burned the outer coffin and burial goods."
Xiàng Yǔ's slaughter of Xiányáng.
The Hànshū says:
"Xiàng Yǔ went west and slaughtered Xiányáng,
burning its palaces and buildings.
The fire lasted for three months without ceasing."
The Flaming Continent blazing brightly,
the Shízhōujì says:
"On Huǒlín Mountain, there is a fire beast resembling a rat,
with fur two to three cùn long.
Spinning it can make fire-cleaning cloth."
Shàngjùn glowing brilliantly.
the Gǔjīnzhù says:
"In the first year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān,
in the sands of Shàngjùn,
at night, there was fire like millet grains,
emerging without heat."
One should prepare baskets and shovels as a precaution,
the Zuǒzhuàn says:

Húmǔ's obtaining of Zǐ Bó,

Sūn Dēng's instruction to Jī Kāng.

When about to part,

'Do you understand fire?
Fire is born with light,
yet it does not use its light;
its reality lies in using the light.
Humans are born with talent,
yet they do not use their talent;
their reality lies in using their talent.
Therefore, using light depends on obtaining firewood,
so as to preserve its flame;
using talent depends on recognizing truth,
so as to preserve one's years.
Now, you have much talent but little recognition,
and will find it difficult to avoid misfortune in this world.'
Kāng could not heed this,
and indeed met an unnatural death."
As for the white-headed bird on Jū Mountain,

Jū,

I admire Zhèng Xuán's foresight,

Bó said:

Zǔ Yíng blocked the window and diligently studied,

Zǔ Yíng loved learning,

His parents feared he would become ill,

Guǎn Níng looked toward an island and arrived there.

Manifesting filial piety in Jūnzhòng,

Zhāng Zhāo,

Zhāo angrily claimed illness and did not attend court.

Quán repeatedly comforted and apologized,

Quán, while passing by his gate, called out to Zhāo,

Quán set fire to his gate,

Níng Fēngzǐ's five colors,

The King of Yuè grasped it to take revenge on Wú,

Praising Shūdù for not prohibiting fires,

Lián Fàn,
styled Shūdù,
served as the governor of Shǔ Commandery.
Chéngdū was cramped with narrow houses,

Laughing at Ānú's inferior strategy.

Zhōu Yǐ's younger brother, Sōng,

Sòng Jī's ominous event at Bó Shè,

Because of that friction wood,

Suddenly spouting from the mouth,

Rěng,

Pressured Zhòng Dū, yet he did not feel the heat.

Metal
Among the fine things of the southwest,
there are the metals and stones of Huàshān.
From the *Erya*.

enduring countless smeltings without losing weight.

yellow metal is the chief.

enduring countless smeltings, it does not lose weight;

The *Shū* says:
"Metal is said to follow transformation."
The commentary says:
"Metal can be changed and altered."
Its worth is sufficient for redemption of punishments.
The *Shū* says:
"Metal serves for the redemption of punishments."
It is responsible for the crafts of casting, forging, bell-making, and sword-making.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
Among the metalworking craftsmen,
the Zhù shì handle the lower alloys,
the Yě shì handle the upper alloys,
the Fú shì make musical sounds,
the Lì shì make measures,
the Duàn shì make farm tools,
and the Táo shì make blades.
There are six proportions for metal alloys.
Six parts metal with one part tin
is called the alloy for bells and tripods.
Five parts metal with one part tin
is called the alloy for axes and adzes.
Four parts metal with one part tin
is called the alloy for dagger-axes and halberds.
Three parts metal with one part tin
is called the alloy for large blades.
Five parts metal with two parts tin
is called the alloy for carving and killing blades.
Equal parts metal and tin
is called the alloy for mirrors and burning-glasses.
The commentary says:
More tin makes a lower alloy,
less tin makes an upper alloy.
A mirror
is a looking-glass.
With more tin, the blade is white and bright.
Inquire into the essence of polished, lustrous, fine, and pure gold.
The *Erya* says:
Yellow gold is called dàng,
the finest kind is called liú.
Ingot gold is called bǎn,
gold of surpassing luster is called xiǎn.
The commentary states:
"Surpassing luster" refers to fine gold,
the most lustrous.
Wáng Yáng was said to be able to make it.
The *Hànshū* says:
Wáng Yáng was fond of fine carriages, horses, and clothing,
but when he moved,
what he carried did not exceed a bag of clothes.
It was commonly said that Wáng Yáng could make gold.
Luán Dà, however, falsely claimed it could be produced.
The *Hànshū* says:
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
Luán Dà said:
"My teacher said:
'Gold can be made,
and the breach of the Yellow River can be stopped.'"
In Póyáng, casting sand yielded sudden finds.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìnshū* says:
Lè'ān in Póyáng produced gold.
Digging over ten zhàng into the earth,
sifting through sand, what was obtained
was as large as beans,
and as small as millet grains.
In Qīnghé, hidden grains of millet caused alarm.
The *Jìnshū* says:
Wáng Tán of Qīnghé,
initially the heir of the Prince of Qīnghé,
had a gold bell on his belt that suddenly developed hidden protrusions,
resembling hemp or millet grains.
His grandmother, the Grand Consort Chén, considered it inauspicious,
so she destroyed it and sold it.
Diviners believed the gold was an auspicious sign of the Jin dynasty's great prosperity,
and that Tán, as a royal descendant,
was its omen.
Destroying and selling it
meant Tán would be deposed,
an omen of an unfinished fate.
As for Yángmài's strange radiance,
the *Sòngshū* says:
Yángmài, King of Fúnán in the South Sea,
while still in the womb,
his mother dreamed of giving birth to a child.
Someone laid him on a gold mat,
its color radiant and beautiful.
The barbarians called the essence of gold "yángmài."
In China, what is called "purple-polished"
was thus used as his name.
The Lánghuǎng night market,
the *Yìwùzhì* says:
The Lánghuǎng people traded with the Han Chinese,
often at night markets.
They sniffed gold with their noses,
knowing its quality.
Biting it yields the image of dried meat.
The *Yìjīng*, "Shìkè" hexagram says:
The sixth line, fifth place:
Biting dried meat,
one obtains yellow gold.
Breaking it has the advantage of shared purpose.
The *Yìjīng* says:
When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal.
Leaping in the great furnace, it is known to be inauspicious.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Now a great smelter was casting metal,
and the metal leaped up and said:
"I will surely become a Mòyé sword!"
The great smelter certainly considered it inauspicious metal.
Raining in Lìyáng was hailed as an auspicious sign.
The *Shǐjì* says:
In the eighteenth year of Duke Xiàn of Qin,
gold rained in Lìyáng.
Considering it an auspicious omen of obtaining gold,
he therefore built the Fūzhì altar in Lìyáng,
to sacrifice to the White Emperor.
As for the ox leaping in Bāqiū,
the *Yōumíng Lù* says:
On Bǎijīn Ridge in Bāqiū County, there was a Gold Pool.
Above the pool was a rapid,
also called the Gold Rapid.
In ancient times, someone fished in this pool
and caught a gold chain.
Pulling it,
it filled an entire boat,
and a golden ox emerged,
its sound and appearance fierce and powerful.
The fisherman was terrified,
and the ox, struggling, leaped back into the pool.
In Línyì, fireflies flew.
The *Liángshū* says:
In the kingdom of Línyì, there is a red mountain,
within which gold is produced.
At night, it flies out,
appearing like fireflies.
Praise Chén Yì for taking nothing.
The *Lújiāng Qīxián Zhuàn* says:
Chén Yì,
courtesy name Zǐchū.
Arriving at Lǎnxiāng,
he saw a sick man beside a horse,
who called out:
"I am Wèi Shǎogōng of Cháng'ān.
Hearing of the delights of Lújiāng,
I came to travel,
but now I am ill and cannot proceed."
Yì welcomed him back,
and cared for him.
There were ten cakes of gold,
and twenty bolts of plain silk.
After he died,
Yì sold the silk to buy a coffin and burial clothes,
placed the gold beneath the coffin,
and rode the horse in and out.
Later, his elder brother, Chánggōng, saw the horse
and reported it.
Officials arrested Yì,
and Yì explained fully.
The gold was found beneath the coffin.
Chánggōng kowtowed in apology,
and threw ten cakes of gold at his gate.
Yì sent them back to Cháng'ān.
Respect Wáng Tún for his honesty.
The *Yìdū Qíjiù Zhuàn* says:
Wáng Tún,
courtesy name Shǎolín.
Going to the capital,
at an inn he saw a traveler gravely ill.
The man thus said to Tún:
"I have ten catties of gold at my waist.
I wish to give it to you,
begging you to collect and bury my bones."
Before he could ask his name,
the man died.
Tún sold one catty of gold,
to provide for the coffin,
and nine catties of floss silk,
placing them at the man's waist.
Then there is the wife of Rǔ Dūn, praised.
The *Liènǚ Zhuàn* says:
The wife of Rǔ of Guǎnghàn
was the wife of Rǔ Dūn.
Dūn gave all the fields, lands, and over three million in slaves he had received
to his elder brother and sister-in-law.
He kept only a few dozen mǔ of garden land,
built a hut and farmed it.
In the soil, he found a vessel of gold.
Dūn showed it to his wife,
and his wife said:
"Originally you said to yield what belonged to our ancestors,
is this alone not also theirs?"
Dūn said:
"That was indeed my intention."
They both carried the gold and delivered it to his elder brother and sister-in-law.
Again, he praised the wife of Yuè Yáng.
The *Liènǚ Zhuàn* says:
Yuè Yángzǐ went out to study,
his wife Zhēnyì,
cut off her hair to supply his expenses.
Later, Yángzǐ obtained a lost gold ingot,
and gave it to Zhēnyì.
Zhēnyì said:
"A gentleman does not stain his conduct for profit."
Yángzǐ was ashamed and discarded it.
Could Zhí Bùyí have stolen from his roommate?
The *Hànshū* says:
Zhí Bùyí served as a court gentleman,
a fellow gentleman in his quarters requested leave to return home,
and mistakenly took a fellow gentleman's gold with him.
The owner suspected Bùyí,
Bùyí bought gold to repay him.
When the one who had requested leave came back and returned the gold,
the one who had lost it was greatly ashamed.
Yáng Zhèn made clear the "Four Knowings."
The *Xù Hànshū* says:
Yáng Zhèn was the governor of Dōnglái,
traveling through Chāngyì.
Previously,
Zhèn had recommended Wáng Mì as an outstanding talent,
Mì was then a magistrate,
and at night he visited Zhèn,
carrying ten catties of gold to give to Zhèn.
Zhèn said:
"Your old friend knows you,
but you do not know your old friend.
Why is that?"
Mì said:
"In the dark of night, no one knows."
Zhèn said:
"Heaven knows,
the spirits know,
you know,
and I know.
That is already four knowings,
how can you say no one knows?"
Mì left in shame.
Some used it to honor Shū Guǎng's request for retirement,
the *Hànshū* says:
the Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Shū Guǎng, and his nephew, the Junior Tutor, Shòu,
begged to retire,
and both were permitted,
granted twenty catties of gold,
and the Crown Prince bestowed fifty catties upon them.
Some used it to reward Shūsūn for establishing the rituals.
The *Hànshū* says:
Shūsūn Tōng drafted the court rituals,
was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and granted five hundred catties of gold.
Then ascend Guō Kuí's terrace,
the *Xīnxù* says:
Yān Zhāowáng placed a thousand catties of gold on a terrace,
to attract scholars from all under heaven,
calling it the Golden Terrace.
He first honored Guō Kuí,
whereupon Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Zōu Yǎn came from Qí,
and Jù Xīn came from Zhào.
Scatter Dòu Yīng's corridor gifts,
the *Shǐjì* says:
When Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
Xiàojǐng appointed Dòu Yīng as Grand General,
and granted him a thousand catties of gold.
Yīng displayed it in the corridor,
and when military officers passed by,
he would let them take what they needed,
none entered his private home.
The *Shū* records three grades,
the *Shū* says:
Between the Huái and the sea is Yángzhōu,
its tribute is the three grades of metal.
The commentary says:
Gold, silver, and copper.
The *Shī* speaks of great bribes.
The *Shī* says:
Those fierce Huái-Yí,
come to offer their treasures.
Great tortoises and elephant tusks,
great bribes of southern gold.
Wéi Xián was not valued for a full hamper,
the *Hànshū* says:
Wéi Xián's youngest son, Xuánchéng,
again through mastery of the classics served successively until becoming Chancellor.
Thus the Zōu-Lǔ proverb says:
"Leaving your son a hamper full of gold,
is not as good as one classic."
Chún says:
Yíng,
a bamboo container,
holds three shēng.
Chén Píng often heard of sowing discord in Chǔ.
The *Shǐjì* says:
the King of Hàn gave Chén Píng forty thousand catties of gold,
to sow discord among the Chǔ ruler and his ministers,
without questioning his expenditures.
Benefit is spoken of as the tripod's ears,
the *Yìjīng*, "Dǐng Guà" says:
Six in the fifth place,
the tripod,
yellow ears,
golden rings,
beneficial and steadfast.
Skill is heard of in wagering with tiles.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Those who wager with tiles are skillful,
those who wager with belt hooks are cautious,
those who wager with gold are confused.
The commentary says:
When the stakes are heavy, the mind becomes arrogant.
Some ingested it and became immortals,
the *Shénxiān Zhuàn* says:
Róng Chénggōng ingested the three huángs and attained immortality.
Meaning realgar, orpiment, and gold.
Some bestowed it and gained land.
The *Shǔ Wáng Běnjì* says:
The King of Qín bestowed a hamper of gold upon the King of Shǔ,
Shǔ responded with gifts,
but they all turned into earth.
The King of Qín was angry,
but his ministers bowed in congratulation, saying:
"Earth,
is land.
Qín is destined to obtain Shǔ."
Obtain Sū Qín's old residence,
the *Jùnguó Zhì* says:
Sū Qín's residence was in Luòyáng's Lìrén Lane.
Later, Wèi's Gāo Xiǎnyè each night saw a red light,
and digging at the place of the light, obtained a hundred catties of gold,
the inscription said "Sū family gold."
Yè built a temple for it.
Obtain Dǒng Zhuó's remaining stronghold.
The *Yīngxióng Jì* says:
Dǒng Zhuó's stronghold had twenty to thirty thousand catties of gold.
Chén Jué sought a wine vessel from the bottom of the waves,
the *Lùnhéng* says:
Lújiāng commoners, young boys named Chén Jué and Chén Tǐng,
were bathing together by the lakeshore.
There was a wine vessel,
its color pure yellow,
submerged in the water.
Jué thought it was bronze,
waded into the water to fetch it, but it was too heavy to lift.
Tǐng went to help him,
the vessel sank further, becoming a sunken plate,
moving into the deep abyss.
Tǐng and Jué stayed looking,
and saw hundreds and thousands of coin-like objects, pure yellow in color,
immediately they gathered them together,
each filling their hands.
Returning home, they showed their families,
and it was gold.
Guō Jù then obtained a cauldron from the earth.
Sòng Gōng's *Xiàozǐ Zhuàn* says:
Guō Jù,
was from Wēn in Hénèi.
His wife bore a son,
and he considered that raising the child would prevent him from managing his livelihood,
hindering his ability to provide for his parents,
so he decided to kill and bury him.
As his spade entered the earth,
there was a cauldron of gold,
on it an iron deed stating:
"One cauldron of gold,
bestowed upon the filial son Guō Jù."
Praise Bǐng Yuán for returning it,
the *Bǐng Yuán Biézhuàn* says:
Yuán, styled Gēnjǔ,
as the chaos of war was raging,
went to Liáodōng.
At that time, his fellow commandery member Liú Jǔ was also in Liáo,
plotting to seize power from the Grand Administrator Gōngsūn Dù,
Dù raided and arrested his family,
but Jǔ escaped,
and in dire straits, returned to Yuán.
The Grand Administrator of Dōnglái, Tàishǐ Zǐyì,
was always righteous,
Yuán entrusted Jǔ to him.
As Jǔ was about to leave,
he gave Yuán three gold ingots from the sword he always carried,
Yuán accepted the gold but declined the sword.
Returning,
he said to Dù:
"General, you ordinarily had no grievance with Jǔ,
yet you wished to kill him,
only fearing he might be like a wasp or scorpion.
Now Jǔ has already left,
if you must detain and confine his family,
their venomous stings will surely grow even stronger."
Dù Jí then took out all his family's wealth,
and returned the gold to him.
He admired Guǎn Níng's disregard for gold.
"Shì Shuō" records:
Guǎn Níng and Huá Xīn were hoeing vegetables together in the garden,
when they saw a piece of gold on the ground.
Guǎn Níng continued hoeing as if it were a tile or stone,
while Huá Xīn picked it up and then threw it away.
Then there was the case of the widow Yìng who discovered gold at the shrine.
The "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
At the beginning of the restoration of the Hàn dynasty,
there was a widow Yìng who had four sons.
She saw a divine light shining on the shrine,
and upon investigating,
found gold.
From then on,
her sons all became officials and scholars,
and gained fame for their talents.
Up to Yáng, for seven generations, they were prominent and illustrious.
The Zhāng family obtained a belt hook.
The "Yōu Míng Lù" says:
In Cháng'ān, there was a man named Zhāng,
who was alone in his room during the day,
when a dove flew in
and perched on the bed opposite.
Zhāng disliked it,
and opened his robe, praying:
"Dove, if you have come
to bring me misfortune, stay on the canopy;
if to bring me fortune, enter my bosom."
The dove flew into his bosom.
When he reached in to feel for it,
it was nowhere to be found,
but he found a golden belt hook instead,
which he treasured.
From then on,
his descendants flourished and prospered.
The King of Qí's gift to Mèngzǐ,
"Mèngzǐ" says:
The King of Qí sent Mèngzǐ a hundred pieces of fine gold.
Note:
Fine gold
is high-quality gold.
King Xiāng of Chǔ's offer to Zhuāng Zhōu.
The "Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn" says:
King Xiāng of Chǔ sent an envoy with a thousand catties of gold and a hundred pairs of white jade to invite Zhuāngzǐ,
wishing to make him his chancellor.
Zhuāngzǐ firmly declined.
As for the burial at Líshān, where wild geese were made,
the "Shǐ Jì" says:
Qín Shǐhuáng was buried at Líshān,
with gold used to make wild geese.
The display in Xiányáng, where the book was completed.
The "Shǐ Jì" says:
Lǚ Bùwéi then had his guests each write what they knew,
compiling it into the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū".
When the book was completed,
it was displayed at the market gate in Xiányáng,
with a thousand pieces of gold hung above it,
promising a reward of a thousand pieces of gold to anyone who could add or remove a single character.
Leaving gold for Léi Yì to test his integrity.
Xiè Chéng's "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
Léi Yì,
styled Zhònggōng,
often helped others.
A man who had been saved from a death sentence later offered him two catties of gold in gratitude.
Yì refused to accept it.
The gold's owner waited until Yì was not home,
and secretly placed the gold on the canopy.
Later, when Yì was repairing his house, he found the gold.
By then, the owner had died,
so Yì handed it over to the county office.
Giving gold to Yuán Shū as a birthday gift.
The "Hàn Shū" says:
Dǒng Yǎn was favored by Princess Guǎntáo.
Yuán Shū of Ānlíng said to Yǎn:
"The Gùchéng Temple is far and has no lodging palace.
Why not advise the princess to offer the Chángmén Garden to the emperor?"
Dǒng Yǎn went in and told the princess,
who offered it.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and renamed it the Chángmén Palace.
The princess was overjoyed,
and had Dǒng Yǎn give Yuán Shū a hundred catties of gold as a birthday gift.
Some accepted by opening their sleeves without refusal.
The "Wèi Lüè" says:
Tián Yù was the governor of Bìngzhōu.
A Hú man secretly carried thirty catties of gold,
saying:
"I offer this to you, sir."
Yù opened his sleeve and accepted it,
acknowledging his kindness.
After the Hú man left,
Yù handed it all over to the authorities,
reporting the matter in detail.
Thereupon,
an imperial edict praised him, saying:
"In the past, Wèi Jiàng opened his bosom to accept the Róng;
now you have opened your sleeve to accept the Dí.
I greatly commend you."
Some threw gold into the garden and refused to accept it.
Xiè Chéng's "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
Zhāng Zǎi,
styled Zhòngzōng,
was the governor of Guǎnglíng.
He recommended Wú Fèng as Xiàolián.
When Zǎi left his post,
Fèng brought gold as a gift.
Zǎi refused to accept it.
Fèng placed it in a bag,
threw it into Zǎi's garden, and left.
Zǎi took the gold back to Guǎnglíng and returned it to Fèng.
Snatching it without fearing the people in the market.
The "Liè Zǐ" says:
A man from Qí desired gold.
One morning, he dressed properly and went to the market,
straight to a gold seller's stall,
snatched the gold, and ran.
The officials caught him
and asked:
"Everyone was there;
why did you snatch someone's gold?"
He replied:
"When I took it,
I saw no people,
only gold."
Melting it is often heard from the mouths of the crowd.
The "Lùn Héng" says:
"The mouths of the crowd can melt gold"
refers to the Five Elements,
the second being fire,
and the Five Affairs,
the second being speech.
Speech and fire correspond,
hence the saying "melt gold."
There is also the case of burying it under the tent.
The "Táng Shū" says:
During the Kāiyuán era,
Dù Xiān was an investigating censor.
He went west to inspect the garrisons,
and the Fān people brought gold to give him.
Xiān firmly refused,
but his attendants said he should not offend the Fān people's feelings.
Xiān accepted it and buried it under his tent.
After he left their territory,
he sent a dispatch ordering them to retrieve it.
Gold growing from a stele.
The "Wèi Zhì" says:
In Fánchāng County, gold grew from the stele marking the abdication,
which was presented to the court.
All the ministers offered congratulations.
Also,
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" says:
At the beginning of the Yǒngjiā era,
in Xiàng County of the Chén Kingdom, gold grew from the stele of Jiǎ Kuí.
People stole it by chiseling it out and selling it.
After it was sold, it grew again.
This was an auspicious sign for Jiāngdōng.
The Jìn dynasty's virtue was metal,
and Yuán Dì restored the dynasty in Jiāngdōng,
hence it was an auspicious sign for Jiāngdōng.
At night, startled by a white rat.
The "Bái Zé Tú" says:
White rats appear at dusk among the hills,
and where they come and go, there is gold inside.
Over the years, it may transform into a yellow dragon.
The "Huái Nán Zǐ" says:
A beautiful stone takes five hundred years to become huángqīng,
another five hundred years to become gold,
and another thousand years to become a yellow dragon.
Note:
A beautiful stone
is a fine gem.
In summer, wearing fur as a principle.
The "Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn" says:
Yánlíng Jìzǐ was traveling in Qí
when he saw lost gold on the road.
He called to a herdsman to pick it up.
The herdsman said:
"How is it that you stand so high
yet see so low!
You appear like a gentleman but speak like a rustic.
You have a lord but do not serve him,
have friends but do not befriend them,
wear fur in the heat of summer—
how could I be one to pick up gold?"
Jìzǐ realized he was a worthy man
and asked his name.
The herdsman said:
"You are a man who judges by appearances;
why bother asking my name?"
Below, we see the demeanor of a noble scholar.
The "Chūnqiū Hòu Yǔ" says:
When Qín besieged Hándān of Zhào,
Wèi sent General Xīnyuán Yǎn into Hándān
to persuade Zhào to honor Qín as emperor.
Lǔ Zhònglián persuaded him to abandon this,
and Hándān was saved.
Lord Píngyuán wanted to enfeoff Zhònglián,
but Zhònglián declined three times and would not accept.
Lord Píngyuán then prepared a banquet,
offering a thousand gold pieces to wish Zhòng Lián longevity.
Zhòng Lián laughed and said:
"What is valued among the gentlemen of the world
is to resolve others' troubles, dispel difficulties, and untangle disputes without seeking reward.
If one seeks reward,
then he is merely a merchant.
Zhòng Lián cannot bear to be such a person."
He then declined and departed.
There are also accumulations amounting to tens of thousands,
as the *Suí Shū* states:
Yáng Sù once ranked first in archery,
and the emperor bestowed upon him a gold-essence plate presented by a foreign state,
worth tens of thousands.
Also, the *Hàn Shū* states:
King Xiào of Liáng
possessed gold counted in tens of thousands.
Bestowed a thousand yì.
The *Hàn Shū* states:
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he appointed Chén Píng as chancellor,
bestowing upon him a thousand yì of gold,
and enfeoffing him with three thousand households.
Considering Wáng Mǎng's defeat,
the *Hàn Shū* states:
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
the gold in the palace, ten thousand catties per chest,
still amounted to sixty chests.
Estimating King Liáng's death,
the *Hàn Shū* states:
When King Xiào of Liáng died,
the remaining gold in his treasury still exceeded three hundred thousand catties.
The yellow birds by the well first flew,
as the *Yì Yuàn* states:
At the well of Wáng Kuàng in Yǒngkāng,
there was a washing stone,
occasionally emitting red vapor.
Later, a foreigner lodged there,
suddenly requesting to buy it.
Before the money could be counted,
the daughter-in-law, Sūn shì, saw two yellow birds fighting on the stone.
She swiftly went to capture them,
and they turned into gold.
The foreigner, unaware,
pressed even more urgently to purchase it.
Once he obtained it,
he broke the stone open,
and inside were precisely the two birds' hollows.
The tall hat beneath the wall suddenly emerged.
The *Sōu Shén Jì* states:
Zhāng Jù of Wèi Commandery sold his house to Chéng Yìng.
The entire household fell ill,
so he sold it to Hé Wén.
Wén alone took a large knife
and entered the north hall at dusk to stay.
In the middle of the first watch,
a figure over ten feet tall,
wearing a tall hat and red headband,
called out to Xìyāo:
"Why is there a human presence?"
The reply was:
"There is none."
Wén asked Xìyāo:
"Who is the tall-hatted one?"
The reply was:
"It is gold,
beneath the wall of the west room."
Wén dug
and obtained three hundred catties of gold.
It is also said to chase Hán Yān's pellets,
as the *Xī Jīng Zá Jì* states:
Hán Yān enjoyed pellet-shooting,
often using gold for pellets,
losing over ten in a single day.
In Cháng'ān, a saying arose:
"If hungry or cold,
chase the pellets."
The children of the capital, whenever they heard Yān was out shooting pellets,
would follow him,
watching where the pellets fell to pick them up.
Presented Liáng Jì's snake,
as Zhāng Fān's *Hàn Jì* states:
The Grand Administrator of Yǒngchāng cast a golden snake
and presented it to Liáng Jì.

Jade
The ancients had a saying:
"The gentleman compares his virtue to jade."
The Book of Rites says:
Zǐgòng asked:
"May I ask why the gentleman values jade and despises mǐn stone?
What is the reason?"
Confucius said:
"In ancient times, the gentleman compared his virtue to jade.
Warm, smooth, and lustrous—
this is benevolence;
dense, fine, and firm—
this is wisdom;
sharp-edged but not cutting—
this is righteousness;
hanging down as if about to fall—
this is propriety;
when struck,
its sound is clear, resonant, and long,
then ends abruptly—
this is music;
flaws do not obscure its beauty,
beauty does not conceal its flaws—
this is loyalty;
its radiance shines forth in all directions—
this is trustworthiness;
its aura resembles a white rainbow—
this is heaven;
its essence is revealed in mountains and rivers—
this is earth;
guī and zhāng jades are presented directly—
this is virtue;
all under heaven value it—
this is the Way.
The Book of Songs says, 'When I think of the gentleman,
his warmth is like jade.'
Therefore, the gentleman values it."
Annotation says:
Lì
means firm appearance.
Guì
means to injure.
Righteousness means not carelessly injuring.
Fúyīn
is read like fúyún (floating clouds).
As for the six ritual vessels of the Zhou officials,
the Rites of Zhou says:
Jade is used to make six vessels to worship heaven, earth, and the four directions.
A dark blue bì is used to worship heaven,
a yellow cóng to worship earth,
a blue guī to worship the east,
a red zhāng to worship the south,
a white hǔ to worship the west,
a black huáng to worship the north.
Daqin has five colors.
The Weilüe says:
The country of Daqin produces jade of five colors.
Zhào's walled cities:
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
King Huìwén of Zhào obtained the Héshì jade disc from Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Qín requested to exchange fifteen cities for the disc.
Zhào sent Lìn Xiàngrú to present the disc to Qín.
Xiàngrú saw that Qín had no intention of giving the cities,
so he said to the King of Qín:
"The disc has a flaw;
allow me to point it out."
The king ordered the disc to be handed over.
Xiàngrú took the disc and stepped back,
leaning against a pillar to reprimand Qín,
intending to smash the disc against the pillar.
The King of Qín, fearing the disc would break,
did not dare to press him.
Xiàngrú then sent someone to secretly carry the disc back to Zhào.
Jìn's Chuíjí.
The Zuozhuan says:
Xún Xī of Jìn requested to use the horses of Qūchǎn
and the jade disc of Chuíjí

to attack Guó.
Some used guàn jiǎ to avert disaster.
The Zuozhuan says:
Bì Zào of Zhèng said to Zǐchǎn:
"Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng will all suffer fire on the same day.
If we use guàn jiǎ and jade zàn,

Zǐchǎn did not give them.
Annotation:
Natural disasters spread;

Some engraved names on Tiáohuá.
The Dūnhuáng Chronicle says:
King Jié attacked Mínshān.
Mínshān gave King Jié two daughters,

King Jié loved the two women,
but they bore no sons.

Tiáo was Wǎn,
Huá was Yǎn.
Loving a huán, Hánzǐ received a gift.
The Zuozhuan says:
Hán Qǐ of Jìn visited Zhèng on a diplomatic mission.
Xuānzǐ had a huán,
and one of its pair was held by a merchant in Zhèng.
Xuānzǐ requested it from the Earl of Zhèng.
Zǐchǎn refused to give it.
Zǐ Tàishū and Zǐ Yǔ urged him to give it.
Zǐchǎn said:
"I have heard that a gentleman does not worry about lacking wealth,
but worries about lacking a good reputation.
I have heard that governing a state does not worry about inability to serve the great and nurture the small,
but worries about lacking propriety to secure its position.
If people from great states make demands on small states,
and all their requests are granted,
how will they be satisfied?
Sometimes granting, sometimes refusing—
this creates even greater offense."
Hán Xuānzǐ privately visited Zǐchǎn
and gave him jade,
saying:
"You ordered me to abandon that jade;
this is giving me jade and sparing my life.
How dare I not express my gratitude with this?"
Annotation:
Xuānzǐ is Hán Qǐ.
Yè
means to request.
Presenting ten jué, the Marquis of Wèi was released.

The Book of Songs says:
When I think of the gentleman,
his warmth is like jade.

It manifests these five virtues.
The *General Meanings of the Five Classics* says:
Jade possesses five virtues:
Warm, moist, and lustrous,
it resembles wisdom;
Sharp but not harmful,
it resembles benevolence;
Firm yet not inflexible,
it resembles righteousness;
Having flaws within,
they are sure to show without,
it resembles trustworthiness;
Hanging down as if falling,
it resembles propriety.
It distinguishes these six ceremonial tokens.

Hard yet not constricted,
the *Guǎnzǐ* says:
The reason jade is precious
is that nine virtues emerge from it.
Warm, moist, and lustrous—
this is benevolence;
Clear and patterned—
this is wisdom;
Hard yet not constricted—
this is righteousness;
Angular yet not cutting—
this is conduct;
Bright yet not soiled—
this is purity;
Can be broken but not bent—
this is courage;
Flaws and perfections both visible—
this is sincerity;
Splendid luster flowing freely without encroaching—
this is tolerance;
When struck, its sound is clear, focused, penetrating, and far-reaching,
pure and not harsh—
this is eloquence.
Therefore, rulers value it,
store it as treasure,
and split it to make auspicious tallies.
Angular yet not cutting.
See the commentary on "The gentleman compares his virtue to jade" above.

Respectfully noted:
Since the sixth year,
stones in the mountains have transformed into jade.
Stone is yīn,

Jade water records square flow,
xuán sources bear round breaks.
Moistening trees makes them more luxuriant,

Jade in the mountain makes the trees moist;

Pearls,
are the yáng within yīn,

jade,

Gathered from Lóngshǒu,
emerging from that Píngqiū,
