Língchāng bore floating.
The *Jìn Shū* says:
Shí Jìlóng built a bridge over the river at Língchāng Ford,
gathering stones for the central pier,
but stones, regardless of size,
sank and were carried away by the current,
and over five million man-days of labor were spent without success.
Shí Jìlóng sent an envoy to perform sacrifices,
and sank a jade disc into the river.
Soon after, the sunken disc floated onto an islet.
Some ascended the terrace and did not take it,
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* says:
King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked Yīn and became Son of Heaven,
ascended a terrace and saw jade,
the King said:
"Whose jade is this?"
Someone said:
"The jade of the feudal lords."
The King did not take it,
but returned it.
All under heaven heard of this,
and said:
"The King is incorruptible with wealth."
Some broke stones and sought it thus.
The *Lùnhéng* says:
Jade changes into stone,
pearls change into gravel,
slander causes this.
Those who gather jade
break stones to extract jade;
those who select scholars
discard the bad and take the good.
Furthermore, there is drinking wine from Yíngzhōu,
The *Shízhōu Jì* says:
Yíngzhōu has jade fat like wine,
called jade wine.
Drinking several shēng
makes one live long.
Observing the sun from Fúsāng.
The *Liáng Sì Gōng Jì* says:
An envoy from the Fúsāng kingdom came to present sun-observing jade.
As large as a mirror,
over a foot square and round,
It is as clear and transparent as glass.
When held against the sun to observe,
one can see palaces within the sun,
distinct and bright.
The Marquis of Jìn received it with a negligent demeanor.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The Son of Heaven sent Duke Shào Wǔ and the Neishi Guò to confer a mandate upon the Marquis of Jìn.
Upon receiving the jade, he was negligent.
Guò said:
"Will the Marquis of Jìn have no descendants?"
The Viscount of Zhū held it and lost propriety.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Duke Yǐn of Zhū came for an audience.
Zǐgòng observed the ceremony.
The Viscount of Zhū held the jade high,
his face looking upward;
the Duke received the jade low,
his face looking downward.
Zǐgòng said:
"Judging by propriety,
these two rulers
will both meet death."
The annotation states:
Jade
is the gift presented by those attending court.
Zhāng Bó concealed it and was exposed.
The Bié Zhuàn of Zhōnglí Yì states:
Yì served as Chancellor of Lǔ.
While inspecting Confucius’s teaching hall,
a man named Zhāng Bó
was weeding beneath the steps
and found seven jade discs in the soil.
He concealed one of them
and presented the other six to Yì.
Yì opened them,
and inside was a plain silk document that read:
"In later generations, the one who will study my writings
is Dǒng Zhòngshū;
the one who will touch my carriage, wipe my shoes, and open my bamboo case
is Zhōnglí Yì of Kuàijī;
there are seven jade discs,
and Zhāng Bó took one of them."
Yì summoned Bó and asked:
"There were seven jade discs;
why did you conceal one?"
Bó kowtowed and produced it.
Yàfù smashed it without regret.
The Hànshū states:
Gāozǔ met Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén.
After Gāozǔ departed,
he sent Zhāng Liáng to present a jade vessel to Yàfù Fàn Zēng.
Yàfù dashed it to pieces,
saying:
"We are destined to become captives."
Some resemble that false jade,
as the Zhànguócè states:
Bone may be mistaken for ivory,
and false jade resembles true jade.
Some are mistaken for Yān stone,
as the Quēzǐ states:
A foolish man of Sòng obtained a Yān stone at Wútái
and stored it as a great treasure.
A visitor from Zhōu heard of it and came to see it.
The host fasted for seven days,
then emerged wearing formal black robes and a ceremonial cap.
He brought out a splendid case of ten layers
wrapped in ten layers of orange silk.
Upon seeing it, the visitor covered his mouth and chuckled,
saying:
"This is Yān stone,
no different from gravel."
The host was greatly angered
and hid it even more securely.
Obtaining it from Chǔ Mountain led to punishment,
as the Hánzǐ states:
A man of Chǔ named Biàn Hé obtained an uncut jade at Chǔ Mountain
and presented it to King Lì.
The king had a jade craftsman examine it.
He said:
"It is stone."
The king considered Hé deceitful
and had his right foot amputated.
When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
he presented it again.
It was examined once more, and they said:
"It is stone."
His left foot was amputated.
When King Wén ascended the throne,
Hé embraced his uncut jade and wept at Chǔ Mountain
for three days and three nights,
until his tears dried and blood flowed.
The king had a jade craftsman work on it,
and a precious jade was obtained,
named Héshì's Jade Disc.
Presenting it to a person of Zhèng to seek its value,
as the Wénzǐ states:
People of Zhèng call uncut jade "pú,"
while people of Zhōu call unprocessed rat meat "pú."
A man of Zhōu carried his "pú" and asked a merchant of Zhèng:
"Do you want this?"
He produced his "pú."
Upon inspection, it turned out to be rat meat.
These are all cases where the genuine and the false are confused
due to lack of discerning knowledge.
There is also the yǎn and jade qìng of Qí,
as the Zuǒzhuàn states:
Jìn and Qí fought at Ān,
and the Qí army was defeated.
The Marquis of Qí sent Bǐn Mèirén to offer a yǎn, a jade qìng, and land as bribes.
"If this is not accepted,
then we will submit to whatever the guests do."
There is also the fányú of Lǔ,
as the Yì Lúnyǔ states:
Fányú
is the treasure of Lǔ.
Confucius said:
"How beautiful!
Fányú.
Viewed from afar,
it is resplendent;
examined up close,
it is serene.
One excels in texture,
the other in brilliance."
Its value exceeds a hundred thousand,
as Huán Tán's Xīnlùn states:
Lǐ Yòubīn of Luòyáng
had a small jade seal case.
Wèi Yèzhě Shǐ Zǐbó,
who was fond of jade objects,
saw it and found it remarkable.
He sent someone to offer thirty thousand coins to purchase it.
Yòubīn said:
"I have shown it to an elder connoisseur,
who valued it at a hundred thousand.
It is not for thirty thousand coins."
The messenger exclaimed in surprise:
"If I saw this on the road,
I would not buy it even for a thousand coins."
Thus, the difference between knowing and not knowing
is vast.
Its fame is renowned throughout the five capitals.
The Yǐnwénzǐ states:
A farmer of Wèi found a jade disc a foot in diameter in the wild.
Not knowing it was jade,
he told his neighbor.
The neighbor deceived him,
saying:
"This is a strange stone.
Keeping it will bring no benefit."
Though the farmer was suspicious,
he still placed it under the eaves.
That night,
the jade illuminated the entire room.
His family was greatly frightened
and hastily discarded it in the wild.
The neighbor stole it
and presented it to the King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi summoned a jade craftsman to examine it.
The craftsman gazed at the jade, bowed twice, and stepped back,
saying:
"I dare to congratulate Your Majesty
on obtaining a treasure of the world.
I have never seen such a thing."
The king asked its value.
The craftsman said:
"This is priceless.
Even the five cities' capitals are only worth a single viewing."
The king immediately bestowed a thousand gold upon the presenter
and granted him a perpetual salary as a senior official.
Distinguish its texture and grain,
as the Shuōwén states:
Jade
is the beauty among stones, possessing five virtues:
Its moist, smooth, and warm nature
represents the aspect of benevolence;
its texture visible from the outside,
allowing one to know its interior,
represents the aspect of righteousness;
its sound, clear and far-reaching,
spreading widely,
represents the aspect of wisdom;
its unyielding nature, breaking without bending,
represents the aspect of courage;
its sharp edges that do not cut, representing the aspect of purity.
Observe its flaws and virtues.
See the annotation on "The gentleman compares virtue to jade."
Recall Lǎodān, who wore coarse cloth,
as the Lǎozǐ states:
Wearing coarse cloth while holding jade within.
Think of Mùmǎn, who examined maps and charts.
The Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn states:
The Son of Heaven held a grand assembly at Huángzhī Mountain,
examined maps and consulted records,
and surveyed the Son of Heaven's treasures: jade fruits and xuán pearls.
The annotation states:
Jade fruits
are jade resembling fruit.
Xuán
is a type of jade.
I have also heard that when holding jade, one does not hasten.
The Book of Rites says:
"When holding jade, one does not hasten."
The commentary states:
"This is because one regards the jade with great importance."
It is received with cupped hands.
The Book of Rites says:
"Those who receive pearls and jade do so with cupped hands."
A hairpin was left behind, and the pavilion was named Zhāolíng.
The Dòng Míng Jì records:
In the first year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the Zhāolíng Pavilion was built. There was a divine maiden
who left a jade hairpin for the Emperor.
The Emperor bestowed it upon Consort Zhào Jiéyú.
By the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
palace ladies still saw this hairpin.
They plotted together to break it.
When they opened the hairpin case to look,
they only saw a white swallow soar straight up to heaven.
Afterwards, palace ladies often made jade hairpins,
and thus they were named 'jade swallow hairpins,'
said to be auspicious.
A jué ring was seen, and the mountain was named Xīlù.
The Suí Cháo Zǐ states:
The Xīlù mountain crumbled,
and Heaven bestowed a jade jué ring upon Yì,
which ultimately led to his mutilation.
Taking this as a blessing,
he ended up with calamity.
Without reason, how could one part with it?
The Book of Rites says:
"A nobleman, without reason,
does not part with his jade."
Awaiting the right price, it should always be kept stored in a case.
The Analects:
Zǐgòng said:
"Suppose there is a beautiful jade here.
Should one store it away in a case,
or seek a good price and sell it?"
The Master said:
"Sell it! Sell it!
I am one who awaits the right price."
Observe it: black as pure lacquer,
white like sliced fat.
Wáng Yì's "Treatise on the Jade Section" says:
Someone asked about the signs of jade.
The reply was:
"Red as a cockscomb,
yellow as steamed millet,
white as animal fat,
black as pure lacquer—
these are the signs of jade."
Emperor Wén of Wèi, in his "Letter to Zhōng Yáo" discussing jade,
also said, "white like sliced fat,
black compared to pure lacquer."
To handle it is to feel its ruggedness.
The Lǎo Zǐ says:
"I desire not to be rugged like jade,
nor common like stone."
Wearing it, it clinks and chimes.
The Book of Songs says:
"About to soar, about to glide,
the girdle gems clink and chime."
The layered city is where it grows.
The Huái Nán Zǐ says:
The Kūnlún mountains have layered cities, ninefold,
where there are pearl trees and jade trees.
On a sea island it was stored.
The History of the Later Wèi states:
Cuī Tǐng was Governor of Guāngzhōu.
In Yè County, there was a man over ninety years old
who came to the provincial seat by wooden carriage.
He claimed that in his youth he had once served as an envoy to Línyì,
and obtained a beautiful piece of jade,
one foot four inches square,
with great luster.
He had hidden it on a sea island
for nearly sixty years.
Rejoicing in the enlightened governance,
he now wished to present it.
Cuī Tǐng said:
"Although my virtue falls short of the ancients,
I cannot consider jade a treasure."
He sent a boat to fetch it;
it was indeed glossy and smooth.
He firmly declined to accept it
and instead memorialized to send it to the capital.
It astounds, like the rainbow's transformation.
The Sōu Shén Jì records:
When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals
and established the Classic of Filial Piety,
upon completion,
he fasted and purified himself to report to Heaven.
Heaven sent down a crimson rainbow,
which transformed into a yellow piece of jade,
three feet long,
with inscriptions on it.
It amazes, like the vanishing of accumulated snow.
The Yì Yuàn records:
When Téng, the Duke of Dōngyíng of Jìn, was stationed in Yè,
there was heavy snow.
Yet, on the ground in front of the gate for several tens of paces, the snow melted and did not accumulate.
Téng found it strange.
He dug there
and found a jade horse,
about a foot tall,
with missing teeth in its mouth.
Téng considered the horse, the surname of the state, an auspicious omen.
Some said a horse without teeth cannot eat again.
Destroyed within its case—how to avoid blame?
The Analects says:
"When a tiger or rhinoceros escapes from its cage,
or when a tortoise-shell or jade is destroyed in its case—
whose fault is it?"
Presented at the palace gate, deception was revealed.
The Book of Hàn states:
When Emperor Wén first visited Yōng,
Xīnyuán Píng, who observed portents, had someone present a jade cup at the palace gate as an offering.
Píng reported to the Emperor, saying:
"There is an aura of precious jade below the palace gate."
Indeed, someone came forward offering a jade cup.
One thinks of the return of the disc at Hàochí.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
In the thirty-sixth year of the First Emperor,
an envoy traveling from east of the pass passed by night through the Píngshū road at Huáyīn.
A man holding a jade disc stopped the envoy and said:
"Take this for me to the Lord of Hàochí."
He then added:
"This year, the First Dragon will die."
The envoy received the disc and reported the matter in full.
The First Emperor ordered the Imperial Treasury to examine the disc;
it was the very disc he had cast into the river while crossing the Yangtze in his twenty-eighth year.
One recalls the fishing for the huáng tablet at Pánxī.
The Shàng Shū Zhōng Hòu states:
Tàigōng went to the waters of Pánxī
and fished by its bank.
He obtained a jade huáng tablet,
inscribed: "The Jī clan receives the Mandate,
the Lǚ clan assists it.
The reward lies in Qí."
Tucking it in the bosom—heard of concerning Shū Dài.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Duke Xiāng died in the Chǔ palace.
Shūzhòng Dài stole his large ceremonial disc
and gave it to a carriage driver.
He tucked it in his bosom and then took it back,
for which he incurred blame.
Pressing against the cord-knot—seen again with King Píng.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
King Gòng of Chǔ had no legitimate heir by his principal wife.
He had five favored sons,
with no one clearly designated as successor.
He then performed a great ceremony to all the mountain and river deities,
praying:
"I beg the spirits to choose from among these five,
to let one preside over the altars of soil and grain."
He then showed a jade disc to all the deities,
saying:
"He who bows with the disc directly in front of him
is the one established by the spirits."
Afterwards,
he secretly buried the disc with Consort Bā in the courtyard of the Grand Chamber.
He had the five sons fast and purify themselves, then enter in order of age to bow.
King Kāng stepped over it.
King Líng's elbow touched it.
Zǐ Gàn and Zǐ Xī both kept their distance.
King Píng was young.
He was carried in,
bowed twice,
and each time pressed against the cord-knot.
When it is put to use,
its aura rises at the Court of Imperial Entertainment.
The Continuation of the Book of the Later Hàn states:
During the reign of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
below the officials' quarters of the Court of Imperial Entertainment,
at night there was a blue aura.
Upon inspection,
they found one jade hook and one jade jué ring each,
their bodies all carved and engraved.
And at the time of being burned,
the fire rages on the Kūnlún peaks.
The Book of Documents says:
"When fire blazes on the Kūnlún peaks,
jade and stone are burned together."
Additionally, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn planted it in his front courtyard.
The Stories of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
The Emperor built a divine chamber,
and in the front courtyard planted a jade tree,
using coral for its branches,
green jade for its leaves.
Its blossoms were blue and red,
made of pearls and jade.
Its center was hollow,
like small bells, producing clinking sounds.
King Chéng of Zhōu displayed it in the eastern chamber.
The Book of Documents, the "Testamentary Charge" chapter, says:
"The great jade, the foreign jade, the celestial sphere, and the River Chart were placed in the eastern chamber."
Chìsōngzǐ ingested it and trod through fire.
The *Biographies of Immortals* states:
Chìsōngzǐ was
the Rain Master during the time of Shénnóng.
He ingested aqueous jade,
instructed Shénnóng,
and could enter fire without being burned.
Yáng Gōng planted it and took a wife.
The *Records of Searching for the Supernatural* states:
Yáng Gōng Yōngbó
was a man from Luòyáng County.
His nature was sincerely filial.
When his parents died,
he buried them on Wúzhōng Mountain,
and subsequently resided there.
The mountain was eighty *li* high,
and atop it there was no water.
The lord drew water
and prepared charitable broth at the head of the slope;
all travelers drank it.
After three years,
a man came to drink,
gave him a peck of pebbles,
and told him to plant them in a high, level, good place where there were stones,
saying jade would grow among them.
Yáng Gōng was not yet married.
He also said:
"You will later obtain a good wife."
When he finished speaking, he vanished.
Later, he planted those stones.
After several years,
he would go from time to time to look,
and jade seeds grew,
though no one else knew.
There was a Xú family,
a prominent clan of Yòuběipíng,
whose daughter was quite renowned.
People of the time sought her hand,
but they were mostly refused.
The lord then tried seeking her from the Xú family.
The Xú family considered him mad,
and thus jokingly said:
"Bring a pair of white jade discs,
and we will consent to the marriage."
The lord went to the place where he had planted the stones,
obtained five pairs of white jade discs,
and presented them as betrothal gifts to the Xú family.
The Xú family was greatly astonished,
and subsequently gave their daughter to the lord as his wife.
The Son of Heaven found this extraordinary,
and appointed him as a Grand Master.
At the place where the jade was planted, they erected large stone pillars at the four corners,
each ten feet tall,
and the central area of one *qing* was called the Jade Field.
Regarding Yú Shùn receiving the Zhāohuá jade,
the *Great Commentary to the Book of Documents* states:
Yáo bestowed the realm upon Shùn,
and presented him with the Zhāohuá jade.
Regarding the Marquis of Qí obtaining the Lóngfǔ jade,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
The Duke bestowed a lamb-fur robe upon Gōngyǎn,
and sent him to present the Lóngfǔ jade to the Marquis of Qí,
whereupon he entered wearing the lamb-fur robe.
The Marquis of Qí was pleased,
and gave him Yánggǔ.
The commentary states:
Lóngfǔ
is the name of a jade.
Yánggǔ
is a city of Qí.
Regarding bestowing five *jué* of jade upon the Duke of Guó,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
The Duke of Guó and the Marquis of Jìn had an audience with the King.
At the feast,
he commanded them to be assisted with wine,
and each received five *jué* of jade.
Regarding bestowing a pair of *hǔ*-shaped jades upon Zǐjiā,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ was ill,
and bestowed gifts upon all the Grand Masters,
but the Grand Masters did not accept them.
He bestowed upon Zǐjiāzǐ a pair of *hǔ*-shaped jades, one ring, one disc, and fine garments;
he accepted them.
Thereupon, all the Grand Masters accepted their gifts.
When the Duke passed away,
Zǐjiāzǐ returned the gifts to the treasury officer,
saying:
"I dared not disobey the lord's command."
All the Grand Masters returned their gifts.
Commentary:
*Hǔ*
is a jade vessel.
Fine garments
are exquisite, fine clothing.
Regarding Wáng Mǎng's hidden treachery with the *zhuì* jade,
the *Book of Hàn* states:
When Wáng Mǎng went to his fief,
Kǒng Xiū was the Administrator of Xīndū.
Xiū paid a visit to Mǎng,
and Mǎng offered him a jade-adorned precious sword.
Xiū was unwilling to accept it.
Mǎng then said:
"Truly, I see your face has a scar;
fine jade can remove it.
I am offering you its *zhuì*."
He then detached its *zhuì*.
Xiū again declined.
Mǎng then smashed it with a hammer,
wrapped it up himself, and presented it to Xiū.
*Zhuì*:
pronounced *wèi*.
Regarding the man of Sòng's lingering affection for carving paper mulberry leaves,
the *Lièzǐ* states:
A man of Sòng carved paper mulberry leaves from jade for his lord;
it took three years to complete them.
The sharp points, stems, and leaves,
the fine tips and lush sheen,
were indistinguishable when mixed among real paper mulberry leaves.
This man thus made his living through his skill in the state of Sòng.
Regarding Jǔ Pú stealing it and fleeing here,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
The Crown Prince of Jǔ fled here with his precious jade.
Regarding Jiāogé demanding it but not receiving it,
the *Hánzǐ* states:
Zhōu possessed a jade tablet.
King Zhòu ordered Jiāogé to demand it,
but King Wén did not give it.
Fèi Zhòng came to request it,
and he then gave it.
This was because Jiāogé was worthy,
while Fèi Zhòng was without virtue.
Zhōu disliked the worthy gaining their ambitions,
so he gave it to Fèi Zhòng.
Regarding taking it to symbolize virtue,
the *White Tiger Discussions* states:
Jade
symbolizes the virtue of a gentleman:
it is not light when dry,
nor heavy when wet;
therefore, rulers treasure it.
Regarding it not being appropriate to change the pace,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
Jì Píngzǐ traveled to Dōngyě.
On his return,
before he arrived,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
he died in Fáng.
Yánghǔ intended to use the *yúfán* jade for his burial accoutrements,
but Zhòngliáng Huái would not give it,
saying:
"A changed pace requires changed jade."
The commentary states:
When Duke Zhāo was exiled,
Jì Sūn performed the duties of the ruler,
wore the *yúfán* jade,
and sacrificed in the ancestral temple.
When Duke Dìng was established,
he resumed his ministerial position.
Changing the ruler's pace,
he should then also have removed the *yúfán* jade.
Regarding having already inspected the palaces of Xiányáng,
the *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
When Gāozǔ first entered the Xiányáng Palace,
he toured the storehouses,
where gold, jade, and precious treasures
were beyond description.
Among the most extraordinary items
were five blue jade lamps.
The lamps were seven feet five inches tall,
depicting coiled *chī* dragons holding the lamps in their mouths.
When the lamps were lit, their scales all moved,
filling the room with brilliant light.
Regarding further viewing the storehouse of Xuāntù,
the *Records of Wèi* states:
During the Hàn, when the King of Fúyú was buried, a jade seal was used,
which was always kept in advance at Xuāntù Commandery.
When the king died, it was fetched for the burial.
Regarding recognizing the white-haired old man,
the *Wú's Materia Medica* states:
White jade's substance is like the white-haired old man.
Regarding seeing the purple-clad divine maiden,
the *Records of the Extraordinary* states:
Jiāng Yán often went to Wú to gather herbs.
When he reached the south of Qīngquán Mountain in Fùchūn County, he saw a beautiful maiden,
clad in purple,
sitting on a rock and singing,
with a sound like that of a stone tablet.
Yán approached,
but before he had gone several tens of paces,
the maiden vanished.
This happened for several days,
so Yán broke open the rock,
and obtained a piece of purple jade,
one foot in width and length.
These are signs of the essence and purity of Heaven and Earth,
which cannot be fully enumerated.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
The jade of Zhōng Mountain,
when heated over furnace charcoal
for three days and three nights, does not change its color and luster,
for it has obtained the essence of Heaven and Earth.
Pearl
When virtue reaches the deep springs,
bright pearls emerge from them.
The *White Tiger Discourse* states:
When virtue reaches the deep springs,
then the rivers yield large shells,
and the sea yields bright pearls.
They dazzle with radiance, illuminating carriages.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
The King of Wèi and King Wēi of Qí met for a hunt in the suburbs.
The King of Wèi said:
"Though my state is small,
I still have ten pearls, each an inch in diameter, that can illuminate twelve carriages both in front and behind.
How can a state with ten thousand chariots have no treasures?"
They emit crystalline brilliance in the enchanting rivers.
Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on Literature" states:
Waters that hold pearls make rivers enchanting;
mountains that contain jade make hills radiant.
They emerge from the Chìyě region.
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
Jade originates from Yúshān,
and pearls originate from Chìyě.
They are produced in the Dānyuān.
The *Rènzǐ* states:
The pearls of Dānyuān
sink into the yellow mud.
They reflect autumn waves with their round fractures.
The *Yǐnzǐ* states:
Wherever water fractures squarely, there is jade;
wherever it fractures roundly, there are pearls.
They wax and wane with the night moon.
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" states:
The pearl-bearing clams and mussels
wax and wane with the moon.
As for listing the tribute of the Huáiyí,
the *Book of Documents* states:
In Xúzhōu,
its tribute includes pearls from the Huái and Yí rivers, and sturgeon fish.
The commentary notes:
Huái and Yí are the names of two rivers.
They stand out as the beauty of Huòshān.
The *Erya* states:
Among the beauties of the western regions,
there are the many pearls and jades of Huòshān.
Recognize the Fúyú pearls resembling dates.
The *Guǎngzhì* states:
The land of Fúyú is beautiful,
and its pearls are like sour dates.
See the Guǎntáo pearls resembling plums.
The *Notes on Ancient and Modern Matters* states:
In the first year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng,
bright pearls emerged in Guǎntáo,
as large as plums,
with brilliant radiance.
In the third year,
bright moon pearls emerged in Hǎihūn, Yùzhāng,
as large as chicken eggs,
with a circumference of four inches and eight-tenths.
Some bury qīnglíng insects in the ground.
The *Records of the Investigation of Things* states:
On the fifth day of the fifth month, take the heads of qīnglíng insects,
bury them in the center of the main gate,
and they all turn into green pearls.
Some gather red clams from the bottom of springs.
The *Records of the Hidden and Visible* states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn visited Hézhǔ,
and heard the sound of string music and singing.
An old man and several young people emerged,
all eight or nine inches tall,
and performed music for the emperor.
The old man ordered someone to fetch the treasure from the cave.
One person accepted the command,
descended to the bottom of the river,
and obtained a large pearl,
several inches in diameter,
with unparalleled brilliance.
The emperor asked Dōngfāng Shuò,
and Shuò said:
"At the bottom of the river, there is a cave,
hundreds of zhàng deep,
containing red clams,
which produce this pearl."
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn received a dream from Kūnmíng.
The *Decisive Records of the Three Capital Regions* states:
In the Kūnmíng Pond, there is a divine spring,
connected to the White Tiger Plain.
When people fished there,
the fishing line would break and the fish would escape,
and they would dream of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
asking him to remove the hooks.
The next day, the emperor was playing by the pond,
and saw a large fish holding the line in its mouth.
The emperor took it and released it.
Three days later,
he found a pair of bright pearls by the pond.
The emperor said:
"This is the fish's repayment."
Mǎ Yuán was slandered over job's tears.
Fàn Yè's *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
While Mǎ Yuán was in Jiāozhǐ,
he often consumed job's tears,
and upon returning,
he loaded a cart with them.
Later, someone submitted a memorial slandering him,
claiming that what he had brought back earlier
were all bright pearls and patterned rhinoceros horns.
As for rejecting Wén Lì's tribute,
the *Records of the Eastern Pavilion* states:
In the fourth year of the Yǒngjiàn era,
Wén Lì, the governor of Hànyáng, presented a large pearl.
Emperor Shùn issued an edict stating:
"The realm is plagued by disasters and anomalies,
yet Lì does not devote loyalty and sincerity,
but instead flatters with auspicious pearls.
Now, the pearl is sealed and returned."
Accepting Sū Zé's words,
the *Records of Wèi* states:
Emperor Wén asked Sū Zé:
"Previously, when the Western Regions sent envoys,
Dūnhuáng presented a large pearl an inch in diameter.
Can we seek to purchase more?"
Zé replied:
"If Your Majesty's virtue flows to the desert,
they will come without seeking;
if sought and obtained,
they are not worthy of value."
The emperor fell silent.
In times of famine, trading for grain is still acceptable.
The *Garden of Stories* states:
Mòzǐ said to Huá Lí:
"In this year of famine,
if someone wanted to give you the Pearl of the Marquis of Suí,
saying it cannot be sold,
but only used as an ornament,
and another wanted to give you a zhōng of grain,
if you take the grain, you cannot have the pearl;
if you take the pearl, you cannot have the grain,
which would you choose?"
Huá Lí said:
"I would take the grain."
But using it to shoot sparrows is inappropriate.
The *Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals* states:
Using the Pearl of the Marquis of Suí
to shoot a sparrow a thousand rèn high,
the world would surely laugh at it.
What is used is heavy,
while what is sought is light.
Wáng Zhāng's orphan,
after gathering pearls, became wealthy;
the *Book of Hàn* states:
During the reign of Emperor Chéng,
Wáng Zhāng died,
and his wife and children were exiled to Hépǔ.
His family gathered pearls,
and amassed wealth worth several million.
After Lǐ Hóngjié's death,
his family sold pearls and was suspected.
The *Book of Táng* states:
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Lǐ Hóngjié, the military governor of Guìzhōu, was known for his purity and caution.
After his death,
his family sold pearls.
When the emperor heard of this, he grew suspicious,
and intended to punish those who had recommended him.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated:
"Your Majesty says this man was not pure,
but no evidence of accepting bribes has been seen.
Moreover, those who remained pure and untainted
were only Qūtū Tōng and Zhāng Dàoyuán.
Now, Tōng's three sons came for selection,
and together they had only one emaciated horse.
Dàoyuán's sons could not sustain themselves,
yet not a word was spoken on their behalf.
But Hóngjié achieved merit,
was greatly rewarded,
and his wife and children bought pearls—
this is not a crime.
Though your hatred of evil runs deep,
your love of goodness is not steadfast."
The emperor praised his words.
Thus, there is anger when pearls are thrown in the dark, and swords are drawn.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
Zōu Yáng's "Letter to the King of Wú from Prison" states:
"If a bright moon pearl
or a night-shining jade
is thrown at someone in the dark on the road,
everyone will draw their swords and glare.
Why?
Because they arrived without cause."
Moved by pure integrity, pearls return to the shore.
Xiè Chéng's *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
Mèng Cháng served as the governor of Hépǔ.
The local custom was to gather pearls to exchange for grain.
Previously, the two-thousand-dàn officials were greedy and corrupt,
ordering people to gather pearls
and hoarding them for themselves.
The pearls suddenly migrated away,
and Hépǔ was left without pearls,
causing countless deaths from famine.
Under Mèng Cháng's transformative governance,
within a year,
The tall man pointed to a sheep beneath the cypress tree in the courtyard,
and ordered him to kneel and stroke the sheep's beard.
After three strokes, he obtained three pearls.
The man instructed him to eat the one he had obtained last,
after which he would no longer feel hunger.
He then continued through the cave,
emerging in Jiāozhōu.
Returning to Luòyáng,
he asked Zhāng Huà,
who said:
"There are nine earthly immortals,
known as the Nine Hall Ministers.
The sheep is the Foolish Dragon.
If you eat the first pearl,
your lifespan will equal that of heaven and earth;
the second will prolong your years;
the last merely cures hunger."
Though fish may hear of calamity,
The Annals of Lü Buwei states:
Sīmǎ Huán of Sòng had a precious pearl.
Convicted of a crime, he fled into exile.
The king sent someone to inquire about the pearl's whereabouts,
so he threw it into a pond.
The pond was then drained in search of it,
and the fish suffered calamity as a result.
The banks may not dry up because of it.
The Da Dai Li Ji states:
Where jade resides in the mountains, the trees are moist;
where pearls are born in the deep, the banks do not dry up.
The tomb of Qín hung with sun and moon,
The Records of Sān Qín states:
In the First Emperor's tomb, luminous pearls served as the sun and moon.
The hall was hung with bright moon pearls,
shining day and night.
Even great Confucians untie skirts and jackets.
Zhuangzi states:
Confucians used the Book of Songs and the Book of Rites to rob tombs.
The great Confucian said:
"The east is growing light;
how goes the affair?"
The lesser Confucian replied:
"The skirt and jacket are not yet untied,
but there is a pearl in the mouth.
The Book of Songs indeed says:
'Green, green the wheat,
growing on the slopes of the hills.
In life you did not give alms;
in death, what use is a pearl in your mouth?'"
It is also heard that Zhū Zhòng came and went in the Hàn court,
The Biographies of Immortals states:
Zhū Zhòng was a pearl merchant from Kuàijī.
During Empress Gāo's time,
when three-inch pearls were sought,
he went to the palace and presented one.
The pearl was exceptionally fine,
and he was rewarded with five hundred gold pieces.
Princess Lǔ Yuán privately paid seven hundred gold to Zhòng for a four-inch pearl.
During Emperor Jǐng's reign, he again presented several dozen three-inch pearls,
then left, and no one knew where he went.
Dǒng Yǎn idled in the princess's residence.
The Book of Hàn states:
Dǒng Yǎn and his mother made a living selling pearls.
When Yǎn was thirteen,
he followed his mother to serve in Princess Guǎntáo's household.
Those around spoke of his beauty,
and the princess summoned him, saying:
"I will raise him."
He gained her favor.
Obtaining the tears of the jiāo people,
The Records of the Investigation of Things states:
The jiāo people emerged from the water,
dwelling among humans,
selling silk for many days.
When about to leave,
they asked their host for a vessel,
wept, and filled the plate with pearls,
which they gave to the host.
Waiting for the Black Dragon to sleep.
Zhuangzi states:
By the river, there was a poor man who made a living by weaving reeds.
His son dove into the deep,
and obtained a pearl worth a thousand gold.
The father said to his son:
"Bring a stone and smash it.
A pearl worth a thousand gold
must lie beneath the Black Dragon's chin in the ninefold depths.
That you could obtain the pearl
was because you caught it asleep.
Had the Black Dragon awakened,
what would have been left of you?"
A hundred strands earned Jì Lún's reward,
The Records of Gleaned Fragments states:
Shí Jì Lún had several dozen beloved maidservants.
Jì Lún once ground aloeswood into dust-like powder,
spread it on an ivory bed,
and had them walk on it.
Those who left no trace were rewarded with a hundred strands of pearls;
those who left traces had their food rationed,
to make their bodies lighter.
Thus, the women in the inner chambers teased each other:
"If not for your slender bones and light body,
how could you obtain a hundred strands of true pearls?"
A hú received as a gift from Sūn Quán.
The Records of Shǔ states:
Zōng Yù again visited Wú as an envoy.
Sūn Quán grasped Yù's hand and said:
"Now you are aged,
and I too am growing old.
I fear we may not meet again."
He gifted Yù a hú of large pearls.
Some crossed the seas to seek them afar,
The Book of Hàn states:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
envoys were sent overseas to purchase bright pearls,
and obtained some
less than two inches in diameter.
Others entered the pass and were discarded.
The Biographies of Exemplary Women states:
The magistrate of Zhūyá died in office,
and his wife and children escorted his coffin back.
According to Hàn law:
bringing pearls into the pass was punishable by death.
The wife discarded her arm-bound pearl.
The son from the former wife, aged nine,
admired it and took it,
placing it in his mother's mirror case,
unknown to her.
At the pass,
the officials searched and found the pearl,
interrogating who should be held accountable.
The son from the former wife, Chū, said:
"I should be held accountable."
The stepmother pleaded with the officials:
"Please do not charge the child.
He truly did not know.
I should be held accountable."
Chū again said:
"My lady pities my orphaned state
and wishes to save my life."
Then he wept bitterly.
Those nearby could not help but shed tears,
and the pass official, holding his brush, could not write a single word.
So they discarded the pearl and let them go.
There is also Cāngwú forming mounds,
Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Gleaned Fragments states:
When Shùn was buried in the wilds of Cāngwú,
birds like sparrows,
called Píngxiāo,
came from Dānzhōu.
Reaching the wilds of Cāngwú,
they carried blue sand pearls, piling them into mounds,
called Pearl Mounds.
Nowadays, beyond Cāngwú,
herb gatherers occasionally find blue stones,
pure as pearls.
Consuming them grants immortality;
wearing them makes the body light.
Jīng and Luò scattering ashes,
The Book of Later Wèi states:
When Ěrzhū Shìlóng was about to be defeated,
a ballad circulated in Luòyáng:
"At the end of the third month, beginning of the fourth,
scatter ashes, winnow dust, searching for pearls."
King of Chǔ's inquiry to Xī Xù,
The New Prefaces states:
Qín sent an envoy to observe Chǔ's treasures.
The King of Chǔ summoned Zǐ Xī and asked him:
"My Héshì jade and Suíhóu pearl—
may I show them?"
Zǐ Xī replied:
"I do not know."
He then summoned Zhāo Xī Xù and asked him,
who replied:
"The state's treasures lie in its worthy ministers.
Pearls and jade are mere playthings,
not the most valuable treasures."
Tàishū accepting from Huán Tuí,
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Wèi's Tàishū Jí fled into exile,
serving in Sòng.
Xiàng Tuí gave him a fine pearl,
along with the city of Chéng Chú.
The Duke of Sòng demanded the pearl,
but Tuí refused to give it,
thus incurring offense.
Note:
Chéng Chú
is a city of Sòng.
Xiàng Wǎng seeking in the Chìshuǐ,
Zhuangzi states:
Huángdì traveled north of the Chìshuǐ,
ascending the heights of Kūnlún,
and lost his dark pearl.
He sent Zhì to search for it,
but it was not found.
He sent Lí Zhū to search for it,
Could not find it.
He sent Xiàngwǎng to search for it,
and then it was found.
Shāngqiū Kāi swimming in the bend of the river.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
A disciple of Zǐhuá pointed to the bend in the river and said to Shāngqiū Kāi:
"There is a precious pearl there,
you can swim to get it."
Shāngqiū Kāi swam for it,
and after emerging,
indeed obtained the pearl.
Also heard of the Zīshuǐ pí fish,
The *Shānhǎijīng* says:
On the Niǎoshǔtóngxué Mountain,
the Zīshuǐ River flows from there,
flowing west into the Hànshuǐ River,
there are many pí fish,
which produce pearls and jade.
Annotation:
Also a type of clam.
Pí is pronounced jūzhī fǎn.
The dark blue wings of Yíngzhōu,
The *Shíyíjì* says:
On Yíngzhōu, there is a bird like a phoenix,
with a dark blue body and red wings,
named Cángzhū,
every time it sings and soars,
it spits out many pecks of new pearls.
Immortals use them to adorn their immortal robes,
light and shining under the sun and moon.
Layered city with rows of trees,
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
There is a nine-layered city,
with a pearl tree to its west.
Yǔ filled the great flood to make mountains,
blocked Kūnlún to make earth,
in the middle stood a nine-layered city,
its height is eleven thousand lǐ,
on it grows the Mùhé,
the grain is five zhàng and five chǐ tall,
pearl trees, jade trees, and immortal trees,
Shātáng, Lánggān, and Jiàngshù are all there.
Kāimíng widely planted.
The *Shānhǎijīng* says:
North of Kāimíng Mountain, there is a pearl tree.
Formed from coughing and spitting,
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Now spittle,
the large ones are like pearls,
the small ones are like mist.
Ranking them in order.
The *Guǎngzhì* says:
There is a bright pearl,
called Yèguāng,
with a diameter of over an inch,
from Huángzhī.
There is a perfectly round pearl,
placed on a flat surface,
it will not stop rolling all day.
Now the imperial workshop names them with jiǎ and yǐ as the order.
The snake knew the kindness of the Suí family,
The *Sōushénjì* says:
The Marquis of Suí was traveling,
saw a large snake injured,
saved and treated it.
Later, the snake brought a pearl in its mouth to repay him,
over an inch in diameter,
pure white,
and glowing at night, lighting up the room,
thus through the ages it is called the Suí pearl.
The crane repaid Kuài Shēn's virtue.
The *Sōushénjì* says:
Kuài Shēn cared for his mother with utmost filial piety.
Once, a black crane was shot by a Róng person,
in distress, it came to Shēn.
Shēn took it in, cared for, and treated it,
and after its wounds healed, released it.
Later, the crane came to his door at night,
Shēn took a candle to look at the crane,
a pair, male and female, arrived together,
each holding a bright moon pearl to repay Shēn.
Also, there is adorning clothing for decoration,
The *Wèizhì* says:
The custom of the Eastern Yí is to use pearls as wealth,
some use them to adorn clothing as decoration,
some hang them on the neck and let them hang over the eyes,
not considering gold, silver, brocade, or felt as precious.
Shining at night for illumination.
The *Wèilüè* says:
The Dàqín state produces night-shining pearls.
The *Mòzǐ* says:
The Héshì jade,
the night-shining pearl,
are treasures of the feudal lords.
Once heard of seeking fire by facing the sun,
The *Tángshū* says:
East of Pólì is the Luóchà state,
its people are extremely ugly,
with red hair and black bodies,
beast-like teeth and eagle-like claws,
they trade with the people of Línyì,
coming at night,
covering their faces.
That state produces fire pearls,
shaped like crystal,
at noon,
using the pearl to catch the shadow,
taking mugwort and placing it on it,
fire emerges.
Moreover, because of buying a sword, it could topple a city.
The *Wúyuèchūnqiū* says:
King Yǔncháng of Yuè hired Ōuyězǐ to forge five swords.
A Qín guest, Xuē Zhú, was skilled at appraising swords,
they showed them to him,
Zhú said:
"Even if you measure out pearls and jade to topple a city,
it still cannot compare."
Adorning the head, showing the appearance of a bùyáo,
The *Shìmíng* says:
The queen's head ornament is called fù.
Fù,
means to cover.
On it hang pearls,
which shake when walking.
Lifting the curtain, hearing the sound of jade pendants.
The *Xījīngzájì* says:
In the Zhāoyáng Hall, pearls were woven into curtains,
when the wind blew, they chimed,
like the sound of kē and pèi jades.
Gathering from turbid water without loss,
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Those who recognize treasures,
must pick bright pearls from turbid water;
those who appreciate fragrance,
must gather fragrant orchids from foul marshes.
Holding the spiritual snake and being proud.
The *Wèilüè* says:
Cáo Zhì wrote to Yáng Xiū:
"Authors of this age,
each claims to hold the pearl of the spiritual snake,
every family claims to embrace the jade of Jīngshān."
Birds gathering at Yānzhāo's hall,
The *Shíyíjì* says:
During the time of King Yānzhāo,
there was a white-headed bird,
that gathered at the king's place,
holding a Dòngguāng pearl in its beak,
one chǐ in diameter,
this pearl was black as lacquer,
and when hung indoors,
no deity could hide its essence.
The phoenix gracing Shàohào's court.
The *Shíyíjì* says:
During Shàohào's time,
a phoenix brought a bright pearl to the court,
Shàohào picked up the pearl and kept it,
it illuminated the world.
These are the wondrous secrets of the nine grades,
truly rare in the world and renowned through the ages.
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's *Nányuèzhì* says:
Pearls have nine grades,
larger than five fēn up to one cùn eight or nine fēn,
are especially considered top grade,
having brilliance.
One side slightly flat like an overturned cauldron,
is called a dāng pearl.
Next to dāng pearls are zǒu pearls,
next to zǒu pearls are huá pearls,
next to huá pearls are lěiluǒ pearls,
next to lěiluǒ pearls are guānliǎng pearls,
next to guānliǎng pearls are shuì pearls,
next to shuì pearls are sōngfú pearls.
Lěi is pronounced láiwěi fǎn.
Luǒ is pronounced láikě fǎn.
Sōng is pronounced sōng.
Brocade
Yīzhī wénzhī zhòng jǐn,
"Shuōwén" yuē:
jǐn,
Xiāngyì zhī wén yě.
Bǐng làn xī zhī xiān lì.
"Shī" yuē:
jiǎo zhěn càn xī,
jǐn qīn làn xī.
Bìxié tiānmǎ zhī qí,
"Tángshū" yuē:
Dàizōng chì yuē:
"Suǒ zhī dà zhāng jǐn, ruǎn jǐn, tòu bèi jí jié záo,
liù pò,
yǐ shàng jǐn bìng yí jìn duàn.
Qí cháng xíng Gāolì bái jǐn, zá sè jǐn děng,
rèn yī jiù zhì.
Qí pán lóng, duì fèng, qílín, shīzi, tiānmǎ, bìxié, kǒngquè, xiānhè, zhīcǎo,
yì yí jìn duàn."
Bóshān jiāo lóng zhī zhì.
"Yèzhōng Jì" yuē:
Zhījǐn shǔ yǒu huáng dì bóshān wén jǐn, dà jiāo lóng, xiǎo jiāo lóng, dà zhūyú, xiǎo zhūyú jǐn.
Kūnzhāo yǒu luán zhāng zhī měi,
"Shíyí Jì" yuē:
Zhōu Língwáng qǐ Kūnzhāo zhī tái,
yǐ xiǎng qún chén.
Zhāng luán zhāng jǐn wén rú luán xiáng.
Yuánjiào yǒu shuāng cán zhī yì.
"Shíyí Jì" yuē:
Yuánjiào zhī shān míng Huánqiū,
dōng yǒu yún shí,
guǎng wǔbǎi lǐ,
yǒu cán cháng qī cùn,
hēisè yǒu lín jiǎo,
yǐ shuāngxuě fù zhī,
ránhòu zuò jiǎn,
cháng yī chǐ,
qí sè wǔ cǎi,
zhī wéi wén jǐn,
rù shuǐ bù rú,
qí zhì qīng nuǎn róu huá.
Bǐ Guǎn Zhòng zhī dēng cháo,
"Huáinánzǐ" yuē:
Guǎn Zhòng,
wén jǐn yě,
suī chǒu dēng cháo.
Zǐ Chǎn,
liàn bó yě,
měi ér bù zūn.
Zhù yún:
Guǎn Zhòng suī bùjí shèng,
yóu wén jǐn yě.
Zǐ Chǎn xiān ēn hòu fǎ,
rú liàn bó yě,
suī wēn,
bùkān wéi zōngmiào fú.
Shěn Yǐn Hé zhī xué zhì.
"Zuǒzhuàn" yuē:
Zǐ Pí yù shǐ Yǐn Hé wéi yì.
Zǐ Chǎn yuē:
"Shǎo,
wèi zhī kě fǒu."
Zǐ Pí yuē:
"Wú ài zhī,
shǐ fú wǎng ér xué yān."
Zǐ Chǎn yuē:
"Wúzǐ ài rén yǐ zhèng,
yóu wèi néng cāo dāo ér shǐ gē yě,
qí shāng shí duō.
Zǐ yǒu měi jǐn,
bù shǐ rén xué zhì yān.
Dà guān, dà yì,
shēn zhī suǒ bì yě,
ér shǐ xuézhě zhì yān,
qí wéi měi jǐn,
bù yì duō hū?"
Xuán Yèzhōng zhī dǒu zhàng,
"Yèzhōng Jì" yuē:
Shí Hǔ dōng yuè shī shú jǐn liúsū dǒu zhàng,
sì jiǎo ān chún jīn lóngtóu,
xián wǔ sè liúsū,
huò yòng huáng dì bóshān wén jǐn,
huò yòng zǐ tí xiǎo míngguāng jǐn.
Yì hùjūn zhī piǎo bèi.
"Wúzhì" yuē:
Jiǎng Qīn wéi yòu hùjūn,
Sūn Quán cháng rù qí nèi,
mǔ shū zhàng piǎo bèi.
Quán tàn qí zài guì shǒu yuē,
chì yùfǔ wéi qí mǔ zuò jǐn bèi,
gǎi yì wéi zhàng.
Sìshí lǐ Shí shì zhī shē,
"Shìshuō" yuē:
Shí Chóng jǐn bùzhàng sìshí lǐ.
Sānshí liǎng Qí Huán zhī guī.

Wèi qiān yú Cáo,

Fūrén zì Xiànyīng,

Cóng wàisūn Húmǔ Chàng shàng fūrén jǐn bèi,

Zhū Chǒng wéi tàiwèi,
jiā pín,

Cháotíng cì jǐn bèi, liáng ròu,

Yù àn bào měirén zhī zèng,

Měirén zèng wǒ jǐnxiù duàn,
hé yǐ bào zhī qīng yù àn.
Huíwén shí Dòu Tāo zhī jì.

Dòu Tāo qī Sū shì,
shàn zhǔ wén.
Fú Jiān shí,

Sū shì sī zhī,

jǐn,

jǐn wén zhūyù chéng qì,

Wéncǎi zhī gōng,
fān hóng zǒu lóng,

Hàn Wǔ qǐ Zhāoxiān líng gé yú Gānquán Gōng,
ér biān cuìyǔ lín háo wéi lián,
yǒu zǒu lóng jǐn,
yǒu fān hóng jǐn.
Shàngfāng jì wén yú Yèxià,

Zhījǐn shǔ zài zhōng shàngfāng.
Dòuchǎng yì liè yú Jiāngdōng.
"Dānyáng Jì" yuē:
Dòuchǎng jǐn shǔ,
píng Guānyòu,
qiān qí bǎi gōng suǒ zhì yě.
Xī zhī jiāng jiàn yú hú bái,
"Lǐ" yuē:
jūn yī hú bái qiú,
jǐn yī yǐ xī zhī.
Jìn zhī kǒng shāng hū nǚgōng.
"Hànshū" yuē:
Jǐngdì èr nián,

"Diāo wén kè lòu shāng nóngshì,
jǐnxiù qí zǔ hài nǚgōng,
yí jìn zhī."
Ruò nǎi chuí jūshì zhī dài,
"Lǐ" yuē:
jūshì jǐn dài.
Zhù:
jūshì,
dào yì chǔshì yě.
Bèi hǔbēn zhī fú,

hǔbēn lángjiàng yī shā hú dān yī,
hǔ wén jǐn kù.
Pútáo xī fènghuáng,
"Yèzhōng Jì" yuē:
jǐn shǔ yǒu pútáo wén jǐn, bān wén jǐn, fènghuáng jǐn, zhūquè jǐn, tāo wén jǐn, táohé wén jǐn.
Míngguāng xī wēn shú,
"Yèzhōng Jì" yuē:
zhījǐn shǔ yǒu dà dēnggāo, xiǎo dēnggāo, dà míngguāng, xiǎo míngguāng jǐn.
Zhāng Wēn biǎo yuē:
Liú Chàn sòng chén wēn shú jǐn wǔ duān.
Huì Xún Yǎn ér jiā bì,
"Zuǒzhuàn" yuē:
Jìn Hóu xiān guī.
Gōng xiǎng Jìn liù qīng yú Púpǔ,
huì Xún Yǎn shù jǐn jiā bì.
Kuì Zuǒshī ér xiān yù.
"Zuǒzhuàn" yuē:
Zuǒshī jiàn fūrén zhī bù mǎ zhě,
wèn zhī,
duì yuē:
"Jūn fūrén shì yě."
Zuǒshī yuē:
"Shéi wéi jūn fūrén,
yú hú fú zhī?"
Yǔrén guī yǐ gào fūrén,
shǐ kuì zhī jǐn yǔ mǎ,
First, there is jade.
There are also coiled dragons arranged in images,
see the annotation below under "tying colorful threads between fingers."
Tower battlements take shape.
The Records of Omissions states:
During the reign of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the country of Yīnzhī presented female artisans,
who could place five-colored silk threads in their mouths,
pull them out with their hands and knot them,
creating patterned brocade.
There was Yúnkūn brocade,
with patterns like clouds and rosy clouds.
There was tower battlement brocade,
and miscellaneous pearl brocade,
with patterns resembling strung pearls.
There was seal script and clerical script brocade,
and Lièmíng brocade,
with patterns like lamps and candles.
Zhēn Chēn delighted in wearing brocade garments in daylight,
The Book of Later Wèi states:
Zhēn Chēn served as the governor of Dìngzhōu,
and upon returning to his hometown,
he wore brocade garments and roamed in daylight.
Xiàng Yǔ also disliked traveling at night.
The Book of Hàn states:
Xiàng Yǔ was in Guānzhōng,
longing to return east,
and said:
"To attain wealth and honor without returning to one's hometown,
is like wearing brocade garments at night."
Brocade was once used to pull carts for Liú Bèi,
The Chronicles of Jiāngbiǎo states:
Lù Xùn attacked Liú Bèi at Yílíng,
Bèi abandoned his ships and fled on foot,
burning leather armor to block the roads,
and had his soldiers use brocade to pull carts,
fleeing into Báidì.
Brocade was also used to moor boats, as told of Gān Níng.
The Records of Wú states:
Where Gān Níng resided,
he often used silk brocade to moor his boats,
and when leaving, he would cut and discard it,
to display his extravagance.
In a dream, he once heard of cutting and discarding,
The Book of Qí states:
When Jiāng Yān was dismissed from his post as governor of Xuānchéng and returned,
he first moored at the shore of Chánlíng Temple,
and at night dreamed of a man who called himself Zhāng Jǐngyáng,
who said to him:
"I previously entrusted a bolt of brocade to you,
now please return it."
Jiāng Yān searched his bosom,
found a few feet and gave it to him,
whereupon this man angrily said:
"How could you have cut it all up?"
He then saw Qiū Chí,
and said to him:
"Since these remaining few feet are useless,
I give them to you."
From then on, Jiāng Yān's literary talent declined.
Washing fish made it appear even more vibrant.
The Discourses of the Recluse states:
To polish jade, one uses stone;
to refine metal, one uses salt;
to wash brocade, one uses fish;
to launder cloth, one uses ash;
thus, there are cases where the ugly improves the beautiful,
and the lowly refines the noble.
As for retrieving a map from the bosom,
The Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
The Emperor saw a small yellow scroll in the handkerchief container of the Queen Mother of the West,
stored in a purple brocade pouch.
The Emperor asked:
"What book is this?"
The Queen Mother said:
"It is the True Form Chart of the Five Sacred Mountains.
Its text is secret and forbidden."
She then ordered her attendant, Sòng Língbīn, to fetch another chart to give to the Emperor.
Língbīn searched her bosom,
retrieved a scroll,
stored in a cloud-patterned brocade pouch.
The Queen Mother gave it to the Emperor.
Tying colorful threads between fingers,
The Records of Omissions states:
The younger sister of Wú's Zhào Dá excelled in calligraphy and painting,
her skill was unparalleled,
she could use colored silk threads between her fingers to create brocade with patterns of clouds, dragons, coiled dragons, and phoenixes,
large ones measuring over a foot,
small ones only an inch square.
The offering of a hundred bolts by King of Zhōu,
The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu states:
On the auspicious day of Jiǎzǐ,
the Son of Heaven held a white jade scepter and a black jade disc to meet the Queen Mother of the West,
and presented a hundred bolts of brocade.
The Queen Mother of the West bowed twice and accepted it.
The gift of a thousand bolts by Lord Liú,
The Records of Shǔ states:
When the Late Sovereign entered Yìzhōu,
he bestowed upon Zhūgě Liàng, Fǎ Zhèng, Zhāng Fēi, and Guān Yǔ a thousand bolts of brocade each.
There is also the case of a youth tying his hair,
The Rites states:
For the attire of a youth,
a black cloth garment,
trimmed with brocade,
a brocade sash with a brocade clasp,
brocade hair ties,
all in vermilion brocade.
The tall lady in a plain overcoat,
The Book of Songs states:
The tall lady is graceful,
wearing a brocade garment under a plain overcoat.
The Rites states:
When wearing brocade, one should cover it with plain silk,
to avoid the ostentation of its patterns.
Brocade sails on dragon ships,
The Records of the Great Enterprise states:
Emperor Yáng traveled to Jiāngdū,
the dragon boat he rode,
had brocade sails and brocade cables.
Brocade curtains in the powder chamber.
The Ceremonial of the Hàn Officials states:
When a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat was on duty,
the palace supplied a brocade curtain.
Jí Rú compared it to wrapping dust,
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity states:
Jí Rú and Dǒng Dèng,
are like brocade and silk wrapping dust.
Yuánfāng was ridiculed for covering with a brocade quilt.
The Forest of Sayings states:
Chén Yuánfāng lost his father,
and became emaciated,
his mother pitied him,
and covered him with a brocade quilt.
Guō Línzōng came to offer condolences,
saw this and reprimanded him,
and guests ceased visiting for over a hundred days.
White ground covering the flagpole,
The Erya states:
Plain brocade covers the flagpole.
Green ground covering the mudguard.
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
when the Heavenly Horse of Èrshī was obtained,
rose quartz was used for the saddle and bridle,
with a green ground,
and five-colored brocade for the mudguard.
Some retrieved it from the Fàn family's treasury,
The Liezi states:
The Fàn family had a fire in their treasury,
Zǐhuá said:
"Whoever can enter the fire to retrieve brocade,
regardless of the amount,
I will give it to them."
Shāngqiū Kāi entered the fire and returned unharmed, his body unburned.
Some washed it on the banks of the Shǔ River.
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Shǔ Capital" states:
The patterned brocade is resplendent,
washed in the colors of the river waves.
Huáinán's reception of the Eight Lords,
The Biographies of Immortals states:
The King of Huáinán prepared brocade and silk curtains for the Eight Lords,
and burned incense of a hundred harmonies.
King Mù of Zhōu's mourning for Shèng Jī.
The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu states:
At the funeral of Shèng Jī,
patterned brocade was used as burial gifts.
The virtuous transformation of Yán Xiàn,
The Chronicles of Huáyáng states:
Yán Xiàn served as the magistrate of Miánzhú,
and transformed people through ritual and deference.
A county resident, Dù Chéng, was walking at night,
found a lost bag of valuables,
containing twenty bolts of brocade,
sought its owner and returned it,
saying:
"The county has a wise ruler,
how dare I betray him!"
The resources for Military Marquis's decisive battles.
The Collected Works of Zhūgě Liàng states:
Now the people are poor and the state depleted,
the only resource for decisive victory is brocade.
The beauty of crimson ground with interwoven dragons,
The Records of Wèi states:
During the Jīngchū era,
the Queen of Wō was bestowed five bolts of crimson ground interwoven dragon brocade,
and three bolts of dark blue ground patterned brocade.
The wonder of tiger head and connected jade discs.
Emperor Wén of Wèi's edict states:
Each time Shǔ brocade was obtained before, it was particularly poor,
even the Xiānbēi would not accept it.
The Wú-woven Rúyì tiger head connected jade disc brocade,
when it arrived in Luòyì,
was also of inferior quality,
being a product of inferior lands,
all had false reputations.
Some took it for the splendor of the heavy Huī and Suī rivers,
The Traditions of Chénliú states:
South of Xiāngyì County is the Huī River,
north is the Suī River,
tradition says:
Between the Suī and Huàn rivers, there are those skilled in literary composition,
hence there are embroidered robes with ornate patterns,
adorned with suns, moons, flowers, and insects,
to serve the Son of Heaven in ancestral temple ceremonies and imperial attire.
Some use this to illustrate the art of elaborate and intricate rhetoric.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Intricate and elegant,
they form this shell-patterned brocade.
Those slanderers,
have also gone too far."
Forgetting the care and nurturing of one's parents,
one grieves for Zǎi Yǔ, who was ridiculed.
The *Analects* says:
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"The three-year mourning period,
is also too long."
The Master said:
"Eating fine rice,
wearing brocade robes,
would you feel at ease?"
He replied:
"At ease."
"If you feel at ease,
then do it."
Silk
Bright and pure white silk threads,
Guō Tàijī's "Poem in Reply to Fù Xián" says:
Bright and pure white silk threads,
Woven into garments for a poor woman.
It is what the woman works on.
The Book of Songs says:
Green are the threads,
It is what the woman works on.
The Zhou official had the duty of distinguishing materials,
The Rites of Zhou says:
The Director of Silk manages the silk brought in and distinguishes its quality,
using price tags to mark it,
oversees its storage and distribution,
awaiting the time for its use in work,
distributes silk to the inner and outer courts,
all according to the material given.
The seasonal ordinance specifies the time for dividing cocoons.
The Book of Rites says:
In the first month of summer, after the silkworm work is completed,
divide the cocoons and weigh the silk.
Only to be dyed with vermilion and indigo,
The Han Records say:
The youth Wèi Zhào sought to serve Guō Tài,
offering to sweep and clean.
Guō Tài said:
"You should focus on studying the classics and lecturing on books,
why come to be near me?"
Zhào said:
"A teacher of classics is easy to find,
a teacher of character is hard to come by,
I wish to bring my plain silk nature close to vermilion and indigo."
Do not discard coarse grasses lightly.
The Zuo Zhuan says:
Even if there are silk and hemp,
do not discard coarse grasses.
The Máng official had a method for boiling silk,
The Rites of Zhou says:
The Máng official boils silk,
soaking the silk in alkaline water,
for seven days,
then hanging it a foot above the ground,
exposing it to the sun,
exposing it to the sun during the day,
soaking it in a well at night,
for seven days and seven nights,
this is called water boiling.
Fāng Chǔ cut it appropriately.
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Han says:
Fāng Chǔ served as a Gentleman of the Interior,
Emperor Zhāng ordered civil officials to stand on the left,
military officials on the right,
Chǔ stood squarely in the middle,
saying:
"I am proficient in both civil and military affairs,
ready to be employed wherever needed."
The emperor praised his talent,
and gave him a tangled mess of silk threads to sort out.
Chǔ drew his sword and cut it three times,
then replied:
"To reverse the order and rely on the situation,
is appropriate when facing matters."
The lamb's fleece,
with five tufts of white silk.
From the Book of Songs,
also five tufts, five bundles.
Issuing orders is like silk expanding into cords,
The Book of Rites says:
The king's words are like silk threads,
their issuance is like cords.
The king's words are like cords,
their issuance is like thick ropes.
The eclipse is further heard of as silk entangling the sun.
See the "Rì Fù" note on "tying the clapper and entangling silk."
Distinguishing nobility and baseness in silk and brocade,
The Shì Wěi says:
Silk all comes from silkworms,
as plain silk it is humble,
as brocade it is noble.
Following the blue and yellow from indigo and amur cork tree,
The Zhèng Bù says:
Bright and pure white silk,
with indigo becomes blue,
with cinnabar becomes red,
with amur cork tree becomes yellow,
with mud becomes black.
Reeling it is seen in the three basins,
The Book of Rites says:
The lady reels silk with three basins of water.
Soaking it is also spoken of as seven days.
See the note above.
Then there is the book mentioning its baskets,
The Book of Documents says:
Qīngzhōu's baskets contain yǎn silk.
The poem records its brightness.
The Book of Songs says:
Silk garments so bright,
wearing caps respectfully.
The note says:
Silk garments,
are sacrificial robes,
qiú sounds like "seek."
Sometimes tangling it makes it more disordered,
The Zuo Zhuan says:
Zhòng Zhòng said:
"Harmonize the people with virtue,
never heard of using disorder.
Using disorder is like trying to sort silk by tangling it."
Sometimes trading it leads to schemes.
The Book of Songs says:
A simple fellow,
carrying cloth to trade for silk.
Not really to trade silk,
but to come and scheme with me.
Inauspicious then ashes float on water,
The Book of Jin says:
Lǚ Guāng usurped the throne west of the Yellow River,
the Palace Library Director Zhāng Zī fell ill,
Guāng extensively sought treatment.
There was a foreign monk Luó Chā,
who claimed he could cure Zī's illness.
Guāng was pleased,
and rewarded him heavily.
Luó Shí said:
"Chā cannot help,
it's just wasteful trouble.
Take five-colored silk to make a rope,
burn it to ashes,
throw it into water,
if the ashes float up and reform into a rope,
the illness cannot be cured."
Shortly after,
the ashes gathered and floated up,
reforming into a rope.
A few days later Zī died.
Auspicious then dreaming of hanging on a mountain top.
The Book of Later Wei says:
The Governor of Yōuzhōu, Zhāng Liàng,
earlier,
there was Xuē Shū,
who dreamed of Liàng hanging silk on a mountain,
woke and told Liàng,
and interpreted it saying:
"Silk on a mountain,
is the character yōu,
will you become Governor of Yōuzhōu?"
Before a year had passed he received the appointment.
Also there is the strength to tie a golden furnace,
The Records of the Four Lords of Liáng says:
The country of Fúsāng offered three hundred catties of yellow silk,
which is silk spun by Fúsāng silkworms,
silk boiled in Fúsāng ash water.
The emperor had a golden furnace,
weighing fifty catties.
Tied with six silk threads to suspend the furnace,
the silk had strength to spare.
Fine as dense rain,
an ancient poem says:
Dense rain like scattered silk.
Straight as a vermilion rope,
an ancient poem says:
Straight as a vermilion silk rope,
pure as jade pot ice.
Also heard of life threads.
The Customs and Manners says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month, five-colored threads are life threads,
commonly said to benefit one's life.
Sometimes spitting it out forms brocade,
see the "Jǐn Fù" note on "towers and battlements taking shape."
Sometimes vomiting it while kneeling by a tree.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
In the land of vomiting silk,
there is a woman kneeling by a tree vomiting silk.
Guō Pú said:
It is like a silkworm.
Shān Tāo accepted Yuán Yì's gift,
The Biographies of the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove says:
The Magistrate of Gé, Yuán Yì, bribed the court,
to build a false reputation,
he gave Shān Tāo a hundred catties of silk,
Tāo, not wanting to be different,
accepted it,
and ordered it stored on a beam in the inner chamber.
Later Yì's deeds were exposed,
officials came to Tāo's place to investigate,
Tāo took the silk down from the beam,
the silk had been there for years,
dusty, yellow, and black,
the seal intact as before,
and handed it to the officials.
Chángqiàn's admonition to Sūn Hóng.
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital says:
Gōngsūn Hóng was recommended as virtuous and capable,
a fellow countryman Zōu Chángqiàn gave him a stalk of white silk as a gift,
and wrote a letter to present to him,
saying:
"Five threads make a niè,
double a niè makes a shēng,
double a shēng makes a yù,
double a yù makes a jì,
double a jì makes a zōng,
Doubling the threads forms an ear of grain,
this is from few to many,
from subtle to prominent.
For a scholar to establish merit and reputation,
it is also like this;
do not consider small acts of goodness insufficient to cultivate,
and therefore not perform them."
You are responsible for these tributes from Chǔ,
Guǎnzǐ says:
Duke Huán of Qí attacked Chǔ,
crossed the Rǔ River,
passed over the Fāngchéng Mountains,
and had silk sent as tribute to the Zhōu court.
Severing that shāng string,
Huáinánzǐ says:
Silkworms feed on silk and the shāng string breaks.
The annotation states:
Shāng is the sound of metal,
spring silkworms produce silk,
metal perishes, hence it breaks.
Mòzǐ saw this and sighed with emotion,
Mòzǐ says:
Seeing someone dyeing silk, he sighed and said:
"Dyed with blue, it becomes blue;
dyed with yellow, it becomes yellow;
after five immersions, it becomes five colors;
one cannot but be cautious.
It is not only dyeing silk;
governing a state is also like this."
Yuánkè reeled it and ascended as an immortal.
Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Yuánkè was
a man from Jìyīn,
handsome in appearance,
many in the town wished to marry their daughters to him,
but he never married.
He once planted five-colored fragrant herbs,
for several decades,
consuming their fruits.
Suddenly, five-colored moths gathered on the fragrant herbs;
Yuánkè collected them and laid them on cloth,
where they produced splendid silkworms.
When it was time for silkworms,
a woman came of her own accord to help Yuánkè raise the silkworms,
also feeding them fragrant herbs,
obtaining one hundred and twenty cocoons,
each cocoon as large as a jar,
each cocoon taking six or seven days to reel all the silk,
after reeling was finished,
this woman and Yuánkè both became immortals and departed.
Suddenly thinking of the virtuous person's sash,
The Shī says:
The virtuous person, the noble man,
his sash is made of silk.
Remotely recalling the year of first taking office.
Xiè Língyùn's "Poem on First Leaving the Commandery" says:
"Tying the silk" was in Yuánxīng,
"removing the tortoise" was in Jǐngpíng.
Lǐ Shàn says:
"Tying the silk"
means first taking office.
Yìng Qú's poem says:
Not mistaken in tying the vermilion silk,
the three offices came seeking.
Fishing has the beauty of the yī mín,
The Shī says:
What is used for fishing?
It is silk, it is the mín.
The qín is known for the beauty of wild cocoons.
Méi Chéng's "Seven Stimuli" says:
The tóng tree of Lóngmén,
a hundred feet tall without branches,
cut to make a qín.
The silk of wild cocoons is used for strings.
The task of silk and hemp,
is also foremost for the livelihood of the people.
The Shū says:
From the valleys of Dài, silk and hemp.
Note:
Quǎn,
means valley.
Qián
In the south there is an insect,
whose form resembles a cicada but larger,
named qīngfú.
Its eggs attach to grass leaves,
like silkworm eggs.
If one obtains the eggs and returns with them,
the mother will fly over to them.
Kill the mother and smear its blood on coins,
and smear the eggs on goods;
when using the coins for market transactions,
they will swiftly return on their own,
hence the technique described in the Huáinánzǐ employs this.
Examining the system of ròu and hào,
the Hànshū states:
The large coin of King Jǐng of Zhōu,
inscribed with the characters "Bǎohuò,"
had both ròu and hào with raised rims.
A note explains:
Ròu refers to
the body of the coin.
Hào refers to
the hole.
Distinguishing the differences among yāo, yòu, and others.
The Hànshū states:
Wáng Mǎng reformed the categories of coins and cloth currency,
the small coin had a diameter of six fēn,
weighed one zhū,
and was inscribed "Xiǎoqián zhí yī."
The next, seven fēn,
three zhū,
was called "Yāoqián shíyī."
The next, eight fēn,
five zhū,
was called "Yòuqián èrshí."
The next, nine fēn,
seven zhū,
was called "Zhōngqián sānshí."
The next, one cùn,
nine zhū,
was called "Zhuàngqián sìshí."
Together with the earlier "Dàqián wǔshí,"
these constituted the six grades of coin currency.
Zhào Qín was offered coins but did not bow.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Zhào Qín, styled Yìqīng,
was the nephew of Liú Cì's elder sister,
and from childhood had lofty aspirations and integrity.
When the tax revenue from Cì's fiefdom happened to arrive,
Qín was present at the time.
Cì pointed to the money and said to Qín:
"Bow,
and I will give you three hundred thousand."
Qín said:
"To obtain money by bowing
is not something to be taken righteously."
He ultimately refused to bow.
Láo Xiānwēng was summoned.
The Gé Xiānwēng Biézhuàn states:
The master took ten coins,
and had someone throw them one by one into a well.
The master, standing above the well, called the coins with a vessel,
and the coins flew out of the well one by one,
entering the master's vessel.
As for accumulating in the Shuǐhéng,
and storing in the Shàofǔ,
the Hànshū states:
During Emperor Yuán's time,
the capital held three billion coins,
the Shuǐhéng treasury held two billion five hundred million,
and the Shàofǔ treasury held one billion eight hundred million.
The emperor was gentle, respectful, and had few desires,
and his rewards and gifts were frugal,
hence the Shàofǔ and Shuǐhéng treasuries had abundant coins.
Treasuring this square enclosure,
the Hànshū states:
Coins are round and enclose a square,
their weight measured in zhū.
A note:
Hán is the same as hán (to contain),
fāng refers to
the hole.
Despising this "ādǔ" thing.
The Jìnshū states:
Wáng Yǎn's wife, Guō shì, was greedy and vulgar.
Yǎn never spoke of money.
His wife waited until he was asleep,
and ordered maids to surround him with coins.
When he awoke,
he said:
"Remove these ādǔ things."
Páng Qiàn dug a well.
The Fēngsútōng states:
Páng Qiàn of Wèijùn lost his father due to turmoil.
At the time, Qiàn was three or four years old.
His mother carried him in swaddling clothes and moved to a guest house.
Digging a well, they obtained over ten million coins,
and thus became immensely wealthy.
While music was played in the hall,
an old servant in the kitchen whispered:
"The old mother in the hall
is my wife."
A maid informed the mother.
She summoned and questioned him about the facts,
and they reunited as husband and wife.
People of the time said of them:
"Páng Gōng of the village,
dug a well and obtained copper,
bought a servant and gained an old man."
Bǐng Yuán tied coins to a tree.
The Bǐng Yuán Biézhuàn states:
Yuán was traveling through Liáodōng,
found some lost coins,
picked them up and tied them to a tree branch.
These coins were not retrieved,
and many others began tying coins there.
Yuán asked the reason,
and they replied:
"We call it a divine tree."
Yuán disliked that this superstitious worship arose because of him,
so he explained the matter in the village,
collected the coins,
and used them for community sacrifices.
Jiābīn distributed them until all was exhausted.
The Shìshuō states:
Xī Yīn was fond of amassing wealth,
and had tens of millions in coins.
He loved his son, Chāo,
and once allowed him to open the treasury and take as he pleased.
Yīn initially thought he would only take a few million.
But Chāo, in a single day, distributed and exhausted it all.
Kǒng Yòu encountered coins but paid no heed.
The Sòngshū states:
Kǒng Yòu of Shānyīn
possessed supreme virtue that communicated with the divine.
He lived in seclusion on Sìmíng Mountain.
Once he saw several hundred hú of coins in a valley,
but regarded them as no different from tiles or stones.
Méng Yán Chǎng returned what was entrusted.
The Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn states:
Yán Chǎng, styled Zǐzhāng,
served as a Wǔguān Yuàn in the commandery.
The Grand Administrator, Dìwǔ Cháng, was summoned to the capital,
and entrusted Chǎng with 1.3 million coins of his salary.
Chǎng buried them in the hall.
Later, Cháng's entire household fell ill and died,
leaving only an orphaned grandson, nine years old.
Before dying, Cháng told his grandson:
"I have three hundred thousand coins entrusted to Yuàn Yán Chǎng."
When the grandson grew up,
he came to seek Chǎng.
Chǎng, upon seeing him, felt both sorrow and joy,
and retrieved the coins to return to him.
The grandson said:
"My grandfather only mentioned three hundred thousand,
but now it is one million three hundred thousand;
I truly dare not take it."
Chǎng said:
"The Grand Administrator was ill and spoke erroneously;
young master, have no doubts."
He had Dìwǔ Lún supervise coin casting.
The Hòuhànshū states:
In Cháng'ān, coin casting was often fraudulent and cunning.
The Prefect appointed Dìwǔ Lún as Supervisor of Coin Casting,
overseeing the Cháng'ān market,
and the market became free from unfairness.
Opening this Lùtái treasury.
The Zhōushū states:
King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
opened the Lùtái treasury of coins,
and distributed the grain from the Jùqiáo granary.
Melting down its bells and stands.
The Hòuhànshū states:
Dǒng Zhuó destroyed the five-zhū coins,
and recast smaller coins,
taking all the bronze figures, bell stands, fēilián sculptures, bronze horses, and the like from Luòyáng and Cháng'ān to use for casting.
Consequently, currency was devalued and goods became expensive,
with grain costing tens of thousands per shí.
Moreover, the coins lacked rims and inscriptions,
making them inconvenient for use.
Some hung them on a staff head and roamed wine shops.
The Jìnshū states:
Ruǎn Fú often hung a hundred coins on his staff head,
went to market shops,
and returned after drinking to his heart's content.
Some stored them in a jar to pave the way to the netherworld.
The Qíshū states:
Zhào Sēngyán dwelled in mountain valleys,
often carrying a jar with him.
One day he told his disciples:
"I shall die tonight.
A thousand large coins in the jar
to pave the way to the Nine Springs;
one stick of candle
to illuminate my seven-foot corpse."
He passed away that night.
Additionally, there is amassing until the strings rot.
The Shǐjì states:
By Emperor Wǔ's time, over seventy years since Hàn's founding,
the state was without major incidents,
and the coins in the capital accumulated to hundreds of millions,
The strings of cash rotted and could no longer be counted.
Scattered like flowing springs,
The Book of Hàn says:
"Goods are more precious than gold,
profit is sharper than a knife,
flows like a spring,
and spreads like a door."
The annotation states:
"Circulates like a spring,
spreading among the people."
Mining mountains without exhaustion,
Bào Zhào's "Rhapsody on the Ruined City" says:
"Goods multiplied in the salt fields,
profits were mined from copper mountains."
Digging the earth to seek it.
The Book of Wèi says:
"Liú Lèi served as the Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng,
and had people dig the earth to seek coins,
so that holes were found everywhere in the markets and neighborhoods."
Fǔguó casting a bell to show an omen,
The Book of Táng says:
During the Qiányuán era,
Lǐ Fǔguó petitioned to cast a bronze bell in the Inner Flying Dragon Stables,
throwing two newly minted Qiányuán coins into the furnace and praying:
"If His Majesty enjoys myriad blessings,
the state's fortune is boundless,
evil is eradicated,
and the four directions are peaceful,
then I hope [the coins] will not melt or burn,
one yin and one yang,
both appearing on the outside."
When the bell was completed,
it was exactly as prayed.
Zǐlián feeding his horse and throwing coins.
The Comprehensive Meaning of Customs says:
"Huáng Zǐlián of Yǐngchuān,
every time he watered his horse,
would throw coins into the water."
Some saw dust accumulating on coins,
The Collection of Yīn Zhòngkān - The Crown Prince's Edict says:
"The court has built a palace for me,
and winter has already arrived.
The workers suffer from the cold and hardship,
so let the Supervisor of Palace Quarters and Attendants reward them twice a month with wine and meat.
I receive a monthly salary,
and dust accumulates on my coins,
as I have no use for them.
They can be used for this purpose."
Some heard of commanding ghosts.
Dù Shù's "Discourse on Substance" says:
"That which can command ghosts
is money.
That which can command spirits
is sincerity."
If little, they are seated in the lower hall,
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Lǚ Gōng of Shànfǔ,
was on good terms with the Magistrate of Pèi,
and sought refuge with him to avoid enemies.
The local elites and officials of Pèi all went to congratulate him.
Xiāo Hé was in charge of receiving gifts,
and ordered the various gentlemen:
'Those who offer less than a thousand coins
shall sit in the lower hall.'"
The annotation states:
"Jìn is the same as jìn (gift)."
If much, they are stored in the capital treasury.
The Book of Hàn says:
"Zhāng Ānshì, because both father and son were enfeoffed as marquises,
held positions of great power,
so he declined to avoid receiving a salary.
An edict ordered the capital treasury to separately store unnamed money of the Zhāng family,
amounting to millions."
The seawall was built thanks to Huá Xìn,
Liú Dàozhēn's Record of Qiántáng says:
"The Discussion Officer Huá Xìn's family was wealthy.
He proposed building a seawall.
When recruitment began,
anyone who delivered one hú of earth or stones
would be given one dǒu of coins.
Within ten days,
people came like clouds.
Before the seawall was completed,
he falsely announced that no more earth would be accepted,
so those who had transported earth all abandoned it and left.
When the seawall was completed,
it blocked lake fish [from escaping],
and the entire region benefited.
The county was originally named Quántíng,
and was then renamed Qiántáng.
The people cherished his virtue,
and erected a stele at the seawall."
The embankment was heard of from Wáng Jì.
A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
"Wáng Wǔzǐ's private residence was near Běimáng.
At that time, population was dense and land was expensive.
Jì enjoyed horse archery,
so he bought land to build an embankment,
and lined coins all over the ground along the embankment.
People of the time called it the 'Golden Embankment.'"
The divination about Emperor Wén of Wèi's family affairs,
The Book of Wèi says:
"Emperor Wén dreamed of grinding coin inscriptions,
wanting to erase them but make them brighter.
Zhōu Xuān divined and said:
'This is Your Majesty's family affair.'"
At that time, the emperor wanted to punish his brother Zhí,
but was pressured by the Empress Dowager,
so he only demoted and reduced his rank.
The gift to the station master of Huáiyīn.
The Book of Hàn says:
"When Hán Xìn was a commoner,
he often relied on the station master of Xiàxiāng Nánchāng for meals.
After several months,
the station master's wife grew annoyed,
so she cooked early and ate in bed.
When Xìn arrived,
she did not prepare food for him.
Xìn was angry,
and left for good.
When Xìn became King of Chǔ,
he summoned the station master,
gave him a hundred coins,
and said:
'You are a petty man,
who does not carry virtue to the end.'"
Some said it rivaled Dài Shuò's son,
The Book of Sòng says:
"Dài Shuò's son Yánshòu was skilled in calligraphy,
and Yánxìng was fond of learning.
In Shānyīn, there was a man named Chén Zǎi,
whose family was wealthy,
possessing thirty million coins.
The locals said:
'Dài Shuò's sons rival Chén Zǎi's thirty million coins.'"
Some said it bought Wáng Dǎo's son.
The Book of Jìn says:
"Wáng Dǎo's son Yuè served as a Palace Gentleman.
Dǎo dreamed that someone offered a million coins to buy Yuè,
and felt very troubled by it.
Later, he dug the ground and found coins,
all of which he stored away and sealed,
and indeed Yuè died."
As for the image of the King of Ānxī's face,
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"The state of Ānxī used silver for coins,
and the coin bore the king's face.
When the king died,
they changed it to the face of the succeeding king."
The shape of a mounted horse from Jìbīn,
The Book of Hàn says:
"The state of Jìbīn used silver for coins,
with the obverse showing a mounted horse,
and the reverse showing a human face."
Mocking Cuī Liè's stench of copper,
The Book of Later Hàn says:
"During Emperor Huán's reign,
the Hóngdū Gate was opened to sell official positions.
Cuī Liè used five million coins to buy an office,
and obtained one of the Three Excellencies.
He asked his son:
'Now that I am one of the Three Excellencies,
what do outsiders say?'
His son replied:
'People dislike Your Excellency's stench of copper.'"
Laughing at Jiāng Lù's bells ringing.
The Book of Liáng says:
