"When Jiāng Lù served as the Administrator of Wǔníng Commandery,
he had considerable assets.
He hoarded coins against a wall,
causing the wall to collapse under the pressure,
and all the bronze objects rang.
People joked:
'This is what is called: When the copper mountain collapses in the west,
the bell in Luòyáng responds in the east.'"
Sending off Xiè Huì and expressing shame,
The Book of Liáng says:
"When Xiè Huì served as the Interior Historian of Dōngyáng,
and upon his return,
the Five Officials sent him ten thousand coins,
but he only kept one hundred.
He replied in a letter:
'The amount sent is large, but what I keep is small;
this makes me even more ashamed.'"
Bidding farewell to Liú Chǒng and surpassing purity.
The Continued Book of Hàn says:
"Liú Chǒng, styled Zǔróng,
was summoned from the post of Grand Administrator of Kuàijī to be the Minister of Works.
The people of Shānyīn lived dozens of lǐ from the administrative seat.
There was the Ruòyē River flowing through the mountains and valleys.
Five or six elders, aged seventy or eighty,
heard that Chǒng was leaving,
and together came to see him off.
Each brought a hundred coins.
Chǒng thanked them,
and selected to accept one large coin from them.
Therefore, during Chǒng's tenure in Kuàijī,
he was called 'Take-One-Coin.'
Such was his purity."
Some heard of Chéng Gōng's treatise,
The Book of Later Wei states:
Yuán Dàn was transferred to be Governor of Qí Province.
While in the province, he was corrupt and tyrannical,
becoming a great affliction to the people.
A Buddhist monk who had been gathering herbs for Dàn
returned to see him.
Dàn asked for news from outside.
The monk replied:
"I only hear that the Prince is greedy;
I wish the Prince would be replaced soon."
Dàn said:
"Qí Province has seventy thousand households.
Since my arrival,
I haven't even obtained three pecks of cash from a single household.
How can you speak of greed?"
A bag of coins makes Zhào Yī lament his poverty.
Zhào Yī's "Rhapsody on Hating Evil" says:
Though one's belly is filled with literary works,
it is not worth a bag of coins.
Shǐxīng teasing Yuán Shū.
The Book of Song states:
Shǐxīng Prince Liú Jùn once sent thirty thousand cash as a gift to Yuán Shū.
The next day, he sent someone to retrieve it,
claiming the messenger had made a mistake,
intending to tease Shū.
Shū sent a letter saying:
"I have heard from former records that
within seven years,
giving once and taking back once
is still criticized by righteous men.
How much more so when it happens so closely within a short span?
How rapid is this increase and decrease!
I fear privately,
how will the various lords view this?"
Jìyǎ congratulating Lǚ Sēngzhēn.
The Book of Liang states:
Sòng Jìyǎ was dismissed from his post as Governor of Nánkāng Commandery.
He bought a house next to Lǚ Sēngzhēn's residence.
Sēngzhēn asked the price of the house.
Jìyǎ said:
"Eleven million."
Sēngzhēn thought it was expensive and was puzzled.
Jìyǎ said:
"One million for the house,
ten million for the neighbor."
When Sēngzhēn had a son,
Jìyǎ went to congratulate him.
He inscribed the envelope: "One thousand cash."
The gatekeeper thought it too little
and refused to announce him.
Only after insisting did he gain entry.
Sēngzhēn suspected something was amiss,
so he opened it himself,
and found it was gold coins.
Profit is sharp as a knife—
see the note above on "scattered like flowing springs."
Its aura can be like clouds.
The Dìjìng Tú states:
The aura of coin copper
appears like blue clouds when viewed from afar.
Thread-strung are the goose-eye coins—
see the note above on "so fine they float on water."
Elm-pod coins and whale-pattern coins.
The Book of Han states:
At the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
considering Qín currency too heavy and difficult to use,
they ordered the people to cast pod coins instead.
The annotation says:
They were like elm pods.
"Whale pattern" see the note above on "blue damask patterned jacket."
Worth a thousand and worth a hundred—
The Book of Later Zhōu states:
In the first year of Dàxiàng,
they cast the Yǒngtōng Wànguó coin,
worth one thousand each,
circulating alongside the Wǔzhū and Dàbù coins.
The Records of Shǔ states:
When the First Sovereign first captured Chéngdū,
military supplies were insufficient.
Liú Bā said:
"We should only cast coins worth a hundred each,
to stabilize the prices of goods."
Liú Bèi followed his advice,
and within a few months,
the treasury was fully stocked.
Thick rims and large wheels—
The Book of Qí states:
Cáo Wǔ served as General of the Right Guard.
In his later years in Yōng Province,
he amassed seventy million in cash,
all with thick rims and large wheels.
To gather all the variations of gold, silver, tortoise, and cowry—
truly difficult to accomplish and fully describe.
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states:
Wáng Mǎng created gold treasure (first), silver treasure (second), tortoise treasure (third), cowry treasure (fourth), cloth treasure (fifth), and spring treasure (sixth).
In total, there were six types of treasure currency in twenty-eight denominations.
Song
As for the Jade Pond and White Clouds,
the Biography of King Mu of Zhōu says:
The Emperor feasted with the Queen Mother of the West upon the Jade Pond,
and the Queen Mother of the West sang for the Son of Heaven, saying:
"White clouds are in the sky,
mountains and hills rise of themselves.
The road is long and far,
mountains and rivers lie between.
If you do not die,
may you yet return."
The Son of Heaven replied:
"I return to the eastern lands,
to harmonize and govern all the Xià.
When the myriad people are equal and balanced,
I shall look to see you again.
After three years have passed,
I shall return to the western wilds."
Regarding Chǔ's "Spring Snow,"
the Biographies of the Elders of Xiāngyáng says:
Sòng Yù understood music and excelled at writing;
King Xiāng loved music and was fond of rhapsodies.
He admired Sòng Yù's talent,
yet disliked his resemblance to Qū Yuán,
so he said to him:
"Why not follow the customs of Chǔ,
so that people may value your virtue?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"In the past, there was a skilled singer in Chǔ—
has Your Majesty heard of it?
At first, he sang 'Xiàlǐ Bārén,'
and tens of thousands in the state sang along in harmony.
Then he sang 'Yáng'ē Xièlù,'
and hundreds in the state sang along in harmony.
Finally, he sang 'Yángchūn Báixuě,'
'Zhāorì Yúlí,'
holding shāng notes and releasing jué notes,
with flawless rhythm and perfect melody—
those in the state who sang along in harmony were no more than a few.
Thus, the higher the song,
the fewer who join in harmony."
Lín Lèi strolled leisurely while gleaning ears of grain.
The Lièzǐ says:
Lín Lèi was nearly a hundred years old
and gleaned leftover ears in the old fields,
singing as he walked forward.
When Confucius went to Wèi,
he saw him in the wilds
and sent Zǐgòng to inquire of him.
Lín Lèi did not stop walking,
nor did he cease singing.
Xuānfù lamented upon capturing the qílín.
the Kǒng Cóngzǐ says:
Shūsūn's charioteer Chú Shāng was gathering firewood in the wilds
and captured a qílín.
No one recognized it,
considering it inauspicious,
and abandoned it at the crossroads of Wǔfù.
Rǎn Yǒu reported, saying:
"A deer-like creature with fleshy horns—
could it be a heavenly portent?"
The Master said:
"Where is it now?
I shall go and see it."
Then he wept, saying:
"I am to people as the qílín is;
this benevolent beast appears only to die—
my Way is at an end."
He then sang:
"In the age of Táng and Yú, qílín and phoenixes roamed;
now is not their time—why have you come?
O qílín, O qílín, my heart is grieved."
Hearing the Yuè women gathering kudzu,
the Annals of Wú and Yuè says:
Gathering Kudzu—
the women of Yuè grieved over King Gōujiàn's earnest efforts,
and composed the 'Rúhé' song, saying:
"Tasting gall is not bitter—its flavor is like sweet syrup;
now we gather kudzu to make thread."
Listening to Zhū Mǎichén carrying firewood,
the Book of Hàn says:
Zhū Mǎichén's family was poor,
but he loved books.
He often cut firewood
and sold it to provide food.
Tying the firewood, he walked while reciting books.
His wife carried burdens and followed him,
often urging Mǎichén not to sing while walking on the road.
Mǎichén only sang more vigorously.
His wife was ashamed of this
and asked to leave.
Mǎichén laughed and said:
"At fifty, I shall attain wealth and honor;
now I am already over forty.
You have suffered long;
wait until I am wealthy and honored to repay you."
His wife angrily said:
"Men like you
will end up starving to death in a ditch."
Mǎichén could not stop her,
so he let her go.
Pitying Zēngzǐ who was beaten with a staff,
the Shuōyuàn says:
Zēng Shēn was weeding melons and accidentally cut their roots.
Zēng Xī was enraged
and took a large staff to strike him.
Zēngzǐ fell to the ground;
after a while, he revived,
rose abruptly,
and came forward, saying:
"Earlier, Shēn offended you, Father;
I hope you have not been harmed?"
He withdrew
and played the qín while singing.
Praising Jì Zūn at pitch-pot,
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Hàn says:
When Jì Zūn was a general,
he selected officers using Confucian methods.
When offering wine and setting out music,
he would always perform elegant songs and pitch-pot.
Shí Chǒng mocking Guō Nè,
Dèng Càn's Annals of Jìn says:
The Crown Prince's Tutor Guō Nè once went to Luòyáng to watch performers sing
and said they were excellent.
Shí Chǒng asked about the tune,
but Nè did not know it.
Chǒng laughed:
"You do not recognize the tune—
how can you say it is excellent?"
Nè replied:
"It is like seeing Xīshī—
must one know her name to recognize her beauty?"
Mèng Jiā's reply to Huán Wēn.
The Separate Biography of Mèng Jiā says:
Huán Wēn asked Jiā:
"When listening to performers,
silk [strings] are not as good as bamboo [pipes],
and bamboo is not as good as flesh [voice]—
what does this mean?"
He replied:
"They gradually approach what is natural."
All present sighed in admiration.
These all excelled at carrying on the sound.
The Rites says:
A skilled singer makes others carry on his sound;
a skilled teacher makes others carry on his will.
They were marvelously able to enter the spiritual.
An ancient poem says:
Clear singing marvelously enters the spiritual.
Also, it is heard that gourd and bamboo instruments are below,
while the human voice is esteemed.
The Rites says:
The singer is above,
gourd and bamboo instruments are below—
this esteems the human voice.
Thus, the hands dance and the feet stamp.
The Preface to the Odes says:
Emotion stirs within,
and takes form in words.
When words are insufficient,
one sighs over it;
when sighing is insufficient,
one sings of it;
when singing is insufficient,
unconsciously the hands dance
and the feet stamp.
Rising as if lifting, falling as if dropping.
The Rites says:
The singer rises as if lifting,
falls as if dropping,
turns as if breaking,
stops as if a withered tree.
Thus, Yáo's people struck the earth.
The Biographies of Reclusive Scholars says:
In Yáo's time, there was an old man of eighty or ninety
who struck the earth and sang:
"I rise at sunrise,
rest at sunset.
I drink from wells I dig,
eat from fields I plow.
What has the Emperor's power to do with me!"
The Hàn palace linked arms.
the Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital says:
Jiǎ Pèilán said that in former times in the palace,
they often amused themselves with string and wind instruments, singing and dancing,
competing in exotic attire
to welcome auspicious times.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, they would enter the Temple of the Numinous Maiden together,
play flutes and strike the zhù,
sing the tune 'Ascending Clouds,'
and link arms together,
stamping the ground in rhythm,
singing 'The Red Phoenix Comes.'
Hearing the gorge's crying gibbons,
the Records of Yídu's Mountains and Rivers says:
In the gorge, gibbons cry, clearing the mountain valleys;
their echoes, clear and cold, never cease.
Travelers sing:
"In Bādōng's Three Gorges, gibbons cry mournfully;
three cries of the gibbon, and tears soak one's clothes."
Hearing the Lǒngtóu's flowing waters.
The Records of Sān Qín by the Xīn family states:
West of the Lǒng Pass,
its slopes wind nine times,
no one knows how many li high it is.
Those who wish to ascend
take seven days to cross.
At the top, there is clear water
flowing down in four directions.
A folk song says:
"The flowing waters of Lǒngtóu,
their murmuring sounds are mournful and choked.
Gazing into the distance toward Qínchuān,
my heart and liver are torn asunder."
The fragrant wind was harmonized by Yú Shùn.
The Annals of Emperors and Kings states:
Shùn was reverent and inactive,
singing the poem "Southern Wind."
The poem says:
"When the southern wind is timely,
it can enrich the wealth of our people.
When the southern wind is fragrant,
it can dispel the grievances of our people."
"The Wheat Sprouts" brought even greater sorrow to Jīzǐ.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Jīzǐ went to pay homage to Zhōu,
passing by the ruins of the former Yīn capital,
where millet and grain grew wild.
Jīzǐ was saddened by this.
He wished to wail but could not,
and weeping would be akin to a woman's behavior.
So he composed the poem "The Wheat Sprouts" to sing of it,
saying:
"The wheat sprouts grow lushly,
the millet and grain are glossy.
That cunning youth,
does not treat me as a good friend."
The so-called cunning youth
refers to Zhòu.
The people shed tears.
The Yōng Gate gained the excellence of Hán É.
The Liezi states:
Hán É traveled east to Qí,
ran out of provisions,
passed by the Yōng Gate,
and sold her singing to borrow food.
Thus, the people of the Yōng Gate excelled in the lingering sounds of É.
Xuē Tán bowed to the extraordinary talent of Qín Qīng.
The Records of Broad Learning states:
Xuē Tán studied singing under Qín Qīng,
but before mastering all his skills, he bid farewell and returned home.
Qīng held a farewell feast for him in the suburbs,
then beat time and sang a mournful song,
its sound shaking the forest trees,
its echo halting the passing clouds.
Tán then apologized and begged to return.
The lyrics of "Auspicious Clouds" and "Heavenly Steed."
The Great Commentary to the Book of Documents states:
Shùn was the guest,
Yǔ was the host,
and the Emperor then sang:
"Auspicious clouds are resplendent,
intertwined and spreading.
The sun and moon shine brightly,
dawn after dawn."
The commentary says:
Yǔ was the host,
receiving the abdication from Shùn.
"Dawn after dawn"
means brightness succeeding brightness.
The Book of Hàn states:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
a horse was born in the waters of Wòwā,
and the "Song of the Heavenly Steed" was composed, saying:
"The heavenly steed comes from the westernmost reaches,
traversing ten thousand li to return to the virtuous.
Bestowing divine might, it subdues foreign states,
crossing the shifting sands, the four barbarians submit."
The auspicious signs of the Precious Tripod and the Divine Fungus.
The Book of Hàn states:
Emperor Wǔ obtained a treasure,
a tripod at Fényīn,
and composed the "Song of the Precious Tripod."
Bān Gù's eulogy for Hàn, discussing merit in song and poetry, the "Song of the Divine Fungus" says:
"From the divine resting place grows the divine fungus,
symbolizing the three virtues, an auspicious response depicted.
Extending lifespan, it glorifies this capital,
matching the Supreme Deity, resembling the Grand Subtlety,
alongside the sun and moon, radiating brilliance."
The dust on the beams flew of its own accord.
Liú Xiàng's "Separate Records" states:
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
the skilled singer Yú Gōng of Lǔ,
whose voice was clear and sorrowful,
could stir the dust on the beams.
None of his students could match him.
The passing clouds halted abruptly because of it.
See the note above on "Xuē Tán and Qín Qīng."
As for Féng Xuān plucking his sword,
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Féng Xuān met Lord Mèngcháng,
who placed him in the guesthouse.
Xuān plucked his sword and sang:
"Long sword, let us return,
for there is no fish to eat."
Lord Mèngcháng moved him to the fortunate quarters,
where there was fish to eat.
He sang again:
"Long sword, let us return,
for there is no carriage to go out."
He was moved to the superior quarters,
where he could come and go by carriage.
He sang again:
"Long sword, let us return,
for there is nothing to support my family."
Lord Mèngcháng was displeased.
Nìng Qī feeding oxen.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
Duke Huán of Qí welcomed guests in the suburbs,
opening the gates at night.
Nìng Qī fed oxen beneath a cart,
saw Duke Huán and felt sorrow,
struck the ox horn and swiftly sang a shāng song:
"The southern mountain is rugged,
the white stones gleam,
born not in the time of Yáo and Shùn's abdication,
in short coarse garments, just reaching the shins.
From dusk feeding oxen till near midnight,
the long night stretches on, when will dawn come?"
Duke Huán heard it and said:
"How extraordinary!
The singer is no ordinary man."
He ordered him to be taken in the following carriage.
The majestic crossing of the Fén River.
The Book of Hàn states:
Emperor Wǔ visited Hédōng,
sacrificed to the Earth Goddess,
looked back at the imperial capital,
joyfully in midstream,
and sang:
"Sailing the tower ship across the Fén River,
crossing midstream, raising white waves."
Lingering while passing by Pèi.
The Book of Hàn states:
Emperor Gāozǔ defeated Qíng Bù,
returned,
passed by Pèi,
set up a feast at Pèi Palace,
and summoned all his old acquaintances.
Elders, youths, and brothers assisted with the wine,
gathering children from Pèi,
obtaining one hundred and twenty of them,
and teaching them songs.
When the wine was in full swing,
the Emperor struck the zhù and sang himself:
"A great wind rises, clouds fly and scatter,
my might covers the land within the seas, I return to my hometown,
how can I obtain fierce warriors to guard the four directions?"
He ordered the children to learn and harmonize with it.
The melodious six yǐn.
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng states:
The first is the "Kōnghóu Yǐn,"
the second is the "Shāng Yǐn,"
the third is the "Zhǐ Yǐn,"
the fourth is the "Yǔ Yǐn."
In ancient times, there were six yǐn,
the "Gōng Yǐn" originally being the second,
the "Jué Yǐn" originally the fourth.
Xiè Língyùn's Music Bureau poem "Huìyín Xíng" says:
"The six yǐn slowly sing clear tunes,
the three modes pause with rich sounds."
The lingering nine autumns.
The ancient Music Bureau poem "The Sun Rises in the Southeast Corner" says:
A mournful song emits a clear sound,
an elegant dance spreads the fragrance of secluded orchids.
Red lips contain the nine autumns,
beautiful rhythm ascends the seven plates.
Dragging shoes, heard of Zēngzǐ.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
Zēngzǐ lived in Wèi,
when he pulled his lapel, his elbows showed,
when he put on his shoes, his heels burst through,
yet he dragged his shoes and sang the "Shāng Odes,"
his voice filling heaven and earth,
as if issuing from metal and stone.
Drumming on a basin, again seen in Zhuāng Zhōu.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
Zhuāngzǐ's wife died,
Huìzǐ came to offer condolences.
He sat with legs sprawled, drumming on a basin and singing.
Huìzǐ said:
"Not weeping is enough,
but singing, is that not excessive?"
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"She now lies peacefully asleep in the great chamber,
and if I were to wail and weep following her,
that would show I do not understand fate,
so I stopped."
As for Shíchéng Mòchóu,
The Record of Ancient and Modern Music states:
"The Mòchóu Lè" is
The crown prince and those who knew of the plan all wore plain white garments and caps to see him off on the banks of the Yì River.
Jīng Kē rose to offer a toast,
and sang:
"The wind soughs and sighs, oh! the Yì River is cold;
The brave warrior, once gone, oh! will not return again."
Gāo Jiànlí struck the zhù to accompany him.
Xìjūn's entry into the felt tent.
The Book of Hàn says:
The Hàn married Xìjūn, daughter of the King of Jiāngdū, to the Wūsūn.
Grieving and sorrowful,
she composed a song herself, saying:
"My family married me off, oh! to a corner of the world,
Sent far away to a remote land, oh! to the King of Wūsūn.
The felt tent is my house, oh! felt is the wall,
Meat is my food, oh! fermented milk is my drink.
Dwelling in constant grief and longing, oh! my heart is wounded within,
I wish to be a yellow swan, oh! and return to my homeland."
Master Yǐ was seen in the tradition as having mastered all subtleties.
The Book of Rites says:
Zǐgòng asked Master Yǐ, saying:
"I, Cì, have heard that songs and chants each have their appropriateness;
For someone like me, what is appropriate to sing?"
Master Yǐ said:
"Yǐ is a lowly musician;
How could I be sufficient to discuss what is appropriate?
I beg to recite what I have heard,
and you, sir, may choose for yourself.
Those who are broad-minded and calm, gentle and upright are suited to sing the Hymns;
Those who are expansive and calm, open-minded and trustworthy are suited to sing the Greater Odes;
Those who are respectful, frugal, and fond of ritual are suited to sing the Lesser Odes;
Those who are upright and calm, incorruptible and modest are suited to sing the Airs;
Those who are straightforward and kind-hearted are suited to sing the Shāng;
Those who are gentle, good, and capable of decision are suited to sing the Qí."
Yánnián was especially skilled and difficult to surpass.
The Book of Hàn says:
Lǐ Yánnián was skilled at singing,
able to create new melodies,
and he and his younger sister were both favored by Emperor Wǔ.
People of the time said:
"One female and one male,
flying in pairs into the Purple Palace."
The Xuánhù Bamboo Hall,
where the purity and beauty of poetic words were appreciated and chanted;
The Book of Later Wèi says:
Emperor Gāozǔ campaigned north of the Yellow River,
and feasted his attending ministers in the great bamboo hall at Xuánhù.
Music was played and wine flowed freely,
Emperor Gāozǔ sang:
"The sun and moon shine in the heavens, oh! there is nothing they do not illuminate,
Yet the region south of the Yangtze, oh! alone remains unlit."
Prince Péngchéng Xié continued the song, saying:
"I wish to follow the sage ruler, oh! ascending to Héng and Huì,
All states hasten in sincerity, oh! merging beyond the sun."
Zhèng Yì sang:
"Clouds and thunder greatly shake, oh! heaven and earth open wide,
All within the realm come as guests, oh! to unify the calendar."
Xíng Luán sang:
"Shùn danced with shield and axe, oh! and all under heaven submitted,
Civil virtue spread far and wide, oh! none do not think of him."
Zhèng Dàozhāo sang:
"The imperial wind, with one drumbeat, oh! envelops the nine lands,
Bearing the sun and leaning on heaven, oh! purifying the six directions."
Emperor Gāozǔ sang again:
"Following those banks of the Rǔ River, oh! in ancient times transformation was pure,
Not like today, oh! where the Way's influence is bright."
Sòng Biàn sang:
"King Wén's governance and teaching, oh! shone upon the rivers and marshes,
How could one know the great transformation, oh! would illuminate the four quarters?"
The bright moon over the northern woods,
containing the empty leisure of a clear melody.
A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
Wáng Tánshǒu, at fourteen or fifteen, could already sing.
Various singing girls praised him to Xiè Gōng,
and Xiè Gōng very much wished to hear him.
But Wáng was from a renowned family and young,
so there was no way to hear him.
The singing girls again fully explained Xiè Gōng's wish to Wáng.
Later, Xiè went out to the earthen hill at the Eastern Administrative Headquarters to enjoy performances,
Wáng at the time wore his hair in two round buns,
dressed in trousers and a jacket,
rode a horse to the Yǔ family's grove of tombs below the earthen hill,
and sang one melody.
It was autumn then, with the moon,
Wáng therefore raised his head to look at the northern woods,
finished the song, and left.
The singing girl reported to Xiè Gōng, saying:
"That was the song of Master Wáng."
There are also the eight pieces of Gětiān,
The Annals of Lü Buwei says:
The eight pieces,
are the songs of Gětiānshì.
Liáng Hóng's Five Sighs,
The Decisive Records of the Three Capital Regions says:
Liáng Hóng traveled east out of the pass,
passed through the capital city,
and composed the song of Five Sighs, saying:
"I climb that Northern Máng, oh!
Sigh!
Gaze back at the imperial capital, oh!
Sigh!
The palace towers are lofty, oh!
Sigh!
The people's toil and hardship, oh!
Sigh!
Vast and endless, oh!
Sigh!"
Emperor Sùzōng heard it and was saddened,
and sought Liáng Hóng but could not find him.
The Master had him repeat it,
The Analects says:
When the Master sang with someone and it was good,
he would certainly have them repeat it,
and only then would he join in harmony.
Jiēyú ended with 'and that's all'.
The Analects says:
The madman of Chǔ, Jiēyú, passed by Confucius singing, saying:
"Phoenix, oh phoenix, oh!
How has your virtue declined?
What is past cannot be remonstrated,
what is to come can still be pursued.
Enough, oh enough, oh!
Those who engage in governance today are in peril, oh!"
Covering Lord È with an embroidered quilt,
The Garden of Stories says:
On the day Lord Xiāngchéng first received his fief,
he wore kingfisher-green robes,
carried a king's jade-adorned sword,
and tread in slippers,
standing above flowing water.
The Chǔ senior official Zhuāng Xīn passed by and admired him,
saying:
"I wish to hold your hand,
may I?"
Lord Xiāngchéng flushed with anger, changed expression, and did not speak.
Zhuāng Xīn stepped back and said:
"Have you alone not heard of Lord È, who was just then riding in a boat of blue waves,
with a kingfisher-green canopy spread,
amid the sounds of bells and drums,
when a Yuè person, embracing an oar, sang:
'What night is this night, oh!
that I pluck the islet midstream.
What day is this day, oh!
that I get to share a boat with the prince.
The mountain has trees, oh! the trees have branches,
my heart delights in you, oh! but you do not know.'
Thereupon, Lord È raised an embroidered quilt and covered him with it."
Picking the purple mushrooms of the southern mountains,
Cuī Qí's Eulogy of the Four Hoaryheads says:
In ancient times there were the Four Hoaryheads of the Southern Mountains,
namely, Master Lùlǐ, Qǐlǐ Jì, Xià Huánggōng, and Dōngyuán Gōng.
The Qín age saw the Way extinguished and virtue dissipated,
with scholars vilified and Confucian arts suppressed,
whereupon they withdrew and composed a song, saying:
"Lush, lush are the high mountains,
the deep valleys winding.
Gleaming, gleaming the purple mushrooms,
they can cure hunger.
The age of Táng and Yú is far,
to where shall I return?
Four horses and a high canopy,
the worries are very great.
Wealth and honor make one fear others, oh!
better poverty and lowliness to follow one's will."
Dreaming of the two pillars, oh! dragging a staff,
The Book of Rites says:
Confucius rose early,
hands behind his back, dragging his staff,
strolling leisurely by the gate,
and sang:
"The Tài Mountain is crumbling, is it not?
The beam and timber are rotting, are they not?
The wise man is withering, is he not?"
Hiding on Shǒuyáng, oh! picking ferns.
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
Bóyí and Shūqí considered it shameful,
and would not eat the grain of Zhōu.
They hid on Shǒuyáng and composed a song, saying:
"We climb that western mountain,
and pick its ferns.
Using disorder to replace violence, oh!
they do not know their error.
Shénnóng, Yú, and Xià,
suddenly vanished, oh!
To where shall we go?"
Observe the resentment of slapping the thigh and plucking the strings,
Comprehensive Meaning of Customs says:
Bǎilǐ Xī became Prime Minister of Qín,
and music was played in his hall.
A hired washerwoman said she knew music,
was called, slapped her thigh,
took up a qín, plucked the strings, and sang:
"Bǎilǐ Xī,
you first married me, oh! for five sheepskins,
when about to part, I cooked a nursing hen,
now you have reached wealth and honor, have you forgotten me?"
Upon inquiry,
it was his wife.
Marvel at the wonder of lingering notes moving leaves.
The Records of Penetrating the Obscure says:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sent Dǒng Yè to ride the Wave-and-Rosy-Cloud Carriage to ascend the altar and await the Queen Mother.
The Queen Mother arrived,
feasted and sang with the Emperor,
performing the music of Spring’s Return.
The sound of the singing encircled the beams three times,
and the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves all stirred.
Admirable was the eloquent woman of the ferry.
The *Biographies of Exemplary Women* states:
When Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào attacked Chǔ in the south,
the ferry officer was drunk and unable to cross him.
Furious, he was about to kill him.
The ferry officer’s daughter Juān, holding an oar, stepped forward and said:
“Formerly, my father heard that you, my lord, were crossing east over treacherous waters.
Fearing the rise of wind and waves,
he therefore prayed to the spirits of the Nine Rivers and Three Huái.
Unable to withstand the libations of wine from the sorcerers’ sacrifices,
he became drunk to this state.
I, your humble handmaid, wish to exchange my lowly body for my father’s life.”
As Jiǎnzǐ was about to cross,
they were short one person to handle the oars.
Juān said:
“I wish to fill the position and handle the oars.”
So she crossed with him.
Midstream, she performed the song “Stirring the River,” singing:
“Ascend that river, oh, gaze westward;
Clear waters raise waves, oh, vast and dim.
Praying for blessings, oh, drunk and unawakening;
Punishment about to befall, oh, my heart is startled.
The horned dragons assist, oh, the lord general returns;
Call for the oars, oh, proceed without doubt.”
Jiǎnzǐ was greatly pleased
and made her his wife.
Great was the chaste wife of Táo.
The *Biographies of Exemplary Women* states:
The wife of Táo Yīng of Lǔ,
when her husband died,
guarded her resolve without wavering.
She composed a song-poem, saying:
“Alas,
the yellow swan’s early widowhood,
for seven years not paired.
With bent neck she sleeps alone,
not mingling with the flock.
At midnight she cries mournfully,
longing for her former mate.
Heaven ordained early widowhood;
sleeping alone, what harm is there?
A widow dwelling on this
sheds tears in many lines.
Woe, alas, how sorrowful—
the dead cannot be forgotten.
Even flying birds are thus,
how much more one’s good spouse.
Though there be worthy males,
in the end one cannot travel paired again.”
Qí Zhuāng stroked the pillar and met with disaster.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
Duke Zhuāng of Qí had an affair with Cuī Jiāng.
Cuī Zhù feigned illness and did not attend to affairs.
The Duke inquired after Cuī Zǐ
and then followed Lady Jiāng into the inner chamber.
The Duke stroked the pillar and sang.
Zhù killed him.
Yuán Rǎng climbed a tree and was ridiculed.
The *Rites* states:
When Yuán Rǎng’s mother died,
he climbed a tree and sang:
“The markings of the lynx’s head, so patterned;
holding your hand, so tightly clasped.”
Therefore it is said: poetry expresses intent;
song prolongs the words.
Its meaning lies herein.
The *Documents* states:
Poetry expresses intent;
song prolongs the words.
Sound follows the prolonging;
pitch harmonizes the sound.
Dance
The Preface to the Odes says:
When singing is insufficient,
one unconsciously moves one's hands and dances with one's feet.
Advancing and retreating in unison,
the Rites say:
Advancing and retreating in unison,
with strings, gourds, sheng reeds, and huang reeds,
the hands join to strike the drum.
Extending the right and raising the left,
the Rites say:
Confucius asked Bīn Móu Jiǎ:
"In the Wǔ dance, one extends the right and raises the left,
why is that?"
He replied:
"That is not the seated posture of the Wǔ dance."
Note:
Wǔ,
is a Zhōu dynasty dance,
meaning there is no seated posture in martial affairs.
Xiàn is read as xuān.
Beginning again, ah, with three steps.
The Rites say:
Three steps to show the square,
beginning again to mark the advance,
returning to disorder to adorn the retreat.
Note:
Three steps are taken before the dance,
one must first lift the foot three times.
Beginning again symbolizes King Wǔ reaching Mèng Jīn,
returning,
after two years,
he then attacked,
thus the Wǔ dance begins again,
starting anew.
Returning to disorder,
means sounding the náo bells and retreating,
to organize the return.
Holding their egret banners,
the Odes say:
Whether winter or summer,
they hold their egret banners.
The commentary says:
Zhí,
means to hold.
Dào,
means a screen,
held by dancers to direct movements.
Dragging these silken threads,
Fù Wǔzhòng's "Rhapsody on Dance" says:
White cranes fly, ah, silken threads are dragged.
Suddenly like a swan soaring and a dragon swimming,
Fù Wǔzhòng's "Rhapsody on Dance" says:
The body like a swimming dragon,
sleeves like plain rainbows.
Cáo Zǐjiàn's "Seven Stimuli" says:
Long robes follow the wind,
mournful songs enter the clouds.
Turning like a swan soaring,
swiftly like a duck diving.
Suddenly swirling like dust and gathering like feathers.
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Omissions" says:
During the time of King Zhāo of Yān,
the state of Guǎngyán presented two dancing girls,
one of their dance tunes was called "Swirling Dust,"
meaning their bodies were so light they mingled with dust and mist.
Another was called "Gathering Feathers,"
meaning they turned gracefully like feathers following the wind.
Raising the zhǐ note, ah, galloping the jué note,
Fù Wǔzhòng's "Rhapsody on Dance" says:
Raise the stirring zhǐ,
gallop the clear jué.
Binding the wind, ah, stirring the Chǔ.
Fù Wǔzhòng's "Rhapsody on Dance" says:
Stirring Chǔ, binding the wind,
the dance of Yáng'ē.
The utmost of human talent,
observing the most exquisite under heaven.
As for inquiring about numbers from Zhòng Zhòng,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
When the temple of Zhòngzǐ was completed, they were about to perform the Wàn dance,
the Duke asked Zhòng Zhòng about the number of feathers,
who replied:
"The Son of Heaven uses eight,
feudal lords use six,
great officers four,
scholars two.
Dance is used to regulate the eight sounds and circulate the eight winds,
thus from eight downward."
Performing the Wàn dance for the Lady.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Chǔ's Lingyǐn Zǐyuán wanted to seduce Lady Wén,
so he built a hall beside her palace,
and performed the Wàn dance there.
The Lady heard it and wept, saying:
"The former lord used this dance
to practice military preparations.
Now the Lingyǐn does not seek out enemies,
but performs it beside this widow,
is this not strange?"
The "One Campaign to Bring Great Peace" of Lóngshuò,
the Táng Shū says:
On the first day of the third month of the first year of Lóngshuò,
the Emperor summoned Lǐ Jì and others to a feast at the city gate,
to watch the newly trained dance of the garrison camps,
named it "The Music of One Campaign to Bring Great Peace,"
all imitating the situation of personally campaigning against Liáodōng and using martial force.
The "Six Harmonies Returning to Purity" of Tiáolù.
The Táng Shū says:
At the beginning of Tiáolù,
the Emperor visited the south tower of Luòchéng,
bestowed a feast,
the Tàicháng performed the "Dance of Six Harmonies Returning to Purity."
Admirable, the Shàngyuán of Táng,
the Táng Shū says:
During the Shàngyuán period,
an edict newly created the "Shàngyuán Dance,"
for the round mound and square marsh,
and sacrifices in the ancestral temple,
then this dance was used,
all other sacrifices stopped it.
The Wénshǐ of Hàn,
the Hàn Shū says:
The temple of Gāozǔ performed the "Wǔdé," "Wénshǐ," and "Wǔxíng" dances.
Bending and stretching,
the Rites say:
Bending and stretching, bowing and rising,
the spacing and speed,
are the appearance of music.
Vigorous and forceful stepping.
The Rites say:
Vigorous and forceful stepping,
is the will of Tàigōng,
meaning his will was to soar like an eagle.
Startled by the sudden arrival of the feathered banner,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
The Duke of Sòng feasted the Marquis of Jìn,
the dance master displayed the feathered banner,
the Marquis of Jìn was frightened,
retreated into a room,
removed the banner,
and finished the feast.
Admiring the beauty of the xiāo and yuè.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Wú Jì Zhá went to Lǔ to observe the music,
saw the dance of xiāo and southern yuè,
and said:
"How beautiful,
yet there is regret."
The note says:
It is the music of King Wén,
regretting that he did not achieve peace himself.
Praising Lù Xùn for receiving a gift,
the Wú Shū says:
Lù Xùn defeated Cáo Xiū,
the Emperor held a grand assembly with his officials,
when the wine was flowing freely,
he ordered Xùn to dance,
and took off his white flying squirrel fur robe to bestow upon him.
Despising Gù Tán for not stopping.
the Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn says:
Sūn Quán summoned Gù Yōng, his son, and his grandson Tán to drink,
Tán was then the Minister of Personnel Selection,
holding an important position.
That day,
Sūn Quán drank to great joy,
Tán became drunk,
danced three times,
and danced without knowing when to stop.
Yōng was inwardly angry,
the next day,
summoned Tán and scolded him:
"The ruler considers tolerance a virtue,
subjects consider respect and caution a principle,
how can one dance without knowing when to stop?
Although it was after drinking,
it was also due to relying on favor,
the one who will ruin our family must be you."
Shī Jīng striking Duke Wén of Wèi,
the Shǐ Jì says:
Shī Jīng played the qin,
and struck Duke Wén of Wèi with the qin,
the Duke was angry.
Jīng said:
"I strike rulers like Jié and Zhòu,
not rulers like Yáo and Shùn."
Duke Wén was pleased,
hung the qin in the room as a warning.
Yànzǐ shaming the Jìn envoy.
the Yànzǐ Chūnqiū says:
Jìn wanted to attack Qí,
sent Fàn Zhāo to observe,
Duke Jǐng hosted him with wine.
Fàn Zhāo requested to drink from the Duke's cup,
the Duke said:
"Agreed."
Told the attendant to pour wine from the cup and present it.
Yànzǐ said:
"Remove the cup and replace it."
Fàn Zhāo said:
"Play the music of Chéng Zhōu,
This dance is named after its tune,
performed by two young girls,
with golden bells adorning their hats,
their clapping and twirling producing sounds.
When they appear,
they are hidden within two lotus flowers,
which part to reveal them,
facing each other in dance,
truly an elegant and wondrous piece among dances.
Such intricate postures in myriad variations,
though swift and agile, are difficult to name.
Qín
This elegant instrument of vermilion strings,
contains the lingering beauty of antiquity.
The *Shuōwén* states:
The qín,
is for restraint,
created by Shénnóng.
It had a hollowed-out soundboard and polished vermilion strings,
and the Zhōu dynasty added two strings.
Striking the clear *zhǐ* note on the Yúnhé,
the *Hánzǐ* says:
Shī Kuàng played the clear *zhǐ* note.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
The qíns and sè of Yúnhé,
were played at the round mound altar on the ground on the winter solstice.
Stirring the flowing spring on the Lǜqǐ.
Fù Xuán's "Qín Fù Xù" says:
Cài Yōng had a Lǜqǐ qín,
a renowned instrument of the world.
The *Qínpǔ* contains the piece "Flowing Spring on the Rock."
The divine maiden and the falling rosy clouds,
the *Dòngmíng Jì* says:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn once gazed at dusk,
and saw azure clouds to the east.
Suddenly, a pair of white swans came soaring and alighted,
and in an instant transformed into two divine maidens,
who danced upon a tower.
Grasping the phoenix-pipe xiāo,
dancing with the falling-rosy-clouds qín,
singing the song of clear Wú spring waves.
Cài Yōng's scorched-tail.
The *Sōushén Jì* says:
A man of Wú was burning tong wood for cooking,
Cài Yōng heard the crackling sound and said:
"This is fine tong wood."
He then carved it into a qín,
but the scorched part remained,
thus it was named the scorched-tail qín,
and it had a sound.
Táo Qián strummed it to convey his thoughts,
the *Sòngshū* says:
Táo Qián did not understand music,
yet he kept a plain qín,
and whenever wine brought him contentment,
he would strum and play it to express his thoughts.
Fúzǐ played it to govern.
The *Jiāyǔ* states:
Fúzǐ Jiàn governed Shànfù,
without descending from his hall,
playing the qín and the district became orderly of itself.
The Duke of Zhōu's excellence in Yuècháng,
the *Qíncāo* says:
The "Yuècháng Cāo",
was composed by the Duke of Zhōu.
King Wén's confinement in Yǒulǐ.
The *Qínlù* says:
King Wén, as the Earl of the West, cultivated virtue and practiced benevolence,
and King Zhòu, angered by his benevolent heart,
summoned him to court,
and confined him in Yǒulǐ.
King Wén, sorrowful and worried,
took up the qín and played it,
composing the "Jūyōu Cāo".
Passing on the ancient method to Jī Kāng,
the *Shìshuō* says:
Hè Sīlìng of Kuàijī was skilled at playing the qín,
and once sat at night under the moon,
playing the strings in the breeze.
Suddenly, a person appeared,
of imposing stature,
wearing fetters,
with a sorrowful countenance,
who praised him from the courtyard.
He then conversed with him,
saying he was Jī Zhōngsàn,
and said to Hè:
"Your playing is extremely swift,
but it lacks the completeness of the ancient method."
He then taught him the "Guǎnglíng Sàn".
Hè thus transmitted it,
and it remains unbroken to this day.
Moved by the spirit of a maiden.
The *Shìshuō* says:
Wáng Jìngbó once moored his boat on an islet,
and went up to a pavilion to stay the night.
That night, the moonlight was radiant and the dew light,
and Jìngbó, feeling serene, played the qín,
which moved the spirit of the deceased daughter of Liú Huìmíng.
In a moment, the maiden arrived,
her form as in life.
Jìngbó strummed the qín and sang:
"Low dew descends on deep curtains,
the hanging moon shines on a solitary qín.
Empty strings increase night's tears,
who pities this night's heart?"
The maiden harmonized, singing:
"The song is plaintive,
the feeling again sorrowful.
I wish to be mist and fog,
swirling in the gentleman's bosom."
As for the design of broad in front and narrow behind,
the form of round heaven and square earth,
the *Qínshū* says:
The qín is three feet six inches long,
modeling the number of days in a year.
Broad in front and narrow behind,
symbolizes the noble and the humble.
Rounded and gathered above,
symbolizes heaven.
Square and level below,
models earth.
Some hung it on the wall as a warning,
the *Shí'èr Guó Shǐ* says:
Zhōu Shījīng served Marquis Wén of Wèi,
and was skilled at playing the qín.
Marquis Wén became engrossed in it,
and began to dance.
Shījīng grew angry,
and struck Marquis Wén with the qín.
The Marquis was enraged,
and had him dragged down from the hall,
intending to kill him.
Shījīng said:
"I beg to speak one word before I die."
Marquis Wén said:
"What is it?"
Shījīng said:
"I struck a ruler like Jié or Zhòu,
I would not strike a lord like Yáo or Shùn."
Marquis Wén said:
"I was at fault."
He then spared him,
and hung the qín on the wall as a warning.
Some removed the tuning pegs to observe a response.
The *Hánshī Wàizhuàn* says:
Confucius traveled to Chǔ,
and reached the pass of Āgǔ,
where there was a maiden wearing a jade pendant washing clothes.
Confucius said:
"That woman can be spoken with."
He took out a qín, removed its tuning pegs, and gave it to Zǐgòng, saying:
"Skillfully compose words,
to observe her reply."
Zǐgòng said:
"Here is a qín without tuning pegs,
I wish to borrow yours to adjust its sound."
The maiden replied:
"I am a person of the wilds and countryside,
ignorant and without intellect,
I do not know the five notes,
how could I adjust a qín?"
The melody of the Wèi maiden longing to return,
the *Yuèfǔ Jiětí* says:
The "Sīguī Yǐn",
tells of a virtuous maiden of Wèi.
King Shào heard of her virtue,
and requested to marry her.
Before she arrived,
the king passed away.
The crown prince intended to take her,
but a minister admonished:
"Now this Wèi maiden is virtuous,
she certainly will not listen to us;
if she listens, she is not virtuous,
and not worth taking."
The crown prince did not listen,
and detained her in the deep palace.
Longing to return but unable,
she took up the qín and composed the "Sīguī" melody,
and hanged herself.
The sorrow of Bóqí being separated from his parents.
Yáng Xióng's *Qín Qīngyīng* says:
Yǐn Jìfǔ's son Bóqí was extremely filial,
but his stepmother slandered him,
and he threw himself into the river.
Clothed in moss and draped with algae,
he suddenly dreamed of a water spirit bestowing fine medicine upon him.
Bóqí, yearning to care for his parents,
raised his voice in a sorrowful song,
which boatmen heard and learned.
Jìfǔ heard the boatmen's song,
and suspected it was Bóqí,
so he took up the qín and composed the "Zǐ'ān" melody.
Admiring it, it had the form of dragons and phoenixes,
the *Xījīng Zájì* says:
Empress Zhào had a precious qín called the phoenix,
with dragons, phoenixes, hornless dragons, and simurghs raised in gold and jade,
and images of ancient worthies and virtuous women.
Listening to it evokes thoughts of integrity and righteousness.
The *Lǐ* says:
The sound of silk strings is sorrowful,
sorrowful,
establishes integrity,
integrity,
establishes resolve.
When a gentleman hears the sounds of qín and sè,
he thinks of ministers of integrity and righteousness.
Shī Xiāng already bowed before the Master,
the *Jiāyǔ* says:
Confucius learned the qín from Shī Xiāngzǐ,
Shī Xiāngzǐ said:
"You have already practiced the zither,
you may progress further."
Confucius said:
"I have not yet grasped its technique."
He was asked again:
"Having already practiced its technique,
you may progress further."
He said:
"I have not yet grasped its spirit."
He was asked again:
"Having already grasped its spirit,
you may progress further."
He said:
"I have not yet grasped the character of its composer."
He was asked again:
"You seem deeply thoughtful,
gazing loftily and distantly."
He said:
"I have perhaps discerned the man:
dark and swarthy,
tall and slender,
with a broad, far-reaching gaze like one overlooking sheep,
encompassing the four directions—who but King Wén could have composed this?"
Master Xiāngzǐ rose from his mat, bowed with clasped hands, and replied:
"You, sir,
are a sage."
The piece handed down is called "The Composition of King Wén."
Bó Yá also grieved for Zǐqī.
The *Family Sayings* states:
Bó Yá played the qin,
and Zhōng Zǐqī listened.
When Bó Yá's mind was on Mount Tài,
Zǐqī said:
"Excellent!
As towering as Mount Tài."
A short while later,
his mind turned to flowing water,
and Zǐqī again said:
"Excellent!
As surging as flowing water."
After Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá broke his qin and severed its strings,
and never played again for the rest of his life.
Then there is the trunk from Hánshān,
Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Seven Summons" says:
The tong wood from Hánshān
originates from Tàimíng.
Note:
Tàimíng
is the north.
The branches from Lóngmén,
the fine wood from Kōngsāng.
The *Rites of Zhōu* says:
Qins and sè made from Kōngsāng wood
are played at the summer solstice at the square mound in the marsh.
Qins and sè made from Lóngmén wood
are played in the ancestral temple.
Also, Méi Shū's "Seven Stimuli" says:
The wood from Lóngmén
is a hundred feet tall without branches.
The wondrous wood from Yìyáng.
The *Book of Documents* says:
The solitary tong tree of Yìyáng.
The commentary states:
On the southern side of Yìshān,
grows a tong tree uniquely suited for qins and sè.
Then there are the nine strings representing the six directions,
The *Qin Treatise* says:
The qin originally had seven strings,
representing gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ, wén, and wǔ.
Later, Cài Yōng of the Eastern Hàn added two more strings,
representing the nine stars,
and in man, modeling the nine orifices.
Also, the *Qin Compositions* says:
Fúxī created the qin,
six cùn wide,
representing the six directions.
It responds to the eight winds and models the four seasons.
The *Qin Treatise* says:
Divide its body into five parts,
three above,
two below,
representing the principle of three heavens and two earths.
Broad above and narrow below,
symbolizes the distinction between noble and base.
The middle section is eight cùn,
representing the eight winds.
The waist is four cùn wide,
representing the four seasons.
The crow once cried at night,
the pheasant also flew at dawn.
The *Explanations of Music Bureau Titles* says:
"The Pheasant's Dawn Flight Composition"
was created by the recluse Dú Mùzǐ
during the time of King Xuān of Qí.
At fifty, he had no wife.
Going out to gather firewood in the wild,
he saw a pair of pheasants, male and female, following each other.
His heart grew sorrowful,
and he looked up to heaven and sighed:
"A sage king reigns above,
his grace extends even to plants and trees.
Birds and beasts are thus blessed,
yet I alone am not."
He took up his qin and sang,
to express his own grief.
"The Crow Cries at Night" is also a tune name.
Bójiē's approval of Gù Yōng.
The *Jiāngbiǎo Biography* says:
Gù Yōng in his youth studied qin playing with Cài Bójiē.
Bójiē held him in high esteem,
and said to him:
"You are sure to achieve greatness,
therefore I give you my name."
Thus Yōng shared the same name as Bójiē.
Zōu Jì's recognition by King Wēi of Qí.
The *Zhōu Documents* says:
Zōu Jì gained an audience with King Wēi of Qí by playing the qin.
King Wēi was pleased with him,
and lodged him in the right chamber.
Shortly after,
the king himself played the qin.
Zōu Jì pushed the door open, entered, and said:
"Excellent!
Your qin playing."
The king suddenly became displeased,
put aside the qin, placed his hand on his sword, and said:
"You, sir, have observed without careful scrutiny,
how do you know it is excellent?"
Jì said:
"The large strings are deep and warm,
the small strings clear and crisp.
You press deeply and release smoothly,
harmonizing them to produce sound.
Large and small complement each other,
intricate yet without discord,
therefore I know it is excellent."
As for the ritual of moving the qin while seated,
The *Rites* says:
If a teacher's qin or sè is placed in front,
one should move it while seated,
being careful not to step over it.
There is also the account of sitting astride a chariot pole.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
Zhāng Gé and Fǔ Lì
again sat astride the chariot pole and played the qin.
In the Hàn dynasty, there was Wénjī.
The *Biography of Cài Yǎn* says:
Yǎn, styled Wénjī,
was from Chénliú.
She was the daughter of Cài Yōng, a General of the Household of the Hàn dynasty.
She was intelligent, kind, and outstanding.
At age six,
Yōng was playing the qin at night
when a string broke.
Yǎn said:
"The second string."
Yōng deliberately broke another string
and asked her,
Yǎn said:
"The fourth string."
Yōng said:
"You merely guessed correctly."
Yǎn said:
"Wú Zhá observed transformations,
and knew the states that would rise and fall.
Master Kuáng blew the pitch pipes,
and discerned that the south wind was not strong.
From this perspective,
how can you say I did not know?"
In the Wèi dynasty, there was the praise of the Lǚ girl.
The *Treatise on Music* says:
Among the palace women of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was a woman named Lǚ,
the elder sister of the late General Yìng Shū.
She entered the Hàn palace at age seven to study the qin,
and excelled at creating new melodies.
Sìzōng's meeting with Sūn Dēng.
The *Biography of Sūn Dēng* says:
Dēng, styled Gōnghé,
lived on Běishān at the end of the Wèi dynasty.
He was often seen with hair loose, sitting upright beneath a cliff,
playing the qin in carefree contentment.
Ruǎn Sìzōng visited him,
and let out a long whistle,
which harmonized with the qin's sound.
Dēng also whistled in response,
their wondrous echoes stirring the forests and valleys.
Mùqiū's welcoming of Hàn Wǔdì.
The *Biographies of Immortals* says:
Master Mùqiū
was a Dàois t priest of Huàshān.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
the master donned a ceremonial cap,
and came forth holding his qin to welcome him.
Pity for the destitute scholar who went to Chǔ.
The *Qin Compositions* says:
"The Composition of the Three Destitute Scholars"
was created by Qí Sī Gézi.
Qí Sī Gézi, Shí Wénzǐ, and Shū Qiānzǐ were three friends who
Hearing that the King of Chǔ was virtuous and fond of scholars,
they all went to see him.
When they reached the rugged mountains,
beneath an empty willow,
they suffered from cold and lacked food.
Judging that they could not all survive,
both men considered Sī Gézi to be the most worthy,
and pushed the clothing and food to him.
The two men then froze and starved to death.
Sī Gézi went to see the King of Chǔ,
who offered fine wine and delicacies,
and set out bells and drums to entertain him.
Gézi, with a sorrowful and grieving expression,
took up the qin and played it,
composing a piece expressing the pain of parting and separation.
The King heard and asked:
"Why is the qin so mournful?"
Gézi set aside the qin, left his mat, knelt upright,
tears streaming down,
and replied:
"I had two friends,
Shí Wénzǐ and Shū Qiānzǐ.
Secretly admiring Your Majesty's lofty righteousness,
they wished to come together to pay their respects.
When we reached the rugged mountains,
we encountered a violent storm,
suffering from cold and lacking food.
We judged that we could not all survive.
The two men did not consider me unworthy,
and pushed the food to me.
The two men then met with freezing and starvation and died.
Now, although Your Majesty has laid out wine, delicacies, and music,
I truly dare not indulge in pleasure."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Alas!
So it was like this."
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Gézi a hundred catties of gold,
ordered his attendants to prepare coffins, gather the two men, and bury them.
He appointed Gézi as his chancellor.
Grieving that Mount Guī obscured Lǔ.
The "Qín Zuǎn" says:
The "Guī Shān Cāo",
was composed by Confucius.
Jì Huánzǐ accepted the female musicians from Qí,
Confucius wished to remonstrate but could not,
withdrew and gazed at Mount Guī, composing a piece,
metaphorically saying the Jì family was like Mount Guī obscuring Lǔ.
As for the five melodies of Guǐgǔ,
the "Qín Zuǎn" says:
Cài Yōng, styled Bójiē,
once entered Qīngxī to visit Master Guǐgǔ.
The mountain where he lived had five bends,
each bend had secluded dwellings and spiritual traces,
for each bend he composed one piece,
completing the melodies in three years.
He showed them to Mǎ Róng, Wáng Yǔn, and Dǒng Zhuó,
who all found them extraordinary.
The "Nǚ Xùn" specifies three endings.
Cài Yōng's "Nǚ Xùn" says:
If the parents-in-law command her to play the qin,
she must sit upright, hold the qin, and perform the piece.
If asked her name,
she should set aside the qin, rise, and reply.
Generally, for small pieces, play five endings;
for large pieces, play three endings and then stop.
Cutting this fine catalpa,
the "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
Mù Jiāng had fine catalpa selected,
to make her own inner coffin and a eulogy qin.
Cutting that paulownia and tong tree.
The "Shī" says:
Paulownia, tong, catalpa, and lacquer trees,
are cut to make qins and sè.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had the "Rào Liáng",
Duke Huán of Qí prized the "Hào Zhōng".
Fù Xiūyì's "Qín Fù" says:
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a qin called "Rào Liáng",
Duke Huán of Qí had a qin called "Hào Zhōng".
Sōng Shí once awaited Sī Huà,
the "Sòng Shū" says:
Xiāo Sīhuà held the position of General of the Left Guard,
once accompanied Emperor Tàizǔ ascending the northern ridge of Zhōngshān,
on the path there was a flat rock and clear spring,
the Emperor had him play the qin upon the rock,
then bestowed upon him silver goblets of wine,
saying:
"I appreciate the sentiment among the pines and rocks."
Lín Jiàn initially followed Dài Yóng.
The "Sòng Shū" says:
Prince Yìjì of Héngyáng garrisoned Jīngkǒu,
Dài Yóng, wearing rustic clothes, played the qin for Yìjì,
including new melodies and varied tunes.
His three modes,
such as "Yóu Xián", "Guǎng Líng", and "Zhǐ Xī",
were all different from the worldly ones.
Emperor Tàizǔ heard of this,
and once said:
"On the day I tour east,
I shall feast at Mount Dài Gōng."
Because of his love for music,
he was long provided with a troupe of orthodox musicians.
Spirit and energy harmonious and balanced,
uniquely attributed to Qiānlǐ;
the "Jìn Shū" says:
Ruǎn Zhān, styled Qiānlǐ,
was skilled at playing the qin.
People heard of his ability,
and many went to listen to him.
Regardless of nobility, baseness, age, or youth,
he would play for them all,
his spirit and energy harmonious and balanced,
making one forget where the listener was.
His brother-in-law Pān Yuè often had him play the qin,
from day until night,
and he never showed a displeased expression.
Grace and refinement pure and far-reaching,
uniquely praised in Shìlóng.
The "Sòng Shū" says:
Imperial Secretary Liǔ Shìlóng achieved fame and merit in youth,
in later years devoted himself solely to discussing principles,
skilled at playing the qin,
the world called Liǔ Gōng's double locks the first among scholars.
He once said of himself:
Horsemanship and lance first,
pure conversation second,
qin playing third.
In court, he did not pursue worldly affairs,
lowering the blinds and playing the qin,
his grace and refinement elegant and far-reaching.
As for the "Water Immortal Prelude",
the "Yuèfǔ Jiětí" says:
The "Shuǐ Xiān Cāo",
Bó Yá studied the qin under Master Chéng Lián,
for three years without success.
Chéng Lián said:
"My teacher Fāng Zǐchūn is now in the Eastern Sea,
he can move human emotions."
So he went with Bó Yá.
Reaching Pénglái Mountain,
he left Bó Yá, saying:
"You stay here and practice,
I will go to fetch him."
He poled the boat and left,
not returning for ten days.
Bó Yá gazed into the distance, seeing no one,
only hearing the sea waters surging and roaring,
the mountain forests dark and silent,
he sighed sorrowfully, saying:
"The master has moved my emotions."
Then he took up the qin and sang,
composing the "Shuǐ Xiān Zhī Cāo".
When the piece ended,
Chéng Lián returned,
poled the boat to meet him and brought him back.
Bó Yá then became the finest in the world.
King Wén's composition,
see the note on "King Wén confined in Yǒulǐ".
Striking and beating considered skillful,
the "Lǐ" says:
Fǔbó, jade chimes, jiējī, large qin, large sè, medium qin, small sè,
are musical instruments of the four dynasties.
Jiē is pronounced as in bāqiè.
Playing the strings with utmost skill.
The "Lǐ" says:
If one does not learn to play the strings,
one cannot properly handle the strings.
Huán Tán was reprimanded for losing his composure,
the "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
The Emperor once asked Sòng Hóng about scholars well-versed in the Way,
Hóng once recommended Tán.
Tán was skilled at playing the qin,
and fond of Zhèng music.
The Emperor listened several times,
and enjoyed it.
Hóng heard of this,
sat in his office,
sent an officer to summon Tán,
and reprimanded him.
Tán kowtowed and apologized,
only after a long time was he dismissed.
Later, at a grand gathering,
the Emperor ordered Tán to play the qin,
Tán saw Hóng,
lost his composure,
the Emperor asked about it.
Hóng explained the reason,
and Tán was no longer allowed to serve as a palace attendant.
Dài Shù followed the sound and responded to the summons.
The "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
Dài Kuí, styled Āndào,
was talented in literature and arts from youth,
skilled at playing the qin.
Grand Tutor Prince Xī of Wǔlíng heard of his qin ability,
and sent someone to summon him.
Kuí, in front of the messenger, broke his qin, saying:
"Dài Āndào does not become an entertainer for princely houses."
Xī was angry,
and instead summoned his elder brother Shù.
Shù was also skilled in music,
and upon hearing the command, went joyfully.
He took his qin and went.
Some say Yànlóng first made it,
as the Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
Dìjùn begot Yànlóng,
who first created the qin and se.
Others say Shénnóng first fashioned it.
The Qīng Qīng Yīng records:
In ancient times, Shénnóng created the qin to settle the spirit,
restrain frivolity and eccentricity,
and remove evil desires, returning one to natural innocence.
Shùn played the five-stringed qin and the world was well-governed;
Yáo added two strings
to harmonize the grace between ruler and minister.
Zhào Shī’s distinction between Wú and Shǔ styles:
The Book of Táng states:
Zhào Shī, styled Yělì,
was skilled at the qin.
In the early Zhēnguàn era,
he stood unrivaled in the capital.
He once said the Wú style is clear and gentle,
like the Yangtze’s broad flow,
lingering and slowly fading,
embodying the demeanor of a state’s scholar.
The Shǔ style is agitated and urgent,
like crashing waves and rolling thunder,
also a moment of outstanding decisiveness.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn’s acquisition of Lóng and Zhào.
Liú Xiàng’s Bié Lù states:
The meaning and affairs of the elegant qin
all come from Lóng Dé’s Miscellaneous Matters of Various Qins.
The Zhào referred to
is Zhào Dìng from Bóhǎi.
During the Yuánkāng and Shénjué eras of Emperor Xuān,
the Chancellor presented those capable of playing the qin:
Bóhǎi’s Zhào Dìng and Liángguó’s Lóng Dé.
Both were summoned to appear in the Warm Chamber,
where they were made to play the qin.
At leisure, they performed sàncāo pieces,
often moving listeners to tears.
Then there were Qiāngōng’s Yùnqìng.
The Guó Shǐ Bǔ states:
Lord Lǐ Qiān, Lǐ Miǎn, was fond of the qin,
carving them himself from paulownia wood,
making as many as several hundred,
giving them to those who sought them.
Among them were peerless ones: Xiǎngquán and Yùnqìng,
which he kept at home.
Zhāng Shēng’s Xiǎngquán.
Zhāng Màoshū’s Record of Xiǎngquán states:
The qins, books, and paintings my family had treasured for generations
were all scattered and lost in the Guāngmíng turmoil.
Among them were two qins:
one named Xiǎngquán,
the other Yùnqìng,
both rare treasures of the age.
Mǐnzǐ was initially startled by catching a rat.
The Kǒng Cóng Zǐ states:
Confucius was resting in his room during the day and playing the qin.
Mǐnzǐ heard it from outside
and told Zēngzǐ:
"Earlier,
the Master’s music was clear, penetrating, and harmonious,
immersed in the ultimate Way;
now
it has changed to a somber, deep sound.
What has moved the Master
to such an extent?
Let us go in and ask him."
Confucius said:
"Yes,
there is a reason.
Earlier I saw a wildcat about to catch a rat,
and hoping it would succeed,
I expressed that in my music.
Which of you two perceived it?"
Zēngzǐ replied:
"Mǐnzǐ."
The Master said:
"He is fit to listen to music."
Cài Yōng was first alarmed by catching a cicada.
The Book of the Later Hàn states:
Cài Yōng’s neighbor invited him for food and drink.
When he arrived,
the wine was already flowing freely.
A guest was playing the qin behind a screen.
When Cài Yōng arrived,
he said:
"You summoned me with music,
yet there is a murderous intent in it.
Why is that?"
He then turned back.
The host pursued him and asked the reason,
and Cài Yōng told him everything.
The qin player said:
"Earlier I saw a mantis facing a singing cicada.
The cicada was about to leave but had not yet flown away,
and the mantis advanced and retreated accordingly.
My heart was tense,
fearing only that the mantis would miss the cicada.
Could this have manifested as a murderous intent in the sound?"
Lamenting Jī Kāng’s execution.
The Biographies of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove states:
As Jī Kāng faced execution,
he looked at the shadow of the sun,
asked for a qin and played it,
saying: [107"Yuán Xiàoní once asked to learn the 'Guǎnglíng Sàn' from me,
but I always stubbornly refused to teach him.
The 'Guǎnglíng Sàn' ends here with me."
Mocking Shī Cáo’s flogging.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
The Marquis of Wèi had a favored concubine
and ordered Shī Cáo to teach her the qin.
Shī Cáo flogged her,
and the Marquis was enraged,
flogging Shī Cáo three hundred times.
Then there is leaning against the screen in sorrow,
listening to the wind.
Ruǎn Jí’s Discourse on Music states:
Emperor Huán of Hàn heard Chǔ-style qin music,
felt mournful and heartbroken,
leaned against the screen in sorrow,
and sighed deeply with emotion:
"Excellent!
If music can be like this, it is enough.
In the past, Jì Liú played the qin facing the wind,
and those who heard it shed tears."
Observing King Wén’s longing for a scholar.
The Qín Lù states:
King Wén met Tàigōng on the north bank of the Wèi River,
was greatly pleased,
and said:
"My ancestor Tàigōng once said
that a sage would come to Zhōu.
Are you the one?"
He then made him his teacher,
calling him Tàigōng Wàng.
Then he took up the qin and played it,
expressing his longing for a scholar,
hence there is the composition "King Wén Longs for a Scholar."
Praising Qín Gāo’s cultivation of nature.
The Qín Shū states:
Qín Gāo used the qin to cultivate his nature.
He first studied at Luófú Mountain,
then traveled throughout the land.
Black cranes dancing at the city gate.
The Hán Zǐ states:
Shī Kuàng played the qin.
With the first performance,
sixteen black cranes came from the south
and gathered at the city gate’s mound.
Receiving the clear breeze from the upper realm.
The Qín Shū states:
A maiden of the Lǐ family in Yǐngyáng,
fifteen years old,
during the Tiānbǎo era, fell ill,
fasted for seven days,
and her soul flew into the darkness,
as if ascending to the upper realm.
Amid clouds and mist,
among female immortals, reeds, lotus roots, and sprouts,
she received fifty pieces, including "Playing with the Clear Breeze."
Then there is Míngguāng’s graceful melody.
Wú Jūn’s Sequel to Tales of Qíxiè states:
Wáng Yànbó once came to the Wú relay station,
moored his boat and tuned his qin,
when he saw a woman lift the curtain and enter.
She took the qin and tuned it—
it resembled a qin but was not quite one—
and its sound was very sorrowful.
Yànbó asked what piece it was,
and she replied:
"This piece is called 'Chǔ Míngguāng.'
Only Jī Shūyè could produce this sound.
Apart from him,
only a few have passed it down."
Yànbó wished to learn it,
but the woman said:
"This is not suitable for the ornate and vulgar;
only those dwelling among cliffs and valleys can enjoy it for themselves."
She played the qin and sang,
and when the song ended,
she rested on the eastern couch.
At dawn, she took her leave.
The Qín Lù states:
Pieces include "Zhōnghuī Qīng,"
"Chàngzhì Qīng,"
"Kànkè Qīng,"
"Wǎnzhuǎn Qīng."
Thunder and kōnghóu.
The Qín Lù states:
"The Thunder Prelude"
was composed when Chǔ Shāngliáng was traveling at the marsh of Jiǔgāo,
encountered wind, thunder, and lightning,
feared it, and returned,
creating this prelude.
It also says:
"The Kōnghóu Prelude"
was composed by Huòlǐ Gāo,
which is the piece "Sir, Do Not Cross the River."
Wind enters through the pines,
spring water flows over rocks.
The *Qín Pǔ* (Manual of the Lute) contains the two pieces "Wind Entering the Pines" and "Spring Flowing Over Rocks."
Jìyīng's lament for Yànxiān.
The *Shì Shuō* (A New Account of the Tales of the World) says:
Gù Róng, styled Yànxiān,
was fond of the lute all his life.
After his death,
his family often placed a lute on the spirit seat.
Zhāng Jìyīng went to mourn him,
overcome with grief,
he went straight up to the bed, played several pieces on the lute,
and said:
"Can Gù Yànxiān still appreciate this?"
Jiǎzǐ's reply to Yìnghóu.
The *Shuō Yuàn* (Garden of Stories) says:
Yìnghóu was sitting with Jiǎzǐ,
when they heard the sound of a lute being played.
Yìnghóu said:
"Why is the lute so sorrowful today?"
Jiǎzǐ replied:
"The strings are taut and the tuning is low,
thus making it sorrowful.
Now, taut strings indicate fine material;
a low tuning
signifies a lowly official position.
To take fine material and assign it a lowly position,
how can it not be sorrowful?"
Yìnghóu said:
"Well said."
There are also the Five Pieces of the Cài Family,
The *Qín Pǔ* (Manual of the Lute) says:
Among lute pieces are the "Five Pieces of Cài Yōng."
Qǐqī's Three Joys.
The *Jiā Yǔ* (School Sayings of Confucius) says:
Confucius was traveling on Tài Shān,
when he saw Róng Qǐqī walking in the wilds of Chéng,
wearing a deerskin robe tied with a rope,
holding a lute and dancing.
Confucius asked:
"What are you doing, sir?"
He replied:
"Heaven gives birth to all things,
but man is the most noble.
Since I am a man,
that is my first joy.
Men are esteemed, women are lowly.
Since I am a man,
that is my second joy.
Some people are born and never see the sun or moon,
or do not survive infancy.
I have lived to ninety-five,
that is my third joy.
Poverty is the constant state of a scholar,
death is the end for all men.
To abide in constancy and reach my end,
what is there to grieve about?"
Confucius said:
"Well said."
Zēngzǐ's "Mutilated Punishment."
The *Qín Lù* (Records of the Lute) says:
The piece "Mutilated Punishment,"
was composed by Zēngzǐ after dreaming of a wildcat,
but not seeing its feet.
He then composed this piece.
Shānglíng's "Parting Crane."
The *Qín Lù* (Records of the Lute) says:
Mùzǐ of Shānglíng had been married for three years without having a child.
His parents wanted him to remarry.
So he took up his lute and played the "Parting Crane."
Shī Wén caused clouds to float and springs to gush;
Hù Bā made birds dance and fish leap.
The *Liè Zǐ* says:
When Hù Bā played the lute,
birds danced and fish leaped.
Shī Wén heard of this,
and studied under Shī Xiāng,
but for three years he achieved nothing.
Not long after,
he saw Shī Xiāng and said:
"I have grasped it."
Thereupon, in spring he plucked the shāng string,
to summon the nánlǚ pitch,
and a cool wind suddenly arrived,
causing plants and trees to bear fruit.
In autumn he plucked the jué string,
and a warm wind slowly circled,
causing plants and trees to bloom.
In summer he plucked the yǔ string,
and frost and snow fell together,
rivers and ponds suddenly dried up.
In winter he plucked the zhǐ string,
and the sun's rays blazed fiercely,
hard ice instantly melted.
As he was about to finish, auspicious winds soared,
auspicious clouds floated,
sweet dew descended,
and sweet springs gushed forth.
Zhōng Yí's playing of southern tunes.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
The Marquis of Jìn was inspecting the military storehouse,
when he saw Zhōng Yí.
He asked about his clan,
and he replied:
"I am a musician."
He gave him a lute,
and he played a southern tune.
The Duke said:
"He is a gentleman.
He speaks of his former duties,
not forgetting his origins;
he plays music of his native land,
not forgetting the old ways."
Shī Kuàng's tuning of the Clear Horn.
The *Hán Zǐ* says:
Duke Píng of Jìn ascended the terrace of Sīqí,
and ordered Shī Kuàng to play the Clear Horn.
Shī Kuàng said:
"It cannot be done.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor assembled spirits and demons on top of the Western Mountains,
riding an elephant-drawn chariot,
with six horned dragons,
Bìfāng by his side,
Chīyóu leading the way,
the Earl of Wind clearing the path,
the Master of Rain sprinkling the road,
tigers and wolves in front,
insects and snakes prostrate on the ground,
phoenixes covering above,
assembling all the spirits and demons,
and composed the Clear Horn.
Now, Your Lordship's virtue is shallow,
and you are not fit to hear it."
The Duke would not listen.
Shī Kuàng, having no choice, played it.
At the first playing,
clouds arose from the northwest.
At the second playing,
a great wind followed,
tearing curtains and canopies,
shattering sacrificial vessels,
and causing roof tiles to fall.
Those seated scattered and fled.
Duke Píng was terrified,
and prostrated himself in the corridor chamber.
Jìn suffered a great drought,
and the land was scorched for a thousand *lǐ*.
The Zhōu people fled to Qí Shān.
The *Qín Cāo* (Lute Pieces) says:
The piece "Qí Shān,"
was composed by the Zhōu people for Tàiwáng.
The infant emperor was abandoned in the great ravine.
The *Shān Hǎi Jīng* says:
Beyond the Eastern Sea is a great ravine.
There, Shàohào, as the infant emperor Zhuānxū's guardian, abandoned his lutes and zithers.
Guō Pú's commentary says:
The meaning of 'rú' (infant/guardian) is not clear.
Playing the "Warm Wind" to dispel resentment.
The *Lǐ* (Book of Rites) says:
Shùn made a five-stringed lute to sing the "South Wind," saying:
"Oh, warm is the south wind,
it can dispel my people's resentment.
Oh, timely is the south wind,
it can increase my people's wealth."
Playing within black curtains to lecture on learning.
The *Zhuāng Zǐ* says:
Confucius wandered in the forest of black curtains,
rested sitting upon the Apricot Altar,
his disciples read books,
while Confucius strummed the zither and sang.
There was also the ode "These Are in Use."
The *Shī* (Book of Songs) says:
"Lutes and zithers are in use,
all is tranquil and good."
Grieving that both were lost.
The *Jìn Shū* (Book of Jìn) says:
When Wáng Xiànzhī died,
his elder brother Wáng Huīzhī rushed to the funeral but did not weep.
He went straight up and sat on the spirit bed,
took Xiànzhī's lute and tried to play it,
but for a long time he could not tune it.
He sighed and said:
"Alas, Zǐjìng,
both the man and the lute are gone."
He then collapsed.
He had a pre-existing back ailment,
which then ruptured,
and he died a little over a month later.
Xiàngrú's seduction of the Zhūo family lady.
The *Shǐ Jì* (Records of the Grand Historian) says:
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú had long been on good terms with Wáng Jí, the magistrate of Línqióng.
The wealthy man Zhūo Wángsūn of Línqióng heard that the magistrate had an honored guest,
and summoned him.
The Zhūo family had a daughter, Wénjūn,
recently widowed,
who was fond of music.
Therefore, Xiàngrú used the lute's heart to seduce her.
Wénjūn secretly peeked through the door,
her heart was delighted,
but she feared it would not be proper.
Jīng Kē stabbed at the King of Qín.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Jīng Kē held the King of Qín with his left hand,
and stabbed at his chest with his right.
The king begged to hear a zither tune before dying,
so he summoned a court musician to play the zither.
The zither’s melody said:
"Silk gauze single-layered robes,
can be torn and severed;
an eight-foot screen,
can be leapt over and crossed;
the sword with the deer-head pommel,
can be carried on the back and drawn."
The king shook his sleeves and fled.
Some say it was passed down from the Pú River.
The Zither Compendium states:
Master Juān transcribed the zither music of the Pú River,
and played it for Duke Píng of Jìn.
Others say it was received from Huáyáng.
The Records of the Supernatural states:
Jī Zhōngsàn once traveled southwest,
several tens of lǐ from Luòyáng, there was a pavilion named Huáyáng,
where he sought lodging.
During the first watch of the night,
he first played several tunes on the zither,
and then heard a voice from the air praising him.
Zhōngsàn stroked the zither and called out:
"Why do you not come here?"
The voice replied:
"I am an ancient person,
who died and was buried here for thousands of years.
Hearing you play the zither,
its melodies serene and harmonious,
I came to listen.
But as my body is decayed and ruined,
it is not fitting to receive a gentleman."
Thereupon, a faint apparition gradually appeared,
holding its own head, and together with Zhōngsàn discussed music.
Then it handed him the zither,
and played many tunes.
None were beyond the ordinary,
except for "Guǎnglíng Sàn," which was peerless.
Zhōngsàn received it,
and by half the night had mastered it entirely,
vowing never to teach it to anyone else.
The King of Jìn moved by Sūn Xī.
The Pure Elegance of the Zither states:
The King of Jìn said to Sūn Xī:
"Can you play the zither in a way that makes me feel sorrow?"
Xī replied:
"Now you reside in high towers and deep halls,
with interconnected rooms and layered doors,
feasting on meat and drinking fine wine,
with musicians performing before you—
it is difficult to make you feel sorrow.
But if one speaks of losing parents in youth,
growing up without elder brothers or sisters-in-law,
living alone by the roadside,
with nowhere to rest at dusk—
such a person can indeed feel sorrow."
Then he took up the zither and played.
The King of Jìn, heart aching and tears flowing, said:
"Why have you come so late?"
Yōngmén moved Mèngcháng to sorrow.
The Garden of Stories states:
Yōngmén Zhōu visited Mèngcháng Jūn with his zither.
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Master, can your zither playing make me feel sorrow?"
Zhōu replied:
"What can make one feel sorrow
is first being noble and later becoming lowly,
first being rich and later becoming poor,
suffering oppression and rejection,
with nowhere to turn for help.
Now you, my lord, are a ruler of a thousand chariots.
Even with the finest zither playing,
it cannot make you feel sorrow.
However, after a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
when your high towers have crumbled,
your winding ponds have filled in,
and your tomb mound has been leveled,
children and woodcutters will tread upon it and sing:
'How could one as noble as Mèngcháng Jūn
end up like this?'"
Mèngcháng Jūn then wept, tears streaming down his face.
Zhōu took up the zither and played,
slowly moving through the gōng and zhǐ notes,
brushing the yǔ and jué notes.
Mèngcháng Jūn’s tears flowed even more sorrowfully.
He stepped down and approached, saying:
"Hearing you play the zither,
I feel like a man whose country has been destroyed and city lost."
Is this not the ultimate wonder of sound,
that hearing it so easily moves one to sorrow?
Flute
Only the tall stalks of the Zhōnglóng bamboo,
grow in the stone ravines of ten thousand fathoms.
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
Only the wondrous growth of the Zhōnglóng bamboo,
on the northern cliffs of the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Perched on the solitary peak of ninefold heights,
overlooking the stone ravines of ten thousand fathoms.
The annotation says:
The "Treatise on Bamboo" says:
Zhōnglóng,
is the name of a bamboo.
Without relying on adornment through carving and engraving,
it possesses the natural endowment of heaven.
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
In ancient times, Páoxī made the qin,
Shénnóng created the sè,
Nǚwā fashioned the shēng,
Bàoxīn made the xūn.
Chuí harmonized the bells,
Shū separated the chime stones,
some smelted metal and polished stone,
with brilliant luster, intricately carved and inlaid.
Exhausting the utmost in skill and beauty,
spending vast amounts of time,
and only then were the instruments completed.
Only the flute, following its natural endowment,
does not alter its material,
is cut and blown,
and its sound is like this.
Learning the dragon's roar, it is similar;
see the annotation below for "flying swan and flowing water."
Cutting the horse's whip, it is easy to hold.
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
Carve its upper hole to make it hollow through,
cut it to serve as a whip, making it easy to hold.
Cài Yōng recognized the exceptional quality of the Gāoqiān bamboo,
The "Biographies of Literary Men" says:
Cài Yōng told a man from Wú:
"I once passed by the Gāoqiān Pavilion in Kuàijī,
and saw that the sixteenth bamboo rafter on the east side of the house could be made into a flute.
I took it and used it,
and indeed it produced an extraordinary sound."
The Han founder tested the wonder of the Zhāohuá flute.
The "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" says:
When Gāozǔ first entered the Xiányáng Palace,
he toured the storehouses,
where gold, jade, and precious treasures were beyond description.
Among the most extraordinary was a jade flute,
two feet three inches long,
with six holes,
inscribed with the words "Zhāohuá's Pipe."
Examining the system of its clear and turbid tones,
The "Compendium of Music" says:
For turbid singing voices, use a long flute;
for clear voices, use a short flute.
Distinguishing the appropriateness of length and shortness.
An ancient song lyric says:
Long flute, short flute,
we always wish Your Majesty boundless longevity.
Then, cutting the emerald bamboo of the Kūn Ravine,
The "Records of the Grand Historian" says:
The Yellow Emperor ordered Líng Lún to cut bamboo in the Kūn Ravine to make flutes,
and when blown, they produced the cry of the phoenix.
Trimming the frosty bamboo of Yúnmèng.
The "Book of Music" says:
The dí (flute),
means to cleanse,
is three feet two inches long,
tuned to the standard pitch,
trimmed from the frosty bamboo of Yúnmèng,
modeled after the wondrous tones of the dragon's roar.
Playing "Qì Chū" and "Jīng Liè,"
Mǎ Róng's "Preface to the Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
While serving as a Dūyóu,
with no pending matters,
