I lay in the Píngyáng Wù in Méi.
A traveler from Luòyáng was staying at the inn,
playing the flute,
performing "Qì Chū" and "Jīng Liè" in harmony.
The annotation says:
"Qì Chū" and "Jīng Liè,"
are the names of two tunes.
Adopting "Yán Lù" and "Bā Rén."
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
Above, it emulates the Sháo Xiāo and Nán Yuè;
in the middle, it takes its measure from "White Snow" and "Green Water";
below, it adopts the forms of "Yán Lù" and "Bā Rén."
Then there is lying in the Píngyáng Wù,
see the annotation above for "Qì Chū Jīng Liè."
Lodging at the Dàijùn pavilion,
The "Records of the Hidden and Dark" says:
Within the boundaries of Dàijùn, there was a pavilion,
often haunted by strange occurrences,
making it unapproachable.
Suddenly, a brave scholar,
singing as he walked, stopped to lodge there.
A ghost played a five-holed flute,
with only one hand,
yet it could not manage to hold the flute properly.
The scholar then laughed and said:
"You only have one hand,
how can you cover all the holes of the flute?
Let me play it for you."
The ghost said:
"Do you think I have too few fingers?"
Then dozens of fingers appeared.
The scholar drew his sword and struck it,
obtaining an old rooster,
with its followers all being chicks.
Listening to Sòng Tóng's new melody,
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" says:
Jìn's Secretariat Director Xún Xù and Secretariat Chief Zhāng Huá,
once had Hǎo Shēng play the zhēng,
and Sòng Tóng play the flute,
performing new melodies in harmony.
Hearing the changing tones of Zhāoxiá.
The "Book of Táng" says:
During the reign of Emperor Wénzōng,
Yún Zhāoxiá was presented for his skill in playing the flute.
The emperor composed new melodies for refined music,
and Zhāoxiá was able to adapt his playing to the changing tones,
quite matching the emperor's intentions,
thus gaining favor.
Truly it can cleanse evil and admit uprightness,
The "Comprehensive Meaning of Customs" says:
The dí (flute),
was made by the craftsman Qiū Zhòng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
originally from the Qiāng region.
Dí,
means to cleanse,
that which cleanses evil filth,
and admits it to elegance and uprightness.
One foot four inches long,
with seven holes.
It is that which stirs things and communicates with spirits.
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Flute" says:
It can communicate with spirits and stir things,
express the spirit and convey meaning.
Cleansing filth and impurity,
washing away grime and dregs.
As for transmitting subtle principles through Mǎ Róng,
Mǎ Róng's "Preface to the Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
I have a natural affinity for music,
and can play the qin and blow the flute.
Praising the fine skill of Qiū Zhòng,
see the annotation for "cleansing evil and admitting uprightness."
Adding to it was done by Jūnmíng himself,
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
Yìjīng Jūnmíng understood musical tones and pitch-pipes,
so originally with four holes, he added one.
The hole added by Jūnmíng appeared later,
this is called the shāng tone,
completing the five notes.
The annotation says:
Jīng Fáng,
styled Jūnmíng,
studied the "Yìjīng,"
hence called Yìjīng.
Reducing it was again due to Xī Zòng.
The "Compendium of Music" says:
The Huángzhōng flute,
during the Jìn dynasty, was three feet eight inches long.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
the Grand Music Director Zhōng Zōngzhī reduced it to three feet seven inches.
In the fourteenth year,
the Secretary Director Xī Zòng again reduced it by five fen,
making it three feet six inches and five fen.
Sometimes it stirs sorrow by the roadside,
The "Compendium of Music" says:
The héngdí (transverse flute),
is a small chí.
A Liáng dynasty song says:
"A swift horse needs no whip,
just break off a willow branch.
Dismount and blow the transverse flute,
sorrow killing the child by the roadside."
Sometimes it aids courage in the army.
The "Compendium of Music" says:
The "Sīmǎ's Art of War" states:
Among the music of the army,
drums and flutes are foremost,
making those who hear them brave and harmonious in joy.
Delicate strings and tall bamboo are not to be used,
for fear that mournful sounds will move people,
causing soldiers to think of returning home.
There is also the establishment of the Yellow Gate,
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" says:
Retiring to manage affairs in the high corridors of the Yellow Gate.
Huán Tán's "New Discourses" says:
The three rulers of Hàn,
internally established Yellow Gate musicians and performers.
The system of the eastern wing,
The "Compendium of Music" says:
Liú Hézhī's eastern wing flute,
was four feet two inches long.
Xiàng Xiù, melancholy and longing for the past,
The "Book of Jìn" says:
Xiàng Xiù's "Preface to the Rhapsody on Longing for the Past" says:
In my youth, I lived close to Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān,
later each met their fate due to certain matters.
I am about to journey westward,
passing by my former dwelling.
At that time, the sun was setting over Yúyuān,
and the icy cold was desolate.
A neighbor was playing the flute,
its sound clear and bright.
Recalling the joys of past outings and feasts,
I was moved by the music and sighed,
thus composing this rhapsody.
Wáng Kǎi, cruel and violent, killed a singing girl.
The *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
The emperor's uncle, Wáng Kǎi, once held a banquet,
and Wáng Dǎo and Wáng Dūn both attended.
A singing girl playing the flute slightly displeased Kǎi,
so he ordered a eunuch to beat her to death.
Everyone present changed countenance,
but Kǎi remained composed.
The one who sang "Quiet Night" already amazed with its divine wonder.
The *Yōumíng Jì* states:
During the Yǒngjiā era,
Cháo Shì of Tàishān, formerly the magistrate of Xiàng County,
resided in Jìnlíng.
A household maidservant was gathering firewood
when suddenly a person followed her home.
He did not allow others to see him;
only the maidservant could see his form.
Whenever he drank and feasted with the maidservant,
he would play the flute and sing,
singing:
"Quiet night, silent and clear,
the long flute bright and resonant.
If you wish to know me,
my surname is Guō, my name is Chángshēng."
The bamboo flute from Bǎoyān suddenly shattered in surprise.
The *Guóshǐ Bǔ* states:
Lǐ Zhōu, fond of curiosities,
once obtained a bamboo flute from a village called Bǎoyān,
cut it to make a flute,
hard as iron or stone,
and gave it to Lǐ Móu.
Móu was the finest flute player in the world.
Once, on a moonlit night, he was boating on the river,
playing the flute with Zhōu,
the sound clear and soaring.
Suddenly, a guest stood on the shore,
calling to the boat to request passage.
Once aboard,
he asked to play the flute.
His music was pure and powerful,
capable of cracking mountains and rocks,
something Móu had never witnessed in his life.
As he reached the climax,
with breath and fingerwork swirling,
the flute shattered under his fingers,
and the guest vanished without a trace.
Zhōu recorded this,
suspecting he was a flood dragon.
Shí Chóng often praised Sòng Wěi.
The *Shìshuō* states:
Among the world's skilled flute players,
Shí Chóng's maidservant Lǜzhū's younger sister was named Sòng Wěi.
The Xiè family once took pride in Ā Jì.
The *Shìshuō* states:
Xiè Rénzǔ's concubine Ā Jì possessed peerless beauty
and was skilled at playing the flute.
After Rénzǔ's death,
Ā Jì vowed never to remarry.
Xī Tán was then the General of the Northern Headquarters.
He employed deceit to lure Ā Jì into becoming his concubine,
but Ā Jì never spoke a word to Tán for the rest of her life.
Lǐ Móu's transcendent thoughts at Guāzhōu.
The *Guóshǐ Bǔ* states:
Lǐ Móu played the flute on an autumn night at Guāzhōu.
The boats were very crowded,
but as he began to play,
all movement ceased;
after several melodies,
a gentle breeze drifted in;
moments later,
boatmen and merchants were heard sighing with sorrow and weeping.
Huán Yī's lingering beauty at Qīngxī.
The *Jìnshū* states:
Huán Yī, styled Shūxià,
was skilled in music
and possessed Cài Yōng's Kētíng flute.
He often played it himself.
When Wáng Huīzhī was traveling to the capital,
he moored his boat by Qīngxī.
Yī did not know him,
but as he passed by on the shore,
Huīzhī sent someone to say to him:
"I hear you are skilled at playing the flute.
Please play a tune for me."
Yī was already esteemed and prominent at the time,
but having long heard of Huīzhī's reputation,
he dismounted, sat on a folding stool, and played three melodies for him.
When finished, he mounted his carriage and left,
without exchanging a single word between guest and host.
Passed down in the Music Bureau,
there are "Breaking the Willow" and "Falling Plum Blossoms";
"Breaking the Willow" and "Falling Plum Blossoms"
are both names of flute tunes.
They originated with the Qiāng people.
See the flying geese and flowing water.
Mǎ Róng's "Rhapsody on the Long Flute" states:
In recent times, the double flute originated with the Qiāng.
The Qiāng people cut bamboo without cease.
The dragon sings in the water, unseen,
but cutting bamboo and blowing it produces a similar sound.
It also says:
Its form resembles flowing water,
and also seems like flying geese.
The drum
is that which stirs,
containing yang and thus stirring.
The Ancient and Modern Record of Music states:
The drum
is that which stirs.
At the winter solstice, yin
causes all things to contain yang and stir.
As for the booming of the alligator drum,
played by the blind musicians in the court,
see the "Líng Tái" ode in the Book of Songs.
It corresponds to the spring equinox and embodies its meaning.
The Shuōwén states:
The drum
is an enclosure.
It is the sound of the spring equinox,
symbolizing all things breaking through their husks and shells to emerge,
hence it is called a drum.
It should be made when the hibernating insects awaken.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
All drumheads must be mounted on the day the hibernating insects awaken.
Hear of the striking of the stone in Línpíng.
The Garden of Marvels states:
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
on the bank at Línpíng in Wújùn commandery,
the mountain collapsed,
revealing a stone drum.
When struck, it made no sound.
They asked Zhāng Huá,
and Huá said:
"Take a paulownia tree from Shǔ,
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and strike it with that; then it will sound."
They followed his advice,
and the sound could be heard for several tens of lǐ.
See the inscribed bronze from Nánjùn.
Yú Xǐ's Forest of Records states:
In the 24th year of the Jiànwǔ era,
a man from Nánjùn commandery presented a bronze drum,
which bore an inscription.
Beating the drum,
beneath Wǎnqiū.
From the "Chén Fēng" in the Book of Songs.
The signalers beat the drums.
The Book of Songs says:
When Fāng Shū led them forth,
the signalers beat the drums,
arraying the troops and addressing the host.
To welcome the Field Ancestor.
The Book of Songs says:
With lutes, zithers, and beating drums,
they welcome the Field Ancestor.
Know the earthen drum and basket-frame drumstick of Yīqí.
The Book of Rites states:
The earthen drum, the basket-frame drumstick, and the reed pipe
were the music of the Yīqí clan.
Examine the fur-covered earthen drum of the Yuèzhāng official.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Yuèzhāng official is in charge of the earthen drum.
Annotation:
With a frame of fur-covered earth,
and a leather surface.
Marvel at the crane flying from the Thunder Gate.
The Record of Línhǎi states:
West of the commandery is White Crane Mountain,
on which there is a stone drum.
During the Yuánjiā era,
local people sacrificed to the mountain god,
and pounded this drum.
It could be heard for tens of lǐ, like the sound of metal or stone.
Tradition says
that a crane from this mountain
flew into the drum at the Thunder Gate in Kuàijī commandery.
When the drum was beaten, the sound was heard in Luòyáng.
Later, the rebel Sūn Ēn hacked this drum open,
and a white crane was seen flying out.
Startle the soaring egret at Jiànkāng.
Liú Huán's Determining Military Rites states:
Some say the egret
is the essence of the drum.
Long ago, King Fūchāi of Wú opened the Snake Gate to suppress the Yuè people.
The Yuè people made a Thunder Gate to exorcise it,
beating a great drum beneath the Thunder Gate,
and the sound was heard at the Snake Gate.
Later, the drum was moved to the Duānmén gate of the Jiànkāng Palace.
A pair of egrets flew out from the drum.
As for the design with a wide head and slender waist,
The Correct Music states:
The waist drum:
the large ones are of pottery,
the small ones of wood,
all with wide heads and slender waists.
The marvel of eight faces and four feet.
The Comprehensive Compilation of Ritual and Meaning states:
The jiàn drum
is a large drum.
In summer, four feet are added,
and it is called a jié drum.
The Book of Music mentions the thunder táo.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The blind musicians are in charge of shaking the táo.
The táo is like a drum but smaller.
A wooden rod is passed through it to serve as a handle,
with four rods on each side,
making eight faces.
Some are shaped like a gaming board.
The Correct Music states:
The jié drum is like a gaming board,
with a round hole in the center,
just large enough to hold the drum, which is struck
to mark the rhythm of the music.
Some have a shape like a musk deer's navel.
The Ancient and Modern Record of Music states:
The qí drum is like a large lacquered bucket.
One end has a flat surface on the drumhead,
like a musk deer's navel,
hence it is called the qí drum.
Strike the small one to lead the large one.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The xuán drum
is the Zhōu drum.
The smaller one is called the yìn.
First strike the small drum
to lead the large drum,
hence it is called the yìn,
also known as the pí.
The yìng drum is in the east, while the xuán drum is hung in the west.
The Book of Rites states:
In the temple hall,
the xuán drum is hung in the west,
and the yìng drum is in the east.
Yáo Hóng was alarmed by the stone's sounding.
The Record of the Later Qín states:
In the first year of the Yǒnghé era of Yáo Hóng,
a stone drum in Tiānshuǐ sounded, heard for hundreds of lǐ,
and wild pheasants all crowed.
Lǐ Líng soon knew his army's spirit had waned.
The Book of Hàn states:
Lǐ Líng attacked the Xiōngnú.
At night, he ordered the drum beaten to rouse the troops,
but the drum did not sound.
Lǐ Líng said:
"Our army's spirit has waned, and the drum does not respond.
Why is this?
Could there be women in the army?"
They searched the army
and found soldiers' wives.
All were executed.
Chéngqián heard Xuánsù's remonstrance.
The Book of Táng states:
The Crown Prince Chéngqián once beat a drum in the palace,
and the sound was heard outside.
Zhāng Xuánsù knocked at the palace gate requesting an audience,
and remonstrated with utmost earnestness.
Chéngqián then brought out the palace drum
and destroyed it in front of Xuánsù.
Sūn Yì suffered Gāo Shuǎng's ridicule.
The History of the Southern Dynasties states:
Sūn Yì was the magistrate of Yánlíng County.
The National University assistant instructor Gāo Shuǎng visited him,
but Yì showed no old friendship.
Shuǎng left,
passed by the gate tower,
took a brush and wrote on the drum face:
"You have only a great big belly,
but truly no liver or guts.
With skin so thick as this,
being beaten will never end."
Then there are those made since Huángdì.
The Imperial Century states:
Huángdì killed the kuí,
using its skin to make a drum,
and the sound was heard for a hundred lǐ.
Beginning with Shàohào.
The Comprehensive Compilation of Ritual and Meaning states:
The jiàn drum,
a large drum,
was made by Shàohào,
serving as the rhythm for all other drums.
Though it is said to not correspond to the five notes,
the Book of Rites states:
The drum does not correspond to the five notes,
yet the five notes cannot achieve harmony without it.
How can one not strike and beat it?
The Book of Songs says:
You have bells and drums,
but do not strike or beat them.
When you lie dead,
others will possess them.
As for the insignia of the wáng, hóu, lù, and bēn,
the Rites of Zhōu states:
The wáng holds the lù,
the hóu holds the bēn,
the army general holds the jìn,
the division commander holds the tí,
the brigade commander holds the pí.
The differences in hanging and placement between Shāng and Zhōu.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Xià added feet to the drum.
The Yīn people set up drums,
the Zhōu people suspended drums.
Commentary:
"Set up" means to plant.
To erect with high teeth,
The Book of Songs says:
"There are blind musicians, there are blind musicians,
in the courtyard of Zhōu.
They set up the frames and stands,
high teeth and feathered decorations,
the Yìng, Tián, and suspended drums."
Mounted on tower carriages.
The Ancient and Modern Commentary says:
The Hàn dynasty had imperial musicians,
also called tower carriages.
Dūtán and Dálà,
The Record of Ancient and Modern Music says:
The Dūtán drum
resembles a waist drum but is smaller,
struck with a small mallet.
It also says:
The Dálà drum,
is wider than the Jié drum but shorter,
played with the fingers,
its sound is very loud,
commonly called the wiping drum.
Jīlóu and Mìxū.
The Music Record says:
The Jīlóu drum,
perfectly round,
and the flat areas at the head and tail that can be struck are several inches wide.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Táng Shū was given the drums of Mìxū."
Commentary states:
Mìxū
is the name of a state.
Mí Héng removed his clothes without shame.
The Book of the Later Hàn says:
Cáo Cāo heard that Mí Héng was skilled at drumming,
so he summoned him to be a drumming official.
During a gathering of guests,
they tested musical rhythms.
All the officials who passed by
were ordered to remove their old clothes
and put on the uniform of Cénmóu Dānjiǎo.
When it was Héng's turn,
he was just about to wield the drumstick and leap forward,
when an official scolded him:
"Drumming official, why don't you change your clothes before lightly advancing?"
Héng then first removed his outer garment,
then took off the rest of his clothes,
stood naked,
slowly took the Cénmóu Dānjiǎo uniform and put it on,
then wielded the drumstick again,
his expression showing no shame.
Cáo laughed and said:
"I originally intended to humiliate Héng,
but Héng instead humiliated me."
Héng replied:
"I dare not use the ceremonial robes of the former kings as the clothes of a musician."
Wáng Gōng raised his drumstick with ease.
The Shì Shuō says:
When General Wáng was young,
he had a reputation for being rustic,
and his speech was also coarse.
Emperor Wǔ summoned contemporary worthies to discuss matters of skill and art,
everyone had something they could do,
only Wáng had nothing he understood,
his expression was particularly unpleasant.
He claimed to understand drumming,
the emperor immediately ordered a drum to be brought for him to play.
From his seat, he shook his sleeves and stood up,
raised his drumstick and struck vigorously,
the rhythm was harmonious and swift,
as if no one else was around.
All those present sighed at his bold and forthright nature.
Beating them deeply,
The Book of Songs says:
"Beating the drums deeply,
shaking the troops with a thunderous sound."
Playing these grandly.
The Book of Songs says:
"Ah, how magnificent,
set up our táo drums.
Playing the drums grandly,
to please our illustrious ancestors."
Some are placed in the western chamber,
The Book of Documents says:
"Large shells and fén drums
are in the western chamber."
Some are arranged below the pipes.
The Book of Documents says:
"Below the pipes are táo drums."
Distinguish between striking alone and shaking the táo,
The Ěryǎ says:
"Striking the drum alone is called è."
Shaking the táo,
see the commentary above on "four legs and eight faces."
Praising the Dēngwén and Gǎnjiàn drums.
The Music Record says:
"The drum on horseback is called the tí drum,
if it cannot be carried,
when placed at court it becomes the Dēngwén drum,
the hearing drum,
the Gǎnjiàn drum."
Also, there is Sīhuà riding the ridgepole,
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng says:
"When Xiāo Sīhuà was about ten years old,
he liked to ride the ridgepole of the house,
beating a slender waist drum."
The King of Chǔ alerting the people,
The Hánzǐ says:
"King Lì of Chǔ had an alarm drum,
to warn the people.
Later, he drank too much and struck it,
the people were greatly alarmed.
He sent someone to stop them, saying:
'I was drunk and struck it as a joke.'
The people all dispersed.
After several months,
when there was an alarm and the drum was struck,
the people did not rise."
Stones in the mountains ringing,
Guō Yuánshēng's Record of Campaigns says:
"Mount Féng is thirty lǐ south of Guǎnggù,
there is a shrine with stone figures and stone drums.
When the Qí dynasty was about to fall into chaos,
the stone figures would beat the drums,
audible for tens of lǐ."
Thunder in the distant wilderness.
The Classic of Divine Marvels says:
"In the wilderness of the eight directions, there are stone drums,
covered with skin,
their sound is like thunder."
King Mù's music at Líqiū,
The Biography of King Mù says:
"The Son of Heaven read at Líqiū,
performed grand music and left his spirit drum."
Wáng Qiáo, the deity of Yè County.
The Book of the Later Hàn says:
"Wáng Qiáo was the magistrate of Yè,
every time he went to court,
the drum at the gate of Yè would sound without being struck.
Heard in the capital,
Emperor Zhāo took it and placed it at the capital pavilion,
and it never made a sound again."
It is also said that copper pellets were thrown,
The Book of Hàn says:
"After the Jiànzhāo era,
Emperor Yuán retained his fondness for music.
Sometimes he placed drums under the palace steps,
and the Son of Heaven himself stood at the balcony railing,
dropping copper pellets to strike the drums,
the sound matching the rhythm of the solemn drums.
None of the palace attendants or those around him who were familiar with music could do it.
But the Prince of Dìngtáo could also do it,
and the emperor repeatedly praised his ability.
Shǐ Dān came forward and said:
'Generally, what is called talent
is being quick and fond of learning,
reviewing the old to know the new—
the crown prince is such a person.
I have not heard of judging a person by his skill with strings, bamboo, drums, and pipes.'"
Regulating them with metal bells,
The Record of Ancient and Modern Music says:
"The master of bó is in charge of the drums for metal performances,
using metal náo to stop the drums,
using metal duó to communicate with the drums,
using metal zhuó to regulate the drums.
As for those using bells and drums,
first strike the bell,
then strike the drum."
Bó is pronounced bó.
Náo,
is pronounced náo.
Zhuó is pronounced zhuó,
also pronounced dú.
The divine bell of Luófú,
The Record of Luófú Mountain says:
"East of the mountain, below the stone tower, there are two stone drums,
when struck, they produce a clear and far-reaching sound,
what is called the divine bell."
The sacred wood of Shǐxīng.
The Record of Jīngzhōu says:
"In Yángshān County of Shǐxīng Commandery, there is a yùzhāng tree,
its trunk diameter can reach two zhàng,
named the sacred wood.
During the Qín dynasty, this wood was cut to make a drum frame,
when the frame was completed, it suddenly ran away,
north to Guìyáng."
Also, Wáng Shāozhī's "Shǐxīng Poem · Preface" says:
"Resting at Línwǔ,
then proceeding to Luòyáng,
hence named the Sacred Drum City.
Now it is in Línwǔ."
The Zhōu officials listed their duties,
recording the differences between thunder, spirit, gāo, and jìn drums;
The Zhōu Rituals says:
"The drum master is in charge of teaching the sounds of the six drums and four metals,
To regulate music with rhythm,
to harmonize military campaigns,
to regulate field labor.
Teach the use of drums,
and distinguish their sounds and functions.
Use léi gǔ to drum for divine sacrifices,
use líng gǔ to drum for earth-god sacrifices,
use lù gǔ to drum for offerings to spirits,
use fén gǔ to drum for military affairs,
use gāo gǔ to drum for labor affairs,
use jìn gǔ to drum for metal performances.
The Ěryǎ is renowned,
listing categories such as fén, yìng, táo, and má.
The Ěryǎ states:
A large drum is called fén,
a small one is called yìng,
a large táo is called má,
a small one is called liào.
End
The Yellow Emperor let robes and garments hang down, and the world was governed,
which likely took inspiration from Qian and Kun.
From the "Book of Changes".
The annotation says:
Upper garment and lower skirt,
represent the images of Qian and Kun.
As for the plain white robe and dark green scarf,
they bring me joy and delight,
from the "Book of Songs".
The annotation says:
Gǎo,
white in color,
is men's attire.
Qí,
pale green like mugwort,
is women's attire.
Some took inspiration from the beauty of Suī and Huàn,
as the "Chénliú Customs Chronicle" states:
The waters of Suī and Huàn in Xiāngyì produce patterns,
hence the embroidered robes, brocades, sun, moon, flowers, and birds,
are used for the ceremonial garments of the Son of Heaven in ancestral temples.
Some imitated the patterns of pheasants.
The "Records of Han Carriages and Attire" states:
The sages observed the patterns of pheasants and the colors of blossoms,
then dyed silk to imitate them,
first creating five-colored garments,
totaling twelve emblems.
Without coarse cloth, how can one survive the year?
The "Book of Songs" says:
In the first month, the wind blows cold,
in the second month, the chill is severe,
without clothes or coarse cloth,
how can one survive the year?
Wearing improper attire brings disaster upon oneself.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
Zhèng Zǐzāng fled to Sòng,
fond of collecting kingfisher-feather caps,
the Lord of Zhèng sent thieves to lure and kill him.
The gentleman said:
"Wearing improper attire,
brings disaster upon oneself."
The wings of the mayfly,
its robes and garments are bright and neat.
From the "Book of Songs".
It also says:
The wings of the mayfly,
its colorful garments.
The mayfly emerges from the ground,
its hemp robes like snow.
Silk floss for the lined jacket and old silk for the robe,
the "Book of Rites" says:
Unless in proper attire, one does not enter the gates of the court,
wearing coarse hemp garments, one does not enter the gates of the court,
wearing mourning attire, one does not enter the gates of the court,
wearing fur robes improperly, one does not enter the gates of the court.
Silk floss for the lined jacket,
old silk for the robe,
unlined for the thin garment,
silk for the lined robe.
Sleeves should conform to the compass, and the collar to the square.
The "Book of Rites: Shēnyī" says:
Sleeves are round like a compass,
the curved collar is like a square.
Zhōngshān then understood its reversal,
as the "Shuōyuàn" says:
Wèi Wénhóu enfeoffed his crown prince Jī in Zhōngshān,
for three years without communication.
His attendant Zhào Cāngtáng was sent as an envoy,
Wénhóu asked:
"How does your lord compare to me in stature?"
Cāngtáng said:
"If you bestow upon him the robes from the outer treasury, he will surpass you."
Wénhóu sent Cāngtáng to bestow a set of robes upon the crown prince,
ordering Cāngtáng to arrive at cockcrow.
The crown prince welcomed and bowed to receive the gift,
opened the chest,
and found the robes all reversed.
The crown prince hurriedly prepared his carriage, saying:
"The gift of robes,
is not because of the cold,
but to summon Jī.
With no one to consult,
he sent you.
As the poem says:
'Before dawn in the east,
robes and garments are reversed.
Reversed and turned,
by the lord's summons.'"
Ruò'áo began with tattered clothes.
See the annotation in "Chē Fù": "Bì heard of the Lord of Chǔ".
Short, but not exposing the skin,
long, but not dragging on the ground,
the "Book of Rites: Shēnyī" says:
In ancient times, there was the shēnyī,
which had its regulations,
short, but not exposing the skin,
long, but not dragging on the ground.
Chān is to cover the front,
as the "Ěryǎ" says:
A garment covering the front is called chān.
Annotation:
Now called a knee cover.
Leg wrappings are worn below.
The "Book of Songs" says:
Red knee covers on the thighs,
oblique leg wrappings below.
Annotation:
Fú,
a large belt,
is the ancient symbol of a knee cover.
Zhōu Yú was bestowed with a hundred sets,
as the "Wú Shū" says:
Sūn Quán often bestowed robes upon Zhōu Yú,
both for cold and heat, each time a hundred sets,
which no other general could match.
Nányuè also received three grades of padded garments.
The "Book of Hàn" says:
The Emperor bestowed upon King Tuó of Nányuè fifty upper-grade padded garments,
thirty middle-grade padded garments,
and twenty lower-grade padded garments.
Annotation:
Garments stuffed with silk floss are called zhǔ.
Astonished at Gěng Gōng's tattered clothes,
the "Book of the Later Hàn" says:
Gěng Gōng returned from Shūlè,
his clothes and shoes torn and worn,
his appearance haggard.
Surprised at Zhāng Róng's coarse and old attire,
the "Book of Qí" says:
Emperor Gāo issued a handwritten edict bestowing robes upon Zhāng Róng, saying:
"Seeing your clothes coarse and old,
truly reflects your simple nature,
but associating with you in tatters,
also damages the court's dignity.
Now I send a set of old clothes,
meaning that though old,
they are better than new.
These are what I wore,
already tailored to fit your body."
Fàn Yè expressed thoughts with precision,
as the "Book of Sòng" says:
Fàn Yè was meticulous by nature,
with refined thoughts,
he adjusted the regulations for robes, utensils, and attire,
and people of the time all followed him.
Dào Gài became famous for his simplicity,
as the "History of the Southern Dynasties" says:
Dào Gài was frugal by nature,
disliking music and beauty,
his room empty with a single bed,
no concubines or attendants beside him,
his hat and shoes replaced once every ten years,
his court robes sometimes worn and patched.
Wearing this embroidered collar,
as the "Ěryǎ" says:
A garment with a turned collar is called ní,
an embroidered collar is called bó.
Covered with this embroidered skirt,
as the "Book of Songs" says:
The gentleman arrives,
in embroidered robes and skirt.
I wear the knee cover, and you wear the pendant,
as the "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
Zhù Mù said to his wife:
"When the world is in order,
I wear the knee cover and you wear the pendant;
when the world is in chaos,
I carry the burden and you wear the hat."
Upper dark and lower yellow,
as the "Records of Carriages and Attire" says:
The Yellow Emperor, Yáo, and Shùn let robes and garments hang down, and the world was governed.
This likely took inspiration from Qian and Kun,
hence the upper garment is dark and the lower garment is yellow.
Laughing at Hé Róng's scorched back,
as the "History of the Southern Dynasties" says:
Hé Jìngróng served as Minister of Personnel,
dignified and solemn by nature,
his attire bright and elegant.
Though Emperor Wǔ of Liáng wore washed clothes,
his attendants' clothes had to be clean and neat.
Once a courtier's belt was wrinkled,
the Emperor angrily said:
"Your belt is like a rope,
what do you intend to bind?"
Jìngróng, seeking favor,
often used glue to groom his beard,
and if his clothes were not neat,
he would lie on the bed to iron them,
sometimes scorching his back in the summer heat.
Surprised at Chén Xuān's ascent to the hall,
as the "Book of Chén" says:
Xú Líng served as Minister of Personnel,
carefully selecting talents,
and the gentry all admired him.
Chén Xuān, with a jade hairpin in his bun,
a red silk cloth wrapped around his head,
his robe sweeping his ankles,
boots reaching his knees,
without announcing his rank or origin,
went straight up to Xú Líng's seat.
Líng did not recognize him,
and ordered an official to take him down.
Xuān walked out slowly,
his demeanor calm and composed,
showing no sign of shame.
He wrote a letter slandering Líng,
which greatly troubled Líng.
Chǔ Zhuāng was seen in a broad robe,
as the "Mòzǐ" says:
"The King of Chǔ wore crimson garments and broad robes."
Shěn Qìng was soon heard of in his hasty attire.
The "Sòng Shū" says:
"Shěn Qìngzhī led troops to guard the eastern gate.
On the evening when Liú Zhàn was arrested,
the gate was opened to summon Qìngzhī.
Qìngzhī entered in military attire, wearing leather boots and bound trousers.
The emperor saw him and exclaimed in surprise:
'Why, sir,
are you dressed in such haste?'
Qìngzhī replied:
'Being summoned as troop commander at midnight,
I had no time to change clothes.'"
As for the various garments of Gēngshǐ,
the "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
"During the Gēngshǐ period,
official titles and ranks were bestowed upon petty merchants, cooks, and butchers.
Many wore embroidered outer garments, brocade trousers, chānyú, and zhūyú.
The wise of the time, seeing this,
considered their attire inappropriate.
The annotation states:
'Zhūyú
are large-sleeved garments,
like the guīyī worn by women.'
The "Fāngyán" says:
'Chānyú,
the shorter ones,
west of the pass are called liúqū.'
Guō Pú notes:
'Commonly known as juéyē.'
Based on this,
it means embroidered skirts added on top of zhūyú,
like today's bànbì.
Chōng is pronounced chōng.
Jué is pronounced qū.
Shēnshēng wore a one-sided garment,
as the "Guóyǔ" says:
'Jìn Xiàngōng sent Crown Prince Shēnshēng to attack Dōngshān,
and had him wear a one-sided garment.'
Dú is pronounced dǔ.
Fēnfēi and shùxuē,
winding and twisting.
The "Zǐxū Fù" says:
'Interwoven fine silks,
hanging like misty gauze.
Winding and twisting,
twisting like valleys.
Fēnfēi and shùxuē,
lifting sleeves, tailored sharply.'
The annotation states:
'The patterns of the garments resemble valleys.'
Fēnfēi
describes the long appearance of garments.
Yáng
means to lift.
Yì
refers to sleeves.
Shùxuē
means tailoring.
Covered with trailing garments,
as the "Shī" says:
'You have robes and skirts,
yet you neither trail nor gather them.'
Delighting in this warmth and comfort,
as the "Shī" says:
'How can I say I have no robes, seven in all?
But they are not as comfortable and auspicious as your robes.'
'How can I say I have no robes, six in all?
But they are not as comfortable and warm as your robes.'
The rituals of Dài are clear in the five principles,
as the "Lǐ·Shēnyī" says:
'The garment is made of twelve panels,
corresponding to the twelve months.
The sleeves are round to correspond to the compass;
the curved collar is like a square to correspond to the square;
the back seam reaches the ankles to correspond to straightness;
the lower hem is balanced like a scale to correspond to levelness.
Thus, the roundness
allows one to raise hands gracefully;
the straight back and square front symbolize upright governance
and righteous principles.
The lower hem balanced like a scale
stabilizes the mind and pacifies the will.
When the five principles are applied,
the sage wears it.'
The state of Qí also provided its three types of garments,
as the "Hàn Shū" says:
'The state of Qí had three types of garments:
officials presented caps and headbands as the primary attire,
plain white silk for winter garments,
and light silk gauze for summer garments.'
As for Yànhuí's yellow silk robe,
the "Sòng Shū" says:
'When Emperor Míng was ill,
he summoned Chǔ Yànhuí.
The emperor sat in his tent, weeping, and said:
"I am critically ill,
so I summoned you,
wishing you to wear the yellow silk robe."
Pointing to a large box by the bed, he said:
"Inside the document box,
I hope this box will never be opened again."
Yànhuí was also overwhelmed with grief.'
The yellow silk robe
was the attire of a wet nurse.
Luó
is pronounced lái kě qiē.
Biān Ràng's chānyú,
as the "Biān Ràng Biézhuàn" says:
'Ràng was talented, eloquent, and outstanding.
Kǒng Róng recommended him to Cáo Cāo, saying:
"Biān Ràng is insufficient to serve as a quilt for the nine provinces,
but more than enough to serve as a single-layer chānyú."'
Merely to display ritual,
as the "Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn" says:
'Attire is used to display ritual.'
Hoping to warm the skin,
as the "Shāng Jūn Shū" says:
'People of ancient times
wore garments that did not warm the skin,
and ate food that did not fill the belly.'
Admiring Zhū Bó's square collar,
as the "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
'Zhū Bó, styled Shūyáng,
at the age of twelve, could recite the "Shī" and "Shū."
He once visited Mǎ Yuán's elder brother, Kuàng.
Bó wore a square-collared garment
and walked with measured steps.'
Annotation:
'A square collar fastened below the neck,
is the attire of scholars.'
Praising Jiāng Chōng's curved hem,
as the "Hàn Shū" says:
'When Jiāng Chōng was first summoned to the Quǎntái Palace,
he wore a gauze silk single-layer garment
with a curved hem trailing behind, intersecting and overlapping,
a cicada-patterned headband and a swaying crown,
and feathered tassels,
his appearance very imposing.
The emperor said to his attendants:
"Yān and Zhào indeed have many extraordinary men."'
Annotation:
'Jiāoshū
resembles swallow tails hanging on both sides,
visible from behind.
The cicada-patterned headband
sways with each step,
and bird feathers are used for tassels.'
Sympathizing with Xīhuá's coarse cloth,
see the annotation for "coarse skirt of Xīhuá" in the "Winter Rhapsody."
The price soared for Wáng Dǎo's coarse silk,
as the "Jìn Shū" says:
'After Sū Jùn was pacified,
the treasury was depleted.
The storehouse only had several thousand bolts of coarse silk,
which could not be sold,
yet state funds were insufficient.
Dǎo, along with court officials, made single-layer garments from coarse silk.
Subsequently, scholars and commoners eagerly vied to wear them,
and coarse silk became expensive,
reaching one gold per duān.'
As for garments shaped like the guī and knife,
the "Shìmíng" says:
'Women's upper garment is called guī,
and the part hanging down
is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom,
like a guī knife.'
Shú
means connected,
the upper and lower garments linked together.
Displaying the designs of eagles and geese,
as the "Táng Shū" says:
'Emperor Dézōng bestowed seasonal garments on military commissioners and observation commissioners.
The imperial workshop weaved and presented them for approval.
The emperor said:
"In recent times, the bestowed garments
have had inconsistent patterns,
which is not according to regulation.
I now think:
military commissioners should have eagles holding ribbon bands,
symbolizing martial prowess to pacify their domains.
Observation commissioners should have geese holding ceremonial wěi,
symbolizing orderly ranks
and the dignity of shepherds."'
Ceremonial wěi
is an auspicious plant.
Criticizing those cormorants,
as the "Shī" says:
'The cormorant is at the weir,
yet its wings are not wet.'
As for one's own child,
Xǐ reported in writing:
"Níng Cháng always wears a black cap, cloth jacket and trousers,
and a cloth skirt.
He moves about the inner courtyards,
able to support himself with a cane,
not requiring assistance.
For the seasonal sacrifices,
he always exerts his own strength,
changing into a padded headcloth.
Thus, in Liáodōng, he had a white cloth unlined garment,
personally presenting the offerings and food,
kneeling and bowing to complete the rites."
He admired Wáng Yǔn's integrity.
The *Weishì Chūnqiū* states:
Wáng Yǔn was an official in the Ministry of Personnel,
selecting commandery governors.
Emperor Míng doubted that his appointments were not in proper order,
but upon summoning him in, his doubts were dispelled.
As he was sent out,
the Emperor, observing his worn clothes,
said:
"He is an honest official."
He recognized Róng Qǐ's straw raincoat.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
Lín Lèi and Róng Qǐqī wore garments of straw and straw raincoats.
He saw Dǒng Wēi's pieced-together silk.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
Dǒng Wēiniǎn arrived in Luòyáng,
lodging at the White Society.
In the market, he obtained torn and tattered silk pieces,
which he would stitch together to make clothes,
calling them the "hundred-patch garment."
As for the plain white garment without pattern,
the *Shìmíng* states:
Zhǎn,
is a garment that is smooth and plain,
flat and pure white without decorative patterns.
Zhǎn is sometimes written as tǎn.
The green outer garment with a yellow lining,
The *Shī* states:
Green is the upper robe, ah!
Green robe with a yellow lining.
Note:
The jū robe is yellow,
the zhǎn robe is white,
the yuán robe is black,
all with plain silk gauze as the lining.
Nowadays, it is not according to regulation,
used as a metaphor for a concubine overstepping her rank.
The clothing bestowed in the ninth month,
The *Shī* states:
In the seventh month, the Fire Star descends,
in the ninth month, clothes are bestowed.
Warning of the threefold stripping.
The *Yì* states:
One may be granted a leather belt,
but by the end of the morning, it is stripped away three times.
The Xiàng says:
To receive garments through litigation,
is also not worthy of respect.
In the state of Qí, it was heard that it reached only to the shin,
see the note on "Níng Shēng feeds the ox" in the *Gē Fù*.
Entering the Hàn palace, it never trailed on the ground.
The *Shǐjì* states:
Emperor Wén wore garments of plain silk.
His favored Lady Shèn,
wore clothes that did not trail on the ground.
Zǐxià, already distressed by his "hanging quail" garment,
The *Sūnqīngzǐ* states:
Zǐxià's family was poor,
his clothes were like hanging quails.
Someone said:
"Why do you not take office?"
He said:
"Among the feudal lords, those who are arrogant towards me,
I will not serve as their minister;
among the high officials, those who are arrogant towards me,
I will not see them again."
Lín Jì also wore garments of reeds.
The *Shuōyuàn* states:
There was a man from Qí named Lín Jì,
who wore reed garments to court when seeing Duke Jǐng.
The Duke said:
"Why do you wear the clothes of a petty man?"
Lín Jì said:
"One who wears a dog-fur robe does not necessarily bark like a dog;
one who wears a sheep-fur robe does not necessarily bleat like a sheep.
Now, my lord, you wear a fox-fur robe,
can you make the sound of a fox?"
The crimson knee-cover appears, coming from afar.
The *Yì‧Kùn* hexagram, second line, nine, states:
The crimson knee-cover comes from afar.
The embroidered robe is heard of in the direct commissioner.
The *Hànshū* states:
At the end of Emperor Wǔ's reign,
bandits and thieves arose in groups throughout the commanderies and kingdoms.
Bào Shèngzhī was appointed as a Direct Commissioner Envoy,
wearing embroidered robes,
and holding an axe to capture them.
Observing the colorful garments of Zhāng Shèng,
The *Nánshǐ* states:
Zhāng Shèng, in his youth, was devoted to filial conduct.
Even after reaching over thirty years of age,
he still wore the patterned clothes of a child and received canings from his father, Mù,
often amounting to several hundred strokes,
yet he wiped his tears and appeared joyful.
Delighting in the bright colors of Láizǐ's garments.
The *Xiàozǐ Zhuàn* states:
Old Láizǐ was seventy years old,
and his parents were still alive.
Láizǐ often wore brightly colored clothes,
and played like an infant.
Furthermore, there was Yuán Zhōng's visit to Wáng Lǎng.
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hànshū* states:
Yuán Zhōng, riding a boat and wearing a bamboo hat, visited Wáng Lǎng.
Seeing that Wáng Lǎng's attendants and servants all wore green and crimson colored clothes,
disapproving of such extravagance and luxury,
he immediately pleaded illness and departed.
Wèi Wén's treatment of Yáng Biāo.
The *Yáng Biāo Biézhuàn* states:
Wèi Wéndì ordered Yáng Biāo to wear a plain cloth unlined garment,
and treated him with the courtesy due a guest.
Jiāng Zhàn, washing his clothes, pleaded illness.
The *Sòng Shū* states:
Jiāng Zhàn, styled Huīshēn,
served as Minister of Personnel.
He had no spare clothes or surplus food.
Once, when summoned by the Emperor,
he happened to be washing his clothes.
He pleaded illness for a whole day,
and only rose after his clothes were ready.
Zǐfú spoke and was imprisoned.
The *Guóyǔ* states:
Jì Wénzǐ served as minister to Xuān and Chéng,
having no concubines clothed in silk,
and no horses fed on grain.
Zhòngsūn Tuó remonstrated, saying:
"People will think you are stingy,
and moreover, that you do not bring splendor to the state?"
Wénzǐ reported this to Mèng Xiànzǐ,
and Xiànzǐ imprisoned him for seven days.
From then on, Zǐfú's concubines wore clothes of no more than seven shēng cloth.
Note:
Zhòngsūn Tuó,
was Xiànzǐ's son, Zǐfú.
Ài,
means stingy.
As for Zhū Bó's large trousers,
The *Hànshū* states:
Zhū Bó was the Governor of Lángyá.
He ordered his subordinates to make many loose robes and large trousers,
which did not conform to regulations.
From then on, he ordered that the clothes of clerks and officials should be three inches from the ground.
Shào,
means trousers,
pronounced shào.
Juàn Shēng in full ceremonial dress,
see the note on "Juàn Shēng wears a quiver" in the *Jiàn Fù*.
Duke Huán of Qí disliked purple.
The *Yǐn Wénzǐ* states:
Duke Huán of Qí liked to wear purple,
and all the people of the state wore it.
The Duke was troubled by this.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Tell your attendants that you strongly dislike the smell of purple."
Thereupon,
within three days, no one within the borders wore purple.
Duke Wén of Jìn corrected customs.
The *Yǐn Wénzǐ* states:
In the past, the state of Jìn suffered from extravagance.
Duke Wén corrected this with frugality.
He then wore no double-layered silk,
and ate no meat with his meals.
Not long after,
all the people of the state wore clothes of coarse cloth
and ate unpolished millet.
The net garment of Xīlún,
The *Shíyí Jì* states:
In the western country of Xīlún,
the customs were pure and harmonious.
People lived to three hundred years of age.
They wove grass and hair into net garments,
like fine silk gauze.
In the sixth year of Yuánshòu,
they presented one set of net garments.
The Emperor, fearing that later generations would demand them,
burned them on the main crossroads.
The smoke had the aura of metal and stone.
The jade of Pínsī.
The *Shíyí Jì* states:
In the early years of Tàishǐ of Jìn,
people from the country of Pínsī came to court.
They used five-colored jade to make clothes,
like armor of today.
Sòng Jǐng's use of kingfisher feathers,
The *Shíyí Jì* states:
Duke Jǐng of Sòng hung clothes for the four seasons.
In spring and summer, they were adorned with pearls and jade;
in autumn and winter, they were warmed with kingfisher feathers.
Tián Wén's criticism of fine silk gauze.
The "Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ" states:
Tián Wén said to his father, Jìngguō Jūn:
"The ladies in your rear palace tread in garments of fine silk and gauze,
yet the scholars cannot even obtain short coarse cloth."
Those riding in great chariots wear garments like reed down.
The "Shī" says:
"Dà Chē" [The Great Chariot],
listens to the disputes between men and women.
The great chariot rumbles,
the felt garments are like reed down.
The great chariot rumbles on,
the felt garments are like crimson jade.
Annotation:
The senior officials of the Son of Heaven wear felt caps when making inspection tours.
Reed down,
refers to the initial growth of reeds.
Crimson jade,
is a reddish color.
Those who sacrifice to the First Silkworm wear garments like oak gall.
The "Zhōu Lǐ" says:
The Inner Department of Attire is in charge of the six garments of the Queen, including the oak gall garment.
Annotation:
The oak gall garment,
is a yellow mulberry garment,
its color is like oak gall dust,
resembling the first growth of mulberry leaves.
Oak gall,
also pronounced qiū liù qiē.
Graceful and majestic,
the ceremonial robe is fitting.
The "Shī" says:
Graceful and majestic,
the ceremonial robe is fitting.
Annotation states:
The ceremonial robe,
refers to the yú dí and quē dí robes.
Adornments of fox tails and tiger patterns,
the "Liáng Jì Biézhuàn" states:
Liáng Jì made a single robe with fox tails,
short on top and long on the bottom.
The "Yúfú Zhì" states:
The Tiger Guard and Martial Cavalry all wear single robes with tiger patterns.
The wonder of pheasant heads and asbestos cloth,
the "Jìn Shū" states:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
the Grand Physician Sīmǎ Chéngjù presented a pheasant head fur coat,
the Emperor considered it a strange skill and unusual attire,
forbidden by the rites and regulations,
and burned it in front of the palace hall.
The "Fùzǐ" states:
"Liáng Jì made asbestos cloth,
wore a single robe to meet guests,
while serving wine he lost a cup and soiled it,
feigned anger,
took off the robe and burned it,
the dirt was completely gone when the fire went out,
and it was brilliantly clean and white."
The distinction between primary colors and intermediate colors,
the "Lǐ" says:
The upper garment is of primary colors,
the lower garment is of intermediate colors.
The etiquette of holding and tucking the lapels,
the "Ěryǎ" says:
Holding the lapel is called jié,
tucking the lapel is called xié.
The system of Shang fire and Xia mountains,
the "Lǐ" says:
The Yǒuyú clan wore the fú,
the Xiàhòu clan wore the mountain pattern,
the Yīn wore the fire pattern,
the Zhōu wore the dragon emblem.
Annotation states:
The fú,
is the bì.
Shùn first made it,
to honor sacrificial garments.
From Yǔ and Tāng to the Zhōu,
added painted patterns.
The regulation of square front and truncated back.
The "Lǐ" says:
The bì,
for the ruler is vermilion,
for senior officials is plain,
for scholars is like a sparrow's color, made of leather.
Round,
tapered,
straight.
For the Son of Heaven, straight;
for dukes and marquises, square front and back;
for senior officials, square front and truncated corners at the back.
For scholars, straight front and back.
The bì,
is a covering,
made of leather.
Recognizing the Táng Emperor's three washings,
the "Táng Shū" says:
Emperor Sùzōng was frugal by nature,
once showed his sleeve to his close ministers and said:
"This garment has been washed three times."
Distinguishing Hàn Gāozǔ's five seasonal garments.
The "Hàn Záshì" says:
During Gāozǔ's time,
the Grand Herald, Minister Zhāng, received an edict at Chánglè Palace,
ordering the ministers to discuss the garments the Son of Heaven should wear to pacify the world.
Herald Zhào Yáo proposed spring,
Lǐ Shùn proposed summer,
Ní Tāng proposed autumn,
Gòng Yǔ proposed winter,
the five seasonal garments began from this.
Meeting Shān Fǔ and seeing mending,
the "Shī" says:
The imperial robes have flaws,
Zhòng Shānfǔ mends them.
Meeting Wǔ Gōng and being remade.
The "Shī" says:
"Zī Yī" praises Zhèng Wǔgōng.
How fitting the black robes are,
when worn out,
I will remake them.
How fine the black robes are,
when worn out,
I will reweave them.
How grand the black robes are,
when worn out,
I will make them anew.
Annotation:
Grand,
means large.
Shāng Zhòu threw himself into the fire covered in precious garments,
the "Liù Tāo" says:
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Zhòu covered himself in precious garments and threw himself into the fire to die.
Sòng Míng hated the wind and used leather.
See the annotation "Sòng Míng Lìngshǐ" in the "Fēng Fù".
Three generations to know about clothing,
the "Wèi Zhì" says:
Emperor Wén's edict stated:
"It takes three generations of elders to know about clothing,
five generations of elders to know about food and drink.
This means clothing and food and drink,
are difficult to understand."
The five colors then show their display.
The "Shū" says:
I wish to observe the images of the ancients,
the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and pheasants,
are depicted,
the ancestral vessels, algae, fire, powdered rice, axe, fu, fine silk, and embroidery,
with the five colors displayed in the five hues,
to make garments,
you make them clear.
Mǎ Yuán's hemp cloth,
the "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
Mǎ Yuán was sent by Wěi Xiāo to Gōngsūn Shù,
Shù arranged a grand display of palace guards to invite Yuán in,
after the exchange of courtesies was completed,
he was sent out to the guesthouse,
and Shù had a hemp cloth single robe made for Yuán.
Annotation:
The "Dōngguān Jì" says dábù.
Dábù,
is white cotton cloth.
Zhòngní's wide-sleeved robe.
The "Lǐ" says:
Confucius said to the Duke of Lǔ:
"I lived in Lǔ when young,
wearing wide-sleeved robes.
I lived in Sòng when grown,
wearing the zhāngfǔ cap."
Annotation states:
Féng means large.
Large-sleeved unlined garment,
worn by gentlemen with virtue and skill.
Coarseness already surprised Empress Mǎ,
the "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
Empress Mǎ of Míngdé,
often wore thick silk,
her skirt without hemming.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, when the various consorts and princesses came to pay respects,
seeing the Empress's robe coarse and rough,
they instead thought it was fine silk and gauze,
upon closer look,
they laughed.
The Empress explained:
"This silk is particularly suitable for dyeing,
so I use it."
All in the six palaces could not help but sigh.
Annotation:
Thick silk,
is heavy silk fabric.
Brightness again praised by Wáng Jí.
The "Hàn Shū" says:
Wáng Jí, styled Zǐyáng,
fond of carriages, horses, and clothing,
his personal upkeep was extremely bright and fresh,
yet when moving, what he carried was no more than a bag of clothes,
the world admired his integrity but found his extravagance strange.
It was rumored that Zǐyáng could make gold.
Some shake it off and thus bathe,
the "Lí Sāo" says:
Those who have just washed their hair must flick their caps,
One who has just bathed must shake out their clothes.
Some inscribed them and had them exchanged.
The *Records of Omissions* states:
Rèn Mù, at the age of fourteen,
was fond of learning.
When reading books, if he came across passages that resonated with him,
he would inscribe them on his clothes and the palms of his hands to record the matter.
His disciples, admiring his diligence in study,
would exchange his clothes for clean ones.
Wáng Dūn removed his old clothes with ease.
The *Book of Jin* states:
Shí Chōng prided himself on his extravagance and luxury.
In his lavatory, there were always over ten maidservants standing in attendance.
When guests used the lavatory,
they would all change into new clothes before leaving.
Most guests felt ashamed to remove their old clothes,
but Wáng Dūn removed his old clothes and donned new ones,
his demeanor showing no shame.
The maidservants said to each other:
"This man is surely capable of becoming a rebel."
Huán Chōng grew angry at the new clothes but was left without a rebuttal.
The *New Account of the Tales of the World* states: Huán Chōng disliked wearing new clothes.
After bathing,
his wife sent him new clothes.
Huán Chōng became angry
and urged her to take them away.
His wife had them brought back,
saying:
"If clothes are not worn new,
how can they ever become old?"
Huán Chōng laughed heartily and put them on.
He concealed his finery and favored the unlined garment,
as seen in the annotation of "the noble lady in her unlined garment" from the *Rhapsody on Brocade*.
He also used military means and discarded the ceremonial apron.
The *Treatise on Carriages and Attire* in the *Book of Han* states:
The Five Hegemons rose in succession,
and warfare did not cease.
The ceremonial apron was not a military adornment,
so it was discarded.
This is how later sages, in their endeavors, worked with hemp and silk,
transforming the primitive materials of feathers and hides from ancient times.
The *Book of Rites* states:
Confucius said:
"In ancient times, before the former kings had hemp and silk,
they clothed themselves in feathers and hides.
Later sages, in their endeavors,
worked with hemp and silk to create cloth and silk."
Crown
The crown is
an ornament for the head that distinguishes an adult.
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
The crown,
is a binding,
used to bind and hold the hair.
When a person demonstrates the completion of rites,
they have refined ornaments and patterns,
thus the crown was created to adorn the head,
distinguishing the adult.
As for the resplendent radiance,
Zuǒ Sī’s *Wèi Dū Fù* says:
Rows of attendants in abundance,
golden sable caps shining together.
Golden cicadas and kingfisher-green tassels,
the *Liáng Shū* states:
The emperor approached the hall,
and crowned the crown prince in the Tàijí Hall.
According to old regulations,
the crown prince wore a yuǎnyóu crown, golden cicada, and kingfisher-green tasseled cords,
and at this time an edict added a golden bóshān.
The wěimào of the Zhōu,
the móuzhuī of the Xià.
The *Lǐ* states:
The wěimào,
is the way of the Zhōu.
The zhāngfǔ,
is the way of the Yīn.
The móuzhuī,
is the way of the Xiàhòu clan.
Móu,
pronounced as móu.
Zhuī,
pronounced as duī.
The zhùhòu huìwén,
is the attire of law enforcement officials and close ministers;
the *Sān Lǐ Tú* states:
The legal crown is called zhùhòu huìwén,
also known as the xièzhì crown.
The pillar,
is five cùn high,
with fine silk as the extended tube,
and iron as the coiled pillar.
Cài Yōng’s *Dú Duàn* states:
The legal crown,
was a Qín institution,
worn by law enforcement officials.
Under Hàn regulations,
shìzhōng and zhōngchángshì all wore the huìwén crown,
with sable and attached cicada.
The gāoshān cèzhù,
is the ceremonial attire of messengers and receptionists.
The *Sān Lǐ Tú* states:
The gāoshān crown,
also called cèzhù.
It is nine cùn high,
with iron as the coiled beam.
Under Qín regulations,
it was worn by messengers and envoys,
and is now worn by receptionists.
Its origin lies in the shrunken seam,
the *Lǐ* states:
In ancient times, crowns had shrunken seams,
now they have horizontal seams,
thus the mourning crown’s reversal to auspiciousness,
is not ancient.
Note:
Explaining the confusion of people of the time,
the mourning crown’s shrunken seam,
is the ancient crown.
It began with the black cloth,
the *Sān Lǐ Tú* states:
The black cloth crown,
is the crown for the first capping.
In antiquity, crowns were made of cloth,
for purification they were dyed black,
as silk and damask were not yet available,
hence hemp was used.
The yellow silk floss like an orange,
the *Suí Shū* states:
All six ranks of miǎn crowns have yellow silk floss,
made of yellow silk,
as large as an orange,
from the crown prince down, all have rhinoceros horn paths and blue cords.
The hanging beads like dew.
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
Niú Hēng asked:
"Why are the miǎn beads called ‘profuse dew’?"
The answer was:
"They hang down attached,
like the profuseness of dew,
hence called ‘profuse dew’."
The Chǔ ruler’s tōngliáng,
the *Huáinánzǐ* states:
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had tōngliáng cords and tassels.
Note:
Tōngliáng,
is the yuǎnyóu crown.
The Lǔ scholars’ zhāngfǔ.
See the note on "Zhòngní’s wide sleeves" in the *Yī Fù*.
Observing the embroidered tassels of the feudal lords,
recognizing the vermilion cords of the Son of Heaven.
The *Lǐ* states:
A black crown with vermilion cord tassels,
is the crown of the Son of Heaven.
A black cloth crown with embroidered tassels,
is the crown of the feudal lords.
The note says:
These are both crowns for the first capping.
Summoning the gamekeeper but he did not advance,
see the note on "the gamekeeper did not advance" in the *Gōng Fù*.
Asking Zhòngní but he remained silent.
The *Jiāyǔ* states:
Duke Āi asked Confucius:
"What crown did Shùn wear in the past?"
Confucius did not reply.
The Duke said:
"I asked you a question,
why do you not reply?"
He replied:
"Shùn as a ruler,
cherished life and abhorred killing,
appointed the capable and entrusted the worthy.
Your lordship disregards this and does not follow it,
yet asks about his crown,
hence I delayed my reply."
The low and narrow had already been transmitted by Liáng Jì,
the *Xù Hàn Shū* states:
Liáng Jì altered the carriage and attire regulations,
making headgear low and crowns narrow.
Could tearing and destroying be endured by the paternal uncle?
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
The king sent Zhān Huánbó to deliver a message to Jìn, saying:
"I am to the paternal uncle,
like clothes having a crown and miǎn,
water and trees having a source and root,
the people having a strategist.
If the paternal uncle tears the crown and destroys the miǎn,
uproots the source and blocks the root,
and abandons his strategist,
even among the Róng and Dí, how could there be any remnant of me?"
As for the wondrous design of wearing the Big Dipper,
Cáo Zhí’s *Letter to Chén Lín* states:
To wear emerald clouds as clothing,
don the Big Dipper as a crown,
gird rainbows as a sash,
and link the sun and moon as pendants,
such attire is not unbeautiful.
However, emperors and kings do not wear it,
because their aspirations differ from heaven,
and their will is severed from the heart.
Inscribing the fine name of the southern department,
the *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
Cuī Lín served as a huángmén attendant,
participating in determining rituals and ceremonies.
The emperor once inspected the old storehouse,
and found an old crown,
inscribed with "Made by Cuī Chěng, Shàngshū of the Southern Department."
Turning to Xiū, he said:
"This is an old matter of your family."
Elegance already astonished Xīntài,
the *Liáng Shū* states:
Zhāng Xīntài served as a direct guard commander,
overseeing the Yǔlín guard,
well-versed in both refined and common matters,
his associations mostly with renowned scholars.
After duty, he wore a deer-skin crown,
carrying a plain qín.
This was reported to Emperor Wǔ,
the emperor said:
"How dare a military family child act like this?"
Simplicity and disregard again astonished Chén Líng.
The *Guóyǔ* states:
King Dìng sent Duke Shàn Xiāng on a mission to Chǔ,
passing through Chén.
Duke Líng of Chǔ, with Kǒng Níng and Yí Xíngfù, wore southern caps to visit the Xià clan.
Duke Shàn returned,
and reported to the king:
"Abandoning the gǔnmiǎn and wearing southern caps to go out,
is that not simplifying and disregarding?"
The note says:
It means simplifying and neglecting regular attire.
Despising Sòng Kāng’s display of bravery,
Huánzǐ’s *Xīn Lùn* states:
King Kāng of Sòng wore a headless crown to display bravery.
Mourning Zǐlù’s tying of the tassel.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
Shí Qǐ and Mèng Yǎn started a rebellion,
Zǐlù attacked them with a halberd,
and his tassel was cut.
Zǐlù said:
"A gentleman dies,
but his crown must not be removed."
He tied his tassel and died.
There was the grand style of Gài Kuānráo,
the *Hàn Shū* states:
When Gài Kuānráo was first appointed as a guard commander,
he wore a large crown,
and carried a long sword.
Slightly heard of Zǐxià’s praise.
The Book of Han states:
Dù Qīn, styled Zǐxià,
was wealthy but blind in one eye.
Mùlíng’s Dù Yè was also styled Zǐxià,
so people of the time called Qīn “Blind Dù Zǐxià”
to distinguish them.
Qīn disliked being insulted for his disability,
so he made a small cap,
only an inch wide.
Thus, the capital began to call Qīn “Small-Cap Dù Zǐxià.”
Dusting it off was indeed an expression to a close friend.
The Book of Han states:
Wáng Yáng and Gòng Yǔ were friends.
When Yáng became Inspector of Yìzhōu,
Yǔ, hearing of it,
dusted off his cap, awaiting Yáng’s recommendation.
Yáng recommended Yǔ to Emperor Chéng,
who summoned him to be a Grand Master.
Urinating in it was not favored by Confucian scholars.
The Book of Han states:
The Lord of Pèi was conquering territory in Chénliú.
A knight under his command, Lì Yìjī,
was from the same village.
Yìjī, seeing him, said:
“The Lord of Pèi is the one I wish to follow.”
The knight said:
“The Lord of Pèi does not like Confucians.
When guests arrive wearing caps,
he often takes off their caps and urinates in them.
You cannot persuade him as a Confucian scholar.”
As for the purple tassels of the State of Lǔ,
the “Jade Ornaments” chapter of the Rites states:
Black caps with purple tassels
began with Duke Huán of Lǔ.
The commentary says:
This was likely usurping the attire of the descendants of the kings of Sòng,
for tassels should use embroidered silk.
The plain silk cap of Duke Wén of Wèi.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The Dí people destroyed Wèi,
and Duke Huán of Qí enfeoffed Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Duke Wén of Wèi wore clothes of coarse cloth
and a cap of plain silk.
Commentary:
He used the mourning attire of feudal lords.
The extraordinary attire and azure clouds.
The Chǔcí states:
From youth I have loved this extraordinary attire,
girded with a long sword, splendid and tall,
crowned with a cap as lofty as the azure clouds.
Ornamented tassels and flying plumes.
Zhāng Héng’s “Seven Arguments” states:
A cap of fine mist,
tassels of flying plumes.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn making a bamboo-skin cap.
The Book of Han states:
Emperor Gāozǔ was a village head,
and made a cap from bamboo skin.
When he became noble,
it was called the Liú family cap.
Later, he ordered that unless one held the rank of Gōngshèng or above,
one could not wear the Liú family cap.
Duàn Jiǒng’s red headband.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Duàn Jiǒng annihilated the Qiāng,
and an edict awarded Jiǒng a red headband and a large cap.
Then there were those who wore this embroidered cap.
The Book of Songs states:
The officers of Yīn were diligent and swift,
performing the libation in the capital.
When they performed the libation,
they always wore embroidered caps.
Commentary:
Embroidered,
white and black.
The cap,
is the Yīn dynasty cap.
Wearing this cap string and covering.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The horizontal pendant, the cap string, and the covering
display their measure.
Commentary:
The cap string is the tassel from bottom to top,
the covering is atop the cap.
The cap officer in charge of the five types of ceremonial caps.
The Zhōulǐ states:
The cap officer is in charge of the king’s five ceremonial caps,
with red lining, extended cover, and loops,
five-colored silk cords,
with twelve clusters.
Commentary:
The extended cover
is the covering of the ceremonial cap.
The loops,
are small knobs.
The hairpin,
is what passes through.
The silk cords,
are made by intertwining five-colored threads,
hanging before and after the extended cover,
each with twelve strands,
which is called the deep-extended cover.
The clusters,
are completed units.
Each wrap of the cord passes through the five colors.
Twelve tassels mean twelve jades.
Yàn Huí’s regret over three cicadas.
The Book of Qí states:
Hé Jì was a Palace Attendant.
The emperor wished to transfer Jì to oversee selections,
and asked the Imperial Secretary Chǔ Yàn Huí.
Considering Jì’s seniority,
he wished to add the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Yàn Huí said:
“In Sòng times, Wáng Qiú went from Palace Attendant and Palace Secretary to solely serving as Minister of Personnel.
His seniority was similar to Jì’s.
Overseeing selections is a minor, light duty,
and does not warrant immediately adding Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
I and Wáng Jiǎn already have left-side cicada ornaments.
If we add Jì,
then among the eight high ministers, there will be three with cicada ornaments.
If we attach the titles of Xiāo or Yóu General,
it would not be too little.”
Thus, Jì was made Minister of Personnel,
with the added title of General of the Xiāo Cavalry.
Was it fear of Guō Zhāng’s cutting off the horn?
The Book of Jìn states:
Liú Tūn, styled Chángshēng,
was transferred to be a Palace Censor.
When the armory caught fire,
the Imperial Secretary Guō Zhāng led a hundred men to protect himself but did not fight the fire.
Tūn sternly questioned him.
Zhāng angrily said:
“I can cut off your horn!”
Tūn flared up and said to Zhāng:
“How dare you rely on favor to act arrogantly and abuse power?
The Son of Heaven’s legal cap, and you wish to cut off its horn?”
He demanded paper and brush to memorialize.
Zhāng prostrated and dared not speak,
and only after many explanations did the matter cease.
Only surprised at Liú Yú’s patching the holes.
The Book of Later Hàn states:
Liú Yú was executed by Gōngsūn Zàn.
Initially,
Yú upheld frugality and simplicity as his conduct.
When his cap was worn, he did not replace it,
but instead patched its holes.
When he was killed,
Zàn’s soldiers searched his inner quarters,
and found his wives and concubines dressed in fine silk and lavish ornaments.
People of the time doubted him for this.
Again, there is the splendor of the Upper Primordial’s nine stars,
the beauty of the Queen Mother’s morning tassels.
The Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
The Lady of Upper Primordial wore a cap of nine-star spirit mushroom and night radiance,
and the Queen Mother of the West wore the Supreme Truth morning tassel cap.
Wèi Shū’s lotus ornament.
The Scripture of Immortal Food and Clothing states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was at leisure in the Wèiyāng Palace,
when someone rode a white cloud chariot,
drawn by a white deer,
wearing a lotus cap,
and said:
“I am Wèi Shūqīng of Zhōngshān.”
The beauty of Jí Rú’s kingfisher feathers.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
During Emperor Gāozǔ’s time, Jí Rú,
and during Emperor Huì’s time, Hóng Rú,
were charming and favored,
sleeping and rising with the emperor.
Thus, during Emperor Huì’s reign,
all palace attendants wore kingfisher-feather caps and shell-decorated belts,
applied powder and rouge,
comparing themselves to Hóng, Jí, and their kind.
Emperor Wén of Sòng removing the sable to receive a subordinate.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn’s Book of Qí states:
The Palace Attendant has always been a close and intimate position.
In Wèi and Jìn, the selection gradually became more splendid and weighty.
During Emperor Wén of Sòng’s Yuánjiā era,
Wáng Tánshǒu, Yīn Jǐngrén, and others all served as Palace Attendants,
and were emotionally close and intimate.
Jǐngrén spoke with the emperor knee to knee.
The sable tail brushed the emperor,
and the emperor removed the sable tail and placed it on the table.
After speaking, he again placed it by hand.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ cutting off tassels to treat his officers.
The Shuōyuàn states:
King Zhuāng of Chǔ feasted his ministers with wine.
At dusk, the candles went out,
and someone tugged at a beauty’s clothes.
The beauty grabbed and broke the man’s cap tassel,
and told the king to quickly bring light to see who had the broken tassel.
The king said:
“I gave them wine,
causing them to get drunk and lose propriety.
How can I display a woman’s chastity and shame an officer?”
He then ordered all to cut off their cap tassels,
and only then relit the candles.
Crows gathering once moved Zēng Shēn,
see the “Crow Rhapsody” note on “gathering in the courtyard during Yú’s time.”
The flying cicada brought even greater joy to Zhū Yì.
The Book of Liáng states:
When Zhū Yì was appointed as a Palace Secretary,
it was during the autumn season when he first received the appointment.
A flying cicada happened to alight on Yì's cap.
At the time, everyone considered it an omen of the cicada ear ornament,
and indeed, later events turned out as predicted.
The names of the shōu and xǔ caps were already different.
The Book of Rites states:
The Zhōu had the biàn, the Yīn had the xǔ, and the Xià had the shōu.
The three kings all used leather caps with plain pleated skirts.
Xǔ is pronounced xǔ.
The styles of Qí and Chǔ were also distinct.
Mòzǐ states:
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí wore a tall cap and broad sash to govern his state.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ wore a bright cap with silk tassels and crimson robes with wide sleeves to govern his state.
Guǎn Zhòng once spoke about correcting faults.
See the annotation for "losing one's cap while drunk" in the "Ode to Wine."
Sūn Áo was just then pleased about carrying out an execution.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
King Zhuāng of Chǔ executed Shǐ Lǐ.
Sūnshū Áo made a cap and washed his clothes.
The annotation says:
Shǐ Lǐ
was a sycophantic minister.
When the wicked man was executed,
he knew he would be employed.
I have heard of Chén Bózhī's otter-skin cap.
The Book of Liáng states:
Chén Bózhī liked to wear an otter-skin cap.
Jiāng Chōng's cicada gauze cap,
see the annotation for "admiring Jiāng Chōng's curved hem" in the "Ode to Clothing."
The censor's zhì horn cap,
The Book of Táng states:
Censor Sòng Fàng requested to restore the placement of red robes and zhì caps in the inner corridor.
When there were offenders of the law,
the censors would wear them to impeach.
The imperial guards' pheasant tail cap,
The Hàn Official Ceremonial states:
The imperial guards' caps were adorned with pheasant tails.
The pheasant
is the most fierce and powerful among birds of prey.
Whenever it seizes something,
its claws shatter it.
The tails
were tributes from Shàngdǎng.
Shì Huì's fú miǎn cap,
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Shì Huì exterminated the Chìdí.
The Marquis of Jìn requested from the king
to bestow upon Shì Huì the fú miǎn cap and appoint him to command the central army,
and also serve as Grand Tutor.
The Marquis of Jìn's duān wěi cap.
The Guóyǔ states:
King Xiāng of Zhōu bestowed upon Duke Wén of Jìn,
commanding the Marquis of Jìn to enter wearing the duān wěi.
The annotation says:
It refers to the xuán duān robe
and the wěi mào cap.
Some were named after Fán Kuài.
Zhōu Qiān's Record of Carriages and Attire states:
Fán Kuài tore his clothes to wrap a shield,
wore it as a cap,
and forced his way into Xiàng Yǔ's camp.
Now the guards at the Sima palace gates wear it,
its design resembling a miǎn cap.
Some took Mùróng as their surname.
The Records of Former Yān states:
Mùróng Huī's great-grandfather Mòhùbá
saw that many youths in Yān and Dài wore bùyáo caps.
He admired them,
so he gathered his hair and adopted the cap.
The various tribes thus called him Bùyáo.
Later, the pronunciation became corrupted,
turning into Mùróng.
Thus, they took Mùróng as their surname.
The hanging tassels already indicated idleness and wandering.
The white band at the base of the cap thus revealed that one was not counted among the ranks.
The Book of Rites states:
Hanging tassels five inches long
are for idle wanderers.
A black cap with a white band at the base
is attire for those not counted among the ranks.
The annotation says:
Idle wanderers
are the indolent people.
Hanging tassels on a white cap,
not counted among the ranks,
is how those who do not follow teachings are banished.
There were also those who wore caps and yet had no ugly gentlemen.
Lù Jī's poem says:
Under caps and coronets, there are no ugly gentlemen;
with long tassels, all are outstanding people.
Losing it indeed signifies a petty man.
The Suǒyǔ states:
Fàn Xiànzǐ divined about hunting.
The divination verse said:
"The gentleman obtains a turtle,
the petty man loses his cap."
Fàn Xiànzǐ went hunting but gained nothing,
and lost his leopard-skin cap.
Yún Gōng was teased about burning the candle.
The Book of Qí states:
Lù Yúngōng was skilled at playing chess.
Once, while attending Emperor Wǔ at night,
his cap touched the candle flame.
The emperor laughed and said to him:
"The candle is burning your sable."
The emperor intended to appoint him as Palace Attendant,
so he teased him with this.
Jiāng Yān alone rejoiced in gathering firewood.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Book of Qí states:
When Jiāng Yān was thirteen years old,
he was orphaned and poor.
He once gathered firewood to support his mother.
While gathering firewood, he obtained a set of sable and cicada ornaments.
He intended to sell them to provide for his mother.
His mother said:
"This is an auspicious sign for you.
With your talent and conduct like this,
how could you remain poor and lowly forever?
You may keep it until you become a Palace Attendant and wear it."
Later, he indeed was appointed Palace Attendant.
Seen as impeaching and governing by the Chancellor of Liáng.
The Book of Hàn states:
Zhāng Chǎng's younger brother Wǔ served as Chancellor of Liáng.
Chǎng sent an official to see him off.
He asked:
"How will you govern Liáng?"
Wǔ said:
"To control a cunning horse,
one benefits from bit and whip.
I shall use the Zhùhòu Huìwén cap to impeach and govern it."
The official returned and reported this.
Chǎng said:
"He will certainly govern Liáng well."
Annotation:
In Qín, it was the law enforcement
cap, the law cap,
now worn by censors.
Following the preferences of Lord Zōu.
Hánzǐ states:
Lord Zōu liked to wear tasseled caps.
His attendants all made long tassels.
The tassels became very expensive,
and Lord Zōu was troubled by this.
Thereupon, Lord Zōu cut off his own cap tassels,
and no one in the state wore them anymore.
Seeing Jí Àn and avoiding the military tent.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
When Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng was received in audience at a banquet,
the emperor sometimes did not wear his cap.
But when it came to Jí Àn's audience,
the emperor would not see him without wearing his cap.
Once, the emperor was sitting in the military tent.
Àn came forward to present a matter.
The emperor was not wearing his cap.
Seeing Àn,
he withdrew into the tent.
Declining Wáng Mǎng and hanging the cap on the east gate.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
When Wáng Mǎng acted as regent,
his son Yǔ admonished Mǎng,
and Mǎng killed him.
Páng Méng said to his friend:
"The three bonds are severed.
If I do not leave,
disaster will befall me."
He then took off his cap, hung it on the east gate, and left.
The jiāo ràng cap understood the principle of seeking the old.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Mǎ Yuán had an old acquaintance with Gōngsūn Shù.
When Yuán entered Shǔ,
Shù met him
and was very pleased.
He wore the jiāo ràng cap
and stood at the position of an old friend.
The branch-wood cap heard the words criticizing the sage.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
Robber Zhí reproached Confucius, saying:
"You craftily fabricate words,
falsely praise King Wén and King Wǔ.
You wear a branch-wood cap,
gird yourself with the ribs of a dead ox,
wag your tongue and drum your lips,
arbitrarily create right and wrong,
to confuse the lords of the world."
Observing its adornment with sable and marmot fur.
Liú Zhēn's "Reply to Emperor Wén of Wèi" states:
The tails of sable and marmot
hang on the headbands of the attending ministers.
Adorned with tortoiseshell hairpins.
Bān Gù's "Letter to Dòu Xiàn" states:
The general, in his compassion,
bestowed upon me the tortoiseshell hairpin that the king personally favored.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Zhào's Lord Píngyuán sent an envoy to Lord Chūnshēn.
The Zhào envoy wanted to boast to Chǔ,
so he made tortoiseshell hairpins.
Lord Chūnshēn had over three thousand retainers,
The distinguished guests all wore pearl-studded shoes,
causing the envoy from Zhào great embarrassment.
Zhuāngzǐ’s mention of “mànhú”
is seen in the annotation “change this mànhú” in the “Ode to the Sword.”
The Qí general’s reply regarding the helmet.
The Qí Shū states:
Zhōu Pánlóng served as the Grand Administrator of Dōngpíng,
requested to be relieved of his duties,
and was granted permission.
He was then appointed as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Emperor Wǔ teased him, saying:
“You now wear the marten-tail and cicada-adorned cap,
how does it compare to a helmet?”
Pánlóng replied:
“This marten-tail and cicada-adorned cap was born from the helmet.”
The Yuǎnyóu crown was bestowed upon Yú Jìn,
as recorded in Emperor Wén of Wèi’s “Edict to Yú Jìn”:
In the past, Emperor Gāo of Hàn removed his own robe to clothe Hán Xìn,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn untied his own sash to bestow upon Lǐ Zhōng,
both instances where the sovereign honored and esteemed meritorious service at the time.
Now, I grant the Yuǎnyóu crown to you, General.
The Jìnxián cap was additionally conferred upon Lǐ Huì.
The Běi Qí Shū states:
When Wénxiāng succeeded to the enterprise,
he took the Jìnxián cap formerly belonging to the former Minister Over the Masses, Hóu Jǐng, and bestowed it upon Lǐ Huì, saying:
“If you serve me with straightforward loyalty,
I shall appoint you as one of the Three Dukes.
Do not follow the example of Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion.”
Some used golden marten-tail ornaments to exchange for wine,
as recorded in the Jìn Shū:
Ruǎn Fú, styled Yáojí,
served as an Adjutant in the Āndōng administration.
With disheveled hair, he indulged in drink,
paying no mind to official duties.
Later, he was appointed as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
His nature being fond of wine,
he once used his golden marten-tail ornament to trade for wine,
was impeached by the relevant officials,
but was pardoned by the emperor.
Some used yak-tail tassels to request punishment.
The Jiāyǔ states:
A senior official requesting punishment wears a white cap with yak-tail tassels.
Furthermore, it resembles the majesty of the Dark Warrior,
as stated in the Chūnqiū Fánlù:
The cap rests upon the head,
symbolizing the Dark Warrior.
The Dark Warrior,
is the most majestic and awe-inspiring in appearance.
Its image is at the rear,
yet it is placed at the head,
signifying the ultimate in martial prowess that remains unused.
