Gathering bamboo from Línglíng,
as recorded in the Zhōu Shū:
When King Chéng was about to undergo the capping ceremony,
the Duke of Zhōu sent someone to Línglíng
to fetch patterned bamboo for making the crown.
Recognizing the black silk cap of the city-dwellers,
as stated in the Shī:
Those gentlemen of the capital,
wear straw hats and black silk caps.
The annotation states:
Zīcuō,
is a black cloth cap.
Observing the straw garments of the rustic folk,
as stated in the Lǐ:
Wearing yellow robes and yellow caps for sacrifice
is to give rest to the field laborers.
The rustic folk wear yellow caps;
yellow caps,
are straw garments.
Following King Zhuāng of Chǔ’s preference,
as stated in the Huáinánzǐ:
King Zhuāng of Chǔ favored the huà crown,
and the state of Chǔ imitated him.
The annotation states:
The huà crown,
is the present-day strongman’s cap,
pronounced hú wǎ qiē.
Laughing at Fūchāi’s desire,
as stated in the Gǔliáng:
Duke Āi met with the Marquis of Jìn and the Viscount of Wú at Huángchí.
King Fūchāi of Wú said:
“Bring fine caps.”
Confucius remarked:
“Fūchāi did not know how to speak of caps,
yet desired caps.”
The annotation states:
He did not understand that caps have distinctions of rank,
and merely desired fine caps.
Wèi Móu’s admonition using the cap-ribbon,
as recorded in Huánzǐ’s Xīnlùn:
Wèi Móu visited the King of Zhào.
The king was having a cap-maker craft a cap before him,
and asked Móu about governing the state.
Móu replied:
“If Your Majesty truly values the state as much as this two-foot cap-ribbon,
then the state will be well-governed and peaceful.”
The king said:
“The altars of soil and grain are of utmost importance;
how can you compare them to a two-foot cap-ribbon?”
Móu said:
“When Your Majesty orders a cap made,
you do not employ those close to you,
but necessarily seek a skilled craftsman.
Is it not because if the ribbon is flawed, the cap cannot be completed?
Now, in governing the state, you do not seek worthy men,
but instead appoint those you privately favor.
Is this not treating the state as less important than the making of a two-foot cap-ribbon?”
The king had no reply.
Wáng Shēng’s words about loving fine silk,
as recorded in the Zhànguó Cè:
Wáng Shēng said to the King of Qí:
“Your Majesty’s love for the state and the people
is not as great as your love for a foot of fine silk.”
The king said:
“What do you mean?”
Shēng said:
“When Your Majesty has a cap made,
you do not employ your close attendants,
but employ craftsmen.
Why is that?
It is because they are capable.
Now, in governing Qí, you employ no one but your close attendants.
Therefore, I say it is not as great as loving a foot of fine silk.”
As for the plain silk tassels and hemp ceremonial caps,
the Wèi Liáozǐ states:
The Son of Heaven wears a black cap with black tassels;
feudal lords wear a plain cap with plain tassels;
senior officials and below wear a bleached silk cap with bleached silk tassels.
The Lúnyǔ states:
Hemp ceremonial caps
are in accordance with ritual.
Nowadays, they are made of silk,
which is more frugal.
Jade-adorned caps and golden-faced ornaments,
as stated in Jìn Chénggōng Suí’s “Seven Songs”:
Jade-adorned caps shine upon the head,
jade tassels illuminate the body.
Xú Yuán’s Shìcí states:
The Tōngtiān crown,
with its golden boshan and cicada ornament, is called the “golden face.”
The four stars of the eunuch constellation
were all added to the Qiǎoshì cap,
as recorded in the Hàn Yúfúzhì:
The Qiǎoshì cap is seven inches high.
It is not worn regularly;
only four eunuch attendants wear it during the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
in the imperial procession,
preceding the imperial carriage,
to correspond to the four stars of the eunuch constellation.
The dancers of the eight-row formation
all wear the Fāngshān cap,
as stated in the Sānlǐtú:
The multicolored Fāngshān cap
is made with its respective colored silk.
In the ancestral temple, the Son of Heaven’s eight-row music
and the Wǔxíng dance are performed by dancers wearing this.
Cherishing this cicada attachment,
as stated in Cài Yōng’s Dúduàn:
Palace Attendants and Regular Palace Attendants all wear the Huìwén cap with the addition of marten-tail and attached cicada.
The rustic fellow’s collection of kingfisher-feather caps,
as recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn:
Zhèng Zǐzāng was fond of collecting kingfisher-feather caps.
The Earl of Zhèng had a thief lure him out and kill him.
The gentleman remarked:
“If clothing is not appropriate,
it brings disaster upon oneself.”
Fànzǐ merely spoke of seeking goods,
as recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn:
Fàn Xiànzǐ sought goods from Shūsūn,
and had someone request a cap.
He took the pattern of his cap
and gave him two caps,
saying:
“That is all.”
Annotation:
Requesting goods
was merely a pretext for asking for a cap.
Master Xǔ was not known for weaving his own,
as recorded in the Mèngzǐ:
Chén Xiàng spoke of Xǔ Xíng’s doctrines to Mèngzǐ, saying:
“Although the Lord of Téng is worthy,
he has not heard the true Way.
A worthy man plows and eats alongside the people.
Now, Téng has granaries and treasuries;
this is exploiting the people to nourish himself.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Does Master Xǔ wear a cap?”
He replied:
“He wears a plain cap.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Does he weave it himself?”
He replied:
“He exchanges grain for it.”
Mèngzǐ said:
“Why does Master Xǔ not weave his own cap?
Why does he busily engage in trade with various artisans?”
He replied:
“The work of the various artisans certainly cannot be done while also farming.”
It is said:
"Can one who governs the world also farm at the same time?"
Chén Sī's wish to wear a military cap,
as recorded in the "Wèi Zhì":
Chén Sī Wáng Zhí submitted a memorial stating:
"If I could resign from my distant travels,
wear a military cap,
remove the crimson sash,
and don the blue silk ribbon,
that would be my greatest wish."
The censor's white brush hairpin.
See the "Bǐ Fù" "Mào bái shí yú Xīn Pí zhù".
All these serve to signify the principles of adulthood,
and fully express the adornment of literary refinement.
Bow
In ancient times, the sages bent wood to make bows,
sharpened wood to make arrows,
as recorded in the *Book of Changes*.
Thus, the world was subdued and the myriad people were governed.
As for the excellence of the six materials and seven types of wood,
the *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"The bow-maker makes the bow,
and must select the six materials in their proper seasons.
Once the six materials are gathered,
the skilled craftsman harmonizes them.
The wood (幹) is for achieving distance,
the horn (角) is for achieving speed,
the sinew (筋) is for achieving penetration,
the glue (膠) is for achieving cohesion,
the silk (絲) is for achieving strength,
and the lacquer (漆) is for withstanding frost and dew."
In general, there are seven types of wood suitable for the bow-stave:
Zhè mulberry is the best,
Yì wood is next,
Yǎn mulberry is next,
orange wood is next,
quince wood is next,
Vitex wood is next,
and bamboo is the lowest.
Note:
"Yì"
is pronounced "yì" (於力反).
"Yǎn mulberry"
is mountain mulberry.
The beauty of the three harmonies and nine balances,
the *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"Superior materials, skillful craftsmanship, and timely production
are called the 'Three Harmonies' (參鈞).
When the horn does not overpower the wood,
and the wood does not overpower the sinew,
this is called the 'Three Harmonies'.
Measuring its strength,
there is again the 'Three Harmonies'.
Three harmonies
are called the 'Nine Balances' (九和)."
Note:
"Again the Three Harmonies"
means that if the wood can withstand one shí,
adding horn enables it to withstand two shí,
and applying sinew enables it to withstand three shí.
Adorned with horn from the 𧤗,
the *Shuōwén* states:
"The horned 𧤗,
a beast resembling a pig,
its horn is excellent for making bows,
and it comes from the Húshī Kingdom.
is pronounced "duān".
The *Continued Book of Hàn* states:
"The Xiānbēi have wild horses, plains sheep, and horned-duān oxen.
Using their horns to make bows,
the world calls them 'horned-duān bows'."
Decorated with ivory弭 (弓弭).
The *Book of Songs* states:
"The four steeds are well-matched,
with ivory弭 and fish-skin quivers."
Note:
"弭" refers to the ends of the bow,
made of ivory.
Embroidered substance and fine materials,
Chén Lín's "Rhapsody on the Armory" states:
"Bows include the Wūháo and Yuèjí,
the Fánruò and Jiǎoduān,
with ivory弭 and embroidered substance,
wisely adorned with patterns."
The Wūháo with its straight grain.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"The Yellow Emperor rode a dragon ascending to heaven.
His minor officials could not ascend,
so they all grasped the dragon's beard.
The beard was pulled out and fell,
and the Yellow Emperor's bow also fell.
The people, gazing at the Yellow Emperor, embraced his bow and wailed.
Later generations thus named his bow 'Wūháo'."
The *Ancient Historical Investigations* states:
"Wūháo:
The branches of the zhè mulberry are long, and crows gather on them.
When about to fly,
the branch springs and hits the crow,
causing the crow to cry out.
Using zhè wood to make a bow,
it was thus named 'Wūháo'."
Some say it is for use in defense against thieves.
The *Astronomical Compendium* states:
"The Bow constellation is for defense against thieves and bandits."
Some record the principle of learning to make baskets.
The *Book of Rites* states:
"The son of a skilled bow-maker
must learn to make baskets."
Rewarding merit includes bestowals of red and black bows.
The *Book of Documents* states:
"King Píng bestowed upon Marquis Wén of Jìn one red bow, one hundred red arrows, ten black bows, and one thousand black arrows."
Shooting far illustrates the principle of the bending and returning body.
The *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"The Director of Bows and Arrows oversees the methods of the six bows, four crossbows, and eight arrows."
The note states:
"The six bows are:
the Wáng, Hú, Jiá, Yǔ, Táng, and Dà.
Those with little outward bend (往體) and much inward return (來體)
are called Wáng and Hú.
Those with much outward bend and little inward return
are called Jiá and Yǔ.
Those where the outward bend and inward return are equal
are called Táng and Dà.
For shooting far, use momentum;
for shooting deep, use direct force."
Obtaining the Fánruò from Fēngfù.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"The Duke of Zhōu assisted the royal house in governing the world,
maintaining harmony in Zhōu.
He bestowed upon the Duke of Lǔ the great carriage and banner,
the Huáng jade of the Xiàhòu clan,
and the Fánruò bow of Fēngfù."
Note:
"Fēngfù
was an ancient feudal lord.
Fánruò
was a great bow."
Using the peachwood bow against the ruler of Chǔ.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"King Líng of Chǔ was stationed at Gānxī.
In the evening,
Yǐn Zǐgé came for an audience.
The king spoke with him, saying:
'In the past, my first ancestor, Xióng Yì,
was secluded in the Jīng Mountains,
traveling in rough carts and worn clothes,
with only peachwood bows and thornwood arrows
to serve the royal affairs.'"
As for the principles of aiming high and shooting low,
see the note on "The Way of Drawing the Bow" in the "Heaven Rhapsody".
The etiquette of holding the弰 (弓弰) and承弣 (承弣),
see the note above on "'The Rites' mark the hanging of帨 (帨)".
Some say it began with Chuí and Yì.
The *Master Xún* states:
"Chuí made the bow."
The *Mòzǐ* states:
"Yì made the bow."
Some transmit that it originated from Bān and Huī.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"Shǎohào begat Bān,
who first made bows and arrows."
Note:
"Bān" is pronounced "bān".
The *Genealogical Records* states:
"Móu Yí made arrows,
Huī made the bow.
Bow and arrow are one implement,
yet two people are credited as makers;
this is questionable in meaning.
This text saying Bān made it
is correct."
Initially observing its curved form,
it bends back gracefully.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The curved bow
is today's弭弓."
Also, the *Records of Yèzhōng* states:
"Shí Hǔ's female riders held雌黃 (雌黃) curved horn bows."
The *Book of Songs* states:
"The well-trimmed horn bow,
bends back gracefully."
Suddenly obtaining its穹隆 (穹隆) shape,
it is received and stored away.
The *Explaining Names* states:
"Bow (弓)
means穹 (穹).
穹
means隆起 (隆起)."
The *Book of Songs* states:
"The red bow is relaxed,
received and stored away."
As for the yǎn mulberry bow, it was seen heralding the fall of Zhōu.
The *Discourses of the States* states:
"During the reign of King Xuān of Zhōu,
there was a children's rhyme:
'Yǎn mulberry bows and jī wood quivers,
will truly destroy the Zhōu state.'
There was a couple selling these implements;
the king arrested and executed them,
and they fled to Bāo.
They found an abandoned girl in the wild and raised her;
this was Bāosì,
who ultimately caused the fall of Zhōu."
The note states:
"Jī (箕) is pronounced 'qī',
a type of wood.
Fú (服)
is an arrow tube."
The Dàqū bow is also heard of being bestowed upon Lǔ.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"The ruler of Chǔ feasted with Duke Zhāo of Lǔ at the new terrace,
He had a man with a long beard act as his minister.
He was fond of using the Dà Qū,
but later regretted it.
Note:
Dà Qū,
is the name of a bow.
Qí Lián stacking four bows,
The "Diǎn Lüè of the Three Kingdoms" says:
Qí Lián Měng of Qi had great courage and strength,
when the Liang envoy came on a diplomatic mission,
there was a martial artist who sought to compete with him,
Měng carried two & - ;,
galloped left and right while shooting,
and took four bows,
stacking them and drawing them together,
the Liang people sighed in admiration.
Chén Qiú’s thousand paces.
The "Hàn Jì" says:
Chén Qiú was in Línglíng,
when the provincial soldiers Zhū Gài and others rebelled,
Qiú defended the city,
stringing a large tree to make a bow,
using feathered spears as arrows,
pulling the mechanism to shoot them,
they shot over a thousand paces,
and beheaded Gài and others.
Summoning the gamekeeper but he did not advance,
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
Duke Jǐng of Qí was hunting at Pèi,
he summoned the gamekeeper with a bow,
but he did not advance,
so the duke had him seized.
The gamekeeper explained:
"A banner is used to summon a senior official,
a bow to summon a scholar,
and a leather cap to summon a gamekeeper.
I did not see a leather cap,
so I dared not advance."
Flattering King Xuān of Qí and thus causing error.
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
King Xuān of Qí was fond of archery,
and delighted when people said he could use a strong bow.
The bow he usually used was no more than three dàn,
but he showed it to his attendants,
and when they tried to draw it,
they only pulled it halfway and stopped,
all saying it was no less than nine dàn,
and that no one but the king could use it.
Thus, King Xuān used a bow of no more than three dàn,
yet for his whole life believed it was nine dàn,
is that not lamentable?
If not an upright scholar,
who could avoid flattering the ruler?
Therefore, the rulers of disordered states
all exist by using three dàn as nine dàn.
As for Jìn Píng’s seven layers of armor,
The "Liè Nǚ Zhuàn" says:
Duke Píng of Jìn had a craftsman make a bow,
which took three years to complete,
but it could not pierce a single layer of armor.
The duke was angry,
and was about to kill the craftsman.
His wife went to see the duke and said:
"My husband made this bow with great effort.
The wood grew in the valleys of Tài Shān,
witnessing three periods of shade and three of sunlight each day,
it was fitted with horns of Yān oxen,
bound with sinews of Jīngmí deer,
and glued with fish glue from the Hé River.
These four materials
are the finest in the world.
If it cannot pierce a single layer of armor,
it is because you do not know how to shoot,
yet you instead wish to kill my husband,
is that not absurd?
I have heard the way of archery is:
the left hand as if pushing away,
the right hand as if clinging to a branch,
when the right hand releases,
the left hand remains unaware,
this is the way of archery."
The duke took her words as guidance,
and pierced seven layers of armor.
The bow craftsman was released,
and was rewarded with three yì of gold.
Note:
Zhá,
refers to armor layers.
Yān horns are excellent,
Chǔ sinews are fine,
Hé River glue is sticky.
Yán Gāo’s six jūn,
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
Lǔ attacked Qí,
and the soldiers were all seated in formation.
Yán Gāo’s bow was six jūn,
and everyone took turns to look at it.
Note:
Thirty jīn make one jūn.
Lín glue and thorn bamboo,
Yáng Shīdào’s "Poem on the Bow" says:
The frost thickens, the lín glue strengthens,
the wind is high, the moon’s shadow is round.
Birds fly following the imperial carriage,
geese fall chasing the singing bowstring.
Shěn Huáiyuǎn’s "Nányuè Zhì" says:
Sòngchāng County has thorn bamboo,
which grows to ten xún,
the locals take it
to make bows.
Yān horns and Chǔ sinews.
The "Liè Zǐ" says:
Jǐ Chāng learned archery from Fēi Wèi,
Fēi Wèi said:
"You must first learn not to blink,
and then you will be able to."
He also made him see small things as large,
Jǐ Chāng hung a louse by the window,
and gazed at it facing south,
after three years,
it appeared as large as a wheel,
then he used a bow of Yān horn,
and an arrow of northern péng grass to shoot it,
piercing the louse.
Chǔ sinews, see above.
Yǐn Xiāng inquiring of Xì Zhì,
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
Jìn and Chǔ fought at Yānlíng,
Xì Zhì encountered the soldiers of the King of Chǔ three times,
and each time he saw the King of Chǔ, he dismounted,
removed his helmet, and bowed respectfully.
The King of Chǔ sent the craftsman Yǐn Xiāng to present him with a bow.
Dù Yù’s note says:
Wèn,
means to give.
Zhū Mù reprimanding the Tiger Guard.
Xiè Chéng’s "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
Zhū Mù was a Shàngshū,
at the beginning of the year, during the百官朝賀 (hundred officials’ court congratulations),
a Tiger Guard stood on the steps,
placed a bow on the ground,
and said to the assembled officials:
"This is the Son of Heaven’s bow,
who dares to transgress?"
All the officials avoided it.
Mù reprimanded him, saying:
"The Son of Heaven’s bow
should be carried on the head,
how dare you place it on the ground?
This is great disrespect."
He immediately arrested the Tiger Guard and sent him to prison for punishment,
and everyone was solemn and respectful.
Then there are those stored in bow-case garments,
The "Shuō Wén" says:
Dú,
is a bow case.
The "Lǐ" says:
Wear it with a bow dú.
The "Shī" says:
Cross two bows in their chàng.
Adorned with gold and jade ornaments.
The "Ěr Yǎ" says:
Those with a rim are called gōng,
those without a rim are called mǐ.
Those adorned with gold are called xiǎn,
those adorned with shèn are called yáo,
those adorned with jade are called guī.
Note:
Yǒu yuán,
now refers to curved bows.
Wú yuán,
now refers to horn bows.
Xiǎn, yáo, guī,
refer to bows decorated with gold, clam shells, or jade at both ends,
hence the names.
Yáo,
pronounced yáo.
Some emphasize the affairs of men,
The "Lǐ" says:
When a boy is born, use a mulberry bow and péng grass arrows,
to shoot six times toward heaven, earth, and the four directions.
Note:
Heaven, earth, and the four directions,
represent all the affairs a man will undertake.
Some belittle the gains of the Chǔ people.
The "Jiā Yǔ" says:
King Gòng of Chǔ went on an excursion,
and lost his Wū Hào bow.
His attendants sought to find it,
but the king said:
"Stop.
A Chǔ person lost the bow,
a Chǔ person will find it,
why search for it?"
Confucius heard of this,
and said:
"What a pity his perspective is not broader,
he should have said, 'A person lost the bow,
a person will find it,'
why must it be Chǔ?"
The bow of Qūlú was presented as a congratulatory gift.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Zigòng persuaded the King of Yuè to send troops to follow Wú in attacking Qí.
The King of Yuè then sent envoys to present the bow of Qín Qūlú and the sword of Bùguāng as congratulatory gifts.
And these were the great bows of Yuèjí.
The Rites states:
The great bows of Yuèjí
are the weapons of war of the Son of Heaven.
When the high-flying birds are exhausted, they are stored away.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn captured Hán Xìn.
Xìn said:
"When the high-flying birds are exhausted,
the good bows are stored away.
When the enemy states are destroyed,
the strategist ministers perish.
Now that the realm is settled,
I should indeed be boiled."
Shooting at the Great Yin to rescue from an eclipse.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Tíngshǐ official is in charge of shooting the demon birds within the state.
If the birds or beasts are not seen,
then they use the arrows for rescuing the moon to shoot at night.
If it is a spirit,
then they use the bow of the Great Yin and the crooked arrows to shoot it.
Commentary:
Demon birds,
refer to owls and screech-owls,
birds with evil cries.
To rescue from a solar eclipse,
they beat drums facing north,
and shoot at the Great Yin.
To rescue from a lunar eclipse,
they beat drums facing south,
and shoot at the Great Sun.
They shoot with these bows and arrows.
As for Dōngmíng striking the water,
The Brief History of Wèi states:
In the north there was the state of Tuólí.
A maidservant of its king became pregnant.
The king wanted to kill her.
The maidservant said:
"There was a vapor like an egg that descended upon me,
therefore I became pregnant."
Later she gave birth to a crown prince.
The king abandoned him in a pigsty,
but pigs warmed him with their snouts;
he was moved to a horse stable,
and horses warmed him with their breath.
The king grew suspicious,
and considering him the crown prince,
ordered his mother to take him in and raise him.
He was named Dōngmíng,
and was often ordered to herd horses.
Dōngmíng was skilled at archery.
The king feared he would seize his state,
and wanted to kill him.
Dōngmíng fled,
reaching south to the Yān River.
He struck the water with his bow,
and fish and turtles surfaced to form a bridge,
allowing Dōngmíng to cross.
The fish and turtles then dispersed,
and the pursuing troops could not cross.
Dōngmíng subsequently established his capital,
ruling the land of Fūyú.
Hùntián pierced the ship.
The Foreign States Record from the Wú period states:
The ancestors of Fúnán
had a woman as their ruler,
named Liǔyè.
There was a man from the state of Mófú,
named Hùntián,
who diligently served the spirits.
The spirits were moved by his utmost sincerity,
and at night he dreamt of them,
who bestowed upon him a divine bow,
instructing him to board a merchant ship and go to sea.
Hùntián entered the temple,
and beneath the divine tree obtained the bow.
He then boarded a large ship and went to sea.
The spirits turned the wind,
causing him to reach Fúnán.
Liǔyè wanted to seize him by force,
but Hùntián raised the divine bow and shot at her,
piercing through the ship from one side to the other.
Liǔyè, terrified, submitted.
Hùntián thus became king of Fúnán.
There must be bows of hemp sinew and poplar wood.
Liú Xiàng's Garden of Stories states:
Qí attacked Lǔ.
Zigòng met with Duke Āi,
requesting aid from Wú.
The Duke said:
"What treasures of our former lords should be used?"
Zigòng said:
"If we use treasures and they give us troops,
this is not something to rely on."
Thereupon, they sent six bows of poplar wood and hemp sinew.
How could there be bows of gold arcs and jade strings?
See the annotation for "How could one use jade vessels" in the "Rhapsody on Boats."
For a twenty-dàn bow, only Yáng Kǎn had one.
The Book of Liáng states:
Yáng Kǎn possessed extraordinary physical strength.
The bow he used reached twenty dàn,
and on horseback he used a six-dàn bow.
For a three-hundred-jīn bow, one also hears of Gài Yán.
The Eastern View Hàn Records states:
Gài Yán could bend a three-hundred-jīn bow.
It also states:
Jì Tóng could draw a three-hundred-jīn bow.
Green sandalwood is both strong and sharp.
The Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú states:
In Hédōng there is Dútóu Mountain,
which has much green sandalwood,
which can be used to make excellent bows.
Lǜchén is also refined and sturdy.
The Extensive Records states:
Lǜchén
is the name of an ancient bow.
Liú Shào's "Rhapsody on Zhào Commandery" states:
Its implements include six bows and four crossbows:
Lǜchén, Huángjiàn, Tángxī, Yúcháng, Dīnglìng, and Jiǎoduān.
The ultimate perfection of principle lies in nine layers of lamination.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Son of Heaven's bow
is formed into a circle by nine layers of lamination,
the feudal lords' by seven layers,
the senior officials' by five layers,
and the gentlemen's by three layers.
Commentary:
If the material is excellent, then fewer laminations are needed.
Exhausting refined thought over three years.
See the annotation above for "Jìn Píng's seven layers of armor."
There is also the creation from Má Lín.
The Lost Records of Yuè states:
Má Lín Mountain,
where Gōujiàn, wishing to attack Wú,
planted hemp to make bowstrings.
The excellence of Yìlóu.
The Records of Wèi states:
Yìlóu bows are four chǐ long,
with power like a crossbow.
Their arrows use kǔ wood,
are one chǐ eight cùn long,
and have arrowheads of blue stone.
This was the ancient state of Sùshèn.
Praising this yang sound.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
In general, when selecting wood for the bow's body,
one desires it to be reddish-black and to have a yang sound.
Reddish-black indicates it faces the heartwood,
and a yang sound indicates it is far from the root.
Treasuring this superior construction.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
A bow six chǐ six cùn long
is called superior construction,
and is worn by upper-grade gentlemen.
Six chǐ three cùn long
is called medium construction,
and is worn by middle-grade gentlemen.
Six chǐ long
is called inferior construction,
and is worn by lower-grade gentlemen.
The Poetry mentions storing them in cases.
The "Zhōu Odes" in the Classic of Poetry states:
Then they put away their shields and spears,
then they cased their bows and arrows.
The Rites mark the hanging of the sash.
The Rites states:
In general, when presenting a bow to someone,
if the bow is strung, the sinew side should be upward;
if unstrung, the horn side should be upward.
The right hand holds the tip,
the left hand supports the grip.
Regardless of rank, the sash is hung.
Commentary:
The sash is a decorative scarf.
When bowing deeply, the sash hangs down.
Xú Yǎn received auspicious signs.
The Records of the Investigation of Things states:
King Xú Yǎn governed his state,
and his benevolence and righteousness were widely known.
Wishing to travel by boat to the central states,
he dredged a canal between Chén and Cài,
and obtained vermilion bows and arrows.
Believing he had received a heavenly omen,
he proclaimed himself King Xú Yǎn.
Tàizōng inquired about the grain pattern.
The Book of Táng states:
Tàizōng said to Xiāo Yǔ:
"From youth I loved bows and arrows,
and thought myself capable of understanding their utmost subtleties.
Recently I obtained over ten fine bows,
and showed them to a bow craftsman.
He said the wood's heart was not straight,
and the grain pattern was all askew.
Although the bows were strong and powerful,
the arrows they shot did not fly straight.
They were not fine bows."
I have pacified the four directions with bow and arrow,
and have used many bows.
The time since I gained the realm is short,
and I have grasped the principles of governance,
so I have not yet attended to the bow.
If even the bow can be neglected,
how much more so governance?"
From then on, he invited officials of the fifth rank and above in the capital to take turns staying overnight in the Secretariat of the Inner Court,
to inquire about the successes and failures of governance and education.
As for the name Tuīwáng,
the "Chūnqiū Zuǒzhùqī" says:
The Heavenly Bow governs the drawing of bows and crossbows,
and its divine name is Tuīwáng.
The name Qūzhāng,
the "Hétú" says:
The bow deity is named Qūzhāng,
which is also seen in "Tàigōng's Art of War."
Leaning against the western wall,
the "Yílǐ" says:
The archery announcer informs the guest:
"The bows and arrows are now prepared,
the officials request to shoot."
The guest and the grandee's bows,
lean against the western wall,
with arrows beneath the bows.
The treasure is in the eastern chamber.
The "Shū" says:
Hé's bow is in the eastern chamber.
Or inserted into a carved quiver,
Bào Zhào's poem says:
A felt belt with a pair of & - ;,
an ivory bow inserted into a carved quiver.
Or hung upon the Fúsāng tree.
Sòng Yù's "Dàyán Fù" says:
A red bow hangs upon the Fúsāng,
a long sword leans beyond the heavens.
Thus, the great target is raised,
the "Shī" says:
The great target is raised,
bows and arrows are drawn.
My bow is drawn.
The "Shī" says:
My bow is drawn,
my arrows are nocked,
I shoot that small boar,
and slay this great rhinoceros.
Then one sees its majestic and dignified bearing,
and the archery arrows are thus excellent.
The "Shī" says:
In archery, one is excellent.
Arrow
As for the arrows of Gōuyuè,
the Kàng Cāng Zǐ states:
The arrows of Gōuyuè,
with arrowheads of fine gold,
and feathers from fierce falcons,
if used to beat or flog, they are no different from withered wood;
but when sweeping away bandits and contending for supremacy,
or when displaying martial prowess to decide victory,
mounted upon powerful crossbows,
then within three hundred paces, no enemy can stand.
The fine products of Kuàijī,
the Ěr Yǎ states:
Among the fine products of the southeast,
are the bamboo arrows of Kuàijī.
The treasured hanging bamboo of the Eastern Chamber,
the Shū states:
The hanging bamboo arrows,
are in the Eastern Chamber.
The stored hù arrows in the courtyard of Chén.
The Guó Yǔ states:
Zhòngní was in Chén,
when a falcon alighted in the courtyard of the Marquis of Chén and died,
pierced by a hù arrow,
the stone arrowhead measured a foot and eight inches.
Chén Huì Gōng sent someone with the falcon to Zhòngní's residence to inquire about it.
Zhòngní said:
"This falcon has come from afar,
this is an arrow of the Sùshèn clan.
In the past, King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
opening roads to the nine Yí and eight Mán tribes,
ordering each to bring tribute of their local products,
not forgetting their duties.
Thus the Sùshèn offered hù arrows and stone arrowheads,
which were divided between Tàijī and Yú Gōng,
and enfeoffed to Chén.
If Your Lordship orders the officials to search the old treasury,
they can be found."
He ordered a search, and in a golden casket,
it was as he said.
Gěng Gōng applied poison,
the Xù Hàn Shū states:
The Xiōngnú defeated and killed King Āndé,
attacking Jīnpú City,
Gěng Gōng applied poison to arrows,
sending word to the Xiōngnú:
"The arrows of Hàn are divine,
those struck will have unusual effects."
Then he fired crossbows at them.
The barbarians struck by arrows,
saw their wounds boil,
and were greatly alarmed.
They said to each other:
"The Hàn soldiers are divine,
truly fearsome."
Thus they withdrew and left.
Láng Jī cut paper,
the Běi Qí Shū states:
Láng Jī, styled Shìyè,
once campaigned westward,
was besieged by bandits,
with provisions and weapons exhausted,
he then whittled wood to make arrows,
cut paper for feathers,
broke the siege and returned to court.
The Vice Director Yáng Yīn consoled him, saying:
"You were originally a civil official,
yet possess military strategy,
whittling wood and cutting paper for feathers,
neither had precedent,
the ingenuity of Bān and Mò,
how could surpass this?"
Fēi Wèi was trapped by Gān Yíng,
the Liè Zǐ states:
Fēi Wèi learned archery from Gān Yíng,
mastering all methods,
except the biting method was not taught.
Wèi secretly held an arrow to shoot Yíng,
Yíng bit and caught the arrowhead,
shot it back,
Wèi ran around a tree,
the arrow also circled the tree.
Yóu Jī excelled over Lǚ Qí.
the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Lǚ Qí shot King Gōng, hitting his eye,
the king summoned Yǎng Yóu Jī,
gave him two arrows,
ordering him to shoot Lǚ Qí.
He hit his neck, felling him onto his quiver,
and returned with one arrow.
Then there is the Xiàfú and Wàngguī already made,
the Zǐ Xū Fù states:
On the left, the carved bow of Wūhào,
on the right, the strong arrows of Xiàfú.
the Xīn Xù states:
The King of Chǔ carried the Fánruò bow,
and Wàngguī arrows,
to shoot rhinoceros in the Mèng marshes.
The three-edged and eight methods already perfected,
the Kāiyuán Wénzì states:
Three-edged,
refers to the arrows used in tube shooting today.
Flat-tipped,
refers to arrows used in sport shooting today.
Edge,
means ridge.
Tip,
means head.
the Zhōu Lǐ states:
The Director of Bows and Arrows oversees the eight arrow methods,
first called wǎng,
second called jié,
third called shā,
fourth called hóu,
fifth called zēng,
sixth called fú,
seventh called cháng,
eighth called bì.
Generally, wǎng and jié are for fire shooting,
used in defending cities and chariot battles.
Shā and hóu are for close-range shooting and hunting.
Zēng and fú are for fowling.
Cháng and bì are for scattered shooting.
These eight arrows,
bows and crossbows each have four,
wǎng, shā, zēng, cháng,
are for bows;
jié, hóu, fú, bì,
are for crossbows.
Releasing them as if breaking,
the Shī states:
Not losing their pace,
releasing arrows as if breaking.
Bundling them densely.
the Shī states:
The horn bow is curved,
the bundled arrows are dense.
Note:
Sōu,
means numerous,
fifty arrows make a bundle.
Hitting the shoulder and pinning the neck,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
The Qí army fled,
Jìn Zhōu Chuò caught up,
shot Zhí Chuò,
hitting his shoulder,
two arrows pinning his neck.
Dòu,
means neck.
Piercing the hub and passing through the shaft,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
The King of Chǔ fought with Ruò'áo,
Bó Fén shot the king,
the arrow passed through the shaft,
piercing the canopy hub.
The king sent a messenger to inspect the troops, saying:
"My late father King Wén conquered Xī,
obtaining three arrows.
Bó Fén stole two of them,
and now they are exhausted."
He beat the drum and advanced,
thus destroying the Ruò'áo clan.
Note:
Yì,
means to pass through,
pronounced yì.
Some turned their boat to face the enemy,
see the "Ode to Boats" note: "Sūn Quán turned it around to receive arrows."
Others followed the water to seek them.
the Zhu Xúnzhī Zhuàn states:
Lǔ Xiù attacked Xiāngyáng,
continuous crossbows fired wildly,
Xúnzhī ordered soldiers to follow the water and collect arrows.
Then there was Lǔ Zhuāng's Púgū,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ used a golden Púgū arrow to shoot Nángōng Cháng Wàn.
Note says:
Name of an arrow.
Hóng Chāo's Qí Wèi,
the Liè Zǐ states:
Péng Méng's disciple named Hóng Chāo,
angry with his wife and to frighten her,
drew the Wūhào bow,
with Qí Wèi arrows,
shot at her eyes.
The arrow tip touched her pupil but her eyelid did not blink,
the arrow fell to the ground without raising dust.
Guān Yǔ was hit and scraped the bone,
the Shǔ Zhì states:
Guān Yǔ was hit by a stray arrow,
piercing his left arm.
The physician said:
"The arrowhead is poisoned,
the bone must be scraped."
He immediately extended his arm to him.
The physician cut the flesh and scraped the bone while Yǔ remained composed.
Xiàng Yǔ shouted and it fell to the ground.
the Hàn Shū states:
Lóu Fán shot at Xiàng Yǔ,
as the bow released and the arrow was about to hit,
Yǔ glared angrily and shouted at the arrow,
causing it to fall to the ground.
Lóufán also feared for his life.
As for the “Flying Duck” and “Lightning Shadow” arrows,
Tàigōng’s *Six Secret Teachings* states:
“To break through strong formations,
to defeat powerful enemies,
the large yellow triple-linked crossbow
is accompanied by ‘Flying Duck’ and ‘Lightning Shadow’ arrows.”
Commentary:
“Flying Duck” arrows
have red shafts and white feathers,
with steel tips.
“Lightning Shadow” arrows
have blue shafts and red feathers,
with copper tips.
Poisoned iron and scorched copper.
*Records of the Investigation of Things* states:
“The mountain tribes of Jiāozhōu are called Lǐzǐ.
Their bows are several feet long,
with scorched copper arrowheads.
They coat the arrowhead tips with poison.
If a person is struck, they die immediately.
If the body is not promptly collected and buried,
it will quickly scorch and completely disintegrate,
leaving only bones behind.
Their custom forbids revealing the poison formula to outsiders.
To treat it,
they drink women’s menstrual blood and feces juice,
and sometimes recover.
Only those who shoot pigs or dogs suffer no harm,
because these animals eat feces.”
Chén Lín’s “Rhapsody on the Armory” states:
“Arrows include those from Shēn and Xī, Sùshèn arrows, Jùnlù arrows, Kōngliú arrows, scorched copper, poisoned iron, Gǎnzú arrows, and Mínghóu arrows.”
“Taking from Dǒngzé, one could never exhaust them.”
*The Zuo Commentary* states:
“During the battle between Jìn and Chǔ,
Chǔ’s Xióng Fùjī captured Zhì Yīng.
Zhì Zhuāngzǐ led his clan to counterattack.
Chú Wǔzǐ drove the chariot.
Every time he shot an arrow,
he selected a fine arrow,
and placed it in Chúzǐ’s quiver.
Wǔzǐ angrily said:
‘You are not seeking to capture the enemy,
but instead cherish the willow arrows.
The willows of Dǒngzé—
could they ever be exhausted?’”
Commentary:
“Zhì Yīng
is the son of Zhuāngzǐ.
Zōu
means fine arrows,
pronounced ‘cè liú’ in reverse.
Fáng
means arrow quiver.
Pú
refers to willow,
which can be used to make arrows.
Dǒngzé is located in Wénxǐ County.”
“Gathering from the Pú Terrace until it is nearly emptied.”
*Records of the Three Qí Regions* states:
“To the southeast of Yàncì lies the Pú Terrace.
Qín Shǐhuáng once halted beneath the terrace
and tied his horse with twisted willow.
To this day, willows grow along both sides of the road for a hundred paces.
Willow resembles water poplar,
but is sturdy enough to make arrows.”
“Some use mulberry bows and mugwort arrows.”
*The Book of Rites* states:
“When a boy is born,
a bow is placed to the left of the door.
After three days, he is carried out.
For a boy’s archery,
he shoots six arrows with a mulberry bow and mugwort arrows,
aiming at heaven, earth, and the four directions.”
Commentary:
“Mulberry bows and mugwort arrows
originate from ancient times.
Heaven, earth, and the four directions
represent the affairs that a man must attend to.”
“Red and black bows are both bestowed.”
See the commentary in “Rhapsody on the Bow”: “For rewarding merit, there is the bestowal of red and black bows.”
“The groom was seen while bathing the horse.”
*The Book of Rites* states:
“During the battle of Chéngqiū,
Xiàn Bēnfù drove the chariot.
The horse bolted and the reins broke,
causing Bēnfù to die.
When the groom bathed the horse,
he found a stray arrow in its flesh.
The lord said:
‘It was not his fault.’
He then composed a eulogy for him.”
“The Hàn general was astonished by shooting a stone.”
See the commentary in “Rhapsody on the Tiger”: “Lǐ Guǎng shooting a stone.”
“Some use it to encourage Zǐlù’s learning.”
*The School Sayings of Confucius* states:
“Zǐlù met Confucius.
Confucius asked:
‘What do you enjoy?’
He replied:
‘I enjoy long swords.’
Confucius said:
‘With your abilities,
if you add learning,
who could surpass you?’
Zǐlù said:
‘The bamboo of the southern mountains
grows straight without support.
Cut it and use it—
it can pierce rhinoceros hide when shot.
From this perspective,
what use is learning?’
Confucius said:
‘If you fletch it with feathers
and sharpen it into an arrowhead,
would it not penetrate even deeper?’”
“Some compare it to Shǐ Yú’s uprightness.”
*The Analects* states:
“Confucius said:
‘How upright Shǐ Yú was!
When the state was well-governed, he was like an arrow;
when the state was poorly governed, he was like an arrow.’”
“Metaphor: following others, and Hóu Jǐng’s ability to speak.”
*The Book of the Later Zhōu* states:
“Hèbá Yuè was killed at Héqū.
Tàizǔ led light cavalry to rush to Píngliáng.
At that time, Qí Shénwǔ sent his Chief Clerk Hóu Jǐng to recruit Yuè’s troops.
Tàizǔ encountered him in Āndìng
and said to Jǐng:
‘Although Hèbá Gōng is dead,
Yǔwén Tài still lives.
What are you doing?’
Jǐng replied:
‘I am like an arrow—
shot by others.
How can I decide for myself?’
He then returned immediately.”
“Metaphor: like an arrow on the string, and Chén Lín was pardoned.”
*Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wei* states:
“Chén Lín wrote a proclamation for Yuán Shào.
After Shào’s defeat,
he surrendered to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ said to him:
‘When you wrote for Běnchū in the past,
you could have just listed my crimes.
Why did you involve my ancestors?’
Lín said:
‘An arrow on the string
must be released.’
Tàizǔ then pardoned him.”
“As for the mighty title ‘Heavenly Strategy’ arrow.”
*The Book of Táng* states:
“Tàizōng campaigned against Liú Hēità in Féixiāng.
There was a fierce general of exceptional bravery
who charged directly at Tàizōng.
Just as their blades were about to meet,
Tàizōng shot him with a great arrow as the Heavenly Strategy Supreme General.
It pierced his heart and exited his back,
and he fell dead with the twang of the bowstring.
This arrow was then displayed to the northern tribes,
and the Turks saw it with awe.”
“The spirit’s name is Xùcháng.”
*Tàigōng’s Art of War* states:
“The spirit of the arrow
is named Xùcháng.”
“Shooting Dīng Hóu caused his illness.”
*Tàigōng’s Golden Coffer* states:
“When King Wǔ attacked Yīn,
Dīng Hóu did not come to court.
Shàngfǔ drew a portrait of Dīng Hóu
and shot at it for thirty days.
Dīng Hóu fell ill
and sent an envoy to offer submission.
Shàngfǔ then, on the days of Jiǎ and Yǐ, removed the head arrow;
on Bǐng and Dīng, removed the eye arrow;
on Wù and Jǐ, removed the belly arrow;
on Gēng and Xīn, removed the foot arrow.
Dīng Hóu’s illness then healed.
The four barbarian tribes heard of this and were terrified,
and Yuècháng offered a white pheasant.”
“Different from the armor-maker’s fear of injury.”
*Mencius* states:
“The arrow-maker is not more inhumane than the armor-maker.
The armor-maker fears injuring people,
while the arrow-maker fears not injuring people.”
“Lǔ Lián’s capture of Liáochéng.”
*The Book of Lǔ Lián* states:
“Yān attacked Qí
and captured over seventy cities.
Tián Dān defeated the Yān army
and recaptured Qí’s cities,
but only Liáochéng remained unconquered.
Lǔ Zhònglián then wrote a letter,
attached it to an arrow,
and shot it into the city.
The Yān general received the letter,
wept for three days,
and then took his own life.”
Regarding Ānyú's preparation of Jìnyáng,
the Hánzǐ states:
Zhì Bó was about to attack Zhào,
and Zhào Xiāngzǐ summoned Zhāng Mèngtán to ask him, saying:
"What shall we do about having no arrows?"
Mèngtán said:
"When Dǒng Ānyú governed Jìnyáng,
he used qiū, hāo, kǔ, and chǔ plants to construct the walls of the ducal palace.
If we dig them up and use them,
we will have more than enough arrows."
The lord said:
"What shall we do about having no metal?"
Mèngtán said:
"When Master Dǒng governed Jìnyáng,
he used refined copper for the pillar bases in the halls of the ducal palace's official residences.
If we dig them up and use them,
we will have more than enough metal."
Qiū is pronounced qiū,
chǔ is pronounced qiáng.
The vanguard was already performed by Wújì,
the Shǐjì states:
Lord Wèi Wújì advanced his troops to attack Qín,
the Qín army retreated and dispersed,
and thus he saved Hándān.
The King of Zhào and Lord Píngyuán personally went to welcome the lord,
and Lord Píngyuán carried a quiver of arrows, acting as the lord's guide.
Note:
Lán,
means a container for crossbow arrows,
pronounced lán.
The one who stayed behind to guard still heard of Níngzhuāng.
See the note on "orderly and patterned" in the "Robe Rhapsody."
There was also the Gāoméi prayer for children,
the Lǐ states:
On the day the dark birds arrive,
a grand sacrifice of a tàiláo is offered to Gāoméi,
the Son of Heaven personally goes,
the empress and consorts lead the nine concubines to attend,
in the ritual, the women the Son of Heaven has lain with,
are girded with a bow case,
and presented with a bow and arrows,
before Gāoméi.
Note:
Swallows, as they come to nest in the halls and eaves during the breeding season,
are an omen of hatching and nurturing offspring.
The officials of the matchmaking office take this as a sign of seasonal change.
Méi is said as méi,
meaning to deify it.
For further meaning, see the note on "sacrificing to Gāoméi" in the "Spring Rhapsody."
The Xià official presented the fú,
the Zhōulǐ states:
The Director of Bows and Arrows,
in mid-autumn presents arrow quivers.
Note:
Fú,
is a container for arrows,
made of animal hide.
Admiring those gǔ tails,
the Wèi Bǎiguānmíng states:
When the Three Excellencies are appointed, it is said,
"Bestow twelve arrows with chún tail, gǔ tail, and xiāo."
Xiāo,
is pronounced xiāo with the qiè.
Heavy are these metal arrowheads.
Yáng Xióng's Fāngyán states:
Metal arrowheads with trimmed feathers are called hóu,
bone arrowheads with untrimmed feathers are called zhì.
Note:
Metal arrowheads,
are now called pī arrows.
Bone arrowheads,
are now called gǔbào arrows, untrimmed,
meaning the bird feathers are naturally shallow and narrow,
and are not trimmed further.
Bào is pronounced báo.
Lǐ Líng's troops exhausted and left empty-handed,
the Hànshū states:
Lǐ Líng attacked the Xiōngnú,
in one day, five hundred thousand arrows were all exhausted.
The enemy attacked fiercely,
Lǐ Líng sighed and said:
"If only I could get a few dozen more arrows,
it would be enough to escape."
Wěi Xiāo, in desperate straits, tore down houses.
The Hànshū states:
Lái Xī attacked Wěi Xiāo,
Xiāo defended Luòyáng,
tearing down houses and cutting wood to make arrows.
Zhāng Hóu already spoke of the arrow piercing his elbow,
the Zuǒzhuàn states:
Jìn fought with Qí,
Xì Kè was wounded,
blood flowed down to his shoes,
yet he did not stop beating the drum,
saying:
"I am injured."
Zhāng Hóu said:
"From the start of the engagement,
an arrow pierced my hand and elbow,
I broke it off and continued driving,
the left wheel is stained dark red,
how dare I speak of injury!
My lord, endure it."
Xiǎndá was even more pleased to have the arrowhead removed from his eye.
The Qíshū, "Biography of Chén Xiǎndá," states:
Xiǎndá went out from the Dù Lǎo residence,
fought a great battle and defeated the bandits,
an arrow struck his left eye,
he pulled out the arrow but the arrowhead did not come out.
An old Fān woman from Dìhuáng Village was skilled in incantations,
first she nailed a nail into a pillar,
the old woman performed Yǔ steps and concentrated her energy,
the nail immediately came out,
then she used incantations to remove the arrowhead from Xiǎndá's eye.
The white ape embraced a tree and wailed,
the Hánzǐ states:
The King of Chǔ had a white ape,
the king shot at it himself,
but it caught the arrows and played with them.
He sent Yǎng Yóujī to shoot it,
as he adjusted his bow and straightened the arrow, before shooting,
the ape embraced a tree and wailed.
The goddess bore a grievance and wept by day.
the Yìyuàn states:
Lǐ Zēng of Yǒngyáng was traveling by a great stream,
two jiāo were in the water,
he drew his bow and shot at them,
hitting one, which died.
Zēng returned,
and then went out again to the market,
there was a woman in plain clothes, tears streaming,
holding the arrow he had shot,
Zēng found it strange and asked her.
The woman replied:
"What is the use of asking?
If it is yours,
I will return it to you."
She handed over the arrow and vanished.
Zēng turned back but before reaching home,
he died suddenly on the road.
Cutting down hāo and kǔ until none remained,
see the note above on "Ānyú prepared Jìnyáng."
Felling the Qí Garden was still not enough.
the Xù Hànshū states:
The emperor appointed Kòu Xún as Governor of Hénèi,
he sent documents to the subordinate counties,
drilling troops and practicing archery,
felling bamboo from the Qí Garden,
making over a million arrows.
As for hitting the turtle's back to present it,
the Zuǒzhuàn states:
Jìn and Chǔ fought,
Yuè Bó challenged to battle,
the Jìn men pursued him,
attacking from left and right.
Yuè Bó shot left at the horses and right at the men,
the attackers could not advance,
and he had only one arrow left.
A mílù appeared before him,
he shot the mílù, hitting its turtle back.
Note:
Lì,
means to hit,
the raised high part of the turtle's back.
Whipping the horse, he spoke of returning,
the Zuǒzhuàn states:
Mèng Zhīcè was the last to enter, acting as rearguard,
he drew an arrow and whipped his horse, saying:
"The horse would not advance."
Falling thickly like rain,
the Hànshū states:
Zuǒxiánwáng surrounded Lǐ Guǎng,
arrows fell like rain,
over half the Hàn soldiers died.
Suddenly like gadflies flying.
the Zhūgézǐ states:
If one can match the strength of three men,
his body and horse like glue and lacquer,
his hand and arrows like flying gadflies,
he truly deserves special favor.
Hitting the shield tile yet still powerful,
the Zuǒzhuàn states:
Zǐyuān Jié of Qí followed Xiè Shēngzǐ,
shot and hit the shield tile.
From the qú, it splashed onto the zhōu,
the bǐ penetrated three inches.
Note: tile,
is the ridge of the shield.
Qú,
is the yoke of the chariot.
Zhōu,
is the shaft of the chariot.
Tài,
means to splash.
Bǐ,
is the arrowhead.
Qú,
is pronounced qú.
Tài,
is pronounced yì.
Piercing through willow leaves without fail.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng of Liáng's "Ode to Bow and Arrow" states:
The bow uses sinew and horn,
The arrow employs skilled craftsmanship.
It also serves to encourage virtue,
Not merely for warfare.
Hitting the willow leaf target,
The ape falls from the vast sky.
Piercing the stone bridge, its force already unmatched.
The "Mǐnzǐ" says:
Duke Jǐng of Sòng commissioned a bowmaker to craft a bow,
After three years, it was presented,
Saying:
"My essence is exhausted in this bow."
After presenting the bow, he returned,
And died three days later.
The duke strung the bow and ascended the Tiger Enclosure Terrace,
Facing east, he shot,
The arrow flew over the Western Frost Mountain,
And landed east of Péngchéng.
Its remaining force, fierce and unrestrained,
Still pierced the stone bridge with its feathers.
To exhaust one's essence on a single bow and die for it,
How much more so for the world—how can it be alone?
Pacifying Tiānshān, even more remarkable.
The "Tángshū" says:
Xuē Rénguì defeated the Tiělè forces at Tiānshān.
At that time, the nine tribes numbered over a hundred thousand,
They sent several cavalrymen forward to challenge,
Xuē Rénguì shot three arrows,
Killing three men,
The rest immediately surrendered.
The army sang:
"The general with three arrows pacified Tiānshān,
The soldiers sang long songs as they entered the Hàn pass."
This is the advantage of the sage carving wood,
Extending its might across the ages.
See the annotation on "bending wood to make a bow" in the "Ode to the Bow."
Sword
In the past, Léi Huàn had obtained the precious swords from Fēngchéng,
and presented one of them to Zhāng Huá.
The Book of Jin states:
Between the constellations Dǒu and Niú, there was often a purple aura.
Hearing that Léi Huàn was exceptionally skilled in interpreting celestial phenomena,
Huá asked him about it.
Huàn said:
"The essence of a precious sword lies in Yùzhāng Fēngchéng."
He then appointed Huàn as the magistrate of Fēngchéng.
Upon arriving at the county,
he excavated the foundation of the prison building,
and found a stone case,
its radiance extraordinary,
containing a pair of swords.
When he wiped the swords with soil from the Western Hills of Nánchāng,
they gleamed brilliantly.
He sent one sword to Huá,
and kept the other for himself.
Upon receiving the sword, Huá replied:
"Upon careful examination of the sword's patterns,
this is indeed Gānjiàng;
why has Mòyé not arrived?
Nevertheless,
divine objects are destined to be reunited."
Huá also believed that the soil from Huàyīn was superior to that of the Western Hills,
so he sent one jin of it to Huàn.
Huàn used it to wipe the sword,
and its brilliance doubled.
Later, Huàn's son, Huá, wore his father's sword and crossed the Yánpíng Ford.
Suddenly, the sword leaped into the water.
He sent someone to dive and retrieve it,
but they saw two dragons,
and fled in fear.
Moreover, it is said:
Since Gélú discovered metal,
and Chīyóu initiated its use,
see the annotation "The Beauty of the Nǚhàn" in the "Ode to Metal."
Exhausting the sharpness of Chǔ's iron,
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
King Zhāo of Qín sighed while holding court,
and Fàn Suī asked for his fault.
The king said:
"I have heard that in Chǔ, iron swords are sharp but entertainers are clumsy.
If iron swords are sharp, the warriors are brave;
if entertainers are clumsy, their plans are far-reaching.
With far-reaching plans to command brave warriors,
I fear Chǔ may plot against Qín."
Draining the excellence of Qí's metal.
The Discourses of the States states:
Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"The state of Qí lacks armor and weapons,
what should be done?"
He replied:
"For minor offenses, impose fines of metal.
Use fine metal to cast swords and halberds,
testing them on dogs and horses;
use inferior metal to cast hoes and plows,
testing them on soil."
Thus, armor and weapons became abundant.
Tempered with clear waves,
honed with Yuè's whetstones.
Zhāng Xié's "Inscription for the Tài'ē Sword" states:
The Tài'ē sword,
its beauty passed down through generations.
Tempered with clear waves,
honed with Yuè's whetstones.
Brilliant as a shooting star,
The Ancient and Modern Annotations states:
Emperor Dà of Wú possessed six precious swords:
named Báihóng, Zǐdiàn, Bìxié, Liúxīng, Qīngmíng, and Bǎilǐ.
Deep and clear as reflecting water.
Liáng's Wú Jūn's "Poem on the Precious Sword" states:
I have a precious sword,
originating from the Kūnwú Stream.
Reflecting people as it reflects water,
cutting jade as if slicing mud.
This is the exquisite sharpness of the sheep's head,
Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Seven Commands" states:
The ingot from Yéxī,
the essence of Chìshān,
refined with a sheep's head,
forged into a blade.
The annotation states:
Refined using sheep's head bones.
The spiritual secret of the water's heart,
see the annotation "Duke of Zhōu built the city of Luòyì" in the "Ode to Spring."
Adorned with seven colors and nine blossoms,
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
Emperor Gāozǔ's serpent-slaying sword was adorned with seven-colored, nine-blossom jade,
and encased in a box of five-colored glass.
The blade always remained like frost and snow,
its radiance shining outward.
When the sheath was opened and the sword drawn,
a gust of wind would shoot forth.
The beauty of tortoise patterns and dragon motifs.
The "Ode to the Capital of Wèi" states:
Among swords, there are treasures of flowing colors,
and treasures of pure substance,
rainbow-like brilliance reflecting like waves,
with tortoise patterns and dragon motifs.
The wonder of raised and sunken patterns,
see the annotation below for "Fēnglóng wields the hammer."
The marvel of purple lightning and white rainbows.
See the annotation above for "Brilliant as a shooting star."
Though said to be a match for one man,
The Book of Han states:
Xiàng Yǔ failed to master swordsmanship,
and said:
"A sword is a match for one man,
not worth learning.
Learn to be a match for ten thousand men."
Moreover, it responds to the energies of the eight directions.
The Records of Omissions states:
King Gōujiàn of Yuè sacrificed white oxen and white horses to the mountain god of Kūnwú,
and forged eight swords,
each responding to the energies of the eight directions.
The first was named Yǎnrì;
pointing it at the sun,
the sunlight would dim even at noon.
The second was named Duànshuǐ;
drawing it across water, the water would part and not rejoin.
The third was named Zhuǎnpò;
pointing it at the moon,
the toad and rabbit would reverse their course.
The fourth was named Xuánjiǎn;
if a flying bird touched its blade,
it would be severed as if cut.
The fifth was named Jīngní;
sinking it into the sea,
whales and sharks would dive deep.
The sixth was named Mièhún;
carrying it while traveling at night,
one would not encounter demons.
The seventh was named Quèxié;
evil spirits would halt upon seeing it.
The eighth was named Zhēngāng;
it could cut jade and sever metal,
as easily as slicing through wood and earth.
Thus, the three worthies received gifts,
The Book of the Later Han states:
Hán Léng served as the Imperial Secretary,
alongside the Deputy Secretary Zhì Shòu and the Secretary Chén Chǒng.
All three were renowned for their talent at the same time.
Emperor Sùzōng once bestowed swords upon the various Secretaries,
but only these three received precious swords,
personally inscribed with their names:
"Hán Léng: Chǔ's Lóngquán,
Zhì Shòu: Shǔ's Hànwén,
Chén Chǒng: Jǐnán's Chuíchéng."
Contemporary commentators believed that Léng was profound and strategic,
hence he received Lóngquán;
Shòu was enlightened and literary,
hence he received Hànwén;
Chǒng was honest and unpretentious,
hence he received Chuíchéng.
And thus, the gentleman uses it for self-defense.
The School Sayings of Confucius states:
Zǐlù, dressed in military attire, visited Confucius,
drew his sword and danced with it,
saying:
"The gentlemen of ancient times
used swords for self-defense."
Confucius said:
"The gentlemen of ancient times
took loyalty as their essence,
and benevolence as their defense.
When faced with wrongdoing, they transformed it with loyalty;
when faced with violence, they resisted it with benevolence.
Why must one rely on a sword?"
Zǐlù straightened his robes and accepted the teaching.
Màoxiān saw it and exclaimed in astonishment:
This must be the essence of Yéxī,
see the annotation above for "the exquisite sharpness of the sheep's head."
The essence of Chìjǐn.
See the annotation below for "Xuē Zhú's appraisal."
The marvel of toppling Qín and leaving Wú,
Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Seven Commands" states:
Some gained fame by toppling Qín,
some flew away at night from Wú.
Annotation:
The King of Wú possessed the Zhànlú sword.
When the king became unrighteous,
the sword flew away at night,
entered the water,
and was obtained by the King of Chǔ.
The King of Qín heard of this,
sought it but could not obtain it,
and raised an army to attack Chǔ,
but ultimately did not acquire it.
The essence of the five mountains and the six directions.
The Annals of Wú and Yuè states:
Gānjiàng forged swords,
gathering the essence of the five mountains,
and the excellence of the six directions.
He observed the heavens and waited for the earth,
until yin and yang shone together.
The vessels of Chúnjūn and Zhànlú,
the names of Háocáo and Jùquè.
The Annals of Wú and Yuè states:
King Yǔncháng of Yuè commissioned Ōuyězǐ to forge five renowned swords,
three large and two small.
The first was called Chúnjūn,
the second Zhànlú,
the third Háocáo,
also known as Pányǐng,
the fourth Yúcháng,
and the fifth Jùquē.
They overshadowed three districts in value,
as Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Seven Commands" states:
"Their form awed Xuē Zhú,
their brilliance startled Fēng Hú.
Their worth surpassed three districts,
their fame outweighed two capitals."
They rivaled a thousand households in soaring renown.
Liáng's Cuī Róng's "Ode to the Sword" says:
"The precious sword emerges from Kūnwú,
with tortoise and dragon flanking the colored pearl.
The five essences first presented their art,
a thousand households vied to discuss the capital.
The aura from its sheath charges the Dipper and Ox,
its mountain-like form turns the pulley.
To know the world's most precious,
take this and ask Fēng Hú."
Dìngguāng was already known from Tàijiǎ,
as Táo Hóngjǐng's "Record of Blades and Swords" states:
"Tàijiǎ, in the year of Jiǎzǐ, cast a sword,
inscribed with the words 'Dìngguāng'."
Zhàodǎn was likewise passed down from Wǔdīng.
"Record of Blades and Swords" says:
"Wǔdīng, in the year of Wùwǔ, cast a sword,
named Zhàodǎn."
When warfare stirs, it flies.
"Records of Omissions" states:
"Zhuānxū possessed the Zhàoyǐng Sword and the Téngkōng Sword.
If there was warfare in any of the four directions,
these would fly pointing to that direction,
hence battles were won.
When not in use,
within their scabbards,
they often sounded like dragons and tigers roaring."
They were forged during a lunar eclipse.
"Book of Hàn" says:
"Censor-in-Chief Xiāo Wàngzhī investigated Hán Yánshòu, former Left Administrator of Féngyì, for taking official copper objects while in Dōng Commandery,
waiting for a lunar eclipse to make blades, swords, hooks, and guards,
imitating the Imperial Workshop.
Yánshòu was sentenced to be beheaded at the waist."
Considering these divine objects,
they are ultimately destined to be reunited.
See the annotation above on "Léi Huàn obtaining the precious swords of Fēngchéng."
Thus, Xuē Zhú's appraisal:
"Chronicles of Wú and Yuè" states:
King Yǔncháng of Yuè commissioned Ōuyězǐ to forge five renowned swords.
He showed Háocáo to Xuē Zhú.
Zhú said:
"Now, precious swords possess the five colors,
but now seeing Háocáo, it is dull and lacks splendor,
its radiance has perished,
its spirit is gone."
He showed him Jùquē.
Xuē Zhú said:
"This is not a precious sword.
For in precious swords, gold and tin are harmoniously combined,
their aura like clouds and mist.
Now its brilliance has already separated."
He showed him Yúcháng.
Zhú said:
"The essence of metal follows its grain,
from base to tip it does not reverse.
Now Yúcháng reverses base to follow the tip,
it is a sword that goes against the grain."
He showed him Chúnjūn.
Zhú, startled, said:
"Brilliant like the blossoms of the bending sun,
deep and serene like lotuses first born in the lake.
Its patterns like the march of arrayed stars,
its light like water overflowing a pond.
This is Chúnjūn."
The King said:
"A guest offered thirty districts, a thousand fine horses, and two cities of a thousand households to buy this sword.
Is it acceptable?"
Xuē Zhú said:
"No.
I have heard that when this sword was first made,
Mount Chìjǐn cracked and yielded tin,
the Ruòyē stream dried up and yielded copper.
The Master of Rain sprinkled the path,
the Duke of Thunder struck the drum,
the Celestial Emperor loaded the charcoal,
and Tàiyī descended to observe."
He showed him Zhànlú.
Zhú said:
"Excellent!
It holds the essence of metal and iron,
emits the spirit of silver and tin.
It can repel enemies and defeat foes.
If a ruler has rebellious schemes, it will leave for another state."
Yǔncháng presented Zhànlú to Wú.
Prince Guāng of Wú assassinated King Liáo of Wú.
Zhànlú left for Chǔ.
King Zhāo awoke and obtained it.
He summoned Fēng Húzǐ and asked him:
"What is this sword worth?"
He replied:
"Mount Chìjǐn has already closed,
the Ruòyē stream is deep and unfathomable.
The host of spirits have ascended to heaven,
Ōuyě has died.
Even if one offered a city's weight in gold,
filled the river with pearls and jade,
one could not borrow it for a single viewing,
let alone for fine horses or cities of ten thousand households?"
Ōuyězǐ's work,
see the annotation above on "Chúnjūn and Zhànlú."
The Táo clan showed no discrepancy in width and narrowness,
see the annotation below on "Zhōu officialdom lists three regulations."
The Zhì clan were especially skilled in polishing and sharpening.
"Book of Hàn" says:
"The Zhì clan, through polishing and sharpening, achieved a tripod feast."
Annotation:
"Polishing and sharpening"
means forging blades and swords.
The Yuè maiden's skill in striking the ape,
"Chronicles of Wú and Yuè" states:
Fàn Lǐ said to the King of Yuè:
"In Yuè there is a maiden,
who comes from within the southern forests.
I wish you would inquire from her the way of hand-to-hand combat."
As the maiden was about to appear,
on the road she met an old man,
who called himself Old Man Yuán.
He said:
"I hear you are skilled with the sword,
I wish to see it once."
Thereupon he pulled up a bamboo grove.
The maiden immediately seized the tip,
the old man grasped the base and thrust at the maiden.
The maiden then raised her staff and struck him.
Old Man Yuán flew up into a tree,
transforming into a white ape.
The maiden went to see the King of Yuè.
The King ordered the most talented of the five commands to learn from her.
At that time,
all called it the Yuè Maiden Sword.
The cruelty of the Lord of Jǔ testing on people.
"Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The Lord of Jǔ, Yǔyú, was cruel and fond of swords.
Whenever he cast a sword,
he would invariably test it on people.
Grand Officer Wū Cún led the people of the state to drive him out."
As for obtaining the iron from Mount Niútóu,
"Record of Blades and Swords" states:
"Kǒng Jiǎ, in the year of Jiǎchén, obtained iron from Mount Niútóu,
and cast a sword,
four feet one inch long."
And acquiring the copper from Jí Commandery,
the annotation to "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"From a tomb in Jí Commandery, a copper sword was obtained,
three feet five inches long,
the so-called Gānjiàng."
Its edge could cut jade.
"Lièzǐ" says:
"King Mù of Zhōu campaigned against the Western Róng.
The Western Róng presented a sword from Kūnwú.
Its blade was red,
cutting jade like cutting mud."
Its inscription was heard to strike a bell.
See the annotation below on "Picking up shoes, how could it be like an awl?"
Though there are those named Zhènshān and Chénshuǐ,
"Record of Blades and Swords" states:
"Dàowǔ of Later Wèi cast two swords,
one named Zhènshān,
the other named Chénshuǐ."
They also cut rhinoceros and intercepted swans.
Cáo Zhí's "Seven Exhortations" says:
"Cutting rhinoceros and elephants on land
is not enough to be called outstanding.
Intercepting swans following the waves,
the water does not moisten the blade."
Wearing the cold stars of the Northern Dipper,
"Chronicles of Wú and Yuè" states:
"Wǔ Zǐxū, crossing the river,
untied his sword and gave it to the old fisherman, saying:
'Within this sword are the seven stars of the Northern Dipper pattern,
its value is a hundred gold.'"
Felling the lush pines of the southern mountain.
"Biographies of Immortals" states:
"Gānjiàng and Mòyé made swords for the Lord of Jìn.
After three years they were completed.
The swords had a female and a male,
renowned vessels of the world.
So they presented the female to the lord,
keeping the male for themselves.
He said to his wife:
'I have hidden the sword in the shade of the southern mountain,
the sunny side of the northern mountain.
Where pines grow upon the stone,
the sword lies within.
If the lord becomes aware,
he will kill me.
With over ten attendants singing and playing the zither,
a sword worth a hundred gold pieces,
he said to his son:
"When I visit you,
you must provide men, horses, wine, and food for a grand feast,
lasting ten days before I depart.
The household where I die
shall receive the sword."
Gāohuáng’s sword was three feet long.
The Book of Hàn states:
Gāozǔ attacked Qíng Bù,
was struck by a stray arrow,
and asked a physician,
who said:
"The illness can be cured."
Gāozǔ said:
"I seized the realm with a three-foot sword,
is this not fate?
Fate lies with Heaven;
what use is even Biǎn Què?"
The Wèi tradition speaks of the Fēijǐng design.
In the Diǎnlùn by Wèi Wéndì, it is said:
Wèi Crown Prince Pī forged a hundred-fold precious sword,
four feet two inches long,
weighing one catty and fifteen liǎng,
quenched in the clear Zhāng River,
whetted on jiānzhū stone,
adorned with patterned jade,
sheathed with rhinoceros horn,
its light like a shooting star,
named Fēijǐng.
Jiānzhū,
is a type of green whetstone,
pronounced jiān zhū.
The Hàn responded to the great horizontal omen.
The Dāojiàn Lù states:
Hàn Wéndì cast three swords,
named Shénguī,
carved with many turtle shapes,
to correspond with the great horizontal portent.
The wearing of oxen has long faded.
The Book of Hàn states:
Gōng Suì was Governor of Bóhǎi,
focused on agriculture,
urged people to sell their swords to buy oxen,
and sell their knives to buy calves,
saying:
"Why wear oxen and carry calves?"
Guarding the road, virtue grows ever brighter.
The Xiánxián Xíngzhuàng states:
Wáng Liè, styled Yànfāng,
in the state there was a man who stole an ox,
the owner caught him,
the thief said:
"I was momentarily confused,
since you have pardoned me,
I beg you not to let Wáng Liè know."
Liè heard of it,
and gave him a bolt of cloth, saying:
"Shame for evil gives rise to goodness,
hence I reward him."
Within a year,
an elderly traveler carrying a heavy load,
a man helped carry it,
for several tens of li.
Shortly after, the old man traveled again,
lost his sword on the road,
a passerby guarded it,
until dusk,
the sword’s owner returned,
saw him,
it was the man who had carried the load before.
The old man told Liè,
who recognized him as the former ox thief.
As for the anger provoked by sleeping and tasting,
see the annotation on "Chǔzǐ zhī jí Pú Xū" in the Chē fù.
Leaning a sword by the door is an old transmitted method.
The Wàn Bì Shù states:
Draw a sword and lean it by the door,
and children will not cry at night.
The White Emperor is called the Great Marsh.
The Book of Hàn states:
Gāozǔ, as a village head, escorted convicts to Líshān,
passed through a marsh at night,
a great serpent blocked the path,
he drew his sword and cut the snake,
the snake split in two,
the path opened.
After traveling several li,
drunk,
he lay down to sleep.
Later travelers reached the snake’s place,
an old woman wept at night,
people asked why she wept,
she said:
"My son was the son of the White Emperor,
transformed into a serpent,
blocking the path,
was killed by the son of the Red Emperor,
hence I weep."
People thought the old woman dishonest,
wanted to trouble her,
but she suddenly vanished.
Zhū Yún requested the Shàngfāng sword.
The Book of Hàn states:
Emperor Chéng’s Chancellor Zhāng Yǔ,
as the emperor’s teacher held the position of Tèjìn,
was highly respected.
Zhū Yún submitted a memorial requesting an audience,
with the high officials present,
Yún said:
"Today’s court ministers cannot rectify the state above,
nor benefit the people below,
all hold sinecures and feed on empty titles.
I wish to request the Shàngfāng beheading sword,
to cut off the head of one sycophantic minister,
to warn the rest."
The emperor was greatly startled,
asking who it was.
He replied:
"Ānchāng Hóu Zhāng Yǔ."
The emperor was enraged.
The Duke of Yú’s endless demands.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Initially,
Yú Shū possessed jade,
the Duke of Yú requested it,
he did not present it,
but later regretted it,
and offered it.
The duke then requested his precious sword,
Shū said:
"This is insatiable,
insatiability will reach me."
Thereupon he attacked the Duke of Yú.
Emperor Xuān’s feelings were unforgettable.
The Hànshū Zhuàn states:
After Emperor Xuān was enthroned,
Empress Xǔ was a Jiéyú,

The emperor then issued an edict seeking the old sword from his humble days,

Wú Jì Zhá passed through Xú,

Jì Zhá knew this,
as he was on a mission to a superior state,

Returning to Xú,

His attendants said:
'The Lord of Xú is dead,

Yáng Xiū was once remembered.

Wèi Wéndì admired Yáng Xiū’s talent,

King Zhāo cast into the Five Peaks.

King Zhāo of Zhōu, Xiá, cast five swords and cast them into the Five Peaks.
Wénmìng hid one in Kuàijī.
The Dāojiàn Lù states:
Xià Yǔ, styled Gāomì,

hid it in the belly of Qínwàng Mountain in Kuàijī,

Harvesting rice, how could it be like a sickle?

The Fēijǐng sword,
its might eclipses the bright sun,
its aura forms a purple rainbow.
Using it to reap harvests,

No distinction.
Note:
Jué,
is a sickle.
Picking up shoes, how could it be like an awl?
The Shuōyuàn states:
Gānjiàng Mòyé made bells that did not ring,
using them to pick up shoes,
It is not even as good as a two-copper awl.
White-haired, he once was pointed at,

The *Yuèjué Shū* says:
The King of Chǔ ordered Fēng Húzǐ to go to Wú,
to see Ōuyě and Gānjiàng,
and have them forge iron swords.
Ōuyě and Gānjiàng excavated Cí Mountain,
drained its streams,
and took iron essence to make three swords:
the first, Lóngyuān;
the second, Tài'ē;
the third, Gōngshì.
When the swords were completed,
Jìn and Zhèng heard of them,
but sought them in vain.
The army of Jìn besieged the city of Chǔ,
and for three years it did not lift.
Then, drawing the sword Tài'ē,
he ascended the city wall and brandished it;
the three armies were defeated and routed,
the soldiers were bewildered,
blood flowed for a thousand *lǐ*,
and the heads of the men of Jìn and Zhèng all turned white.
The King of Chǔ asked Fēng Hú:
"Now, a sword—
it is merely iron—
can it truly possess spirit and essence?"
Fēng Hú said:
"Shénnóng used stone to make weapons,
Huángdì used jade to make weapons,
Yǔ used bronze and iron to make weapons,
and all under heaven submitted.
This too is the spirit of bronze and iron,
the virtue of jade and stone."
How valiant was Zhūxū!
The *Shǐjì* says:
Zhūxū Hóu Zhāng resented the Lǚ clan's monopoly of power.
He often attended Empress Lǚ's drinking feasts.
Empress Gāo had Zhāng serve as the wine officer.
Zhāng said:
"Your subject is of military stock;
I request to enforce the drinking according to military rules."
Empress Gāo permitted it.
When the wine was in full swing,
Zhāng rose to dance and said:
"I request to sing a song of plowing the fields."
The Empress Dowager laughed and said:
"How would you know about farming matters?
Try and tell me."
Zhāng said:
"Plow deep and sow thickly,
plant the seedlings sparsely;
those that are not of the proper kind,
hoe them up and remove them."
Empress Gāo fell silent.
After a while,
one of the Lǚ clan members avoided drinking.
Zhāng chased him, drew his sword, and beheaded him.
Since the Empress Dowager had already permitted Zhāng to enforce the drinking by military law,
she had no grounds to punish him.
Xiàng Zhuāng merely acted thus.
The *Hànshū* says:
The Lord of Pèi, with over a hundred horsemen, went from Bàshàng to see Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén.
Yǔ then detained the Lord of Pèi for a drink.
Fàn Zēng repeatedly signaled Yǔ to attack the Lord of Pèi,
but Yǔ did not respond.
Fàn Zēng rose and went out,
and said to Xiàng Zhuāng:
"Our king is too soft-hearted.
You go in,
perform a sword dance,
and take the opportunity to attack the Lord of Pèi,

Zhuāng entered,
and offering a toast, said:
"In the army, there is nothing for entertainment;

He then drew his sword and began to dance.
Xiàng Bó also rose to dance,
constantly using his body to shield and cover [the Lord of Pèi],
and thus Gāozǔ managed to escape.
Melting one's body to achieve something,
the *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* says:
When Gānjiàng was forging a sword and had not yet succeeded,
he then said:
"In the past, when my master practiced smelting,
the essence of metal and iron would not melt,
and both husband and wife entered the smelting furnace."
Mòyé said:
"Our master personally melted his body to complete the object;
what difficulty would I have?"
Thereupon, Gānjiàng and his wife cut off their hair and clipped their fingernails, throwing them into the furnace.
They had three hundred maidens blow the bellows and load the charcoal,
and the metal and iron then melted,
thus completing the swords.
The male was called Gānjiàng,
and bore a tortoise-shell pattern;
the female was called Mòyé,
and bore a smooth grain.
Gānjiàng hid the male sword and presented the female,

How can a substitute form be pursued?
The *Shénxiān Zhuàn* says:
When a true person departs from the world,
they often use a sword to substitute their form.
After five hundred years,
the sword can also become spiritually transformed.
Once Shǔlòu was bestowed,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
When Wú was about to attack Qí,
the ruler of Yuè led his multitude to pay court.
The people of Wú were all pleased,
but only Zǐxū feared, saying:
"This is fattening Wú [for the slaughter]."
The king was angry,
and sent someone to bestow upon him the sword Shǔlòu to die by.
Note:
Shǔlòu
is a sword.
Just then, Dùyóu was presented as a gift.
The *Shǐjì* says:
King Zhāo of Qín sent Bái Qǐ to attack Hándān.
He declined and refused to go.
So he sent Wáng Hé to replace him,
and the Qín army was indeed defeated.
Qǐ said:
"You did not heed my plan;
now what do you think?"
The King of Qín heard this and was furious.
He stripped him of rank to become a common soldier,
and exiled him to Yīnmì.
When he reached Dùyóu, ten *lǐ* west of Xiányáng,
he was given a sword to kill himself.
Juàn shēng wore a léijù sword,
the *Hànshū* says:
Bào Shèngzhī was a direct imperial envoy,
touring the commanderies and kingdoms.
He had long heard of Juàn Bùyí's worthiness.
When he reached Bóhǎi,
he sent an official to request an audience with him.
Bùyí wore a *jìnxián* cap,

The note says:
Léijù
is a sword with a wooden pommel.
Léi means imposing and grand.
Hán soldiers obtained Tángxī.
The *Zhànguó Cè* says:
The swords of Hán soldiers came from Míngshān, Tángxī,
Mòyáng, Yuǎnféng, Lóngyuān, and Tài'ē.
They could sever horses and oxen on land,
and cut through wild geese in water.
They were famous implements under heaven.
The knight was merely said to be bestowed,
the *Dōngguān Hànjì* says:
During the time of Shìzǔ,
a vassal king presented a famous horse and a precious sword,
worth a hundred pieces of gold.
The emperor used the horse to pull the drum carriage,
and bestowed the sword upon a knight.
Hēi Luǎn ultimately suffered no loss.
The *Lièzǐ* says that Wèi's Hēi Luǎn, harboring a grudge, killed Qiū Bǐngzhāng.
Qiū Bǐngzhāng's son, Lái Dān, plotted to avenge his father.
But Dān's spirit was very fierce,
his form very exposed,
and he was also ashamed to borrow strength from others,
vowing to kill Hēi Luǎn with his own hand and sword.
But Hēi Luǎn had the strength to resist a hundred men,
and he viewed Lái Dān as if he were a fledgling chick.
Lái Dān shed tears and plotted with his friend Shēn Bào.
Shēn Bào said:
"I have heard that Wèi's Kǒng Zhōu's ancestor obtained three precious swords from Yīn.
A child wearing them
could repel the multitudes of three armies.
Why not request them?"
Lái Dān went to Wèi,
saw Kǒng Zhōu,
performed the rites of a servant,
and requested first to hand over his wife and children,
then speak of his desire.
Zhōu said:
"I have three swords;
you may choose among them.
The first is called Hánguāng.
Looking, it cannot be seen;
wielding it, one does not know what it touches.
Void and without boundary,
it passes through things without being felt.
The second is called Chéngyǐng.
At the transition of dawn,
at the time between dusk and light,
facing north to observe it,
dimly, as if something exists,
but it has no discernible form.
When it touches an object,
there is a faint sound,
and it passes through the object without harming it.
The third is called Xiāoliàn,
By day it shows its shadow but not its light,
by night it shows its light but not its form.
When it touches an object, it passes through with a swishing sound,
closing up again immediately after passing,
so swift that it feels no pain and leaves no bloodstain on the blade.
These three treasures have been passed down for thirteen generations,
yet they have never been put to use.”
Lái Dān requested the lowest-grade sword,
so Kǒng Zhōu returned his wife and children to him,
knelt down, and presented him with the lowest-grade sword.
Lái Dān bowed twice and accepted it.
Carrying the sword, he followed Hēi Luǎn.
Hēi Luǎn was drunk,
lying on his back beneath the window.
Lái Dān struck Hēi Luǎn three times from the neck to the waist.
When Hēi Luǎn awoke,
he angrily said to his wife:
“You let me fall while I was drunk,
making my throat sore and my waist stiff.”
Note:
Hidden resentment,
private hatred.
Lù,
means weak.
Huō,
pronounced as xiū bó fǎn.
Never put to use,
means unable to harm anything.

The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
In Jīng, there was a man named Cì Fēi,

Xīndū praised fine jade,
see the annotation in “Ode to Jade”: “Wáng Mǎng concealed treachery in the mallet and pig.”
Féng Shí received a patterned rhinoceros horn.

Féng Shí inherited the title of Mǔ Gōngzhǔ and was enfeoffed as Huòjiā,

Léi Gōng struck the drum,

Fēng Lóng wielded the mallet.

Then forged and smelted,

Fēng Lóng wielded the mallet,

Lingering brocade, stars aligned,

Its light like scattered lightning,

icy blade, dew formed.

The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
Wǔ Yún fled from Chǔ,

After crossing the river,

Wǔ Yún untied his sword and gave it to him,
