and a thousand yì of gold.
How could it be worth merely a thousand-gold sword?”
In the end, he did not accept it.
When Zhāng Huà saw it,
he was filled with admiration and awe.
Delving into the profound principles,
savoring the dazzling splendor.
A guest, influenced by this legacy,
pondered it repeatedly,
a spiritual connection across a thousand years.
Daring to raise a humble tune,
he composed a song as follows:
“Guǎn Cén shines with five colors,
The *Jìn Shū* says:
Liú Yào of the Former Zhào,
considering himself different from others in appearance,
feared he would not be accepted by society,
so he hid in Guǎn Cén Mountain,
devoting himself to music and books.
Once, while resting at night,
two young boys entered and knelt, saying:
‘The King of Guǎn Cén sends his humble servant to pay respects to the Zhào Emperor.’
They presented a sword,
placed it before him, bowed twice, and left.
By candlelight, he examined it:
the sword was two zhang long,
with extraordinary luster,
a red jade scabbard,
and an inscription on the back,
saying:
‘Wield this divine sword,
to dispel all poisons and shine brightly.’
He then wore it.
The sword changed into five colors with the four seasons.
The *Zhōu Guān* lists three grades.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* says:
The Táo shì made swords,
with the blade five times the length of the hilt,
weighing nine luè,
this was the upper grade,
worn by upper-ranking officers.
With the blade four times the length of the hilt,
weighing seven luè,
this was the middle grade,
worn by middle-ranking officers.
With the blade three times the length of the hilt,
weighing five luè,
this was the lower grade,
worn by lower-ranking officers.
Note:
The hilt is five cun long,

Guard,
is what people hold above the tán.
Luè,

Already skilled in sugarcane technique,

When Emperor Wén was crown prince,

When Hóu Jǐng usurped the throne,

The sword worn by Hóu Jǐng,

Lǒngxī entrusted with decisive authority,
The *Jìn Shū* says:
Zhāng Guǐ governed Liángzhōu,

Prince Mó was very pleased,

Hénèi added sighs of sorrow.
Xiè Chéng’s *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Zhāng Yè of Wújùn, styled Zhòng Shū,

Grieving that his father’s body was not returned,

he would take his father’s sword to Hénèi,
and pour libations at the place where his father died,

Zhōu Yú once held and wielded it,
The *Dāo Jiàn Lù* says:
During Sūn Quán’s Chìwū era, someone obtained Hán Xìn’s sword,

Táo Jūn was forging and refining.
The *Dāo Jiàn Lù* says:
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng ordered Táo Hóngjǐng to forge thirteen divine swords,
symbolizing the intercalary months.
Already indebted to Mèng Cháng’s favor,
Shěn Yuē’s “Memorial to the Crown Prince Thanking for the Bestowal of Mèng Chángjūn’s Sword” says:
Tián Wén valued spirit and reputation,
surpassing even the Four Lords.
With a precious sword at his side,
he could intimidate Qín and Chǔ.
A man of high stature, deeds of great renown,

I respectfully and carefully admire and wear it,

I am also moved by the gift of the square mirror.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng wrote in his "Letter of Gratitude for the Gift of the Square Mirror Sword":
As soon as the jade case was opened,
exquisite wonders dazzled the eyes;
when the ivory clasp was first unfastened,
beautiful adornments were displayed in all their splendor.
Yánpíng eventually transformed and departed,
see the annotation above on "Léi Huàn obtaining the precious sword from Fēngchéng."
The armory was suddenly burned and abandoned.
The *Book of Jìn* states:
The armory caught fire,
and treasures from successive dynasties,
including Confucius's shoes, Emperor Gāozǔ's serpent-slaying sword, and Wáng Mǎng's head, were all consumed by the flames.
Zhāng Huà saw the dragon sword fly out through the door.
I shall thus continue this ode to the spring sun,
though I feel ashamed before the beauty and elegance of your song.
A jī (small table) is a guǐ (support),
something used to support objects.
From the Shìmíng.
Guǐ means gé (pavilion, shelf),
pronounced guǐ.
Thus, for auspicious events, the jī is changed,
for inauspicious events, the jī remains the same.

For auspicious events, the jī is changed;
for inauspicious events, the jī remains the same.
Some are used to manifest the rites of sacrifice,
some are used to provide for the rituals of feasting and archery.
The Zhōulǐ states:
The Spring Offices are in charge of jī and yán,
overseeing the five types of jī.
For the great court audience,
the great feasting and archery,
the enfeoffment of states and appointment of feudal lords,
at the king's position,
to the left and right are placed jade jī.
For feudal lords' sacrifices,
to the right is a carved jī.
For the zuò (guest) mat,
to the left is a red jī.
For the diàn (hunting) service,
on a bear mat,
to the right is a lacquered jī.
For mourning events,
on a reed mat,
to the right is a plain jī.
The loss of one's counterpart was transmitted by Nánguō.

Nánguō Zǐqí leaned on a jī and sat,

Mèngzǐ did not respond,

Mèngzǐ said:

he could not have put Zǐsī at ease.
If Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng had no one by Mùgōng's side,
they could not have secured their own persons.
You, sir, consider the elder,
yet do not reach the level of Zǐsī.
Are you, sir, cutting off the elder?
Or is the elder cutting you off?"
Note:
Zhòu is a city of Qí.
As for the ornamentation of crane-knees and fox-paws,
the Yǔlín states:
Rén Yuánbāo was Guānglùxūn.
Sūn Féngyì went to visit him,
and saw the gate officer leaning on a jī looking at him.
Sūn entered and said to Rén:
"The officer's jī facing the guest is discourteous."
Rén then beat him.
The officer replied:
"Having been punished, my body aches,
so I use a horizontal piece of wood for support,
it is not leaning on a jī."
Sūn said:
"A vertical piece of wood placed horizontally,
supporting both feet,
then it is a leaning jī.
Why must it have fox-paws and crane-knees,
with curved wood embracing the waist?"
The marvels of white jade and green stone,
the Hàn Jiùyí states:
For sacrificing to Heaven, a jade jī is used.
The Nányuè Jì states:
In the stone chamber of Héng Shān, there are stone beds and stone jī.
They are dusted before being presented.
The Lǐ states:
One who presents a jī or staff dusts it.
They are also carried along when following.
The Lǐ states:
When consulting with an elder,
one must carry a jī and staff to follow him.
Some are used to convey summons from the netherworld.
The Yìyuàn states:
Lìyáng Shí Xiùzhī of Shàn
saw a person wearing a píngjīn and kùzhě,

"I have heard your skill matches Bān and Ěr,

That person then left.
After several decades,
Zhèng indeed died.
Liú's making of jī was famous,
thus it led to his death.
Some are used to record admonitory and recited words.
The Guóyǔ states:
Historian Zuǒ Yǐxiāng said:
"Leaning on a jī, there are admonitions and recited warnings."
The Nèizé mentions folding the mat.
The Lǐ‧Nèizé states:
When parents and parents-in-law sit, the attendant
lifts the jī and folds the mat.
The seasonal ordinance speaks of nurturing the aged.
The Lǐ states:
In the eighth month's node,
nurture the aged and feeble,
and confer jī and staff.
Observe the substance of yellow gold.
The Hàn Wǔ Nèi Zhuàn states:
The Emperor received the Wǔyuè Zhēnxíng Jīng from the Queen Mother of the West,
and placed it on a yellow gold jī.
The covering of cloud-patterned silk.
The Shíyí Jì states:
South of Yíngzhōu is the Jīnluán Observatory,
within which is a precious jī,
covered with plain cloud-patterned silk.
Learning was esteemed by Línshì.

Shěn Línshì devoted himself to diligent study,
often leaning on a plain jī and playing a plain qín.
Fame is ascribed to Zhuómào.
The Dōngguān Hàn Jì states:
Emperor Guāngwǔ appointed the former magistrate of Mì, Zhuó Mào, as Grand Tutor,

and bestowed upon him a jī and staff.

The Jìnshū states:
When Sīlì Liú Yì died,
Emperor Wǔ stroked a jī and exclaimed in shock:
"I have lost my famous minister,
he did not get to become one of the Three Dukes in his lifetime."
Striking it revealed Zhū Jūn's anger.
The Hànshū states:
Zhū Bó was transferred to be governor of Lángyé.
In the Qí region, they were relaxed and cultivated reputation.
The Right Section officials all claimed illness and lay in bed.
According to precedent,
when a new official of two-thousand-picul rank arrives,
officials are sent to inquire and convey greetings,
then they rise and take up their duties.
Bó, shaking his beard and striking the jī, said:
"Do you Qí fellows think this is the custom!"
He dismissed all the sick officials.
As for the Yellow Emperor establishing the method,
Lǐ Yóu's "Jī Míng Xù" states:
In ancient times, Emperor Xuānyuán, benevolent and wise,
observing that affairs had deficiencies,
created the methods for carriages and jī.
Zhāng Huá composed an inscription.
Zhāng Huá's "Yǐ Jī Míng" states:
The leaning jī is set up,
set up but not leaned upon.
Making the vessel here,
completing the rites there.
Xún Yīng threw it and angered Shì Gài.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The Marquis of Jìn met with the feudal lords at Zhā.
Jìn's Xún Yǎn and Shì Gài requested to attack Bīyáng,
and enfeoff Sòng's Xiàng Xū there.
Xún Yīng said:
"The city is small but strong.
Victory over it is not martial,
defeat would be laughable."
They insisted on requesting,
besieged it,
but could not capture it.
Yǎn and Gài requested to withdraw the army.
Zhì Bó was angry,
threw a jī at them,
which flew between them,
and said:
"You urged the ruler and mobilized the feudal lords,
dragged this old man here.
Having no martial defense,
you now wish to shift the blame onto me, saying:
'It was he who withdrew the army,
otherwise, we would have captured it.'
If you do not capture it in seven days,
I will surely take it from you."
They then destroyed Bīyáng.
Lǚ Bù chopped it and reprimanded Chén Dēng.
See the note "hungry and thus used" in the "Yīng Fù".
As for its tiger-attached two heads,
the Kuàijī Diǎnlù states:
Immortal Gě leaned on a white paulownia jī and studied the Way for several years.
Ascending to immortality in broad daylight,
he nearly transformed into a white tiger,
with three legs and two heads,
often seen by people.
Flowers clustered in five colors,
as recorded in the Yèzhōng Jì:
The tables on which Shí Hǔ sat were all lacquered and carved,
all adorned with five-colored flowers.
Some were made of zǐ wood for practical use,
as noted in the Jìn Shū:
Wáng Xīzhī, whose courtesy name was Yìshǎo,
once visited a student’s home,
saw a smooth and clean zǐ wood table,
and thus wrote on it,
mixing regular and cursive scripts.
Later, the student’s father mistakenly scraped it off,
leaving the student shocked and regretful for days.
Some were adorned with tí silk as decoration.
As recorded in the Xījīng Zá Jì:
According to Han dynasty regulations,
the Son of Heaven used jade tables,
which in winter were covered with tí brocade,
called tí tables.
Dukes and marquises all used wooden tables,
which in winter were covered with fine woolen bags.
The dài shèng was already seen on the Queen Mother,
as recorded in the Shānhǎi Jīng:
The Queen Mother of the West leaned on a table and wore the dài shèng.
Annotation:
“Leaning” means to rely on.
The literary style was still passed down by Ruǎn Jí.
As noted in the Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn:
“When Wèi enfeoffed the Prince of Jìn,
the prince declined,
and all the ministers were to convey the imperial intent.
Minister Zhèng Chōng urgently sent a messenger to Ruǎn Jí to request his composition,
waiting immediately.”
Ruǎn Jí was staying at Yuán Xiàoní’s home at the time,
drunk,
helped to rise,
wrote on a table board as his composition,
without any revisions,
and handed it over to the messenger.
There is also Máo Jiè’s ancient style,
as recorded in the Wèi Zhì:
When Tàizǔ served as Minister and Chancellor,
Máo Jiè was the Eastern Section Clerk.
After Tàizǔ pacified Liǔchéng,
distributing the captured artifacts,
he specifically gave a plain screen and a plain leaning table to Máo Jiè,
saying:
“You possess the style of the ancients,
so I bestow upon you the objects of the ancients.”
Yáng Biāo’s longstanding virtue,
as recorded in the Xù Hàn Shū:
Emperor Wén of Wèi bestowed a table and staff upon Yáng Biāo,
to honor his longstanding virtue.
Wèi Shū’s retirement from office,
as recorded in the Jìn Shū:
Wèi Shū, citing old age and illness, retired from office,
and an edict bestowed upon him a table and staff, exempting him from court attendance.
The King of Wú feigned illness.
As recorded in the Hàn Shū:
The King of Wú, Liú Bì, feigned illness and did not attend court.
When the investigation proved untrue,
Emperor Wén reprimanded the Wú envoy.
The envoy said:
“To see the fish in the deep abyss
is inauspicious.”
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven bestowed a table and staff upon the King of Wú.
Kǒng Língchǎn received a gift for knowing contentment,
as recorded in Wú Jūn’s Qí Chūnqiū:
Kǒng Língchǎn was appointed Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments,
but understanding the principle of contentment,
he refused to accept the position.
Tàizǔ bestowed upon him a white yak-tail fan and a plain table,
saying:
“Because you possess the style of the ancients,
I bestow upon you the objects of the ancients.”
Wáng Chōng received an honor for his seniority.
As recorded in the Chén Shū:
Wáng Chōng served as Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and Emperor Wǔ, regarding Wáng Chōng as a minister from a previous dynasty,
specially extended respect for seniority.
Upon ascending the throne,
he showed even greater reverence.
Once, while accompanying the emperor to the residence of Minister Xú Dù,
during a banquet,
he was bestowed a table.
This was to demonstrate the emperor’s favor and honor,
and to show kindness to the elderly in their leisure and comfort.
Staff
The staff is
used to honor the venerable elders
and manifest virtuous conduct.
The Records of Wei states:
Emperor Wen summoned Yáng Biāo, the Grand Commandant of Han,
treated him with the courtesy due a guest,
and bestowed upon him an armrest and a staff.
The imperial edict said:
"The former kings established the bestowal of armrests and staffs
to treat the elderly with guest-like respect
and to honor the venerable elders.
In the past, Kǒng Guāng and Zhuó Mào
both received this special gift due to their virtuous conduct and advanced age.
We now bestow upon you, Duke, a longevity staff and an armrest."
Therefore, at sixty, one receives a staff in the village;
at seventy, one receives a staff in the state.
The Rites: Royal Regulations states:
At fifty, one receives a staff in the household;
at sixty, one receives a staff in the village;
at seventy, one receives a staff in the state;
at eighty, one receives a staff at court.
There is also the title 'Yánnián' (Prolonging Years) staff,
see the annotation above.
It is bestowed for court attendance.
The Book of the Later Han states:
Zhēn Chēn was appointed as Palace Attendant.
Due to his old age and frailty,
an imperial edict bestowed upon him a staff from the Imperial Storehouse,
to be used when entering and leaving court for duty.
Carrying a weeding tool, he was seen by an old man.
The Analects:
Zǐlù, following behind,
encountered an old man
carrying a weeding tool over his shoulder with his staff.
Zǐlù asked:
"Have you seen my master?"
The old man said:
"With limbs that do not toil,
and unable to distinguish the five grains,
who is your master?"
He planted his staff and began weeding.
Blowing fire, one still hears of Tàiyī.
The Records of Omissions states:
Liú Xiàng, in the final years of Emperor Chéng's reign,
was collating texts in the Tiānlù Pavilion,
concentrating deeply and pondering intently.
At night, an old man appeared,
dressed in yellow robes,
holding a goosefoot staff.
Fire emerged from the tip of the staff,
which he used to illuminate Xiàng.
He fully recounted matters from before the creation of the world.
Xiàng thus received the text of the "Five Phases and Great Plan."
Fearing the explanations were too extensive and complex,
Xiàng tore his robe and sash
to record the words.
At dawn, the man departed.
Xiàng asked his name.
He replied:
"I am the essence of Tàiyī.
The Celestial Emperor heard that the Jīnmǎo surname had a learned scholar,
and sent me down to observe."
He then took out a bamboo tablet from his bosom,
containing writings on celestial patterns and terrestrial maps,
and bestowed them upon him.
As for Liú Xīn, Xiàng's son,
he received the arts from his father,
but also did not speak of them to others.
As for the Qióng bamboo arriving from Dàxià,
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Zhāng Qiān said:
"When I was previously in Dàxià,
I saw Qióng bamboo staffs and Shǔ cloth.
I asked how they obtained these."
The people of Dàxià said:
'Our merchants go to Shèndú to buy them.'"
Shèndú is said to be several thousand lǐ southeast of Dàxià.
Língshòu staffs come from Jiǔzhēn.
The Extensive Records states:
Jiǔzhēn produces língshòu staffs.
As for gold, there was the extravagance of Shǎoqiān.
In Search of the Supernatural states:
Emperor Wén of Han, traveling incognito and carrying gold, passed by Lǔ Shǎoqiān.
Shǎoqiān, leaning on a gold staff, came out to the gate to meet him.
As for goosefoot grass, there was the poverty of Yuán Xiàn.
The Zhuangzi states:
Zǐxià, riding in a large horse-drawn carriage too wide for the lane,
went to see Yuán Xiàn.
Yuán Xiàn, leaning on a goosefoot staff, came to the gate.
As for carving it into the shape of a pagoda, a novel form,
The Records of Pagodas and Temples states:
Xiè Shàng once dreamed that his father told him:
"A malign energy will come from the southwest.
Whoever it strikes will surely die.
Do not confront its force.
Building a pagoda temple can avert it.
If you lack time to build a temple,
you can carve the top of a staff into the shape of a pagoda.
When you see the energy coming, point it at it."
Shàng did as he was told.
He placed the staff beside him.
Indeed, a black energy rushed towards Shàng's house.
Shàng pointed the staff at it.
The energy immediately dispersed.
His entire household was spared.
The places the energy passed through
were left with not a single survivor for several lǐ.
Adorned with a dove, an ancient design.
The Continued Book of Han: Treatise on Rituals states:
In mid-autumn, according to household registration,
people aged seventy are granted a jade staff,
the top of the staff adorned with a dove.
The dove is a bird that does not choke,
wishing that the elderly will not choke.
The unicorn horn was transmitted by Liú Xiàng.
Liú Xiàng's Separate Records mentions a unicorn horn staff.
The peach branch is also heard of with respect to Wèi Wǔ.
In the Letter from Emperor Wǔ of Wèi to Yáng Biāo, it says:
"Now I bestow upon you, sir, one silver-cornered peach branch staff."
Thrown into Gě Bēi, it suddenly transformed.
Biographies of Divine Immortals states:
Hú Gōng sent Fèi Chángfáng on his return journey,
giving him a bamboo staff,
saying:
"Ride this to return home,
then throw it into Gě Bēi."
Chángfáng rode the staff,
suddenly feeling as if asleep,
and soon arrived home.
He threw the staff into Gě Bēi.
Looking back at it,
it had become a blue dragon.
Discarded in Dèng Forest, it grew luxuriantly on its own.
See the annotation "Discarded staff heard of regarding Kuāfù" in the "Rhapsody on the Sun."
Chángfáng obtained it and experienced spiritual transformation.
Biographies of Divine Immortals states:
Fèi Chángfáng wished to seek the Way,
but was concerned about his family.
Hú Gōng then cut a green bamboo staff
equal to Chángfáng's height,
and had it hung behind his house.
His family saw it,
thought he had hanged himself,
and all, young and old, cried out in shock,
then buried it.
Chángfáng stood beside them,
but no one saw him.
Later, Chángfáng returned.
His family did not believe it was him.
They then opened the previous burial site,
and the bamboo staff was still there.
Jiè Xiàng gave it to him for distant travel.
Biographies of Divine Immortals states:
Jiè Xiàng had a man ride a green bamboo staff
from Wú to Shǔ.
Then there was the bestowal upon Zhuó Mào,
see the annotation "Name praised Zhuó Mào" in the "Rhapsody on the Armrest."
Bestowed upon Yuán Féng.
Huá Qiáo's Book of the Later Han states:
During the Jiāpíng era,
Yuán Féng served as one of the Three Elders,
and was bestowed a jade staff.
In accord with Yáng Pèi's auspicious dream.
The Records of Wei states:
Zhōu Xuān was a commandery clerk.
The Grand Administrator Yáng Pèi dreamed a man said:
"On the eighth day of the eighth month, Lord Cáo will arrive.
He will surely give you a staff
and have you drink medicinal wine."
Xuān interpreted it, saying:
"The staff supports the weak,
medicine cures people's illnesses.
On the first day of the eighth month,
the Yellow Turbans will surely be defeated."
When the time came,
the rebels were indeed defeated.
Repaying Mí Zhú's hidden merit.
The Records of Omissions states:
Mí Zhú employed the strategies of Táo Zhūgōng,
growing richer daily,
possessing a thousand treasure storehouses.
Zhú relieved the living and cared for the dead.
Beside his family's stables was an ancient grave.
At night, he heard weeping.
Searching for it,
he saw a woman,
who pleaded, saying:
"At the end of the Han, I was killed by the Red Eyebrows.
My coffin was opened and I was stripped.
I beg for a worn garment to cover myself."
Zhú complied with her request.
He saw the woman again, who said:
"You are destined to suffer a fire calamity.
Now, with one green reed staff,
nine chǐ long,
I repay your kindness of clothing."
Zhú took the staff and returned.
Later, a neighbor saw a green vapor like the form of a dragon or snake at Zhú's house.
Within ten days, fire broke out from the storehouse.
They burned their pearls and jades,
leaving only one-tenth behind.
When the fire was at its peak,
they saw over ten blue-clad youths come to extinguish the flames,
and also saw a blue mist like clouds covering the fire,
whereupon the fire immediately died out.
It is said that Confucius once rested his hands behind his back.
The Book of Rites records:
Confucius rose early,
rested his hands behind his back and dragged his staff,
strolling leisurely by the gate,
singing:
"Mount Tài is crumbling,
the great beams are breaking,
the wise man is withering away."
He then fell ill and passed away after seven days.
There is also the story of hanging coins at the Ruǎn family.
See the annotation "or hung on the head of a staff" in the "Ode to Coins."
Shānbīn responded to Jùyuán's gaze.
The Tán Sǒu records:
In Later Wèi, Xíng Luán, styled Shānbīn,
once fell ill
and used a mountain peach staff.
The emperor asked:
"What kind of staff is this?"
He replied:
"A Jùyuán staff."
Emperor Tàiwǔ's personal name was Tāo,
hence the reference.
Chāngyì sought the design of a bundled bamboo staff.
The Xīn Xù records:
When the King of Chāngyì was summoned to become emperor,
upon reaching Xíngyáng,
he purchased two bundled bamboo thorn staffs.
Gōng Suì admonished him:
"Bundled bamboo thorn staffs
are for arrogant and unruly youths.
Your Majesty is in the midst of a great mourning period,
and should use a bamboo staff."
He recited the inscription of King Wǔ ascending the throne.
The Dà Dài Lǐ records:
When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
the inscription on his staff read:
"How can one lose the Way through desires?
Forgetting each other in wealth and honor."
He practiced the ritual of the village drinking ceremony.
The Analects state:
During the village drinking ceremony,
when the elders with staffs leave,
then one may leave.
When presenting a staff, one holds the tip.
The Book of Rites states:
When presenting a staff, one holds the tip.
It is also placed in a case for ceremonial use.
The Zhōu Lǐ records:
The Yīqíshì was in charge of major state sacrifices,
and provided the staff cases.
Annotation:
Although elder ministers may use staffs at court,
when serving spirits, they remove them.
Officials store them in cases,
and return them after the ceremony.
Confucius established the rites,
and in his inquiries, there were distinctions of nobility and commonality.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū records:
When Confucius's disciples came from afar,
Confucius would lean on his staff and ask:
"Are your parents well?"
Then he would set aside his staff and ask:
"Are your siblings well?"
Thus, Confucius used a six-foot staff
to discuss the distinctions of nobility and commonality,
and to differentiate the principles of closeness and distance.
Lù Jiǎ wrote books,
and used it in times of peril.
The Xīn Yǔ states:
Those in high positions
must ensure their own stability;
those treading on dangerous ground
must rely on a staff that is firm.
If one is not stable, they will fall;
if the staff is not firm, they will stumble.
Therefore, when sages occupy high positions,
they use benevolence and righteousness as their nest;
when facing danger and instability,
they use sages and worthies as their staff.
Fan
That fine silk fan,
is indeed a treasure.
It resembles the full moon in its constant roundness,
Xú Gàn's "Ode to the Round Fan" says:
Only the marvelous fan of shared joy,
originates from the delicate silk of Yīluò.
Looking up to the bright moon to take its form,
it follows the round shape's proper measure.
It emits a gentle breeze and becomes ever newer.
Cáo Zhí's "Ode to the Nine-Flower Fan" says:
Following the fair wrist as it slowly turns,
it releases the lingering coolness of a gentle breeze.
Some use it to record Yáng Fú's snow,
The "Shì Shuō" says:
Yáng Fú wrote "In Praise of Snow," stating:
"Drawing purity to transform,
riding the air to drift lightly.
Encountering images, it can freshen,
touching cleanliness, it becomes radiant."
Huán Yī then wrote it on a fan.
Some use it to inscribe Liǔ Yùn's clouds.
The "Liáng Shū" says:
Liǔ Yùn's poem says:
"By the pavilion's shore, tree leaves fall,
over the ridge's head, autumn clouds fly."
Lángyé's Wáng Róng saw it and sighed in admiration,
then wrote it on his study wall and on the white round fan he held.
Think of Wáng Mǎng's face screen,
The "Hàn Shū" says:
Wáng Mǎng had a court attendant skilled in arts at the Yellow Gate,
someone asked about Wáng Mǎng's appearance,
the attendant said:
"Wáng Mǎng is what they call owl-eyed with a tiger's mouth,
a voice like a jackal or wolf,
thus he can devour people,
and will also be devoured by others."
The questioner then reported this,
Wáng Mǎng executed the attendant,
and enfeoffed the informant.
Later, he often concealed himself behind a mica face screen,
so that none but his close associates could see him.
Note:
The face screen is like a fan,
it is a type of fan.
Think of Liáng Jì's body-concealing fan.
The "Continued Hàn Shū" says:
Liáng Jì made a body-concealing fan.
Then there is Jièzǐ declining an official salary,
The "Liè Xiān Zhuàn" says:
Jiè Tuī entered Jiè Mountain to wander with Bó Yáng,
later generations saw him selling fans in the Eastern Sea.
Hé Zhí living in poverty,
The "Jìn Shū" says:
Zhí, styled Yuángàn,
often made a living by binding brushes and weaving fans,
to support his family.
Zhāng Fū wrapped in grief over his mother's death,
The "Liáng Shū" says:
Zhāng Fū was born after his mother died,
when he was a few years old and heard of it,
though still a child, he showed a mournful expression.
By around ten years old,
he sought his mother's remaining belongings,
but they had already been dispersed and given away.
He only obtained one painted fan,
which he then sealed and kept,
whenever he felt longing,
he would open the chest and shed tears.
Huáng Xiāng gaining fame for attending to his parents.
The "Dōng Guān Hàn Jì" says:
Huáng Xiāng was extremely filial,
in summer, he would fan beside his parents.
Túxiū's reverse shadow,
The "Shí Yí Jì" says:
During King Zhāo of Zhōu's time,
the country of Túxiū presented a red swan,
at summer solstice, they took the swan's wings to make a fan,
one name was "spreading wind,"
one name was "feathered wings,"
one name was "reverse shadow."
Dīng Huǎn's lacquered wheels,
The "Gǔ Jīn Zhù" says:
Cháng'ān's clever artisan Dīng Huǎn made a seven-wheel fan,
connecting seven wheels,
each about a zhang in diameter,
one person operating it,
would make the whole hall shiver with cold.
Yànhuí blocking the sun,
The "Qí Shū" says:
Liú Xiáng, styled Xiǎnwēi,
spoke lightly and acted recklessly,
not avoiding high or low.
During the Jiànyuán era,
he served as a proper staff officer.
Minister Chǔ Yànhuí entered court,
using a waist fan to block the sun,
Liú Xiáng passed by his side,
saying:
"Making such gestures,
ashamed to show your face to people,
what good is blocking with a fan?"
Yànhuí said:
"Impoverished scholar, how insolent."
Liú Xiáng said:
"Unable to sell out Yuán and Liú,
how can one avoid being an impoverished scholar?"
Zhūgě commanding the army.
The "Yǔ Lín" says:
Marquis Wǔ of Zhūgě battled Emperor Xuān of Jìn by the Wèi River,
riding a plain carriage,
wearing a coarse headscarf,
holding a white feather fan,
directing the three armies.
Some paint the Qín maiden on it,
The "Gǔ Shī" says:
The silk fan is like a round moon,
coming from the loom's plain silk.
Painted as the Qín king's daughter,
riding a phoenix into mist and haze.
Some give it to Mǎichén.
The "Gǔ Jīn Zhù" says:
Zhū Mǎichén was the governor of Kuàijī,
carrying his seal and ribbon to Jīntíng,
but the locals did not yet know.
Qián Bó saw his worn-out appearance,
then consoled him, saying:
"Aren't you tired?"
And gave him a fine silk fan.
When Mǎichén arrived at the commandery,
he invited him as an honored guest.
Xiè Ān admiring Yuán Hóng's eloquence,
see the note on "fan given to Yuán Hóng" in the "Ode to the Wind."
Wáng Dǎo shielding from Yuánguī's dust.
The "Jìn Shū" says:
Yǔ Liàng went out to garrison the frontier,
as the emperor's uncle, he held court power internally.
Wáng Dǎo was displeased,
whenever he encountered a west wind,
he would raise his fan to shield himself, saying:
"Yuánguī's dust sullies people."
As for the crown prince's unique fan of shared heart,
The "Dōng Gōng Jiù Shì" says:
When the crown prince first received his appointment,
he was provided with one lacquered waist fan,
and one green bamboo fan each.
When the crown prince took a consort,
he was provided with thirty shared-heart fans,
and twenty single bamboo fans.
Bān's creation of the shared-joy fan,
Bān Jiéyú's "Fan Poem" says:
Newly made from Qí's fine silk,
bright and pure as frost and snow.
Cut to make a shared-joy fan,
round and round like the bright moon.
In and out of your bosom and sleeves,
swaying, it emits a gentle breeze.
Cáo Zhí's precious nine-flower fan,
Cáo Zhí's "Ode to the Nine-Flower Fan" says:
In the past, my late father, a constant attendant,
gained favor with Emperor Huán of Hàn,
was bestowed a Shangfang bamboo fan,
named Nine-Flower,
thus he wrote an ode, saying:
"Shape of five separations and nine folds,
bamboo strips split and threads part.
Imitating the coiling of horned dragons,
following the dense mist of clouds and rainbows.
According to form, achieving beauty,
not constant in its appearance.
Square does not match the square,
round does not fit the compass."
Xiāngdōng's inscription of eight characters,
The "Liáng Shū" says:
Prince Línchuān Hóng,
styled Zhèngbiǎo,
often held a white round fan,
Prince Xiāngdōng took it and inscribed eight characters, treasuring it for enjoyment.
Yáng Xīn not writing and remaining aloof,
The "Liáng Shū" says:
Yáng Xīn, styled Jìngyuán,
the heir of the Prince of Kuàijī, Yuán Xiǎn, often had him write on fans,
but he usually did not comply.
Yuán Xiǎn was angry,
then appointed him as a rear army office attendant.
Zǐ Xiǎn with one wave and a haughty glance.
The "Qí Shū" says:
Xiāo Zǐ Xiǎn rather prided himself on his talent,
when in charge of selections,
seeing guests of the nine schools,
he would not speak with them,
but merely raise his fan and wave it once.
The gentry resented him.
Created by King Wǔ,
The "Shì Běn" says:
King Wǔ first made fans.
Banned by the Jìn emperor,
The "Jìn Zhōng Xīng Shū" says:
During the Yìxī era of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
silk fans and gambling were banned.
Greatly seen in Fúnán,
He excelled in painting,
depicting landscapes on fans,
within the span of a foot,
one could feel the vastness of ten thousand miles as if it were distant.
He could dispel the heat of midsummer and welcome the coolness of late autumn,
a feat unmatched by any other.
Brush
The Book of Rites states:
The scholar carries words,
the scribe carries the brush.
In ancient times, it was considered capable of narrating events and words,
hence it was called "narrate."
The Shìmíng says.
It was also considered capable of fully depicting the forms of all things,
thus also called "fully."
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Preface to the Brush Rhapsody" states.
Therefore, in Qín it is called bǐ,
in Chǔ it is called yù,
and in Wú it is called bùlǜ.
The Shuōwén says:
In Chǔ it is called yù,
in Qín it is called bǐ,
in Wú it is called bùlǜ,
in Yān it is called fú.
As for the excellence of lacquered tubes and deep green,
Wáng Xīzhī's "Brush Classic" states:
Someone presented me with a deep green lacquered bamboo tube and an engraved tube,
which I have kept for many years,
and they are truly delightful to admire.
Must they be carved from gold and jade to be considered precious?
The distinctions of patterned rhinoceros horn and elephant ivory,
the Fùzǐ states:
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
a brush case,
carved from gold,
adorned with hé jade,
inlaid with Suí pearls,
and decorated with delicate kingfisher feathers.
If not a stem of patterned rhinoceros horn,
then certainly a tube of elephant ivory,
a shaft of rich fox fur,
and autumn hare's fur.
Bóshān as a stand,
the Dōnggōng Jiùshì states:
When the crown prince was first appointed,
he was given four lacquered brushes,
with a copper Bóshān brush stand as an accessory.
Inlaid treasures as the base.
The Xījīng Zá Jì states:
According to Hàn regulations,
the emperor's brush had a base inlaid with treasures,
the hairs were all made from autumn hare's fur,
crafted by the official artisan Lù Hù.
Also, a case made of assorted treasures,
adorned with jade discs and kingfisher feathers,
each worth a hundred gold.
The quiet maiden once gifted a red tube,
the Shī says:
The quiet maiden is lovely,
she gifted me a red tube.
Zhōu Gōng once wrote on a turtle's shell.
the Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
A black turtle emerged carrying a chart,
Zhōu Gōng took up a brush and wrote on it in timely script.
As for the hairs from Zhōngshān,
the Shǐjì states:
The First Emperor ordered Méng Tián and Crown Prince Fúsū to build the Great Wall,
Méng Tián took hairs from Zhōngshān rabbits to make brushes.
The manufacture of Běigōng,
the Hànshū states:
The Shàngshū Lìng, Pú, Chéng, and Láng were given a pair of large brushes monthly,
inscribed with seal script: "Made in Běigōng."
The beginning of creation by General Méng Tián of Qín,
the Gǔjīn Zhù states:
In the past, when Méng Tián made brushes,
he used mulberry wood for the tube,
deer hair for the core,
and sheep hair for the outer layer,
not rabbit hair and bamboo tubes.
The exquisite craftsmanship of the official artisan Lù Hù.
See the note above on "inlaid treasures as the base."
Zhōu Shě held it to oversee faults,
the Hánshī Wàizhuàn states:
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had a minister named Zhōu Shě,
who stood at the gate for three days and three nights,
Jiǎnzǐ asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"I believe,
a minister who speaks frankly,
holding ink brush and writing tablets,
follows behind his lord,
watches for his lord's faults and records them."
Bān Chāo cast it aside to establish his career.
the Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Bān Chāo's family was poor,
he worked as a copyist,
and once stopped writing, threw down his brush, and sighed:
"A man should be like Fù Jièzǐ and Zhāng Qiān, achieving merit in foreign lands to earn a marquisate,
how can I long engage with brush and inkstone?"
Enraged, Wáng Sī chased away a fly,
the Wèishū states:
Wáng Sī was impatient by nature,
once while holding a brush to write,
a fly landed on the tip of the brush,
he drove it away but it returned.
Sī became angry,
chased the fly but could not catch it,
took the brush and threw it to the ground, destroying it.
Grieved Shèng Jí to the point of shedding tears.
See the note on "Shèng Jí's calligraphy" in the "Winter Rhapsody."
Startled Hé Yàn so that he suddenly dropped it,
the Wèimò Zhuàn states:
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng wanted to execute Cáo Shuǎng,
called Hé Yàn to draft a memorial, saying:
"You should write your lord's name."
Yàn dropped the brush to the ground.
Terrified Cáo Gōng so that he suddenly dropped it.
the Wúzhì states:
Cáo Gōng heard that Sūn Quán had provided Liú Bèi with Jīngzhōu,
just as he was writing,
his brush fell to the ground.
Ruǎn Yǔ's proclamation, astonishingly completed instantly,
the Wénshì Zhuàn states:
Ruǎn Yǔ licked the brush and drafted a proclamation instantly.
Cáo Gōng sought a brush to make changes,
but ultimately found no place to add a stroke.
Mí Hé's rhapsody, written without pause.
the Hòu Hànshū states:
Huáng Zǔ's eldest son, Shè,
had Mí Hé compose the "Parrot Rhapsody,"
the brush never paused,
the text required no corrections.
As for the three grades of Xiāngdōng,
the Liángshū states:
When Emperor Yuán was Prince of Xiāngdōng,
he loved literature,
and often recorded loyal ministers, righteous men, and beautiful writings.
Brushes were of three grades,
some adorned with gold and silver carvings,
others made of mottled bamboo tubes.
For those who were completely loyal and filial,
he used gold tubes to write.
For those with pure and refined virtue,
he used silver tubes to write.
For those with abundant and elegant writings,
he used mottled bamboo tubes to write.
Four brushes in the Eastern Palace,
see the note above on "Bóshān as a stand."
Holding the brush tip, lost in thought,
Lù Shìhéng's "Wénfù" states:
Sometimes holding the brush tip, lost in reverie.
Grasping the tube, pacing back and forth.
Yú Shìnán's "Brush Essence" states:
A brush's length is no more than five or six inches,
the part grasped is no more than two inches.
Yáng Xuán stained blood to write on silk,
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū states:
Yáng Xuán, styled Jīpíng,
pacified the rebels in Línglíng,
and became Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Zhào Kǎi falsely accused him,
he was arrested and transported in a cage cart,
and his brush and inkstone were confiscated.
So he bit his arm to draw blood,
used a white-haired brush from a ledger to stain the blood and write on silk,
detailing the situation of defeating the rebels,
and stating that he was framed by Kǎi,
gave it to his disciples,
who went to the court to plead his case,
and an edict pardoned him.
Táo Jǐng used reeds to draw in ashes.
the Táo Hóngjǐng Zhuàn states:
When Hóngjǐng was four or five years old,
he often used reeds as brushes,
drawing in ashes to practice writing,
and eventually became skilled in clerical script.
Observe it staining the faint smoke of clear pine,
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Discarded Old Brush Rhapsody" states:
Staining the faint smoke of clear pine.
Offering the accumulated moisture of fine hairs,
Xú Chī's "Ode to the Brush" poem states:
Fine hairs offer accumulated moisture,
delicate substance disperses fragrant smoke.
The wonder of white ivory and green carvings,
the Jǐnglóng Wénguǎn Jì states:
Emperor Zhōngzōng ordered the scholars to enter the Gānlù Hall,
on its north wall were rows of bookshelves,
before the shelves was a silver inkstone,
ten green-carved ivory tubes,
and a silver case containing dozens of types of paper.
White ivory,
see the note below on "yet lapis lazuli seems heavy."
The excellence of chicken spur and deer hair.
Bái Lètiān has a "Chicken Spur Brush Rhapsody."
Wáng Yǐn's "Brush Inscription" states:
Must brush-making,
necessarily use rabbit hair?
Hard to adjust and not easily worn,
there is also deer hair.
Wáng Chōng's doors, windows, walls, and partitions,
the Hòu Hànshū states:
Wáng Chōng loved truth and reality,
closed his door to ponder deeply,
placed knives and brushes on doors, windows, walls, and partitions,
and wrote the eighty-five chapters of the Lùnhéng.
Zuǒ Sī's courtyard gates and latrines.
the Jìnshū states:
"The use of the brush lies in the heart;
if the heart is upright, the brush will be upright."
The emperor changed his expression,
knowing it was a brush remonstrance.
Surprised by the flies gathering on Fú Jiān,
the *Jìn Shū* states:
Fú Jiān secretly discussed matters with Wáng Měng and Fú Róng on the open terrace,
when a large blue fly entered through the window,
its buzzing sound was very loud,
it gathered on the brush and then flew away,
and in the marketplace, it turned into a small child in black clothes,
shouting:
"The officials will now grant a great amnesty."
Divined the snake carrying the brush for Guǎn Lù.
The *Wèi Zhì* states:
Guǎn Lù went to see the governor of Ānpíng, Wáng Jī,
Jī asked him to perform a divination,
Lù said:
"On the bed, there should be a large snake carrying a brush,
everyone, young and old, will see it,
but it will disappear in a moment."
He said:
"The snake
is the old scribe."
Zhòngjiāng paid careful attention to craftsmanship,
Wéi Zhòngjiāng wrote the *Bǐ Mò Fāng* (Brush and Ink Method),
already seen in the annotation for "Tòng Jié wéi Jiā."
Zhìgōng sought it but was firmly refused.
Xīzhī's *Bǐ Fǎ* (Brush Method) states:
I once made a brush myself,
which was very usable.
Xiè Ānshí and Yǔ Zhìgōng often came to me seeking it,
but I refused and did not give it to them.
Passed on Máo Yǐng to Lord Hán,
Hán Yù wrote the *Máo Yǐng Zhuàn* (Biography of Máo Yǐng).
Named the brush "háo zhuī" by Bái Fù.
Bái Lètiān and Yuán Wēizhī were about to take the imperial examination,
each had a fine-tipped, slender brush,
which they carried to the examination,
and whenever they looked at each other, they would laugh,
calling it "háo zhuī" (brush awl),
hence the poem presented to Prime Minister Yuán says:
"The strategy paper is pierced like a slip,
the brush tip is sharp as an awl."
Yìshǎo was astonished by the seven-tenths penetration into the wood,
the *Jìn Shì* states:
For the northern suburban sacrificial text,
it was ordered to be rewritten,
and when the craftsman scraped it,
Xīzhī's brush had already penetrated seven-tenths into the wood.
Zhòngní stopped at the single phrase "capturing the qílín."
The *Chūnqiū Xù* states:
He ceased writing at the single phrase "capturing the qílín,"
moved by what he felt,
and thus made it the end.
This is the use of the moistened brush,
truly an urgent task for writers.
Inkstone
Mining the hidden jade from the Yīn Mountains,
Fù Xuán's "Inkstone Rhapsody" says:
Mining the hidden jade from the Yīn Mountains,
inquiring about the suitability of various materials.
Establishing square and round to fix the form,
borrowing metal and iron to make the ink pool.
Carving a round pool like the water of a jade disc,
Yáng Shīdào's "Poem on Inkstones" says:
"The round pool resembles the water of a jade disc,
light brushes are stained with misty blossoms.
The general seeks to secure distant lands,
abandoned, it should not be far away."
Now there are those round as a cup,
with a raised center,
water encircling it,
called the Bìyōng inkstone,
also known as the Fēntí inkstone.
Creating an ink sea from a single knob,
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor obtained a jade knob,
and fashioned it into an ink sea.
Its seal script inscription reads: "The inkstone of Emperor Hóng."
Matching the three legs of the Xià tripod.
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Eulogy" says:
Casting three legs like the Xià tripod,
resembling the mutual support of stars and constellations.
Selected from Fǔkē,
Liǔ Gōngquán's "Discourse on Inkstones" states:
Inkstones come from Fǔkē Mountain,
the place where the chess game was observed.
Placed on a silk-covered table,
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" says:
The Son of Heaven's jade table is adorned with silk brocade,
using jade for inkstones,
and wine as writing fluid,
all chosen for their resistance to freezing.
Some are mined beneath the mountains of Wúdū,
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
Wúdū has inkstone mountain stone.
Others are taken from the streams of Yǒngjiā.
"Records of Yǒngjiā" says:
Yànxī, one source, has many stone inkstones.
As for shapes like lotus leaves or horse hooves,
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Eulogy" says:
Some are round like horse hooves,
pointed like lotus leaves.
Forms of round heaven and square earth,
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Eulogy" says:
Some thin, some thick,
some round, some square.
Square like the image of earth,
round like the light of heaven.
For wood, its softness is valued,
Fù Xuán's "Inkstone Rhapsody" says:
For wood, its softness is valued,
for stone, its moist firmness is admired.
Adding vermilion lacquer for solidity,
containing the pure mystery of inner virtue.
For jade, its resistance to freezing is chosen.
See the note on "silk-covered table" above.
Pigeons have been heard carrying water,
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
At Lántián Yùshùn Mountain's Wùzhēn Temple, a high monk was copying the "Nirvana Sutra,"
and a flock of pigeons carried water from the sky to replenish the inkstone.
It is said to have been passed down by monks of that mountain,
and also appears in Bái Jūyì's hundred-rhyme poem.
Ants have been seen sinking fishing nets.
"Records of the Extraordinary" says:
There was a man named Xú Xuánzhī,
reading by moonlight,
who saw several hundred cavalry warriors
ascend his bed,
and hunt extensively on a flowered carpet.
They then climbed onto his desk,
cast fishing nets in the inkstone,
and caught hundreds of thousands of fish.
A king looked at Xuánzhī,
angered by his disrespect,
and imprisoned him.
The next day,
Xuánzhī dug into the ground,
found an ant nest,
and burned it all.
Dripping the accumulated moisture of the toad,
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" says:
In the past, someone secretly excavated the tomb of Duke Líng of Jìn,
and obtained a jade toad,
as large as a fist,
its belly holding five shēng of water,
moist as new jade,
taken as a water-dropper vessel.
Dotting the cold stars of the mynah bird.
Liǔ Gōngquán once discussed inkstones, saying:
Stones from water,
their color is blue.
Stones from halfway up the mountain,
their color is purple.
Those from the mountain peak are especially moist,
those like the color of pig liver are excellent.
Where water is stored, there are red, white, and yellow dots,
commonly called mynah bird eyes.
If the veins are yellow,
they are called golden threads.
As for the style of the court official,
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Eulogy" says:
Slightly indented at the waist,
it is called the court official style.
The form of the Zhōngkuí,
"Comprehensive Statutes" says:
Guó Prefecture tributes twenty Zhōngkuí stone inkstones.
Empress Zhēn used it as a daily tool,
"History of the Wèi" says:
Empress Zhēn loved writing from a young age,
often using her elder brothers' brushes and inkstones.
Her brothers teased her, saying:
"Do you want to become a female scholar?"
The Empress replied:
"In ancient times, virtuous women
always studied past histories to observe successes and failures."
Yǔwén could not long endure such affairs.
"History of the Suì" says:
Yǔwén Qìng said in his youth:
"Writing is enough to record names,
why should one long engage with brush and inkstone?"
Liú Hóng once associated with Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
"History of the Jìn" says:
Liú Hóng often resided in Luòyáng,
living in the same lane as Emperor Wǔ,
sharing inkstone and mat for writing.
Also, "Anecdotes of the Age" says:
Cáo Shuǎng and Emperor Míng of Wèi also shared this.
Péngzǔ once shared with Emperor Xuān.
"History of the Hàn" says:
Zhāng Péngzǔ once shared an inkstone and mat with Emperor Xuān of Hàn in their humble days.
After ascending the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángdū due to old favor.
Lú Xié angrily threw it,
"History of the Táng" says:
During Emperor Xīzōng's reign,
Lú Xié and Zhèng Tián served as chancellors but were at odds.
Arguing over the matter of Huáng Cháo,
Lú brushed his sleeves and stood up,
throwing the inkstone at him.
Hán Yù recounted its prior burial.
Hán Yù's "Burial of the Inkstone" says:
Lǒngxī's Lǐ Yuánbīn traveled through the Bāo Valley,
accidentally damaged his inkstone box,
and swept and buried it in the capital.
Hán Yù praised and recorded it, saying:
"Earth formed into substance,
fired into a vessel,
the vessel returns to its substance,
not of the class of life and death.
Preserving its use,
destroyed, yet cannot bear to discard,
burying and recording it,
is the righteousness of benevolence."
As for Emperor Wǔ of Liáng not treasuring the soaring phoenix,
"History of the Liáng" says:
Emperor Wǔ was pure and frugal by nature.
Táng Yǒng, magistrate of Wú, presented a cast bronze dragon brazier
and a soaring phoenix inkstone cover,
and the emperor decreed lifelong imprisonment for him.
Dàozhī first obtained it from a floating catalpa,
"Garden of Marvels" says:
Xīn Dàozhī saw a floating catalpa by the water,
took it to make an inkstone,
shaped like a fish,
and placed Taoist talismans and confessions
all in the fish inkstone.
Suddenly it was lost,
and he dreamed of someone saying:
"I briefly traveled to the Xiāng River,
detained by the two consorts.
Now I return,
you may seek me by the water's edge."
Dàozhī went to the water's edge at dawn,
saw a fisherman catch a carp.
He bought it, cut it open,
and found the previous talismans and confessions.
He then understood,
but lost it again.
Someone passing by the Xiāngjūn Temple
saw this fish inkstone beside the two consorts.
A clam gifted to Yǔ Yì,
"History of the Jìn" says:
Yǔ Yì was young when he served as a palace attendant,
valued by Yuán Huàn,
who gifted him a deer-horn book,
a clam inkstone,
and an ivory brush holder.
Iron gifted to Hóngyá.
"Biography of Master Hóngyá" says:
The master wished to return to Hénèi,
when attendant Liú Shǒuzhāng, Taoist Wú Kè, and scholar Zhāng Yǐn came to visit,
gifting the master Yáng Xióng's iron inkstone,
along with the Four Hoaryheads' deer-horn pillow.
Admiring the faint golden threads,
see the note on "mynah bird cold stars."
Re-emphasizing the green blossoms of the droplets.
Táng Dynasty poet Lǐ Hè has a poem titled "Song of the Blue-Flowered Purple Stone Inkstone" which says:
Duānzhōu stoneworkers are skilled as gods,
treading the heavens, grinding swords to slice purple clouds.
Behind gauze curtains, days warm, ink flowers bloom in spring,
light bubbles, faint froth, scented with pine and musk.
It is also heard that Chóusāng produces fine stone.
Táng Dynasty Lǐ Kuāngwén's "Zī Xiá" says:
Chóusāng inkstones began in the early Yuánhé era.
Because my great-uncle served as magistrate of Zhūyáng in Guó Prefecture,
the various Ruǎn family members, in their leisure from attending to warmth and coolness [i.e., filial duties], would always seek out mountains and waters.
One day by a stream bank, they found a stone.
They often carried carving tools with them,
so they inscribed their surnames and the year and month of their mountain excursion.
They realized the stone was beautiful and could be carved into an inkstone,
but it was too large to transport.
They also found many smaller ones, fist-sized,
and brought them to the county seat.
There was a clerk who could carve them,
and selling them brought great profit.
Chóusāng stone inkstones began from this.
Xīngpíng's blue stone:
Liú Chéngzhī's "Record of Jiāngzhōu" says:
South of Càizǐ Pond in Xīngpíng County is a stone cavern,
over two hundred zhàng deep.
The stone is blue in color,
suitable for making writing inkstones.
The brush moves, the ink stains.
Wáng Càn's "Inkstone Inscription" says:
The ink flows, the brush stains,
honor and disgrace serve as warning.
Floating moisture makes the ink gleam.
"The Compendium of Ink" says:
For all writing,
choose a fresh stone for the inkstone,
combining moistness and astringency,
and one that makes the ink gleam with floating moisture.
When studying, one waits for the inkstone to thaw.
"Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" says:
In the first month, the inkstone thaws;
send young children to elementary school.
In the eleventh month, the inkstone is icy cold;
have young children study the "Classic of Filial Piety" and the "Analects."
The washing place is often known for its black water.
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
The Jièzhū Temple in Yuèzhōu is the former residence of Wáng Xīzhī.
There is a pond for washing inkstones,
and to this day the water remains constantly black.
Zhāng Huá was bestowed with a qilin-hair brush along with it.
"Records of Omissions" says:
When Zhāng Huá completed his "Treatise on Curiosities,"
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn bestowed upon him a qilin-horn brush holder,
which was a tribute from Liáoxī.
A green iron inkstone,
made from iron tributed from Yútián.
Ten thousand sheets of cèlǐ paper,
a tribute from Nányuè.
Cèlǐ,
also called zhìlí,
or zhìlǐ,
is a type of seaweed.
Wáng Cí obtained a plain qín along with it.
"Book of Qí" says:
When Wáng Cí was eight years old,
his maternal grandfather, Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià of the Sòng dynasty, brought out treasures
and let him take whatever he wished.
Cí only took a plain qín and a stone inkstone,
and Yìgōng praised him for it.
Those who obtain Duānxī stone value it at a thousand gold.
Liǔ Gōngquán's "Discourse on Inkstones" says:
Using Duānxī stone for inkstones
is most excellent for enhancing ink,
and the blue-purple ones can be worth a thousand gold.
Those from Qīngzhōu are ranked first in fame.
Liǔ Gōngquán's "Discourse on Inkstones" says:
Qīngzhōu stone dust inkstones are the best,
with Jiàngzhōu's coming second.
Some are moved to increased emotion because of ancestors.
"Records of Chénliú" says:
When Fàn Qiáo was two years old,
his grandfather Xīn was on his deathbed.
Patting his head, he said:
"My regret is not being able to see you grow up."
He gave him the inkstone he had used.
When Qiáo turned five,
his grandmother told him about this.
Qiáo held the inkstone and wept.
Some are suddenly lost because of thunder.
Liǔ Gōngquán's "Discourse on Inkstones" says:
Fǔkē Mountain produces stone inkstones.
In the past, when people gathered them,
they would always offer a medium-grade sacrifice.
If not, thunder would suddenly arise,
and the stone would disappear from its place.
As for the exquisite nature of Fénshuǐ,
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
People from Jiàng County are skilled at making chéngní inkstones.
They sew a silk bag and place it in the Fén River,
retrieving it after a year or more.
By then, the mud has already filled the bag.
They fire it into an inkstone,
and it never dries out.
The method for jìn mud is superb.
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
The method for making chéngní inkstones:
Take jìn mud in a double-layered cloth bag,
swing it in water,
obtain the fine particles,
let the clear water settle out,
allow it to dry slightly,
add yellow lead oxide,
knead it like dough,
place it in a mold and press,
making it very firm,
carve it into an inkstone shape with a bamboo knife,
let it dry slightly in the shade,
shape it with a sharp knife,
then sun-dry it.
Pile thickly with rice chaff
and mix with yellow ox dung to fire it.
After one cycle [i.e., a day and night],
then add ink wax,
store it in rice vinegar and steam it five to seven times.
It retains moisture and enhances blackness,
not inferior to stone.
Shè Mountain is esteemed for Lóngwěi stone.
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
Shèzhōu Lóngwěi stone is second only to Duānxī.
In the Western Regions, they only use bamboo joints.
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
The Western Regions have no paper or brush,
only ink.
They use tile shards
or bamboo joints
as their inkstones.
The smoothness and fineness of the Sparrow Platform is kept secret.
"Treatise on the Four Treasures of the Study" says:
At the site of the Wèi dynasty Bronze Sparrow Terrace,
people often excavate its ancient tiles,
carve them into very fine inkstones,
which hold water for several days without drying.
It is traditionally said
that when people built this terrace in the past,
they had potters refine the mud for the tiles, filtering it through coarse and fine hemp cloth,
and added walnut oil to knead it,
hence they differ from other tiles.
Treasure the moistness and purity of Lìgāng.
Lǐ Bái's poem "In Response to Yīn the Eleventh's Gift of a Lìgāng Inkstone" says:
Lord Yīn, a profound scholar of the Three Mysteries,
gifted me a Lìgāng inkstone.
It wets the Zhōngshān hare-hair brush,
its glow outshines silk from Wúmén.
In cold weather, the water does not freeze;
daily use brings no weariness of heart.
Carrying this to the inkstone pool,
it is like facing you once more.
This is why it serves as the city moat in the brush battle array.
Wáng Xīzhī's "Brush Battle Array Diagram" says:
Take the water and inkstone as the city moat.
It is not merely comparing graphite to slanderous talk.
"The Golden Coffer of Tàigōng" says of the inkstone:
Graphite adheres and becomes black;
wicked hearts and slanderous words stain whiteness without waiting.
Paper
The substance of square silk floss,
the Tōngsú Wén states:
square silk floss is called paper.
Smooth as a whetstone,
the Shìmíng states:
paper,
is like a whetstone,
smooth as a whetstone.
In antiquity it did not exist,
only bamboo and wooden slips.
The preface to the Chūnqiū states:
major affairs were written on bamboo slips bound together,
minor affairs on bamboo or wooden slips only.
As for the cèlǐ paper of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
see the note on "Zhāng Huà's lín bǐ" in the Yàn Fù.
The hètí paper of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
the Hànshū states:
Consort Zhào was jealous,
the women of the rear palace, Fù Néng, could bear children,
an edict sealed a small green box,
inside were two pills of medicine,
a hètí document stated:
"Tell Fù Néng to strive to drink the medicine."
Note:
hètí,
is thin, small paper.
Hè is pronounced like hè,
tí is pronounced like tí.
Sōnghuā and phoenix-tail,
the Zīxiá states:
Sōnghuā paper,
its origin is old,
the world considers it Xuē Tāo paper,
which is mistaken.
Lù Guīméng's Cóngshū states:
phoenix-tail approval,
from Jìn until Liáng and Chén times,
was the correspondence of princely residences.
Phoenix-tail refers to the text of the approval.
Approval is like today's system of "permitted."
Phoenix-tail paper,
should be layered thin, light in texture,
exquisitely crafted.
Jade dust and fragrant bark.
Liú Xún's Lǐngbiǎo Yìlù states:
Guǎngzhōu has much zhànxiāng wood,
suitable for making paper,
named fragrant bark.
Also, in Shǔ there is jade dust,
called dust bone.
Yì Qí tore it to foretell defeat,
the Shénxiān Zhuàn states:
the first ruler of Shǔ wished to attack Wú,
asked Lǐ Yìqí,
Yìqí requested paper,
drew several tens of soldiers,
tore them to pieces.
Then drew a great man,
and tore it again.
The first ruler sent troops,
and indeed was defeated.
Zhū Zhān swallowed it to relieve hunger.
the Yánshì Jiāxùn states:
Yìyáng's Zhū Zhān loved learning,
his family was poor,
when there was no cooking for days,
he swallowed paper to fill his stomach,
when cold he embraced a dog to sleep,
later became prominent through learning.
As for Pínghuái peach blossom,
the Huán Xuán Wěishì states:
Huán Xuán issued an edict to Pínghuái,
to make peach blossom paper,
in pale green, green, blue, red, and other colors.
Dōngyáng fish roe,
the Mòshǒu states:
paper made from Dōngyáng fish roe,
is light, soft, smooth, and clean.
Duàn's cloud-blue,
Duàn Chéngshì's preface to the quatrain "Cloud-Blue Paper to Wēn Tíngyún" states:
I was in Jiǔjiāng,
conceived and made cloud-blue paper,
though lacking Zuǒ Bó's method,
and entirely without Zhāng Yǒng's skill,
I sent fifty sheets.
The poem says:
"When the thirty-six scales serve as messengers,
several times still can wrap longing.
Wait until the robe and jacket are recopied,
to write all of Xiāngyáng's bō nuò lyrics."
the Wénfáng Sì Pǔ states:
now in Fēiqīng's collection there are jué zhè lyrics,
fearing the characters bō nuò are mistaken.
Lord Wáng's silkworm cocoon,
the Shìshuō states:
Wáng Xīzhī wrote the Lántíng Xù,
using silkworm cocoon paper and mouse-whisker brush,
vigorous, graceful, and robust,
unmatched in any generation.
Golden flower and Xuē bone,
Shàn vine and hemp surface.
the Dūyáng Biān states:
in Emperor Dézōng's temple a vermilion bird came,
often ate jade dust,
its voice very clear and melodious.
When attacked by a bird of prey,
the palace women all wrote the Heart Sūtra on golden flower paper to pray for its afterlife blessings.
Also, the Guóshǐ Bǔ states:
among fine papers,
there are Yuè's Shàn vine and moss paper,
Shǔ's hemp surface, Xuē bone, golden flower, fish roe, and ten-color paper.
Distinguishing gravity by white and yellow,
the Yùshǐ Gùshì states:
for impeachment memorials,
white slips were for grave matters,
yellow paper for light matters.
Now uniformly white paper,
without distinction.
Following flexion and extension in unrolling and rolling.
Fù Xián's Zhǐ Fù states:
grasp it and it unrolls,
release it and it rolls up.
As for Gān Bǎo being granted two hundred,
Gān Bǎo's memorial states:
I previously wished to compile records of ancient and modern strange and extraordinary events,
extensively inquiring among the knowledgeable,
scraps of paper and incomplete lines,
each matter different.
Also lacking paper and brush,
sometimes writing on old paper.
An edict granted two hundred sheets of paper.
Táo Kǎn presenting three thousand,
see the note on "Táo Kǎn presented it to the Jìn emperor" in the Mò Fù.
The beauty of Qīngtóng's lánggān,
the Yǒuyáng Zázǔ states:
at Lóngmén in the Eastern Capital there was a household,
traditionally said to be where Guǎngchéngzǐ resided.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
the Yǎ Chánshī lived there.
The courtyard had many ancient paulownia trees,
when the paulownia bloomed, there were strange bees,
their sound like human chanting.
The Chánshī observed closely,
they had human form,
so he rolled bamboo screens and spread nets to capture them.
Placed in a gauze cage,
thinking they liked paulownia flowers,
he gathered and placed them nearby.
Suddenly several bees flew and gathered,
comforting and encouraging through the cage.
One said:
"I was playing chess with Lord Qīngtóng,
won and obtained ten sheets of lánggān paper,
when you go out, write the 'Starlight' lyrics for me."
Their speech was not of human worldly affairs,
the monk then raised the cage and released them.
Fàn Nìng's vine-corner's elegance.
Fàn Nìng's instruction states:
coarse paper cannot be used for official documents,
all must use vine-corner paper.
Five colors first seen in a phoenix's beak,
the Yèzhōng Jì states:
Shí Hǔ issued an edict to place five-color paper in the mouth of a phoenix chick.
Pure white sometimes suffers insect damage.
the Tángshū states:
Emperor Gāozōng's Shàngyuán edict states:
"Edicts and decrees for implementation,
since they are permanent models.
Recently using white paper,
often suffers insect damage,
henceforth all should use yellow paper."
Tribute to Héxī,
the Dōngguān Hànjì states:
when Empress Héxī Dèng attended court,
she ordered all tribute from myriad states completely halted,
only paper and ink were to be offered annually.
Requesting from the secret repository,
Yú Yù's memorial states:
the secret repository has over thirty thousand sheets of cloth paper,
unsuitable for writing imperial documents,
I beg four hundred sheets to be given to the historiography clerks to write the daily records.
Commending Dù Xiān's hundred sheets,
the Tángshū states:
Dù Xiān was a military advisor in Wùzhōu,
when his term ended and he was to return,
the clerks gave him ten thousand sheets of paper as a gift,
Xiān only accepted one hundred sheets.
People sighed and said:
"How is this different from the honest official of old accepting a single large coin?"
Praising one case from Wèi Wǔ.
Wèi Wǔ's order states:
now all subordinate officials, attendants, and regional inspectors shall each month at court present gains and losses,
each given one paper case.
As for enjoying this smoothness,
Liú Xiàowēi's "Thanks for Official Paper" states:
even if it were the phoenix-held paper of the Yè palace, the fishnet paper of the Hàn court, the peach blossom paper of Pínghuái, or the grain-tree paper of the central palace,
I would still be ashamed before this smoothness,
and thank you for this fresh splendor.
Observing this frugal squareness,
Fù Xián's Zhǐ Fù states:
Having created notches to replace knotted cords,
they also made paper to serve as bamboo slips.
Its integrity is square and substantial,
its pliant nature wholly genuine.
It contains elegance and harbors refinement,
truly fond of this culture.
Xuē Tāo boasted of the Shǔ style,
the Zīxiá Lù states:
In the early Yuánhé era,
Xuē Tāo enjoyed composing short poems,
but regretted that the paper sheets were too large,
not wishing to have excessive leftover space,
so she made them narrower and smaller.
The talented scholars of Shǔ found this convenient,
and later, when reducing other letter papers, they did the same,
specifically naming them Xuē Tāo jiān.
Sēngqián flaunted the silver light.
The Dānyáng Jì states:
In Jiāngníng County there was a Paper Office,
the place where Emperor Gāo of Qí made paper.
He once had níngguāng paper made and bestowed it upon Wáng Sēngqián,
also called yínguāng.
That which came from the Jìn dynasty was a gift to Shān Tāo,
Shān Jiǎn’s Memorial states:
My father Tāo,
received a handwritten imperial edict on blue paper from the late emperor.
That which fell in Chēnzhōu was an auspicious sign for Wēn Yù.
The Yīnhuà Lù states:
In the Dàzhōng era,
Kǒng Wēn Yù was demoted to Chēnzhōu for forthright admonishment,
when a magpie appeared joyfully in the courtyard,
his children and grandchildren bowed to it,
and it flew away.
It dropped a small piece of paper,
on which were the characters “bǔ quē.”
Not long after,
he was recalled to court,
and indeed received that appointment.
Praise the piǎo red of the Eastern Palace,
the Dōnggōng Jiùshì states:
When the Crown Prince first received his appointment,
he was given one hundred sheets each of red paper and piǎo red hemp paper.
Value the Yúnyáng of Liùhé.
the Guóshǐ Bǔ states:
Yúnyáng has Liùhé jiān,
and also Púzhōu white thin paper, and double-copied Línchuān smooth thin paper.
There were even tree leaves especially prized,
the Línyì Jì states:
In Jiǔzhēn custom,
they wrote on tree leaves as paper.
Also, Zhèng Qián, as a Guǎngwén academician,
studied calligraphy,
but suffered from lack of paper.
Learning that Cí’ēn Temple had several rooms full of persimmon leaves,
he then borrowed a monk’s dwelling,
took the red leaves to practice calligraphy,
and over the years nearly covered them all.
Mulberry root was even cleaner,
the Wénfáng Sì Pǔ states:
Léi Kǒngzhāng’s great-grandson Mùzhī
still possessed a letter from Zhāng Huà to his grandfather,
which was on mulberry root paper.
Cài Hóu first marveled at its fresh splendor,
the Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Eunuch Cài Lún oversaw the Imperial Workshop,
and made paper,
what is called Cài Hóu paper.
the Yúfú Zhì states:
Cài Hóu paper used old hemp,
called hemp paper.
Tree bark,
called gǔ paper.
Old fishing nets,
called net paper.
Zǐliáng again praised its exquisite perfection.
Xiāo Zǐliáng’s Reply to Wáng Sēngqián states:
Zǐyì’s paper,
is beautiful, exquisite, and radiant.
Zhòngjiāng’s ink,
a single dot is like lacquer.
Because of Xiàngrú it became even more prized,
the Hànshū states:
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú composed the “Zǐxū Fù,”
Yáng Déyì recited it,
the emperor admired its diction,
and throughout the capital it was copied and circulated,
making paper expensive.
Meeting Xīzhī, it was used without restraint.
the Yǔlín states:
Wáng Yòujūn was in Kuàijī,
Xiè Gōng requested letter paper,
the storehouse had ninety thousand sheets,
and he gave them all to him.
Huán Xuānwǔ said:
“Yìshǎo shows no restraint.”
Yáng Xù mended his quilt, his virtue lofty,
Xiè Chéng’s Hòu Hànshū states:
Yáng Xù served as governor of Nányáng,
in purity leading his subordinates,
he only slept under a single cloth cover,
when it frayed and tore,
he pasted paper to mend it.
Gě Hóng sold firewood, his ambition earnest.
the Bàopǔzǐ states:
Gě Hóng’s family was poor,
he cut firewood and sold it,
to afford paper and ink.
He often lacked paper,
what he wrote was on both sides, with characters overlapping,
few could read it.
This can supply daily use in the garden of letters,
and hand down an endless fragrance of noble deeds.
Ink
The Declarations of the Perfected states:
Ink is the image of yin.
The Declarations of the Perfected states:
Why is ink commonly used for writing today?
Because literary compositions belong to yin,
and ink
is the image of yin.
The Explanation of Names says:
Ink carries the meaning of darkness.
The Explanation of Names says:
Ink
means darkness.
It is said to resemble things being dark and silent.
Lù Yún obtained it from the Wèi Terrace.
In Lù Shìlóng's Letter to His Elder Brother, it is said:
One day I went up to the Three Terraces,
where Lord Cáo had stored hundreds of thousands of catties of graphite.
Now I am sending two snail-shells of it.
Táo Kǎn presented it to the Jìn Emperor.
The Manual of the Four Treasures of the Study says:
Táo Kǎn presented to the Jìn Emperor three thousand sheets of fine paper
and twenty pellets of ink,
all of the utmost exquisite quality.
Some were famously called Zhòngzhāngjīn.
In Shí Chóng's Bond for a Slave, it is said:
Zhòngzhāngjīn is fine ink;
passing through the market, several snail-shells were sold.
Some were marvelously called Zǔshì.
The Manual says:
The Zǔ clan originally hailed from Yángdìng;
they were official ink-makers of the Táng dynasty.
The world considered their Yìshuǐ ink superior,
and the name of the Zǔ clan became renowned throughout the land.
Wáng Lǎng received gracious gifts.
The Biographies of Elders from Chénliú says:
Wáng Lǎng was resolute and fierce,
capable of unraveling tangled knots
and breaking through difficult points.
Investigating the rebellion plot of King Yīng of Chǔ,
which implicated over a thousand people,
when the matter was concluded and he was summoned,
his interrogations were flawless.
Upon the first audience, he was bestowed with the imperial brush and ink;
upon the second audience, he was bestowed with a girdle;
upon the third audience, he was appointed as the Clerk of the Western Section of the Minister over the Masses.
Zhāng Yǒng also transmitted his ingenious ideas.
The Book of Sòng says:
Zhāng Yǒng excelled in clerical script,
and also possessed ingenious ideas.
Both paper and ink were of his own making.
Whenever the Emperor received Zhāng Yǒng's memorials or petitions,
he would hold and admire them, sighing in admiration,
lamenting that what was supplied to the imperial court could not compare.
Staining a fan and thereby creating a dappled ox.
The Book of Jìn says:
Wáng Xiànzhī was writing on a fan for Huán Wēn,
when he accidentally stained it with ink.
He then turned it into a dappled cow,
which was very skillfully done.
Also, Cáo Xìng was painting a screen,
when he accidentally stained it,
and turned it into a fly,
which Emperor Wén flicked with his hand.
Emerging from a pond and startling a youth.
The Manual says:
During the Yìxī era,
the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra resided at Minister Xiè's Temple in Jiànyè,
where he built the Hall of Protecting Purity,
and translated the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Suddenly, a pond manifested below the hall,
from which a dark-clad youth often emerged,
sweeping and grinding ink for the monks.
Wáng Yuǎn wrote on it and the ink entered the wood.
The Biographies of Divine Immortals says:
Emperor Huán of Hàn summoned the immortal Wáng Yuǎn,
who then inscribed over four hundred characters on the palace gate.
The Emperor disliked them and had them scraped off,
but while the outer characters were removed,
the inner characters reappeared,
as the ink had all penetrated deep into the wood.
Bān Mèng sprayed it and it formed characters.
The Biographies of Divine Immortals says:
Bān Mèng could chew ink,
and with one spray, it would all form characters,
filling the paper with meaningful text.
There are also two snail-shells and nine sons.
The two snail-shells are mentioned above in the note on "Lù Yún obtained it from the Wèi Terrace."
The Manual says:
In ancient times, there was the ink of nine sons,
used to wish newlyweds many children,
a symbol of good prayers.
The blessing said:
"The ink of nine sons,
made from pine soot.
May the family line be long-lived,
with descendants flourishing along the borders."
Also, Duàn Chéngshì, in sending ink to Wēn Fēiqīng, wrote:
"Famed as the nine sons,
shaped differently from the two snail-shells."
Shàngdǎng Yúmí.
The Manual says:
Pine hearts from Shàngdǎng make especially fine ink.
The Book of Hàn says:
The Imperial Secretary, his deputies, and the court gentlemen were monthly bestowed one large Yúmí ink stick and one small Yúmí ink stick.
Duàn Chéngshì, in sending ink to Wēn Fēiqīng, wrote:
"Yúmí pine knots,
long since ceased to exist.
Its hardness is like jade,
its grain like rhinoceros horn."
The Manual says:
In the region of Yīshè, there was a man named Lǐ Chāo,
originally from Yìshuǐ.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, he wandered displaced,
and eventually settled in Shè,
where he made exceptionally marvelous ink,
its hardness like jade,
its grain like rhinoceros horn.
There is also that which is spat from the belly of a fish.
Táo Yǐnjū's Commentary on the Materia Medica says:
The cuttlefish has ink in its belly,
which is now used to make fine ink.
Grinding it on the shield's nose.
The Manual says:
Xún Jì of Yǐngchuān had an old acquaintance with Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
but the Emperor always looked down on him.
When Liáng received the abdication,
he went north.
It is said
he once ground ink on the nose of a shield,
to write a proclamation against Liáng.
Blending the soot of Duke Jì's two liǎng.
The Ink Method of Duke Jì:
Two liǎng of pine soot,
a small amount each of clove, musk, and dried lacquer,
mixed with glue water to form sticks,
then fumigated over fire smoke,
usable after one month.
Adding purple grass powder makes it purple;
adding ash bark powder makes it blue.
Proud of Zhòngjiāng's dot of lacquer.
Xiāo Zǐliáng's Writings say:
Zhòngjiāng's ink,
a single dot is like lacquer.
Yáng Xióng received a gift and viewed books in the stone chamber.
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital says:
An edict ordered the Imperial Secretary to bestow upon Yáng Xióng brushes and ink,
to view books in the stone chamber.
Wáng Sù communicated with spirits and annotated the Book of Changes in the eastern studio.
The Records of Geography says:
During the Hàn dynasty, Wáng Lǎng was the Governor of Kuàijī,
and his son Sù accompanied him to the commandery,
residing in the eastern studio.
At night, a woman emerged from the ground,
claiming to be the daughter of the King of Zhào.
She spoke with Sù,
and at dawn, bid farewell, gifting him a pellet of ink.
Sù was just about to annotate the Zhouyi,
and because of this, felt his talent and thoughts become enlightened.
Thus, there were collars and sleeves as black as dye,
and lips and teeth all blackened.
Zhào Yī's "Against Cursive Script" says:
"One brush every ten days,
several pellets of ink per month.
Collars and sleeves as black as dye,
lips and teeth all blackened."
As for storing it for ten years on Lú Mountain,
The Ink Compendium says:
Lú Mountain pine soot,
and Dàijùn deer antler glue,
aged over ten years,
hard as stone,
is marvelous.
Supplying four pellets to the Eastern Palace.
The Records of the Eastern Palace say:
When the Crown Prince was first appointed,
he was supplied with four pellets of fragrant ink.
Wáng Bó's filled sleeves.
The Book of Táng says:
When Wáng Bó was young,
he once dreamt that someone gave him ink pellets filling his sleeves,
and afterwards, his literary compositions greatly advanced.
The Xīn dynasty's defiling of the imperial tomb walls.
The Book of Hàn says:
When Guāngwǔ rose,
Wáng Mǎng ordered ink to be used to defile the surrounding walls of the Wèi and Yán tombs.
There is also breaking marrow to clarify one's will.
Sòng Yún's Travel Record says:
The King of Móxiū in the Western Heavens broke his marrow to make ink,
to write the Mahāyāna Sūtra.
Cutting out the heart to express piety.
The Records of the Neglected says:
In the past, Lǎojūn resided on Jǐngshì Mountain,
and with five old men, discussed the numbers of heaven and earth,
composing scriptures totaling nearly a hundred thousand words.
Two divine beings from the country of Xītí
brought forth a golden pot,
inside which was ink,
resembling thick lacquer,
with which they wrote.
When the golden pot's ink was exhausted,
The two men then carved out their hearts and drained their blood,
using it in place of ink.
The Five Elders are the interpretations of the Five Heavens,
Jǐngshì,
Tàishì and Shàoshì.
Selling firewood to establish a livelihood,
see the note on "Gě Hóng selling firewood" in the "Rhapsody on Paper."
Drinking water to punish faults.
The "Northern Qi Court Assembly Ritual" states:
After the various commandery governors had finished their reports,
they were sent to present local products.
If there were errors in the characters or the calligraphy was poor,
they were invariably ordered to drink one shēng of ink.
Xuánguāng has a biography by Wén Sōng,
and Wén Sōng wrote "A Brief Biography of Marquis Sōngzī Yì Xuánguāng," which says:
His courtesy name was Chǔhuì,
and he was a man of Yān.
His ancestor was called Qīngsōngzǐ.
Xuánguāng and Shí Xūzhōng of Nányuè were friends who studied the clouds and waters together,
and he was a companion in literary refinement with Máo Yuánruì of Xuānchéng.
The Son of Heaven valued Confucian scholars,
enfeoffing Xuánguāng as Marquis of Sōngzī,
and he was prominently employed for his literary talent.
The green pine recites the verses of Cáo Zhí.
Cáo Zhí's "Music Bureau Poem" says:
Ink comes from the smoke of green pines,
the brush comes from the fur of cunning hares.
This is the helmet and armor of the brush formation.
Xī Zhī's "Diagram of the Brush Formation" says:
Ink is
the helmet and armor.
It truly precedes all in the literary garden.
Boat
In ancient times, the sages hollowed out wood to make boats,
benefiting all generations.
The Book of Changes states:
"Hollowing out wood to make boats,
sharpening wood to make oars;
the utility of boats and oars
is to cross what is impassable."
Some say it originated with Yú Xǔ and Gōng Chuí.
The Annals of Lü Buwei states:
"Yú Xǔ created boats."
The character Xǔ is pronounced qú,
also pronounced xǔ.
The Mozi states:
"Gōng Chuí created boats."
Some say it began with Huò Dí and Gòng Gǔ.
The Shiben states:
"Gòng Gǔ and Huò Dí,
two ministers of the Yellow Emperor,
first made boats."
Although it began with hollowed wood,
the Huainanzi states:
"The ancients saw hollowed wood floating and thus made boats."
Some boasted of floating earth.
The Shiben states:
"Lǐnjūn, named Xiāng,
of the Bā clan,
along with the Fán, Shěn, Xiāng, and Zhèng clans,
five clans in total, contended for divinity.
They made boats from earth,
carved and painted them.
Whose boat floated,
the gods would make him ruler.
Only Lǐnjūn's boat floated,
so he was established as ruler."
Then there were the Yúhuáng of Wú,
the Zuozhuan states:
"Chǔ defeated Wú,
capturing their boat Yúhuáng."
And the Yúnmǔ of Hàn.
The Shiyi Ji states:
"Emperor Chéng of Hàn adorned the prow with yúnmǔ,
naming it the Yúnmǔ Boat."
The white fish auspicious for Zhōu leapt thus,
the Zhōushū states:
"King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
crossing the river,
a white fish leapt into the king's boat.
The king took it and burned it with firewood."
The yellow dragon, moved by Yǔ, came to bear him.
The Annals of Lü Buwei states:
"Yǔ traveled south,
just crossing the Jiāng River,
a yellow dragon bore the boat.
The people on the boat were terrified.
Yǔ looked up to heaven and sighed:
'I received the mandate from heaven,
exerting myself to nourish the people.
Life
is nature;
death
is fate.
Why worry about the dragon?'"
The dragon lowered its ears, trailed its tail, and departed.
