If one drifts aimlessly without attachment,
the Zhuangzi states:
"The skillful toil, the wise worry;
the incapable have no desires.
Eating and wandering freely,
drifting like an untethered boat."
Then even if struck, one feels no anger.
The Zhuangzi states:
"Crossing a river by boat,
if an empty boat comes and strikes,
even a narrow-minded person
will ultimately not be angry.
But if suddenly there is a person aboard it,
then angry shouts follow.
Previously not angry, now angry;
previously empty, now real."
As for Dào Jì's zéměng boat,
the Yìyuàn states:
"Tán Dào Jì, during the Yuánjiā era, garrisoned Xúnyáng.
Someone cast a net in Cháisāng,
recovering a large ship,
its holes drilled as if new.
He had craftsmen make a zéměng boat,
but the workers mistakenly cut both ends,
deeming it inauspicious,
and killed three skilled hands.
When he entered court,
he was indeed executed."
Huáng Gài's méngchōng ships,
the Records of Wú states:
"Zhōu Yú opposed Lord Cáo,
his general Huáng Gài took several dozen méngchōng warships,
filled them with firewood and grass,
poured oil inside,
wrapped them with curtains,
raised command flags atop,
rode the wind to release them,
setting them ablaze simultaneously.
The wind was fierce then,
burning all the shore camps,
Lord Cáo's army retreated in defeat."
Xú Xuān rode the waves with valor,
the Records of Wèi states:
"Xú Xuān was promoted to Colonel Director of the Retainers.
Following Emperor Míng to Guǎnglíng,
the six armies rode boats,
when wind and waves suddenly arose,
the emperor's boat capsized.
Xuān's boat was behind,
but rode the waves forward.
No other officials reached him,
and the emperor admired his courage."
Dèng Tōng held the oar with ease.
The Book of Hàn states:
"Dèng Tōng, as a huángtóu láng, rowed boats."
Note:
"Earth overcomes water,
its color is yellow,
so all boatmen wore yellow caps."
Moored at Wūjiāng awaiting Xiàng Yǔ,
the Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Xiàng Yǔ was defeated,
wishing to cross east over the Wū River.
The Wūjiāng station master moored a boat and waited."
Burning Chìbì to drive off Lord Cáo.
The Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn states:
"Zhōu Yú defeated the Wèi army.
Lord Cáo wrote again to Sūn Quán:
'At the battle of Chìbì,
there happened to be plague.
I burned the boats and retreated myself,
unjustly letting Zhōu Yú gain this fame in vain.'"
Greatly seen galloping horses,
the Book of Jìn states:
"Emperor Wǔ planned to attack Wú,
ordering the Governor of Yìzhōu, Wáng Jùn, to repair warships.
Jùn then made large ships joined as rafts,
one hundred twenty paces square,
carrying over two thousand people.
With wood as walls,
raising towers and watchtowers,
opening four gates,
upon which horses could gallop back and forth.
Also painted yì-shou and strange beasts on the prows,
to frighten the river god.
The magnificence of boats and oars
was unprecedented since ancient times."
Auspiciously heard gathering bees.
The Yǔlín states:
"King Wǔ of Zhōu campaigned east,
crossing the river at night.
The moon was bright as day then,
the eight hundred troops all offered treasures and sang.
A large bee, resembling a crimson bird,
flew and gathered on the king's boat.
Thus they painted birds on the banners.
The next day, they beheaded Zhòu,
naming their boat the Bee Boat."
The people of Zhèng attacked Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào,
capturing his Bee Banner,
which was of the same kind."
Thus one can ride swift currents,
Mǎ Róng's "Guǎngchéng Ode" states:
"Square yúhuáng boats,
joined qiōng boats.
Spread cloud-like sails,
set up rainbow canopies.
Subdue the swift wind,
ride the rapid currents.
Raise oar songs,
release water chants."
Those that ride the long wind.
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" states:
"Polemen and oarsmen,
selected from Mǐnyú.
Riding the long wind,
frolicking with Líng Xū."
Then floating on the river for a thousand lǐ,
the Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Wǔ floated on the river shooting flood dragons,
with ships stretching a thousand lǐ."
Note:
"Zhú,
the stern where the rudder is held.
Lú,
the bow where the oar is plied."
Attacking Chǔ with ten thousand vessels,
the Shǔ Wáng Běnjì states:
"Qín made ten thousand bó ships,
intending to attack Chǔ."
Water so shallow it can only float mustard seeds,
the Zhuangzi states:
"If the accumulation of water is not deep,
then it lacks the strength to bear large boats.
Pour a cup of water in a hall's depression,
and a mustard seed becomes a boat;
place a cup there and it sticks."
The water is shallow, yet the boat is large.
The river is wide, yet it cannot even accommodate a small boat.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Who says the river is wide?
It cannot even accommodate a small boat."
As for the method of the shātáng wood,
the *Shí Yí Jì* says:
Emperor Chéng of Hàn often frolicked with Zhào Fēiyàn in the Tàiyè Pond,
using boats made of shātáng wood,
valued for not sinking.
The beauty of the mùlán wood,
Rěn Fǎng's *Shù Yì Jì* says:
Lǔ Bān carved a boat from mùlán wood,
and the mùlán boats spoken of by poets originate from this.
The names of the cǎilíng and xiángfèng boats,
the *Xījīng Zá Jì* says:
In the Tàiyè Pond, there are cǎilíng boats.
Táo Jìzhí's *Jīng Bāng Jì* says:
When Emperor Wǔ of Sòng crossed the Liùhé River,
there were three thousand four hundred and fifty vessels, from dragon boats to xiángfèng boats and below,
such abundance of boats and oars
was unprecedented in previous eras.
The designs of the zhǐnán and cháng'ān boats.
The *Jìn Gōng Gé Jì* says:
In the Língzhī Pond, there are mínghè boats and zhǐnán boats.
In the Dū Pond, there are huárùn boats and cháng'ān boats.
The terms liánglì and Jìn bó.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
A liánglì is not used to assault a city wall.
Annotation:
Lì
means a small boat.
The *Fēngsú Tōng* says:
In Jìn, it is called bó.
Categories like Wú diāo and Yuè nǚ boats.
Zhāng Yī's *Pí Yǎ* says:
Diāo
is a Wú boat,
pronounced diāo.
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* says:
In the Tàiyè Pond, there are Yuè nǚ boats.
Some carry real firewood and set fires,
see the annotation for "Huáng Gài méngchōng."
Some erect banners and streamers to reflect in the water.
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* says:
In the Kūnmíng Pond, there are several hundred gē boats,
bearing spears and halberds,
with banners hanging from all four corners,
streamers, feathered canopies, and command flags,
illuminating the banks.
Mào,
pronounced ěr.
Lǐ and Guǒ sailed together and ascended as immortals.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Guǒ Línzōng traveled to Luòyáng,
and upon first meeting the Governor of Hénán, Lǐ Yīng,
Yīng greatly admired him,
and they became close friends.
Thus, his fame shook the capital.
Later, when he returned to his hometown,
the gentry and scholars saw him off to the riverbank,
with thousands of carriages.
Línzōng only crossed the river in the same boat as Yīng,
and the guests watching them
thought they were immortals.
Hú and Yuè being of one mind and crossing together.
Wáng Bì's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
Sharing a boat to cross together,
then why worry about Hú and Yuè having different minds?
Delighting in this qīngkuàng boat.
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* says:
In the Tàiyè Pond, there are mínghè, róngyǔ, qīngkuàng, cǎilíng, and other boats.
Praising its lightness and speed.
Liáng Wáng Yún's poem "In Response to Línrǔ Hóu's Command, Singing of the Light and Fast Boat" says:
My lord adorns the light and fast boat,
rocking and swaying, surpassing flying clouds.
Riding the waves, adorned with yì birds' colors,
reflected in the water, glowing with dragon patterns.
Bǔ Shì's practice in Bóchāng.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
Bǔ Shì wished to practice archery with Línzī.
Those in Bóchāng who practiced boating died in Nányuè.
Hè Qí's extravagance with crimson curtains.
The *Wú Zhì* says:
General Hè Qí
was fond of luxury and finery,
the boats he rode were carved and painted red,
with green canopies and crimson curtains,
méngchōng assault ships and dòujiàn warships,
looking from afar like mountains.
Yán Huí speaking of Cì's arrival.
The *Chōng Bō Zhuàn* says:
Confucius sent Zǐgòng to Wú,
but he did not return for a long time,
so he told his disciples to divine,
and they encountered the Dǐng hexagram,
all saying "without feet, he will not come."
Yán Huí covered his mouth and laughed, saying:
"Without feet
means he comes by boat."
Zǐgòng arrived in the morning,
just as Huí had said.
Guō Fān forcing Yǔ Yì to stoop.
The *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
Ānxī Yǔ Yì, relying on his status as the emperor's uncle,
personally went to pressure Guō Fān,
wanting to force him to take office.
Fān's boat was narrow and small,
and Yì wanted to lead him onto a larger boat,
but Fān said:
"Since you, sir, do not disdain my lowliness and have condescended to visit,
this is indeed the boat of a rustic."
Yì stooped and entered his boat.
Singing of cassia oars and seeing the *Chǔ Cí*.
The *Chǔ Cí* says:
Cassia oars and orchid rudders,
cutting through ice and piling snow.
Wearing leopard fur to greet the Jìn envoy.
The *Shuō Yuàn* says:
Jìn Pínggōng sent Shū Xiàng on a mission to Wú,
and the people of Wú decorated boats to welcome him,
with five hundred men on each side,
some wearing embroidered clothes and leopard fur,
others in brocade clothes and fox fur,
Shū Xiàng returned and reported to Pínggōng, saying:
"Wú is likely to perish!"
For great rivers, the way is manifested in Fù Yuè.
The *Shū·Yuè Mìng* says:
If crossing a great river,
I use you as boat and oar.
For the Five Lakes, achievement is completed by Fàn Lǐ.
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* says:
After Fàn Lǐ destroyed Wú,
he then took a small boat,
went out through the Three Rivers,
entered the Five Lakes,
and no one knew where he went.
Also heard of Gān Níng's brocade cables displaying extravagance.
The *Wú Shū* says:
Gān Níng often used silk brocade to moor his boat,
and when leaving, he would cut and discard it,
to display his extravagance.
The Gù family's cloth sail being unharmed.
The *Shì Shuō* says:
Gù Chángkāng served as an assistant to Yīn Jīngzhōu,
and requested leave to return east,
at that time, cloth sails were not usually provided,
but Gù pleaded hard for one.
Upon reaching Pòzhǒng,
he encountered a great storm and was in distress,
so he wrote a letter to Yīn, saying:
"The traveler is safe and sound,
the cloth sail is unharmed."
Wind and waves had already drowned Dù Jī.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
Attendant-in-Chief Dù Jī built an imperial tower ship,
and while testing it on the Táo River,
encountered a storm and drowned.
Emperor Wén issued an edict, saying:
"Míng diligently performed his duties and died in water,
Jì sowed the hundred grains and died on a mountain.
Dù Jī was the epitome of loyalty."
Are boats and oars truly superior to the Liáng Prime Minister?
The *Shuō Yuàn* says:
The Prime Minister of Liáng died,
and Huìzǐ wanted to go to Liáng,
but fell into the water while crossing the river.
A boatman saved him,
asking:
"Where are you going in such a hurry?"
He replied:
"Liáng has no prime minister,
I wish to go and become its prime minister."
The boatman said:
"You were drowning amidst the boat and oars,
without me, you would have died,
how can you be prime minister of Liáng?"
Huìzǐ said:
"When it comes to staying amidst broad boats and long oars,
then I am not as good as you,
but when it comes to stabilizing the state and benefiting the altars of soil and grain,
you are as blind as one who has never seen a dog compared to me."
Sūn Quán turned back and received arrows.
The *Wèi Lüè* says:
Sūn Quán came on a large ship to observe the army,
and Lord Cáo ordered crossbowmen to shoot wildly,
arrows struck his ship,
causing it to list heavily and nearly capsize.
Quán then turned the ship around,
and had the other side receive arrows,
until the arrows were evenly distributed and the ship leveled,
before returning.
Cāngshū carved and weighed an elephant.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
Duke Āi of Dèng, named Zhòng, styled Cāngshū,
was as intelligent as an adult by age five or six.
Sūn Quán once sent a giant elephant,
and Tàizǔ wanted to know its weight,
consulting his subordinates,
but none could figure out a method.
Zhòng said:
"Place the elephant on a large boat and mark the waterline,
then weigh objects to load it,
and the comparison can be known."
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and immediately implemented it.
The fool was heard of seeking the sword,
The Annals of Lü Buwei says:
A man of Chǔ was crossing a river,
his sword fell from the boat into the water,
he hastily carved a mark on the boat, saying:
"This is where my sword fell."
The boat moved on,
and he entered the water from the carved spot to seek it.
Was that not confused?
The wise man observed him taking off his clothes.
The Book of Hàn says:
Chén Píng fled back to Hàn,
crossing a river,
the boatman suspected he had gold,
and secretly intended to harm him.
Chén Píng took off his clothes and poled the boat,
thus avoiding harm.
The Hàn River has the blame of the sinking glue boat,
The Records of Emperors and Kings says:
King Zhāo was crossing the Hàn River,
the boatman hated him,
and presented him with a glue boat.
Midstream, the boat disintegrated,
and the king drowned in the water.
The river has the poem of the floating cypress boat.
The Book of Songs says:
Floating that cypress boat,
in the middle of that river.
Note:
The boat in the middle of the river,
is like a woman in her husband's home,
which is her constant place.
There are also cables seen tying it,
The Book of Songs says:
Floating, floating, the poplar boat,
cables tie it.
Note:
Fú,
is a large rope.
Lí,
is to tie.
Stems and stems connect.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
Stems and stems connect,
for ten thousand lǐ, masts link.
I have heard of Yuè's qiōng and Shǔ's líng,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Yuè's qiōng and Shǔ's líng,
cannot travel without water.
How could one use jade ships and jade oars?
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity says:
Jade ships and jade oars,
have no use for crossing rivers;
golden bows and jade strings,
have no ability to shoot arrows.
Therefore, those who are upright and pure but lack governance skills,
are not instruments for restoring order;
those who are refined and elegant but lack administrative strategies,
are not talents for assisting and illuminating.
There is also Cài Jī seen rocking,
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
The Marquis of Qí and Cài Jī were boating in the garden,
she rocked the lord,
the lord, frightened, changed color,
forbade her but she would not stop,
the lord, angry, sent her back.
The Qín general once burned,
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Qín's Mèng Míng attacked Jìn,
crossed the river and burned the boats,
took Wángguān and Jiāo.
Floating these five-joined,
Zhōu Chù's "Records of Local Conditions" says:
Small ones are called zhōu,
large ones are called chuán.
Wēnmá five-joined,
Yǒngníng County produces Yùzhāng timber,
joining five planks to make a large boat,
thus named five-joined.
Chénfú,
is the name of a large green paulownia boat,
the duck-head boat made by Zhūgě Kè.
Hàopiāo,
means the boat on the water,
like lotus flowers scattered and floating on the river.
Holds ten thousand people.
The "Notes on Hàn Palaces" says:
Emperor Wǔ made the Kūnmíng Pond,
forty lǐ in circumference,
built Yùzhāng large boats,
capable of carrying ten thousand people,
with palaces built on the boats.
Fēiyún was seen in the state of Wú,
The "Chronicles of Jiāngbiǎo" says:
Sūn Quán rode the Fēiyún large boat,
with Zhāng Zhāo, Lǔ Sù, and others chasing to see off and bid farewell.
Qīnghàn was heard of from È Jūn.
See the note on "È Jūn's Embroidered Quilt" in the "Rhapsody on Songs."
There is also Emperor Hàn Wǔ's song of crossing the Fén River,
see the note on "The Fén River's Majestic Beauty" in the "Rhapsody on Songs."
Guǎng Dé had the admonition at the Biànmén.
The Book of Hàn says:
The emperor was offering libation sacrifices at the ancestral temple,
exited through the Biànmén,
intending to ride a tower ship.
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief Xuē Guǎngdé faced the imperial carriage,
removed his cap and admonished, saying:
"You should take the bridge."
The edict said:
"Grandee, put on your cap."
Guǎngdé said:
"If Your Majesty does not listen to your servant,
your servant will cut his own throat and stain the carriage wheels with blood,
and Your Majesty will not enter the temple."
The emperor was displeased.
The Grandee of the Palace Garrison Zhāng Měng advanced and said:
"Your servant has heard that when the ruler is sage, the ministers are upright.
Riding a boat is dangerous,
taking the bridge is safe,
a sage ruler does not take risks.
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief's words can be heeded."
The emperor said:
"Persuading people should indeed be like this."
Then he took the bridge.
Mù Mǎn's riding dragon and bird,
The Biography of King Mù says:
The Son of Heaven rode bird boats and dragon boats, floating on the great marsh.
Note:
Boats shaped like dragons and birds,
like today's Wú's qīngquè fǎng.
Shānsōng's gazing at ducks and geese.
See the note on "Xīlíng Winding Around" in the "Rhapsody on the River."
Some used it to cut timber from Jiānglíng,
The Book of Hàn says:
Wǔ Bèi said:
"The King of Wú cut timber from Jiānglíng to make boats."
Some used it to practice the battle of Kūnmíng.
The Book of Hàn says:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
Yuè wanted to engage in naval warfare with Hàn,
so he greatly repaired the Kūnmíng Pond,
with pavilions surrounding it,
built tower ships over ten zhàng high,
with flags and banners added on top.
As for soaring chī and red horses,
The Forest of Sayings says:
Emperor Hàn Wǔ first dug the Kūnmíng Pond,
floated soaring chī boats,
at that time the sun had already set westward,
cool wind stirred the water,
female musicians sang very clearly.
The emperor, recalling that companions like Lady Lǐ could no longer be obtained,
sadly composed the song "Fallen Leaves and Mournful Cicadas."
The Explanation of Names says:
Boat names: qīnghàn, qiānyì, chìmǎ.
Yìshǒu and duck-head,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Dragon boats and yìshǒu.
Note:
Yì,
is a water bird,
its image painted on the bow of the boat.
The Records of Wú says:
Zhūgě Kè made duck-head boats.
Floating the King of Yuè's three wings,
The Lost Records of Yuè says:
Yuè made large-wing, medium-wing, and small-wing boats for battle.
Liáng Xiàowáng's "Poem on Boat Names" says:
"The sky darkens, floating clouds fly,
three wings chase each other."
Supervising Sūn Quán's five-story tower ships.
The Records of Wú says:
Cáo Gōng went out of Rúxū,
Sūn Quán sent Dǒng Xí to supervise five-story tower ships to join the battle.
First to board is called,
The Jìn Statutes say:
In naval warfare,
there are small boats that board first,
fēiniǎo boats, fēiyún boats, cāngsǔn boats,
each separated by forty-five steps.
Favorable crossing is the plan.
The Yìjīng, Zhōngfú hexagram says:
Favorable to cross the great river,
riding a wooden boat,
is empty.
Also heard of cāngsǔn and chénfú,
Wáng Càn's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
Riding a cassia boat,
a chénfú vessel.
Cāngsǔn see above.
Flying hut and qīngquè,
The Explanation of Names says:
The house on a boat is called a hut,
a double house is called a flying hut.
The Book of Jìn states:
Táo Kǎn attacked the Shǔ rebel Wáng Zhēn,
and Zhēn hooked and captured Kǎn’s qīngquè boat,
but Kǎn escaped by boarding a small craft.
Some construct them to form bridges.
The Book of Songs says:
“He went to meet her by the Wèi River,
and made boats into a bridge.”
Some hide them in ravines.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
“Hiding a boat in a ravine,
or a mountain in a marsh,
may be called secure;
yet in the middle of the night a strong man may carry them away,
and the ignorant know nothing of it.”
The Tiānyuān Pool was graced by flying-dragon boats,
and the Língzhī Pool also floated with singing-crane boats.
The Records of the Jìn Palaces and Pavilions states:
“The Tiānyuān Pool has Zǐgōng boats, Shēngjìn boats, Yàoyáng boats, Fēilóng boats, and Shèliè boats.
The Língzhī Pool has Mínghè boats.”
People on the shore were astonished.
Dài Yánzhī’s Record of a Western Campaign states:
“Tánshān faces Kè,
and the waterway passes through Yíyáng’s Sānlè.
The men, women, old, and young of Sānlè had never seen a boat before.
Upon hearing that the Jìn envoy was sailing upstream,
they all gathered like ants along the riverbank,
bending and straightening, leaning and laughing.”
Dragons leaped in the water.
The Book of Jìn states:
“When Jìn was about to attack Wú,
there was a children’s rhyme that said:
‘Ātóng, oh Ātóng,
carrying a knife, floating across the river;
not fearing the tiger on the cliff,
but fearing the dragon in the water.’
Later, Wáng Jùn built large linked vessels in Yìzhōu,
sailed down the river,
and thus achieved the merit of conquering Wú.
Ātóng
was Jùn’s childhood name.”
Thus, they float across vast waters and traverse impassable places,
bringing broad benefits.
Chariot
The sage created boats and carriages to overcome impassable places,
thus carriages began with the solid-wheeled cart.
The Preface to the *Wén Xuǎn* says:
"The solid-wheeled cart is the beginning of the grand carriage."
They were inspired by the flying tumbleweed.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"Seeing the tumbleweed turn,
they knew how to make a carriage."
The metal carriage has nine rows of tassels on the horse's breastband.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* says:
"The officer of the chariots is in charge of the king's five types of carriages.
The first is the jade carriage,
with a forehead ornament,
twelve rows of tassels on the breastband,
and the Great Banner is raised for sacrifices.
The metal carriage,
with a throat-latch,
nine rows of tassels on the breastband,
the Great Flag is raised,
for receiving guests,
and for enfeoffing those of the same surname.
The ivory carriage,
with red decorations,
seven rows of tassels on the breastband,
the Great Red Banner is raised,
for court audiences,
and for enfeoffing those of different surnames.
The leather carriage,
with a dragon-patterned bridle,
five rows of cord tassels on the breastband,
the Great White Banner is raised,
for military expeditions,
and for enfeoffing the four guards.
The wooden carriage,
with a front black and swan-colored tassel,
the Great Command Banner is raised,
for hunting,
and for enfeoffing the feudal states."
Commentary:
"Where the king is present, it is called a carriage.
The forehead ornament,
is made of gold carved for the horse's face.
The breastband,
is read as 'pán',
it is the horse's large belt.
The tassel,
is on the chest.
The throat-latch,
is the throat strap.
'For receiving guests',
means to meet with guests.
The ivory carriage,
with red decorations,
means the bridle is adorned with red.
The dragon-patterned bridle,
is a dragon-colored horse,
meaning the bridle is adorned with mixed black and white colors.
The cord,
is read as 'tāo',
meaning the tassel is adorned with silk cords.
The front,
is read as 'jiǎn',
meaning light black.
The swan-colored tassel,
means the tassel is adorned with swan color.
The Plough Root carriage has a green base and three layers.
The *Regulations for the Imperial Procession* says:
"The Plough Root carriage has a green base,
with a three-layered canopy,
the rest is the same as the jade carriage,
it is provided for the imperial ploughing ceremony."
Some are drawn by black horses below.
Shěn Yuē's *Treatise on Carriages and Attire* says:
"The palanquin carriage,
is the carriage of the queen's five types of carriages in the *Zhōu Lǐ*.
The queen resides in the palace,
it is for leisurely travel,
not the king's carriage.
According to Hàn regulations,
the emperor used it,
sometimes pulled by people,
sometimes drawn by black horses below.
Some pull it from within the shafts.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Jiāng Gé encountered turmoil,
and because his mother was old, he did not want to jostle her,
so he himself pulled the carriage from within the shafts,
without using oxen or horses,
and the villagers praised him as Jiāng Jùxiào.
To avoid stirring dust beyond the tracks,
the *Lǐ* says:
"Within the state, use a broom-tipped whip to gently urge the horses,
so dust does not fly beyond the tracks."
They should strike the hubs to change customs.
The *Yànzǐ* says:
"The people of Qí enjoyed striking carriage hubs against each other for fun,
and prohibitions could not stop it.
Yànzǐ prepared a new carriage with fine horses,
went out and collided with someone, saying:
'Those who strike hubs bring misfortune.'
He then dismounted and left it,
after which the people of the state ceased the practice."
As for red tassels and green cords,
the *Shī* says:
"The lord's chariots, a thousand in number,
with red tassels and green cords."
Commentary:
"Red tassels,
are spear ornaments.
Green cords,
are ropes."
Patterned mats and long hubs,
the *Shī* says:
"The covered trace, the silver-linked traces,
patterned mats and long hubs,
drive my piebald horses."
Commentary:
"Covered,
means concealed traces.
Traces,
are what pull.
Silver,
is white metal.
Linked,
means traces.
Long,
means extended."
For dukes and marquises, a purple canopy with red lining,
the *Hòu Wèi Shū* says:
"The comfort carriage has a purple canopy with red lining,
the same as for dukes and marquises,
for viscounts, a black canopy with green lining."
The imperial carriage has a yellow roof and left yak-tail banner.
The *Sòng Shū* says:
"According to Hàn regulations,
the imperial carriage,
has a kingfisher-feather canopy with yellow lining,
which is called the yellow roof.
A yak tail is added,
as large as a dou measure,
placed on the left horse's yoke,
which is called the left yak-tail banner.
Yak,
is pronounced 'māo'.
In fierce battle, the wheels are stained crimson with blood.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"Jìn attacked Qí,
they fought at Ān.
Zhāng Hóu said to Xì Xiànzǐ:
'Since the battle began,
an arrow pierced my hand and elbow,
I broke it off and continued driving,
the left wheel is stained crimson,
how dare I speak of injury?
Please endure it, my lord.'"
When slander spreads, a pile of light things can break an axle.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
Zhōngshān Jìngwáng Shèng said:
"Piled feathers can sink a boat,
a heap of light things can break an axle.
Many mouths can melt metal,
accumulated slander can destroy bones."
Fúbō's longing for the Xiàzé carriage,
see the annotation for "Mǎ Yuán Làng Bó" in the *Ode to Dew*.
The Chǔ lord reaching Pú Xū.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"The lord of Chǔ sent Shēn Zhōu on a mission to Qí,
saying:
'Do not ask for passage through Sòng.'
Shēn Zhōu said:
'Zhèng is clear-sighted,
Sòng is deaf,
the Jìn envoy will come to no harm,
but I will surely die.'
The king said:
'If they kill you,
I will attack them.'
When he reached Sòng,
the people of Sòng killed him.
When the lord of Chǔ heard of it,
he flung his sleeves and rose,
his shoes caught up with him at the palace gate,
his sword caught up with him outside the chamber door,
his carriage caught up with him at the market of Pú Xū."
Just as they apply grease and set the linchpin,
the *Shī* says:
"Apply grease and set the linchpin,
turn the carriage and journey far."
How can one not gallop and not drive?
The *Shī* says:
"You have carriages and horses,
yet you neither gallop nor drive."
Displaying silk ribbons and hanging jade discs,
with parted feathers and flowing tassels.
The *Continued Hàn Shū: Treatise on Carriages and Attire* says:
"The funeral carriage,
its decorations are like the golden-rooted carriage;
silk ribbons are added,
the ribbons connect jade discs,
interlaced at the four corners,
The golden dragon head holds a jade disc in its mouth,
dangling with five-colored tassels,
and feathered streamers.
Chén Píng often associated with elders;
the *Hànshū* states:
Chén Píng’s home was in a poor alley against the outer city wall,
with a mat serving as the door,
yet there were many ruts from the carriages of elders at his gate.
Wheelwright Biǎn once mocked the ancient books.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
Duke Huán was reading,
while Wheelwright Biǎn was carving a wheel in the hall below.
Putting down his mallet and chisel, he said to the duke:
"What you are reading,
is merely the dregs of the ancients.
Judging from my own work,
when carving a wheel, if you go too slowly, it feels smooth but is not firm;
if too fast, it feels rough and does not fit.
Neither too slow nor too fast,
the skill lies in the hands,
and responds to the heart.
Words cannot describe it,
for there is an art within it.
Yet I cannot explain it to my son,
nor can my son receive it from me.
The ancients and what they did not transmit have perished,
hence it is called dregs."
In the Hàn, the jiéyú declined the imperial carriage.
The *Hànshū* states:
Emperor Chéng was touring the rear palace,
and wished to share his carriage with Bān Jiéyú.
She declined, saying:
"Looking at ancient paintings,
wise and sagely rulers
all had renowned ministers by their side.
The last rulers of the Three Dynasties
had favored concubines instead.
Now, if I were to share your carriage,
would it not resemble that?"
The emperor praised her words,
and desisted.
In Wèi, the former lord shared a carriage.
The *Shǔzhì* states:
Lord Cáo returned from campaigning against Lǚ Bù,
and appointed the former lord as General of the Left,
treating him with increasing respect,
so that when they went out, they shared the same carriage.
Startling was that man thrown at others;
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
When Chǔ fought with Jìn,
Shūshān Rǎn seized a man and threw him,
hitting a carriage and breaking its yoke.
Frightening was this cart loaded with ghosts.
The *Yì* states:
Seeing pigs covered in mud,
a cart loaded with ghosts.
Some were called "pursuing the wind";
the *Fùzǐ* states:
The pursuing wind carriage had a full canopy,
and was used for urgent travel.
Some were like flowing water.
See the annotation "Féng's traveling carriage" in the *Water Rhapsody*.
Some were made high because of Shū'áo;
the *Shǐjì: Sūn Shū'áo Biography* states:
The Chǔ custom favored low carriages,
but the king considered them inconvenient for horses and carriages,
and wanted to issue an order to make them higher.
Shū'áo said:
"If orders are issued repeatedly,
the people will not know what to follow;
it cannot be done.
If the king truly wishes to raise the carriages,
I request to instruct the neighborhoods
to raise their thresholds.
Those who ride carriages are all gentlemen,
and gentlemen cannot frequently dismount."
The king agreed.
After half a year,
the people all raised their carriages themselves.
Some despised Qìng Fēng's fine carriage.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
When Qí's Qìng Fēng came on a visit,
his carriage was fine.
Shūsūn said:
"Fine attire that does not match one's status
will surely end in misfortune.
What use is a fine carriage?"
One must not speak hastily;
the *Lúnyǔ* states:
When mounting a carriage, one must stand straight and hold the strap,
not look back inside,
not speak hastily,
and not point with the hand.
Nor should one point recklessly.
The *Lǐ* states:
In a carriage, one should not cough loudly,
nor point recklessly.
Shěn Qìngzhī rode a pig-nosed carriage;
Shěn Yuē's *Sòngshū* states:
Whenever Shěn Qìngzhī attended court celebrations,
he often rode a pig-nosed carriage without a canopy,
with only three to five horsemen accompanying him.
When walking through fields and gardens,
especially during busy farming months,
no one followed him,
and passersby did not know he was one of the Three Dukes.
After he was dismissed,
the emperor bestowed upon him a three-view carriage.
He said to others:
"Whenever I traveled,
walking through fields and gardens,
when there were people, I and my horse made three,
when there were none, I and my horse made two.
Now, riding this carriage,
where am I to go?"
Wáng Dǎo drove with a fly-whisk handle.
The *Jìnshū* states:
Wáng Dǎo's wife, Cáo, was jealous,
and Dǎo feared her,
so he secretly established a separate residence for his concubines.
When Cáo found out,
and was about to go there,
Dǎo, fearing his concubines would be humiliated,
hurriedly ordered his carriage prepared.
As it was delayed,
he used the handle of his fly-whisk to drive the ox forward.
Cài Mó heard of this,
and teased Dǎo, saying:
"The court wishes to bestow upon you the Nine Gifts."
Dǎo did not realize it,
and merely modestly declined.
Mó said:
"I have not heard of other items,
only a short-shafted calf carriage
and a long-handled fly-whisk."
Dǎo became greatly angered.
Red silk netting;
the *Regulations on Ceremonial Systems* states:
For all carriages,
first rank: green oiled silk, crimson canopy with red lining and red silk netting;
third rank and above: green full canopy with red lining;
fifth rank and above: green partial canopy with blue-green lining;
sixth rank and below: none may use a canopy.
The black-eared carriage paced back and forth.
The *Jìn Gōngqīng Lǐzhì* states:
When Ānpíng Wáng Fú passed away,
for his burial,
he was provided with one black-eared carriage that paced back and forth.
The *Fù Chàng Gùshì* states:
The carriage of the Imperial Secretary had black ears and a rear door.
A reed carriage was used by the Chancellor of Pèi;
the *Hòuhànshū* states:
Yuán Zhōng served as Chancellor of Pèi,
and arrived at his post in a reed carriage,
gaining a reputation for integrity.
A wicker carriage was heard of from the Chǔ lord;
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
Ruò'áo and Fénmào used wicker carriages and ragged clothes to open up mountains and forests.
Annotation:
Ruò'áo and Fénmào
were ancestors of Chǔ.
Wicker carriage
means a crude cart.
Ragged clothes
means tattered garments.
The grand carriage displayed frugality;
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
The pure temple had a thatched roof,
the grand carriage used rush mats,
the grand broth was not overly seasoned,
the millet food was not finely polished,
to display frugality.
The pole-rubbing carriage was an arrogant imitation;
the *Dǒng Zhuó Biézhuàn* states:
Dǒng Zhuó arrogantly imitated carriage and attire,
riding a carriage with a golden canopy and green cover,
with painted wheels.
People of the time called it the pole-rubbing carriage.
Zhào Jiǎn favored worn-out carriages;
the *Shuōyuàn* states:
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ rode a worn-out carriage,
a lean horse,
and wore a sheepskin robe.
His steward admonished him:
"A new carriage is safe,
a fat horse travels swiftly,
and a fox or leopard robe is warm and light."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I have heard that
when a gentleman wears fine attire, he becomes more respectful;
when a petty person wears fine attire, he becomes more arrogant.
Now, I prepare myself thus,
fearing I might develop the heart of a petty person."
Tián Chà despised extravagance.
The *Shuōyuàn* states:
Jìn Pínggōng made a racing carriage,
adorned with rhinoceros hide,
inlaid with feathers,
and placed it in the palace courtyard,
where all ministers could view it.
Tián Chà passed by three times without looking,
and Duke Píng was greatly angered.
Chà said:
"Jié perished due to extravagance,
Zhòu fell because of lavishness,
and thus I dared not look."
Duke Píng said:
"Well said."
He then removed the carriage.
The great army had the formation at Mùyě,
and the *Book of Documents* says:
King Wǔ had three hundred war chariots,
three hundred tiger warriors,
and fought Shòu at Mùyě.
For long journeys, there was the sacrifice of Zǔ Bá.
The *Rites of Zhōu* says:
The Grand Driver uses the jade carriage for sacrifice,
and when reaching the Bá,
then drives it away.
Commentary:
Crossing a mountain is called Bá.
To "reach" it means
to mound earth into the shape of a mountain,
using grass, thorns, and cypress as the spirit tablet,
and after sacrificing,
to drive the carriage over it and depart,
symbolizing no perilous difficulty.
The *Jìn Shū* says:
According to old accounts, Léi Zǔ, son of the Yellow Emperor, loved distant travels,
died on the road,
and thus was worshipped as the road deity.
As for Cháo watching the Jìn army,
the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
The King of Chǔ ascended a cháo chariot to observe the Jìn army.
Commentary:
A cháo chariot
is a chariot with a lookout tower.
The tower called out to the Sòng people,
the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
Ascended the tower chariot,
and had them call out to the Sòng people to inform them.
Chén Zūn detained guests by throwing away the linchpin,
see the note on "Chén Zūn Throws the Linchpin" in the *Ode on the Well*.
Zhāng Gāng offered uprightness and buried the wheel.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Zhāng Gāng, styled Wénjì,
along with Dù Qiáo and six others, received an edict to travel throughout the realm,
and were called the Eight Envoys.
The other seven all followed orders,
but only Gāng buried his carriage wheel at the Dūtíng in Luòyáng,
saying:
"When wolves block the road,
why ask about foxes?"
He then impeached Liáng Jì and others for their crimes,
shocking the capital.
As for Xī Zhòng's initial creation,
the *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
Pānyú gave birth to Xī Zhòng,
Xī Zhòng gave birth to Jí Guāng,
who first made chariots from wood.
Commentary states:
The *Shìběn* says:
Xī Zhòng invented chariots.
This mentions Jí Guāng,
clarifying that father and son together conceived the idea.
Also, the *Continued Hàn Shū: Treatise on Carriages and Attire* says:
Xī Zhòng served as Chariot Master,
preparing materials according to the season,
all six materials being excellent.
Xuānyuán first made them,
the *Gǔshǐ Kǎo* says:
The Yellow Emperor made chariots,
in Shǎohào's time oxen were added,
in Yǔ's time Xī Zhòng drove horses,
expanding the chariot system.
Also, the *Shìmíng* says:
The Yellow Emperor created chariots,
hence he was called Xuānyuán.
The *Book* records the beginning of harnessing,
the *Book* says:
Begin to harness oxen to carts,
travel far to trade,
to support and care for your parents.
The *Odes* praise their great abundance.
The *Odes* say:
The war chariots are very numerous,
footmen and drivers never weary.
The metaphor of pig fat and thorn axle,
the *Shǐjì* says:
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Pig fat on a thorn axle
is used for smoothness,
yet it cannot turn a square hole."
The pleasure of cutting fresh meat at the salt marsh and staining the wheels.
The *Rhapsody on Zǐxū* says:
Galloping across the salt marsh,
cutting fresh meat and staining the wheels.
Commentary:
Cutting raw meat,
rubbing it on the chariot wheels,
salting it and eating it.
Rubbing,
pronounced ruán.
Some drove with rush-wheeled carriages,
the *Shǐjì* says:
For the fēng and shàn sacrifices, rush-wheeled carriages were used,
to avoid harming soil, stones, plants, and trees.
Also, the *Hàn Shū* says:
Rush-wheeled comfort carriages were used to summon worthies.
Some rode in leather canopied carriages.
The *Hàn Guān Jiě* says:
Horses have stables,
carriages have storehouses; leather canopies
use tiger skin for the canopy.
The Chancellor's tolerance of the driver,
the *Hàn Shū* says:
Bǐng Jí was Chancellor,
his driver was fond of wine,
often negligent.
Once accompanying Jí out,
he got drunk and vomited on the Chancellor's carriage mat.
The Western Section head clerk proposed to dismiss him,
but Jí said:
"To dismiss a man for a fault of drunkenness and fullness,
where would such a man find acceptance again?
The Western Section should just endure it;
it merely soils the Chancellor's carriage mat."
Yǐn Xǐ's divination about Lǎojūn.
The *Guānlìng Nèi Zhuàn* says:
Yǐn Xǐ once ascended a tower,
saw purple qi from the eastern extremity moving westward,
and said:
"A sage should be passing the capital."
Indeed, he saw Lǎojūn coming by in a blue ox cart.
Huán Róng studied antiquity and received gifts,
the *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Huán Róng was Junior Tutor,
and was granted a curtained carriage and horses.
Róng gathered his many students,
displayed the carriages, horses, seals, and ribbons, saying:
"What I receive today
is due to the study of antiquity;
can one not strive hard?"
Wèi Shū lost his son and received grace.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
Wèi Shū's son died,
an edict granted him a yángsuì sìwàng carriage,
to go out and observe,
dispersing his grief.
Chúnyú was likened to a heated grease pot,
the *Shǐjì* says:
Chúnyú Kūn in his remonstrances
admired Yàn Yīng's character,
yet focused on observing expressions and adapting,
so the people of Qí called him "heated grease pot."
A grease pot
is a container for axle grease on a chariot;
when heated, it does not empty completely,
still having some flow left,
meaning Kūn's wisdom was like this.
Wú Qǐ was also known for moving the shaft.
The *Hánzǐ* says:
Wú Qǐ was governor of Xīhé,
Qín had a small fort,
he wished to attack it,
so he moved a chariot shaft outside the north gate,
and ordered:
"Whoever can move this to outside the south gate
will be granted a superior residence."
None of the people moved it.
When someone moved it,
he was rewarded as ordered.
Then he placed a stone,
and again ordered:
"Whoever moves this
will be rewarded as before."
The people competed to move it.
Then he ordered:
"Tomorrow morning we attack the fort;
whoever ascends first
will be granted a superior residence and superior fields."
The people competed to ascend,
and the fort was taken in one morning.
Straight as if growing and curved as if attached,
the *Rites of Zhōu* says:
The carriage maker makes the chariot:
the wheels,
round parts match the compass,
square parts match the square,
vertical parts match the plumb line,
horizontal parts match the level,
straight parts are as if growing,
curved parts are as if attached.
Commentary states:
It refers to working the material;
"as if growing"
means like wood growing from the ground,
"attached" means like branches attached to a tree.
Square symbolizes earth and round symbolizes heaven.
The *Rites of Zhōu* says:
The squareness of the carriage body
symbolizes the earth.
The roundness of the canopy
symbolizes the heavens.
The twenty spokes of the wheel
symbolize the sun and moon.
There are also bells to sound the chimes;
the *Dà Dài Lǐ* says:
"When the king ascends his carriage, he hears the harmonious sound of the chimes,
so that improper thoughts find no entry."
The horses move and the chimes ring,
the chimes ring and harmony responds.
Upon boarding, the harmonious chimes set the rhythm;
upon alighting, the jade pendants set the measure.
Adorned with mica,
the *Yuánzǐ Zhèngshū* says:
"Carriages adorned with mica
are called mica carriages.
Ministers may not ride them;
they are bestowed upon princes and dukes."
Also, the *Jìn Shū* says:
"When Xiè Xuán defeated Fú Jiān at the Féishuǐ,
he captured the mica carriage he rode."
Double hubs with layered rims;
the *Yúfú Zhì* says:
"The imperial golden-root carriage has five vehicles,
all with vermilion-patterned wheels,
double hubs with layered rims."
Leaning dragons and crouching tigers.
The *Yúfú Zhì* says:
"The patterns on various carriages:
the imperial carriage has leaning dragons and crouching tigers,
with divine patterns painted on the shafts.
The crown prince, princes, and feudal lords
have leaning tigers and crouching deer,
with divine patterns painted on the carriage sides.
Dukes and marquises have leaning deer and crouching bears,
with black carriage sides and vermilion-patterned wheels."
It is also heard that Cháng Wàn fled with his mother in a carriage;
the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"Nángōng Cháng Wàn of Sòng fled to Chén,
using a carriage to transport his mother,
arriving in a single day."
Kǎoshū contended and grasped the shaft.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"Gōngsūn È contended with Yǐng Kǎoshū over a carriage.
Yǐng Kǎoshū grasped the shaft and ran away,
while Zǐdū drew a halberd to pursue him."
Traveling through marshes, one desires thin wheels;
traveling through mountains, one desires even wheels.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* says:
"The wheelwright makes wheels.
For traveling marshes, one desires thin wheels;
for traveling mountains, one desires even wheels.
Thin wheels for marshes
are like knives cutting through mud,
so mud does not cling.
Even wheels for mountains
are like rounded thickness for traveling over stones,
so even when worn, the wheel does not break at the mortises."
Note:
"Thin" means to make the part that treads the ground slender.
"Even"
means uniform thickness above and below.
"Rounded"
means thick and circular.
"Break" also means wear;
thick wheels do not wear out at the mortises."
Looking forward should not exceed five guī;
the *Lǐ* says:
"Standing, look forward five guī;
bowing, look at the horse's tail;
turning the head should not pass the hubs."
Driving must involve three circuits.
The *Lǐ* says:
"Drive the bride's carriage,
and the groom hands over the reins;
drive the wheel for three circuits."
Then there is the south-pointing chariot indicating direction;
Zuǒ Sī's *Wú Dū Fù* says:
"Yu riders gallop on the road,
the south-pointing chariot indicates direction."
The carriage emerges, rumbling;
armored soldiers, clanging.
Originating from Zhuōlù,
Cuī Bào's *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
"Huángdì battled Chīyóu in the fields of Zhuōlù.
Chīyóu created a great fog,
and the soldiers all lost their way.
The emperor made the south-pointing chariot."
Four horses to draw it;
the *Lǔbù Lìng* says:
"The south-pointing chariot is drawn by four horses,
with one master craftsman
and fourteen drivers."
The signal banner is observed.
The *Shùzhēng Jì* says:
"Inside the northern gate of the imperial workshop is the south-pointing chariot.
On the chariot is a wooden immortal
holding a signal banner.
As the chariot turns, the figure always points south."
Witnessing Sùshèn's offering of pheasants;
the *Guǐgǔzǐ* says:
"The Sùshèn tribe offered white pheasants to King Wén.
Fearing they would lose their way back,
the Duke of Zhōu made a south-pointing chariot to send them off."
Hearing of the Zhèng people fetching jade.
The *Guǐgǔzǐ* says:
"When the Zhèng people fetch jade,
they must carry a south-pointing chariot,
to avoid confusion."
Mǎ Jūn already understood its intricacies;
the *Wèi Shū·Mǎ Jūn Zhuàn* says:
"Sir Mǎ argued with Gāotáng Lóng and Qín Lǎng,
mentioning the south-pointing chariot.
The two said it never existed in antiquity,
that records were false.
Sir Mǎ said:
'It existed in antiquity.'
Emperor Míng then ordered Sir Mǎ to make one,
and the chariot was indeed completed."
Xiè Fēi also spoke of its details.
The *Hòu Zhào Lù* says:
"Imperial Workshop Director Xiè Fēi,
ingenious as a deity,
with wondrous and extraordinary ideas,
built a south-pointing chariot."
Further, there are carriages prepared in five colors;
Yìng Shào's *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
"The Son of Heaven has five-colored carriages,
all drawn by four horses."
Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū* says:
"Standing carriages in five colors,
sedan carriages likewise,
all are the Son of Heaven's carriages."
Named the seven-fragrance carriage;
Cáo Cāo's *Letter to Yáng Biāo* says:
"Now I present to you two four-view, fully-canopied seven-fragrance carriages
and two black oxen."
Equipped with yokes and collars;
the *Lúnyǔ* says:
"A large carriage without a yoke,
a small carriage without a collar,
how can they proceed?"
Measured by yin and yang.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* says:
"The hub
is for smooth turning.
In the method of cutting hubs,
one must measure their yin and yang.
The yang side
has dense grain and is hard;
the yin side
has loose grain and is soft.
Therefore, use fire to nurture the yin
and balance it with the yang,
so the hub, even when worn, does not warp."
A hub small and long is narrow;
large and short is tight.
Dense,
pronounced jìn.
Warp,
pronounced hào.
Narrow,
pronounced zhà gé fǎn.
Tight,
pronounced zhì.
Dù Lín pushed a deer cart;
the *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* says:
"Dù Lín resided with Wěi Xiāo yet never yielded his integrity.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
his younger brother Chéng passed away,
and Wěi Xiāo allowed Dù Lín to escort the funeral eastward.
After sending him off, he regretted it
and ordered assassin Yáng Xián to intercept and kill him at Lǒngdǐ.
Xián saw Dù Lín personally pushing a deer cart carrying his brother's remains
and sighed:
'In this present age,
who upholds righteousness?
Though I am a petty man,
how can I bear to kill a righteous man?'
He then fled."
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn was drawn by a goat;
the *Jìn Shū* says:
"In Emperor Wǔ's harem,
many were favored,
and he knew not whom to visit.
He rode a goat cart, letting it go where it pleased.
The palace ladies then placed bamboo leaves at their doors
and sprinkled salt water on the ground
to attract the emperor's cart."
Hearing of Zhāng Tāng's misfortune, an ox-drawn cart;
the *Hàn Shū* says:
"Chief Clerk of the Chancellor Zhū Mǎichén and two others investigated and arrested Tián Xìn for profiting with Zhāng Tāng from hoarding goods.
The emperor reprimanded Zhāng Tāng,
and Zhāng Tāng committed suicide.
His mother was buried with an ox-drawn cart,
with a coffin but no outer coffin.
The emperor heard of this
and executed the three chief clerks."
The people of Zhèng bribed the Marquis of Jìn with guǎng-chariots and tún-chariots,
each fully equipped with fifteen,
complete with armor and weapons.
Note:
Guǎng and tún
are both names of war chariots.
Sometimes lù-chariots and píng-chariots vary in prestige,
as the Yuánzǐ Zhèngshū states:
In the Hàn dynasty, lù-chariots were considered lowly while zī-píng chariots were esteemed;
in the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, píng-chariots were considered lowly while lù-chariots were esteemed.
Sometimes spokes converge at the hub,
as the Lǎozǐ says:
Thirty spokes converge at a single hub,
and it is precisely where there is nothing that the usefulness of the chariot lies.
Sometimes the crossbar is paired and the axle-pin is hooked.
Bào Míngyuǎn’s “Rhapsody on the Ruined City” says:
In those days of its full flourishing,
chariots hooked their axle-pins,
men jostled shoulder to shoulder,
houses and alleys covered the ground,
singing and piping filled the sky.
The alleyway exit of chariots originated from the people of Zhèng.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and the people of Zhèng divined about suing for peace, but it was inauspicious.
They divined about weeping at the great ancestral temple,
and also about sending chariots out through the alleyways,
which was auspicious.
The disorder of wheel tracks was discerned by Cáo Guì.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Qí and Lǔ fought at Chángsháo,
and the Qí army was utterly defeated.
The Duke was about to pursue them,
but Cáo Guì said:
"Not yet."
He looked down at their wheel tracks,
then mounted the chariot rail and gazed afar,
saying:
"Now it is permissible.
The enemy of a great state is hard to fathom;
I feared there might be an ambush.
I observed that their tracks were disordered,
and looking, I saw their banners drooping,
so I pursued them."
As for the bone of Fángfēng that filled a whole chariot,
the Jiāyǔ says:
Wú attacked Yuè,
destroyed Kuàijī,
and obtained a section of divine bone
that filled a whole chariot.
They sent an envoy to Lǔ to inquire of Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Long ago, Yǔ assembled his ministers at Túshān;
Fángfēng arrived late,
and was executed.
His bone filled a whole chariot."
The eyebrows of the tall Dí were seen.
The Gǔliángzhuàn says:
There were three brothers of the tall Dí,
who rampaged through the Central States,
and tiles and stones could not harm them.
Shūsūn Déchén shot one in the eye,
and his body lay across nine mǔ.
They cut off his head and carried it,
and his eyebrows were visible over the chariot rail.
When serving in office, one might soon hear of ears growing on the chariot.
The Yìyǔ says:
If one’s official career does not cease,
ears grow on the chariot.
Auspicious signs might appear as hanging tassels.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì says:
When virtue reaches the mountains and hills,
then the mountains produce root-wood chariots,
which are fit to carry all things.
Golden chariots
appear when the kingly ruler’s conduct reaches the utmost in benevolence and virtue.
Yú Shùn’s virtue flourished in the mountains and hills,
so mountain chariots appeared.
Mountain chariots
are natural objects,
the essence stored within mountains,
and resemble elephant-drawn chariots.
Shùn’s benevolence and virtue flourished,
so mountain chariots hung with tassels.
Yet at Ránqiū, hard metal was used for the felloes.
The Shíyíjì says:
In the sixth year of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the state of Ránqiū presented bǐchì birds,
caged with jade.
The envoys from that state wore cloth of cloud and mist,
passed through over a hundred states,
and only then reached the capital.
They crossed the Iron Ridge,
sailed the Boiling Sea,
and passed Snake Isle and Bee Peak.
The Iron Ridge was sharp and abrasive;
the chariot wheels all had felloes of hard metal,
but by the time they reached the capital,
the felloes were nearly worn away.
The Boiling Sea surges up as if boiling and seething;
the skin and bones of its fish and turtles are hard as stone
and can be used for armor.
When sailing the Boiling Sea,
they sheathed the boat bottoms with copper,
so that flood dragons could not approach.
Passing Snake Isle,
they used leopard skins to make shelters,
and pushed the chariots from within the shelters.
Passing Bee Peak,
they burned húsū wood.
The smoke of this wood can kill a hundred insects.
The journey took fifty years to reach Luòyáng.
The Jīgōng people followed the wind to fly.
See the note on "flying chariots first startled the Jīgōng" in the "Rhapsody on the Wind."
We admire Yànzǐ’s ability to decline.
The Shuōyuàn says:
When Yànzǐ attended court,
he rode in a worn-out chariot
drawn by a nag.
Duke Jǐng sent him a fine chariot with horses,
but he refused three times, saying:
"As for fine chariots and horses,
if the ruler rides them,
the high ministers will also ride them.
If the common people lack righteousness,
extravagant in food and clothing without regard for their conduct,
how can they be restrained?"
In the end, he did not accept.
We praise Zǎiyǔ for his perceptive refusal.
The Kǒngcóngzǐ says:
Confucius sent Zǎiyǔ to Chǔ,
and King Zhāo of Chǔ wished to present Confucius with a comfortable carriage adorned with ivory.
Zǎiyǔ said:
"My Master has no use for this.
My Master’s words never stray from the Way,
his actions never violate benevolence.
His wife does not wear colorful silks,
his concubines do not wear fine silk.
His chariots and vessels are not carved,
his horses do not eat grain.
As for observing the beauty and extravagance of things,
or listening to seductively subtle, floating music,
my Master encounters them but does not heed them.
Thus I know my Master will not use this carriage."
There are uses for the Evil-Warding and Mile-Recording chariots.
The Lǔbùlìng says:
The Mile-Recording, White Egret, and Phoenix-Banner chariots,
among others, are all drawn by four horses.
On the Evil-Warding chariot,
one Grand Diviner official stands in the chariot holding a bow and arrows.
On the Leather Canopy chariot,
one Company Commander from the Left or Right Jīnyǔ Guard stands in the chariot holding a bow.
There are the insignia of the Yellow Battle-Axe and the Leopard Tail.
The Lǔbùlìng says:
On the Yellow Battle-Axe chariot,
also called the Golden Battle-Axe chariot,
one Company Commander from the Left Martial Guard stands in the chariot’s second position.
On the Leopard Tail chariot,
one Company Commander from the Right Martial Guard stands in the chariot,
both wearing martial caps with red tassels.
Thus the grandeur of the state’s ceremonial display
is seen in the manifest display of cultural artifacts.
Dǐng
As for the tripod,
it is cast from the metal of the nine provinces and used to harmonize the five flavors.
The Shuōwén states:
The tripod,
with three legs and two ears,
is a precious vessel for harmonizing the five flavors.
In ancient times, Yǔ collected metal from the nine provinces
and cast tripods at the foot of Jīngshān.
When people entered the mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
demons and spirits could not encounter them.
The Xià clan depicted creatures on them.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Wángsūn Mǎn visited Chǔzǐ,
and Chǔzǐ inquired about the size and weight of the tripod.
He replied:
"It lies in virtue, not in the tripod.
In ancient times, when the Xià dynasty possessed virtue,
distant regions depicted creatures,
presented metal from the nine provinces,
and cast tripods depicting these creatures.
When Jié had depraved virtue,
the tripod was transferred to Shāng.
When Shāng Zhòu was tyrannical,
the tripod was transferred to Zhōu.
When virtue is splendid and enlightened,
even if small, it is heavy;
when it is treacherous, depraved, and chaotic,
even if large, it is light.
King Chéng established the tripod at Jiárǔ,
divining thirty generations,
and seven hundred years,
as decreed by Heaven.
Although the virtue of Zhōu has declined,
the Mandate of Heaven has not changed.
The weight of the tripod
cannot be inquired about."
The people of Zhèng cast penal laws.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The people of Zhèng cast penal laws onto a tripod,
making it the constant law of the state.
Lǔ had the bribe of Shòumèng.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Duke Xiāng of Lǔ entertained the six ministers of Jìn,
bribing Xún Yǎn with bundles of brocade, jade, and horses,
preceded by the tripod of Shòumèng of Wú.
Wèi had the inscription of Kǒng Kuī.
The Lǐ states:
The inscription on the tripod of Kǒng Kuī of Wèi says:
The lord said:
"Your ancestor Zhuāngshū,
assisted Duke Chéng,
followed him in hardship to Hànyáng,
and served at the ancestral court of Zhōu.
He toiled tirelessly,
opening the way and assisting Duke Xiàn.
Duke Xiàn then commanded Chéngshū
to continue the duties of your ancestor.
Your father Wénshū,
revived old desires.
He diligently served the public household,
day and night without rest.
I grant you this inscription,
to continue the duties of your father."
Kuī bowed and touched his head to the ground,
diligently fulfilling the great command on the sacrificial tripod.
Danger is seen as fish swimming.
Qiū Xīfàn's "Letter to Chén Bózhī" states:
General, you are like fish swimming in a boiling tripod,
or swallows nesting on a flying curtain.
An omen is heard of a pheasant ascending.
The Shū states:
Emperor Gāozōng sacrificed to Chéng Tāng,
and a flying pheasant ascended to the ear of the tripod and crowed.
Note:
An anomaly of deafness.
Yìshǎo recorded calligraphy.
The Dǐnglù states:
Wáng Xīzhī cast a calligraphy tripod,
inscribing it in his own regular and clerical script,
describing his calligraphic achievements,
and sank it in the Jiǔjiāng River.
Zhāng Líng engraved alchemical scriptures.
The Dǐnglù states:
Zhāng Líng obtained ten immortal tripods,
engraved with alchemical scriptures,
and buried them at the foot of Yúntáishān.
Recognizing Yuáncháng's gift.
The Dǐnglù states:
Zhōng Yáo, styled Yuáncháng,
was given a five-cooked tripod by Emperor Wén of Wèi while he was crown prince.
Lamenting Zhǔfù being boiled.
The Hànshū states:
Zhǔfù Yǎn said:
"A man, if not eating from five tripods in life,
will be boiled in five tripods in death."
As for its form, observe the attached ears.
The Ěryǎ states:
A tripod extremely large
is called nài.
Round and covered on top,
is called zī.
With ears attached on the outside,
is called yì.
The note says:
The tripod ears are on the surface.
Zī is pronounced zī,
yì is pronounced yì.
The image shows a broken leg.
The Yì states:
When the tripod's leg breaks,
it overturns the duke's stew.
Some are engraved with "ten thousand years of longevity."
The Dǐnglù states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn ascended Tàishān,
cast a tripod,
made of copper and silver,
shaped like a jar,
inscribed "Ascended Tàishān,
boundless longevity.
The four seas are tranquil,
the divine tripod spreads fragrance."
Some are inscribed with "five cooked."
The Dǐnglù states:
Emperor Jǐng of Hàn cast a tripod,
named the food tripod,
made of copper, gold, and silver,
shaped like a vase,
without legs.
Inscribed "Supports the five cooked,
the sovereign's meal."
Then there is Lù Xùn defeating Bèi.
The Dǐnglù states:
Wú's Lù Xùn defeated Liú Bèi's army,
cast a tripod,
inscribed "Tripod of Defeating Bèi."
Xiāo Hé recorded achievements.
The Dǐnglù states:
Xiāo Hé served as chancellor,
cast a tripod,
as large as a three-dàn jar,
recording his own achievements,
inscribed "Tripod of Recorded Achievements."
Some say "at dawn yet still negligent."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Jìn's Shū Xiàng said:
"The inscription on the Chán tripod says,
'At dawn, greatly illustrious,
yet later generations are still negligent.'"
Some say "with three appointments, becoming more respectful."
The Lǐ states:
The tripod inscription of Sòng's Zhèng Kǎofù says:
"With one appointment, I stooped;
with two appointments, I bent;
with three appointments, I bowed.
Walking along the wall,
none dared to insult me.
With congee here,
with gruel here,
to fill my mouth."
Wángsūn Mǎn reprimanding Chǔzǐ,
see the note above on "Xià clan depicting creatures."
Zāng Āibó admonishing Duke Lǔ.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Sòng's Huáfǔ Dū assassinated Duke Shāng,
bribed the duke with the great tripod of Gào,
and placed it in the grand temple.
Zāng Āibó admonished:
"King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
moved the nine tripods to Luòyì.
Righteous men still criticized it,
how much more so displaying a bribe vessel of transgression and chaos in the grand temple?
What is to be done?"
Again, it is heard lifted by King Xiàng.
The Hànshū states:
Xiàng Yǔ could lift a tripod.
Lifted by Qín Wǔ.
The Shǐjì states:
King Wǔ of Qín and Mèng Shuō lifted a dragon-patterned tripod,
and died from a broken shin.
Given to Zǐchǎn.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Zhèng's Zǐchǎn visited Jìn,
Hán Xuānzǐ spoke privately,
saying:
"Our sovereign lies ill,
dreaming of a yellow bear entering the bedroom door.
What fierce ghost is this?"
He replied:
"In ancient times, Yáo executed Gǔn at Yǔshān,
his spirit transformed into a yellow bear,
entering the abyss of Yǔ,
and was indeed sacrificed to in the Xià郊祀.
Three dynasties sacrificed to him.
Jìn, as the leader of the alliance,
perhaps has not sacrificed to him?"
Hánzǐ sacrificed to the Xià郊祀.
The Marquis of Jìn recovered,
and gave Zǐchǎn two square tripods of Jǔ.
The note says:
Square tripods,
Presented by Jǔ.
To honor the ancestor of Wèi.
The *Dǐng Lù* says:
Wèi Wǔ created a dǐng at Báilù Shān,
one zhàng high,
recording the feats of campaigns and battles.
It also bears the name of the Grand Preceptor.
The *Dǐng Lù* says:
Dǒng Zhuó, as Grand Preceptor,
cast a dǐng,
inscribed with the words "Grand Preceptor."
It was also cast for Wáng Shāng.
The *Dǐng Lù* says:
Wáng Shāng served as Chányú Chief,
the emperor ordered a dǐng to be cast,
engraving his merits to encourage loyal ministers.
Then, its bronze stand grew hair.
The *Dǐng Lù* says:
During Hàn Xuāndì's reign, the bronze human stand at Jiànzhāng Palace grew hair,
considered an auspicious omen,
so a golden dǐng was cast,
and buried at Jiànzhāng Palace.
The jade huáng emerged from the Wèi River.
The *Dǐng Lù* says:
Tàigōng obtained a jade huáng in the Wèi River,
cast a dǐng,
and inscribed it with the words "Huáng Dǐng."
Seen at Fényīn.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
Hàn Wǔdì obtained the precious dǐng from Fényīn,
stored it at Gānquán,
and the assembled ministers offered congratulations:
"Your Majesty has obtained the Zhōu dǐng."
Wúqiū Shòuwáng said:
"It is not the Zhōu dǐng."
The emperor was angered.
He replied:
"Heaven blesses the virtuous,
the precious dǐng emerges of itself,
this is Heaven bestowing it upon Hàn,
it is the Hàn dǐng,
not the Zhōu dǐng."
Lost in the Sì River.
The *Shǐ Jì* says:
The shrine at Tàiqiū perished,
and the dǐng sank into the Sì River beneath Péngchéng.
Qín Shǐhuáng passed Péngchéng,
fasted and prayed,
wishing to retrieve the Zhōu dǐng,
sent a thousand men into the water to seek it,
but it was not found.
It also says:
During Emperor Wén's time,
Xīnyuán Píng said:
"The Zhōu dǐng is lost in the Sì River,
now the Yellow River overflows and connects to the Sì,
I see a golden treasure aura directly northeast at Fényīn,
could it be that the Zhōu dǐng will emerge?
If the omen appears and is not welcomed,
then it will not come."
Thereupon, an envoy was sent to establish a temple at Fényīn,
facing south toward the river,
wishing to pray for the emergence of the Zhōu dǐng.
Displayed at Bǎiqǐn.
The *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* says:
Lújiāng presented a dǐng,
an edict summoned Zhèng Zhòng,
asking: "Duke Huán of Qí's dǐng is at Bǎiqǐn Terrace,
in which book is this seen?
How many dǐng matters are in the *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn*?"
Zhòng answered the inquiry,
and was appointed Lángzhōng.
Displayed for the yuè sacrifice.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
During Emperor Míng of Hàn's time,
a precious dǐng emerged from Wángluò Shān,
an edict stated:
"The dǐng symbolizes the Three Dukes,
could it be that the dukes and ministers, fulfilling their duties, have achieved proper governance?
On the day of the Tàicháng's yuè sacrifice,
display the dǐng in the ancestral temple,
to prepare the ritual vessels.
Bestow upon the Three Dukes fifty bolts of silk,
and half that to the Nine Ministers and officials of two thousand shí rank."
Moving it certainly requires ninety thousand men.
The *Zhànguó Cè* says:
Qín raised an army,
demanding the Nine Dǐng from Zhōu,
Yán Shuài said to the King of Qí:
"The ministers of Zhōu internally deliberated,
that giving the dǐng to Qín
is not as good as returning it to a great state,
I hope Your Majesty considers this."
The King of Qí dispatched troops to rescue Zhōu,
and the Qín army withdrew.
Shuài went to Qí and said:
"We wish to present the Nine Dǐng,
but do not know by which route your great state can receive them?"
The King of Qí said:
"I will send them via Liáng."
He replied:
"That will not do.
The ministers of Liáng desire to obtain the Nine Dǐng,
they have plotted at Tántái below,
and above Shǎohǎi,
for a long time now.
Once they enter Liáng, the dǐng will certainly not come out."
The King of Qí said:
"Then I will send them via Chǔ."
He replied:
"That will not do.
The ministers of Chǔ desire to obtain the Nine Dǐng,
they have plotted within Huátíng,
for a long time now.
If they are to enter Chǔ,
the dǐng will certainly not come out.
A dǐng is
not like a vinegar pot or sauce jar,
that can be tucked away and carried.
It is not like birds gathering or flying,
rabbits leaping or foxes vanishing,
that it can reach Qí.
In the past, when Zhōu attacked Yīn,
they obtained the Nine Dǐng.
For one dǐng, ninety thousand men pulled it,
nine times nine is eight hundred ten thousand men,
with all the necessary equipment and mechanisms accordingly."
The king then stopped.
Tán,
pronunciation: tán dàn qiē.
Lifting it also requires twelve.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* says:
The king daily presents one set of dǐng,
with twelve items,
each having a zǔ stand.
Note:
nine main dǐng,
three supplementary dǐng.
It neither draws water yet fills itself,
nor is it heated yet constantly boils.
The *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
The divine dǐng is
an instrument of benevolence.
It can be light or heavy,
can rest or move.
Without heating it boils,
without drawing water it fills itself.
The subtle, ethereal energy
is naturally produced.
In times of chaos, it hides in deep mountains;
in times of civilization, it responds to destiny and arrives.
Therefore, Yǔ cast a dǐng to symbolize it.
Obtaining one at Měiyáng reveals the deceased minister.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
During Emperor Xuān's time,
a dǐng was obtained at Měiyáng and presented.
Zhāng Chǎng deliberated:
"The dǐng has an inscription: 'The king commands the deceased minister,
to govern this Xúnyì,
bestows upon you a luán banner,
and embroidered robes with carved spears.'
This dǐng is likely how Zhōu rewarded the descendants of feudal lords,
engraving inscriptions to commemorate former merits."
Casting one at Jīngshān aligns with the celestial order.
The *Shǐ Jì* says:
Huángdì mined copper from Shǒushān,
and cast a dǐng at the foot of Jīngshān.
When the dǐng was completed,
a dragon descended with drooping beard,
to welcome Huángdì.
Emerging from Yǒushēn, seen carried.
The *Shǐ Jì* says:
Yī Yǐn wished to serve Tāng,
so he became a retainer of the Yǒushēn clan,
carrying a dǐng and zǔ stand, using flavors to persuade Tāng,
guiding him toward the kingly way.
Traveling to Jìbīn, not yet ceased.
Sūn Chàngzhī's *Shù Shū* says:
Yǔ cast the Nine Dǐng.
People did not notice the dǐng moving,
yet each day it moved five steps.
Since Zhōu's Jiárù, it has moved southeast,
who knows to which state it has reached now?
The monk Shāng's travel account says:
The dǐng is in Jìbīn,
northwest of Yángzhōu.
Liáng Wǔdì copying the immortal scriptures.
The *Dǐng Lù* says:
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng cast a golden dǐng,
inscribed with the five thousand characters of Lǎozǐ.
Xiāo Zǐyún wrote them,
and it was sunk in the Jiǔjiāng River.
The Chǔ lord seeking the ritual vessels.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
The Chǔ lord said to Right Minister Zǐ Gé:
"Now I send a man to Zhōu to request a dǐng as a ritual vessel,
will the king give it to me?"
He replied:
"He will give it to Your Majesty!"
Observing the images, the xī trigrams change.
The virtue of gold and jade is beneficial,
as the *Book of Changes* says:
The cauldron has yellow ears and golden rings,
which is beneficial for steadfastness.
With jade rings,
there is great good fortune,
and nothing is unfavorable.
When used in service to the royal house,
there is the distinction of Chóng and Guàn.
The *Book of Rites* says:
The Chóng cauldron and the Guàn cauldron
are vessels of the Son of Heaven.
Note:
Chóng and Guàn are both names of states.
Chá
As for its ability to cleanse vexation and cure thirst,
the "Book of Táng" states:
Cháng Lǔ was an envoy to the Western Barbarians,
and once brewed tea in a tent.
He said to the barbarians:
"This cleanses vexation and cures thirst—
this is what is called tea."
The barbarians replied:
"We have this here too."
They ordered some to be brought out,
and pointed, saying:
"This is from Shòuzhōu,
this is from Gùzhǔ,
and this is from Qímén."
As for transforming the bones and lightening the body,
Táo Hóngjǐng's "Miscellaneous Records" states:
Bitter tea lightens the body and transforms the bones;
in the past, Dānqiūzǐ and Huángshān Jūn consumed it.
The benefits of tea,
its efficacy is like that of the divine.
The "Shuōwén" states:
"Tú"
means bitter tea,
which is what is now called tea.
Then there is Qújiāng thin slices,
the "Tea Manual" states:
Qújiāng thin slices,
eighty pieces per pound.
Xīshān white dew,
the "Tea Manual" states:
Xīshān in Hóngzhōu produces white dew.
Clouds hang with green stems,
the "Tea Manual" states:
At the boundary bridge in Yuánzhōu,
its fame is great,
but it is not as good as Húzhōu's ground paste purple shoots;
when brewed, green stems hang down.
Fragrance floats on emerald milk.
The "Tea Manual" states:
Wùzhōu has Jǔyán tea;
its leaves are square and fine,
and though the yield is small,
its flavor is extremely sweet and fragrant;
when brewed, it resembles emerald milk.
Scoop this frosty splendor,
the "Tea Manual" states:
Fù Xùn's "Seven Admonitions" says:
Grapes, Wǎnnài plums, Qí persimmons, Yān chestnuts, Chángyáng yellow pears, Wūshān red tangerines, tea seeds from the southern regions, and stone honey from the western extremes—
after both cold and warm dishes are served,
one should present frosty splendor tea.
It dispels this oppressive summer heat.
The "Tea Manual" states:
The stone nanmu of Chángshā,
its buds are picked for tea.
The people of Xiāng pick yángtóng grass on the fourth day of the fourth month,
pound its juice, mix it with rice, and steam it,
similar to rice cakes or gruel.
One must drink this tea
to dispel wind ailments,
and it is especially suitable for drinking in the hot months.
Elegant writings have been passed down by Dù Yù,
Dù Yù's "Ode to Chuǎn" says:
It harmonizes the spirit and soothes the inner self,
dispelling weariness and fatigue.
Profound thoughts are also heard from Lù Yǔ.
The "Tea Manual" states:
Táng dynasty Lù Yǔ wrote the "Classic of Tea" in three volumes.
As for plucking this gāolú,
the "Guǎngzhōu Records" state:
Gāolú
is another name for tea,
its leaves are large and astringent,
and southern people drink it.
Brewing this bitter tea,
the "Ěryǎ" states:
"Jiǎ"
means bitter tea.
Annotation:
The tree is small, resembling gardenia;
early-picked leaves are called "chá,"
late-picked leaves are called "míng" or "chuǎn,"
and people of Shǔ call it bitter tea.
Evaluate its purple and green hues,
rank its curled and open leaves.
Lù Yǔ's "Classic of Tea" states:
Purple leaves are superior,
green leaves are second.
Shoots are superior,
buds are second.
Curled leaves are superior,
open leaves are second.
Tóngjūn's records place particular importance on it,
the "Records of Tóngjūn" states:
Bādōng has true fragrant tea;
brewing and drinking it keeps one from sleeping.
There is also white tea,
shaped like gardenia,
its color slightly white.
The immortal's palm is hard to surpass.
The "Tea Manual" states:
At Qīngxī Mountain in Dāngyáng County, an immortal
tends to tea.
Lǐ Bái has a poem about it.
The fine sweet dew of Yùzhāng,
the "Sòng Records" state:
Prince Zǐluán of Xīn'ān and Prince Zǐshàng of Yùzhāng
visited the monk Tánjì at Bāgōng Mountain.
Tánjì served tea,
and Zǐshàng, tasting it, said:
"This is sweet dew,
why call it tea?"
Wáng Sù's fondness for the "buttermilk slave."
Yáng Xuànzhī's "Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luòyáng" states:
Wáng Sù was fond of fish,
and Péngchéng Prince Xiào once teased Sù, saying:
"You do not value the great states of Qí and Lǔ,
but love the small states of Zhū and Jǔ."
Sù replied:
"What is esteemed in one's hometown,
one cannot help but love."
Xiào then said to him:
"If you visit me tomorrow,
I will prepare a meal of Zhū and Jǔ for you,
and also have the 'buttermilk slave.'"
Hence, tea was also nicknamed the "buttermilk slave."
At the time, the Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat Liú Gǎo admired Sù's style
and devoted himself to drinking tea.
Péngchéng Prince said to Gǎo:
"You do not admire the eight delicacies of nobles and princes,
but prefer the servant's water vessel."
The Péngchéng Prince's household had a Wú singing girl,
and he used these words to tease him.
From then on, at banquets of the court nobility,
though tea was served,
they felt ashamed to drink it.
Later, when refugees from south of the river came to surrender from afar,
the Palace Attendant Yuán Chà wanted to serve them tea.
He first asked:
"How much of the water vessel do you drink?"
Xiāo Zhèngdé did not understand Chà's meaning,
and replied:
"Although I was born in a region of waters,
since establishing myself,
I have never suffered the calamity of Yánghóu."
The entire gathering laughed.
Also, the "Wèi Records" state:
Lángyá's Wáng Sù once served in the Southern Dynasties,
and was fond of drinking tea and eating water shield soup.
After crossing to the north,
he also grew fond of lamb and buttermilk.
He once said:
"Lamb
is the chief of land produce;
fish
is the foremost of aquatic creatures.
Lamb is comparable to the great states of Lǔ and Qí,
fish to the small states of Zhū and Jǔ.
Only tea is not worthy—
it can only serve as a slave to buttermilk."
Wait for spears and banners to pick,
the "Tea Manual" states:
Tuánhuáng tea has the name "one banner, two spears,"
meaning one leaf and two buds.
Facing the tripod and cauldron to blow and sip.
Zuǒ Sī's "Poem of the Lovely Daughters" says:
In my home there are lovely daughters,
radiant and ever fair-skinned.
The elder is named Wánsù,
her speech clear and articulate.
Eager to run in wind and rain,
swiftly she goes back and forth a hundred times.
Her heart is stirred by tea,
blowing and sipping at the tripod and cauldron.
Then there is curing that hú-jiǎ ailment,
the "Sequel to Records of Searching for Spirits" states:
Huán Xuānwǔ had a commanding officer
who, after contracting a seasonal illness, suffered from residual heat.
He could then drink a large amount of tea,
requiring one hú and two dǒu to feel full.
If reduced by even a shēng or a gě,
he felt greatly unsatisfied.
Later, a guest visited him,
and offered him an additional five shēng.
He then vomited profusely.
Something came out,
as large as a shēng measure,
with a mouth-like shape,
its texture wrinkled and shriveled,
resembling an ox's stomach.
The guest then had it placed in a basin,
and poured two dǒu of tea over it.
The thing sucked it all up and then stopped.
Feeling slightly bloated,
he added another five shēng,
and it all gushed out from his mouth in a chaotic manner.
After vomiting this thing,
his illness was cured.
Someone asked him:
"What illness was this?"
He replied:
"This illness is called the 'hú míng' abdominal mass."
Troubled by this water affliction,
The *Shishuo* states:
Jìn dynasty Wáng Méng was fond of drinking tea,
and whenever guests arrived, he would invariably order them to drink it.
The scholar-officials all suffered from this,
and whenever they intended to visit him,
they would inevitably say:
"Today there is a water calamity."
Plucked from those shady groves,
Lù Yǔ's *Chájīng* states:
To cultivate tea plants for luxuriance,
the method is like planting melons;
after three years they can be picked.
[Grow them on] sunny banks and in shady woods;
purple [sprouts] are superior,
green ones are next.
Obtained from crumbly rock.
Lù Yǔ's *Chájīng* states:
The superior [tea] grows on crumbly rock,
the medium grows on gravelly soil,
the inferior grows on yellow earth.
First apply fire to process it,
and pick it when thunder arrives.
The *Chápǔ* states:
In Yǎzhōu of Shǔ, there is Mount Méng,
the mountain has five peaks,
and on the peaks there are tea gardens.
The central peak is called Shàngqīng Peak.
In the past, there was a monk who suffered from chills for a long time.
He once met an old man,
who said to him:
"For the tea on the central peak of Méng,
often, before and after the Spring Equinox, gather many laborers,
wait for the thunder to sound,
and with joined hands pick for three days and then stop.
If you obtain one liǎng,
decoct it with water from that place and take it,
and it will immediately be able to dispel chronic illnesses.
Two liǎng will ensure freedom from illness before one's destined lifespan ends,
three liǎng can certainly transform one's bones,
four liǎng will make one an earthbound immortal."
This monk therefore went to the central peak,
built a hut to wait,
and when the time came, obtained a little over one liǎng.
Before he had finished taking it, his illness was cured.
When he came to the city market,
people saw his appearance:
he always looked like someone over thirty years old.
His eyebrows and hair were green in color.
Afterwards, he entered Qīngchéng to seek the Way,
and no one knows where he ended up.
Nowadays, the tea gardens on the four other peaks are picked without cease,
but the central peak has dense, luxuriant vegetation,
obscured by clouds and mist,
fierce beasts often appear,
and human footprints rarely reach it.
Nowadays, Méngdǐng tea has Wùsuōyá and Jiǎnyá varieties,
both are said to be 'before fire',
meaning processed before the Cold Food Festival fire prohibition.
The worry of the Wú ruler for Wéi Yào,
initially bestowed special favor;
The *Wúzhì* states:
Sūn Hào, at every banquet when drinking,
[guests] could not avoid it.
He always set seven shēng as the limit per person,
even if it wasn't all drunk,
[the wine] was poured out until finished.
Wéi Yào's capacity for drink did not exceed two shēng.
Initially, he was treated with special courtesy,
and was secretly granted tea to substitute for wine.
Later, when favor declined,
he was further coerced,
and this was then held as a crime.
Lù Nà's treatment of Xiè Ān,
truly displayed frugal virtue.
The *Jìnshū* states:
When Lù Nà was Governor of Wúxīng,
General of the Guards Xiè Ān once wished to visit Nà.
Nà's nephew Lù Chù thought it strange that Nà had made no preparations,
but did not dare ask,
so privately made arrangements himself.
When Ān arrived,
what Nà had set out was only tea and fruit.
Chù then presented a lavish feast,
with all kinds of delicacies fully prepared.
After Ān left,
Nà caned Chù forty strokes,
saying:
"Since you were unable to bring honor to your uncle,
why did you defile my simple way of life?"
There is also that produced at Yùlěi,
The *Chápǔ* states:
Outside Yùlěi Pass, on Bǎotáng Mountain, there are tea trees,
growing on cliffs.
The shoots are three cùn long,
and only after five cùn does one or two leaves appear.
Processed by that Golden Sand [spring],
The *Chápǔ* states:
At Zhuómù Ridge in Chángxīng County, Húzhōu, there is the Jīnshā (Golden Sand) Spring,
which is where tea is processed every year.
