The two prefectures of Hú and Cháng meet their boundary here.
In that land there is the Jìnghuì Pavilion,
and every tea season,
the two prefectural governors both come here.
This spring,
lies amidst sand,
and normally has no water.
When about to process tea,
the Governor performs the ritual procedures, bows, and offers a sacrifice to the spring.
Shortly after,
it begins to flow from the source,
and by that evening it is clear and overflowing.
When the processing for the imperial tribute is finished,
the water immediately diminishes slightly;
when the processing for the prefectural hall is finished,
the water is already half gone;
when the Governor's processing is finished,
it dries up completely.
If the Governor delays his return beyond schedule,
then it shows changes of wind and thunder,
or one may see fierce beasts, poisonous snakes, or tree spirits.
Three grades are designated,
The *Chápǔ* states:
In Línqióng, Línxī, Sī'ān, and Huǒjǐng of Qióngzhōu,
there are Zǎochūn (Early Spring), Huǒqián (Before Fire), and Huǒhòu (After Fire) Nènlǜ (Tender Green) teas, which are superior, medium, and inferior grades.
Five-petaled to form a flower.
The *Chápǔ* states:
Among the different kinds of tea,
Zhǐkéyá, Gǒuqǐyá, and Pípáyá
all treat wind ailments.
There are also Zàojiáyá, Huáiyá, and Liǔyá,
which are made by picking their buds in early spring
and blending them with tea.
The Wǔhuā (Five-Flower) tea
has leaves shaped like five-petaled flowers.
The Zǎochūn (Early Spring) from Bīnhuà,
The *Chápǔ* states:
Fúzhōu produces three kinds of tea:
Bīnhuà is the best,
processed in early spring.
Next is Báimǎ,
and the lowest is Fúlíng.
Héngwén (Horizontal Stripe) produced on the Yángpō (Sunny Slope).
The *Chápǔ* states:
In Xuānchéng County there is Yāshān small square cakes,
with tea buds laid horizontally covering the surface.
The eastern side of this mountain is illuminated by the morning sun,
and is called Yángpō (Sunny Slope).
Its tea is the most excellent.
The Governor once recommended it to the capital Luòyáng,
and men of note inscribed it:
"Yāshān Yángpō Héngwén tea."
Also heard of is the Hángāo (Containing Paste) product from Yōnghú,
The *Chápǔ* states:
Yìxīng has the Hángāo from Yōnghú.
The name Qíhuǒ (Straddling Fire) from Lóng'ān.
The *Chápǔ* states:
Lóng'ān has Qíhuǒ tea,
which is the best.
It is said it is not processed before the fire [prohibition],
nor after the fire [prohibition].
The fire is changed at Qīngmíng,
hence the name 'fire'.
Bǎiyán and Hèlǐng,
The *Chápǔ* states:
Fúzhōu's Bǎiyán is extremely fine.
Also, Hóngzhōu's Xīshān Báilù and Hèlǐng teas are supremely wonderful.
Jiūkēng and Fèngtíng.
The *Chápǔ* states:
Mùzhōu's Jiūkēng is extremely fine.
The *Chájīng* states:
[Tea] growing on Fèngtíng Mountain at the Fēiyún and Qūshuǐ temples,
and on the Qīngxiàn and Zhuōmù ridges,
is the same as that from Shòuzhōu.
Praising the delicate tenderness of the Quèshé (Sparrow's Tongue),
admiring the ethereal lightness of the Chányì (Cicada's Wing).
The *Chápǔ* states:
Shǔzhōu's Quèshé, Niǎozuǐ, and Màikē,
are generally made from tender buds,
because their buds resemble those things.
There is also Piànjiǎ,
where buds and leaves clasp together like armor scales.
Chányì,
where the leaves are tender and thin like a cicada's wings.
Dōngyá (Winter Bud) early flourishing,
The *Chápǔ* states:
Mount Méng has Yāgāolùyá, Bùyāgāolùyá, and also Dōngyá,
meaning the buds split open in deep winter.
Màikē (Wheat Grain) first to form.
See the note above.
Some valued the price of the Western Garden,
The *Jiāngshì Zhuàn* states:
Jiāng Tǒng was promoted to Tutor to the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái,
and once submitted a memorial admonishing, saying:
"Now the Western Garden sells vinegar, noodles, tea, vegetable baskets and such things,
damaging the dignity of the state."
Some rival the shape of a round moon.
The *Chápǔ* states:
In Héngzhōu's Héngshān,
In Fēngzhōu's western region,
tea is made by grinding it into a paste,
all formed into round cakes like the moon.
They brighten the eyes and enhance thinking.
The "Běncǎo Shíyí" says:
Gāolú tea is bitter and neutral,
it quenches thirst and dispels phlegm,
prevents sleepiness,
benefits the waterways,
and brightens the eyes.
Huà Tuó's "Shí Lùn" says:
Long-term consumption of bitter tea benefits thought.
Could it deplete qi and harm essence?
The "Táng Xīnyǔ" says:
Right Supplements Officer Mǔ Jǐng was erudite,
possessing talent for writing,
and by nature did not drink tea.
He wrote the "Cháyǐn Xù," saying:
"To relieve stagnation and dissolve blockages,
the benefit for a day is temporarily good;
but depleting qi and harming essence,
the lifelong burden is great indeed.
When benefits are gained, credit is given to tea's power;
when harm is incurred, it is not called a tea disaster.
Is it not that blessings near are easy to know,
while calamities far are hard to see?"
There is also the Shǔgāng Niú Ridge.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
At Chánzhì Temple in Yángzhōu,
the former Suí dynasty palace,
the temple rests on Shǔgāng,
where there is a tea garden,
its flavor sweet and fragrant like Méngdǐng tea.
Also, the Niú'ě Ridge in Shèzhōu is especially fine.
Hóngyǎ and Wūchéng.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
In Hóngyǎ and Dānlíng Chānghé of Méizhōu, they also make cake tea,
using methods like Méngdǐng.
The "Wúxīng Jì" says:
Twenty lǐ west of Wūchéng County is Wēn Mountain,
which produces imperial chuǎn tea.
Bìjiàn is recorded by name.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
There are names like Xiǎojiāng Garden, Míngyuè Liáo, Bìjiàn Liáo, and Zhūyú Liáo.
Zǐsǔn is praised.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
Méngdǐng has yángāo tea,
made into slices for tribute,
also called zǐsǔn.
Ascending immortal cliffs where flowers fall.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
At Púcūn Péngkǒu in Péngzhōu,
its gardens have names like Cliff and Stone Flower.
Consuming Dānqiū tea gives wings.
The "Tiāntāi Jì" says:
Dānqiū produces great míng tea,
consuming it grows wings.
As for flying from within a prison,
the "Guǎnglíng Qílǎo Zhuàn" says:
During the reign of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
there was an old woman
who each morning carried a vessel of míng tea to the market to sell.
People in the market competed to buy,
from morning till dusk,
the vessel never diminished.
The money she gained she scattered by the roadside for orphans, the poor, and beggars.
Someone seized and imprisoned her,
but at night she lifted the vessel of tea she sold and flew away from the window.
Brewing amidst bamboo.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
Emperor Sùzōng of Táng once bestowed upon the recluse Zhāng Zhìhé a male and female servant each,
Zhìhé paired them as husband and wife,
naming them Yútóng and Qiáoqīng.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"Yútóng is to hold the fishing rod and gather the line,
rowing among the reeds.
Qiáoqīng is to gather orchids and cut cassia,
brewing tea amidst bamboo."
Its effect lies in preventing sleep.
The "Bówù Zhì" says:
Drinking true tea
makes people sleep less.
Its merit lies in gladdening the spirit.
The "Shénnóng Shíjīng" says:
Tea míng should be taken long-term,
it makes people strong and gladdens the spirit.
Some speak of poetry as repayment.
The "Chá Pǔ" says:
There was a man named Hú,
who made a living as a tinker,
living near Báipínzhōu,
beside an ancient grave.
Whenever he drank tea,
he would pour a libation to it.
Suddenly he dreamed of a person who said to him:
"My surname is Liǔ,
in life I was skilled at poetry and loved tea,
moved by your kindness of tea,
having nothing to repay,
I wish to teach you poetry."
Hú declined, saying he could not,
but Liǔ insisted,
saying:
"Just follow your thoughts and speak,
and you will achieve it."
Hú later became skilled at poetry.
People of the time called it Hú the Tinker's poetry.
This Liǔ must be Liǔ Yùn.
Some received money as a gift.
The "Yìyuàn" says:
Chén Wù's wife in Shàn County was widowed young,
living with her two sons,
and loved drinking tea.
At home there was an ancient grave,
and each time she drank she would first offer to it.
Her two sons wanted to dig it up,
but their mother stopped them.
At night she dreamed of a person expressing gratitude, saying:
"Though I lie hidden in decayed soil,
how could I forget repaying kindness from the mulberry shade?"
At dawn,
in the courtyard she obtained a hundred thousand coins,
seeming long-buried,
only the string was new.
Also said: leaves like gardenia,
flowers like roses.
The "Chá Jīng" says:
Tea is
a fine tree of the south,
from one or two chǐ to several tens of chǐ tall,
in Bāchuān and Xiáshān there are trees so large two people can embrace them.
Cut and pluck them,
the tree is like guālú,
leaves like gardenia,
flowers like white roses,
fruit like bīnglǘ,
stem like clove,
root like walnut.
Its names: one is chá,
two is jiǎ,
three is shè,
four is míng,
five is chuǎn.
Note:
shè is pronounced shè.
The beauty of light breezes and floating clouds,
the difference of frosty stalks and bamboo sheaths.
The "Chá Jīng" says:
Tea comes in thousands of forms,
briefly speaking,
some are like Tartar boots, wrinkled and shrunken;
like bison chests, angular and sharp;
like floating clouds emerging from mountains, swirling and rolling;
like light breezes skimming water, rippling and undulating—these are the fine and excellent teas.
Those with bamboo sheaths
have stems and branches hard and solid,
difficult to steam and pound,
hence their shape is coarse and sifted.
Those like frosty stalks
have stems and leaves withered and drooping,
their appearance altered,
hence their shape is wilted and withered—these are the thin and old teas.
From plucking to sealing,
seven steps.
From Tartar boots to frosty stalks,
eight grades.
Líshī,
pronounced lí shī.
Only fragrant tea is of use,
indeed it is a resource for drink and food.
As for wine,
Fish are caught in the weir,
Catfish and carp.
The nobleman has wine,
Fine and plentiful.
From the *Shī*.
As for Yí Dí’s initial creation,
the *Zhànguócè* says:
The emperor’s daughter Yí Dí made wine and presented it to Yǔ.
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
Yí Dí brewed excellent wine,
but Yǔ distanced himself from it.
Shào Kāng began its production,
the *Shìběn* says:
Yí Dí first made fermented wine,
transforming the five flavors.
Shào Kāng made millet wine.
Nine infusions, the essence of a hundred varieties,
the *Jiǔjīng* says:
Empty mulberry tree and spoiled rice,
fermented with millet and wheat,
to become rich wine—
this is the beginning of wine.
Black plum and female yeast, sweet and mellow,
nine infusions, clarified from a hundred varieties—
this is the culmination of wine.
“䴷” is pronounced huǎn,
“醹” is pronounced rǔ.
The beauty of one night’s triple fermentation.
The *Shuōwén* says:
Tú,
is wine yeast.
Lǐ,
is wine fermented for one night.
Láo,
is the liquid,
the sedimented wine.
Zhòu,
is triple-fermented wine.
Lí,
is thin wine.
Xǔ,
is strained wine.
Tú,
pronounced tú.
pronounced suō.
Since yīn and yáng interact,
the *Chūnqiūwěi* says:
When millet is made into wine,
yáng relies on yīn to be able to stir,
hence using yeast to ferment millet into wine.
Note:
Yeast,
is yīn,
they combine and bubble—
this is its stirring.
It also gives rise to fortune and misfortune.
The *Shuōwén* says:
Wine,
is “jiù” (to approach),
thus it approaches the goodness or evil of human nature.
Another interpretation is “zào” (to create),
that from which fortune and misfortune are created.
Draw from this and think of gentleness,
the *Shī* says:
The rhinoceros-horn cup is curved,
fine wine, think of gentleness.
The note says:
Drinking fine wine, one thinks of obtaining gentle, compliant harmony,
to share joy with it.
The rhinoceros-horn cup,
is a penalty vessel.
Recite this and shame the opposite.
The *Shī* says:
All who drink this wine,
some are drunk, some are not.
Having established overseers,
some assist with recorders.
Those drunk are not good,
the sober are instead shamed.
Note:
Among drinkers, some are drunk, some are not,
so overseers are established to watch them.
Also assisted by recorders,
to supervise the drinking,
ordering all to get drunk,
shaming those not drunk.
Shame,
means to penalize them.
Then there was favoring Wéi Yào by granting chuǎn tea,
see the “Wú zhǔ zhī yōu Wéi Yào” note in the *Chá Fù*.
For Mù Shēng, setting out sweet wine.
The *Hànshū* says:
King Yuán of Chǔ respectfully treated Shēn Gōng and others,
Mù Shēng did not enjoy wine,
each time wine was set out,
he would prepare sweet wine for Mù Shēng.
When King Wù ascended the throne,
he often did so.
Later he forgot to set it out,
Mù Shēng withdrew and said:
“It is time to leave.
Sweet wine is not set out,
the king’s intention has slackened.
If I do not leave,
the people of Chǔ will clamp me in the market.”
He then claimed to be ill in bed.
Dìng Guó drank several shí yet remained clear-minded,
the *Hànshū* says:
Yú Dìngguó drank wine up to several shí without confusion,
and handled legal cases with even greater acuity.
Zhèng Xuán one hú and was dignified and imposing.
The *Hànshū* says:
Grand General Yuán Shào commanded troops in Jìzhōu,
sent an envoy to invite Zhèng Xuán,
gathered many guests for a grand feast,
Xuán arrived last,
so they rose and invited him to the upper seat.
He was eight chǐ tall,
drank one hú of wine,
had elegant eyebrows and bright eyes,
with a dignified and imposing demeanor.
The three-day vice director,
the *Jìnshū* says:
Zhōu Yǐ frequently had lapses due to wine,
serving as vice director,
almost never sober,
contemporaries called him the “three-day vice director.”
Yǔ Liàng said:
“In his later years, Marquis Zhōu
could be said to have declined in phoenix virtue.”
A hundred coins, Ruǎn’s son.
See the “huò guà zhàng tóu” note in the *Qián Fù*.
Chén Jiàn often sang “Huíbō”,
the *Tángshū* says:
Lǐ Jǐngbó, during the Jǐnglóng era, served as remonstrance counselor,
Emperor Zhōngzōng once held an inner banquet with favored ministers and noble relatives,
wine flowed freely,
they took turns singing the “Huíbō Lè”,
it became very noisy and improper.
When it came to Jǐngbó’s turn,
he sang:
“Huíbō at this time with wine cups,
my humble duty lies in admonition and guidance.
Proper drinking should be only three rounds,
ruler and subjects mingling chaotically is not fitting.”
The banquet then disbanded.
Contemporaries praised him.
Nourishing nature also washes away piled-up lumps.
The *Shìshuō* says:
Wáng Xùn asked Wáng Chén:
“How does Ruǎn Jí compare to Sīmǎ Xiàngrú?”
Chén said:
“Ruǎn Jí has piled-up lumps in his chest,
so he needs to wash them away.
Speaking of similarity to Xiàngrú,
only the wine differs.”
Thus, take joy in this at Hào,
the *Shī* says:
The king is at Hào,
joyfully drinking wine.
Draw from this like the Miǎn River.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
The Marquis of Jìn feasted with the Marquis of Qí,
Zhōngháng Mùzǐ assisted,
they played pitch-pot,
the Marquis of Jìn went first,
Mùzǐ said:
“There is wine like the Huái River,
meat like a mound,
if my lord hits this,
he will lead the feudal lords.”
He hit it.
The Marquis of Qí raised his arrow and said:
“There is wine like the Miǎn River,
meat like a hill,
if I hit this,
I will succeed you in rising.”
He also hit it.
Emulate Zhèng Jūn’s ability to brew,
the *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Zhèng Jūn’s method of brewing wine:
When the wine is ready,
add monkshood and licorice into the wine,
expose it to dry,
until it forms balls the size of chicken eggs,
one ball thrown into one dǒu of water
instantly becomes fine wine.
Recall Liú Líng’s remedy for hangover.
The *Shìshuō* says:
Liú Líng suffered from wine sickness,
was very thirsty,
and asked his wife for wine.
His wife held the vessel and tearfully admonished:
“You drink too much wine,
it is not the way to nurture life.”
Líng said:
“I cannot restrain myself,
only by praying to ghosts and spirits and swearing an oath.
You may prepare wine and meat.”
He followed her advice.
Líng knelt and prayed:
"Heaven gave birth to Liú Líng,
making wine his fame.
With one drink, a dàn he drains,
five dǒu to sober from his pains.
The words of a woman,
must never be heeded."
Then he drank wine and ate meat,
collapsing drunk once more.
Shān Tāo was known for eight dǒu,
The Book of Jin says:
Shān Tāo drank wine,
and only became drunk after eight dǒu.
The Emperor wanted to test him,
gave him eight dǒu of wine to drink,
secretly adding more wine.
Tāo stopped when he reached his original capacity.
Lù Nà's capacity was merely two shēng.
The Book of Jin says:
Lù Nà was about to become Governor of Wúxīng,
went to bid farewell to Huán Wēn,
and asked Wēn:
"How much wine can you drink to get drunk, my lord?
And how much meat can you eat?"
Wēn said:
"In my old age, three shēng of wine makes me drunk,
and plain pork no more than ten slices.
And you, how about you?"
He replied:
"I have never been able to drink much,
only up to two shēng,
and meat is not worth mentioning."
Later, waiting for a moment when Wēn was free,
he said:
"I have a modest gift outside,
as I am about to guard a distant commandery,
I wish to get drunk with you once,
to express my humble feelings."
Wēn gladly accepted.
At the time, Wáng Tǎnzhī and Diāo Yí were present,
and when the gift was received,
there was only one dǒu of wine,
and one plate of venison,
the guests were astonished.
Nà calmly said:
"My lord recently said you drink three shēng,
I can only manage two shēng,
now there is one dǒu,
to prepare for extra cups and leftover drops."
Wēn and the guests all sighed at his simplicity and sincerity,
Wēn further ordered the inner kitchen to prepare fine delicacies,
and the feast ended with great joy after hearty drinking.
Táo Kǎn would stop once he exceeded his limit,
The Book of Jin says:
Táo Kǎn always had a limit when drinking wine,
often still cheerful but his limit already exhausted.
Yīn Hào urged him to drink a little more,
Kǎn sadly said:
"When I was young, I often made mistakes due to wine,
my kind mother set restrictions,
so I dare not exceed them."
Kǒng Yǐ, however, could stay drunk for a full month without sobering.
The Book of Song says:
Kǒng Yǐ served as Chief Clerk of the commandery,
although drunk most days,
he understood government affairs clearly,
and his decisions when sober were never obstructed.
Everyone said:
"Lord Kǒng is drunk twenty-nine days a month,
better than ordinary people being sober for twenty-nine days."
Wénjǔ mocked Lord Cáo's prohibition,
The Annals of the Nine Provinces says:
Lord Cáo instituted a wine prohibition,
and Kǒng Róng wrote mocking him:
"Heaven has the Wine Banner star,
earth has the commandery of Wine Spring,
people have the virtue of fine wine,
thus Yáo could not achieve his sageliness without a thousand zhōng.
Moreover, Jié and Zhòu lost their states because of lust,
yet now you do not prohibit marriage."
Although Tàizǔ outwardly tolerated him,
inwardly he was displeased.
Jiǎn Yōng ridiculed the First Ruler's punishment.
The Records of Shu says:
The First Ruler prohibited wine due to drought,
officials found brewing equipment in people's homes,
some argued they should be punished the same as those who made wine.
Jiǎn Yōng was accompanying the First Ruler on an excursion,
saw a man walking on the road,
and said to the First Ruler:
"He intends to fornicate,
why not bind him?"
The First Ruler said:
"How do you know that?"
He replied:
"He has the equipment,
same as those who intend to brew."
The First Ruler laughed heartily and pardoned those who intended to brew.
Chopping wood hǔ hǔ,
straining wine, fine and good.
From the commentary on the Book of Songs,
shāi,
pronunciation suǒ qǐ qiē,
using a basket is called shāi,
using a strainer is called xǔ.
yù,
means beautiful appearance.
Pour from the cup of the distant wilderness,
The Classic of Divine Marvels says:
In the northwestern wilderness there is a Wine Spring,
this wine is as fine as meat,
clear as a mirror.
Above it is a jade cup,
take one cup,
and another cup refills,
sharing endless life with heaven and earth,
drinking this wine grants immortality.
Gather the tree from within the sea.
The History of the Southern Dynasties says:
In the southern sea is the country of Dùnxùn,
located on a coastal promontory.
There is a wine tree resembling a pomegranate,
collect its flower juice and store it in jars,
after several days it becomes wine.
The Three Yǎ are known from Liú Biǎo,
The Discourse on Classics says:
Liú Biǎo had three wine cups,
the large called Bó Yǎ,
the middle called Zhòng Yǎ,
the small called Jì Yǎ.
Bó Yǎ holds seven shēng, Zhòng Yǎ six shēng,
Jì Yǎ five shēng.
He also placed a large needle on the end of a staff,
whenever a guest had wine, he would prick them with it,
to test if they were drunk or sober.
A hundred kē are still told of Zǐlù.
See note below for "Táng Yáo's thousand zhōng."
Praise Zhōng Huì for not bowing,
A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
Zhōng Yù and Zhōng Huì were renowned from a young age,
their father was napping during the day,
so they together stole medicinal wine to drink.
Their father woke at the time,
but pretended to sleep to observe them.
Yù bowed and then drank,
Huì drank without bowing.
Their father asked the reason,
Yù said:
"Wine is for completing rites,
I dare not not bow."
He asked Huì,
Huì said:
"Stealing wine is not according to rites,
therefore I did not bow."
Admire Mèng Jiā for grasping the essence.
The Book of Jin says:
Mèng Jiā served as Huán Wēn's Army Advisor,
Jiā loved drinking to his heart's content,
the more he drank, the more composed he remained.
Wēn asked Jiā:
"What is good about wine,
that you are so fond of it?"
Jiā said:
"My lord, you have not yet grasped the essence within wine."
Drink this and become a sage within,
The Records of Wei says:
Xú Miǎo served as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat,
at the time laws prohibited wine,
yet Miǎo drank privately until heavily drunk.
Commandant Zhào Dá asked him about official matters,
Miǎo said:
"I am a sage within."
Dá reported this to Tàizǔ,
Tàizǔ was very angry.
The Liaodong General Xiānyú Fǔ interceded:
"Ordinary drunkards,
call clear wine 'sage,'
and turbid wine 'worthy.'
Miǎo is by nature cultivated and cautious,
these were merely drunken words."
For this, he was pardoned.
Later, Emperor Wén visited Xǔchāng,
saw Miǎo and asked:
"Do you still occasionally become a sage within?"
Miǎo replied:
"In the past, Zǐ Fǎn died at Gǔyáng,
Yù Shū was punished for drinking,
my fondness is the same as these two men,
I cannot restrain myself,
and from time to time still become one within.
However, the woman with the permanent tumor was remembered for her ugliness,
while I am remembered for my drunkenness."
The Emperor laughed heartily,
looked to his attendants and said:
"His reputation is not undeserved."
He bestowed upon him the finest wine.
The Book of Han says:
Emperor Chéng sent an edict reprimanding Chancellor Zhái Fāngjìn,
and had the Imperial Secretary bestow ten dàn of the finest wine,
Raising a cow,
it was said:
"You, sir, should carefully consider your position."
Fāng Jìn committed suicide that very day.
Regarding Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's praise of Zāng Dùn,
the Book of Liáng states:
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng gathered over twenty promising younger men,
set out wine, and composed poems.
Zāng Dùn failed to finish his poem,
and was fined one dǒu of wine.
He drank it all without his complexion changing,
talking and laughing as usual.
Xiāo Jiè took up the brush and finished immediately,
his writing flawless without revision.
The emperor praised them both, saying:
"Zāng Dùn's drinking,
and Xiāo Jiè's writing,
are the beauties of this gathering."
Regarding Xiè Yì pressuring Huán Wēn.
The Book of Jìn states:
Xiè Yì served as Huán Wēn's Military Advisor,
and was called the 'Otherworldly Military Advisor'.
Once, using wine, he pressured Huán Wēn,
who fled into Princess Nánkāng's gate to avoid him.
Xiè Yì then took one of Wēn's soldiers and drank with him in the main hall,
saying:
"Losing one old soldier,
gaining another old soldier,
what is so strange about that?"
Regarding enforcing the military law of Zhūxū,
see the annotation for "How mighty was Zhūxū" in the "Ode to the Sword".
Regarding getting drunk in the chancellor's rear garden.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Cáo Shēn succeeded Xiāo Hé as Chancellor,
strictly adhering to Hé's established rules,
drinking mellow wine day and night.
Ministers and guests, seeing Shēn not attending to affairs,
all wished to speak to him.
When they arrived,
Shēn would get them drunk,
so they ultimately could not speak.
The Chancellor's residence's rear garden was near the officials' quarters.
The officials drank, sang, and shouted daily.
Shēn's attendants disliked this,
and invited Shēn to stroll in the garden.
Hearing the officials drunk, singing, and shouting,
they hoped he would summon and reprimand them.
Instead, he fetched wine, set out mats, and drank,
also singing and shouting,
harmonizing with them.
Some, by casting wine into the river, inspired loyalty.
The Records of Huáng Shígōng state:
In ancient times, when a fine general led troops,
someone presented him with a single dān of wine.
He had it cast into the river,
ordering the officers and men to approach and drink from the downstream flow.
A single dān of wine cannot flavor a whole river,
yet the three armies were willing to die for him,
not because the taste reached them.
Some, by raising a cup, killed a man.
The Book of Liáng states:
Prince Shàolíng, Lún, was stationed in Yǐngzhōu,
and invited Wú Xīng's Wú Guī as a guest.
When Zhāng Zuǎn was appointed to Xiāngzhōu,
his route passed through Yǐngzhōu,
and Lún held a farewell feast for him.
Zuǎn saw Guī seated there,
suddenly raised his cup and said:
"Wú Guī,
this wine celebrates your being able to attend today's feast."
Guī soon rose and returned home.
His son, Wēngrú, seeing his father unhappy,
asked and learned the reason.
Wēngrú, choked with anger,
died that very night.
Guī, resenting Zuǎn and grieving for his son,
was overwhelmed with sorrow and rage.
Within a few days,
he too perished.
Guī's wife, deeply mourning her husband and son,
died the next day.
People of the time said Zhāng Zuǎn, with one cup of wine,
killed three members of the Wú family.
Xiè Fěi was once heard pointing to his mouth,
The Book of Qí states:
Xiè Fěi was appointed to Wú Xīng.
Parting from his brother Xiè at Zhēnglǔ Zhǔ,
he pointed to Xiè's mouth and said:
"This is only fit for drinking wine."
After Fěi arrived at the commandery,
he sent several hú of wine,
with a letter saying:
"Drink this with all your might,
do not involve yourself in human affairs."
Guǎn Zhòng once worried about ruining himself.
The Guǎnzǐ states:
Duke Huán of Qí drank with Guǎn Zhòng.
Zhòng discarded half his wine,
saying:
"Your servant has heard: wine enters, the tongue comes out;
the tongue comes out, words are lost;
words are lost, the self is ruined.
Your servant believes ruining oneself is worse than discarding wine."
Drinking is most harmonious,
The Book of Songs says:
The wine is both mild and fine,
drinking it is most harmonious.
Enjoying it this very night.
The Book of Songs says:
Enjoy the wine this night,
the noblemen are feasting.
Building that hill of dregs,
The History of the Southern Dynasties states:
Chén Xuān was a man of outstanding literary talent but excessively addicted to drink.
His nephew Xiù sent a letter admonishing him to stop,
Xuān replied in a letter:
"Quickly build me a hill of dregs,
I shall grow old there."
Drowning in the underground chamber.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The Earl of Zhèng, Yǒu, was fond of wine.
He built an underground chamber,
and drank wine at night,
striking bells.
Morning came and he had not yet stopped.
Annotation:
The underground chamber,
was a cellar.
Zǐ Liáng holding the wine vessel and suddenly advancing,
The Book of Qí states:
Emperor Gāo visited the Eastern Palace,
summoned the various princes for a feast and drink,
and then toured the Xuánpǔ Garden.
Prince Chángshā, Huǎng, held the canopy,
Prince Línchuān, Yìng, held the pheasant-tail fan,
Prince Wénxǐ, Zǐliáng, held the wine vessel,
and Prince Nánjùn served the wine.
Emperor Wǔ, along with Prince Yùzhāng, Yí, and Wáng Jìngzé, personally presented the dishes.
Emperor Gāo drank heavily,
bestowed wine upon Emperor Wǔ and the others,
and all became thoroughly drunk, enjoying themselves fully.
Yán Zhī leaning on the saddle at ease.
The Book of Sòng states:
Yán Yánzhī enjoyed riding horses and roaming the lanes,
whenever he met an old acquaintance, he would lean on his saddle and demand wine,
upon receiving it, he would drain it completely,
delighting in his own contentment.
Having already managed the five types of filtered wine,
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Director of Wine is in charge of the regulations concerning wine,
distinguishing the names of the five types of filtered wine:
first, the floating filtered wine,
second, the sweet filtered wine,
third, the white filtered wine,
fourth, the reddish filtered wine,
fifth, the settled filtered wine.
Annotation:
The floating type is finished with dregs floating about,
like the present-day Yíchéng unfiltered wine.
The sweet type is finished with juice and dregs mixed together,
like the present-day sweet wine.
The white type is finished with a pure, lush, scallion-white color,
like the present-day Cuó white wine.
The reddish type is finished with a red hue,
like the present-day lower-grade wine.
The settled type is finished with settled dregs,
like the present-day clear-brewed wine.
The pronunciation of 'filtered' is jì,
the pronunciation of 'reddish' is tǐ.
Also evenly blending the six ingredients.
The Book of Rites states:
In the first month of winter, order the officials:
the glutinous rice and ordinary rice must be uniform,
the yeast and malt must be timely,
the soaking and heating must be clean,
the water and spring must be fragrant,
the pottery vessels must be excellent,
the degree of heating must be precise,
combining these six ingredients,
the wine officials supervise it,
so there is no error.
Presenting wine to Yáng Hù without suspicion,
The Book of Jìn states:
Wú's Lù Kàng and Jìn's Yáng Hù maintained a friendship like that of Jī Zǐ and Zhá.
Kàng once sent Hù wine,
Hù drank it without suspicion.
When Kàng fell ill,
Hù sent him medicine,
Kàng also trusted him and took it.
People of the time considered it a reappearance of Huá Yuán and Zǐ Fǎn in their day.
Refuting Zhāng Zhāo and repeatedly defeating him.
The Records of Wú states:
Sūn Quán once ordered Zhūgě Kè to serve wine.
When he came before Zhāng Zhāo,
Zhāo already showed signs of drink,
and refused to drink,
saying:
"This is not the proper way to treat the elderly."
Quán said:
"You must make Lord Zhāng admit defeat,
Then we should drink it."
Zhūgě Kè challenged Zhāng Zhāo, saying:
"In ancient times, Master Shàngfǔ was ninety years old,
still holding his commander's banner and battle-axe,
and had not yet declared himself old.
Now in matters of military affairs, the general stays behind,
in matters of wine and food, the general comes first—
how can this be called not caring for the elderly?"
Zhāng Zhāo ultimately had no reply,
and so drained his cup.
He praised Huángfǔ for his simple honesty.
The Book of Northern Qí says:
Huángfǔ Liàng was by nature simple, pure, and honest.
He never once spoke with artifice or pretense.
Once an edict was issued ordering each department to report diligence and indolence,
Liàng did not go to the ministry for three days.
Emperor Wénxuān personally questioned him on the reason.
Liàng said:
"One day it rained,
one day I was drunk,
one day I was ill from drink."
Emperor Wénxuān, because of his honesty,
treated him leniently.
He despised Wáng Kūn for his stinginess.
The Book of Qí says:
Wáng Kūn was frugal with money and goods.
He would drink no more than two cups of wine,
and would always say, "This wine is hard to come by."
There was also Bì Zhuó who slept by the wine jar.
The Book of the Jin Restoration says:
At the end of the Tàixīng era,
Bì Zhuó was a Vice Director in the Ministry of Personnel.
The wine brewed by the official in the neighboring residence was ready.
Bì Zhuó, being drunk,
went at night to the jar area to take wine and drink it.
The wine steward thought he was a thief,
and seized and bound him.
The official went to look,
and it turned out to be Vice Director Bì.
Bì Zhuó then led the host to feast by the side of the jar,
got drunk, and left.
He entered the Infantry Commandant's kitchen.
A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
Ruǎn Jí heard that the Infantry Commandant's kitchen had stored several hundred hú of wine and a skilled brewer,
so he requested to be made an Infantry Commandant.
He drank the Jade Nectar of Yíngzhōu,
see the "Yíngzhōu Drinks Wine" note in the "Rhapsody on Jade."
He ladled the Jade Cream of Nányuè.
The Biography of the Lady of Nányuè says:
The Lady served Wáng Zǐqiáo Jade Cream and Green Wine.
We also hear of losing one's cap while drunk.
Hán Fēizǐ says:
Duke Huán of Qí was drinking wine and got drunk,
and lost his cap.
Ashamed of this,
he did not hold court for three days.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This is not a shame for a ruler of a state.
Why does Your Lordship not wash it away with governance?"
The Duke said:
"Good."
Thereupon he opened the granaries to give to the poor,
reviewed the prisons,
and released those with minor offenses.
After three days, the people sang:
"Why does our Lord not lose his cap again?"
He put a cap on a jar's head.
The Book of Later Wèi says:
Ruǎn Fú was by nature quick-witted and eloquent,
fond of wine,
short in stature and bald.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu was particularly fond of him.
He often placed ten jars of wine in a room,
each jar holding one hú,
and put caps on top of them,
wanting to tease Ruǎn Fú.
Ruǎn Fú happened to enter the room,
saw them and immediately said with delighted surprise:
"My brothers are very rude.
Why have they sneaked into the Prince's house,
sitting properly facing each other?
They should return home early."
Thereupon he took the wine and left.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
The silver goblet favored Sīhuà,
see the note "Quánshí fāng qī yú Sīhuà" in the "Rhapsody on the Qin."
The pale green wine was bestowed upon Cuī Hào.
The Book of Later Wèi says:
Emperor Tàizōng summoned Cuī Hào to discuss affairs.
They talked until midnight.
Emperor Tàizōng was greatly pleased,
and bestowed upon Cuī Hào ten hú of pale green wine
and one liǎng of crystal salt from Róng,
saying:
"I savor your words
like this salt and wine,
therefore I share their flavor with you."
Péi Càn then diligently offered his sincerity.
The Book of Later Wèi says:
Péi Càn was Central Drafting Official.
When the Emperor went to the banks of the Luò River,
Péi Càn bowed twice and offered a longevity toast.
The Emperor said:
"In the past, when the Prince of Běihǎi came to court,
he temporarily usurped the imperial authority,
and you said:
'I admonish you with wine.'
Now why do you want me to drink?"
Péi Càn said:
"The Prince of Běihǎi's aim was to indulge in drink,
so I admonished him on his fault.
Your Majesty is sagely and restrained,
therefore I dare to offer my slight sincerity."
The Emperor drank for him.
Yīn Kēng was benevolent and received recompense.
The Book of Liáng says:
Yīn Kēng often drank at banquets with guests and friends.
Seeing the wine server,
he turned and gave him his wine and roasted meat.
All the guests laughed.
Yīn Kēng said:
"We drink to our hearts' content all day,
yet the one holding the cup does not know its taste—
this is not human feeling."
When the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng occurred,
Yīn Kēng was once captured by the rebels,
and someone saved him, allowing him to escape.
Yīn Kēng asked who it was,
and it was the wine server.
He encountered Kuò Jǐng with Sīmǎ Xiāonàn.
The Book of Northern Qí says:
The Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Sīmǎ Xiāonàn, once visited Gāo Jìshì.
He drank heartily with him and stayed overnight.
The inner and outer gates were both closed.
He took a cart wheel and put it around Xiāonàn's neck,
and also put one around his own neck.
Xiāonàn had no choice,
and laughingly went along with it.
He saw Cìdào who would exhaust his family's stores.
The Book of Jin says:
Hé Chōng, styled Cìdào,
could drink wine,
and was highly esteemed by Liú Huī.
Liú Huī often said:
"Seeing Cìdào drink
makes one want to exhaust the family's brewing."
This speaks of his ability to be gentle and restrained.
We also hear of Kǒng Qún comparing it to meat in distiller's grains.
A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
Kǒng Qún, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, was fond of drinking wine.
Wáng Dǎo said:
"You are always drinking wine.
Haven't you seen the cloth covering the wine jars at the tavern?
It rots before long."
Kǒng Qún said:
"Haven't you seen the meat in the distiller's grains?
It lasts even longer."
Kǒng Qún often wrote to relatives and old friends:
"This year the fields yielded seven hundred dàn of glutinous rice,
still not enough for the business of brewing."
Sūn Cháo accumulated years of yeast seals.
The Book of Lièzǐ says:
Zǐchǎn's elder brother was called Gōngsūn Cháo.
He gathered a thousand zhōng of wine,
accumulated yeast into mounds.
A hundred paces from his gate,
the smell of distiller's grains and liquor assailed people's noses.
When he was lost in wine,
he did not know the safety or danger of governance,
the regrets or faults in human affairs,
whether there was anything in his household,
or the closeness or distance of his nine kinship groups.
Even if flood, fire, or weapons clashed before him,
he would not know.
Xiǎnfǔ's farewell with a hundred pots,
The Book of Songs says:
The Marquis of Hán went forth on his ancestral journey,
and lodged at Tú.
Xiǎnfǔ bid him farewell,
with clear wine, a hundred pots.
Emperor Yáo of Táng's lifting of a thousand zhōng.
The Kǒng Cóngzǐ says:
Lord of the Plains drank with Zǐgāo,
and pressed Zǐgāo to drink, saying:
"There is a proverb:
'Yáo drank a thousand zhōng,
Confucius drank a hundred gū,
Zǐlù chattered away,
yet still drank a hundred kē.'
The wise and sage of antiquity
all could drink without exception.
Why do you decline?"
Did he care for Jìyīng's reputation after death?
A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
Zhāng Jìyīng was unrestrained and uninhibited.
People of the time called him the 'Infantry Commandant of Jiāngdōng.'
Someone said to him:
"You indulge your whims for the moment,
do you not care for your reputation after death?"
Zhāng replied:
"If I were to have a reputation after my death,
it would be better to have a cup of wine right now."
And he got drunk in Gāo Huān's hand.
The Book of Later Wei says:
Emperor Shénwǔ of Qí once feasted court officials in Sīzhōu,
raised his cup and said to Biéjià Sòng Yóudào:
"Whoever drinks the wine from Gāo Huān's hand
is a true man.
Your character
is worthy of drinking this wine."
Responding to that east wind,
see the annotation "Responding to the sound of wine overflowing" in the "Ode to the Wind."
Brewing this maddening liquor,
The Book of Jin says:
Sūn Jìshū once drank with Shí Chóng,
and his arrogance was excessive.
Chóng wanted to report him,
but Péi Kǎi said:
"To give someone maddening liquor
and then blame them for not observing proper etiquette,
is that not contradictory?"
Chóng then stopped.
Brewed in winter and matured in summer,
The Rites of Zhou says:
Distinguish the three types of wine:
the first is shìjiǔ,
the second is xījiǔ,
the third is qīngjiǔ.
The annotation says:
Shìjiǔ is like today's yìjiǔ.
Xījiǔ
is aged wine,
like today's old yìjiǔ.
Qīngjiǔ
is today's wine brewed in winter and matured in summer.
Fénqīng and Yèzhuó.
The Book of Northern Qi says:
Emperor Wǔchéng was fond of Hé’nán Wáng Yú,
and once wrote to him by hand in Jìnyáng:
"I drink two cups of Fénqīng,
and urge you to drink two bowls of Yèzhuó."
It is also said that Wáng Zhān had three skills,
The Book of Liang says:
Wáng Zhān served as Minister of Personnel,
and was quite fond of wine.
Whenever he drank,
he could remain clear-headed all day,
and still handle official documents.
Emperor Wǔ often praised Zhān for having three skills:
archery, chess, and wine.
Fēng Shū's five crimes,
The Zuo Tradition says:
The Marquis of Jìn was about to attack Lù Fēng Shū,
and the ministers all said:
"Fēng Shū has three outstanding talents."
Bó Zōng said:
"The Dí have five crimes:
though they have many talents,
what good does it do?
Not offering sacrifices,
is the first.
Being addicted to wine,
is the second.
Abandoning Zhòng Zhāng and seizing the land of the Lí clan,
is the third.
Mistreating our Bó Jī,
is the fourth.
Injuring their ruler's eyes,
is the fifth.
Relying on their talents
without cultivating virtue,
only adds to their crimes."
The Hàn had the etiquette of Chánglè,
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
Emperor Gāozǔ abolished the harsh laws of Qín,
making them simple and easy.
The ministers drank and argued over their merits,
and the emperor was troubled by this.
Shūsūn Tōng knew the emperor was increasingly annoyed,
and advised him:
"I wish to establish court etiquette with my disciples."
In the seventh year of Hàn,
when Chánglè Palace was completed,
all ministers attended court in October.
Ritual wine was set out again,
and all ministers seated in the hall bowed,
offering toasts in order of rank.
After nine rounds of toasts,
the herald announced, "The wine is finished,"
and the censors enforced the rules,
removing anyone who did not follow etiquette.
Throughout the court banquet,
no one dared to breach etiquette.
Emperor Gāozǔ then said:
"Only today do I realize the dignity of being an emperor."
Wú had the gathering at Diàotái.
The Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wú says:
Sūn Quán was in Wǔchāng,
drinking at Diàotái.
He got heavily drunk
and ordered water to be splashed on the ministers,
saying:
"Today we drink to our hearts' content,
and only stop when we fall drunk from the terrace."
Zhāng Zhāo looked stern and said nothing,
then went outside and sat in his carriage.
Quán sent someone to call Zhāo back,
and said to him:
"We were just having fun together,
why are you angry?"
Zhāo replied:
"In the past, King Zhòu had hills of dregs and ponds of wine, drinking all night long,
and at the time, no one thought it was wrong."
Quán fell silent, looking ashamed.
A dou of Hé’dōng wine as a gift,
The Book of Later Zhou says:
Emperor Wén heard that Wéi Xiòng lived in seclusion and refused office,
and even an imperial summons could not bend him.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he treated him with even greater respect
and composed a poem for him.
Xiòng received the emperor's poem
and expressed his willingness to attend court occasionally.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and ordered the officials to give him a dou of Hé’dōng wine daily,
calling him "The Duke of Freedom."
A thousand-day drunkenness in Zhōngshān.
The Records of Diverse Matters says:
Liú Xuánshí once bought wine at a tavern in Zhōngshān,
and the tavern keeper gave him thousand-day wine to drink.
When he returned home, he was heavily drunk,
and his family did not know,
thinking he was dead,
and buried him.
Later, the tavern keeper calculated that nearly a thousand days had passed,
went to see him,
and was told:
"He has already been buried."
So they opened the coffin,
and he began to wake from his drunkenness.
It is commonly said:
Xuánshí drank wine
and was drunk for a thousand days.
Sū Wēi became ill from it,
The Book of Song says:
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì was always fond of wine,
and was rarely sober.
Emperor Wén reprimanded him, saying:
"General Sū Wēi became ill from excessive drinking,
and is waiting for death day and night.
No one in our family has ever drunk like this,
where did you learn it?"
Qìng Fēng exchanged wives because of it.
The Tradition says:
Qí Qìng Fēng loved hunting and was addicted to wine.
He moved his household to Lú Pú Piè's home,
exchanged wives, and drank.
Annotation:
Household,
refers to treasures, wives, and concubines.
He moved to live in Piè's home.
As for the thirst of the old Qiāng,
The Records of Omissions says:
In Jìn, there was a Qiāng man named Yáo Fù,
courtesy name Shìfēn,
who worked as a stable hand.
Whenever drunk, he liked to talk about the rise and fall of kings.
He often said:
"The water of the nine rivers is not enough to soak the yeast,
the wood of the eight marshes is not enough to make firewood,
the deer of the seven marshes are not enough to fill the kitchen."
He only spoke of his thirst for wine.
People called him "Thirsty Qiāng."
Later, Emperor Wǔ appointed him as the governor of Zhāogē,
but Fù wished to remain a stable hand,
and be given fine wine to enjoy his remaining years.
The emperor said:
"Zhāogē
is the old capital of King Zhòu,
and there is a wine pond there,
so the old Qiāng will no longer cry thirst."
He firmly declined,
and was transferred to be the governor of Jiǔquán.
There was a clear pond there,
whose taste was like wine,
and Fù, while drunk, bowed and accepted the appointment.
Cìgōng's madness,
The Book of Han says:
Píng’ēn Hóu Xǔ Bó moved into his new mansion,
and all officials from the chancellor down came to congratulate him.
The Sīlì Gài Kuānráo sat alone facing east.
Xǔ Bó poured wine himself and said:
"Lord Gài has arrived late."
Kuānráo said:
"Don't pour too much for me,
I am a wine madman."
Chancellor Wèi Hóu laughed and said:
"Cìgōng is mad even when sober,
why blame the wine?"
Cìgōng,
I dare not allow myself leisure and ease,
let alone dare to indulge in drinking.
Bǐng Yuán had the worry of abandoning his studies.
The *Records of Wei* states:
Bǐng Yuán initially left home to seek learning.
Yuán originally had a nature for drinking alcohol,
but after setting out,
for eight or nine years,
he did not bring wine to his lips.
Traveling alone on foot, carrying his books,
when he reached Chén, he studied under Hán Zǐzhù;
in Yǐngchuān, he revered Chén Zhònggōng;
in Rǔnán, he befriended Fàn Mèngbó;
in Zhuōjùn, he became close with Lú Zǐgàn.
At parting,
his teachers and friends, because Yuán did not drink,
gathered rice and meat to send Yuán off.
Yuán said:
"I originally could drink,
but fearing it would distract my thoughts and abandon my studies,
I therefore cut it off.
Now that we are about to part far away,
and seeing your farewell gifts,
I can drink at a feast once."
Thereupon he sat calmly and drank,
all day without becoming drunk.
Fàn Tài expounded the principle of harming life.
The *Book of Song* states:
Fàn Tài initially served as a Grand Academy Erudite.
His younger cousin, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Chén, requested him to be the Prefect of Tiānmén.
Chén was fond of drinking,
and when drunk, it would last for tens of days.
Upon sobering up,
he would be solemn and dignified.
Tài stated that wine harms life,
and one should deeply guard against it.
His words were very earnest.
Chén sighed for a long time,
and said:
"Many have admonished me,
but none have been like this."
If one forgets the warning of soaking one's head,
the *Book of Changes* says:
Drinking wine soaks the head,
not knowing moderation.
One will bring about the death of rotting ribs.
The *Book of Jin* states:
Zhōu Yǐ was skilled at drinking,
up to one dàn.
After crossing the river,
he often claimed to have no match.
Later, an old drinking rival came from the north.
Yǐ happily brought out two dàn of wine,
and they drank together until finished.
The next day, Yǐ was as before,
but saw that the guest had already died of rotting ribs.
Therefore, after three cups, one withdraws.
The *Book of Rites* says:
When a gentleman drinks wine,
after receiving one cup, his countenance is respectful;
after two cups, his speech is harmonious;
after three cups, he withdraws with ease.
Note:
"Respectful" means
a solemn and reverent appearance.
"Harmonious,"
pronounced yín,
"harmonious" means
a gentle and respectful appearance.
"With ease" means
a respectful and pleased appearance.
And with a hundred bows, the ritual is completed.
The *Book of Rites* says:
In the ritual of one offering,
the guest and host bow a hundred times,
drinking all day without becoming drunk.
Therefore, it is compared to soldiers and likened to water.
The *History of the Southern Dynasties* states:
Chén Xuān was fond of drinking and deeply indulged.
His nephew Xiù sent a letter admonishing him.
Xuān replied in a letter, saying:
"I have often likened wine to water.
Water can carry a boat,
but can also overturn it.
Therefore, Advisor Jiāng said:
'Wine is like soldiers.
Soldiers may not be used for a thousand days,
but cannot be unprepared for a single day.
Wine may not be drunk for a thousand days,
but when drunk, one must not fail to get drunk.'
How admirable, Lord Jiāng!
One can discuss wine with him."
Fèng
The divine bird with nine attributes,
as stated in the *Lúnyǔ Zhāi Shuāi Shèng*:
the phoenix has six resemblances and nine attributes.
The six resemblances:
its head resembles heaven,
its eyes resemble the sun,
its back resembles the moon,
its wings resemble the wind,
its feet resemble the earth,
its tail resembles the weft.
The nine attributes:
its mouth contains destiny,
its eyes harmonize with measures,
its ears are keen and penetrating,
its tongue can bend and stretch,
its colors are radiant,
its crest is short and crimson,
its spurs are sharp and hooked,
its voice is stirring and resonant,
its belly bears patterned markings.
Sòng Jūn notes:
"weft" refers to
the five weft stars.
"Measures" refers to
celestial measures.
"Crimson"
should be read as "vermilion,"
and "markings" are the patterns through which things pass.
It embodies the pure essence of utmost yang.
The *Hèguànzǐ* states:
the phoenix,
the bird of the Chúnhuǒ constellation,
is the essence of yang.
It bears ritual and treads upon faith,
and also upholds benevolence and is adorned with righteousness.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
the phoenix's head is green, upholding benevolence,
its neck is adorned with white, representing righteousness,
its wings are red, bearing ritual,
its breast is black, facing wisdom,
and its feet are yellow, treading upon faith.
Gazing toward Xuánhù, it comes in contemplation.
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
Huángdì fasted in his palace,
seated at Xuánhù,
when a great bird appeared,
with a rooster's head and a swallow's beak,
a turtle's neck and a dragon's form,
its body adorned with five colors,
and it alighted in Huángdì's eastern garden.
Seeing the yellow sash, it was certain to arrive.
The *Hánshī Wàizhuàn* states:
When Huángdì ascended the throne,
the world was peaceful,
but the phoenix had not yet appeared.
So he summoned Tiānlǎo and asked him:
"What is the phoenix like?"
Tiānlǎo replied:
"The phoenix's head upholds virtue,
its neck displays righteousness,
its back bears benevolence,
its feet tread upon uprightness,
with a swan's front and a qilin's rear,
a snake's neck and a fish's tail,
dragon patterns and a turtle's body,
a swallow's jaw and a rooster's beak."
Huángdì donned yellow robes,
wore a yellow sash,
and put on a yellow crown,
fasting in his palace,
and the phoenix arrived, obscuring the sun.
Thus, with Lízhū, it took turns feeding.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
In the south, there is a bird,
named the phoenix,
for which heaven created food,
its tree named Qióngzhī,
bearing fruit of qiúlin and lánggān.
Heaven also created Lízhū,
a being with three heads,
who took turns sleeping and rising,
to feed the lánggān.
Together with Mèngkuī, it departed.
The *Kuòdìtú* states:
Mèngkuī had a human head and a bird's body,
his ancestors tamed a hundred birds for the Yú clan.
At the end of the Xiàhòu era,
people began eating eggs,
so Mèngkuī left,
and the phoenix followed him,
settling at Dānshān,
eighteen thousand lǐ from Jiǔyí.
This mountain abounded in bamboo,
a thousand rèn tall,
the phoenix ate bamboo fruit,
and Mèngkuī ate tree fruit.
As for being moved by the Liùyīng and dancing,
the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
Dìkù had sagely virtue,
and composed the music Liùyīng,
and the phoenix flapped its wings and danced.
Hearing the Jiǔchéng, it came in reverence.
The *Shū* states:
When the Xiāosháo music reached its ninth movement,
the phoenix came in reverence.
Responding to the ascent to heaven, it descended and alighted.
The *Lǐyùn* states:
When one ascends to heaven,
the phoenix descends,
and the turtle and dragon appear.
Observing the radiance of virtue, it descends.
Jiǎ Yì's *Diào Qūyuán* states:
The phoenix soars a thousand rèn high,
observing the radiance of virtue before descending.
Lamenting the absence of the Hétú,
the *Lúnyǔ* states:
The Master said:
"The phoenix does not come,
the Hétú does not emerge from the river,
it is all over for me."
Knowing the decline of the Zhōu virtue.
The *Lúnyǔ* states:
"Phoenix, oh phoenix,
how has virtue declined?"
It once roamed the wilds,
as the *Lǐ* states:
When heaven does not withhold its way,
earth does not withhold its treasures,
and people do not withhold their true feelings,
then the phoenix dwells in the wilds,
and the eggs and offspring of birds and beasts can be observed up close.
How could it gather at the fence?
Sòng Yù's *Reply to King Xiāng of Chǔ* states:
The phoenix soars nine thousand rèn high,
piercing the clouds and rainbows,
bearing the azure sky;
how could the sparrow at the fence measure the height of heaven and earth with it?
Then there is Yáng Xióng's spitting,
as the *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
Yáng Xióng, while writing the *Tàixuán*,
dreamed of spitting out a white phoenix.
And Xiāo Shǐ's playing.
The *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
Xiāo Shǐ and Lòngyù lived together for decades,
playing the flute with phoenix-like sounds,
and phoenixes came to their house.
They built a phoenix tower,
and the couple resided atop it,
one day following the phoenixes and flying away.
Appreciating Sēngchuò's play,
the *Sòngshū* states:
Wáng Tánshǒu gathered with his brothers,
and the children played as they pleased.
Sēngdá jumped to the ground pretending to be a tiger,
Sēngduī stacked twelve game pieces,
and when they fell, he did not stack them again.
Sēngchuò collected wax beads to make a phoenix,
and Sēngdá snatched it into his arms,
yet Sēngchuò did not mind.
His uncle praised him as a magnanimous person.
Seizing Xún Xù's pond.
The *Jìnshū* states:
Xún Xù was transferred from Zhōngshū Jiān to Shàngshū Lìng,
a position he held for a long time.
At Zhōngshū, he was solely in charge of confidential matters.
Losing it,
he felt very disoriented.
Some congratulated him,
but Xún Xù said:
"You have taken my Phoenix Pond from me,
and yet you congratulate me?"
Appearing in a dream, it was named by Zhāng Zhuó.
The *Tángshū* states:
Zhāng Zhuó, styled Wénchéng,
was exceptionally intelligent and alert,
and there was no book he had not read.
As a child,
he dreamed of a large purple bird,
with patterns of five colors,
descending into his family courtyard.
His grandfather said to him:
"Five colors with red patterns
signify a phoenix.
Purple patterns
signify a yuèzhuó,
an assistant to the phoenix.
My child, you will bring literary auspiciousness to the imperial court."
Thus, he was given this name.
As an auspicious sign, it once brought honor to Liú Mùzhī.
The *Yìyuàn* states:
Liú Mùzhī,
styled Dàomín,
originally lived in Jīngkǒu.
A phoenix alighted in his courtyard,
and the physiognomist Wéi Sǒu said:
"You will certainly assist in great plans."
Again, there is the one moved by Táng Yáo and bearing the chart.
The *Héchéngtú* states:
Yáo sat in a boat,
with Grand Commandant Shùn observing the phoenix bearing the chart.
He received the diagram from Yáo,
using red jade for the case,
a golden clasp,
and a white jade cord.
Its inscription read, "Heaven's Mandate, the Imperial Seal," five characters in total.
He served as calendar official for Shàohào.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Tánzǐ replied to Confucius:
"When my ancestor Shàohào ascended the throne,
the phoenix happened to arrive.
Therefore, he established bird officials and gave them bird names.
The phoenix
was the official in charge of the calendar."
It sang on that high ridge.
The Shī says:
"The phoenix sings,
on that high ridge.
The paulownia grows,
facing the morning sun."
It ate the bamboo seeds.
The Hánshī Wàizhuàn states:
"During Huángdì's time,
a phoenix alighted in the emperor's eastern garden,
perched on a paulownia tree,
and ate bamboo seeds."
Sometimes there were five chicks or ten offspring.
The Yìlín states:
"The phoenix had ten offspring,
sharing the same nest and mother."
It also says:
"The phoenix gave birth to five chicks,
raised in the southern suburb.
The nobleman enjoyed peace and prosperity,
joyful and honored."
Sometimes it had three patterns and five colors.
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"Huángdì was seated at Xuánhù,
when a great bird appeared,
its shape resembling a crane,
its body adorned with five colors and three patterns.
The pattern on its head read 'Compliance and Virtue,'
on its back 'Trust and Righteousness,'
on its breast 'Benevolence and Wisdom.'
It was indeed a phoenix."
It descended upon Chánglè and alighted at Shànglín.
The Hànshū states:
"In the third year of the Wǔfèng era,
phoenixes gathered at Chánglè Palace,
lingering for over ten ke,
then gathered again at Shànglín."
It surveyed the Nine Provinces and observed the Eight Extremities.
Tiānlǎo's reply to Huángdì states:
"The phoenix can investigate all things,
penetrate heaven and earth,
harmonize the five notes,
survey the Nine Provinces,
and observe the Eight Extremities."
Sometimes it soared high over the wilderness of Dàhuáng.
The Chǔcí states:
"Have you not seen the phoenix soaring high over the wilderness of Dàhuáng,
circling the four extremities,
descending only upon witnessing great virtue?"
Sometimes it was heard of in the Land of Gentlemen.
The Shuōwén states:
"The phoenix is a divine bird."
Tiānlǎo said:
"It emerges from the Land of Gentlemen in the east."
Again, it nested at the pavilion's eaves.
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
"During Huángdì's time,
the heavenly qi flowed harmoniously,
the Five Phases transformed in their seasons,
and phoenixes nested at the pavilion's eaves."
It alighted in the eastern garden;
see the note above on 'gazing at Xuánhù.'
Sometimes a hall was built because of it.
The Hànshū states:
"During Yuándì's time,
phoenixes gathered at Shànglín,
so he built the Phoenix Hall."
Sometimes the reign title was changed because of it.
The Hànshū states:
"During Yuándì's time,
phoenixes gathered five times,
so he changed the reign title to Wǔfèng (Five Phoenixes)."
It was depicted in paintings within the palace.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"Guāngwǔ was born in Jìyáng.
Previously, phoenixes had gathered in Jìyáng,
so phoenixes were painted throughout the palace."
Further, bronze phoenixes were cast before the hall.
The Wèilüè states:
"When Wéndì wished to receive the abdication,
the commanderies and kingdoms reported thirteen sightings of phoenixes.
Míngdì cast bronze phoenixes,
over five zhang in size,
and placed them before the hall."
There were also those that drank from the rapids at Dǐzhù.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"When the phoenix soars,
it is the ultimate virtue.
It passes by the sparse gardens of Kūnlún,
the rapids at Dǐzhù."
It washed its feathers in the Ruòshuǐ.
The Shuōwén states:
"Tiānlǎo said:
'The phoenix displays all five colors,
soars beyond the Four Seas,
passes Kūnlún,
drinks at Dǐzhù,
washes its feathers in Ruòshuǐ,
rests at night in the Wind Cave,
and when it appears, the world is at peace.'"
Sometimes it came because of aversion to killing.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn states:
"Shùn cherished life and abhorred killing,
so phoenixes nested in his trees."
Sometimes it alighted because of a love for culture.
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"When the ruler loves culture, the phoenix soars."
Sometimes glue was boiled to mend bowstrings.
The Shízhōu Jì states:
"Fènglínzhōu lies in the midst of the Western Sea,
surrounded on all sides by Ruòshuǐ,
where not even a goose feather can float, making it impassable.
It abounds with phoenixes and qílín,
gathering in flocks of tens of thousands.
Immortals boil phoenix beaks and qílín horns,
combining them to make a glue,
called 'mending-string glue,'
or 'gold-joining paste.'
It can mend broken bowstrings
and rejoin severed blades of swords."
Sometimes its feathers could save one from death.
The Shíyí Jì states:
"King Zhāo of Zhōu made two robes from blue phoenix feathers,
one called 'Warm Substance,'
the other 'Comforting Skin.'
When King Lì was exiled to Zhì,
people obtained them.
Those facing capital punishment
could redeem themselves with blue phoenix feathers,
a single feather being worth a thousand gold."
Wáng Cí deftly responded regarding the comparison to a chicken.
The Sòngshū states:
"Wáng Sēngqián's son, Cí,
studied calligraphy in his youth with his cousin, Jiǎn.
Xiè Fèng's son, Chāozōng, once visited Sēngqián
and went to the eastern study to see Cí,
who was practicing calligraphy.
Chāozōng asked:
'How does your calligraphy compare to your father's?'
Cí replied:
'My calligraphy compared to my father's
is like a chicken compared to a phoenix.'"
Chéngtiān dispelled ridicule with the phrase "leading nine chicks."
The Sòngshū states:
"Hé Chéngtiān served as Assistant Editor.
He was already old,
while the other assistants were all young men from famous families.
Xún Bózǐ of Yǐngchuān ridiculed him,
often calling him 'wet nurse.'
Chéngtiān retorted:
'You should say the phoenix leads nine chicks;
what does the wet nurse have to say?'"
Chāozōng was praised for possessing "phoenix feathers."
The Sòngshū states:
"Xiè Fèng's son, Chāozōng, was gifted in writing.
He was appointed as Attendant to the Prince of Xīn'ān
and composed the 'Lament for the Royal Consort Yīn Shūyí.'
The emperor greatly admired it,
saying to Xiè Zhuāng:
'Chāozōng truly possesses phoenix feathers.'
At the time, General of the Right Guard Liú Dàolóng was present at the imperial seat.
He went to see Chāozōng and said:
'I heard you possess a rare object;
may I see it?'
Chāozōng replied:
'In a house as empty as a hanging chime,
how could there be any rare object?'
Dàolóng, being a military man,
was uncultured
and inadvertently touched upon his father's name, saying:
'Just now, during the banquet,
His Majesty said you have phoenix feathers.'
Chāozōng fled barefoot back inside.
Dàolóng thought he had gone to fetch the feathers
and waited until dusk,
but when Chāozōng did not return, he left."
Jiāngxià was also skilled at learning the "phoenix-tail" signature.
The Qíshū states:
"Prince Fēng of Jiāngxià,
at the age of five,
was upright and disciplined,
and fond of studying calligraphy.
Emperor Gāo had him learn the 'phoenix-tail' signature."
He mastered it upon first study,
and Emperor Gāo was greatly pleased,
bestowing upon him a jade qílín,
saying:
"I reward the phoenix's tail with a qílín."
Observing its upholding of virtue and righteousness,
its adherence to justice and benevolence,
consulting Tiānlǎo to understand its form,
see also the annotation above on "gazing at the yellow sash."
It brings auspiciousness to Emperor Shùn and heralds the dawn.
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
Emperor Shùn said:
"I am not skilled in the affairs of the hundred beasts and the phoenix at dawn."
The annotation says:
The hundred beasts dance in unison,
and the phoenix heralds the dawn.
How could it then compete for grain with chickens and ducks?
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
If the luán and phoenix compete for grain in the courtyard,
they will be humiliated by ducks and chickens.
Could it mingle with wild geese and ducks?
The Chǔcí states:
Wild geese and ducks all peck at millet and algae,
while the phoenix soars high and flies away.
As for its cry resembling flutes and pipes,
the Dìwáng Shìjì states:
During the time of Huángdì,
the phoenix nested in the pavilion,
and when it ate and drank,
it would always sing and dance,
its sound like flutes and pipes.
Its sound is akin to metal drums,
the Tiānlǎo Duì Huángdì states:
The phoenix's small sound is like metal drums.
It relies on the long wind to lift its wings,
the Tángshū states:
Emperor Tàizōng once reflected on the hardships of founding the dynasty,
and the contributions of his ministers,
so he composed the "Wēifèng Fù" and bestowed it upon Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
saying:
"There is a majestic phoenix,
resting its wings in the morning sun.
It roams the purple mist at dawn,
and drinks the dark frost at dusk.
It relies on the long wind to lift its wings,
and soars high along the heavenly path."
It gathers on Xuānqiū and dances.
The Shānhǎijīng states:
On Xuānyuán Hill,
the luán sings by itself,
and the phoenix dances by itself.
Its feathers flutter,
the Shī states:
The phoenix flies,
its feathers fluttering.
Its cry is melodious,
the Zuǒzhuàn states:
A diviner of the Chén state married his daughter to Jìngzhòng,
and his wife divined, saying:
"Auspicious.
The phoenix flies,
its harmonious cry is melodious.
The descendants of Guī,
will be nurtured among the Jiāng."
Its morning cry heralds a prosperous age,
the Lúnyǔ Zhāi Shuāishèng states:
When the phoenix cries while flying, it is called 'guīxī';
when it cries while resting, it is called 'tífú';
when it cries at night, it is called 'shànzāi';
when it cries at dawn, it is called 'hèshì'.
When it gathers, it is called 'guīchāng'.
The Tiānlǎo Duì Huángdì states:
When the phoenix cries at dusk, it is called 'gùcháng';
when it cries at dawn, it is called 'fāguāng';
when it cries during the day, it is called 'bǎozhāng';
when it cries while soaring, it is called 'tǔxiáng';
when it cries while gathering, it is called 'guīchāng'.
When the planet Zhènxīng moves in its proper order, it will surely arrive,
the Yuèdòng Shēngyí states:
If Zhènxīng does not move retrograde, the phoenix will arrive.
When the celestial pivot is in place, it descends and soars.
The Yùndǒu Shū states:
When the celestial pivot is in place,
the phoenix soars.
It emerges from Dānxué with abundant virtue,
the Shānhǎijīng states:
On Dānxué Mountain, there is a bird,
with five colors and patterns,
named the phoenix.
The pattern on its head is called 'virtue',
the pattern on its wings is called 'obedience',
the pattern on its back is called 'righteousness',
the pattern on its breast is called 'benevolence',
the pattern on its belly is called 'faithfulness'.
It descends upon the purple court, and its virtue shines brightly.
Cài Yōng's Qíncāo states:
King Chéng of Zhōu's "Qín Gē" says:
"The phoenix soars in the purple court,
what virtue do I possess to move the spirits?"
It leads nine fledglings and arrives together,
the Èrshí Wěishì states:
In Yè, there was a phoenix leading nine fledglings,
west of the road outside Yánmíng Gate.
It joins the four auspicious creatures in manifesting good fortune.
The Lǐyùn states:
The four auspicious creatures are kept as domestic animals.
What are the four auspicious creatures?
The qílín, phoenix, turtle, and dragon are called the four auspicious creatures.
Some carve its likeness in wood,
and place edicts in its mouth;
the Yèzhōng Jì states:
Shí Jìlóng and the empress were on the tower,
placing a five-colored paper edict in the phoenix's mouth,
and attendants lowered it with a hundred-zhàng crimson rope and a pulley.
Some make its image in gold,
and cast it from a tower into the Zhāng River.
The Yèzhōng Jì states:
Fèngyáng Gate had a five-story tower,
with two golden phoenixes installed.
When Shí Hǔ's reign declined,
one flew into the Zhāng River,
and on clear days, it could be seen in the water.
The other had its feet nailed with iron,
and it remains to this day.
Crane
The crane is the patriarch among feathered creatures,
as stated in the Huáinán Bāgōng's Classic of Crane Physiognomy:
The crane,
patriarch among feathered creatures,
is the qílín steed of immortals.
It is a transcendent bird born through transformation.
Bào Zhào's "Rhapsody on the Dancing Crane" says:
Scattering the arcane classics to examine things,
there is a transcendent bird born through transformation.
It roams afar alongside the luán and phoenix.
The Classic of Crane Physiognomy says:
The crane, at sixteen hundred years old,
drinks but does not eat,
and flocks together with the luán and phoenix.
It soars close to the Milky Way, flying high alongside them.
The Classic of Crane Physiognomy says:
In its second year, the crane sheds its down feathers,
and its black spots change;
in its third year, it produces and broods again;
in its fifth year, its wings and feathers are fully restored;
in its seventh year, it flies close to the Milky Way.
It receives its essence from metal and fire,
and also imbibes the vital breath of yáng and yīn.
The Classic of Crane Physiognomy says:
The crane
is a yáng bird,
yet it roams in the realm of yīn,
relying on the energy of metal and the essence of fire to nourish itself.
As for raising its rounded throat,
and lifting its slender toes,
The Classic of Crane Physiognomy says:
Tall legs with thick joints,
broad thighs and slender toes,
are the marks of a well-formed crane.
It stirs the mournful melody of Shānglíng,
see the annotation "Shānglíng's Parting Crane" in the "Rhapsody on the Zither."
It dances to the pure zhǐ mode of Jìn Píng.
See the annotation "Shī Kuàng's Pure Jué" in the "Rhapsody on the Zither."
Also called the pure zhǐ.
Its soaring and gathering was already heard of in the case of Jiè Xiàng.
The Biographies of Immortals says:
After Jiè Xiàng died,
Emperor Dàdì of Wú missed him,
and made the house where Xiàng had lived into a temple,
often going there to offer sacrifices.
A white crane would come and alight on the mat.
Its power to summon was also transmitted in the story of Xiāo Shǐ.
The Biographies of Arrayed Immortals says:
Xiāo Shǐ excelled at playing the panpipes,
and could attract white cranes.
It was the mourning guest at Táo Kǎn's grave mound,
The Separate Biography of Táo Kǎn says:
While Táo Kǎn was observing mourning for his mother,
at the gravesite,
suddenly two guests came to offer condolences.
They did not weep but withdrew,
their appearance and demeanor strikingly unusual.
Knowing they were no ordinary men,
he sent someone to look,
and saw only a pair of cranes soaring into the sky and departing.
It was the gentleman in Zhōu Mù's army.
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity says:
When King Mù of Zhōu campaigned south,
his entire army transformed:
the gentlemen became apes and cranes,
the petty men became insects and sand.
As for alighting on Lányán and looking back while pacing,
Wáng Sháozhī's Records of Divine Realms says:
Over a hundred lǐ south of Xíngyáng Commandery is Lányán,
where a pair of cranes was often seen,
with pure white feathers, gleaming brightly,
flying and gathering together, their shadows paired day and night.
Tradition says
that in the past, a husband and wife both lived in seclusion here,
reaching an age of several hundred years,
and transformed into these cranes.
It pauses at the Golden Grotto and wheels in flight.
The Inner Biography of Máo Jūn says:
Máo Yíng stayed at Jūqū Mountain,
and told his two younger brothers:
"I have official duties,
and cannot come and go frequently."
The elders sang:
"Máoshān connects to Jīnlíng,
the rivers and lakes lie downstream.
The three divinities ride white cranes,
each atop a mountain peak.
The white crane soars to the Golden Grotto,
when will it come roaming again?"
How could it again fear the nets of quails and wrens?
The Separate Biography of Bǐng Yuán says:
Lord Bǐng is what is called a white crane amidst the clouds,
not something the nets of quails and wrens can ensnare.
Truly, it knows the roundness and squareness of heaven and earth.
The Lí Sāo says:
With one ascent of the yellow crane,
it knows the winding course of mountains and rivers;
with a second ascent,
it knows the roundness and squareness of heaven and earth.
There is also the offering of drink from Jùsōu,
The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu says:
When he reached the people of Jùsōu,
the people of Jùsōu offered the blood of a white crane
for the Son of Heaven to drink.
And the enjoyment of the dance at Kūnlún.
The Charts of Auspicious Responses says:
The Yellow Emperor assembled at Kūnlún to make the multitude of spirits dance,
and two times eight dark cranes soared to his right.
Tián Ráo compared himself to it and left Lǔ.
The Outer Commentary to the Book of Songs by Hán Yīng says:
Tián Ráo served Duke Āi of Lǔ but was not recognized.
He said to Duke Āi:
"The rooster possesses five virtues,
yet you, my lord, still boil and eat it,
because it comes from nearby.
It is not like the yellow crane,
which with one ascent travels a thousand lǐ.
If it alighted in your garden pond,
pecked at your rice and grain,
you, my lord, would still value it,
because it comes from afar.
I am about to leave you, my lord;
the yellow crane ascends."
Zhuāng Xīn used it as a metaphor to persuade Chǔ.
The Strategies of the Warring States says:
Zhuāng Xīn said to King Xiāng of Chǔ:
"The yellow crane is born by the rivers and seas,
pecking down at catfish and carp,
snapping up water caltrops and lotus roots from above,
thinking itself free from trouble,
unaware that the archers are just then preparing their bows and arrows,
making their silk-attached arrows,
to bring it down from ten thousand rèn above.
Thus it roams the rivers and lakes by day,
but by evening is seasoned in the tripod and chopping block."
From the northwest it comes from afar to gather,
as an ancient song lyric says:
Flying comes the white crane,
from the northwest direction.
In tens and fives,
they array themselves in rows.
My wife suddenly fell ill,
and could not follow along.
At five lǐ I turned back to look,
at six lǐ I paced in hesitation.
I wish to carry you in my beak,
but my mouth is locked and cannot open.
I wish to bear you on my back,
but my feathers daily crumble and decay.
It soars afar over rivers and seas,
see the annotation above for "Zhuāng Xīn persuades Chǔ."
It takes leave of the Wú market with its clamor,
The Annals of Wú and Yuè says:
King Héliǘ of Wú was eating steamed fish with his wife and daughter.
The king once gave half of his portion to his daughter.
The daughter complained, saying:
"The king feeds me leftover fish and humiliates me;
I cannot bear to live long,"
and then killed herself.
Héliǘ grieved for her,
and buried her west of the capital,
sending her off with treasures of gold tripods, jade cups, silver goblets, and pearl-embroidered jackets.
He had white cranes dance in the market of Wú,
ordering the myriad people to follow and watch,
then had them enter the tomb passage together with the cranes,
and blocked it up to send off the dead.
It emerges from the Thunder Gate and soars aloft.
See the annotation "Cranes fly from Thunder Gate" in the "Rhapsody on Drums."
There is the drinking at the house of the Mèng clan by King Zhōu,
The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu says:
The Son of Heaven drank at the house of the Mèng clan,
and received a dance by two times eight white cranes.
And the altar of the Hàn emperor at Dàizōng.
The Records of the Eastern Lodge of Hàn says:
When Emperor Zhāng reached Dàizōng, after the burnt offering and the gaze,
thirty white cranes came from the southwest,
passing over the sacrificial altar.
At Gōushān, one recognizes the arrival of Wáng Qiáo,
see the annotation "See Wáng Qiáo at Gōushì" in the "Rhapsody on Mountains."
In Liáodōng, one sees the return of Dīng Lìng.
The Continued Records of Searching for the Divine says:
On the ornamental pillar at the gate of Liáodōng city, a white crane suddenly came and alighted.
Someone wanted to shoot it,
but the crane sang in the air:
"There is a bird, there is a bird, Dīng Lìngwēi,
left home a thousand years ago, now returns.
The city walls are as of old, but the people are not;
why not learn the way of immortality, amidst the累累 mounds of graves?"
Furthermore, its cry surely warns of dew,
see the annotation "The night watch hears the white crane" in the "Rhapsody on Dew."
Its whiteness is not from daily bathing.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
The crane does not bathe daily yet is white;
the crow is not blackened daily yet is black.
Sometimes it is ridden at the tower of Jiāngxià,
The Records of the Strange says:
Xún Huán, styled Shūwěi,
lived in seclusion and abstained from grains.
Once while traveling east,
he rested at the Yellow Crane Tower in Jiāngxià.
Gazing southwest, something drifted down from the heavens,
arriving in a moment—
it was a guest riding a crane.
The crane halted beside the door,
and the immortal took his seat.
Clad in feathered robes and rainbow garments,
host and guest conversed joyfully.
After a while, he bid farewell,
mounted the crane, and soared into the sky,
vanishing into the mist.
Some fed them with the millet of Tángāo.
The Shíyí Jì states:
During the reign of King Zhāo of Zhōu,
the state of Túxiū presented a green phoenix and a red crane,
each a male and a female.
They were fed with the millet of Tángāo
and given water from the Róngxī to drink.
Observing their slender heads and exposed eyes,
the Xiàng Hè Jīng states:
The finest features of a crane
are a slender head and a vermilion crown,
with exposed eyes and black pupils.
Abundant feathers and sparse flesh,
the Xiàng Hè Jīng states:
Cranes soar among the clouds,
hence their feathers are abundant and their flesh sparse.
They possess the wings of a phoenix and the back of a turtle,
as well as the breast of a swallow and the belly of a softshell turtle.
From the Xiàng Hè Jīng.
King Xuān was admonished by the sound reaching the heavens.
The Shī states:
"The Crane Calls,"
admonishing King Xuān.
"The crane calls in the nine marshes,
its voice is heard in heaven."
Wáng Mǎng sought immortality by soaking grain in crane marrow.
The Hànshū states:
Wáng Mǎng soaked grain seeds in crane marrow to learn immortality.
As for comparing the crane's leg to the duck's as longer,
the Zhuāngzǐ states:
"The duck's leg is short,
but to lengthen it would cause distress;
the crane's leg is long,
but to shorten it would bring sorrow."
They cannot be confused with a flock of chickens.
The Jìnshū states:
When Jī Shào first entered Luòyáng,
someone said to Wáng Róng:
"Yesterday among the crowd, I saw Jī Shào for the first time—
towering and noble, like a wild crane among chickens."
Wáng Róng replied:
"You have yet to see his father."
The rhapsody extols the beauty described by Bào Zhāo,
who wrote the "Rhapsody on the Dancing Crane."
Poetry spreads the virtue of Qí Gāodì.
The Sòngshū states:
When Qí Gāodì was stationed in Huáiyīn,
he was suspected by Emperor Míng of Sòng,
summoned to serve as a court official,
and deeply troubled.
Seeing a flock of cranes on the open marsh,
he took up his brush and chanted:
"Dancing on the eight winds with strong wings,
sporting clear calls across the nine wilds.
Once their cloud-soaring ambition is crushed,
they become captive birds in your garden."
Yáng Gōng was astonished that it did not dance.
The Shìshuō states:
Yīn Zhōngjūn once praised Liú Zūnzǔ before Yǔ Gōng,
who was very pleased
and appointed him as an assistant.
When introduced,
Liú sat alone on a couch and spoke with him.
That day, Liú performed far below expectations,
leaving Yǔ somewhat disappointed,
so he nicknamed him "Yáng Gōng's Crane."
Long ago, Yáng Shūzǐ had a crane that could dance,
and he often praised it to guests.
When guests arrived,
he tried to have it driven out,
but it merely fluffed its feathers and could not dance.
Yǔ Yù was once startled by a sudden sighting.
The Liángshū states:
Yǔ Yù's mother loved the cry of cranes,
so Yǔ, while in office, sought them diligently,
never tiring in his efforts,
until one day a pair of cranes descended.
Crying in the nine marshes with a clear, distant call,
see above.
Departing from Huátíng with graceful elegance.
The Bā Wáng Gùshì states:
When Lù Jī was executed by Prince Chéngdū,
he looked around and sighed:
"Now, to hear the crane's cry at Huátíng
is something I can never experience again."
Traveling in Wèi and riding in a carriage.
The Zuǒzhuàn states: When the Dí people attacked Wèi,
Duke Yì loved cranes,
and some cranes even rode in carriages.
As battle approached,
the men of the state who received armor all said:
"Send the cranes!
The cranes truly hold rank and salary—
how can we fight?"
Heading toward Yēxī to retrieve an arrow.
The Kuàijī Jì states:
South of Shèdì Mountain lies Báihè Shān,
