where this crane fetched arrows for an immortal.
Zhèng Hóng, Grand Commandant of Hàn, once gathered firewood
and found an arrow.
Soon after, a deity arrived
and asked what he desired.
Zhèng Hóng replied:
"I have often struggled to transport firewood along the Ruòyēxī—
I wish for a south wind in the morning
and a north wind in the evening."
Later, this indeed came to pass.
Truly, with one flight, it travels a thousand miles—
how could it be a mere plaything for the senses?
The Shìshuō states:
Monk Zhī Dàolín loved cranes.
Once, someone gifted him a pair of cranes,
but their wings grew long, and they wished to fly.
Dàolín, reluctant to part with them,
clipped their flight feathers.
The cranes tried to soar but could no longer rise,
so they spread their wings and looked back,
appearing as if filled with regret.
Dàolín said:
"Since they possess the grace to reach the clouds,
why would they consent to be mere playthings for human senses?"
He nurtured them until their feathers regrew,
then set them free to fly away.
Eagle
The fierce bird of Zhōngshān,
according to Suí Wèi Yànshēn's "Ode to the Hawk," says:
This bird's transformation and nurturing,
indeed originates from Zhōngshān.
It draws upon the fierce energy of the metal direction,
and excels in the fiery essence of the fire virtue.
It receives the vigorous energy of the metal direction,
contains the bright radiance of the fire virtue,
see the annotation above.
It embodies the purity of Yáoguāng.
The "Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū" says:
The Yáoguāng star disperses to become hawks.
Some are heard to become green after a thousand days,
Suí Wèi Yànshēn's "Ode to the Hawk" says:
After two weeks, they become sparrowhawks,
after a thousand days, they become green.
Some value their talons as heavy as a cross.
Wèi Yànshēn's "Ode to the Hawk" says:
Talons heavy as a cross,
tail valued like a Hélú.
As for the appearance of speckled blood and scattered flowers,
Wèi Yànshēn's ode says:
White like scattered flowers,
red like speckled blood,
large patterns like brocade,
fine spots like tie-dye.
Names like "grass eyes" and "golden spurs,"
the "Xījīng Zájì" says:
Lǐ Tíng, a young man from Màolíng, loved racing and chasing,
hawks and sparrowhawks,
all had fine names.
Hawks had types like "green wings," "grass eyes," "green abyss," "golden spurs," and so on.
Already in the south, they become sparrowhawks,
the "Jìnshū" says:
Cuī Hóng was pure, stern, and upright,
serving as the Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
people of the time said of him:
"Thorns and brambles grow,
come from Bólíng.
In the south, they are sparrowhawks,
in the north, they are hawks."
Also considered brothers with sparrowhawks.
The "Ancient Music Bureau Poems" say:
The leopard is the tiger's younger brother,
the hawk is the sparrowhawk's elder brother.
There are also those that strike from the glove and hit the mark,
the "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
Zhào Qín, styled Mèngqīng,
Prefect Huán Yú appointed him as the Inspector,
whereupon corrupt officials reprimanded themselves,
returned their seals and ribbons, and left.
Yú sighed and said:
"A good official is like using a fine hawk,
it strikes from the glove and hits the mark."
Painted on a wall as if real.
The "Chénshū" says:
Qí Guǎngníng King Cún Héng enjoyed composing literature,
and had artistic skills.
Once, he painted a green hawk on the wall of the main hall himself,
those who saw it all thought it was real.
Aiding Wáng Sēngdá in hunting,
the "Nánshǐ" says:
Wáng Sēngdá had a fondness for hawks and hounds,
Hé Shàngzhī retired from office,
once entered the fasting chamber,
gathered many court officials,
personally performed the incense offering,
then went to Sēngdá,
and said:
"I hope, sir, you will release your hawks and hounds,
and no longer go hunting."
Teaching Xíngfǔ how to serve his lord.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
Jì Wénzǐ replied to Duke Xuān, saying:
"The late senior official Zāng Wénzhòng taught Xíngfǔ the rites of serving a lord,
Xíngfǔ upheld them in all his dealings,
not daring to neglect or lose them.
He said, when seeing someone who treats his lord with propriety,
serve him like a filial son caring for his parents;
when seeing someone who treats his lord without propriety,
punish him like a hawk or sparrowhawk chasing small birds."
In the Táng, they cut the tethers and released them,
the "Tángshū" says:
When Tàizōng first ascended the throne,
in the old imperial park, there were caged hawks,
he cut all their tethers and let them go,
and fine hounds were also unleashed and released.
In the Hàn, they were sold off and not used.
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
When Héxī Empress Dowager presided over the court,
all the hawks and hounds of the Shanglin Park were sold off.
Chasing a yellow hound out the eastern gate,
the "Shǐjì" says:
Lǐ Sī, facing execution, sighed and said:
"I long to lead a yellow hound, arm a green hawk,
and go out the eastern gate of Shàngcài,
but it is no longer possible."
Striking a young roc in Yúnmèng.
The "Yōumíng Lù" says:
King Wén of Chǔ loved hunting,
someone presented him with a hawk,
they hunted in Yúnmèng,
smoke and flames filled the sky,
furred and feathered creatures fought and struggled.
This hawk stared into the clouds,
with no intention to fight or seize.
The king said to the presenter:
"Are you trying to deceive me?"
He replied:
"If it were only effective against pheasants and hares,
how would I dare present it?"
Soon, there was something in the clouds,
hovering, bright and white,
its form indistinguishable.
The hawk then raised its wings and soared,
in a moment, feathers fell like snow,
blood rained down,
and a great bird fell to the ground.
Measuring its two wings spanned tens of lǐ,
none could recognize it.
A learned gentleman said:
"This is a young great roc."
Then he richly rewarded him.
As for Liáng Jì, greedy and demanding,
the "Yìdū Qíjiù Zhuàn" says:
Féng Hào of Guǎnghàn was an Attendant,
pursuing the Chányú to Yúnzhōng.
General-in-Chief Liáng Jì sent someone to request a hawk,
staying at the Jìnyáng lodge.
The person did not avoid Hào,
Hào arrested him,
and had someone strike the hawk, causing it to flee,
Hào pursued and captured it urgently,
Liáng Jì's plea then stopped it.
Dàliàng, loyal and not presenting it,
the "Tángshū" says:
Tàizōng said to his attending officials:
"Lǐ Dàliàng can be called loyal and upright,
I sent an envoy to his place,
seeing he had a fine hawk,
hinted for him to present it to me,
Dàliàng then secretly submitted a memorial reprimanding me, saying:
'Your Majesty has long ceased hunting,
yet the envoy seeks a hawk,
if this is Your Majesty's intention,
it deeply contradicts your former decree;
if he acted on his own,
then it is appointing the wrong envoy.'
I read the memorial and praised him,
unable to contain myself.
With such a minister,
what more do I worry about?"
Then he bestowed upon him a golden pot,
to commend his loyal and forthright speech.
Mǎ Róng praised its release from the cage,
Mǎ Róng's "Letter to Bó Shì" says:
Troubled and sorrowful thoughts,
still cannot dispel my cares.
Thinking of being among bamboo,
releasing hounds to chase deer.
Late autumn turning to winter,
the great green one emerges from the cage.
Yellow thorns beneath, rabbits,
mixed with dried vegetables.
To pass the remaining days,
this joy is endless.
Yāolí is also heard to strike the hall.
The "Zhànguócè" says:
Táng Jū said to the King of Qín:
"When Yāolí was about to assassinate Qìngjì,
a green hawk struck in the hall."
Thus its might equals Shàngfǔ,
the "Shī" says:
Ah, Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ,
at that time, like a hawk soaring.
Its name is passed down through Zhì Dū,
the "Hànshū" says:
Zhì Dū was the Governor of Jǐnán,
people of the time called him the "Green Hawk."
Emperor Wèi valued it for its autumn cry,
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Reply to Fán Qīn's Letter" says:
The autumn wind shakes the branches,
the Qín hawk cries in autumn.
Hóu Wén executed with severe frost.
See the annotation for "Hóu Wén's duty" in the "Ode to Autumn."
Zhī Dùn loved its divine vigor,
the "Jiànkāng Shílù" says:
Zhī Dùn enjoyed keeping hawks and horses but did not ride or release them,
someone asked him why,
he said:
"I love their divine vigor."
Yuán Tǎn indulged in hunting and fishing.
The "Sānguó Diǎnlüè" says:
Yuán Tǎn was the Governor of Jìzhōu,
he did not care for people's affairs,
his nature loved hunting and fishing,
not a day went by without going out,
hawks and hounds often numbered in the hundreds,
nets and traps over ten carts,
he himself said he would rather go three days without food,
Not a day passes without hunting.
As for not missing the transformation into a dove at the awakening of insects,
The Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances says:
On the day of the awakening of insects,
hawks transform into doves.
At the end of heat, there is no deviation in sacrificing birds.
The Book of Zhou says:
On the day of the end of heat,
hawks sacrifice birds.
Pursuing the unrighteous, Zǐchǎn
The Zuo Commentary says:
Zǐchǎn first knew Rán Míng,
and asked about governance.
He replied:
"Treat the people as your children;
when you see the unrighteous, punish them,
like hawks and falcons pursuing small birds."
The one named Shuǎng Jiū is Shàohào.
The Zuo Commentary says:
Shàohào was the master of birds and named them.
Shuǎng Jiū,
was the minister of justice.
Note:
A hawk.
Also, if the wings are short, flight is swift;
if the legs are long, takeoff is slow.
Wèi Yànshēn's rhapsody says:
Those with long legs take off slowly,
those with short wings fly swiftly.
Females are large, males small.
Yànshēn's rhapsody says:
Females have large bodies,
males have small forms.
Add feathers, reduce flesh.
Yànshēn's rhapsody says:
By day, they never leave the hand;
by night, they stay by the fire.
Slightly increase their feathers,
slightly reduce their flesh.
The seasonal ordinance is passed down for learning.
The Book of Rites says:
At minor heat, hawks learn to fly.
The Erya also calls them "flying huī."
The Erya says:
Hawks and falcons,
their flight is huī.
Note:
Flapping wings swiftly, huī-huī.
Also heard to dislike those with yellow feet,
Yànshēn's rhapsody says:
Red eyes, yellow feet,
slender bones, small elbows,
cannot be called to stay,
cannot be raised to run.
Such as these,
better not to have.
Wanting them to eat swiftly,
Yànshēn's rhapsody says:
Swift eating, quick digestion,
this is fate.
Rabbit neck, monkey stance,
this is without illness.
Nets are set after transformation.
The Book of Rites: Monthly Ordinances says:
In the seventh month, doves transform into hawks,
then set nets.
Arrow traps are forbidden before striking.
The Book of Han says:
Before hawks and falcons strike,
arrow traps are not set on paths.
Hungry, they are useful;
suspicion and defense are seen in Lord Cáo.
The Records of Wei says:
Lǚ Bù sent Chén Dēng to see the Grand Ancestor,
Dēng thus described Bù as brave but without strategy,
and that he should be dealt with early.
The Grand Ancestor was pleased.
Bù initially sent Dēng to seek the governorship of Xúzhōu,
but did not obtain it.
When Dēng returned,
Bù drew a halberd and struck the table, blaming him.
Dēng said:
"I saw Lord Cáo and said:
'Treating the general is like raising a tiger;
you must feed it meat,
otherwise it will bite people.'
Lord Cáo said:
'Not so.
It is like raising a hawk:
hungry, it is useful;
full, it flies away.'"
Bù then understood.
Full, it soars high;
the analogy is also heard from Quán Yì.
The Book of Jin: Records says:
Mùróng Chuí requested to go to Yè to visit his ancestors' tombs,
Fú Jiān permitted it.
Quán Yì advised:
"Chuí is like a hawk:
hungry, it clings to people;
full, it soars high.
If it encounters a stormy meeting,
it will surely have aspirations to reach the clouds.
Only by tightening its tether
can its desires not be indulged."
Jiān did not listen,
and when he left, he indeed did not return.
The colorful essence of the chicken,
the Ěryǎ says:
chicken,
the large ones are called Shǔ,
the Shǔ chicks,
those not yet fully grown are called Liàn,
the exceptionally strong ones,
are called Fèn.
Pronounced Nài.
Its essence descends into the stars of the Jade Balance.
The Yùndǒushū says:
the Jade Balance stars scatter to become chickens.
It takes the image of Xùn.
The Yì says:
Xùn represents the chicken.
Note:
It means the chicken knows the time and gives the signal.
It receives the essence of fire.
The Chūnqiū Shuōtící says:
the chicken is accumulated yang,
the image of the southern direction,
therefore when yang emerges the chicken crows,
responding through resonance.
Its resounding voice is seen in its title.
The Lǐ says:
the chicken in the ancestral temple is called Hànyīn.
Candle of the night is its name.
The Gǔjīn Zhù says:
the chicken is also named Zhúyè.
Bīng Mèng already observed the severed tail,
the Zuǒzhuàn says:
Bīng Mèng went to the suburbs,
saw a rooster severing its own tail,
and asked about it.
The attendant said:
"It fears being used as a sacrifice."
Zhōu Chuò also imitated its crowing first.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Duke Zhuāng of Qí held court,
pointed at Zhí Chuò and Guō Zuì and said:
"These are my champions."
Zhōu Chuò said:
"If my lord considers them champions,
who dares not be a champion?
However, your servant is not clever,
but in the battle of Píngyīn,
I crowed before these two men."
Note:
Jìn attacked Qí,
reached Píngyīn,
Zhōu Chuò captured Zhí Chuò and Guō Zuì,
thus comparing himself to a rooster winning a fight by crowing first.
Some use it to predict signs of war horses,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
if a rooster crows at night,
the army moves and war horses are startled.
Some mistake it for the sound of flies.
The Shī says:
"The Cock Crows",
is about longing for a virtuous consort.
The cock has already crowed,
the court is already full,
it is not the cock that crows,
but the sound of flies.
As for those with five toes and golden shanks,
the Guǎngzhì says:
chickens have breeds like Húgōu, Wǔzhǐ, Jīnqiāo, and Fǎnqiào.
Flower crests catching dew,
the Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn says:
Nánjùn presented a long-crowing dew-catching chicken.
The Nányuè Zhì says:
the chicken's comb opens in four parts like a lotus flower,
its clear crowing sound is penetrating.
Jì Píng already boasted of mustard-sprinkled feathers,
the Hòu clan also bragged of their metal spurs.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
the chickens of the Jì and Hòu clans fought,
the Jì clan sprinkled mustard on their chicken,
the Hòu clan fitted theirs with metal spurs.
Some raise them to ward off fire,
the Shānhǎijīng says:
the Bìzhì, also called the mountain chicken, raising it wards off fire,

Some paint them and paste them on doors.

Mèng Cháng imitated it and gained escape,
the Shǐjì says:
Mèng Chángjūn reached the pass,
the pass law stated,
guests depart at cockcrow.
Among Mèng Chángjūn's guests was one from the lower ranks who could imitate a cockcrow,
and thus they issued the pass and departed.
Yān Dān did this and managed to cross.
the Yāndānzǐ says:
Crown Prince Dān of Yān was a hostage in Qín,
fled and reached the pass,
Dān imitated a cockcrow,
and thus managed to cross early.
As for those three chǐ tall called Kūn,
the Ěryǎ says:
a chicken three chǐ tall is called Kūn.
Kūn,
pronounced Kūn.
On New Year's Day, dismembered at the gate,
see the note on "hanging sheep and dismembering chickens" in the Chūn Fù.
Its nature is solely to oversee the night,
the Hánzǐ says:
make the chicken oversee the night,
order the cat to catch mice,
both use their abilities.
Its duty is to herald the dawn.
the Tàixuánjīng says:
the hen crows at dawn,
the rooster bends its neck.
Observing the celestial star to announce amnesty,
the Běiqí Shū says:
Wǔchéng ascended the throne at Nángōng,
granted a great amnesty.
Erected a golden chicken outside the palace gate,
not understanding its meaning,
he asked the Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments Sīmǎ Yīngzhī,
who replied:
"The sea star divination says:
when the Celestial Chicken star moves,
there should be an amnesty,
the emperor uses it as an omen."
Paired with the golden horse to become a spirit.
the Hànshū says:
the fāngshì said:
in Yìzhōu there is the spirit of the Golden Horse and Jade Chicken,
which can be summoned by sacrifice.
Emperor Xuān sent Wáng Bāo to go and sacrifice there.
Furthermore, there is the Yuèxī long-crower,
the Xījīng Zá Jì says:
during the reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Jiāozhǐ and Yuèxī presented a long-crowing chicken,
when placed under a water clock to test it,
not a moment was off.
One crow, one feeding,
long spurs, good at fighting.
Mǎhán fine-tailed,
the Wèi Zhì says:
Mǎhánguó produces fine-tailed chickens,
their tails are all over five chǐ long.
Zǐlù wore it to show courage,
the Shǐjì says:
Zǐlù's nature was crude,
fond of courage and strength,
wore a rooster crest,
carried a boar's tusk,
and bullied and insulted Confucius.
Confucius set up rituals and righteousness to gradually guide him,
Zǐlù then presented gifts and requested to become a disciple.
Huángfù wore it and devoured ghosts.
the Shényì Jīng says:
in the east there was a man,
seven zhàng tall,
wearing a chicken on his head,
in the morning devoured three thousand evil ghosts,
in the evening three hundred,
named Huángfù,
also named Shíxié,
using ghosts as food,
using dew as drink.
Zǔ Tì then danced upon hearing the night crow,
the Jìn Shū says:
Zǔ Tì and Liú Kūn were registrars in Sīzhōu,
shared a blanket and slept together.
In the middle of the night hearing a wild cock crow,
Tì kicked Kūn awake and said:
"Is this not a stirring sound?"
Then they rose and danced.
Yǔ Yì was angry at their love for pheasants.
the Jìn Shū says:
Yǔ Yì practiced calligraphy,
in his youth was equally famous with the Right General.
The Right General later advanced,
Yǔ still did not distinguish himself.
In Jīngzhōu he wrote to people in the capital:
"The youngsters,
despise the domestic chicken,
love the wild pheasant,
all study Yìshǎo's calligraphy,
when I come down,
I will compare with them."
To abandon it is a pity:
the land of Hànzhōng;
the Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū says:
the King of Wèi entered Hànzhōng to attack Liú Bèi,
could not advance,
wanted to defend but it was difficult,
intended to abandon it,
then issued an order saying:
"Chicken ribs."
The officials did not understand.
The Registrar Yáng Xiū said:
"Chicken ribs,
to abandon them is a pity,
to take them gains nothing,
using this to compare to Hànzhōng."
The king wished to depart. "
Then he ordered the army to be on alert,
and the king subsequently returned.
The reason they cannot be unified
is the situation in Shāndōng.
The *Strategies of the Warring States* states:
King Huì of Qín said to Hánquánzǐ:
"Sū Qín deceived our state,
wishing to use the wisdom of one man
to sway the rulers of Shāndōng back and forth.
That the feudal lords cannot be unified
is like tethered chickens that cannot all roost together."
Some eat them by the thousands.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
A good learner
is like the King of Qí eating chicken:
he eats several thousand of their feet before being satisfied.
Some serve them daily in pairs.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
The daily court meals include a pair of chickens.
Their crowing is as punctual as wind and rain.
The *Shī* says:
The wind and rain are dark as night,
yet the cock crows without cease.
Holding them must be the duty of artisans and merchants.
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
Artisans and merchants hold chickens.
The commentary explains:
This is because they keep time and act accordingly.
There is also the cockfight at Yánggōu.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
The cock of Yánggōu,
after three years becomes a champion.
Those who judge it
say it is not a good fighting cock,
yet it often defeats others
because wildcat fat is smeared on its head.
Commentary:
Yánggōu
is a place for cockfighting.
Zhū
means champion.
Chickens fear wildcat fat.
There is also the raising at Shīxiāng.
The *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
Zhùjīwēng
was a man from Luòyáng
who lived north of Shīxiāng mountain.
He raised chickens, each with a name,
over a thousand in total.
They roosted in trees at night,
and were let loose to feed during the day.
When he wanted to catch one,
he would call its name and it would come.
He sold chickens and their eggs,
earning millions in cash,
then would leave the money and depart.
Some crow in the clouds.
The *Shùyì Jì* states:
On Jìyáng mountain is the immortal place of Mágū.
Folklore says that when a thousand years pass on the mountain, a golden cock crows and a jade dog barks.
The *Lùnhéng* states:
Tradition says
that when Huáinánwáng ascended to immortality,
the crowing of cocks and barking of dogs
were all heard in the clouds.
Some are buried on mountains.
The *Yìyuàn* states:
Zhū Wénxiù and Luó Zǐzhōng were friends,
both serving in Liáng.
After Wénxiù died,
Zǐzhōng mourned him,
and that night both passed away.
Seven lǐ south of Liáng is Jīshān (Chicken Mountain),
where Wénxiù was buried.
Nine lǐ north is Zhìjiàn (Pheasant Stream),
where Zhōng was interred.
Wénxiù's spirit transformed into a chicken,
Zhōng's soul turned into a pheasant.
Their clear cries and mournful calls
passed back and forth without end.
Thus a poem says:
"From Chicken Mountain, a parting flight's cry,
with Pheasant Stream's clear notes harmonize."
Hear their fluttering sounds.
An ancient verse says:
Fluttering, bustling, the cock first crows;
scattered, strewn, the stars toward dawn.
Listen to their clucking.
The *Shī* says:
The wind and rain sough and sigh,
the cock crows cluck-cluck.
Abandoned, one turns to seek the phoenix's warning.

To abandon the dawn cock and await the phoenix's alert
is like abandoning the genuine talents of the present age,
awaiting an old acquaintance to hold power.
Why use an ox-cleaver for slaughtering a chicken?
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
When the Master went to Wǔchéng
and heard the sounds of strings and singing,
he smiled and said:
"Why use an ox-cleaver to slaughter a chicken?"
As for roosting in a tree within the palace hall,

Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī jointly managed crucial affairs.
Xiàhóu Xiàn and Cáo Zhào were inwardly discontent.
There was a chicken roosting in a tree in the palace hall.

"This has also been here a long time;
how much longer can it last?"
pointing at Zī and Fàng.
There is herding at Lóumén.

The ruins of Jībēi outside Lóumén
is where the king herded chickens.

Liú Bīn, governor of Píngyuán,

a bird with vermilion body,
feathers dark and yellow,
crowing without missing its hour.
This is a pheasant feather."
There is inquiry into the divination of Yuè witches.
The *Shǐjì* states:
Yuè witches established Yuè sacrifices
and used chicken divination.
The emperor believed in it.
Jiāng Yóu tethered them and set a fire.

Fù Yǎn cut one open to decide a lawsuit.

Fù Yǎn, styled Jìguī,
was magistrate of Shānyīn.
Two old villagers disputed over a chicken.

the other said beans.
Yǎn had the chicken cut open,
found millet,
and punished the one who said beans.
Observe Fèngxiān's cockfighting.

Formerly, Xǔ Fèngxiān loved cockfighting.

he made Fèngxiān's daughter a Jiéyú,

Fèngxiān was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Record the raising by the King of Yuè.
The *Yuèjué Shū* states:
Jīshān (Chicken Mountain)
was where Gōujiàn raised chickens,
intending to attack Wú,
to feed his death-defying warriors.
Tiānyuān Pool once delighted Lù Jī.

At Tiānyuān Pool, they raise pheasants,
which are quite amusing.

On Chéncāng mountain there is a stone chicken,

Some say it is a jade chicken.
On Chéncāng city wall is a divine chicken.

If one gets the male, he becomes king;

Duke Mù obtained the female,

Duke Wén of Qín obtained a stone-like object

Its spirit sometimes did not come for years,

Its sound rumbling,
then wild pheasants all crowed at night.
There are also long-crowing and far-flying ones.
Long-crowing: see the note above.

The far-flying chicken
returns at dusk to rely on people,
but at dawn flies far to the four seas,
going in the morning and returning at dusk.
Yellow crown, green tassels.

The fir chicken has a yellow crown and green tassels,

On its head are long yellow feathers like a crown,
its head and neck are a pure blue-green like hanging tassels.

Zǐlù encountered an old man,

killed a chicken and cooked millet to feed him.

it signifies the decline of the household.
There is also the case of the crown withering after being cut against the grain.
The *Jìn Shū* says:
After Huán Xuán was killed,
Emperor Ān was restored to the throne,
the remaining rebels who held forces and assumed false titles were all pacified,
and the Huán clan was thus exterminated.
During the Yuánxīng era,
in Héngyáng, a hen transformed into a rooster,

When Huán Xuán established his state in Chǔ,

From his usurpation to his defeat,

Then there is the one that only crowed upon reaching the northern dike.

Emperor Wǔ once visited Lángyé City,

In the seventh year,

established a county,
moved people from Fēng to populate it,

There is the legend of what Zhū Gōng transformed.

Calling chickens "Zhū Gōng,"

Lè Yángzǐ's wife,

Also, like keeping watch at night is called faithfulness,

having a crown on its head signifies civility,
having spurs on its feet signifies martial prowess,
daring to fight when an enemy is before it signifies courage,

And foretelling the tide shows its peculiarity.
The *Yìwù Jì* says:
The tide-watching chicken,
crows when the tide rises.

"The stone rooster's clear cry responds to the tide" refers to this.
Driving them is compared to governing the people.

Observing a child driving chickens,

if too hasty they become alarmed,
if too slow they become sluggish,
if gentle they become calm.
Dreaming of them also brings worry about military officials.
The *Mèng Shū* says:
The chicken represents military officials,

Dreaming of a rooster,
brings worry about military officials.
As for dancing upon seeing its reflection,

the south presented a pheasant.

Wéi Zhòngjiāng composed a rhapsody about this event.
And drowning while admiring its reflection in water.
The *Bówù Zhì* says:
The pheasant has beautiful feathers,
loves its own feathers,
admires its reflection in water all day,
becomes dizzy and drowns.
Fú Lǎng knew it was half-exposed.

Fú Lǎng was skilled at discerning flavors.
Prince Dàozǐ of Kuàijī killed a chicken to feed him,

Lǎng said:
"This chicken often roosted half-exposed."
Upon checking, it was verified.
Jì Shěng nurtured its complete virtue.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
Long ago, Jì Shěngzǐ raised fighting cocks for King Xuān of Zhōu,
after ten days he was asked:
"Is the cock ready to fight?"
He said:
"Not yet,
it is still vainly arrogant and relies on its spirit."
After ten more days he was asked again,
he said:
"Not yet,
it still glares fiercely and is full of spirit."
After ten more days he was asked again,
he said:
"Almost there,
even if other cocks crow,
it shows no change,
looking at it, it seems like a wooden cock.

Hántú was known for making them able to speak.

The country of Hántú is seventy thousand lǐ from the royal capital,
its people are skilled at taming birds and beasts,
they make chickens and dogs all able to speak.
Táodū is also known for heralding the sunrise.

In the southeast is Táodū Mountain,
on it is a great tree,
named Táodū,
its branches span three thousand lǐ.
On it is a heavenly rooster,
when the sun first rises,
shines upon this tree,
the heavenly rooster crows,

The right guǎng harnessed upon its crow.

The ruler of Chǔ had twenty chariots called guǎng,

Zǐ Fǎn then ate upon its crow.

Jìn and Chǔ fought from dawn,
until stars appeared without ceasing.
Zǐ Fǎn ordered officers to inspect the wounded,
replenish soldiers and chariots,
eat at cockcrow,
and be ready to obey orders.
Seen in the origins of events,
Cuī Guāng knew the meaning of many wings and feet;
The *Hòu Wèi Shū* says:
Cuī Guāng, styled Chángrén,
in the summer of the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
the clerk Shi Xiǎn presented a chicken with four feet and four wings,
an edict inquired of Guāng,

"Many wings and feet,
is an image of subordinates inciting each other.
The feet are rather small,
their influence is still slight,
easy to control."
Several days later,
Rú Hào and others were all executed for their crimes,
and thereafter Guāng was treated with even greater respect.
Placed by the window,
the Sòng clan gained benefit from conversation.
The *Yōumíng Lù* says:
Sòng Chùzōng, Governor of Yǎnzhōu during the Jìn, once bought a long-crowing rooster,

kept it in a cage placed by the window,

extremely eloquent,
ceaselessly all day.
Chùzōng's speaking skills greatly improved because of this.
Wild goose
Harmoniously honking wild geese,
soar in accordance with the seasons.
The Book of Songs says:
"Harmoniously honking wild geese,
as the rising sun begins to dawn."
The Eastern Sea offered songs to Emperor Wǔ of Hàn;
The Book of Hàn states:
In the third year of the Tàishǐ era of Emperor Wǔ,
a red wild goose was captured in the Eastern Sea,
and the "Song of the Red Wild Goose" was composed.
In Suīyáng, they were reared by King Liáng.
The Book of Hàn says:
King Xiào of Liáng built a pond for ducks and wild geese within his domain of Suīyáng.
To congratulate Duke Mù of Qín on obtaining a worthy man,
The Garden of Stories says:
Duke Mù of Qín obtained Bǎilǐ Xī,
Gōngsūn Zhī returned to fetch a wild goose to congratulate him, saying:
"You have obtained a minister for the altars of soil and grain,
truly a blessing for the altars of soil and grain."
The duke did not decline,
but bowed twice and accepted it.
Mourning for Yú Gù, who followed the funeral.
The Records of Kuàijī says:
Yú Gù, styled Jìhóng,
was filial from a young age.
He served as the Grand Administrator of Rìnán,
and there were often wild geese resting in his official hall.
Whenever he traveled through the counties,
they would fly after him.
When he died in office,
the wild geese followed the funeral to his tomb in Yúyáo,
and only left after two years.
Some call them "jià'é" (wild geese),
The Expanded Erya says:
"Jiā'é"
means wild goose.
"Jiā" is the same as "jià."
They are also said to have webbed feet.
The Erya says:
Ducks and wild geese are similar,
their feet are webbed.
The annotation says:
Between their toes, there is a webbed membrane connecting them.
"Pǔ" is pronounced "bǔ."
Having heard that they are bound with cords and adorned with cloth,
The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial says:
When ministers meet, they use a wild goose,
adorned with cloth,
and bound with cords,
as if holding a pheasant.
Annotation:
Wild geese know the seasons,
and their flight is orderly.
Adorning them with cloth
means sewing a garment around their body.
"Wéi" means tying their feet together.
This is also similar to the three silks and five jades.
The Book of Documents, "Canon of Shùn," says:
"Cultivate the five rites, five jades, three silks, two living animals, and one dead animal."
Annotation:
The two living animals:
High ministers present lambs,
and ministers present wild geese.
They can be fed with chaff,
The Writings of Jiǎ Yì says:
Duke Mù of Zōu ordered that ducks and wild geese must be fed with chaff,
and no one dared to use grain.
It is not suitable to feed them grain.
The Records of Diverse Matters says:
If wild geese eat grain,
their wings become heavy,
and they cannot fly.
As for entering Liángzhōu and crossing the frontier,
The Records of Liángzhōu says:
Within the boundaries of Liángzhōu County, there is a Wild Goose Mountain.
Tradition says this mountain has a large pond,
where wild geese gather and roost,
hence it is named Wild Goose Frontier.
Passing Gāoliǔ, they know the gate.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
Wild Goose Gate Mountain,
where wild geese emerge from between its peaks,
lies north of Gāoliǔ.
Responding to late winter, they face north.
The Book of Rites says:
In the month of late winter,
wild geese face north.
Awaiting the White Dew, they arrive as guests.
The Book of Zhōu says:
On the day of White Dew, the wild geese come.
If the wild geese do not come, people will rebel.
Presenting to Bóyáng to hear governance.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
When Cáo Bóyáng ascended the throne,
he enjoyed hunting and archery.
A man from the borders of Cáo, Gōngsūn Qiáng, was fond of archery.
He captured a white wild goose and presented it,
and spoke of the pleasures of hunting and archery.
Bóyáng then consulted him on governance,
greatly pleased with him,
favored him,
and had him hear governance.
Advising Lord Liáng against killing a man.
The New Discourses says:
Lord Liáng went out hunting,
saw a white wild goose,
and wanted to shoot it himself.
Someone on the road startled the wild goose, frightening it away.
Lord Liáng was angry,
and ordered this person to be shot.
His charioteer, Gōngsūn Lóng, admonished him, saying:
"In the past, during the time of Duke Wén of Wèi,
there was a great drought for three years.
Divination said a human sacrifice was necessary.
Duke Wén said:
'Seeking rain is for the people.
To kill someone now would be inhumane;
I shall take the responsibility myself.'
Before he finished speaking,
rain fell.
Now, you value a wild goose and kill a person—
how is this different from a tiger or wolf!"
Lord Liáng led Lóng into his carriage and entered the city walls,
exclaiming, "Long live!" and said:
"Excellent!
Today's hunt has yielded good words."
Now, there is the clear order of their ranks,
The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial says:
Using a wild goose as a gift,
takes from their orderly ranks.
Distinguishing the order of elders and juniors.
The Garden of Stories says:
Using a wild goose as a gift
embodies the rites of elders and juniors.
Seeing that being killed is far different from the mountain trees,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Zhuāngzǐ was walking in the mountains,
and saw a large tree.
Woodcutters stopped beside it,
but did not take it.
Asked why,
they said:
"It is useless scattered wood, unfit for timber."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"This tree, by being unfit for timber, can live out its natural lifespan."
Leaving the mountains,
and reaching a town,
he stayed at an old friend's home.
The old friend was pleased,
prepared wine and meat,
and ordered a servant to kill a wild goose and cook it.
The servant asked:
"One wild goose can honk,
the other cannot honk.
Which should I kill?"
The host said:
"Kill the one that cannot honk."
The next day,
a disciple asked:
"Yesterday, the mountain tree, by being unfit for timber, lived out its natural lifespan,
but the host's wild goose, by being unfit, died.
Where will you position yourself, Master?"
Zhuāngzǐ sighed and said:
"I, Zhōu, will position myself between being fit and unfit for timber."
In use, they are similar to the pheasant for scholars.
The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial says:
Ministers use a wild goose as a gift,
scholars use a pheasant.
Symbolizing that a woman is timely,
The Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall says:
Using a wild goose as a gift
takes from their moving south and north with the seasons,
not losing their proper time,
signifying that a woman's timeliness should not be taken away.
Only ministers use it as a gift.
See the annotation above for "In use, they are similar to the pheasant for scholars."
Following the wind, some first, some after,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Wild geese fly with the wind,
to conserve their energy.
The Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn says:
For all gifts,
ministers use a wild goose,
resembling elders among the people,
who must have precedence and sequence.
Following the sun, they fly and rest.
The Spring and Autumn Explanatory Texts says:
Wild geese go south and north,
moved by the sun.
The rites were slighted by the Grand Administrator,
The Book of Later Hàn says:
General Dùliáo Huángfǔ Guī resigned and returned to Āndìng.
A fellow villager had bought the position of Grand Administrator of Wild Goose Gate with money,
and also left his post to return home.
He wrote a card and requested an audience with Guī.
Guī lay down and did not welcome him.
After he entered, Guī asked:
"Did you enjoy eating wild geese when you were in the commandery before?"
No regard was shown in the presence of the Master.
The Family Sayings of Confucius says:
When Confucius went to Wèi,
the Duke of Wèi spoke with Confucius,
but upon seeing a flying goose pass by, he looked up at it,
his attention no longer on Confucius.
Confucius then departed.
As for encountering Míngyuè and having two fall together,
the *Book of Northern Qí* states:
Húlǜ Guāng accompanied Wénxiāng out into the wilderness,
where they saw two geese flying toward them.
Wénxiāng ordered Míngyuè to gallop and shoot at them,
with two arrows,
and both fell.
Gathering at Héxī in five colors,
the *Book of Hàn* states:
Emperor Xuāndì built the Shìzōng Temple in Xīhé,
and when offering sacrifices and prayers,
five-colored geese gathered before the hall.
Entering Shàngyú to tend the fields,
the *Records of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
In Shàngyú, there were geese
that helped the people tend the fields,
plucking out weed roots in spring,
and pecking away the waste in autumn.
Therefore, the local officials forbade the people from harming these birds without cause,
and violators were punished without pardon.
In Nánkāng, floating on stone.
The *Records of Nánkāng* states:
In Pínggù County, there is Fùsì Mountain,
on which there is a lake
several tens of lǐ in circumference.
There is a stone goose floating on the lake,
and every autumn,
the stone goose flies and cries,
as if marking the season.
Soaring over vast marshes,
they often avoid arrows by carrying reeds in their beaks;
the *Huáinánzǐ* states:
Geese carry reeds in their beaks while flying,
to avoid arrows and nets.
Coming from distant frontiers,
they also deliver letters with silk attached.
The *Book of Hàn* states:
Sū Wǔ was among the Xiōngnú,
and Emperor Zhāodì sent an envoy to seek peace through marriage.
Cháng Huì met the Hàn envoy at night,
and the envoy said to the Chányú:
"The Son of Heaven was hunting in the Shanglin Park,
and caught a goose,
on whose foot was attached a silk letter,
stating that Sū Wǔ and others were in a certain marsh."
The envoy spoke as instructed,
and the Chányú was greatly astonished,
then allowed Sū Wǔ to return.
Bird
The crow, that filial bird of dark plumage,
The Book of Songs says:
"None are black but the crows."
The Chunqiu Yuanming Bao says:
"The crow,
is a filial bird.
It embodies the pure essence of utmost Yang."
The Yuanming Bao says:
"Flowing fire becomes the crow,
the essence of Yang,
residing within the sun,
shining down from heaven."
It receives its endowment from the Yáoguāng star,
The Yundou Shu says:
"The Yáoguāng star scatters and becomes crows."
It also corresponds in harmony with the Wéi stars.
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu says:
"When the Wéi stars are bright,
then the sun and moon are luminous.
When crows have three legs,
ritual and righteousness are cultivated,
and all creatures are in harmony."
The people of Zhèng once observed the Chu army's tents,
The Zuozhuan says: Chǔ Zǐyuán attacked Zhèng,
the feudal lords came to its rescue,
and the Chu army fled by night.
The people of Zhèng were about to flee to Tóngqiū,
when a spy reported:
"There are crows on the Chu tents."
They then stopped.
The Jìn army also watched for signs at the Qí city walls.
The Zuozhuan says:
Jìn attacked Qí,
and the Qí army fled by night.
Shī Kuàng informed the Marquis of Jìn:
"The cries of the birds and crows are joyful,
the Qí army must have fled."
Shūxiàng informed the Marquis of Jìn:
"There are crows on the city walls,
the Qí army must have fled."
As for the crows on the city walls with tails all aflutter,
The Xu Hanshu says:
During Emperor Huán's time, a children's rhyme said: "Crows on the city walls,
tails all aflutter,
one year they hatch their young.
The lord becomes an official,
the son becomes a conscript.
One conscript dies,
a hundred chariots come."
And the crows at the yamen morning and evening.
The Hanshu says:
During Emperor Chéng's time, Hé Wǔ requested that the Yùshǐ Dàfū be made Dà Sīkōng,
to complete the three ducal offices.
At that time, cypress trees stood in rows at the Yùshǐ yamen,
and several thousand wild crows often roosted upon them,
leaving at dawn and returning at dusk,
they were called the 'Morning and Evening Crows'.
When the crows left and did not return for several months,
the elders found it strange.
Moved by Yáng Yán's filial piety, their beaks were injured,
The Yiyuan says:
Yáng Yán was renowned for his pure filial piety.
Later, crows carrying drums in their beaks
gathered in the village where Yán lived.
The crows' beaks were all injured.
The image of carrying drums
was to make the deaf hear from afar.
A county was then established at that place,
named Wūshāng (Crow-Injured).
Wáng Mǎng changed it to Wūxiào (Crow-Filial),
to manifest his conduct.
For Yān Dān, their heads turned white.
The Yandanzi says:
Crown Prince Dān of Yān was a hostage in Qín.
The King of Qín treated him discourteously.
Unhappy with his situation,
he wished to return home.
The King of Qín would not permit it,
and deceitfully decreed:
"When crows' heads turn white,
and horses grow horns,
then you may go."
Dān looked up to heaven and sighed.
The crows' heads immediately turned white,
and horses immediately grew horns.
Qín had no choice but to send him away.
Zǐtuī was once seen shielded by smoke,
The Shiyi Ji says:
Duke Wén of Jìn set fire to the mountain seeking Zǐtuī.
Zǐtuī embraced a tree.
A white crow came and shielded him with smoke.
When Tuī died,
Duke Wén ceased using fire for a month in his honor.
The Queen Mother of the West is also heard of in tales of fetching food.
The Kuodi Tu says:
Mount Kūnlún lies within the Ruòshuǐ waters.
None can reach it unless riding a dragon.
There, three-legged divine crows fetch food for Xīwángmǔ.
As for borrowing a tree in a poem,
The Tangshu says:
Lǐ Yìfǔ was summoned for an audience.
Tàizōng tested him by ordering him to compose a poem on crows.
He said:
"In sunlight, they display morning splendor;
Amidst zither strings, they accompany night's cries.
How many trees in Shànglín Park,
yet not one branch is lent for me to perch."
The Emperor said:
"I shall lend you the entire tree,
how could it be just one branch!"
And composing a rhapsody when they gathered at his hut,
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on the Crow - Preface" says:
"Filial crows gathered at my hut.
Crows are virtuous birds,
and I praise them,
therefore I composed this rhapsody."
They are observed in their resting places,
The Book of Songs says:
"Look at the crows, where they rest,
upon whose house?"
And heard of in their returning to feed their parents.
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu says:
"The crow belongs to Yang.
Yang energy is benevolent,
therefore they feed their parents in return."
Furthermore, dreaming of Fēngyì presaged the rise of Hàn,
The Diwang Shiji says:
The grandfather of the Lord of Pèi had his home in Fēng.
His wife once dreamed of a red crow sporting like a dragon.
Afterwards, she gave birth to Zhíjiā,
who became Tàigōng.
And their arrival in Wǔchāng brought auspicious signs to Wú.
The Wú Zhi says:
Red crows were seen in Wǔchāng,
and accordingly the reign title was changed to Chìwū (Red Crow).
When pigs arrived, the flying essence vanished without trace,
Guō Pú's Donglin says:
General Níngyuǎn Jǐng Zé
had a sister who was ill for over forty years.
I divined for her,
obtaining the hexagram Míngyí changing to Xiǎoguò.
According to the hexagram, a single-hoofed pig should be obtained and reared.
They acted accordingly.
Later, the woman began to sleep,
and saw a man
dressed entirely in black.
The woman told him to come forward.
He would not,
saying there was something he feared.
He then wept and left.
Her illness began to slightly abate.
I once discussed this matter.
The crow
is a creature of the sun;
the pig
is a creature of the moon.
Water and fire are mutually averse,
a natural principle.
Taking a creature of hidden Yin
to dissipate the flying essence of the Great Yang.
In the sun, there are three legs,
therefore it is countered by a creature with a single hoof.
When a sparrow gave birth to a crow, it meant the ruin of Xià.
The Shuoyuan says:
Confucius said:
"Preservation and ruin, calamity and fortune, all depend on oneself.
In the time of Dì Xīn,
a sparrow gave birth to a crow at a city corner.
The diviner said:
'The small gives birth to the great,
the state is sure to receive blessings.'
Dì Xīn believed this,
and did not govern the state well,
leading to its destruction.
This is turning calamity into fortune deceptively."
Cutting their wing feathers to make them tame,
The Hánzǐ says:
"If you tame a crow by cutting its lower wing feathers,
then it must depend on people for food.
How can it not become tame?
An enlightened ruler nurturing his ministers is also like this."
Retracting their claws, they are naturally classified among the 'chǒu' category.
The Erya says:
"Crows and magpies are of the 'chǒu' category,
their claws retract."
Annotation:
"In flight, they retract their feet beneath their belly."
They nested in Emperor Yáng's curtains and tents,
The Suishu says:
Emperor Yáng built a palace in Dānyáng,
intending to travel to Jiāngzuǒ.
Crows and magpies nested in his curtains and tents,
and driving them away did not stop them.
They were moved by King Wén's filial piety and fraternal duty.
The Ruiying Tu says:
In King Wén's time, blue crows appeared.
When the king is filial and fraternal, they arrive.
Responding to prophecies, they flocked and gathered on towers,
The Sanguo Dianlue says:
Hóu Jǐng usurped the throne,
He ordered the decoration of the Zhūquè Gate.
On that day, tens of thousands of white-headed crows gathered on the gate tower.
A children's rhyme said:
"White-headed crow,
sweeping past Zhūquè,
returns to Wú."
It was revealed that one of its feet was fake and fell to the ground.
The "Tángshū" states:
In the first year of the Tiānshòu era,
someone presented a three-legged crow,
and Empress Wǔ Zétiān considered it an auspicious omen for the Zhōu dynasty.
When Zhōngzōng was still the crown prince,
he said that one of its feet was fake,
and Empress Wǔ was displeased.
Shortly after,
one of the crow's feet indeed fell off.
It is also said that Yì shot the sun,
see the annotation "Yì Céng Jiàn Shè" in the "Rì Fù."
Loving the crow on the roof,
as stated in Tàigōng's "Liù Tāo":
King Wǔ ascended the Xiàtái to oversee the people of Yīn,
and Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"I have heard that if you love someone,
you will also love the crow on their roof;
if you hate someone,
you will hate even their servants."
The gathering of crows in the courtyard was praised during the time of Yǒuyú.
The "Bàopǔzǐ" states:
Why does the crow have three legs?
It is because the number three is odd and represents yang.
Thus, due to Yǒuyú's utmost filial piety,
a three-legged crow gathered in his courtyard;
when Zēngzǐ was hoeing melons,
a three-legged crow perched on his hat.
It is also said that a crow snatched meat from a village head.
The "Hànshū" states:
Huáng Bà served as the governor of Yǐngchuān,
and he sent an official to investigate something.
The official did not dare to stay at the postal station,
so he ate by the roadside.
Nearby,
a crow snatched his meat.
When the official met Huáng Bà,
Huáng Bà greeted him and said:
"How hard you have worked!
Eating by the roadside,
a crow stole your meat."
The official was greatly astonished,
and from then on, he dared not hide anything.
The pure white crow was mentioned in Fàn Yún's response.
The "Qíshū" states:
During Emperor Gāo's reign, someone presented a white crow.
The emperor asked:
"What auspicious omen is this?"
Fàn Yún, though of low rank,
stepped forward and replied:
"I have heard that when a ruler reveres the ancestral temple,
white crows will arrive."
The red crow is mentioned in Xuē Zǒng's words.
Xuē Zǒng's "Chì Wū Sòng" states:
Majestic red crow,
essence of the sun.
With red feathers and crimson form,
it appears once in an age.
To attain longevity, one must feed on its red flesh.
The "Bàopǔzǐ" states:
Take a crow that has not yet grown feathers,
mix cinnabar with beef and feed it to the crow.
When it grows up,
its feathers will all turn red.
Kill it,
dry it in the shade, grind it, and consume it,
and you will live for five hundred years.
Sometimes, flocks of crows are mistaken for banners.
The "Běishǐ" states:
Gāo Shìbiàn of Qí was timid by nature.
When the Zhōu army entered Yè,
Shìbiàn led over a thousand cavalry to scout.
He climbed to a high point and looked west,
and from afar, he saw a flock of crows flying up.
Mistaking them for banners,
he immediately galloped back,
not daring to look back.
They waited for Zōng Lǐn's weeping.
The "Hòuzhōushū" states:
Zōng Lǐn was mourning his mother's death,
and he wept until he vomited blood.
Every time, thousands of crows gathered at his residence,
arriving when he wept
and leaving when he stopped.
They also shared Xiāo Fàng's sorrow.
The "Běishǐ" states:
Xiāo Fàng of Qí was known for his filial piety during mourning.
While he resided in a hut, two kind crows came and perched in front,
tamingly drinking and pecking in the courtyard.
Whenever the mourning time approached,
they would spread their wings and cry mournfully,
entirely like grieving and weeping.
Some pecked at Sīmǎ Shēn's mouth.
The "Chénshū" states:
Sīmǎ Shēn slandered Máo Xǐ before the later ruler,
causing him to be dismissed and confined.
Once, Shēn was napping in the daytime at the Shàngshū Shěng,
and a crow pecked his mouth until it bled.
Contemporary opinion held it was retribution for slandering the virtuous.
Some perched on Zēngzǐ's hat.
See the annotation above for "the gathering of crows in the courtyard was praised during the time of Yǒuyú."
Wáng Jí shot one and always hit his target.
The "Hànmíngdì Qǐjū Zhù" states:
The emperor traveled east to Mount Tài,
and upon reaching Xíngyáng,
a crow flew crying over the imperial carriage.
The imperial guard Wáng Jí shot it down,
and he prayed:
"The crow cries 'yā yā,'
I draw my bow and shoot it.
Piercing its left flank,
may Your Majesty live for ten thousand years,
may I serve as a two-thousand-dàn official,
and be granted two million coins."
Péi Xiá pointed at them and was able to speak.
The "Běishǐ" states:
Péi Xiá of Western Wèi could not speak until he was seven years old.
Later, he saw a flock of crows darkening the sky west of Luòchéng,
raised his hand to point at them, and began to speak.
From then on, he became exceptionally intelligent compared to other children.
They even built a city in Tián Xù's territory.
The "Tángshū" states:
During Dézōng's reign,
flocks of crows from Zhèng and Biàn prefectures all entered the territories of Tián Xù and Lǐ Nà,
carrying wood to build a city,
two or three feet high,
and over ten miles square.
Xù and Nà ordered it burned,
but after two nights, it was restored as before,
and the crows' mouths were all bleeding.
They also gathered on halberds at Liǔ Zhòngyǐng's gate.
The "Tángshū" states:
After Liǔ Zhòngyǐng was appointed as a remonstrance official,
every time he was promoted,
large flocks of crows gathered at his residence in Shēngpíng Lǐ,
filling the courtyard trees and halberd racks.
Later, when he became the military governor of Tiānpíng,
the crows did not gather,
and he died at his post.
Some carried a jade tablet and descended to the altar.
The "Mòzǐ" states:
A red crow carried a jade tablet and descended to the Qí altar of Zhōu,
commanding the attack on Yīn.
Some gathered on mulberry trees to make bows.
See the annotation "Wū Hào Jìng Lǐ" in the "Gōng Fù."
The imperial enterprise flourished,
and at Wángwū, a flowing fire was once observed.
The "Shàngshū Zhōnghòu" states:
When the Zhōu crown prince Fā crossed the Mèngjīn,
fire descended from above onto Wángwū,
transforming into a red crow.
The imperial residence was magnificent,
and the Língtái also relied on a wind vane.
The "Shùzhēng Jì" states:
The wind vane crow was placed on the Língtái,
and it would move when a thousand-mile wind blew.
Magpie
People resorted to cannibalism.
Magpies nested on their trebuchets,
and the people's hearts grew estranged.
The government troops beheaded their leader,
and sent his head to the capital.
Some gained fame from the divine maiden,
as the *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
"The magpie,
also called the divine maiden."
Some dwell together with nesting crows.
The *Suí Shū* says:
Guō Jùn, styled Hóngwén,
was from Tàiyuán.
His household was harmonious and amicable,
seven generations lived together,
dogs and pigs suckled each other's young,
crows and magpies shared nests,
and people of the time considered it a response to righteousness.
The province reported the matter,
and the emperor dispatched Duke Píngchāng, Yǔwén Bì, to his home to offer commendation.
Bì is pronounced bì.
They gather millet atop Huánqiū,
as the *Shíyí Jì* records:
The mountain Yuánqiáo is named Huánqiū.
Upon it lies a lake,
a thousand *lǐ* square.
There are many large magpies,
ten feet tall,
flying in flocks by the lake's edge,
gathering millet from Bùzhōu atop Huánqiū.
They carry fire by the side of Qīngxī.
The *Dòngmíng Jì* says:
The emperor bestowed the Mínghóng dagger upon Dōngfāng Shuò,
and Shuò said:
"This dagger was forged from the metal of Shǒushān;
the male flew away,
while the female remained alone.
The metal came from Jiǔtāng Qīngxī,
where magpies carried fire above Qīngxī."
They attest to the marvelous skill of Zǐxìn,
as the *Běi Qí Shū* records:
Imperial guard Xī Yǒngluò was sitting opposite Zhāng Zǐxìn of Hénèi,
when a magpie cried in a tree in the courtyard,
fought, and fell.
Zǐxìn said:
"The magpie's words are inauspicious;
if a wind comes from the southwest toward evening,
passing through the trees and brushing the corner of the hall,
then tonight someone will summon you,
and you must not go."
After Zǐxìn left,
indeed a wind came,
and at night, Gāo Yǎn sent someone to summon Yǒngluò,
claiming it was an imperial summons.
Yǒngluò intended to go,
but his wife pleaded with him to stay,
saying he had fallen from a horse and broken his back,
thus avoiding disaster.
They reveal the keen insight of Guǎn Lù.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
Guǎn Lù went to the residence of District Magistrate Liú Chángrén of Ándé,
when a magpie came crying on the roof of the pavilion,
its call very urgent.
Lù said:
"The magpie says a woman in the northeast killed her husband yesterday,
and is implicating the western neighbor;
the revelation will come before the sun sets at Yúyuān."
At that time, indeed a fellow villager from the northeast came to report
that a neighboring woman had killed her husband with her own hands,
and falsely claimed the western neighbor killed her husband.
They journeyed to the western lands,
and once heard the chant of the Queen Mother;
the *Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn* says:
When the Queen Mother of the West returned,
the people chanted with sorrow:
"Journeying to those western lands,
dwelling in the wilds.
Leopards and tigers as companions,
with magpies we abide.
A noble fate does not return,
I, the emperor's daughter."
Yú is read as wū.
Examining the *Guófēng*,
they are also likened to the virtue of a lady.
The *Shī* says:
"The Magpie's Nest,"
speaks of the virtue of a lady.
The ruler accumulates deeds and merits,
to attain rank and position,
and the lady rises from her household to dwell therein.
Swallow
That mysterious bird, the swallow—
the Guangya states:
“The mysterious bird
is the swallow.”
It is the essence descended from the Jasper Light.
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu says:
“The Jasper Light Star scattered and became swallows.”
It was celebrated in verse by Zhuāng Jiāng sending off a concubine.
The Book of Songs says:
“The Swallows,”
is about Wèi Zhuāng Jiāng sending off a returning concubine.
“The swallows are flying,
their wings uneven.
This lady is returning home,
I escort her far to the wilds.
The swallows are flying,
their calls rising and falling.”
It was swallowed by Jiǎn Dí, who gave birth to Shāng.
The Book of Songs says:
“Heaven commanded the mysterious bird,
to descend and give birth to Shāng.”
Also, the Records of the Grand Historian states:
“Dì Kù’s junior consort, of the Yǒusōng clan, was named Jiǎn Dí.
The mysterious bird left an egg,
which Jiǎn Dí swallowed,
and gave birth to Xiè.”
It left behind a cinnabar text.
The Tián Qiúzǐ states:
“In the time of Shǎohào,
a red swallow perched at the door,
leaving behind its cinnabar text.”
It was covered with a jade basket.
The Lüshi Chunqiu states:
“The Yǒusōng clan had two beautiful maidens,
who built a nine-tiered tower.
Whenever they ate or drank, drums were sounded.
The Emperor ordered a swallow to observe them.
Its call was like ‘yì yì.’
The two maidens loved it and fought to catch it,
covering it with a jade basket.
After a short while, they opened it to look,
and the swallow had left two eggs,
then flew north,
and never returned.
The two maidens composed a song:
‘The swallow, the swallow, flew away,’
which truly began the northern music.”
Note:
“The music of the northern states.”
Some, from carrying mud, became bald-headed;
others were injured in the eye by a thrown hairpin.
The Xuyi Ji states:
“The wife of Mr. Sūn, née Huáng,
saw a child before her,
and threw a hairpin at it.
It leaped into the clouds and vanished.
At night, she heard singing outside:
‘In the past, I filled the Xià family’s grave,
carrying mud till my head went bald.
Now I lodge at the Huáng family’s home,
unexpectedly, you injured my eye.’”
Searching the nest,
she found a white swallow,
with its left eye injured.”
“The swallows are flying,
their wings uneven,”
see the note above.
The Wú palace resented being burned.
The Wúdì Jì states:
“Chūnshēn Jūn made the Wú palace his capital,
and embellished it with skillful decorations.
After Chūnshēn died,
officials, illuminating a swallow’s burrow, caused a fire,
and it burned down.”
The Wèi widow was also known for tying a thread.
The History of the Southern Dynasties states:
“The wife of Xiāngyáng’s Wèi Jìngyú was sixteen when Jìngyú died.
Her parents and in-laws all wished her to remarry,
but she vowed not to consent,
cutting off her ear and placing it on a tray as a pledge,
so they desisted.
At the house where she lived, there was a swallow’s nest,
and a pair always came and went.
Later, one suddenly flew alone.
The woman, moved by its solitary perch,
tied a thread to its leg as a marker.
The following year, this swallow indeed returned,
still bearing the previous thread.
The woman then composed a poem:
‘In past years, you left without a mate,
this spring, you still return alone.
The kindness of my departed one is deep,
I cannot bear to fly in pairs again.’”
Praise Guǎn Lù for his skillful divination.
The Records of Wèi states:
“Zhūgě Yuán once took swallow eggs and placed them in a vessel,
asking Guǎn Lù to divine what was inside.
Lù divined and said of the swallow eggs:
‘Containing life, awaiting change,
nestled under the eaves.
Male and female distinguished,
wings not yet spread.
These are swallow eggs.’”
Admire Wáng Wēi for his ability to compose rhapsodies.
The Bié Zhuàn of Wáng Wēi states:
“A white swallow came flying,
and he was ordered to compose a rhapsody on it.”
As for observing the maidens of the Yǒusōng clan,
see the note above on “Jiǎn Dí gave birth to Shāng.”
It piled up the walls of Qūfù.
The Běi Liáng Lù states:
“Once, a man lost his way at sea,
and reached Dǎnzhōu,
where he saw Zhòngní and his seventy disciples traveling on the sea.
They gave a man from Lǔ a wooden staff,
telling him to close his eyes and ride it,
and return to inform the Marquis of Lǔ
to build walls against invaders.
The man from Lǔ left the sea,
threw the staff into the water,
and it turned into a dragon.
He reported everything in detail,
but the Marquis of Lǔ did not believe him.
Soon after, tens of thousands of swallows came carrying earth to pile up the walls,
and the Marquis of Lǔ believed.
The great walls of Qūfù were completed just as the Qí invaders arrived,
but they attacked Lǔ without success and retreated.”
Nesting on a tent canopy is already perilous.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
“The Wú prince Zhá, traveling from Wèi to Jìn,
was about to lodge at Qī,
when he heard bell sounds.
He said to Sūn Wénzǐ:
‘How strange!
For you to be here
is like a swallow nesting on a tent canopy.’”
Perching on a balance, it is even lighter.
The Jiǔzhāng Suànshù states:
“Five sparrows and six swallows fly and perch on a balance,
and the balance is exactly level.
If one sparrow and one swallow fly and exchange places,
then the sparrow is heavy and the swallow light.”
It rises suddenly, riding on rumbling thunder.
See the note on “stone swallows flying” in the “Rhapsody on Rain.”
It congratulates the completion of a great mansion.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
“When a great mansion is completed, swallows and sparrows congratulate each other;
when hot bath water is prepared, lice and fleas mourn each other.”
As for its form divided into tail and wings,
the Shuōwén states:
“The swallow,
is the mysterious bird.
It has a forked mouth,
spread wings,
and a branched tail, pictographic.”
It instinctively knows the days of Wù and Jǐ.
The Bówùzhì states:
“Swallows do not carry mud to plaster their nests on Wù and Jǐ days.
This is not due to intelligence,
but comes naturally.”
It soars through the mist and clouds of Jǐngsù.
The Tán Sǒu states:
“Sòng Xuānwáng Jǐngsù garrisoned Zhūfāng,
and once was with Liú Jìn in a small study.
Swallows gathered on the ceiling,
flying and calling in pursuit.
Jǐngsù said:
‘All things have their own spiritual nature,
why is it bestowed only on scaled and feathered creatures?
Like this bird,
it roams above the mist and clouds,
rests beneath the woods and trees,
pecks when hungry,
drinks when thirsty,
its form unburdened by things,
gain and loss unrelated to its heart,
how joyful it is!’”
It perched on Mǎ Shū’s desk.
The Book of Chén states:
“The noble scholar Mǎ Shū,
whose eyes were often yellow,
could see in the dark.
There was a pair of white swallows
that nested in the courtyard tree,
tame and familiar with the railings and corridors,
often alighting on his desk.
They came in spring and left in autumn,
for nearly thirty years.”
It serves Shǎohào in managing the equinoxes.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
“Tánzǐ said:
‘Shǎohào
had bird officials and bird names.
The mysterious bird official
manages the equinoxes.’”
Note:
“It comes at the spring equinox,
and leaves at the autumn equinox.”
It is sacrificed to at the high禖 altar.
See the note on “praying for children at the high禖 altar” in the “Rhapsody on Arrows.”
It is also heard that after eating it, one should not enter water.
The *Records of Diverse Matters* states:
If a person eats swallow meat, they must not enter water,
for they will be devoured by flood dragons.
Digging them up can relieve hunger.
The *Book of Jin* states:
During the chaos and turmoil in the Central Plains,
the villagers jointly recommended Xī Jiàn as their leader,
and they took refuge on Yì Mountain in the State of Lǔ.
The mountain had multiple layers of perilous terrain,
and the people suffered from famine.
The wilderness had no living grass,
so they dug up wild mice and hibernating swallows to eat.
How could one know the ambition of the swan goose?
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
Chén Shèng stopped plowing,
sighed, and said:
"How could sparrows and swallows know the ambition of the swan goose!"
Their killing is often due to caltrops.
The *Records of Hidden Proofs* states:
A man named Zhōu from the State of Pèi had three mute sons,
all unable to speak.
A visitor came to beg for a drink,
heard the sounds of the children,
asked about it,
and was told the whole truth.
The visitor said:
"Sir, please go inside and reflect on your faults."
Finding his words strange,
he realized this was no ordinary person.
After a long while, he came out and said:
"I truly cannot recall any wrongdoing."
The visitor said:
"Try to think back to your childhood."
He went inside,
and after the time it takes to eat a meal, came out and said:
"I remember when I was a child,
there was a swallow's nest by the bed,
containing three fledglings.
When the mother went out to fetch food,
I took three caltrops and gave one to each.
They swallowed them and died immediately.
When the mother returned,
she could not find her young,
cried mournfully, and flew away.
I have often regretted and blamed myself for this."
The visitor transformed into the appearance of a Daoist,
and said:
"Since you have realized your remorse and guilt,
it is now forgiven!"
The sons were then able to speak.
Jīng Fáng's arts were profound,
and he spoke of the heavenly maiden.
Jīng Fáng's *Divinations of the Changes* states:
If a white swallow appears in the mountains,
the ruler should obtain a noble maiden.
The annotation says:
Nowadays, swallows are commonly called heavenly maidens.
Lord Máo ascended as an immortal,
having once eaten divine mushrooms.
The *Inner Biography of Lord Máo* states:
On Jùqū Mountain, there are five types of divine mushrooms.
The third is called the swallow-embryo mushroom.
Its color is purple,
its shape resembles sunflower leaves,
and on its leaves is the image of a flying swallow,
luminous and translucent.
Eating one stalk
grants the title of Grand Clarity Dragon-Tiger Immortal Lord.
Sparrow
The fluttering small bird,
is indeed the descent of the Star of Jade Radiance.
The *Chūnqiū Yùndǒu Shū* states:
The Star of Jade Radiance scatters and becomes sparrows.
It is also called the Píngxiāo bird.
The *Shíyí Jì* states:
When Shùn was buried in the wilderness of Cāngwú,
there was a bird like a crimson sparrow,
which came from Dānzhōu,
spewing five-colored vapor,
misty and dense like clouds,
named the Píngxiāo sparrow,
capable of flying in flocks,
carrying earth to form a burial mound.
It is also called the "esteemed guest."
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
The sparrow is also called the "esteemed guest,"
meaning it dwells in people's homes like a guest.
Its transformation is known to occur upon entering water.
The *Lǐ* states:
In late autumn,
sparrows enter the great waters,
and transform into clams.
Their soaring and gathering are further seen as relying on humans.
The *Shuōwén* states:
The sparrow
is a small bird that relies on humans.
There is also the story of repaying Yáng Bǎo by carrying rings.
The *Xù Qíxié Jì* states:
Hóngnóng's Yáng Bǎo, at the age of nine,
went north of Huàyīn,
and saw a yellow sparrow being attacked by an owl,
falling under a tree,
and besieged by ants.
Bǎo took pity on it,
took it home,
placed it in a handkerchief box,
and fed it yellow flowers.
After over a hundred days,
its feathers grew fully,
and it would leave in the morning and return at dusk.
One night at the third watch,
while Bǎo was reading and had not yet slept,
a child in yellow robes bowed and said:
"I am an envoy of the Queen Mother,
sent to Pénglái,
but carelessly attacked by an owl.
Your benevolence and kindness saved me."
He gave Bǎo four white rings, saying:
"May your descendants rise to the rank of the Three Excellencies,
just like these rings."
Bǎo begot Zhèn,
Zhèn begot Bǐng,
Bǐng begot Cì,
Cì begot Biāo,
four generations of renowned lords.
There is also the story of entering the curtains for Wáng Xiáng.
The *Jìn Shū* states:
Wáng Xiáng's stepmother, Madame Zhū, craved roasted yellow sparrows.
Suddenly, several dozen yellow sparrows flew into her curtain,
allowing him to serve them to his mother.
The villagers believed it was due to his filial piety.
Some sparrows come from Kūnqiū.
The *Hànwǔ Nèizhuàn* states:
Among the immortal medicines of the Queen Mother of the West is the divine sparrow of Kūnqiū.
Some are produced in Tiáozhī.
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
In the second year of the Yǒngyuán era,
the king of Ānxī presented a large sparrow from Tiáozhī,
whose eggs were as large as jars.
Praise for Bùyí's ode.
The *Xiānxián Zhuàn* states:
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was an auspicious sign of white sparrows.
Zhōu Bùyí had already composed an ode.
Lord Cáo suddenly gave him paper and brush,
immediately ordering him to compose another.
After it was completed,
Cáo Cāo was greatly amazed.
Admiration for Gōnggàn's poem.
Liú Gōnggàn's poem states:
Fluttering wild blue sparrows,
nest and hide among thorns and brambles.
In the morning, they gather grains from the flat fields,
in the evening, they drink from the winding pool's springs.
Humbly emerging from the overgrown weeds,
they reach the edges of Dānqiū.
Taking and returning them is praised regarding Qí Jǐng.
The *Yànzǐ Chūnqiū* states:
Duke Jǐng of Qí took a fledgling sparrow,
but it was weak,
so he returned it.
Yànzǐ bowed twice,
congratulating him, saying:
"My lord possesses the virtue of a sage!
Taking the fledgling sparrow,
seeing it weak,
and returning it—
this shows respect for the young and old.
If he treats birds and beasts this way,
how much more will he treat people!"
Being cautious about whom to follow is heard from Zhòngní.
The *Jiāyǔ* states:
Confucius saw that the sparrows caught by a hunter were all fledglings.
Confucius asked:
"Why are all the fledglings caught, but not the adult sparrows?"
The hunter replied:
"If the fledglings follow the adult sparrows, they cannot be caught;
if the adult sparrows follow the fledglings, they can be caught."
Confucius turned to his disciples and said:
"A gentleman must be cautious about whom he follows."
As for Xī nú's long whistle,
the *Yì Yuàn* states:
Shàngyú's Sūn family had a Xī nú skilled in various arts.
When he whistled long into the air,
flocks of sparrows would gather.
When he cried at night,
mosquitoes and gnats would all die beside him.
Hénán's young archer.
The *Běi Shǐ* states:
In the Later Wèi, Hénán Prince Yào, at the age of five,
once shot sparrows before Dàowǔ,
hitting his target,
and the emperor was amazed.
Upstairs, Lián Fàn was already worried.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
Yáng Yóu,
a native of Shǔ Commandery,
served as a literary official.
In the commandery, there was a large sparrow
that gathered on the treasury building at night.
Grand Administrator Lián Fàn asked Yóu about it,
and Yóu replied:
"This portends minor military disturbances within the commandery,
but they will not cause harm."
Over twenty days later,
the barbarians of Guǎngróu County rebelled,
killing and injuring officials.
Under the dǒu, Sīhuà was also alarmed.
The *Sòng Shū* states:
When Xiāo Sīhuà was in Qīngzhōu,
he often used a bronze dǒu,
which was overturned under the medicine cabinet.
Suddenly, two dead sparrows were found under the dǒu.
Sīhuà sighed and said:
"The dǒu overturned,
two sparrows perished—
is this not an ill omen?"
Soon after, he was imprisoned.
There is also the story of befriending different species on the cold ridge.
The *Shāzhōu Jì* states:
The cold ridge is thirty lǐ from Tàiyángzhōu,
where sparrows and rats share the same burrow.
The sparrows resemble house sparrows,
small and white in color;
the rats resemble house rats,
yellow in color and tailless.
Adorning with five colors in Hándān.
The *Kǒngcóngzǐ* states:
The people of Hándān presented sparrows to the King of Zhào on the first day of the first month,
adorned with five colors,
and the king was greatly pleased.
Shēn Shū told Zǐ Shùn:
"Why did the king do this?"
Zǐ Shùn replied:
"Releasing them on New Year's Day
symbolizes life."
Zǐ Shùn said:
"This is a vulgar custom of the back alleys,
not the law of the ancient kings."
Descending upon the Hánzhāng Palace Gate.
The *Suí Shū* states:
During the Kāihuáng era,
a divine sparrow descended upon the Hánzhāng Gate.
Emperor Gāozǔ summoned all officials for a banquet,
and Xǔ Shànxīn requested paper and brush at his seat,
composed an ode, and presented it.
Emperor Gāozǔ joyfully said:
"The writing flows without pause,
the brush never stops—
I have long heard of such skill,
and now I witness it."
He then bestowed two hundred bolts of silk.
Carrying the immortal text of the *Língbǎo*.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
The *Língbǎo Jīng*
is a text of immortal arts.
When the King of Wú quarried stone to build his palace,
he found a book with purple script and golden slips inside the stone,
but could not read it.
He sent someone to ask Confucius,
saying:
"A red sparrow carried this book and placed it before the hall.
I do not understand its meaning,
so I have come from afar to consult you."
Confucius said:
"This is the method of immortality,
which Yǔ practiced."
Yǔ was about to ascend as an immortal,
and sealed it in a stone casket within a famous mountain.
Now a red sparrow has carried it in its beak,
which must be a heavenly bestowal."
Also, there is the story of shooting with a bright pearl,
as stated in the Tàixuán Jīng:
"Using a bright pearl to shoot at a sparrow
is a mismatch of value."
It transformed into yellow jade,
as recorded in the Chūnqiū Kǒng Yǎn Tú:
"A bird transformed into a book,
which Confucius reverently presented to heaven.
A red sparrow alighted on the book,
and it transformed into yellow jade."
Guō Pú's divination about the gathering of sparrows,
from Guō Pú's Dònglín:
"In the Chancellor's residence, there was a hen with chicks.
A sparrow flew and alighted on its back.
Driven away, it returned again,
repeating this several times.
They ordered Guō Pú to divine it,
and he said:
'This is an omen of the Prince of Jin ascending the throne.'"
Yáng Xuān's knowledge of overturned grain.
From the Yìdū Qíjiù Zhuàn:
"Yáng Xuān was the Governor of Hénèi.
While touring the county,
he saw a flock of sparrows chirping on a mulberry tree.
Xuān said to his officials:
'Ahead, there is overturned cart grain,
and these sparrows are following each other, wanting to go eat it.'
After traveling a few li ahead,
they indeed found overturned grain."
Presenting literary elegance in Yǒng'ān,
from the Dōngguān Hànjì:
"In the seventeenth year of Yǒng'ān,
the dukes and ministers, because divine sparrows of five colors soared and gathered in the capital,
raised their cups to offer longevity toasts,
and ordered Jiǎ Kuí to compose the 'Ode to the Divine Sparrows.'"
Soaring with white feathers in the Eastern Garden.
From the Yān Shū:
"During Emperor Mǐn's reign, due to an unusual sparrow, the Eastern Garden was renamed the White Sparrow Garden."
Holding a slingshot, hearing Zhuāng Xīn's persuasion,
from the Zhànguó Cè:
"Zhuāng Xīn said to the King of Chǔ:
'The sparrow pecks downward at a hundred grains,
rests upward in lush trees,
flaps its wings and spreads its feathers,
thinking itself free from worry.
It does not know that the young nobles, left hand holding a slingshot,
right hand gripping pellets,
will aim at its neck.'"
Staining clothes, hearing Shàorú's words.
See the annotation in the "Lù Fù": "Shàorú borrowed words about catching sparrows."
The marvel of Jùgōng in Dōnglái,
from the Hànwǔ Gùshì:
"Sūn Qīng was appointed as a court gentleman,
holding a tally to await the spirits.
From Tàishì to Dōnglái,
he said he saw a man,
five zhàng tall,
who called himself Jùgōng,
leading a yellow dog and holding a yellow sparrow,
saying he wished to see the Son of Heaven,
then suddenly disappeared."
In the Western Regions, there was Bān Chāo's tribute.
From the Cáo Dàgū Collection:
"Elder brother Chāo was Protector of the Western Regions,
and presented a large sparrow.
An edict ordered Dàgū to compose an ode."
Nesting on a cassia tree, forming a poem,
from an ancient poem:
"The cassia tree bears no fruit in autumn,
a yellow sparrow nests atop its peak."
Gathering in Bùqí, composing an ode.
From Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū:
"Dǒng Zhòng of Lángyá was the magistrate of Bùqí.
A red sparrow nested and fed its young on a mulberry tree in front of the hall.
The people composed a song and ode for him."
There were also those born by the Sān Hé, flapping their wings,
from Sīmǎ Biāo's poem "To Shān Jùyuán":
"Graceful wild green sparrow,
your nature is solitary and extraordinary.
Once born by the side of the Sān Hé,
you flap your wings in the emperor's domain."
Emerging from Bèiduō, skilled in dancing,
from the Shùyì Jì:
"In the first year of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the people of Bèiduō presented dancing sparrows.
The Duke of Zhōu ordered them returned."
Hearing of alighting on the shoulder of Pān Lè,
from the Běishǐ:
"Pān Lè,
courtesy name Xiàngguì.
At his birth,
a sparrow alighted on his mother's left shoulder.
Diviners all said it was an omen of wealth and nobility,
hence he was named Xiàngguì,
later used as his courtesy name."
Seen entering the bosom of Tángzǔ.
From the Tángshū:
"Emperor Gāozǔ executed Wáng Wēi in Tàiyuán,
and a white sparrow flew into Emperor Gāozǔ's bosom."
Flowing fire was heard of with Tàibó,
from the Shàngshū Zhōnghòu:
"Heaven descended its mandate,
Tàibó went out hunting,
reaching Xiányáng.
Heaven thundered greatly,
fire descended,
transforming into a white sparrow,
which carried a tally and alighted on the official carriage.
The writing said:
'Tàibó,
a hegemon.'"
Probing for nestlings also passed down about Zhǔfù.
From the Shǐjì:
"King Wǔlíng of Zhào styled himself Zhǔfù.
He deposed his eldest son Zhāng and passed the state to Prince Hé.
Zhǔfù traveled to Shāqiū,
Prince Zhāng rebelled,
fought with Hé,
and was defeated.
Zhāng fled to Zhǔfù,
Zhǔfù opened the door to him,
and Hé then besieged Zhǔfù.
Starving, he probed for sparrow nestlings to eat them.
After more than three months,
he eventually starved to death at Shāqiū."
If one idly roams within the fence,
how can one know the soaring of the roc!
They are called the Four Divine Creatures.
If kept as domestic animals, then beasts will not run wild.
The *Book of Rites* says:
If the qilin is kept as a domestic animal,
then beasts will not run wild.
"Xuè,"
pronounced as "hū jué" in reverse.
Whenever they fight, the sun will inevitably lose its light.
The *Chūnqiū Kǒng Yǎn Tú* says:
The qilin
is the essence of wood.
When they fight, the sun loses its light.
The annotation says:
The qilin and dragon, as the essence of lesser yang, fight on the earth,
then the sun and moon will also contend in the heavens.
They roam in the suburban wilderness.
The *Book of Rites* says:
Heaven does not withhold its ways,
earth does not withhold its treasures,
and humans do not withhold their true feelings.
Therefore, qilin and phoenixes roam in the suburban wilderness,
while tortoises and dragons dwell in palace ponds.
They stay far from nets and traps.
The *Qílín Zàn* by Wǔzhāo Wáng of Xīliáng says:
They roam only in chosen lands,
soaring before settling.
They do not enter pitfalls,
nor are they ensnared by nets.
Arriving without virtue,
they break their legs for it.
Thus, they presented their essence at the Hàn court,
as seen in Mèngjiān's rhapsody.
Bān Gù's *Liǎng Dū Fù* says:
The qilin of Jiǔzhēn,
the horses of Dàyuān.
Elephant
Among the beauties of the south,
are the rhinoceroses and elephants of Liáng Shān.
From the Ěryǎ.
Zhōu Chéng submitted a memorial,
saying they could be washed to cure illness;
The Táng Shū says:
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng,
the state of Zhōu Chéng sent an envoy to present a memorial stating:
"In the state of Hējiā, there is a white elephant,
possessing both majestic power,
and the ability to avert disasters and calamities.
If one washes its tusks with water,
and drinks it, illnesses are cured.
We request troops be dispatched to welcome and retrieve it for presentation."
The Emperor said:
"Sources of no benefit
must not be indulged."
He rewarded the envoy and sent him away.
Cāng Shū was wise,
and also weighed an elephant by marking a boat.
See the note on "Cāng Shū Weighs an Elephant" in the "Rhapsody on Boats".
Then there is binding blades to the trunk,
The Sān Guó Diǎn Lüè says:
The Zhōu army approached Jiānglíng,
and the Liáng forces came out to battle.
Liáng armored two elephants,
bound blades to their trunks,
and ordered Kūnlún slaves to drive them into battle.
Yáng Zhōng shot at them,
and the elephants turned and fled.
Tying torches to the tail.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
When Wú attacked Chǔ,
Zhēn Yǐngù was in the same boat as the king.
The king ordered him to drive torch-bearing elephants to charge the Wú army.
Although its substance is larger than an ox,
the Wénzǐ says:
Seeing an elephant's tusk,
one knows it is larger than an ox.
Yet its eyes are no bigger than a pig's.
Wàn Zhèn's Nán Zhōu Yì Wù Zhì says:
The elephant as a beast
has a particularly strange form.
Its body is several times that of an ox,
