its eyes no bigger than a pig's,
its trunk serves the mouth,
looking at the head, it resembles a tail,
it bears heavy loads over great distances,
moving like a mountain shifting.
It gives birth once and nurses for three years.
The Shuōwén says:
Elephants
give birth once every three years.
Ultimately, it is burned for its body because of its tusks.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
The elephant has tusks,
which cause its body to be burned.
As for releasing them on the sunny side of Jīng Shān,
the Táng Shū says:
Since the Yǒnghuī era,
the state of Wéndān repeatedly presented tame elephants,
thirty-two in total,
all kept within the palace grounds,
some quite skilled at dancing.
When Emperor Dézōng ascended the throne,
he considered it contrary to their nature,
and released them on the sunny side of Jīng Shān.
Raising them in marshlands.
The Jìn Zhū Gōng Zàn says:
During the Jìn dynasty, Nányuè presented an elephant,
which was raised in marshlands.
Although it receives its essence from Yáoguāng,
the Chūnqiū Yùndǒu Shū says:
The Yáoguāng star scattered and became elephants.
In the end, it is controlled by Yuè children.
The Lùnhéng says:
An ox ten arm-spans around
is driven by a shepherd boy;
an elephant several yards tall
is hooked by Yuè children.
As for emerging from the long isle of the Yī Shuǐ,
Wáng Sháozhī's Shǐxīng Jì says:
The Yī Shuǐ has an isle,
the isle is ten lǐ wide,
with herds of elephants and wild oxen.
Born in the foreign land of Qiántuó,
the Hòu Wèi Shū says:
The state of Qiántuó was fond of warfare,
possessing seven hundred battle elephants.
Ten men rode one elephant,
all holding weapons.
Its gall bladder shifts with the moon,
the Lǐng Biǎo Yì Lù says:
Elephant meat has twelve kinds.
The gall bladder is attached to the liver,
shifting with the moon
among the various meats.
The trunk serves the mouth.
See the note above on "eyes no bigger than a pig's".
Encountering a lion, it must flee,
the Sòng Shū says:
Zōng Què attacked the southern barbarians.
The barbarians armored their elephants,
forming an endless front and rear.
Què knew that lions could subdue all beasts,
so he ordered lion dancers to perform before the formation.
The elephants all turned and fled,
and he thus defeated them.
Looking at its shed tusk, it still cherishes it.
The Yì Wù Zhì says:
When an elephant's tusk falls out yearly, it still cherishes it,
digging the ground to hide it.
People make fake tusks to secretly replace them.
Seeing its skin, it weeps.
Jiǎng Jì's Wàn Jī Lùn says:
Zhuāng Zhōu sang when his wife died.
Now an elephant weeps upon seeing its calf's skin.
How could Zhōu bear it!
Fighting for the trunk to eat.
The Lǐng Biǎo Yì Lù says:
People of Cháo and Xún captured an elephant,
and fought to eat its trunk,
saying it was fat and delicious.
Facing execution, its weeping blood is heard,
the Jìn Zhū Gōng Zàn says:
During the Jìn dynasty, Nányuè sent a tame elephant.
Later, the elephant used its trunk to strike and kill a person.
The authorities petitioned to have it killed.
The elephant wept, blood flowing to the ground,
and did not dare move.
Thereupon, they all returned it to Yuè.
Losing its mate also leads to continuous tears.
the Bówù Zhì says:
Elephants each have mates, male and female.
When one female dies,
for over a hundred days,
refuses to drink wine or eat meat alone.
If asked the reason,
it immediately sheds tears as if in mourning.
They come from Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán,
the Wú Lù ‧ Dìlǐ Jīng says:
The Jiǔzhēn commandery has many elephants,
Rìnán also abounds with them.
They plow in Cāngwú and Kuàijī.
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
Shùn was buried in Cāngwú.
Below, herds of elephants plowed the fields.
Entering his dream thoughts,
it already foretold disaster for Zhāng Mào;
the Jìn Shū says:
Zhāng Mào once dreamed of a great elephant,
and asked Wàn Tuī about it.
Tuī said:
"You will become a grand administrator,
but will not fare well.
Now the elephant
is a great beast.
'Beast'
means 'to guard'.
Yet it is burned for its body because of its tusks.
You will surely later be killed by others."
Mào later became grand administrator of Wúxīng commandery.
When Wáng Dūn harbored imperial ambitions,
Mào held firm and would not yield.
Dūn destroyed him.
Causing them to lead the dance,
is also credited to Hè Qí.
the Wú Shū says:
Hè Qí was grand administrator of Xīndū.
Sūn Quán came out to bid him farewell,
and had a musical performance with elephant dancers.
Quán said to Qí:
"Now the realm is pacified,
causing distant customs to present treasures,
and cunning beasts to lead the dance—
if not you, then who!"
Tiger
The fierce devouring of the striped tiger
evokes the descent of the Pivot Star.
The *Yun Dou Shu* states:
"The Pivot Star disperses and becomes the tiger."
It is already regarded as the chief of beasts.
The *Feng Su Tong* states:
"The tiger is a yang creature,
the chief of all beasts."
It is also called the Lord of the Mountains.
The *Shuō Wén* states:
"The tiger
is the lord of mountain beasts."
Its gaze is fiercely intent.
The *Yì* states:
"The tiger gazes fiercely,
its desires are pressing."
Its stripes are beautifully patterned.
The *Kǎo Yì Yóu* states:
"Three times nine is twenty-seven;
yang energy is complete,
therefore the tiger is born in the seventh month.
Yang is established in seven,
therefore the tiger's head and tail are seven feet long.
The striped pattern
is a mixture of yin and yang."
Niú Āi transformed his body after seven days.
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* states:
"In the past, Niú Āi was ill for seven days
and transformed into a tiger.
His elder brother opened the door and entered;
the tiger pounced and killed him.
While he was a tiger,
he did not know he had once been a man;
while he was a man,
he did not know he would become a tiger."
Fēng Shào devoured people in a single day.
The *Shù Yì Jì* states:
"Fēng Shào, the Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng in the Hàn,
one day suddenly transformed into a tiger
and devoured the people of the commandery.
The people cried out, 'Lord Fēng!'
People of the time said:
'Do not become a Lord Fēng,
who in life did not govern the people but instead devoured them.'"
Then there is carving jade to form its fur.
The *Shí Yí Jì* states:
"In the second year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
a painter from the state of Jiǎn Xiāo named Liè Yì
carved two white jade tigers.
Their fur appeared lifelike,
but he did not dot their two eyes.
Shǐ Huáng sent other artisans to dot them at night.
At dawn,
the tigers flew away.
The following year,
Nánjùn presented two white tigers.
Upon looking at them,
they were the jade tigers.
He ordered their eyes to be removed,
and then they could not fly away again."
There is casting bronze to make vessels.
The *Xī Jīng Zá Jì* states:
"Lǐ Guǎng was hunting north of Míng Shān
and saw a crouching tiger.
He killed it with a single arrow,
used its head as a pillow
to show he had subdued the fierce beast.
He cast a bronze likeness of its form
to use as a chamber pot,
to show his contempt and humiliation of it."
Lǐ Yǔ entered the pit and cut the rope.
The *Hàn Shū* states:
"Lǐ Yǔ was brave.
The Emperor summoned him and ordered him to stab a tiger.
He was lowered into the enclosure by rope;
before reaching the ground,
an edict was issued to pull him out.
Lǐ Yǔ cut the rope with his sword,
intending to stab the tiger.
The Emperor admired his courage."
Zhū Hài in the cage split his eyelids.
The *Liè Shì Zhuàn* states:
"Qín summoned Lord Wú Jì,
but he did not go,
instead sending Zhū Hài to present a pair of jade discs.
The King of Qín was furious
and had Zhū Hài placed in a tiger enclosure.
Hài glared at the tiger,
his eyelids splitting and blood splattering,
but the tiger ultimately did not dare to move."
There is also the endangerment of Empress Lǐ within the palace.
The *Yōu Míng Lù* states:
"Lǐ Tàihòu, mother of Jìn Xiàowǔ, was originally of low status.
Jiǎn Wén had no sons,
so he once ordered skilled physiognomists to examine the palace women.
Lǐ Tàihòu, serving as a menial laborer, was not among them.
The physiognomist pointed at her:
'This one shall bear a noble son,
but will suffer a tiger calamity.'
The Emperor thus favored her,
and she gave birth to Xiàowǔ and Lord Dào Zǐ of Kuàijī.
After ascending to the honored position,
believing the physiognomist's prediction,
she wondered about the tiger harm,
as she had never seen a tiger in her life.
She then ordered someone to paint a tiger,
and while playfully striking the tiger with her hand,
her hand swelled and became painful.
She then fell ill and passed away."
Licking Jiè Xiàng in the mountains.
The *Shén Xiān Zhuàn* states:
"Jiè Xiàng entered the mountains
hoping to encounter immortals.
Lying on a stone,
a tiger came
and licked Xiàng's forehead.
Xiàng awoke
and said to the tiger:
'If Heaven sent you to guard me,
then stay;
if the mountain spirit sent you to test me,
then go away on your own.'
The tiger then left."
How could it climb a tree?
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* states:
"A snake cannot be made to have feet,
a tiger cannot be made to climb trees."
It can only generate wind.
The *Wàn Bì Shù* states:
"When a tiger roars, valley winds arise."
Bowing its head and submitting to punishment.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"Tóng Huī, styled Hàn Zōng,
was the magistrate of Bùqí.
A householder had been harmed by a tiger,
so he set a trap and captured it,
taking two tigers alive.
Huī cursed the tigers, saying:
'Heaven gives birth to all things,
but humans are the most precious.
Tigers and wolves should eat the six domestic animals,
yet you brutally harm humans.
The king's law: those who kill humans shall die;
those who injure humans shall be judged by law.
If you are the killer, you should bow your head and submit to punishment;
if you know you are not, you should cry out and proclaim your innocence.'
One tiger lowered its head and closed its eyes,
appearing terrified,
and he immediately killed it.
The other leaped up vigorously,
so he released it."
Wagging its tail and begging for food.
The *Hàn Shū – Sīmǎ Qiān's Letter* states:
"A fierce tiger in the mountains
terrifies all beasts,
but when in a cage or pit,
it wags its tail and begs for food—
this is the gradual effect of accumulated intimidation and constraint."
Sēng Zhào recognized the roar from Nán Shān.
The *Sú Shuō* states:
"Shěn Sēng Zhào of Qí once went on an inspection hunt
but returned midway.
His attendants asked:
'What is the reason?'
He replied:
'The state has border affairs;
I must return to handle them.'
They asked:
'How did you know?'
He said:
'Just now I heard the roar of a tiger from Nán Shān, that's how.'
Shortly after, a messenger arrived."
Lǐ Guǎng shot the stone in Běipíng.
The *Hàn Shū* states:
"Lǐ Guǎng was out hunting in Běipíng
and saw a stone in the grass.
Thinking it was a tiger, he shot it,
the arrow piercing the stone up to its feathers.
Upon looking, it was a stone.
The next day he shot at it,
but ultimately could not pierce it."
Eating meat, then Shì Zǔ ordered it shot.
The *Wèi Míng Chén Zòu* states:
"During Shì Zǔ's time, someone presented a tiger.
He asked what the tiger ate.
The reply was:
'It eats meat.'
The edict stated:
'The common people are weary of chaff and husks;
how can we bear to feed meat to a tiger?'
He then ordered the Tiger Guard to shoot it."
Climbing the saddle, then Zhāng Zhāo changed countenance.
The *Wú Zhì* states:
"Sūn Quán often went hunting
and would ride a horse to shoot tigers.
A tiger once charged and climbed, grasping the horse's saddle.
Zhāng Zhāo changed countenance and remonstrated.
Quán apologized, saying:
'In my youth, I did not consider matters far enough.'
Yet he still could not stop."
Then he made a tiger-hunting chariot.
Some call it Lǐ Ěr,
as the Customs and Manners states:
"Tigers are called Lǐ Ěr."
Folklore says tigers were originally transformed from a Mr. Lǐ of Zhōnglú in Nánjùn,
so calling them Lǐ Ěr
pleases them;
calling them Bān
angers them.
Also, the Dialects says:
Between the Jiāng, Huái, and Southern Chǔ regions, they are called Lǐ Ěr.
When a tiger is eating and hears its name, it stops immediately,
because it touches upon its taboo.
Some call it Wūtú.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Dòu Bóbǐ had relations with a woman of Yún,
and she gave birth to Wén.
The Lady of Yún had him abandoned in the marsh.
A tiger suckled him.
The Lord of Yún was hunting
and saw him,
so he had him taken in.
The people of Chǔ call milk "gǔ",
and call a tiger "wūtú",
so they named him Dòu Gǔ Wūtú.
Note:
"Mèng" means
marsh.
"Gǔ"
is pronounced nǎihòu qiē.
"Tú" is pronounced like "tú".
Some are born on Mèng Mountain.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
Mèng Mountain,
the mountain where birds and rats share burrows,
has many white tigers on its summit.
Some are kept in Dōngyú.
The Biography of King Mù says:
There was a tiger in the reeds.
Gāo Bēnróng, one of the Seven Elite Warriors,
captured it alive and presented it.
The Son of Heaven ordered it caged and kept in Dōngyú,
which was called "Tiger Prison".
There was even Zhōnghuáng who could wrestle them.
The Shīzǐ says:
Zhōnghuáng Bó said:
"I hold the monkey of Tàiháng in my left hand,
and wrestle the dappled tiger with my right,
only the elephant I have yet to try."
Féng Fù was skilled at capturing them.
The Mèngzǐ says:
Féng Fù was skilled at wrestling tigers.
Once, a crowd was chasing a tiger.
Seeing Féng Fù,
they hurried to welcome him.
Lǚ Méng explored the den without fear.
The Records of Wú says:
Lǚ Méng wished to join the army.
His mother tried to stop him.
Méng said:
"If one does not enter the tiger's den,
how can one obtain the tiger's cub?"
Wáng Róng approached the cage without fear.
The Biographies of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove says:
Emperor Míng of Wèi had a cage set up on the Xuānwǔ Grounds for tiger fights,
ordering strong men to wrestle them.
Róng was seven years old
and also went to watch.
The tiger seized a moment, pressed against the cage, and roared.
Its voice shook the earth.
All the spectators were terrified and fell over,
but Róng stood calmly unmoved.
The Emperor saw him from the tower,
sent someone to ask his name, and thought him extraordinary.
The mournful weeping moved even Zhòngní.
The Book of Rites says:
Confucius passed by the side of Tài Mountain.
There was a woman weeping mournfully at a grave.
The Master was moved and listened.
He sent Zǐgòng to ask her:
"Your weeping
seems as if you have suffered repeated misfortunes?"
She replied:
"Yes.
Formerly, my father-in-law died by a tiger.
My husband also died by a tiger,
and now my son has died the same way."
The Master said:
"Why not leave this place?"
She said:
"There is no oppressive government here."
The Master said:
"Remember this, my children:
Oppressive government is more fearsome than a tiger."
Bound tightly, he evoked even more pity from Lǚ Bù.
The Records of Heroes says:
Lord Cáo captured Lǚ Bù.
Bù looked at Liú Bèi and said:
"Xuándé,
you are a guest seated above,
I am a surrendered captive.
The ropes bind me so tightly;
can you not say a single word?"
Cáo said:
"Binding a hungry tiger must be done tightly."
Then he ordered Bù's bonds loosened.
As for Liáng Yǎng, he reared them with method.
The Lièzǐ says:
Liáng Yǎng's method of rearing tigers
was that generally, complying with them pleased them,
opposing them angered them—
such is the nature of creatures of blood and energy.
Those who feed tigers dare not give them living creatures,
for fear of arousing their killing rage.
They dare not give them whole creatures,
for fear of arousing their tearing rage.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ stabbed them appropriately.
The Later Tales of the Spring and Autumn says:
King Huì of Qín said to Chén Zhěn:
"Now Hán and Wèi are attacking each other.
A year has passed without resolution.
Some tell me it is expedient to rescue them,
others say it is not expedient to rescue them.
You devise a plan for me."
Zhěn said:
"Formerly, Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was about to stab a tiger,
when a young servant stopped him, saying:
'Two tigers are just now eating an ox.
The ox is sweet, so they will surely fight over it.
Fighting will lead to combat.
In combat, the larger will be injured,
the smaller will die.
Then stab the injured one;
with one move, you will gain the fame of getting two tigers.'
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ thought this right
and stood waiting.
After a while,
the two tigers indeed fought.
The larger was injured,
the smaller died.
With one move, he indeed achieved the feat of two tigers.
Now Hán and Wèi are attacking each other.
A year has passed without resolution.
This will surely result in the larger state injured,
the smaller state destroyed.
Attack the injured one then;
with one move, you will gain two substantial results.
This is like the case of Biàn Zhuāngzǐ stabbing the tigers."
The King said:
"Good."
Misled by slander, he spoke of tigers in the market.
The Hánzǐ says:
Páng Gòng was a hostage with the crown prince in Hándān.
He said to the King of Wèi:
"If one person says there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The King said:
"No."
"If two people say it,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The King said:
"No."
"If three people say it,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
"I would believe it."
Páng Gòng said:
"That there is no tiger in the market is clear,
yet three people saying it creates a market tiger.
Now Hándān is farther from Wèi than the market,
and those criticizing me number more than three.
I hope Your Majesty will examine this."
When Páng Gòng returned from Hándān,
he indeed was not allowed to enter.
Moved by magical arts, he returned the child.
The Continued Records of Searching for the Divine says:
Wú Měng possessed magical arts.
Zōu Huìzhèng of the same county invited Měng
and at night burned incense in his courtyard.
Suddenly a tiger came, picked up Zhèng's child, and leapt over the fence.
Měng said:
"Do not worry;
he will return shortly."
The tiger went several tens of paces,
then suddenly brought the child back.
Zhèng then devoted himself earnestly
and begged to become a good Daoist.
Though its patterned fur is not yet formed,
it already has the spirit to devour an ox.
The Shīzǐ says:
The cub of a tiger or leopard,
though its patterns are not yet formed,
already has the spirit to devour an ox.
When claws and teeth are fully equipped,
then it fully possesses the power to subdue dogs.
The Hánzǐ says:
The reason a tiger can subdue a dog
is its claws and teeth.
If the tiger were deprived of its claws and teeth
and the dog were given them,
then the tiger would instead be subdued by the dog.
The ruler uses punishments and rewards to control his ministers.
If you, my lord, lose control over punishments and rewards,
and let your ministers wield them,
then you, my lord, will instead be controlled by your ministers.
As for Zhí Fǎxióng quelling violence,
the *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Fǎ Xióng was the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
The commandery bordered the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers, with the Yúnmèng marshes and lakes,
where tigers and wolves caused much violence.
The previous administrator offered rewards and recruited people to set traps and hunt them,
but many people were instead harmed by them.
Xióng sent a dispatch to the subordinate counties, saying:
"Tigers and wolves are in the mountains and forests,
just as people dwell in cities and towns.
In the eras of perfect transformation in antiquity,
fierce beasts did not cause disturbances,
all because benevolence extended to the flying and running creatures.
Although I, the Grand Administrator, lack virtue,
how dare I forget this principle?
Upon receipt of this dispatch,
you are to destroy the cages and pits,
and must not recklessly hunt."
After this, the harm from tigers gradually ceased.
Avoiding Liú Líng and moving far away,
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Liú Líng of Yùzhāng,
styled Mènggāo,
served as the Chief of Ānchéng in Chángshā.
Previously, there were many tigers,
and the common people suffered from them,
all moving to other counties.
When Líng took office,
he cultivated virtuous governance.
After over a month,
all the tigers left the territory,
and the people all returned.
Moved by Liú Kūn's governance in Hóngnóng,
the *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Liú Kūn, styled Huángōng,
served as Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng during the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
Previously, the post roads of Xiáo and Miǎn had many tigers,
and travel was blocked.
Kūn governed for three years,
benevolent transformation became widespread,
and the tigers all carried their cubs across the river.
Later, he was summoned to be the Superintendent of the Imperial Household.
An imperial edict questioned Kūn, saying:
"Previously, in Jiānglíng,
you reversed the wind and extinguished a fire;
later, as Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng,
the tigers crossed north over the river.
What virtuous governance did you practice to achieve this?"
Kūn replied:
"It was merely by chance."
Those around him all laughed at his simple and inarticulate manner,
but the Emperor sighed and said:
"These are the words of a gentleman of noble character."
He ordered them recorded in the official records.
Recognizing Sòng Jūn's administration in Jiǔjiāng,
the *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Sòng Jūn was transferred to Jiǔjiāng.
The commandery had much violence from tigers,
which repeatedly plagued the people.
Traps and pits were often set up with rewards,
yet many injuries and deaths still occurred.
When Jūn arrived,
he issued a dispatch to the subordinate counties, saying:
"Tigers and leopards are in the mountains,
turtles and fish are in the water,
each has its place of reliance.
To laboriously set traps and hunt them
is not the fundamental way of showing compassion and concern.
You must strive to expel the treacherous and greedy,
and think of promoting loyalty and goodness.
You may remove all traps and pits,
and abolish the hunting quotas."
Afterwards, it was reported that the tigers together floated east and crossed the river.
Burning tiger skin to ward off evil,
the *Fēngsú Tōng* says:
If a person suddenly falls ill,
burn tiger skin and drink the ashes.
Wearing it on one's clothing
also wards off evil,
and it is very effective.
Hanging a tiger nose aids in having sons.
The *Hé Tú* says:
Hang a tiger nose above the door,
it benefits officials and their descendants,
who will wear official seals and ribbons.
Hang a tiger nose inside the door,
after a full year,
take it down, burn it into powder,
and give it to your wife to drink.
Within two months, she will bear a son, a noble child.
Do not let others know,
for if it is divulged, it will not be effective.
Also, do not let your wife see it.
Fúnán is known for deciding lawsuits,
the *Yì Yuàn* says:
Fán Xún, King of Fúnán, often kept tigers and crocodiles.
If there was a lawsuit and the right and wrong were unknown,
he would throw the parties to the fish [crocodiles] and tigers.
If the fish and tigers did not devour them,
then they were in the right.
The people of Huìmò
worship the tiger as a god,
there must be a reason for it.
Dùshuò is also said to feed on ghosts.
The *Fēngsú Tōng* says:
Peachwood figures, reed ropes, and painted tigers are placed at doors.
According to this, in the time of the Yellow Emperor,
there were two brothers, Shén Shū and Yù Lǜ,
whose nature enabled them to capture ghosts.
Under a peach tree on Dùshuò Mountain, they examined all the ghosts.
Those who without reason brought calamity upon people
were bound with reed ropes
and given to the tiger to eat.
Therefore, officials often at the year-end La festival adorned peachwood figures
and painted tigers on doors.
Lifespan reaching a thousand years,
the *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Tigers, deer, and rabbits all live a thousand years.
Those reaching five hundred years turn white.
Length exceeding a hundred lǐ,
the *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Cài Dàn entered the mountains,
and upon returning home,
said he had been exiled to Kūnlún.
At the foot of Kūnlún Mountain, there were white tigers and boa constrictors over a hundred lǐ long,
their teeth as large as boats holding three hundred hú.
Shí Qián leaped and pulled out arrows,
the *Shì Shuō* says:
When Huán Shíqián was a child,
he followed his father, the General Who Conquers the West, on a hunt.
There was a tiger hit by several arrows,
lying on the ground.
The generals challenged Shíqián, saying:
"Can our fierce young man pull out the tiger's arrows?"
Shíqián went to the tiger and pulled out one arrow.
The tiger leaped,
and Shíqián also leaped,
leaping even higher than the tiger.
The tiger lay down again,
and Shíqián pulled out another arrow.
Yí Jiù shouted and made it flatten its ears.
The *Suǒ Yǔ* says:
The King of Zhōu wanted to kill Prince Yí Jiù and establish Bó Fú.
He released a tiger to seize him,
but Yí Jiù shouted at it,
and the tiger flattened its ears and submitted.
Some were startled and released in the market,
the *Guǎnzǐ* says:
In the time of Jié, there were thirty thousand female musicians.
He released tigers in the market,
to watch people's terror.
Some swayed and crossed water.
The *Fēngsú Tōng* says:
Sòng Jūn was Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng,
and tigers carried their cubs across the river.
According to this, tiger fur sways,
how could it brave the waves of Yáng Hóu?
A local saying goes:
"The fox wishes to cross the river,
but what can it do about its tail?"
Even boatmen are afraid,
let alone a tiger!
As for Guō Wén removing a bone,
the *Xiàozǐ Zhuàn* says:
Guō Wén removed a bone stuck in a tiger's throat,
and the tiger brought a deer to repay him.
Zǐhuá cut a sheep.
The *Shāng Shì Shì Zhuàn* says:
Liàng, styled Zǐhuá,
studied the *Gōngyáng Commentary* in his youth,
and was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt at fourteen.
Arriving at Yángchéng, he encountered tigers fighting over a sheep.
Liàng then pressed his sword, glared fiercely,
cut the sheep's belly,
and the tigers each took half and left.
Some assisted Qū Bǎo's sacrifices,
Wáng Fú's *Ānchéng Jì* says:
There was a man named Dū Qū Bǎo,
a person of the Later Hàn.
While in mourning for his father,
neighbors were hunting a tiger.
The tiger ran and entered his hut,
so he immediately covered and hid it with a straw raincoat.
The neighbors followed the tracks and asked Bǎo,
but Bǎo said:
"How could a tiger be something worth caring for and hiding?"
Later, this tiger sent birds and beasts to assist Bǎo's sacrifices.
His filial and compassionate will
communicated with the spirits,
and he became known for this.
Some escorted Wáng Yè's funeral.
The *Chénliú Qíjiù Zhuàn* says:
Wáng Yè, styled Zǐxiāng,
was Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and had virtuous governance.
He died in Zhījiāng,
There were three white tigers,
lowering their heads and dragging their tails,
keeping guard by his side.
After the funeral procession departed,
once they crossed the prefectural border,
they suddenly vanished.
Together, they erected a stele inscription,
naming it the "Zhījiāng White Tigers."
Some practiced the art of subduing with red blades.
The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
Jū Dàolóng was skilled in illusionary arts,
and once said that a man from the Eastern Sea, Huáng Shào, excelled in illusions.
At the end of the Qin dynasty, a white tiger appeared in the Eastern Sea,
and an imperial decree sent Huáng Gōng with a red blade to subdue it.
When his art failed,
he was killed by the tiger.
The people of the Sānfǔ region customarily used this as entertainment.
Some wore the seal of the Yellow God.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
Those entering the mountains wear the Yellow God Yuèzhāng seal,
which is four inches wide,
with one hundred and twenty characters inscribed.
Sealed with clay,
and placed in all four directions around their dwelling within a hundred paces,
then tigers and wolves dare not approach.
Was it only the purple kudzu that verified the transformation in Jiānglíng?
The *Records of the Broadly Learned* states:
In Jiānglíng, there were fierce people
who could transform into tigers.
It is also said that tigers transform into humans,
fond of wearing purple kudzu garments,
and lacking heels on their feet.
Or perhaps the white substance served as an auspicious sign for the Wei dynasty.
The *Weilüe* states:
When Emperor Wén intended to accept the abdication,
the commanderies and kingdoms reported twenty-seven appearances of white tigers.
Horse
The cavalryman captured Cáo Cāo but did not recognize him,
and asked:
"Where is Governor Cáo?"
The reply was:
"The one riding the yellow horse is he."
Thus, Cáo Cāo escaped.
Swift and majestic, half-skyward,
Yán Yánnián, by imperial decree, composed the "Ode to the Chestnut-White Horse," saying:
Distinguished from the herd, surpassing the multitude,
swift and majestic, peerlessly lofty.
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital" says:
The dragon-sparrow coils and winds,
the heavenly horse reaches half the sky.
Majestic and prancing, soaring high.
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Plowing" says:
The golden carriage shines with brilliant light,
the dragon-steed prances, majestic and soaring.
Resembling the moon in swiftness,
"Chūnqiū Shuōtící" says:
The essence of earth becomes the horse,
born in the twelfth month,
responding to yin and harmonizing with yang to unite their achievements.
The moon moves swiftly,
therefore the horse is good at running.
Traversing the earth without bounds.
"The Book of Changes · Kūn Hexagram" says:
The mare is of the earth's kind,
traversing the earth without bounds.
Some depict the image of a white horse,
"The Book of Changes" says:
A white horse, pure as feathers.
Some transmit the verse of lushness.
"The Book of Songs" says:
My horse is a dappled gray,
the six reins are lush and glossy.
Praising Bóhòu for resembling a dog,
Xiè Chéng's "Hòu Hànshū" says:
Zhū Zhèn, styled Bóhòu,
was of a stern and fierce nature.
Initially serving as an attendant,
he impeached Shàn Kuāng, the governor of Jìyīn, for corruption,
and implicated Kuāng's brother, the Palace Attendant and General of Chariots and Cavalry, Chāo.
A saying among the Three Ducal Offices went:
"The carriage like a chicken roost, the horse like a dog,
hating evil like the wind is Zhū Bóhòu."
Admiring Zhāng Huàn for resembling a sheep.
See the annotation in the "Ode to Gold": "Entering the bosom, as seen with Zhāng Huàn."
Additionally, there is Zhèng Zhuāng setting up relay stations,
"Hànshū" says:
Zhèng Dāngshí served as a Gentleman of the Heir Apparent.
On the fifth day, during the washing and resting period,
he often stationed relay horses in the suburbs of Cháng'ān,
to receive and send off guests,
day and night without cease.
Wànshí showing respect to carriage horses,
"Hànshū" says:
Wànshí Jūn Shí Fèn,
when passing palace gates, would always dismount from his carriage and hasten on foot,
and upon seeing carriage horses, would always show respect.
Drinking from the springs of the Great Wall,
an ancient Music Bureau poem exists titled "Drinking Horse at the Great Wall Springs."
Galloping along the road to Zhāngtái.
See the annotation in the "Ode to the Fan": "The Capital Governor galloping on horseback."
Swift as the passing wind,
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
The team of green dragons,
the steed of the passing wind,
unless one first becomes the Son of Heaven,
cannot be fully obtained.
The annotation states:
Qīnglóng and Yífēng,
are both names of horses.
Lofty as the flying hare.
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
If one must wait for Yǎoniǎo and Fēitù to harness them,
then the world would have no carriages to ride.
Practicing on ant hills and thus prevailing,
"Jìn Jì" says:
Wáng Zhàn possessed hidden virtue.
His nephew Wáng Jì was fond of horses,
and the steed he rode was swift and excellent,
which he cherished greatly.
Zhàn said:
"Recently, I saw the postal superintendent's horse,
which should surpass this one."
Jì did not believe him.
He took the postal superintendent's horse and tested it with Zhàn.
Zhàn said:
"Galloping straight on level ground,
how can one distinguish the horses?"
Thereupon, they raced on an ant hill,
and Jì's horse indeed stumbled.
Regretting the splashboard and refusing to cross.
"Jìnshū" says:
Wáng Jì was skilled in understanding horse nature.
Once, he rode a horse
fitted with a linked splashboard.
When they came to water ahead,
the horse absolutely refused to cross.
Jì said:
"This must be because it regrets the splashboard."
He had someone remove it,
and the horse then crossed.
Therefore, Dù Yù said that Jì had a horse obsession.
The two central horses leading the way,
"The Book of Songs" says:
The uncle goes hunting,
driving a team of bays,
the two central horses lead the way,
the two side horses follow like geese in flight.
Eight bells regulating the pace.
Yán Yánnián's "Ode to the Chestnut-White Horse" says:
Reining the five commands to march in order,
the sound of eight bells regulates the pace.
The chariot of Qiándàn and Dàbǐng,
see the annotation for "surpassing the kūn and jī birds at Gūyú."
The driving of Wáng Liáng and Zàofǔ.
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
Wáng Liáng
and Zàofǔ were charioteers.
Mounting the chariot and taking the reins,
adjusting their steps in harmony,
the labor and ease were as one.
Galloping with the sun, the suspended peaks do not press close,
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
The sun's course,
one does not see it move.
A fine steed galloping with its back to the sun,
the grass and trees are swept aside,
the suspended peaks have not yet pressed close, yet the sun is already ahead.
Annotation:
Xuánfēng,
refers to the chicken-tongue shape under the horse's hoof.
Becoming a dragon, then auspicious clouds distantly cover it.
"Tángshū" says:
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Huángfǔ Wéimíng, the military commissioner of Lǒngyòu, reported:
"Kùdí Xiàoyì, a man from Lóngzhī County,
had a horse that gave birth to a dragon colt.
After nine days,
its body had scales but no hair grew.
I went to inspect it,
and at that time, five-colored auspicious clouds distantly covered the horse,
lingering without dispersing for a long time.
I request this be recorded by the Historian."
Also, there is Xiàng Jǐ's dappled horse,
"Shǐjì" says:
King Xiàng's fine horse was named Zhuī.
Surrounded at Gāixià,
he sang a sorrowful and indignant song:
"My strength plucked up mountains, my spirit overshadowed the world;
the times are unfavorable, my Zhuī does not advance."
When he reached Wūjiāng,
he said to the village elder:
"I have ridden this horse for five years,
it faced no match,
once galloping a thousand lǐ in a day.
I cannot bear to kill it,
and give it to you, sir."
The Bào family's piebald horse,
"Lièyì Jì" says:
The former Colonel Bào Zǐdū,
when young, was recommended for the annual accounting.
On the road, he encountered a scholar
who suddenly suffered heart pain.
Zǐdū dismounted and massaged him,
but the man abruptly died,
and his name was unknown.
He had a scroll of plain writing
and ten ingots of silver.
Zǐdū sold one ingot
to fund the burial,
placed the rest as a pillow for the deceased,
laid the scroll on his abdomen,
and buried him.
Before reaching the capital,
a piebald horse followed him.
He stayed overnight at the home of a Marquis Within the Passes.
The Marquis asked:
"How did you, sir, come by this horse?"
Zǐdū then explained.
The Marquis was astonished and said:
"This was my son."
He had the coffin brought,
opened it,
and saw the silver and scroll as described.
The Marquis then recommended Zǐdū for an official post,
and he rose to Colonel.
His son Yǒng and grandson Yù both became Colonels,
and they also rode piebald horses.
Thus, a song in the capital went:
"The Bào family's piebald,
three times entering the Colonelcy,
twice entering the Ducal Office.
Though the horse is lean,
its steps are skillful."
Chāngyì rode it under the fruit trees,
"Hànshū" says:
King Hè of Chāngyì summoned the imperial carriage's fruit-tree horse and rode it.
Shí Qìng counted them in the carriage.
The Book of Hàn says:
Shí Qìng was the Grand Coachman.
When driving the carriage out,
the Emperor asked:
"How many horses are in the carriage?"
Qìng counted the horses with his whip and finished,
saying:
"Six horses."
Some run for a whole day without tiring.
The Records of Penetrating the Obscure says:
Dōngfāng Shuò traveled to the land of Jíyún,
east beyond Fúsāng,
and obtained a divine horse,
nine chǐ tall,
with whorled hair on its thighs resembling the shapes of the sun and moon.
The one like the moon
glows at night;
the one like the sun
shines during the day.
Its coat color changes with the four seasons.
The Emperor asked,
and Shuò said:
"Long ago, the Queen Mother of the West rode in her Língguāng carriage to visit the dwelling of the King Father of the East.
She rested this horse in the Zhītián fields where it ate zhī grass.
The King Father became angry,
and abandoned the horse at the Qīngjīn Heavenly Shore.
I arrived at the King Father's altar,
and thus rode it back,
circling the sun three times.
This horse entered the Hàn frontier pass,
and the pass gate was already half-closed."
The Emperor asked its name,
and he said it was Bùjǐng.
Some conceal their form in the void.
The Records of Penetrating the Obscure says:
In the country of Xiūmí, there is a horse like a dragon,
soaring through the void chasing the sun,
sometimes concealing its form in the air,
with only its sound heard.
Viewed like a bolt of white silk,
The Balanced Discourses says:
Confucian texts claim that Confucius and Yán Yuān together ascended the Eastern Mountain of Lǔ,
and looking towards the Chāng Gate of Wú, he said to Yuān:
"What do you see?"
He said:
"A bolt of white silk with something blue in front of it."
The Master said:
"It is a white horse and reed fodder."
Appearing like a swimming dragon.
See the annotation for "Mǎ Shì's traveling carriage" in the "Rhapsody on Water."
As for holding the reins like silk cords,
the two outer horses dancing,
this comes from the Book of Songs.
Three sharing the same trough,
The Book of Jìn says:
Cáo Cāo observed that Sīmǎ Yì had ambitions of heroism and dominance,
and once dreamed of three horses eating from the same trough,
which he greatly detested.
He thus said to Crown Prince Cáo Pī:
"Sīmǎ Yì is no ordinary minister,
he will certainly interfere in your family's affairs."
Five floating across the river.
In the first year of the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn (307 CE),
Emperor Yuán first crossed the river to garrison Jiànyè.
Earlier, during the Tài'ān era of Emperor Huì, a children's rhyme said:
"Five horses float across the river,
one horse transforms into a dragon."
The Emperor, along with the Kings of Xīyáng, Rǔnán, Nándùn, and Pèiyáng, managed to cross,
and Emperor Yuán ultimately ascended the great throne.
Jīsī presented it to please Zhòu,
The Six Secret Teachings says:
King Zhòu of Shāng imprisoned Xībó (King Wén of Zhōu) at Yǒulǐ.
Tàigōng (Jiǎng Zǐyá) and Sǎn Yíshēng offered ten yì of gold,
seeking rare treasures from the world,
and obtained the patterned horse of the Quǎnróng,
with eyes like yellow gold,
a neck like a pheasant's tail,
named Jīsī,
and presented it to the King of Shāng,
thus securing Xībō's release.
Patterned teams were sent to him, leading to Lǔ's downfall.
The School Sayings of Confucius says:
When Confucius was minister of Lǔ,
the people of Qí feared he would make it hegemonic.
Wishing to ruin his proper governance,
they selected eighty women,
dressed them in patterned garments to dance the "Róngjī,"
along with forty teams of patterned horses,
to present to the ruler of Lǔ.
They displayed the female musicians
and arrayed the patterned horses outside the southern high gate of the Lǔ city wall.
The ruler of Lǔ made a circuit to view them,
neglecting government affairs,
and Confucius subsequently departed.
The annotation states:
"Róngjī"
is a dance tune.
Fed with dìhuáng root,
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity says:
Hán Zǐzhì once fed dìhuáng root and licorice to a fifty-year-old horse,
which then gave birth to three foals,
and lived another one hundred and thirty years before dying.
Fed with jujube paste.
See the annotation below for "Yōu Mèng speaking of its funeral rites."
Qí's ancestor, the Soaring Dragon,
The Book of Qí says:
Prince Yáng killed Cāngwú, the King of Sòng.
The Grand Ancestor (Emperor Gāo of Qí) rode his usual red horse into the palace at night.
When he ascended the throne,
he named this horse "General Soaring Dragon."
Xiūzhī's "Displaying Might."
The Continued Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn says:
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī fled to Guǎnggù.
Mùróng Chāo wanted to harm him,
but Xiūzhī was unaware.
The piebald horse he usually rode suddenly neighed continuously and refused to eat,
staring fixedly at the saddle.
Xiūzhī tried putting the saddle on it,
and sat back down,
but the horse became agitated and jumped again.
He then tried riding it to look around.
Just as he went out the gate,
the horse galloped several lǐ.
Looking back at his dwelling place,
soldiers had already arrived.
He then fled south,
and escaped.
Later, he bestowed upon the piebald horse the title "Displaying Might."
In the morning, one only sees its tracks,
by evening, one knows not where it has gone!
Bólè's Classic of Horse Physiognomy says:
A horse born falling to the ground without hair
will travel a thousand lǐ.
One that raises a leg while urinating
will travel five hundred lǐ.
One with prominent sinews stands out for a thousand lǐ.
Knees like round yeast cakes,
a thousand lǐ.
The three armies cannot pursue it,
they only know from where it started,
but not where it rests.
Another version says hooves round like yeast cakes.
There are yīn, xiá,
zhuī, and pī.
The Book of Songs, "Odes of Lǔ" says:
Sturdy are the stallions,
in the distant wilds.
Of those sturdy ones,
there are yīn and xiá,
diàn and yú.
It also says there are zhuī and pī.
The annotation states:
Black mixed with white hair,
is yīn.
Red mixed with white hair,
is xiá.
Blue-gray mixed with white hair,
is zhuī.
Yellow mixed with white hair,
is pī.
Some were revived by meeting Guō Pú,
The Book of Jìn says:
Guō Pú visited General Zhào Gù,
who happened to have his fine horse die.
Pú said:
"I can revive the horse.
Get twenty or thirty strong men,
each holding a long pole.
Go east for thirty lǐ,
where there is a hill, woods, and a village shrine.
Then use the poles to beat and slap about.
You should catch a creature.
Quickly bring it back,
and the horse will revive."
As instructed, they caught a creature,
resembling a monkey.
Seeing the dead horse, it blew on and sucked its nose.
The horse arose,
vigorous and swift as usual,
and the creature from before was no longer seen.
Some rescued Yú Jǐn from peril.
The Book of the Later Zhōu says:
Yú Jǐn once led cavalry in pursuit of the Rúrú,
fighting seventeen battles in total,
and completely subjugating their forces.
He was once surrounded by bandits.
Jǐn rode a fine horse, one purple and one yellow-black,
which the bandits recognized first.
He then had two men each ride one of the horses and charge out of the formation.
The bandits, thinking it was Jǐn,
all rushed to pursue them.
Jǐn then entered the frontier pass.
Yànzǐ with one word ensured punishments were meted justly,
The Annals of Master Yàn says:
Duke Jǐng of Qí had a man care for his beloved horse.
The horse fell ill and died.
The Duke was angry
and ordered the man killed.
Yànzǐ requested to enumerate his crimes, saying:
"You have three capital offenses:
I had you care for the horses,
and you killed one—
that is the first offense deserving death.
Moreover, you killed the horse most beloved by our lord—
that is the second offense deserving death.
If our lord were to kill a man over the matter of a single horse,
the common people would surely resent and rebel,
and the feudal lords would look down upon and attack our state—
that is the third offense deserving death."
The lord sighed and said:
"Pardon him."
Sūn Shū'áo, at three years old, did not know the difference between male and female horses.
The "Zōu Zǐ" states:
Dǒng Zhòngshū did not look beyond his garden gate for three years,
and when riding a horse, did not know its gender.
Also, Zhūgě Liàng taught, saying:
"In the past, Sūn Shū'áo rode a horse
for three years without knowing its gender—
this is praised as a mark of his virtue."
There is also the account of Guāngwǔ's drum carriage,
see the annotation to "the knight is merely said to be bestowed" in the "Ode to the Sword."
Hàn Wén declined tribute;
the "Hàn Shū" states:
During Emperor Wén's reign,
someone presented a thousand-li horse.
The edict said:
"With the phoenix banners ahead
and the accompanying carriages behind,
on auspicious journeys we travel fifty li per day.
If I were to ride a thousand-li horse, where would I go alone ahead?"
Thus, he returned the horse.
And at the sandy plain, he drank blood;
the "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" states:
On the day xīnchǒu,
the Son of Heaven
was thirsty at the sandy plain.
Before water could be fetched,
Gāo Bēnróng, a warrior of the Seven Elite Troops,
stabbed the neck of the left trace horse
and drew its clear blood
for the Son of Heaven to drink.
At Jùsōu, he washed with milk.
The "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" states:
When the Son of Heaven reached Jùsōu,
the people of Jùsōu used the milk of their cattle and horses to wash the Son of Heaven's feet.
Dòng
means milk,
pronounced dòng.
To save Wú Hàn, he clung to the horse's tail;
the "Dōngguān Hàn Jì" states:
Wú Hàn's troops were defending Chéngdū.
Gōngsūn Shù's general Yán Cén dispatched surprise troops to attack from behind Hàn's forces,
defeating Hàn in an assault.
Hàn fell into the water
and escaped by clinging to a horse's tail.
To save Fú Jiān, the horse lowered its bridle.
The "Yì Yuàn" states:
Fú Jiān was attacked by Mùróng Chōng.
Jiān galloped his horse and fell into a ravine.
The pursuing troops nearly caught up,
and he saw no way out.
The horse then hesitated at the edge of the ravine,
lowering its bridle to Jiān,
but Jiān could not reach it.
The horse knelt again,
and Jiān climbed onto it,
managing to ascend the bank and flee westward.
If virtue reaches the mountains and hills,
the "Xiàojīng Yuán Shénqì" states:
When the king's virtue reaches the mountains and hills,
then divine horses emerge from the marshes.
When governance is proclaimed as harmonious and peaceful,
the "Lǐ Dǒu Wēiyí" states:
When the ruler rides fire and becomes king,
his governance is harmonious and peaceful,
and the southern seas present dappled horses.
Thus, the category of earth,
the "Yì" states:
The mare belongs to the category of earth,
traversing the earth without bounds.
The essence of the moon,
the "Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu" states:
Yin combines with eight,
eight combines with yang nine,
eight and nine make seventy-two.
Two represents earth,
earth governs the moon,
the moon's essence is the horse.
The moon's number is twelve,
thus the horse is born after twelve months.
The king rides horses,
thus the character for horse is formed with the component for king.
The spirit of the river water,
the "Ruìyìng Tú" states:
The dragon horse
is a benevolent horse,
the essence of the river water.
It has wings on its forehead,
and hanging hair on its sides.
Its cry produces nine tones.
It appears when there is an enlightened king.
The essence of bronze vessels,
the "Dìjìng Tú" states:
The essence of bronze vessels appears as a horse.
Drenched in red sweat, they arrive in numbers;
the "Hàn Shū·Tiānmǎ Gē" states:
Drenched in red sweat,
foaming with crimson.
Held by strong reins, they come to court.
Méi Chéng's "Qī Fā" states:
The stallions of Zhōng and Dài,
colts at the age of prime teeth,
front like flying birds,
rear like the jùxū beast,
held by strong reins,
attached to smooth roads,
with Wáng Liáng and Zàofǔ as drivers,
and Qín Quē and Lóu Jì as attendants.
Note:
The "Hàn Shū" states:
In Zhào territory, Zhōng and Dài have stones,
northward turning, near the Hu barbarians.
Then there were Tàizōng's ten steeds,
the "Táng Shū" states:
During the Zhēnguàn era, Gǔlìgàn sent envoys to present ten fine horses.
Tàizōng named them the ten steeds:
first, Téngshuāngbái; second, Jiǎoxuěcōng; third, Nínglùcōng; fourth, Xuánguāngcōng; fifth, Juébōyú; sixth, Fēixiábiāo; seventh, Fādiànchì; eighth, Liújīnzhōu; ninth, Xiánglínzǐ; tenth, Bēnhóngchì.
He also composed a text to narrate the event.
Qín Shǐhuáng's seven famous horses,
the "Gǔjīn Zhù" states:
Qín Shǐhuáng had seven famous horses:
first, Zhuīfēng; second, Báitù; third, Nièyǐng; fourth, Zhuīdiàn; fifth, Fēihé; sixth, Tóngquè; seventh, Chénfú.
Cáo Zhēn's title Jīngfān,
the "Gǔjīn Zhù" states:
Cáo Hǔzhēn had a fine horse,
named Jīngfān (Startling Sail).
Wèi Wǔ's title Báihè.
The "Shíyí Jì" states:
Cáo Hóng and Wèi Wǔdì rode a horse named Báihè (White Crane).
People of the time had a saying:
"Leaping through empty space,
the Cáo family's White Crane."
Some followed the westward migration and became kings of the land;
the "Sòng Shū" states:
The Xiānbēi chieftain's eldest son by the principal wife was Ruòluòwěi,
and the eldest son by a concubine was Tǔyùhún.
The horses of the two tribes fought and injured each other.
Wěi became angry,
and Hún then gathered the horses and traveled west.
Wěi regretted it,
and sent his senior official Yǐnàlóu to pursue Hún and order him to return.
Hún said:
"I am of lowly birth,
and by principle cannot coexist as equals.
Now that the horses have caused this separation,
it is likely heaven's will.
You all try to gather the horses and make them go east.
If the horses return east,
I will follow."
Immediately, two thousand cavalry together herded the horses to turn them back.
The horses turned back less than three hundred paces,
then suddenly cried sorrowfully and ran west,
their sound like a collapsing mountain.
This happened over ten times.
Lóu knelt and said:
"Khagan,
this is no longer a matter of human affairs."
Thus, he became king in the western barbarian lands.
Some built a city following the traces of a running horse.
The "Sōushén Jì" states:
In the past, the Qín people built a city within the Wǔzhōu Pass to guard against the Hú.
The city was about to be completed but collapsed several times.
A horse ran about,
circling and turning repeatedly.
The elders found it strange.
They then built the city following the horse's tracks,
and the city became stable.
Thus, it was named Mǎyì (Horse City).
Praising Wǔ Lún's pure sincerity,
the "Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
Someone asked Dì Wǔ Lún:
"Do you have any private interests?"
He replied:
"In the past, someone offered me a thousand-li horse.
Although I did not accept it,
whenever the Three Dukes made recommendations for office,
my mind could not forget it,
yet I still never used it."
Commending Zhuó Mào's non-contention.
The "Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
Zhuó Mào served as a clerk in the Chancellor's office.
Once while traveling,
someone claimed his horse.
Mào asked:
"How long ago did you lose your horse?"
The man replied:
"Over a month ago."
Mào had owned the horse for several years,
and knew in his heart the claim was false,
but silently untied it and gave it to him,
pulling the carriage away himself.
Looking back, he said:
"If this is not your horse,
please return it to me at the Prime Minister's residence."
Another day, the horse's original owner found his lost horse elsewhere,
and went to the residence to return the horse,
kowtowing in apology.
Qìng Zhèng knew the defeat at Huánníng.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Qín and Jìn fought at Hán.
The Duke Huì of Jìn rode a small steed,
a horse from Zhèng.
Qìng Zhèng said:
"In ancient times for great affairs,
one must ride horses bred in one's own land.
Born of its water and soil,
they know the hearts of its people;
accustomed to its training,
and familiar with its ways.
Now riding an alien breed,
to engage in warfare,
when frightened they will change,
and act contrary to their rider.
Their disordered spirit becomes treacherous and agitated,
their dark blood surges throughout,
their vessels swell and burst forth,
strong on the outside but dry within.
They can neither advance nor retreat,
nor maneuver about.
You will surely regret it."
He did not listen.
When battle was joined,
the duke's horse circled in the mud and halted.
Xíng Bó recognized the sound of a night retreat.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
The Marquis of Jìn attacked Qí.
The Qí army retreated at night.
Xíng Bó told Zhōngháng Bó:
"There is the sound of horses neighing to each other,
the Qí army is likely retreating."
Annotation:
At night during retreat, horses cannot see each other,
so they neigh to distinguish themselves.
Therefore, in spring they sacrifice to the Celestial Steed,
in summer to the First Herdsman,
in winter they practice driving,
and in autumn they select charioteers.
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
In spring, sacrifice to the Horse Ancestor,
and restrain the foals.
In summer, sacrifice to the First Herdsman,
distribute horses and geld the stallions.
In autumn, sacrifice to the Horse Spirit,
and select charioteers.
In winter, sacrifice to the Horse Guardian,
present horses,
and practice driving.
Annotation:
The Horse Ancestor
is the Celestial Steed.
Restraining the foals:
In the spring mating season,
the foals are weak,
their blood and vital energy not yet settled,
to prevent them from being injured by mating.
The First Herdsman
was the first to raise horses.
Gelding the stallions:
After the summer mating season,
they geld the stallions
to prevent kicking and biting.
The Horse Spirit
was the first to ride a horse.
Xiàng Tǔ created riding horses.
Selecting charioteers:
means examining the drivers of the five chariots.
The Horse Guardian
is a spirit that causes disasters for horses.
Presenting horses:
means showing the mature horses to the king.
Practicing driving:
practice means training and drilling.
After removing the bedding and consecrating the stables with blood,
see the annotation below for "entrusting to the encircling army."
They also adorned worn-out horses and held whips.
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
The Stable Master adorns the ceremonial horses,
and follows them holding a whip.
Annotation:
Ceremonial horses
are horses given to people in place of silk gifts.
Some are born in the wilds of Táolín,
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
North of Kuāfù Mountain is Táolín,
spanning three hundred lǐ in breadth,
where many horses dwell.
Some emerge from the valley of Pōlí.
The Táng Shū says:
The country of Tǔhuǒluó has Mount Pōlí.
In the caves of the southern cliffs dwell divine horses.
The people of that country often pasture mares nearby,
and they sometimes give birth to famous foals,
all of them sweat-blood horses.
There are those with the belly of a qílín and the chest of a tiger,
the head of a dragon and the eyes of a bird.
Liú Wǎn's "Rhapsody on Horses" says:
I have a fine steed,
named Qíxióng.
It has a dragon's head and bird's eyes,
a qílín's belly and tiger's chest.
Its tail is like a cloud comet,
its ears like inserted tubes.
Guō Jí arrived in the commandery and rode bamboo horses.
The Hòu Hàn Shū says:
Guō Jí was Governor of Bìngzhōu.
While touring his jurisdiction,
he arrived at Měijì in Xīhé.
Several hundred children,
each riding bamboo horses, lined the roadside to welcome and bow to him.
They asked:
"When will the Governor return?"
Guō Jí told his Assistant Inspector,
to calculate the date and inform them.
Upon his return,
one day ahead of schedule,
Guō Jí stopped at a roadside pavilion,
waiting until the appointed day to enter.
Zhào Gāo, disloyal, pointed to a deer as a horse.
The Shǐ Jì says:
Zhào Gāo wished to rebel,
but feared the ministers would not obey.
So he first set a test,
presenting a deer to the Second Emperor,
saying:
"It is a horse."
The Second Emperor laughed and said:
"The Chancellor is mistaken,
calling a deer a horse."
He asked his attendants,
some remained silent,
some said it was a horse,
to flatter and comply with Zhào Gāo.
Those who said it was a deer,
Gāo secretly found legal pretexts to punish them.
They ransomed Huá Yuán with a hundred teams of horses.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
The people of Sòng used one hundred teams of fine horses to ransom Huá Yuán from Zhèng.
When half had been delivered,
Huá Yuán escaped and returned.
They fed the followers with Qǐfú.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
The Marquis of Wèi came and presented his carriage horse named Qǐfú.
It fell into a pit and died.
The duke intended to make a coffin for it.
Zǐjiā Zǐ said:
"The followers are suffering,
please let them eat it."
Annotation states:
Qǐfú
is the horse's name.
Fell into a pit:
means it fell into a pit.
Coffin:
means a coffin.
Yōu Mèng then spoke of its funeral rites.
The Shǐ Jì says:
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a beloved horse.
He clothed it in embroidered silk,
housed it under a magnificent roof,
and fed it dates and dried meat.
When the horse died,
he wished to bury it with the rites of a senior official.
The entertainer Yōu Mèng entered the palace gate,
and wailed loudly, saying:
"Please bury it with the rites of a ruler,
with a coffin of carved jade,
an outer coffin of patterned catalpa,
a protective enclosure of camphorwood,
mobilize armored soldiers to dig the grave,
and have the old and weak carry the earth.
When the feudal lords hear of this,
they will all know that Your Majesty values horses and despises men."
The king said:
"What should I do then?"
He replied:
"Allow me to advise Your Majesty:
for the burial of the six domestic animals,
use a stove mound as the outer coffin,
a copper cauldron as the coffin,
season it with ginger and cinnamon,
and present it with magnolia,
Clad in firelight,
buried in human bellies.
The king then entrusted the horses to the Grand Provisioner."
䥶 pronounced lì.
Mǎ Fáng then clarified the matter of grain provisioning for horses.
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
The emperor initially wished to campaign against the Xiōngnú,
and discussed troop deployment and logistics with Dòu Gù and others,
all believing that the grasslands beyond the frontier were lush,
so grain might not be necessary.
When Gù and others led troops to Dūnhuáng,
and were about to exit the frontier,
they requested horse grain.
The emperor, because Gù's words contradicted his earlier statements,
was angered and refused to provide grain.
All said that according to precedent, armies exiting the frontier did not provide grain for horses.
Mǎ Fáng stated,
during Emperor Xuān's time, five generals campaigned against the Xiōngnú,
Xiōngnú scouts obtained dung from Hàn horses,
and seeing millet within it,
knew the Hàn troops were advancing,
and therefore withdrew.
Based on this,
horses should be provided with grain.
The emperor praised the subtlety of his reasoning,
and ordered grain to be provisioned for the horses.
In warfare they unite their strength,
in hunting they match their pace,
from the *Ěryǎ*.
How could one again compete in skill with a lame cat?
The *Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò* states:
The Swift Cavalry General challenged the various Erudites,
Shuò replied:
"Qílín, Lǜ'ěr, Fēihóng, Huáliú,
are the finest horses under heaven,
but if catching rats within the deep palace,
they are not even as good as a lame cat."
How could one race them alongside Hán Lú!
The *Discourse of Kǒng Róng* states:
Among dogs, there is Hán Lú,
among horses, there is qíjì,
among men, there are sages,
their reputations are equivalent.
Suppose a qíjì and Hán Lú ran together,
could they possibly keep head and tail aligned,
eight feet moving as one,
without any perception of who leads or follows?
As for dividing into three classes,
the *Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ* states:
Tián Jì and the various young lords of Qí raced horses with heavy wagers,
Sūn Bìn observed their horses' speeds were not very far apart,
and there were upper, middle, and lower classes.
Thereupon Bìn said to Tián Jì:
"Sir, just place heavy wagers,
I can make you win."
Tián Jì raced with the king and the various young lords,
wagering a thousand gold at the contest.
Bìn said:
"Take your lower team against their upper team,
take your upper team against their middle team,
take your middle team against their lower team."
After the three classes finished,
he lost one but won two.
Jì obtained the thousand gold.
Note:
Heavy wagers,
means wagering heavily to win.
Driving seven outriders,
the *Huáinánzǐ* states:
In late autumn, they conduct hunts to practice the five weapons,
ordering the charioteers and seven outriders all to drive, bearing banners.
Crossing the ferry bridge in a leap,
the *Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn* states:
Sūn Quán campaigned against Héféi,
was defeated,
and reached the ferry bridge on horseback.
The southern section of the bridge had been dismantled for over a zhang,
with no planks.
Gǔ Jílì was behind the horse,
had Quán hold the saddle and loosen the reins,
then whipped from behind,
to assist the horse's momentum,
and thus they leaped across.
Drinking from the Zhàn River until it ceased to flow.
The *Hánzǐ* states:
Zhòu had armor for a million men,
on the left watering horses at the Zhàn,
on the right watering horses at the Huán,
the Huán River dried up,
the Zhàn River ceased to flow,
King Wǔ with three thousand armored soldiers defeated him and became king.
Mòdú belittled gifts from neighboring states,
the *Shǐjì* states:
Dōnghú sent a request for Mòdú of the Xiōngnú's thousand-lǐ horse,
Mòdú asked his ministers,
they said:
"A thousand-lǐ horse,
is a treasure of the Xiōngnú,
do not give it."
Mòdú said:
"When dealing with a neighboring state,
why begrudge a single horse."
Thereupon he gave it to them.
Dōnghú thought Mòdú feared them,
and further wanted to obtain one of his yānzhī,
Mòdú again asked his attendants,
the attendants were all angry,
and requested to attack them.
Mòdú said:
"Why, when dealing with a neighboring state,
begrudge a single woman!"
He gave her,
Dōnghú grew even more arrogant.
Between them and the Xiōngnú was some abandoned land,
they wanted that too,
Mòdú asked his ministers,
some said:
"This is abandoned land,
giving it is fine,
not giving it is also fine."
Mòdú was greatly angered,
said:
"Land,
is the foundation of a state,
how can we give it away."
Those who spoke of giving it were all beheaded.
Thereupon he attacked Dōnghú by surprise,
and annihilated them.
Èrshī was stingy regarding the Hàn envoy's request.
The *Shǐjì* states:
Dàyuān had fine horses,
in the city of Èrshī,
they hid them and were unwilling to give them to Hàn.
The Son of Heaven sent strong men like Chē Lìng and others bearing a thousand gold and a golden horse to request Dàyuān's fine horses.
The Dàyuān state council deliberated together, saying:
"The Èrshī horses,
are Dàyuān's treasure horses."
Thereupon they refused to give them to Hàn.
The Hàn envoy was angered,
spoke recklessly,
smashed the golden horse and left.
Dàyuān nobles attacked the Hàn envoy,
seizing the valuables.
The Son of Heaven was greatly angered,
appointed Lǐ Guǎnglì as General Èrshī,
mobilized cavalry from dependent states and tens of thousands of unruly youths from commanderies and kingdoms to attack Dàyuān,
expecting to storm the city of Èrshī,
and obtain the fine horses.
Grazing on the bean leaves of the threshing floor and tethered,
the *Shī* says:
Bright, bright the white colt,
grazes on the bean leaves of my threshing floor.
Tether it, tie it fast,
to prolong this evening.
Longing for stable beans and lingering.
The *Jìn Jì* states:
Cáo Shuǎng and others followed in paying respects at Gāopínglíng.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng raised troops to execute Shuǎng.
Huán Fàn went out to join Shuǎng,
Xuānwáng said to Jiǎng Jì:
"The brains are going over!"
Jì said:
"Brains he has, indeed,
but a nag longs for stable beans,
he certainly cannot be employed."
Zhūgě had not yet obtained but first gave thanks,
the *Wú Shū* states:
Zhūgě Kè served as a general,
a Shǔ envoy arrived,
the sovereign said to the envoy:
"Yuánxùn serves as general,
when you return to Shǔ, you may report to the Prime Minister,
to send fine horses."
Kè rose and expressed thanks,
the sovereign said:
"You have not yet obtained the horses,
why give thanks?"
He replied:
"Shǔ is Your Majesty's outer stable,
Your Majesty has issued an edict,
your subject is sure to obtain them,
therefore I give thanks."
Dù Lín accepted them and was sure to repay.
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
Dù Lín and Mǎ Yuán were from the same locality,
and had always been close and affectionate.
When Yuán returned from the south,
at that time Lín's horse happened to die,
Yuán ordered his son to take a horse and give it to Lín, saying:
"Among friends, there is the gift of carriage and horse,
it can temporarily serve to prepare against want."
Lín accepted it.
After several months,
Lín sent his son to present a letter, saying:
"General, internally you provide for the nine clans,
externally you sustain guests and friends,
those looking to your kindness are many.
My father and I, two people, eat from the ranks of the ministers,
our salaries are often ample,
now I send fifty thousand cash."
Yuán received it,
and said to his son:
"People should take this as a model."
As for the five directions of the Xiongnú having different colors,
the Shǐjì says:
Mòdú besieged Gāozǔ at Píngchéng,
his cavalry in the west were all white horses,
in the east all blue dragons,
in the north all black steeds,
in the south all red horses.
Gōngsūn's cavalry were all white.
The Yīngxióng Jì says:
Whenever Gōngsūn Zàn heard of border alarms,
he would immediately become stern and rouse his spirit as if going to face an enemy.
He always rode a white horse,
and also selected several dozen white horses for riders and archers,
calling them the "White Horse Righteous Followers,"
using them as his left and right wings.
The Hú people greatly feared them,
and told each other:
"We must avoid the White Horse Chief Clerk."
Tethering vicious horses,
training colts and taming stallions,
the Zhōulǐ says:
The Horse Assessor is in charge of tethering vicious horses.
Annotation:
This means using a halter rope to tie and familiarize them.
It also says:
The Stable Master is in charge of taming stallions, training colts, and controlling foals.
Annotation:
Taming stallions,
means using them without making them overly fatigued,
to calm their vital energy.
Training colts,
means beginning to ride and accustom them.
Controlling foals,
means castrating those that kick and bite and separating them.
Two-year-olds are called foals,
three-year-olds are called colts.
Even if one is as skilled at driving as Dōngyě,
one must have the foresight of Yán Huí.
The Jiāyǔ says:
Duke Dìng of Lǔ asked Yán Huí:
"Have you not heard of Dōngyě Bì's skill at driving?"
He replied:
"Skilled he is indeed,
but even so, his horses will surely bolt."
Later, Dōngyě Bì's horses bolted,
the two outer horses dragging the two inner ones,
into the stable.
The Duke summoned Yán Huí and asked him,
and he replied:
"I knew it from governance.
In ancient times, Emperor Shùn was adept at employing the people,
and Zàofù was adept at employing horses.
Shùn did not exhaust his people,
Zàofù did not exhaust his horses,
therefore Shùn had no people who bolted,
and Zàofù had no horses that bolted.
Now, Dōngyě Bì's driving,
mounting the horses, grasping the reins and bit,
his posture is correct;
walking, trotting, galloping,
the courtly rituals are complete;
traversing dangers and reaching far places,
the horses' strength is exhausted.
Yet his mind still seeks more from the horses without cease,
this is how I knew."
Thus, among mounts there are inferior and superior,
among things there are poor and good.
As for having prominent knee bases,
long sweat grooves,
Mǎ Yuán's "Bronze Horse Physiognomy Method" says:
The sweat groove should be deep and long,
the knee base should be prominent.
Eyes having a purple glow,
Bólè's "Classic of Horse Physiognomy" says:
The eyes should be like hanging bells,
with a purple glow.
Mouth having a red light,
Mǎ Yuán's "Bronze Horse Model Method" says:
The mouth being red and having light,
this is a thousand-lǐ horse.
Therefore, the head should be square,
the belly should be expansive,
the nostrils should be large,
the spine should be strong,
the ears should be close and small,
Bólè's "Classic of Horse Physiognomy" says:
The horse's head is the king,
it should be square.
The belly is the city walls,
it should be expansive.
The spine is the general,
it should be strong.
The nostrils should be large.
The ears should be close together and erect forward,
small and thick.
The lips should be tight and square,
the "Bronze Horse Physiognomy Method" says:
The upper lip should be tight and square.
Possessing all these traits,
ultimately they will be truly excellent.
If it has large haunches and short ribs,
shallow hips and thin thighs,
a mouth with elm writing,
eyes with tear-catching,
crow bit and short life,
flying snake and inauspiciousness,
weak spine and small neck,
large head and drooping ears,
Bólè's "Classic of Horse Physiognomy" says:
The method of judging horses,
first eliminate the three emaciations and the five inferiorities,
then judge the rest.
Large head and small neck,
is the first emaciation;
weak spine and large belly,
is the second emaciation;
small neck and large hooves,
is the third emaciation.
Large head and drooping ears,
is the first inferiority;
long neck that does not bend,
is the second inferiority;
short upper and long lower,
is the third inferiority;
large haunches and short ribs,
is the fourth inferiority;
shallow hips and thin thighs,
is the fifth inferiority.
White forehead entering the mouth,
one name is elm writing,
one name is target skull,
if a slave rides it, he will die on the road,
if the master rides it, he will be executed in the market.
Curved hair under the eyes,
named tear-catching,
is inauspicious for people.
Having black in the mouth is called a crow-driven horse,
short-lived.
In spring, it should be like a crouching turtle,
having curved hair on both sides is called a flying snake,
it kills its master.
This is the lowest grade of eight hundred,
the "Chronicles of the Elders of Chángshā" says:
Yú Zhī,
the province appointed him as an attendant in Nányáng.
Prefect Zhāng Zhōng was connected by marriage to the royal house,
his crimes were serious.
Zhī, according to the law, handled the case,
the Inspector, fearing the power, summoned Zhī,
Zhī said:
"As years pass, ambition fades,
just like an eight hundred coin horse, its life and death have the same value,
and I wish to establish merit in enlightened times!"
Thereupon, he cast aside his credentials and left.
Perhaps ten days of driving will just reach it.
The Sūnqīngzǐ says:
A steed travels a thousand lǐ in a day,
an inferior horse driving for ten days will also reach it.
As for selecting its six sections,
distinguishing its four seasons,
the Zhōulǐ says:
The Horse Driver is in charge of assisting in the selection of fine horses,
and selecting their six sections,
distinguishing the management of their dwellings in the four seasons.
Annotation:
Selecting the six sections,
means grading the king's horses into six classes.
Dwelling,
refers to the places for spring collection and summer sheds.
Management,
refers to spring foal handling, summer stallion control, and the like.
Master Chén Bēi's expertise in legs and feet,
the Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
Ancient horse judges,
Hánfēng judged mouth and teeth,
Má Cháo judged cheeks,
Nǚ Lì judged mouth,
Guǎn Qīng judged lips,
Chén Bēi judged legs and feet,
Qín Yá judged the front,
Zàn Jūn judged the rear,
each knowing one aspect.
Learn Xiè's expertise in lips and mane.
The Hòuhànshū says:
Mǎ Yuán was skilled at distinguishing famous horses,
in Jiāozhǐ he obtained a Luòyuè bronze drum,
and cast it into a horse model.
Presenting it in a memorial, he said:
"I served Yáng Zǐ'ā,
and obtained Zǐyú of Xīhé's bone method for judging horses.
Formerly, during Emperor Wǔ's time, Dōngmén Jīng cast a bronze horse method and presented it,
an edict erected it outside the Lǔ Bān Gate,
and renamed the gate the Golden Horse Gate.
I humbly followed Yí's expertise in the bridle path,
Zhōngbó's expertise in mouth and teeth,
Xiè's expertise in lips and mane,
Dīng's expertise in the body's center,
Take the bone structure of these several breeds as the standard."
The horse stands three feet five inches tall.
An imperial edict placed it beneath the Xuāndé Hall,
to serve as the model for famous horses.
Jī,
pronounced jū qí qiē.
If the one holding the reins is not the right person,
The "Chǔ Cí" says:
"Yet they reject the qíjì and do not ride them,
Instead urging on the nútái to take the road.
Seeing the one holding the reins is not the right man,
Therefore the colt leaps and flees far away."
Or one holds a knife and eyes it.
The "Yán Tiě Lùn" says:
A qíjì pulling a salt cart hangs its head on the slope of Tàiháng Mountain,
A butcher holds a knife and eyes it.
Therefore, Zhuōzǐ controlled its advance and retreat,
and Zàofǔ, seeing this, shed tears.
The "Hánzǐ" says:
Qiānlíng Zhuōzǐ rode a black dragon and Páifù's carriage,
With hook ornaments in front,
and spiked whips behind.
When the horse wished to advance, the hook ornaments restrained it;
when it retreated, the spiked whips pierced it.
Zàofǔ saw this and wept, saying:
"This is like a man living in troubled times yet not knowing the way."
Some say he rode Qúfù's carriage.
Offered the Zhūzé to supply provisions,
The "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" says:
The Son of Heaven campaigned north,
and lodged at Zhūzé,
fishing in the flowing water.
The people there offered three hundred food horses.
Note:
To supply the kitchen's provisions.
Threw into the Suī River to establish authority.
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
A man of Sòng who was taking a road,
his horse would not advance,
so he beheaded it and threw it into the Suī River.
He again took to the road,
his horse would not advance,
so again he beheaded it and threw it into the Suī River.
He again took to the road,
his horse would not advance,
so again he beheaded it and threw it in.
This happened three times.
Even the method Zàofǔ used to intimidate horses
could not surpass this.
Not attaining Zàofǔ's way,
and merely obtaining his intimidation,
is of no benefit to charioteering.
An unworthy ruler,
not attaining the way,
and merely increasing his intimidation,
finds his intimidation increasingly useless.
In the end, the shadow is extinguished by the firelight,
See the note above on "Yōu Mèng".
And the body is consigned to a worn-out curtain.
The "Lǐ" says:
"A worn-out curtain is not discarded,"
meaning to bury a horse.
"A worn-out cover is not discarded,"
meaning to bury a dog.
As for harnessing the Fúhuáng,
The "Ruì Yìng Tú" says:
The Fúhuáng
appears when the king's carriages and attire are of proper measure.
The Yǎoniǎo,
a divine horse,
is the same as the Fēitù,
signifying that an enlightened ruler possesses virtue.
Harnessing the Zǐyàn,
See the note on "Hàn Wén Jiǔ Liáng".
Controlling Péi Guǒ's Huángcōng,
The "Sān Guó Diǎn Lüè" says:
Péi Guǒ of Zhōu, styled Róngzhāo,
in the army rode a Huángcōng horse,
wearing a blue robe.
Each time he charged the enemy ranks first,
people of the time called him "Huángcōng Youth".
Driving Chángsūn's Shǎndiàn,
The "Suí Shū" says:
Chángsūn Shèng followed Prince of Jìn to defeat the Tūjué,
The Prince invited Shèng to a banquet.
A Tūjué dignitary came to attend,
and said that the Tūjué greatly feared Commander Chángsūn,
hearing the sound of his bow,
they called it thunder,
seeing his running horse,
they called it lightning.
The Prince laughed and said:
"The General's majestic wrath,
his authority extends beyond the borders,
thus compared to thunder and lightning,
how magnificent!"
The Marquis of Wèi's tail and mane were all dyed red,
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
The Duke of Wèi had four white horses,
The Duke favored Xiàng Tuí,
Tuí desired them,
so the Duke took them and dyed their tails and manes red to give to him.
Xuē Gōng came and went unseen.
Huán Tán's "Xīn Lùn" says:
Xuē Gōng was
an expert horse physiognomist in Cháng'ān.
He obtained a fine horse from a border commandery,
rode it into the market,
coming and going, people did not see him.
Later, when questioned,
and asked to see the horse,
the old man said:
"You gentlemen have no eyes,
it is not worth showing."
Established a model at the Golden Horse Gate,
Set a standard at the Xuāndé Hall.
Both see the note above on "Xiè Shì's lips and mane".
As for Yǔ Liàng's Lú,
The "Jìn Shū" says:
The horse Yǔ Liàng rode was a Lú,
Yīn Hào considered it inauspicious,
and urged him to sell it.
Liàng said:
"How can one shift one's own misfortune
onto another!"
Wáng Róng's Bādiān,
The "Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn" says:
Wáng Róng was simple and unrestrained,
not adhering to formal appearances,
fond of riding a Bādiān horse.
Although he held the rank of Sānsī,
he would casually travel privately.
Inspecting his fields and gardens,
not accompanied by a single person,
he would tuck a handkerchief in his belt himself.
To Huángchí where it sprayed jade,
The "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" says:
The Son of Heaven traveled east to Huángzé,
lodged at Xīluò,
and sang:
"The pools of Huáng,
their horses spray sand,
the august men's majestic bearing;
The marshes of Huáng,
their horses spray jade,
the august men's life-giving grain."
Drinking from the Wèi River and tossing coins.
The "Sān Fǔ Jué Lù" says:
Xiàng Zhòngshān of Ānlíng watered his horse at the Wèi River,
first tossing three coins.
Yān Zhāo died yet still purchased,
The "Zhàn Guó Cè" says:
King Yān Zhāo sent a palace attendant with a thousand gold to purchase a thousand-lǐ horse from a remote land.
Upon arrival, it had died,
so he used five hundred gold to buy its head and return.
The world heard of this,
and considered the King a lover of horses.
Thus, before a year had passed,
there were three who offered thousand-lǐ horses.
Zǐfāng grew old yet still pitied.
The "Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn" says:
Tián Zǐfāng went out,
saw an old horse on the road,
and asked the driver,
who said:
"It is a beast of the state,
worn out and no longer useful,
therefore turned out to pasture."
Zǐfāng said:
"In youth it exhausted its strength,
in old age its body is cast aside,
a benevolent man does not do this."
He used a bundle of silk to ransom it.
Impoverished scholars heard of this,
and knew where to turn their hearts.
Harnessed to a salt cart and hesitating,
ascending Tàiháng and delaying.
The "Zhàn Guó Cè" says:
Hàn Míng met Chūnshēn Jūn and said:
"That steed's teeth show its age has come,
pulling a salt cart,
ascending Tàiháng,
on the middle slope it delayed,
bearing the shafts it could not ascend.
Bólè encountered it,
descended his carriage, grasped it and wept,
took off his ramie coat and covered it.
Then it lowered its head and snorted,
raised its head and neighed,
its sound reached the heavens,
rejoicing that Bólè knew its worth."
Wishing for a single glance to increase its value,
even the worthy and eminent are all thus.
The "Chūnqiū Hòu Yǔ" says:
Sū Dài wished to see the King of Qí,
and persuaded Chúnyuán Kūn, saying:
"A man had a fine horse he wished to sell,
and seeing Bólè, said:
'For three mornings I have stood in the market,
and no one has spoken to me.
I wish you would return and look at it,
leave and glance back at it,
I will offer you the wages of a single morning.'
Bólè did as he said,
and in one morning the horse's price increased tenfold.
Now I wish to present a fine horse to the king,
but there is no one to introduce me.
Would you be willing to act as my Bólè?
I offer a pair of white jade discs,
and ten yì of gold,
as fodder for the horse."
Chúnyú Kūn spoke to the king and had him introduced.
Note:
Fodder for the horse,
a euphemism, not wishing to state it directly.
As for trampling on fodder being punishable,
the Rites say:
Trampling on the fodder of the king's horse is punishable.
Checking teeth at the pass,
the Book of Hàn says:
Wèi Wǎn reported that the horse's teeth were not yet flat,
and it could not pass through the gate.
Note:
A horse's teeth become flat at ten years of age.
Swift as crossing a clod,
fleeting as a shadow vanishing.
See the previous note on "chariot attendant at dawn."
There is also the distinction of three types,
the Zhōu Lǐ says:
The horse assessor is in charge of assessing horses,
evaluating three types.
The first is the war horse,
the second is the hunting horse,
the third is the inferior horse,
each with its own price.
The note says:
Price,
refers to appearance and value.
Regulating the six stables,
the Zhōu Lǐ says:
The Son of Heaven has twelve stables,
with six types of horses.
The feudal states have six stables,
with four types of horses.
The nobles have four stables,
