with two types of horses.
Some were tied with halberds and charged into battle,
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū says:
Chángshā King Sīmǎ Wánghú fought against Chéngdū King's vanguard Mǎ Xián.
Hú tied halberds to the saddles of several dozen horses,
and stabbed them from behind,
causing the horses to panic and charge into Xián's army,
defeating them.
Some spat out diagrams and approached the altar.
the Shū Zhōng Hòu says:
Yáo sank jade discs into the river,
and a dragon horse with red patterns and green color
approached the altar and spat out a diagram.
Some urged them to follow the steed,
Yángzǐ says:
To govern oneself, follow Zhòngní;
to lead horses, follow the steed,
is that not appropriate!
Some compared it to aspiring to Yán.
Yángzǐ says:
A horse that aspires to be a steed
is also a steed's mount;
a person who aspires to be like Yán
is also a follower of Yán.
Shī Kuàng had a discussion resembling the bó,
the Shuō Yuàn says:
Jìn Pínggōng went hunting,
and saw a nursing tiger crouching motionless.
Upon returning, he said to Shī Kuàng:
"When a hegemon king emerges,
fierce beasts crouch and dare not rise,
could this be it?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Magpies eat hedgehogs,
hedgehogs eat jūnyí,
jūnyí eat bó,
bó eat tigers.
The bó's appearance resembles a jiào horse.
Today, our lord must have ridden a jiào horse when he went out?"
Pínggōng said:
"Indeed."
Gōngsūn had the theory that white is not a horse.
the Kǒng Cóngzǐ says:
Gōngsūn Lóng argued that a white horse is not a horse.
Some said this argument destroys the great way.
Zǐgāo went to Zhào,
and said to Lóng:
"I have long wished to study under you,
but what prevents me from accepting you as my teacher
is your claim that a white horse is not a horse.
If you could abandon this,
I would become your disciple."
Lóng said:
"If I were to abandon it,
I would have nothing to teach."
Jī Shào did not keep a swift steed,
the Jìn Shū says:
The royal army was defeated at Dàngyīn,
and Jī Shào was killed.
Initially, the attendant Qín Zhǔn said to him:
"Today we face danger,
do you have a fine horse?"
Shào sternly replied:
"The imperial carriage is on a personal campaign,
it is reasonable to expect an advance without battle.
If the imperial carriage were to be lost,
my duty as a minister is clear,
what use is a swift horse!"
Huáiyuǎn only feared stumbling and startling.
the Táng Shū says:
Lǐ Huáiyuǎn, though long holding a prestigious position,
increasingly valued simplicity.
He once rode a slow horse,
and the Left Vice Director Dòulú Qīn said to him:
"You are so honored and noble,
why not buy a fine steed?"
He replied:
"This horse fortunately avoids stumbling and startling,
there is no need to seek another."
Those who heard this could not help but admire him.
As for those coming from the northwest,
the Book of Hàn says:
Initially,
the Son of Heaven opened the Book of Changes and it said:
"Divine horses should come from the northwest."
They obtained Wūsūn horses,
and called them heavenly horses.
When they obtained the sweat-blood horses of Yuān,
they renamed the Wūsūn horses as western extreme horses,
and called the Yuān horses heavenly horses.
Note:
Opening the Book of Changes,
refers to divining by opening the Book of Changes.
Death is feared on Rénshēn day,
the Shuō Wén says:
Ào,
is a fine horse.
It dies on Rénshēn day,
and those who ride horses avoid this day.
Ào,
pronounced wǔ dāo qiē.
Some used green silk to bring disaster to Liáng,
the Sān Guó Diǎn Lüè says:
During the Liáng's Pǔtōng era,
a children's rhyme said, "green silk, white horse."
Hóu Jǐng often rode a white horse,
using green silk as a bridle,
to fulfill the rhyme.
Some used yellow spots to prophesy Chén.
the Chén Shū says:
Initially, there was a children's rhyme:
"Yellow-spotted green-maned horse,
sets out from the banks of Shòuyáng,
arrives when autumn has not yet come,
leaves when spring winds begin."
Later, the Chén ruler was indeed defeated by Hán Qínhǔ.
Qínhǔ,
refers to the yellow spots.
After capturing Jiànkāng,
he again rode a green-maned horse,
and the timing of his coming and going matched the rhyme.
Entrusted to the stable master,
the Zhōu Lǐ says:
The stable master is in charge of teaching,
the grooms to care for horses.
In spring, remove bedding,
consecrate the stables,
and begin grazing.
In summer, shelter the horses.
In winter, present the horses.
Note:
Bedding,
refers to horse mats.
At midday, take the horses out and remove them.
Consecration,
is to make them sacred.
Shelter,
is a shed,
to provide shade and coolness for the horses.
Shelter is pronounced yá.
Managed by the horse official.
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
The horse official manages the king's horses,
distinguishing six types of horses.
Breeding horses are one type,
war horses are one type,
ceremonial horses are one type,
travel horses are one type,
hunting horses are one type.
Note:
Breeding,
refers to the best, resembling the mother;
the jade carriage is drawn by breeding horses.
The war carriage is drawn by war horses.
The gold carriage is drawn by ceremonial horses.
The imperial carriage road uses imperial horses.
The field road uses field horses.
Inferior horses are assigned to palace duties.
The Qiūcí horses numbered in the tens of thousands, filling the stables.
The *Nán Qín Lù* states:
Lǚ Guāng campaigned against the Western Regions,
and pacified them.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"Only Qiūcí lies at the heart of the thirty-six states.
Entering its capital city,
heavenly steeds, dragon-lin, yǎoniǎo, and red-maned horses numbered in the tens of thousands, filling the stables.
Even if Bó Yì were reborn,
or Wèi Cì reappeared,
they could not distinguish them all."
The Érzhū horses were grouped by color.
The *Sānguó Diǎnlüè* states:
Gāo Huān returned to Érzhū Róng.
Róng seated Huān below the bed,
dismissed his attendants, and inquired about current affairs.
Huān said:
"I hear you have horses filling twelve valleys,
each grouped by color.
What do you intend to do with them?"
Róng said:
"Speak your mind."
Huān said:
"Now the Son of Heaven is foolish and weak,
the Empress Dowager is licentious and corrupt,
turmoil clouds the four directions,
and court governance is ineffective.
With your heroic prowess,
seize the moment and rise to action.
Simply use the pretext of punishing Zhèng Yǎn and Xú Hé,
and raising your whip will be enough to stabilize the realm.
This is Hè Liùhún's idea."
Róng said:
"Your idea is my idea."
It is also said that when the world lacks the Way, warhorses are born in the suburbs.
The *Lǎozǐ* states:
When the world has the Way,
galloping horses are retired to fertilize the fields.
When the world lacks the Way,
warhorses are born in the suburbs.
When sages emerge, even Feīhuáng serves in the stables.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
When the world has the Way, Feīhuáng serves in the stables.
It also says:
In the time of Huángdì,
Feīhuáng served in the stables.
Ascending Qiūshān without losing the horses.
The *Fúzǐ* states:
I and Xuánzǐ were viewing the Eastern Sea,
released the team and ascended Qiūshān.
Midway, we forgot about the horses.
Fúzǐ sent men to search for them,
but they were not found.
He sent ghosts to seek them, and they were found.
Fúzǐ said:
"The six directions cannot be forgotten,
thus we know the fine horses are within them.
Let us observe them with the perspective of the six directions."
Releasing the old horse of Gūzhú to find the way.
The *Hánzǐ* states:
Qí Huán attacked Gūzhú.
He set out in spring and returned in winter,
lost and confused about the way.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The wisdom of an old horse can be used."
So they released an old horse and followed it,
and thus found the way.
There are also Yìqú Zībái horses,
The *Zhōushū* states:
The Yìqú Zībái
is a white horse with serrated teeth,
and eats tigers and leopards.
Hànhǎi Cōngjū horses,
The *Suíshū* states:
Tǔyùhún has a Qīnghǎi,
over a thousand *lǐ* in circumference.
In its center is a small mountain.
Their custom is to release mares there in winter,
saying they obtain dragon offspring.
Once they obtained a Persian mare,
released it into the sea,
and it gave birth to a cōngjū,
which could travel a thousand *lǐ* a day.
Thus it was called the "Hànhǎi Cōng Horse."
Qūchǎn horses borrowed the road,
see the note on "Jìn's Chuíjí" in the *Yù Fù*.
Xiānlí horses were sent to Wú.
The *Wèi Zhì* states:
In *Emperor Wén's Letter to Sūn Quán*:
The Xiānlí horse,
which I often ride myself,
is well-trained and runs excellently.
Selected from tens of thousands,
it is truly a delight.
Though the Central Plains abound in horses,
those known for unmatched speed
are also occasionally found.
Fú Jiān demonstrated his lack of desire.
The *Zǎijì* states:
During Fú Jiān's time, Dàyuān presented heavenly steeds and thousand-*lǐ* colts,
all sweat-blood, red-maned, five-colored, with phoenix chests and dragon bodies,
along with over five hundred kinds of rare treasures.
Jiān said:
"I recall Hàn Wén returning the thousand-*lǐ* horse,
sighing in admiration and praise.
Now that horses are presented,
let them all be returned,
so that I may emulate the former kings
and resemble the ancients."
He then ordered his ministers to compose a *Stop the Horses Poem* and sent them back,
demonstrating his lack of desire.
Emperor Gāozōng clarified his surplus.
The *Tángshū* states:
During the Yǒnghuī era,
Tǔyùhún sent an envoy presenting fine horses.
The emperor asked about the breed of the horses.
The envoy replied:
"They are the finest in our country,
hence we present them."
The emperor said:
"Fine horses are what people desire.
How can we stop their insufficiency
and add to our surplus?"
He then ordered them returned.
One must heed the prohibition on double silkworms.
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
The horse officer prohibits double silkworms.
Note:
Yuán
means again.
In astronomy, Chén corresponds to the horse.
Silkworm texts say silkworms are the essence of dragons.
When the moon aligns with Dàhuǒ, the silkworm eggs are bathed.
Thus silkworms and horses share the same *qì*.
No thing can achieve two greatnesses.
Prohibiting double silkworms
is to avoid harming horses.
One should verify the writing in the golden pot.
The *Yànzǐ Chūnqiū* states:
Duke Jǐng traveled to Jì,
obtained a golden pot,
opened it and looked inside,
finding cinnabar writing,
which said:
"Do not eat fish twice,
do not ride inferior horses."
Yànzǐ said:
"Not eating fish twice
means not exhausting the people's strength;
not riding inferior horses
means not employing the unworthy at one's side."
The duke said:
"Jì had this writing,
so why did it perish?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Jì had this writing,
but hid it in a golden pot.
If it did not perish, what else could it expect!"
Even deaf creatures can be taught.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
When horses are colts,
they leap, kick up their hooves, raise their tails, and run,
and humans cannot control them.
Their biting can pierce muscles and shatter bones,
their kicking can break skulls and crush chests.
But when grooms tame them,
and skilled drivers train them,
covering them with yoke and collar,
connecting them with reins and bit,
then even crossing dangers and leaping ditches,
they dare not refuse.
Thus, though horses cannot be transformed, they can be harnessed,
which is the result of training.
Horses are deaf creatures and cannot communicate their will,
yet they still require training to become useful.
How much more so for humans!
Note:
Deaf creatures
means without understanding.
Like drumstick and drum matching each other.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
A skilled craftsman and a thousand-*lǐ* horse
must meet to achieve greatness,
like a drumstick and a drum.
High integrity and dying for righteousness
are also the thousand-*lǐ* horse among scholars.
Those who can make scholars travel a thousand *lǐ*
are surely the worthy.
Thus, assisted by Bēnróng,
The *Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn* states:
Bótiān masters the chariot,
Cānbó drives on the left,
Bēnróng serves on the right.
Aided by Hán'āi,
see the previous note on "Cānshèng Dàn."
How can one compare ability with kuǎnduàn horses?
See the note on "Mǎ Yuán Làngbó" in the *Wù Fù*.
Among the largest of creatures,
its form resembles clouds hanging from the sky.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
There is a yak,
its size like clouds hanging from the sky.
The Lǐ records that for three months it is kept in the cleansing pen.
The Lǐ says:
If the sacrificial bull for the Emperor is inauspicious,
it is replaced by a bull for the God of Grain.
The Emperor's bull must be kept in the cleansing pen for three months,
while the Grain God's bull need only be complete,
to distinguish between serving the heavenly deities and human spirits.
The Shī says: "Ninety are the black-lipped."
The Shī says: "Who says you have no oxen?
Ninety are the black-lipped."
Note:
A yellow ox with black lips is called a rún.
Those with cloven hooves are of heaven;
those with pierced noses are of man.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Oxen have cloven hooves and bear horns,
horses are covered in hair and have complete hooves—
this is of heaven.
Bridling a horse's mouth,
piercing an ox's nose—
this is of man.
Some, adorned in embroidered robes, enter the grand temple.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Chǔ sought to employ Zhuāngzǐ.
Zhuāngzǐ responded to the envoy, saying:
"Have you seen the sacrificial ox,
clothed in embroidered silks,
fed with hay and beans,
raised within the pen's confines?
When it is led into the grand temple,
though it may wish to be a solitary calf,
can it possibly be so?"
Some, made into drums, command the three armies.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Strip the ox hide,
tan it to make drums,
to command the masses of the three armies.
For the ox's own sake,
it is better to submit to the yoke.
Your oxen come,
their ears moist.
From the Shī.
The shrew mouse, fearing injury,
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
A shrew mouse gnawed the horns of the suburban ox,
so another ox was divined for.
The shrew mouse gnawed its horns again,
and the ox was spared.
Even the wind-blown horse knows they do not meet.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
The Marquis of Qí attacked Chǔ.
The Lord of Chǔ sent a messenger to address the army, saying:
"You dwell by the northern sea,
I dwell by the southern sea,
this is like the wind-blown horse and ox that do not meet.
I did not expect you to tread upon my land.
Why is this?"
Striking the horns, expressing Nìng Qì's plight.
See the "Song and Rhapsody" note on "Nìng Qì Feeds the Ox."
Burning tails to save Tián Dān's crisis.
See the "Fire Rhapsody" note on "Tián Dān Releases the Oxen."
Some serve as omens for military affairs.
The Jìnshū says:
In the state of Fúyú, if there are military matters,
they slaughter an ox to sacrifice to heaven,
using its hooves to divine good or ill fortune.
If the hooves separate, it is inauspicious;
if they remain together, it is auspicious.
Some indicate the timing of farming.
The Lǐ says:
In late winter, an earthen ox is brought out.
To show the earliness or lateness of farming.
Fearing that mǎotóu,
The Sōushénjì says:
In Wǔdū Gùdào, there was a shrine to the Angry Bull,
atop which grew a catalpa tree.
Duke Wén of Qín sent men to fell it,
but the tree's wounds healed as they were made,
and for days it could not be cut.
So they increased the axemen to forty,
yet still it could not be cut.
The men, weary, rested.
One among them injured his foot,
could not rise,
and lay beneath the tree.
He heard ghosts conversing, saying:
"Tiring, this battle?"
One of them said:
"What is there to tire of?"
A man said:
"If they wear russet robes and scatter ashes,
what will you do?"
Then they fell silent.
The recliner reported this,
so they ordered the workers to all wear russet,
and as they chopped the wounds,
scattered ashes upon them.
The tree was cut,
and transformed into a black ox.
They sent cavalry to attack it,
but could not prevail.
Some fell to the ground,
their topknots loosened, hair disheveled.
The ox feared this,
and plunged into the water.
Thereupon, Qín established the mǎotóu cavalry.
Rather be a chicken's beak.
The Shǐjì says:
Sū Qín persuaded the King of Hán, saying:
"A common saying goes, 'Rather be a chicken's beak,
than an ox's rear.'
Now, to serve Qín facing west,
how is that different from being an ox's rear?"
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn used green hemp to display virtue.
The Jìnshū says:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
officials reported that the green silk reins of the imperial ox had broken.
An edict ordered them replaced with green hemp.
Hé Zēng was impeached for using bronze hooks.
The Jìnshū says:
Hé Zēng was extravagant and haughty.
Capital Official Liú Xiǎng impeached Hé Zēng for using bronze hooks for carriage traces,
and polishing the ox's hooves and horns.
As for wounding the mouth and changing the divination,
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
The suburban ox's mouth was wounded,
so another ox was divined for.
Using a calf values sincerity.
The Lǐjì says:
For suburban sacrifices, a red ox is used,
esteeming the color red;
using a calf,
values sincerity.
Some, holding the horns, cannot sell it.
The Fēngsútōng says:
When selling an ox, do not hold its horns,
or it will not sell.
This is because it fears goring people,
so people will not take it.
Some, cutting its flesh, it grows back.
The Xuánzhōngjì says:
In Dàyuèzhī and the Western Hú, there is an ox
called the fǎn ox.
If you cut three or four catties of its flesh today,
by tomorrow the flesh has regrown,
and the wound is healed.
Admirable is Liú Kuān's far-reaching magnanimity.
The Hòuhànshū says:
Liú Kuān was once traveling
when someone who had lost an ox
came to his cart to claim it.
Kuān said nothing,
dismounted, and walked home.
After a while,
the claimant found his ox and returned it,
apologizing, saying:
"I am ashamed to have wronged you, elder."
Kuān said:
"Things may resemble each other,
mistakes can happen.
Fortunately, you troubled to return it;
why apologize?"
Envying Lǔ Gōng's governance in practice.
The Hòuhànshū says:
Lǔ Gōng was magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
Once, a village head borrowed an ox from someone and did not return it.
The ox owner brought a complaint to Gōng.
Gōng summoned the village head three times to return the ox,
but he still did not return it.
Gōng wept, saying:
"This shows that moral instruction is not effective."
He wished to resign and leave.
The village head returned the ox
and went to prison to accept punishment.
Gōng pardoned him and did not pursue the matter.
Thereafter, the officials and people respected and trusted him,
and none were willing to deceive.
Praising Guō Shū's leniency.
The Jìnshū says:
Guō Shū
once had a villager who stole and ate his ox.
When discovered,
the man came to apologize.
Shū said:
"You were hungry,
that is why you ate the ox.
The remaining meat we can share."
Admiring Zhū Chōng's non-contention.
The Jìnjì says:
Zhū Chōng of Nán'ān
had a villager who lost a calf,
which resembled Chōng's calf.
The man came to claim it,
and Chōng did not argue.
Later, the calf was found beneath solid ice.
Qiú,
means end,
the ox used for concluding affairs,
refers to that which is used for unraveling.
Zhí is read as zhí,
zhí refers to a stake,
which can be used to tether an ox.
The zhí person refers to the herdsman.
The fēng person supplies fodder,
see the note above on "setting up the fú héng."
Yànhuí did not look at the fallen well,
the Sòng Shū says:
Chǔ Yànhuí,
was the son of Zhàn Zhī.
Zhàn Zhī had an ox,
which he cherished greatly,
that fell into the well in front of the hall for no reason,
Zhàn Zhī led his attendants to personally rescue it,
causing a commotion in the commandery,
but Yànhuí lowered the curtain and did not look.
Lú Kǎi did not cook it but pitied its old age.
The Suí Shū says:
Lú Kǎi accompanied Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu at the Yúnyáng Palace,
where an order was issued to the various garrisons to select old oxen,
intending to feast the soldiers.
Kǎi remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Tián Zǐfāng ransomed an old horse,
and gentlemen considered it a beautiful tale.
Now, having received a clear edict,
to feast the soldiers with old oxen,
would damage benevolent governance."
The emperor praised his words and stopped the order.
He was then transferred to become the Minister of Rites.
Some collapse on a pig,
the Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
People from Zhū and Jǔ went to Jìn and said:
"Lǔ attacks us morning and evening,
nearly destroying us."
Shūxiàng of Jìn came to deliver a message, saying:
"Our ruler has four thousand chariots of armored troops,
even if they act without principle,
they are surely fearsome.
How much more if they follow the Way,
what enemy could withstand them?
Even if an ox is lean,
if it collapses on a pig,
would it not fear death?"
Some place it atop a tree.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
In Wú, there was Xú Suí,
who lived in Dāntú.
Zuǒ Cí passed by Suí's gate,
where there were six or seven guest carriages,
and they deceived Cí, saying:
"Lord Xú is not here."
Cí left.
The guests all saw oxen atop poplar trees,
and chariot hubs sprouting thorns.
The guests were afraid,
chased after Cí,
and kowtowed to apologize.
When the guests returned,
they saw the oxen as before,
and the hubs no longer had thorns.
Zhān Hé recognized it by its white hooves,
the Hánzǐ says:
Zhān Hé was sitting,
with disciples in attendance,
when an ox bellowed outside the gate.
A disciple said:
"It is a black ox,
with white on its hooves."
Zhān Hé said:
"Indeed."
They looked and it was true.
Gě Lú also discerned its three sacrifices.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Jiè Gě Lú came to court,
heard an ox bellow,
and said:
"This one gave birth to three sacrificial animals,
all of which have been used,
its sound says so."
They inquired and it was true.
Sùshèn divined by it and came to offer tribute,
the Jìnyáng Qiū says:
The state of Sùshèn,
during Emperor Wǔ's time and Emperor Yuán's restoration,
both came to offer tribute.
During Emperor Chéng's time, they also communicated tribute to Shí Jìlóng,
saying:
"For three years, we have observed oxen and horses sleeping facing southwest,
thus knowing the location of the great state,
and so we have come."
Xián Gāo used it to provision the army.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
Qín secretly attacked Zhèng,
reaching Huá,
when the Zhèng merchant Xián Gāo encountered them,
he first presented four hides,
then twelve oxen to provision the army,
and also sent a swift messenger to inform Zhèng.
The Qín general Mèng Míng said:
"Zhèng is prepared."
They destroyed Huá and returned.
Separately, Péngzǐ was placed in charge to establish his enterprise,
the Hòu Hàn Shū says:
Liú Péngzǐ initially, with his elder brother Mào, was subordinate to the Right Battalion officer Liú Xiáqīng,
in charge of herding oxen,
and was called the Ox Official.
When he was established as emperor,
he was fearful and wanted to cry,
and immediately returned to rely on Xiáqīng.
Emperor Guāngwǔ rode it to raise troops.
The Hòu Hàn Shū says:
When Emperor Guāngwǔ first raised troops,
he rode an ox,
killed the Xīnyě Commandant,
and then obtained a horse.
Some dreamt of it by Jiǎng Yǎn,
the Shǔ Zhì says:
Jiǎng Yǎn once dreamt of an ox,
with blood flowing from its head, horns, and mouth.
Zhào Zhí said:
"Ox horns and mouth,
form the character 'gōng.'
Blood,
indicates clarity of affairs.
The dream is auspicious."
Some understood it through the butcher.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
The butcher dissected an ox for Lord Wénhuì,
saying:
"My knife has been used for nineteen years,
dissecting thousands of oxen,
yet its edge is as if newly sharpened.
The joints have spaces,
and the knife edge has no thickness;
using no thickness to enter spaces,
there is ample room to maneuver."
Observe its Yùzhāng tying silk,
the Qí Shū says:
Yùzhāng, the presented king Liáo, was Governor of Yángzhōu,
he paid respects at the temple of Jìzǐ of Yánlíng,
observed the boiling well,
when an ox charged into the ranks,
the guards seized the ox for questioning,
but the king did not permit it,
instead took a bolt of silk,
tied it across the ox's horns,
and released it to return home.
A rush saddle hanging books.
The Táng Shū says:
Lǐ Mì once sought Bāo Kǎi,
riding a yellow ox,
covered with a rush saddle,
and hung a volume of the Hàn Shū on its horn,
holding the ox's reins with one hand,
and flipping through the book with the other to read.
The Minister of Works, Duke Yuè, Yáng Sù, saw him on the road,
and followed from behind, reining in his horse to catch up.
When he caught up,
he asked:
"What scholar is this,
so devoted to learning?"
Mì recognized Duke Yuè,
dismounted from the ox,
bowed twice,
and stated his name,
then was asked:
"What book are you reading?"
He replied:
"The biography of Xiàng Yǔ."
White then recognized Lǐ Bīng's ribbon,
the Fēngsú Tōng says:
King Zhāo of Qín appointed Lǐ Bīng as Governor of Shǔ,
who opened the two rivers of Chéngdū,
to irrigate fields.
The river god demanded two young girls annually as wives.
Bīng went to the temple,
and reprimanded the god.
After a long while,
two gray oxen fought on the riverbank.
After a moment,
Bīng, sweating, said to his officials:
"I am fighting to the utmost,
you should assist me.
The one with the white on its southern waist,
is my ribbon."
The Registrar stabbed the one facing north,
and the river god died.
Green then drove Lǎozǐ's carriage.
See the note on "Yǐn Xǐ divined Lǎojūn" in the "Chē Fù."
Jìzhī, upon one strike, reflected on his faults,
the Biànzǐ says:
Guō Línzōng said to Qiú Jìzhī:
"Have you ever had faults?"
Jìzhī said:
"I once fed an ox,
but the ox would not eat,
One seized the ox's ear. "
Jiāng Zhàn only gave it water and no fodder.
The Book of Sòng states:
Jiāng Zhàn was honest and frugal by nature,
and served as Minister of Personnel.
His ox was hungry,
and the groom asked for grass.
After a long while, Jiāng Zhàn said:
"You may give it water to drink."
There is also the story of trampling stones to form flowers.
The Records of Penetrating the Obscure states:
During the Yuánfēng era,
Dàqín presented an ox.
It was good at running and very strong.
It was made to pull carts of copper and iron to build the Wàngxiān Palace.
Its hoofprints on the stones
all resembled flower shapes.
Therefore, outside Yángguān there is the Flowery Ox Ford.
There is also smearing mud to pray for rain.
The Records of Guǎngzhōu states:
In the prefecture there was a stone ox.
Whenever there was a drought, they would kill an ox,
mix its blood with mud, and smear it on the stone ox's back.
Once this was done,
rain would immediately fall.
It would only stop once the mud was washed away.
There is also the case of practicing deception by writing on silk.
The Discourses on the Principles of Things states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn appointed Shào Wēng as General Wénchéng.
Shào Wēng wrote on silk, fed it to an ox,
and proclaimed that this ox was extraordinary.
When it was killed and examined,
a silk document was found inside.
The Emperor recognized his handwriting.
As the situation became critical,
Shào Wēng confessed.
Thereupon, Wénchéng was executed and the affair was concealed.
There is also the case of contending for precedence and killing the driver.
The Book of Jìn states:
Shí Chóng once contended with Wáng Kǎi over entering Luòchéng.
Shí Chóng's ox was swift as a flying bird,
and Wáng Kǎi simply could not keep up.
So Wáng Kǎi secretly bribed someone from Shí Chóng's entourage
and asked him the reason.
The man replied:
"The ox's running is not inherently swift.
It is truly because the driver, unable to keep up, instead restrains it.
If you let it gallop freely, it will be fast."
Wáng Kǎi followed this advice,
and thus contended for precedence.
Shí Chóng later found out
and killed the informant.
There is the ox that wielded its horns like spears to protect its calf.
The Record of Strange Creatures from Yùlín states:
What is a Zhōuliú?
It is actually a water buffalo with blue-gray hair and a boar's body.
Its horns are like shouldered spears.
It protects its calf
and is the enemy of the tiger.
There is also the case of forming a battle array to repel a tiger.
Bàopǔzi states:
The wise bird carries reeds in its beak to foil nets.
The water buffalo forms a battle array to repel a tiger.
As for placing it on the basin and bamboo basket,
The Rites of Zhōu states:
For all sacrifices, provide the oxen victims' frames,
along with the basins and bamboo baskets for the proceedings.
The commentary states:
The basin
is for holding blood.
The bamboo basket
is a cage for receiving meat.
The frame
is like the meat racks used by butchers today.
There is the ox growing old in the pen.
The Spring and Autumn Annals of Yànzǐ states:
Duke Jǐng's ox grew old in the pen,
and could no longer bear the yoke.
His carriage was moth-eaten among tiles and stones,
and could no longer bear being ridden.
There is the horn not lacking the three colors.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
A horn two feet five inches long,
not lacking the three colors,
is called 'an ox wearing an ox.'
Commentary:
The three colors are:
white at the base,
blue in the middle,
and rich at the tip.
'Wearing an ox'
means the horn is worth an ox.
Its fragrance is uniquely praised among the four fats.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
In spring, use fragrant fat.
In summer, use rank fat.
In autumn, use raw-smelling fat.
In winter, use gamy fat.
Commentary:
Ox fat is fragrant,
pig fat is rank,
dog fat is raw-smelling,
and sheep fat is gamy.
There is encountering Kuí and posing a question.
Zhuāngzǐ states:
Shēng's ox escaped at night and encountered Kuí.
It stopped and asked him:
"I have four feet,
and move about clumsily.
You have one foot and leap swiftly.
How is this so?"
Kuí said:
"With my one foot,
I surpass you."
There is panting at the moon to decline labor.
See the note on "applying Jìn Wǔ's colored glaze" in the "Rhapsody on the Wind."
The one renowned for discerning judgment was Xuē Gōng.
The Classic of Ox Physiognomy states:
The Ox Classic was transmitted from Nìng Qī to Bǎilǐ Xī.
In the Hàn dynasty, Xuē Gōng obtained this book and used it to judge oxen,
with not a single error in a thousand.
The one who studied the transmitted text was the Jìn Ancestor.
The Classic of Ox Physiognomy states:
In the Wèi dynasty, Gāotáng Shēng obtained Xuē Gōng's book
and transmitted it to Jìn Gāozǔ.
Later, Wáng Kǎi kept the book secret.
There is the saying that it cannot catch rats.
Zhuāngzǐ states:
The yak is as large as a cloud hanging from the sky.
It can achieve greatness,
but cannot catch rats.
It is also said to be difficult for chasing hares.
Jiāo Gòng's Forest of Changes states:
Killing an ox to chase a hare
wastes time and achieves nothing.
There is the case of forming Niú Hóng's magnanimity.
The Book of Suí states:
Niú Hóng's younger brother, Bì,
was fond of drink and given to drunken violence.
Once, while drunk,
he shot and killed the ox pulling Niú Hóng's carriage.
When Niú Hóng returned home,
his wife met him and said:
"Your younger brother shot and killed the ox."
Niú Hóng heard this
and, showing no surprise or questioning,
simply replied:
"Make dried meat."
When he sat down,
his wife said again:
"Your younger brother suddenly shot and killed the ox.
This is a very strange affair."
Niú Hóng said:
"I already know."
His countenance remained unchanged,
and he continued reading without pause.
There is the case revealing Lú Chānghéng's benevolence and forbearance.
The Book of Suí states:
Lú Chānghéng was Governor of Xúzhōu.
Once, while traveling to Jùnyí,
the horse he was riding was gored by another man's ox
and consequently died.
The ox's owner apologized
and asked to pay compensation.
Lú Chānghéng said to him:
"For beasts of burden to gore each other
is hardly a matter of human intent.
Why should you apologize?"
He refused and did not accept.
As for possessing a thousand feet and being wealthy,
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
A thousand horses with cloven hooves,
a thousand oxen feet,
this is also comparable to a family with a thousand chariots.
If it bellows at night, its meat is putrid.
The Rites of Zhōu states:
If an ox bellows at night, its meat is putrid.
Commentary:
Yóu
means the stench of rotten wood.
Pronunciation: yóu.
As for Gù Xiàn and Zhòng Wén,
both decided lawsuits and people submitted.
The Book of Sòng states:
Gù Xiànzhī,
during the Yuánhuī era, served as Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
There was a cattle thief at the time
who disputed ownership of an ox with its original owner.
Each claimed it as his own property.
The testimonies and evidence from both families were equal,
and previous magistrates had been unable to decide the case.
When Gù Xiànzhī arrived,
he reviewed the case,
then ordered the ox untied and allowed to go wherever it wished.
The ox went straight back to its original home.
The thief confessed his crime.
The Book of Later Wèi states:
Yú Zhòngwén was transferred to become Grand Administrator of Āngù.
The Rén and Dù families had each lost an ox.
Later, an ox was found,
Both families claimed ownership,
and the prefecture and commandery could not settle the matter for a long time.
Zhòng Wén ordered both families to drive their herds of cattle to the location,
then released the claimed ox,
which went toward the Rén family’s herd.
He also secretly had someone slightly injure the ox;
the Rén family sighed in distress,
while the Dù family remained indifferent.
Zhòng Wén then interrogated the Dù family,
and the Dù family confessed their guilt.
Regarding Shí Miáo and Yáng Shì,
both served as officials but left their calves behind.
The *Wèi Lüè* states:
Shí Miáo of Jùlù served as the magistrate of Shòuchūn,
and when he first took office, he rode a female ox.
After a little over a year, it gave birth to a calf.
When his term ended,
he left the calf behind and departed.
The *Jìn Shū* states:
Yáng Piān served as an official with integrity and caution.
He had a private ox that gave birth to a calf in the official residence.
When he left his post,
he left it behind.
There is also Chéng Zhèng’s “Jiāng Jié,”
the *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
“Ox Drinking Water”
refers to how in the past, Chéng Zhèng watered his ox here,
and the river dried up because of it,
hence the name.
Lóu Tí measured by the valley,
the *Hòu Wèi Shū* states:
Lóu Tí was heroic and outstanding,
with insight and judgment.
He had several thousand servants,
and his oxen and horses were measured by the valley.
Also, the *Shǐ Jì* states:
Wūshì Luǒ sought rare silk goods,
and secretly presented them to the Róng king.
The Róng king repaid him tenfold,
giving him livestock measured by the valley for oxen and horses.
Observing the qi to discern the signs of the northern barbarians,
the *Yúnqì Zhàn* states:
Zhào’s cloud resembled an ox.
Also, the qi of the northern barbarians resembled an ox.
Divination signs as an auspice for the Minister of War.
The *Jìn Shū* states:
When Táo Kǎn was still obscure,
his mother passed away,
and as he was about to bury her,
he suddenly lost an ox.
He encountered an old man who said:
“On the hill ahead, I saw an ox
lying in a mountain hollow.
Whoever buries there
will reach the highest ministerial rank.”
He also pointed to another mountain and said:
“This is the second-best site,
producing officials of two-thousand-bushel rank.”
After speaking, he vanished.
Kǎn soon found the ox
and buried his mother there himself.
He told Zhōu Fǎng about the other mountain,
and Fǎng buried his parent there.
Kǎn rose to Grand Minister of War,
and Fǎng also served as a provincial governor for generations.
As for praising its gentle and cautious nature,
the *Shuōwén* states:
“Rào ox.”
“Rào” is pronounced rào,
meaning gentle and cautious.
Pitying its trembling fear.
The *Mèngzǐ* states:
The King of Qí was sitting in his hall
when someone led an ox past below.
The king saw it
and asked:
“Where is the ox going?”
The reply was:
“It will be used to consecrate the bell.”
The king could not bear to see it trembling, innocent yet going to its death,
and wanted to substitute a sheep.
Mèngzǐ said:
“This is the method of benevolence,
for you saw the ox but not the sheep.”
Some trespassed on fields and had their ox seized,
the *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
The King of Chǔ, due to the disorder caused by the Xià clan in Chén,
attacked Chén.
He killed Xià Zhēngshū
and annexed Chén as a county.
Shēn Shūshí said:
“Yet there is a saying:
‘If someone leads an ox to trample another’s field,
and you seize his ox.
The trespasser is indeed at fault;
but seizing his ox
is an overly severe punishment.’”
The king then restored Chén.
Some washed their ears as an insult.
See the annotation on “Xǔ Yóu washing his ears” in the *Shuǐ Fù*.
Bǐng Jí already toiled by inquiring about panting,
the *Hàn Shū* states:
Bǐng Jí once served as chancellor.
Once, going out, he encountered a brawl,
with dead and injured lying across the road.
Jí passed by
without asking.
Going further,
he met someone driving an ox,
the ox panting with its tongue out.
Jí sent a mounted officer to ask:
“How far has the ox traveled?”
Some criticized Jí,
but Jí said:
“When people brawl, kill, or injure,
it is the duty of the Cháng’ān magistrate and the Jīngzhào governor to prohibit, pursue, and arrest;
at year’s end, the chancellor merely evaluates their performance.
Now it is early spring, with young yang in effect,
and it should not be hot yet.
I feared the ox had traveled nearby in the heat, hence its panting.
If the seasonal qi is disordered,
I fear there may be harm.
The Three Dukes are responsible for harmonizing yīn and yáng,
which is what I should be concerned about.”
Gōng Suì further admonished by wearing a plow.
See the annotation on “Wearing an ox has long transformed” in the *Jiàn Fù*.
The Zhōu officials divided duties,
and the ox keeper was in charge of leading and assisting;
the *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
The ox keeper, for all assemblies, military campaigns, and labor duties,
provides the oxen for war chariots,
along with those to lead and assist,
to carry the duke’s equipment.
Annotation:
“Leading and assisting”
refers to oxen pulling outside the shafts.
A person driving in front is called “leading,”
and one at the side is called “assisting.”
Among the worthies of the Jìn court,
Hé Qiáo was also diligent and hurried.
The *Jìn Jì* states:
Pān Yuè was appointed magistrate of Héyáng,
and by official seniority, he should have been a court gentleman,
but he was dissatisfied.
At the time, Shān Tāo oversaw appointments,
and Yuè privately criticized him,
secretly composing a rhyme:
“East of the gallery path,
there is a great ox.
Wáng Jì holds the breast strap,
Péi Kǎi the crupper,
and Hé hurriedly prods,
never resting.”
Yáng
The Book of Changes says:
“Dui represents the sheep.”
The Book of Changes: Shuogua states.
Those with great strength are called fèn,
The Erya says:
An immature sheep is called zhù,
Those with utmost strength are called fèn.
Its meaning is derived from auspiciousness.
The Shuowen says sheep,
Means auspiciousness.
It resembles the shape of four legs, horns, and a tail.
Confucius said:
The characters for ox and sheep are formed based on their shapes.
Having heard of them carrying whips to drive,
The Liezi says:
When Yáng Zhū first met King Liáng,
He said governing the world was as easy as turning something in the palm of his hand.
The King said:
“You, sir, have one wife and one concubine,
Yet cannot manage them;
A garden of three mǔ,
Yet cannot tend it.
To speak of governing the world,
How is that?”
He replied:
“Have you seen shepherds?
A hundred sheep form a flock,
Let a child of five chǐ,
Carry a whip and follow them,
They will go east if desired,
And west if desired.
If Yáo were to lead one sheep,
And Shùn carried a whip to follow it,
Even they could not make it go forward.”
Also because of them carrying bamboo slips and losing sheep.
The Zhuangzi says:
Two men, Zāng and Gǔ,
Went together to herd sheep,
And both lost their sheep.
Asked what Zāng was doing,
He was carrying bamboo slips and reading;
Asked what Gǔ was doing,
He was playing dice and wandering.
The two men’s activities differed,
But their loss of sheep was the same.
Do not be clad in a tiger’s skin,
The Fayan says:
A sheep’s substance in a tiger’s skin.
Sees grass and rejoices,
Sees a jackal and trembles,
Forgetting its skin is that of a tiger.
Better to be autumn frost.
The Book of the Later Han says:
When Emperor Guāngwǔ passed away,
Prince Jīng of Guǎnglíng wrote a secret letter plotting rebellion, saying:
“One should be autumn frost,
Not a penned sheep.”
Note:
Autumn frost,
Is severe and destructive to things.
A penned sheep,
Is controlled by others.
Seen in adjudicating cases by Gāo Yáo,
The Lunheng says:
The xièzhì,
Is a one-horned sheep,
Innate in knowing guilt.
When Gāo Yáo tried cases,
Those whose guilt was doubtful,
He would have the sheep butt them.
Heard of litigation being settled in Qí Zhuāng.
The Mozi says:
Qí Zhuānggōng’s ministers Wáng Guóbēi and Zhōnglǐ Xí litigated for three years without a verdict.
Fearing to wrongly convict the guilty,
They had the two men share a sheep to swear an oath at Qí’s altar.
The two men followed each other, sprinkling the altar with sheep’s blood.
After reading Wáng Guóbēi’s statement in full,
And before Zhōnglǐ Xí’s statement was half done,
The sacrificial sheep rose and butted Zhōnglǐ Xí.
The people of Qí considered it divine.
Bearded then refers to the Registrar,
The Gǔjīn Zhù says:
Sheep are also called the bearded Registrar.
Thin ones are called Doctor.
The Dōngguān Hànjì says:
Zhēn Yǔ was appointed Doctor.
Each year at the Là festival, an edict granted each Doctor a sheep,
The sheep varied in size and fatness.
At that time, the Doctors and the Jìjiǔ discussed killing the sheep,
Weighing and dividing the meat,
Zhēn Yǔ said:
“That won’t do.”
They then wanted to draw lots,
But he felt ashamed of that.
Zhēn Yǔ first took the thinnest one,
From then on there were no more disputes.
Later, when summoned to an assembly,
The edict inquired about “the thin sheep Doctor Zhēn.”
Zhígōng differed from our village,
The Analects says:
Shègōng told Confucius:
“In our village there is a man named Zhígōng,
His father stole a sheep,
And the son testified against him.”
The Gùsuò ritual is still passed down for the love of propriety.
The Analects says:
Zǐgòng wanted to abolish the sacrificial sheep for the Gùsuò ceremony,
The Master said:
“You love the sheep,
I love the ritual.”
A one-year-old is called zhào,
The Guangya says:
For Wú sheep, a male one-year-old is called zhào,
A three-year-old is called dī.
A female one-year-old is called zì,
A three-year-old is called zāng.
Three hundred form a flock.
The Book of Songs says:
Who says you have no sheep?
Three hundred form a flock.
When Jìn Wǔ conquered Wú,
Palace women vied for bamboo leaves;
When Wèi Jiè was in Luò,
All the shops gazed at the jade-like man.
Both seen in the “Chē Fù” note on “Jìn Wǔ driving them with sheep.”
There is also plucking the beard to obtain a pearl,
See the “Zhū Fù” note on “using that sheep’s beard.”
Butting the fence and entangling its horns.
The Book of Changes says:
A ram butts the fence,
And entangles its horns.
Scolding the white stone in Jīnhuá,
See the “Shí Fù” note on “Chūpíng scolding sheep.”
Losing the jade essence at the Western Peak.
The Zhōuyì Shìmóu Lèi says:
Tàishān lost the golden rooster,
The Western Peak lost the jade sheep.
Zhèng Xuán notes:
The golden rooster and jade sheep,
Are the essences of the two mountains.
The Rites mark it as a gift,
The Chūnqiū Fánlù says:
For gifts, ministers use lambs,
Lambs suckle from their mothers on bended knees,
Resembling those who know propriety.
Also, sheep in speech means auspiciousness,
Hence used as gifts.
The Book of Songs praises their coming.
The Book of Songs says:
Your sheep come,
Their horns jostling.
Residing in a thousand-year-old tree,
The Xuánzhōng Jì says:
A thousand-year-old tree,
Its essence becomes a green sheep.
Selling the skin of five rams.
See the “Niú Fù” note on “Bǎilǐ carried to the Qín state.”
Yǐn Xǐ once sought Lǎozi,
The Yǐn Xǐ Nèizhuàn says:
Lǎozi parted with Xǐ, saying:
“Seek me at the green sheep market in Chéngdū.”
Xǐ later sought and found him.
Cáo Gōng struggled to capture Zuǒ Cí.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Cáo Gōng captured Zuǒ Cí,
Cí fled into a flock of sheep,
And Cí’s whereabouts were lost.
The pursuers suspected he had transformed into a sheep,
So they ordered the sheep to be counted,
Originally there were a thousand sheep,
But the tally showed one extra,
Knowing he had transformed into a sheep.
They then said:
“If it is Master Zuǒ,
Just come out without suffering.”
One sheep knelt and said:
“Is it really so?”
The pursuers wanted to seize it,
Whereupon all the sheep knelt and said:
“Is it really so?”
The pursuers then left.
How could one see leading wolves,
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
Qíng Bù rebelled,
He wanted to have the Crown Prince lead troops,
And go attack him.
The Four Haos said to Marquis Jiànchéng:
“Now all the generals are Your Majesty’s former peers,
To have the Crown Prince lead these men,
Is no different from making a sheep lead wolves.”
Could they withstand tigers?
The Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ says:
Zhāng Yí said to the King of Chǔ:
“Those forming alliances,
Are no different from driving a flock of sheep to a live tiger,
That tigers and sheep cannot withstand each other is clear.
Now if Your Majesty does not side with the tiger but with the sheep,
I privately think Your Majesty’s strategy is mistaken.”
Praising Bǔ Shì for having spoken,
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
Bǔ Shì herded a hundred sheep,
and after more than ten years, they increased to over a thousand.
The Emperor said:
"I have sheep in the Shànglín Park,
I order you to herd them."
He was then appointed as a court gentleman.
Bǔ Shì, wearing cloth clothes and straw sandals, herded the sheep.
After over a year,
the sheep were all fat.
The Emperor passed by his sheep,
and praised them.
Bǔ Shì said:
"It is not only with sheep,
governing the people is also like this.
Let them rise and rest according to the seasons,
and remove the bad ones."
He was appointed as the magistrate of Gōushì.
Why did Yáng Zhēn not receive his share?
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Huá Yuán killed a sheep to feed his soldiers,
but his charioteer Yáng Zhēn did not receive any.
When they went to battle,
he said:
"In the past, with the sheep, you were in charge;
today, with this matter, I am in charge."
He drove the chariot into the Zhèng army,
thus causing defeat.
The Zhōulǐ already records the decoration of lambs,
The Zhōulǐ says:
The sheep officer is in charge of sacrificial rituals and decorating lambs.
Seasonal ordinances also mention suitability with millet.
The Zhōulǐ says:
Eating lamb is suitable with millet.
Some took the tongue to form a clan,
The Lièxiānzhuàn says:
In the past, there was a sheep thief,
who gave a sheep to Shū Xiàng.
Shū Xiàng's mother buried it,
and did not eat it.
Three years later,
the sheep theft incident came to light,
and they pursued and searched Shū Xiàng's home.
Examining the sheep, the bones and flesh were all gone,
only the tongue remained.
The people of the state found it strange,
and thus took "Yángshé" (sheep tongue) as their clan name.
Some cut open the liver and found earth.
The Hánshī Wàizhuàn says:
Lǔ Āigōng sent people to dig a well,
for three months they did not find water,
but obtained a live sheep.
The Duke ordered a shaman to drum and dance,
wanting it to ascend to heaven.
The sheep could not ascend.
Confucius saw it and said:
"The essence of water is jade,
the essence of earth is sheep,
this sheep's liver is earth."
The Duke ordered the sheep killed,
and upon looking at the liver, it was indeed earth.
The one who dug a well and obtained it was Jì Huán,
see the annotation in the "Jǐng Fù": "Obtaining a sheep already startled Jìzǐ."
The one who held the envoy's staff and herded was Sū Wǔ.
The Hànshū says:
Sū Wǔ was sent as an envoy to the Xiōngnú,
the Xiōngnú wanted to make him surrender,
but Wǔ refused to submit.
They sent him to herd in a deserted place by the North Sea,
saying he could return only when the ram bore milk.
Wǔ was at the sea,
official rations did not arrive,
he dug up wild mice and grass roots to eat,
and leaning on the Hàn envoy's staff, he herded sheep.
Giving it served as a warning against not sacrificing,
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
Tāng asked Gé Bó:
"Why do you not sacrifice?"
He said:
"I have nothing to offer as sacrificial animals."
Tāng gave him a sheep.
Killing it also cautioned against doing so without reason.
The Lǐ says:
A senior official does not kill a sheep without reason.
Some had the nickname "bearded gentleman,"
The Shùyìjì says:
Sheep without horns are called jiāo sheep,
also known as "húxū láng" (bearded gentleman).
Some spread the name "rotten stomach."
The Hòuhànshū says:
Gēngshǐ appointed only merchants and cooks,
a saying in Cháng'ān went:
"The kitchen boy,
becomes a general of the palace guard.
The rotten sheep stomach,
becomes a cavalry commander.
The rotten sheep head,
becomes a marquis within the passes."
Chanting the white silk in five strands,
The Shī says, the "Gāoyáng" (Lamb),
is the result of the "Quècháo" (Magpie's Nest),
the governance of Zhàonán,
those in office were all frugal and upright,
their virtue like that of a lamb.
The skin of the lamb,
white silk in five strands.
Gazing at the large head under three stars.
The Shī says:
The ewe has a large head,
three stars are in the eaves gutter.
In herding, it reveals the decline of an age,
The Zhōushū says:
Xià Jié's virtue declined,
wild sheep were in the pastures,
and flying locusts filled the fields.
Whipping the rear clearly illustrates nurturing life.
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Nurturing life is like herding sheep,
whip the ones lagging behind.
Shān Bào lived among cliffs and drank water,
at the age of seventy,
he had the complexion of an infant,
but a tiger ate him.
Zhāng Yì had high gates and hanging curtains,
there was none he did not approach,
yet he died from internal heat.
Shān Bào nurtured his inner self,
but a tiger injured his outer self;
Zhāng Yì nurtured his outer self,
yet died from internal heat.
Both failed to whip their rears.
Ending Shěnyóu's morning watering,
looking up to Xuānní's model and punishment.
The Sūnqīngzǐ says:
Zhòngní was the minister of justice of Lǔ,
Shěnyóu did not dare to water his sheep in the morning.
Dog
The Book of Changes says:
"Gen represents the dog."
The "Explaining the Trigrams" chapter of the Book of Changes says:
Gen represents the dog.
Among domestic animals, it corresponds to Metal.
The Comprehensive Meaning of Customs says:
Killing a dog
is an act of exorcism.
The dog
is a Metal animal;
exorcism
means to repel,
restraining Metal to prevent harm.
It receives its essence from the Dipper.
The Apocrypha on the Spring and Autumn Annals: The Conveyance of Anomalies says:
Seven times nine is sixty-three,
the yang energy circulates,
therefore the Dipper moves,
and the dog is born after three months.
Commentary:
The dog
is born from the essence of the Dipper.
The Rúhuáng of Jīngchǔ;
Liú Xiàng's Garden of Stories says:
The King of Jīng obtained a dog named Rúhuáng,
and sharp arrows from Wǎnlù,
and went hunting in Yúnmèng,
not returning for three months.
Bǎoshēn knelt and caned the king,
then went out and drowned himself in a stream.
The King of Jīng then killed the dog and broke the arrows.
The huge-mouthed dogs of the Xiōngnú.
The Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters says:
Jiǎo,
means a young dog.
The Xiōngnú lands have jiǎo dogs,
with huge mouths and black bodies.
Following the Giant Lord, it roamed by the sea;
The Story of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn says:
Gōngsūn Qīng arrived at Dōnglái,
and said he saw a man,
five zhang tall,
who called himself the Giant Lord,
leading a yellow dog,
holding a yellow sparrow,
saying he wished to see the Son of Heaven,
then suddenly disappeared.
Chasing the Eastern Hare, it ran around the mountain.
The Strategies of the Warring States says:
Qí wanted to attack Wèi,
Chúnyú Kūn said to the King of Qí:
"Hán Lú
is the strongest dog in the world.
The Eastern Hare Qūn circled the mountain three times,
leaped over mountains five times,
the hare exhausted itself ahead,
the dog grew tired behind,
both dog and hare were spent,
each dying where they were.
An old farmer saw them,
without the toil of weariness,
and took the prize.
Now Qí and Wèi have been locked in stalemate for a long time,
I fear that powerful Qín and great Chǔ,
will rise to take advantage of the aftermath,
and gain the old farmer's reward."
The King of Qí was afraid,
dismissed his generals and rested his troops.
Then there is Pánhù of Gāoxīn,
The Records of the Mysterious Middle says:
In the past, during the time of Gāoxīn,
the Dog Róng caused rebellion,
the Emperor said:
"Whoever subdues them,
I will give him a beautiful woman in marriage,
and enfeoff him with three hundred households."
The Emperor had a dog named Pánhù,
who disappeared for three months and then killed the Dog Róng,
bringing back their leader's head.
The Emperor gave him his daughter in marriage,
and enfeoffed him with three hundred lǐ of land in the sea southeast of Kuàijī,
their sons were dogs,
their daughters were beauties,
and they were enfeoffed as the Dog clan.
Húcāng of Lord Xú,
The Records of the Investigation of Things says:
A palace maid of Lord Xú became pregnant and laid an egg,
considering it inauspicious,
abandoned it by the water's edge.
A lonely old woman had a dog named Húcāng,
who hunted by the water's edge,
found the abandoned egg,
and carried it back in its mouth.
The old woman thought it strange,
covered it to keep it warm,
and it turned into a small child,
born lying face up,
hence he was given that name.
When he grew up, he was benevolent and wise,
and succeeded to the lordship of Xú.
Later, when Húcāng was about to die,
he grew horns and nine tails,
truly a yellow dragon.
King Yǎn buried him within the borders of Xúliáng,
and today there is a Dog Mound.
Stretching and shaking vigorously,
Jiǎ Dàizōng of Wèi's "Rhapsody on the Great Dog" says:
At times stretching and shaking vigorously,
like a responding dragon leaping and tossing.
Alert, swift, tame, and good.
Zhōu Chù's Records of Local Conditions says:
Among dogs there are the Green Harrier, White Sparrow, Flying Dragon, and Tiger Cub,
tame, good, alert, and swift,
difficult to befriend but easy to command.
Dù Yù then hated that they tied a gourd to it;
The Book of Jìn says:
Dù Yù had a goiter illness,
when first attacking Wú,
the people of Wú feared his wisdom,
and tied a gourd to a dog's neck to show him.
After Wú was pacified,
Dù Yù had them all killed.
Dīng Fěi was then used to preserve the sack intact.
The Records of Wèi says:
Tàizǔ said:
"I have Dīng Fěi,
just as a household has a thieving [dog],
a dog good at catching rats,
though causing minor damage, preserves my sack of clothes intact."
Shǐ Àn tested it for Jiǎnzǐ;
The Discourses of the States says:
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was hunting at Lóu,
Shǐ Àn waited at the gate with a dog.
He said:
"I obtained a dog,
and wish to test it in the park."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Why didn't you report it?"
He said:
"My lord was about to go to Lóu, and the park keeper did not hear of it,
how dare I trouble the officer of the day?"
Jiǎnzǐ then returned.
Commentary:
Lóu,
is the park of the Jìn ruler.
Lù,
is the official in charge of the park.
This means the lord hunted in the ruler's park,
without having the park keeper inform the ruler,
therefore the minister also dared not trouble the officer of the day to explain himself.
The people of Juàn Hán presented them to King Mù.
The Biography of King Mù says:
The people of Juàn Hán presented seventy fine dogs to the Son of Heaven.
Juàn,
is pronounced zhī rán qiē.
It is called 'led from the left';
The Book of Rites: The Details of Rites says:
Those presenting horses or sheep,
lead them with the right hand;
those presenting dogs,
lead them with the left hand.
It is also called 'broth offering'.
The Book of Rites: The Details of Rites says:
In all sacrifices, dogs are called broth offerings.
Gān Shǐ then fed it spiritual medicine;
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity says:
Gān Shǐ fed newly hatched chickens and dogs with medicine from past years,
and they did not grow,
feeding a white dog made its fur black.
Hánzǐ then raised its long feathers.
The Biographies of Immortals says:
Hánzǐ
was a man of Shǔ,
fond of letting dogs roam.
A dog ran into a mountain cave,
Hánzǐ followed it,
traveled several hundred lǐ and emerged,
at the mountain top were palace halls and government offices,
with immortals, officials, and envoys very strict.
He saw his former wife in charge of washing fish,
who gave Hánzǐ a box of medicine,
opening the box,
it contained fish roe.
Placing it in a pond to raise it,
after a year they all became dragons.
Hánzǐ later returned the box to the mountain,
saw the dog's color had turned redder,
with long feathers following,
Hánzǐ then stayed on the mountain.
From time to time he came down to protect his clan,
and the people of Shǔ built a shrine for him.
And as for the Jìn envoy biting the shield,
The Zuǒ Tradition says:
The Marquis of Jìn gave Zhào Dùn wine to drink,
having埋伏 soldiers to attack him.
His right-hand attendant Tímí Míng knew of it,
hurried forward and said:
"Your servant attends the ruler at a feast,
exceeding three cups,
is against ritual."
Then he was supported and descended.
The lord set his hound on him,
and Míng fought and killed it.
Dùn said:
"Abandoning men and using a dog,
though fierce, what use is it!"
Jié's hound barked at Yáo,
the Records of the Grand Historian states:
Emperor Gāozǔ ordered Qí to arrest Kuǎi Tōng,
when Tōng arrived,
the emperor said:
"Did you teach Huáiyīn Hóu to rebel?"
He replied:
"Jié's dog barked at Yáo,
not because Yáo was unkind,
but because a dog naturally barks at those not its master.
At that time,
I only knew Hán Xìn,
I did not know Your Majesty."
Regarding the glaring eyes of the Wèi Tái,
the Wèi Lüè states:
During Emperor Míng's time, slanderous writings said:
"Three dogs in the Tái,
their glaring eyes are unbearable;
one dog relies on Diǎn to act as a maggot bag."
The three dogs refer to Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, and Dīng Mì.
Diǎn refers to
Cáo Shuǎng's childhood name.
Mì especially flattered Shuǎng.
Hearing of the carefree life in the Qí state.
the Sānguó Diǎn Lüè states:
Qí Gāo Wěi bestowed the Persian dog with the titles Chìhǔ Yìtóng and Xiāoyáo Jùnjūn,
often placing a cushion on horseback to hold it.
White Sparrow, Green Falcon, Flying Dragon, Tiger Cub,
see the note on "alert, swift, tame, and good" above.
Majestic appearance and fierce countenance,
Wèi Jiǎ Dàizōng's "Great Dog Rhapsody" states:
Its head,
cannot be fully described;
its bone structure,
cannot be clearly distinguished and explained.
CH0F0237 Suō & - ; Cùqiàng,
majestic appearance and fierce countenance.
Difficult to befriend but easy to command.
See the note on "alert, swift, tame, and good" above.
Again, there is the growling that none may approach,
the Chǔcí‧Jiǔ Biàn states:
How could I not be melancholy and think of my lord?
The lord's gate has nine layers.
Fierce dogs growl and bark in welcome,
the passes and bridges are closed and impassable.
Línglíng is praiseworthy,
the Shī states:
The black dog's collar rings línglíng,
its master is handsome and kind.
Note:
Lú,
hunting dog.
Attacking Shí Liáng's house,
the Hànshū‧Wǔxíng Zhì states:
In the first year of Hépíng under Emperor Chéng,
Cháng'ān men Shí Liáng and Liú Jìn lived together,
something resembling a human form appeared in their house,
they struck it,
it turned into a dog,
and ran away.
Then several men wearing armor and carrying bows and crossbows came to Liáng's house,
Liáng and others struck them, some were wounded,
all were dogs.
This lasted from the second month to the sixth month before stopping.
According to the Hóng Fàn,
these were all dog calamities.
Entering Huà Chén's house.
the Zuǒzhuàn states:
The people of the Sòng state chased a rabid dog,
it entered Huà Chén's house,
the people followed it,
Huà Chén was afraid,
and fled to Chén.
Then there is the barking at the black-clothed man,
the Lièzǐ states:
Yáng Zhū's younger brother was called Bù,
he went out wearing white clothes.
It rained,
he took off his white clothes,
and returned wearing black clothes.
His dog came to meet him and barked,
Yáng Bù was angry,
and was about to beat the dog.
Yáng Zhū said:
"Do not beat it,
if earlier your dog had seen you go out white,
and come back black,
how could it not be strange!"
Again, disaster began with the plum blossom.
the Shùyìjì states: The dog at Zhū Xiū's house sang:
"You say I cannot sing,
listen to me sing of the plum blossom.
This year may still be fine,
what about next year?"
The family killed the dog,
the next year they all died.
Sīmó once guarded the north gate,
the Tángshū states:
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Míníshú Kèhán Lǐ Sīmó,
was granted land by imperial decree,
south to the great river,
north to the Báidào Chuān.
Later, when returning to his state,
he addressed the emperor saying:
"I have undeservedly received grace,
been made a tribal chief,
I truly hope my descendants will serve the state with utmost loyalty,
becoming one of the state's dogs,
guarding and barking at the north gate."
Yànzǐ once mocked the Chǔ state.
the Yànzǐ states:
Yànzǐ was short,
and was sent to Chǔ.
The Chǔ people made a small gate next to the main gate,
and invited Yànzǐ to enter.
Yànzǐ said:
"Those sent to a dog state,
enter through the dog gate.
Now I am sent to Chǔ,
I should not enter through this gate."
The weeping of the three Miáo, though perhaps it became an omen,
the Suícháozǐ states:
In ancient times, when the three Miáo were in great chaos,
a dragon was born in the temple,
and dogs wept in the marketplace.
The calamity of Shūjiān, how could it overcome virtue?
the Fēngsútōng states:
Lǐ Shūjiān, Governor of Guìyáng, was an official,
his family had a dog that walked like a man,
his family said it should be killed.
Shūjiān said:
"Dogs and horses are compared to gentlemen,
the dog sees men walking,
and imitates them,
what harm is there?"
Shortly after,
the dog put on Shūjiān's hat and ran,
the family was greatly alarmed.
Shūjiān said:
"It accidentally touched the hat,
and the tassel got caught on it."
The dog also kept the fire going in front of the stove,
the family became even more anxious.
Shūjiān again said:
"The children and servants are all in the fields,
the dog helps keep the fire going,
fortunately we need not trouble the neighbors,
what evil is there in this?"
After several days,
the dog suddenly died on its own,
and the family ultimately suffered not the slightest mishap.
Again, there is the name "kòu qì",
the Shuōwén states:
Gǒu (dog),
means kòu,
kòu qì means barking to guard.
Called "xuán tí",
the Shuōwén states:
Quǎn,
refers to dogs that have xuán tí.
Heard of "gǎn shuì",
the Shī states:
Do not lift my handkerchief,
do not make the long-haired dog bark.
Seen holding clothes in its mouth.
the Wú Zhì states:
Sūn Jùn plotted to kill Zhūgě Kè.
On the night before Kè was to have an audience,
his spirit was restless,
he could not sleep all night.
After dressing, he hurried out,
a dog held his clothes in its mouth and pulled,
Kè said:
"Does the dog not want me to go?"
He returned and sat down,
after a while he got up again,
the dog again held his clothes in its mouth,
Kè ordered his attendants to drive the dog away,
then ascended his carriage.
Indeed, he met with disaster.
The worn cover is recorded in the Lǐ,
see the note on "lún qū bì wéi" in the "Horse Rhapsody".
Double rings are seen in the Shī.
the Shī states:
The black dog's collar has double rings and double chains.
Advising against Qí Jǐng's burial,
the Yànzǐ states:
Duke Jǐng's hunting dog died,
he ordered an outer coffin and inner sacrificial offerings.
Yànzǐ advised that this was not permissible,
and the duke followed his advice.
Seizing Gōngsūn's calf.
the Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ states:
Diāo Bó often slandered Tián Dān at court,
so Tián Dān summoned him and asked about it.
Diāo Bó said:
"Indeed, a dog of Zhí can be made to bark at Yáo,
not because Zhí is esteemed and Yáo is despised,
but because a dog naturally barks at those who are not its master.
Moreover, Gōngsūnzǐ is virtuous while Xúzǐ is unworthy,
yet when Gōngsūnzǐ fought with Xúzǐ,
Xúzǐ's dog seized Gōngsūnzǐ's calf and bit it.
If one were to abandon the unworthy and become virtuous,
would the dog only seize and bite?!"
Tián Dān then recommended Diāo Bó to the king.
Suí ascended to immortality with Liú Ān,
as recorded in the Shù Yì Jì:
at the immortal site of Má Gū on Jìyáng Mountain,
it is commonly said:
after a thousand years, the golden rooster crows,
and the jade dog barks.
It is also said:
at the immortal site of Huáinán King Liú Ān,
roosters crow in the heavens,
and dogs bark among the clouds.
This alludes to the homeless dog of Zhòngní.
The Shǐ Jì states:
When Confucius went to Zhèng,
he became separated from his disciples,

"Using Qín to govern the feudal lords,
is like unleashing a Hán Lǔ hound to chase a lame rabbit."
Lǐ Sī's words from Shàngcài.
The "Shǐjì" says:
Lǐ Sī, leaving prison,
turned and said to his son:
"I wish with you,
to again lead the yellow hound out the eastern gate of Shàngcài,
to chase the cunning rabbit,
how could that be possible now!"
Liáng Jì built a park for them,
Zhāng Fán's "Hànjì" says:
Liáng Jì established a rabbit park,
issued proclamations everywhere,
requisitioned live rabbits,
and marked their fur.
Any commoner who violated this,
was sentenced to death.
Once a foreign merchant from the Western Regions came,
unaware of the prohibition,
accidentally killed a rabbit,
word spread,
and over ten people were executed for this.
Prince Xiào created a garden for them.
Xiè Huìlián's "Snow Rhapsody" says:
The King of Liáng was displeased,
and went to roam in the Rabbit Garden.
As for the "Shī" calling it 'this head',
the "Shī" says:
There is a rabbit, this head,
roast it, broil it.
'Sī' is pronounced 'xiān'.
The "Lǐ" marks it as 'bright-eyed',
the "Lǐ" says:
in sacrifices, the rabbit is called 'bright-eyed'.
It should not emerge from the moon,
the "Yùndǒushū" says:
If the conduct of Yáoguāng is errant, then the rabbit emerges from the moon.
Annotation:
Because yin does not contain yang, the rabbit emerges from the moon.
How could it exist in water?
The "Lùnhéng" says:
Confucian scholars say there is a rabbit in the moon,
but the moon,
is water,
a rabbit in water,
none can survive.
The rabbit,
is merely the essence of the moon.
As for Shū Lín, one was born beneath his bed,
Xiè Chéng's "Hòuhànshū" says:
Rú Shū Lín was governor of Dōngjùn,
a red crow nested on his roof beam,
and a rabbit was born beneath the trees.
Cài Yōng had one tamed beside his dwelling.
The "Hòuhànshū" says:
Cài Yōng was deeply filial by nature,
his mother was once ill for three years,
Yōng, unless the seasons of cold and heat changed,
never loosened his girdle,
and did not sleep for seventy days.
When his mother died,
he built a hut by her grave mound,
his every action followed ritual,
and a rabbit became tame beside his dwelling.
The red one manifests the auspicious sign of a flourishing king,
the "Ruìyìngtú" says:
the red rabbit,
is an auspicious beast,
it arrives when the king's virtue is flourishing.
The black one is the portent of a dynastic change.
The "Jìnshū ‧ Zǎijì" says:
During Shí Lè's time,
Magistrate Shī Huān of Rènpíng captured a black rabbit,
some considered it an auspicious sign of Lè's dynastic change.
For Jìn, water succeeded metal.
The rabbit,
is a beast of yin essence,
black is the color of water,
therefore he changed the reign title to Tàihé.
Bestowed upon a general's concubine,
the "Diǎnlüè" says:
Zhōu ordered Yùchí Jiǒng to attack Shǔ,
Tàizǔ saw him off west of the city,
saw a running rabbit,
and ordered his younger brother, the Central Army Commander Gāng, to shoot it.
Gāng vowed:
"If I catch this rabbit,
we will surely defeat Shǔ."
He caught it as he spoke.
Tàizǔ joyfully said:
"When the matter is settled,
I will reward you with a fine person."
After conquering Shǔ,
he bestowed two serving maids.
Tribute of beauties from a neighboring state.
The "Hòuwèishū" says:
A rabbit entered the rear palace,
the gate officials were questioned,
but it had no way to enter.
Tàizǔ ordered Cuī Hào to deduce the ominous sign.
Hào believed it meant a neighboring state would offer beauties.
The next year,
Yáo Xìng indeed came to present a woman.
Also, there is one dwelling in the belly of the moon,
see the annotation in the "Moon Rhapsody": "The gazing rabbit ascends with essence."
Its fur comes from Xuāntù.
The "Fànzǐ Jìrán" says:
Rabbit hair comes from Xuāntù and Lèlàng.
A metaphor for attaining the Way by forgetting the snare,
the "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
The snare is what is used for the rabbit,
having caught the rabbit, one forgets the snare.
Annotation:
The snare,
is a rabbit net.
Despising the fool who guarded the stump.
The "Hánzǐ" says:
A man of Sòng was plowing,
in his field was a stump,
a rabbit ran and hit it,
broke its neck and died.
He then abandoned his plow to guard the stump,
hoping to get another rabbit.
As for overtaking the sun and chasing the wind,
the "Huáinánzǐ" says:
With the rabbit's running,
If it were as large as a horse,
it would catch up with the sun and chase the wind;
but when it becomes a horse,
it no longer runs.
Running through the streets and piled up in the market,
the *Shènzǐ* says:
"A single rabbit running through the streets
is chased by a hundred people;
but when rabbits are piled up in the market,
people pass by without even looking.
It is not that they do not desire to obtain them,
but because their shares are already determined."
People have the name "Mǎorì,"
the *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"In the mountains, the one called 'Zhàngrén' on the Mǎorì day is the rabbit."
Its fine hair is praised as the finest in Zhàoguó.
The *Guǎngzhì* says:
"When the various commanderies of Hàn presented rabbit hair
to inscribe the Hóngdū Gate,
only the hair from Zhàoguó was suitable for use."
Huá Qiū threw himself into the task and captured a rabbit,
the *Suíshū* says:
Huá Qiū,
a man from Jíjùn.
When his mother passed away,
he carried earth to build her grave,
and built a hut beside the tomb.
If anyone tried to assist him,
Huá Qiū would bow and stop them.
Once, a hunter was chasing a rabbit,
which ran into Huá Qiū's hut
and hid beneath his knees.
The hunter, astonished, spared it.
From then on, this rabbit often stayed in the hut.
Stationed at Shèquǎn, it was certain to die.
The *Xiàndì Chūnqiū* says:
Suī Gù, a general under Zhāng Yáng, was stationed at Shèquǎn.
A shaman warned him, saying:
"General, your original name is Báitù (White Rabbit).
When a rabbit sees a dog, it is sure to panic.
It is not suitable for you to stay here."
Suī Gù did not heed this.
Lord Cáo said:
"The rabbit has entered the dog's city."
He advanced his army, attacked, and pacified the area.
In Zhāng Huá's *Bówùzhì*,
the birth of young rabbits was once seen in the mouth;
the *Bówùzhì* says:
"The rabbit conceives by gazing at the moon,
and gives birth from its mouth.
I had long heard of this tale,
and today I have witnessed it."
Fù Xuán composed a song,
and the pounding of medicine is still heard within the moon.
Fù Xuán's *Gēcí* says:
"What is there to say of the rabbit pounding medicine in the moon,
what is there to say of the divine crow frolicking among the clouds!"
Grass
Lush and verdant grow the spring grasses,
Yet the noble wanderer does not return.
These are lines from Liú Ān's "Summoning the Recluse."
Exuding fragrance and spreading their splendor,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park" says:
Mingled with méiwú,
Mixed with liúyí.
Bending with the wind,
Exuding fragrance and spreading their splendor.
Covering the banks and cliffs.
Zhāng Píngzǐ's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" says:
Among the grasses are zhēn, suō, jiān, and biāo,
Wēi, jué, lì, and háng,
Dense and luxuriant,
Covering the banks and hills.
Thoughts of the Jiangnán in late spring,
Qiū Xīfàn's "Letter to Chén Bózhī" says:
In the third month of late spring,
In Jiangnán the grasses grow tall,
Mixed flowers bloom on the trees,
Flocks of orioles flit about.
The sorrow of the frontier beyond the pass in the cool wind.
Lǐ Líng's "Letter to Sū Wǔ" says:
In the ninth month, the cool wind blows,
Beyond the pass the grasses wither.
Unable to sleep at night,
I listen intently into the distance,
The sound of Hú jiā pipes intermingling,
The mournful whinnying of pasturing horses.
That which communicates with the spirits is the wēnzǎo.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
The plants from mountain streams, ponds, and islets—pín, fán, wēn, and zǎo—
Can be offered to ghosts and spirits,
Can be presented to kings and lords.
That which manifests auspicious omens is the xíuzhī.
The Ěryǎ says:
Xíu,
Is zhī.
Commentary:
The zhī blooms three times a year,
An auspicious plant.
Pointing to the east gate for steeping jiān,
The Shī says:
The pool by the east gate,
Can be used to steep jiān.
Climbing the southern mountains to gather wēi.
The Shī says:
Climb that southern mountain,
To gather its wēi.
Now, on the mound there is the lovely tiáo,
The Shī says:
On the dam there is a magpie's nest,
On the mound there is the lovely tiáo.
In the lowlands there is the chángchǔ,
The Shī says:
In the lowlands there is the chángchǔ,
Graceful are its branches.
Gathering blue dye, not yet filling a lapful,
The Shī says:
All morning gathering blue,
Not filling a lapful.
Planting huì, soon flourishing over a hundred mǔ.
The Lísāo says:
Having already cultivated orchids over nine wǎn,
And planted huì over a hundred mǔ.
Mùxu sways with the wind,
The Xījīng Zá Jì says:
In the Lèyóu Garden grew wild rose trees,
Under the trees was much mùxu,
Also called huáifēng.
Sometimes it was said that radiant wind was among them,
Always rustling, shining with its brilliance,
Hence called mùxu huáifēng.
People of Màolíng called it liánzhīcǎo.
Ránghé thrives in the shade.
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Life of Leisure" says:
Ránghé relies on shade,
While huò faces the sun.
The gé has already spread in the valley,
The Shī says:
The gé vine spreads long,
Spreading in the valley,
Its leaves so lush.
Orchids also grow clustered below the hall.
Qū Píng's "Nine Songs" says:
Autumn orchids and méiwú,
Grow clustered below the hall.
Those luxuriant artemisias,
With one shot, five boars.
From the Shī.
The book-binding grass of Bùqí,
The Sān Qí Lüè Jì says:
East of Bùqí City is the mountain where Zhèng Xuán taught.
At the foot of the mountain grew a grass like xiè,
Its leaves over a chǐ long,
Exceptionally tough and pliant,
The locals named it Kāngchéng's book-binding grass.
The screen grass of Jìnyáng.
The Bówùzhì says:
North of Tàiyuán and Jìnyáng grows screen grass.
If the Way prevails, why be ashamed of a lí staff?
See the annotation in "Rhapsody on the Staff": "Lí signifies Yuán Xiàn's poverty."
When virtue flourishes, then appears the hào palace.
The Dà Dài Lǐ says:
When the virtue of Zhōu was harmonious and pervasive,
The hào grew large,
And was used as palace pillars,
Named the hào palace,
This was the Lùqǐn of the realm.
Clearing them meets the duty of the tì official,
See the annotation in "Rhapsody on Winter": "Following the tì official's removal of grasses."
Tasting them also began with Shénnóng.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Shénnóng first tasted the hundred herbs,
Encountering seventy poisons in one day.
Then there is the surplus grain of the sea,
The Bówùzhì says:
On the sea there is a grass,
Named shī,
Its seeds eaten are like barley,
Ripening in the seventh month,
Called zìrán gǔ,
Or called Yǔ's surplus grain.
Shī is pronounced shī.
The fúlǎo by the wellside,
The Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn says:
Cài Shùn, styled Jūnzhòng,
Was extremely filial.
The well-sweep at his dwelling was old,
He wished to replace it,
But dared not because it was within his mother's lifespan.
One day, suddenly a fúlǎo vine grew and entwined it,
And a turtledove nested upon it.
Marveling that the overgrown path is hard to travel,
The Guóyǔ says:
King Dìng sent Duke Dān Xiāng on a mission to Sòng,
Who then borrowed passage through Chén to go on a mission to Chǔ.
When the Fire Star appears at dawn,
The path is overgrown and impassable.
Duke Dān returned and reported to the king, saying:
"Now in the state of Chén, the Fire Star appears at dawn,
Yet the roads seem blocked,
This is to abandon the teachings of the former kings,
How can it last long!"
In the ninth year,
The Viscount of Chǔ entered Chén.
Commentary:
Grasses and weeds blocking the road is called fú.
Lamenting that the wall-thorns are not swept away.
The Shī says:
"The Wall Has Thorns,"
The people of Wèi satirize their superiors.
The wall has thorns,
That cannot be swept away.
The xuān planted in vain behind the house,
The Shī says:
Where can one get xuān grass,
To plant behind the house.
The Yǎngshēng Lùn says:
Héhuān dispels anger,
Xuān grass makes one forget sorrow.
Can the quán perceive my true feelings?
The Lísāo says:
The quán does not perceive my innermost feelings,
Instead believes slander and rages.
Commentary:
Quán is a metaphor for the ruler.
Tying the secluded orchid, I linger long,
From the Lísāo.
Eating the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums.
From the Chǔcí.
Hearing of killing by gōuwěn,
Yet tales of prolonging life by huángjīng.
The Bówùzhì says:
Tiān Lǎo said to the Yellow Emperor:
"The grass of the Great Sun is named huángjīng,
Consuming it can lead to long life.
The grass of the Great Yin is named gōuwěn,
Entering the mouth brings instant death.
People believe gōuwěn kills,
But do not believe huángjīng prolongs life,
Is this not delusion?"
In Jìyīn, some marveled at their soldier-like forms,
The Fēngsútōng says:
In the seventh year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng,
On the roadsides of various commanderies in Chénliú and Jìyīn, grasses grew in human shapes,
Holding spears, crossbows, and myriad forms of oxen and horses, all fully equipped.
Later, Guāndōng rose against Dǒng Zhuó,
Chénliú and Jìyīn abandoned friendship for arms,
Officials and people were slaughtered and maimed,
The rise of grass portents,
How could it be without some truth!
The Eight Dukes were also startled by human-like forms.
The Jìnshū says:
Fú Jiān arrived at Shòuchūn,
And with Fú Róng ascended the wall to observe the royal army,
Seeing the formations orderly and aligned,
The officers and soldiers elite and sharp.
Looking north again at the plants and trees on Bāgōng Mountain,
All resembled human forms.
He turned and said to Róng:
"This is also a formidable enemy;
how can you call it few!"
He stroked his beard with a fearful expression.
He feared the early fall of autumn frost.
The Fúzǐ says:
A neighbor said to Zhǎn Qín:
"Lǔ has offered you a position,
yet you were dismissed three times without showing any sign of worry—why?"
Qín replied:
"When the spring wind blows,
and all plants flourish luxuriantly,
I do not know their lushness;
when autumn frost descends,
and all plants wither and fall,
I do not know their decay.
Decay and lushness are not the sorrow or joy of the four seasons;
how can glory and disgrace know the worry or delight in my heart?"
He feared the early call of the tíjué bird.
The Lísāo says:
I fear the tíjué's early call,
which makes all plants lose their fragrance.
Note:
The tíjué often calls at the spring and autumn equinoxes.
As for being born in a land of gentlemen,
the Kuòdìtú says:
The people of the gentleman's land carry swords and lead two striped tigers,
wear wild silk,
and their territory spans a thousand li square,
with abundant xūnhuā grass,
which is yielding,
hence it is called the Land of Gentlemen.
Xūnhuā grass
blooms in the morning and dies by evening.
It illustrates the virtue of petty men.
See the Lúnyǔ.
Lush is that Yān Mountain,
Jiāng Yān's "Imitating Guō Pú's Roaming Immortal Poem" says:
Yān Mountain has many spiritual herbs,
and the seashore abounds with strange stones.
Abundant is this orchid marsh.
An ancient poem says:
The orchid marsh has many fragrant grasses.
Some do not bend even in the wind,
the Shuǐjīng says:
In Wèixīng,
Xīyì Mountain grows much wēihéng grass,
which does not bend in the wind,
but sways alone when there is no wind.
Some stand straight without support.
The Fēngsútōng says:
When artemisia grows among hemp,
it stands straight without support.
On the plain, thoughts of parting stir,
