an ancient poem says:
Lush, lush the grass on the plain,
dense, dense the willows in the garden.
By the riverbank, one delights in the verdant color.
An ancient Yuèfǔ poem says:
Verdant, verdant the grass by the riverbank.
By day you gather thatch,
by night you twist ropes.
From the Shī.
Note:
Táo means
to twist,
twisting thatch into ropes.
Some have patterns like the yìshòu grass,
the Ěryǎ says:
Yìshòu.
Note:
Small flowers,
with variegated colors,
resembling a ribbon.
Some are colored like a green robe,
an ancient poem says:
Gentle, gentle the clear wind arrives,
blowing the hem of my silk skirt.
The green robe is like spring grass,
its long strands swaying in the wind.
Some thread orchids to wear as adornments,
from the Chǔcí.
Some fill their waists with mugwort.
The Chǔcí says:
Adorned with mugwort filling the waist,
saying the secluded orchid cannot be worn.
As for Zāng Wén's concubine weaving mats,
the Zuǒzhuàn says:
Zhòngní said:
"Zāng Wénzhòng has three acts of unkindness:
demoting Zhǎn Qín, abolishing the six passes, and having his concubine weave mats—
these are the three acts of unkindness."
Bó Yǒu's gate grew weeds.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Zhèng's Gōngsūn Huī passed by Bó Yǒu's house,
and weeds grew at his gate.
Zǐyǔ said:
"Are the weeds still there?"
Note:
This metaphorically refers to Bó Yǒu.
Bó Yǒu was extravagant,
and they knew he could not last long.
Hearing of the jǐngtiān grass that warns of fire,
the Běncǎo says:
Jǐngtiān,
also called jièhuǒ,
also called shuǐmǔhuā,
primarily improves eyesight and lightens the body.
Recognizing the bāomáo grass used for straining wine.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
The Marquis of Qí attacked Chǔ,
and said to Chǔ:
"You have not presented the bāomáo grass as tribute,
so the king's sacrifices are not supplied,
and there is nothing to strain the wine—
this is what I demand."
As for the differences between cloth and silk,
and the distinctions between lún and zǔ,
the Ěryǎ says:
Lún resembles lún,
zǔ resembles zǔ,
and they exist in the Eastern Sea.
Note:
Lún is the twisted blue silk ribbon worn by today's village officials.
Zǔ
is a ribbon.
In the sea, grass grows in colors,
and its patterns resemble these,
hence the names.
It also says:
Bó resembles bó,
bù resembles bù,
and they exist on Huà Mountain.
Note:
Some grasses have leaves resembling cloth or silk,
hence the names,
and they grow on Huà Mountain.
Adorned with jiānglí and bìzhǐ,
from the Lísāo.
Planted in rows are liúyí and jiēchē.
From the Lísāo.
Note:
Liúyí and jiēchē are both fragrant herbs.
The pond inspired Huìlián's dream,
Xiè Língyùn's "Poem on Ascending the Pond Tower" says:
"Spring grass grows by the pond,
and garden willows change the singing birds."
This line came to him in a dream about Huìlián.
Mugwort and weeds encroached upon Zhòng Wèi's dwelling.
The Sānfǔ Juélù says:
Zhāng Zhòngwèi,
a man of Pínglíng.
He lived in seclusion and did not serve in office.
Mugwort and weeds overgrew his dwelling, covering it entirely.
The mushrooms of Luòyuè,
the qǐ of Yúnmèng.
The Wúyuè Chūnqiū says:
Among delicious vegetables,
there are the mushrooms of Luòyuè,
and the qǐ of Yúnmèng.
Pronounced qǐ.
Suījiāng already perfumes the mouth,
the Shuōwén says:
Suī
is a type of ginger,
and can perfume the mouth.
Fúyǐ is also said to aid childbirth.
The Shī says:
Plucking, plucking the fúyǐ,
let us gather it.
Note:
Fúyǐ,
also called chēqián,
is beneficial for pregnancy.
Resting on thistles makes it hard to seek peace,
the Yì says:
Trapped among rocks,
resting on thistles,
entering his house,
he does not see his wife—
ominous.
Gathering fēng and fěi without discarding the lower parts.
The Shī says:
Gather fēng, gather fěi,
do not discard the lower parts.
Note:
These two vegetables,
are types like turnip and fú.
Both the upper and lower parts are edible,
but their roots can be good or bad at times.
The auspicious míngjiá and qūyì,
míngjiá is mentioned in the Yuèfù note for "verifying the míng on the steps without error."
The Bówùzhì says:
When a flatterer enters the court,
the qūyì grass points at him.
It grew during the time of the Yellow Emperor.
The auspicious kuòdá and huápíng.
The Báihǔtōng says:
When the king's succession is peaceful,
then bīnlián kuòdá grows at the door.
The "Ruì Yìng Tú" states:
When the ruler's mechanisms are orderly,
and men and women are distinguished,
then the bīnlián kuòdá grows in the chamber.
Also called liándá,
it symbolizes that the queen and consorts are disciplined.
It also says:
Huápíng,
its branches are even!
When the ruler's governance and decrees are equitable, it grows.
The "Yuán Shén Qì" states:
When the ruler's virtue reaches the earth,
then huápíng flourishes.
The "Sòng Shū ‧ Fú Ruì Zhì" states:
During the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén,
twin lotus flowers shared a single stem.
The "Ruì Yìng Tú" states:
Twin lotus flowers are called píng.
Brewing wine in the land of Yáokūn,
the "Dòng Míng Jì" states:
Tiánxī water is like honey;
Dōngfāng Shuò traveled to this water,
and brought back several hú to present to the emperor.
The emperor poured it into a yīn well,
and the well thereafter became sweet and cold,
washing flesh to make the skin soft and smooth.
Yáokūn is ninety thousand lǐ from Yùmén,
where there is green grass like wheat;
cutting it to brew wine,
one hé will cause one to remain unconscious for thirty days,
but drinking sweet water will awaken them.
Feeding horses in the land of Jíyún.
The "Dòng Míng Jì" states:
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"I have ten qǐng of jíyún grass,
transplanted from the marsh of Jíyún to the east of Jiǔjǐng Mountain,
which blooms once every two thousand years;
one must fetch water from the surface stream of Zhāngláng Mountain to the east to sprinkle on it,
I request to go and harvest it."
He left in the morning,
and returned carrying it in the evening;
its leaves resemble wheat and are golden in color.
Cutting it to feed horses,
makes the horses plump and glossy.
The sunflower has the reputation of protecting its feet,
and the bean has the inclination to face the sun.
Both are seen in the annotation of "sunflower and bean leaning and relying" in the "Rì Fù."
Such varieties are numerous,
hence called bǎi zǒng.
The "Shuō Wén" states:
Huì,
is the general name for grass.
Bamboo
Among the beauties of the southeast,
there are the bamboo arrows of Kuàijī.
From the Ěryǎ.
The two consorts wept for him at Cāngwú.
The Bówùzhì says:
Shùn died at Cāngwú.
His two daughters wept at Dòngtíng.
They shed tears upon the bamboo,
and the bamboo became entirely mottled.
A fief of a thousand households was granted for it at Wèichuān.
The Shǐjì says:
A thousand mǔ of bamboo in Wèichuān
is equivalent to a marquis with a thousand households.
Líng Lún gathered it in Xiègǔ.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
The Yellow Emperor commanded Líng Lún to establish the pitch pipes.
From west of Dàxià to the northern slopes of Yuán and Yú,
he took bamboo from the mountain streams and valleys,
selecting pieces with uniform wall thickness,
cutting between two nodes,
their length being three inches and nine tenths,
and blew them.
Note:
Dàxià, Yuán, and Yú are all mountain streams.
Sometimes written as Xiè.
Cài Yōng recognized it at Gāoqiān.
See the note on "Cài Yōng recognized Gāoqiān" in the Dí Fù.
Féi Chángfáng obtained it and used it to transform his shape.
See the note on "Féi Chángfáng obtained it and it manifested spiritual transformation" in the Zhàng Fù.
Lí Lóu ingested it and became an immortal.
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Lí Lóugōng ingested bamboo sap and took cassia to become an immortal.
Then there is that which emerges from Gònggǔ.
The Shānhǎijīng says:
West of Chángshí Mountain is Gònggǔ,
within which there is much bamboo.
South of Wèiqiū Mountain lies the bamboo forest of Dì Jùn,
large enough to make boats.
Note:
Jùn is the character for Shùn.
Planted on the southern slope of the mountain.
The Shùzhēngjì says:
Northeast of Shānyáng County, the garden and residence of Jī Kāng are now all ruins,
yet the elders still call it Jīgōng's Bamboo Grove.
The Shū mentions jùn lù.
The Shū says:
The tribute of Jīngzhōu consists of jùn lù
and hù.
Note:
Jùn lù
is fine bamboo.
The Yì praises the cāng láng.
The Yì says:
Zhèn represents the cāng láng bamboo.
Sometimes it is killed to make slips.
The Fēngsútōng says:
Killing the green,
means making slips for writing.
New bamboo has sap;
later it all becomes worm-eaten,
so those who make slips dry it over fire.
Sometimes it is inserted to lead sheep.
See the note on "Jìn Wǔ drove it with sheep" in the Chē Fù.
It can be used to drill for fire.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Dry bamboo contains fire,
but without drilling it will not ignite.
It cannot obtain water.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Tiles are formed by fire,
but cannot obtain fire;
bamboo is born from water,
but cannot obtain water.
The white tiger had an auspicious omen for the Hàn court.
The Shīyì says:
In the southern regions grows the mother-child bamboo,
which is now the cí bamboo.
In the third year of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
mother-child bamboo grew before the White Tiger Hall.
It was then called filial bamboo,
and the assembled ministers composed the "Ode to Filial Bamboo."
Yóuwú has the beauty of Wú's capital.
Zuǒ Sī's "Wūdū Fù" says:
"Yóuwú has its huáng."
Sometimes it is bundled to administer punishment.
The Tángshū says:
Nánzhào had no penal names or implements of shackles.
Those guilty of crimes were bound with five stalks of bamboo,
and those who confessed were flogged on the back.
Sometimes it is cut to make arrows.
The Hòuhànshū says:
Kòu Xún was the governor of Hénèi.
He sent documents to the subordinate counties,
to drill troops and practice archery,
and cut bamboo from the Qí Garden to make arrows.
Above the Music Pond of King Mù of Zhōu.
The Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn says:
The Son of Heaven campaigned westward,
reaching Xuánchí.
The Son of Heaven rested by Xuánchí,
then performed the Grand Music,
which lasted three days and concluded.
This was called the Music Pond.
He then planted bamboo there,
and this was called the Bamboo Grove.
Within the Hare Garden of King Xiào of Liáng.
The Hànshū says:
King Xiào of Liáng's Hare Garden had many planted bamboos,
which was the so-called Tall Bamboo Garden.
Bīngzhōu riding a horse.
See the note on "Guō Jí reached the commandery and rode bamboo" in the Mǎ Fù.
Gěbēi transforming into a dragon.
See the note on "Cast into Gěbēi and suddenly transformed" in the Zhàng Fù.
Sometimes it symbolizes the Way and models Heaven.
Jiāng Yōu's "Zhú Fù" says:
Hollow within to symbolize the Way,
with a round substance to model Heaven.
Sometimes it wards off dew and invites the wind.
The Chǔcí, "Seven Remonstrances" says:
The graceful bamboo grows by the river pool.
Above, lush and warding off dew;
below, cool and inviting the wind.
And then cutting the Qí Garden.
The Hànshū says:
During Emperor Wǔ's reign, the Yellow River breached.
The emperor sent tens of thousands of soldiers
to dam the Hùzǐ River,
using bamboo from the Qí Garden as pilings.
Burning Shēnchí.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Jìn attacked Qí,
and burned the bamboo and trees of Shēnchí.
Meeting the blade, then the Jìn minister metaphorized victory.
The Jìnshū says:
Wáng Jùn campaigned against Wú.
Many commanderies and prefectures submitted upon hearing the news.
Dù Yù said:
"The might of our army is already felt.
It is like splitting bamboo:
after a few sections,
it all meets the blade and splits open,
with no place left to apply force."
The fishing rod, then a Wèi woman longed to return.
"The Bamboo Rod"
is about a Wèi woman longing to return.
Long and slender the bamboo rod,
to fish in the Qí.
Zhào Xiāngzi split it and found red writing.
The Shǐjì says:
Zhì Bó led Hán and Wèi to attack Zhào Xiāngzi.
Xiāngzi fled to Jìnyáng.
Yuán Guò arrived later,
and saw three men visible from the belt up,
but not from the belt down.
They gave Yuán Guò three sections of bamboo,
with no opening.
They said:
"Give this to Zhào Wúxù."
Xiāngzi himself split the bamboo,
and there was red writing.
A woman split it and obtained an infant.
The Huáyáng Guózhì says:
There was a Bamboo King,
who arose at Dùnshuǐ.
There was a woman washing by the riverside.
Three large bamboos flowed between the woman's feet.
She pushed them but they would not go away.
She heard the sound of a child.
She took them home,
split the bamboo, and obtained a boy.
He grew up with military talent,
and then dominated the Yí and Dí tribes.
He took Bamboo as his clan name.
The split bamboo in the wild formed a forest,
which is now the Bamboo Grove at the king's shrine.
Yá hollow, biǎo solid.
The Zhúpǔ says:
Biǎo and yóu yá,
their bodies are both large,
their circumference sometimes accumulating to a chǐ.
Biǎo solid, yá hollow,
the dwellings of Nányuè
are supplied with their beams and pillars.
Note:
Both bamboos are large.
Biǎo has small pores,
nearly solid inside;
yóu yá is hollow inside, somewhat larger.
The solitary pipe and side branches.
The Zhōulǐ says:
The pipes of solitary bamboo,
the qín and sè of Yúnhé,
the dance of Yúnmén,
on the winter solstice,
are performed at the round mound on the earth.
The pipes of silk and bamboo,
the qín and sè of Kōngsāng,
the dance of Xiánchí,
on the summer solstice,
are performed at the square mound in the marsh.
The pipes made of yīn bamboo,
the qín and sè zithers from Lóngmén,
the songs of the nine virtues,
and the dances of the nine chimes,
are performed within the ancestral temple.
Note:
Gūzhú bamboo
grows alone.
Sūnzhú bamboo,
grows from the root's end.
Yīnzhú bamboo,
grows on the northern side of mountains.
The dense bamboo groves of Hù and Dù,
as stated in the "Treatise on Geography":
In the land of Qín, there are bamboo groves in Hù and Dù,
with tán and zhè trees on the southern mountains,
known as the "Land of Abundance."
The accumulation of bamboo in Tánxī.
As recorded in the Book of Liáng:
When Emperor Wǔ governed Yōngzhōu,
he ordered the felling of many trees and bamboos,
which were sunk into Tánxī,
and covered with thatch, piling up like hills,
all unused.
When he raised an army,
he took all the bamboo from Tánxī,
fashioned it into boats and ships,
and covered them with thatch,
completing the task swiftly.
Covering with crimson curtains to observe the pitch pipes,
as stated in the Méizǐ:
Bamboo from Jīnmén Mountain in Yíyáng County, Hóngnóng, is used to make pitch pipes.
Reed pith from Hénèi can be made into ash to observe the seasonal qi.
Take the ash and fill the end of the pipe,
place it in a deep chamber,
cover it with crimson curtains,
and do not let it be exposed to wind.
When the solar term arrives,
the ash will fly, and the pipe will resonate.
Adding feathers and penetrating rhinoceros hide.
See the annotation in the "Ode to the Arrow": "Or to encourage the studies of Yóu."
There are also the stems of péngshān fúyún bamboo,
as recorded in the Shíyí Jì:
Péngshān has fúyún bamboo stems,
with green leaves,
purple stalks,
and seeds as large as pearls,
where blue luan birds gather.
Below is sandy gravel,
fine as powder.
When a fierce wind arises,
the bamboo branches sway,
brushing the fine sand like snowflakes.
Immortals come to watch and play,
and when the wind breaks the bamboo,
the sound resembles bells and chimes.
The species of zhōnglóng bamboo from Luófú.
As recorded in the Nányuè Zhì:
Bamboo growing on Luófú Mountain is all seven or eight arm-spans in circumference,
with nodes one or two chǐ long,
called zhōnglóng.
Bó Zhēn wrote on leaves to study diligently,
as recorded in the Book of Jìn:
Xú Bózhēn was orphaned and poor in his youth,
and had no paper for studying calligraphy.
He often practiced writing on bamboo arrows, ruò leaves, sugarcane, and the ground.
Tiān Shēng sharpened bamboo tips to demonstrate courage.
As recorded in the Book of Sòng:
Bǔ Tiānshēng served as a squad leader in his youth,
with ten men sharing a fire.
Behind the house was a pit,
over two zhàng wide.
The ten men all jumped across,
but only Tiānshēng fell in.
Tiānshēng then took solid kǔzhú bamboo,
sharpened its tip,
making it sharp,
and laid it crosswise in the pit.
He called his comrades to jump again,
but they were all afraid and dared not.
Tiānshēng then jumped again,
back and forth over ten times,
without any hindrance.
As for the fame of áo water,
as recorded in the Shānhǎi Jīng:
On Bōzhǒng Mountain,
along the Áo River,
there is much táozhī bamboo.
The beauty of Cénhuá,
as recorded in the Shíyí Jì:
Cénhuá Mountain lies west of the Western Sea,
where màn bamboo is used to make flutes and pipes,
and when blown, they sound like the cries of a flock of phoenixes.
Bówàng saw it in Dàxià,
as recorded in the Book of Hàn:
When Zhāng Qiān reached Dàxià,
he saw Shǔ cloth and Qióng bamboo canes.
He inquired about them,
and it was said:
"Merchants bought them from the Shēndú Kingdom."
Thus, he advised Emperor Wǔ to engage with the southwestern tribes to open up the Western Regions.
Zhāng Zhì planted it in Yǒngjiā.
As recorded in the Yǒngjiā Jùn Jì:
Lèchéng's Zhāng Zhì,
lived in seclusion, nurturing his aspirations.
His family owned dozens of qǐng of kǔzhú bamboo,
and he built a house within the bamboo grove,
often residing there.
Wáng Yòujūn heard of him and visited,
but Zhì hid in the bamboo grove,
refusing to meet him.
The entire commandery hailed him as a noble scholar.
Moreover, bamboo forms groves in six years,
as recorded in the Shānhǎi Jīng:
When bamboo blooms,
it withers that same year.
Bamboo renews its roots every sixty years.
Renewal must involve bearing fruit and withering,
the seeds fall to the ground and regrow,
forming groves again in six years.
It takes three years to become a pole,
as an ancient poem says:
Plant bamboo deep in a well,
and in three years, it becomes a pole.
Wèi Wǔ used it to make armor,
as recorded in the Shì Shuō:
Wèi Wǔ had several tens of hú of bamboo strips,
all several cùn long.
Everyone said they were useless,
fit only for burning.
Tàizǔ deeply regretted this,
and pondered how to use them.
He thought they could be made into bamboo armor,
but did not voice this idea.
He sent a messenger to ask his chief clerk, Yáng Dézǔ,
and Dézǔ's thoughts aligned with his.
Hàn Gāozǔ used it to make a crown.
As recorded in the Book of Hàn:
When Gāozǔ was a village head,
he made a crown from bamboo bark.
There is also Yuán Gōng who stabbed a maiden with it,
see the annotation in the "Ode to the Sword": "The skill of the Yuè maiden striking the ape."
Zǐyóu called it "this gentleman."
As recorded in the Book of Jìn:
Wáng Huīzhī often lived in an empty house,
and would have bamboo planted there.
Hearing its sound, he chanted and recited,
pointing at the bamboo, saying:
"Not a single day can pass without this gentleman."
Some gather phoenixes and bear fruit,
as stated in the Zhuāngzǐ:
The yuānchú bird will only eat liànshí.
Note:
Liànshí,
refers to bamboo fruit,
chosen for its purity and whiteness.
Some compare it to ritual and speak of its sheath.
As stated in the Lǐjì:
Ritual, in relation to people,
is like the sheath of a bamboo arrow.
The filial piety of Yúnhuá,
illuminated the night and suddenly flourished;
as recorded in the Book of Jìn:
Prince Zǐhǎn of Nánhǎi, styled Yúnhuá,
the eleventh son of Emperor Wǔ,
was quite learned.
When his mother was chronically ill,
Zǐhǎn prayed day and night.
At that time, bamboo was used to make a lamp frame to illuminate the night.
This frame's branches and leaves suddenly grew lush overnight,
and his mother's illness also recovered.
It was believed to be the result of his filial piety.
The tears of Mèng Zōng,
also revived bamboo in the midst of winter.
As recorded in the Chu Guó Xiānxián Zhuàn:
Mèng Zōng, styled Gōngwǔ,
was extremely filial.
His mother loved eating bamboo shoots.
Zōng entered the forest and wept bitterly.
In the midst of winter,
shoots emerged for him,
which he used to provide for her.
People of the time believed it was the result of his filial piety.
Wood
That fine tree,
is the element of the east.
The Shuōwén says:
“Mù (wood)
means mào (to emerge).
It emerges from the earth and grows,
the element of the east.
It embraces the nature of bending and straightening.”
The Shū says:
“Wood is said to bend and straighten.
Bending and straightening produces sourness.”
It bears the fine name of rěnrǎn.
The Shī says:
“The rěnrǎn supple tree,
the nobleman plants it.”
Note:
“Rěnrǎn
means broad and gentle in appearance.”
Wood,
like yī, tóng, zǐ, and qī,
must await the craftsman’s measurement.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
“The mountain has trees,
the craftsman measures them.”
We also hear that fire is born from it.
The Yīnfújīng says:
“Fire is born from wood,
when calamity erupts, it will certainly overcome it.”
How can it choose birds?
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
“Birds can choose trees,
but how can trees choose birds?”
It can only follow the marking line.
The Shū says:
“Wood follows the marking line and becomes straight;
the ruler follows remonstrance and becomes sage.”
Although zhīqiàn can bring wealth of a thousand chariots,
the Hànshū says:
“Zhīqiàn amounting to a thousand dàn
is comparable to a household of a thousand chariots.”
Yet the timber for the court and temple cannot be formed from a single branch.
The Shènzǐ says:
“The timber for the court and temple
is not from the branch of a single tree.”
Planting zhēn, lì, yī, tóng, zǐ, and qī
comes from the Shī.
Some are used to obtain the functions of yīn and yáng.
The Zhōulǐ says:
“In midwinter, fell yīn wood;
in midsummer, fell yáng wood.”
Some are used to symbolize the virtue of the queen and consorts.
The Shī says:
“The ‘Jiūmù’
is about the queen and consorts reaching down to those below.
In the south is the jiū tree,
with gé lěi vines clinging to it.”
Note:
“A tree bending downward is called jiū.”
Jade nectar irrigates the roots of the dān tree.
The Shānhǎijīng says:
“On Mìshān, there are many dān trees,
with round leaves, red stems, and yellow flowers.
Their fruit is like malt sugar;
eating it prevents hunger.
Jade nectar irrigates the dān tree.
After five years, the dān tree
becomes clear in five colors
and fragrant in five flavors.”
A golden knife cuts open the fruit of the rúhé tree.
The Shényìjīng says:
“In the southern wilderness, there is the rúhé tree.
It blooms at three hundred years,
and bears fruit at nine hundred years.
Its pit is shaped like a jujube,
five feet long.
If cut with a golden knife, it becomes sweet like malt sugar;
otherwise, it is pungent.
Eating it enables one to become an earthbound immortal.”
There is the fragrance of cassia beams and orchid rafters.
The Chǔcí says:
“Cassia beams and orchid rafters,
magnolia lintels and peony chambers.”
Note:
“Yào
refers to white stamens,
pronounced wò.”
There is the beautiful ornamentation of painted brackets and patterned rafters.
The Lúnyǔ says:
“Mountain-like capitals and painted brackets.”
Cáo Zhí’s “Qī Qǐ” says:
“Vermilion galleries and purple pillars,
patterned rafters and ornate beams.”
As for the beauty of this jiāoràng tree,
the Xúnyángjì says:
“On Huángjīnshān, there is a nán tree.
One year, the east side flourishes while the west side withers;
the next year, the west side flourishes while the east side withers.
This happens every year.
Zhāng Huá called it the ‘jiāoràng tree.’”
Sheltering under an inauspicious tree brings misfortune.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
“Those who assist in sacrifices get to taste;
those who intervene in fights get injured.
Sheltering under an inauspicious tree,
one is struck by thunder and lightning.”
It has rooted deeply and raised its trunk,
and also displays blossoms and emits fragrance.
Zhāng Héng’s “Nándū Fù” says:
“Rooted deeply, raising its trunk,
with hanging branches, graceful and elegant.”
It also says:
“Shaded and luxuriant, lush and dense,
displaying blossoms and emitting fragrance.”
As for praising that which is tall,
the Shū says:
“In Yǎnzhōu, the trees are slender;
in Yángzhōu, the trees are tall.”
Cherish this, for it can be knotted.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
“Winter ice can be broken,
summer trees can be knotted.
When trees are in full flourish,
picking all day, one does not notice;
when autumn winds bring frost,
they wither overnight.”
Some have interlocking branches or shared limbs.
The Tángshū says:
“During the Zhēnguàn era,
Shānnán presented a tree with interlocking branches,
intertwined and exquisite.
It resembled a luómù tree,
with a trunk one zhàng tall,
and over twenty places where branches were shared.”
Some have gnarled roots and tangled joints.
The Hòu Wèishū says:
Zhēn Chēn submitted a memorial stating:
“Whenever one sends someone to work on hard wood,
one must select a good axe for them.
Now, Hénán Commandery is Your Majesty’s hard wood from Tiānshān,
with gnarled roots and tangled joints,
mixed and planted within.
The six department captains are the sharp tools for tackling hard tasks;
without integrity, firmness, and precision,
they cannot manage it.”
Indeed, accumulating the small leads to greatness and height.
The Yì, “Shēng” guà says:
“Wood growing from the earth
is Shēng (ascending).
The nobleman, by following virtue,
accumulates the small to achieve greatness and height.”
And the tree that takes two arms to encircle begins from a tiny sprout.
The Lǎozǐ says:
“The tree that takes two arms to encircle
grows from a tiny sprout.”
Recognize that thousand-year tree.
The Yídū Shānchuān Jì says:
“On Héngshān, there is a strange tree;
no one has seen it decay.
Its name is ‘thousand-year.’
Its leaves resemble the jujube,
its color resembles the mulberry.
It is green in winter and summer,
firm and strong with few knots.”
Observe this ten-thousand-year tree.
The Jìn Gōnggé Míng says:
“In Huálín Garden, there are fourteen ten-thousand-year trees.”
Xiè Tiǎo’s poem says:
“The wind stirs the ten-thousand-year branches.”
Adorn silver fruit on the píngzhòng,
and tie gourd-like seeds on the jūnqiān.
Zuǒ Sī’s “Wúdū Fù” says:
“Píngzhòng and jūnqiān.”
The note says:
“The fruit of the píngzhòng is like silver;
the seeds of the jūnqiān are like gourds.”
The Wèiwáng Huāmù Zhì says:
“The jūnqiān is slender like the sweet banana,
with seeds like horse milk.”
Praise the ‘Gāntáng’ for hearing lawsuits.
The Shī says:
“The ‘Gāntáng’
praises Shào Bó.
Lush is the sweet pear tree;
do not cut it, do not fell it,
for Shào Bó rested beneath it.”
Commend the Wēnshì for its silence.
The Hànshū says:
“Kǒng Guāng, returning home on his day off,
would chat with his brothers, wife, and children,
but never mention court or government affairs.
Someone asked Guāng:
‘What trees are in the Wēnshì and the provincial office?’
Guāng remained silent and did not answer,
instead responding with other topics.”
As for selecting the yīwú and awaiting the phoenix,
Yán Yánnián’s “Qiū Hú Shī” says:
“The yīwú leans for the lofty phoenix,
the cold valley awaits the singing pitch-pipe.”
Snap the ruòhuā to brush against the sun.
The Chǔcí says:
Before the sun charioteers Xi Hé have risen,
how can the Ruòhuā tree shine with light?
Note:
This says that before the sun has risen,
the Ruòmù tree can have a bright red radiance.
It also says:
Break off a branch to brush against the sun.
Pluck the nine-forked paths of the Ruòshuǐ River.
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
There is a tree like an ox,
pulling its bark is like a tassel,
named Jiànmù,
located on the Ruòshuǐ River.
Green leaves,
purple stems,
dark flowers,
red fruit.
A hundred rèn high without branches.
Above it has nine vertical supports,
below it has nine forked paths.
Zhú,
pronounced zhì yù fǎn.
Admire the five colors of the Mìshān mountain.
See the note above for "jade ointment irrigates the roots of the dān tree."
As for the Héhuān dispelling anger,
Jī Kāng's "Essay on Nourishing Life" says:
Xuāncǎo makes one forget sorrow,
Héhuān dispels anger.
Wúhuàn drives away evil.
The Gǔjīn Zhù says:
Chéng Yǎ asked:
"The Lú tree is called Wúhuàn,
why is that?"
The reply was:
"In the past, there was a spirit medium named Bǎo Mào,
who could use charms to subdue hundreds of ghosts.
When he caught a ghost, he would use this wood to make a club,
and beat it to death.
People in the world vied to take this to make utensils,
to suppress and ward off evil spirits,
hence it was called Wúhuàn."
Distinguish the differences between Cōng and Guì,
The Ěryǎ says:
Cōng,
pine needles, cypress trunk.
Guì,
cypress needles, pine trunk.
Discern the distinctions between Qiū and Jiǎ,
The Ěryǎ says:
Large and cracked,
is Qiū;
small and cracked,
is Jiǎ.
Paddle a boat of Mùlán wood,
Rěn Fǎng's Shùyì Jì says:
The Mùlán River is in the Xúnyáng River,
with many Mùlán trees.
Also, on Qīlǐzhōu island, there is a boat carved from Mùlán wood by Lǔ Bān,
which remains on the island to this day.
Poets' reference to "Mùlán boats" originates from this.
Drive a carriage of Xīnyí wood.
The Chǔcí says:
Riding a red leopard, followed by a patterned wildcat,
a Xīnyí carriage with a cassia banner tied.
The nine Jǐ thorns mark the positions of the Gū and Gōng.
The Zhōulǐ says:
The Cháoshì official is in charge of the laws for the outer court of the state.
On the left are nine Jǐ thorns,
where the positions of the Gū, Qīng, Dàfū are;
on the right are nine Jǐ thorns,
where the positions of the Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ, Nán are.
The three Jīng thorns flourish in the Tián family's home.
The Xiàozǐ Zhuàn says:
In ancient times, there were brothers,
who suddenly wanted to separate.
Going out the door, they saw three Jīng thorn trees sharing one trunk,
their leaves connected, providing shade together.
They sighed and said:
"Even trees happily grow together,
how much more should we, who are different!"
So they returned to harmony.
Another version says they were the Tián Zhēn brothers.
When borers flourish, one sees the onset of decay.
The Fúzǐ says:
Trees produce borers,
when borers flourish, the tree decays;
stones produce metal,
when metal gleams, the stone erodes.
When the tip is large, there is lamentation over breakage.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
For plants and trees, the thick part is the root,
and the slender part is the tip;
for birds and beasts, the large part is the head,
and the small part is the tail.
If the tip is larger than the root, it will break;
if the tail is larger than the waist, it cannot be swung.
Therefore, feed the mouth and all joints become plump,
irrigate the root and the branches and leaves become beautiful.
There is also Guāngláng tree flour,
The Shǔ Zhì says:
Xīnggǔ Nánhàn County has Guāngláng trees,
which produce flour,
with large ones yielding up to a hundred hú.
Wénráng tree rice,
The Wú Lù ‧ Dìlǐ Zhì says:
Jiāozhǐ has Ráng trees,
whose bark contains something like white rice grains.
Dried,
and washed with water,
it resembles flour,
and can be made into cakes.
Zhè can be used to make bows,
The Zhōulǐ ‧ Dōngguān says:
The bow-maker distinguishes six materials,
Zhè is the best.
Gǔ is suitable for making paper.
The Shīyì Shū says:
In Yōuzhōu it is called Gǔsāng,
or Chǔsāng.
In Jīng, Yáng, Jiāo, and Guǎng, it is called Gǔ.
Nowadays, in Jiāngnán, its bark is woven to make cloth.
Also, pounded to make paper,
several zhàng long,
clean, white, and glossy.
The Míngguāng Hall plants the Chángshēng tree.
The Luòyáng Jì says:
In front of the Míngguāng Hall, there are two Chángshēng trees.
The Huálín Garden arrays the Jūnzǐ tree.
The Jìn Gōnggé Míng says:
In the Huálín Garden,
there are three Jūnzǐ trees.
Also heard is the calamity of the withered mulberry extending to the old turtle.
The Yìyuàn says:
During Sūn Quán's time,
a man from Yǒngkāng entered the mountains,
encountered a large turtle,
and immediately bound it to take home.
The turtle then spoke, saying:
"My travels did not meet with a good time,
and I was caught by you."
The man found it very strange.
Carrying it out,
he intended to present it to the King of Wú.
At night, they moored at Yuèlǐ,
tying the boat to a large mulberry tree.
In the middle of the night,
the tree called to the turtle, saying:
"Tired, Yuánxù?
What brings you here?"
The turtle said:
"I have been captured and bound,
and am about to be cooked into soup.
Even if all the firewood from the southern mountains were used,
it could not boil me."
The tree said:
"Zhūgě Yuánxùn is knowledgeable,
he will surely cause you suffering and seek someone like me.
What plan do you have?"
The turtle said:
"Zǐmíng, say no more,
disaster will reach you."
The tree fell silent and stopped.
Upon arrival,
Sūn Quán ordered it boiled.
After burning ten thousand cartloads of firewood,
it still spoke as before.
Zhūgě Kè said:
"Burn it with old mulberry wood, then it will cook."
The presenter then recounted the conversation between the turtle and the tree.
Sūn Quán immediately sent someone to fell and fetch it.
Boiling the turtle,
it immediately fell apart.
The strange Wénzǐ tree fears being entangled by silk threads.
See the note for "fearing that hairy head" in the "Ox Rhapsody."
The peculiarity of the Mígǔ tree shining in four directions,
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
On Zhāoyáo Mountain, there is a tree,
its flowers shine in four directions,
its name is Mígǔ.
Wearing it, one does not get lost.
The wonder of the Wényù tree's five colors.
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
North of Kāimíng, there is a Wényù tree,
of five colors.
Observe that Gūyóu tree,
The Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn says:
The Son of Heaven fished in the river,
to observe the Gūyóu tree.
Note:
Gūyóu,
is a large tree.
Exhaust this Xīsī tree.
The Guǎngyǎ says:
Qīngtán resembles Xīsī.
A saying goes:
"The Qí people cut Tán,
Xīsī is exhausted first."
Draw wine from Dùnxùn,
The Liáng Shū says:
In the southern country of Dùnxùn, there is a wine tree,
resembling a pomegranate,
its flower juice is collected in a cup,
and after several days it turns into wine,
delicious and intoxicating.
Also, the *Bówùzhì* mentions the country of Diǎnxùn.
It tells of plucking children from the sea.
The *Tángshū* says:
The Persians saw a square stone in the western sea,
upon which grew a tree,
with a red trunk,
and green leaves.
On the tree, small children suddenly appeared,
six or seven inches tall,
who laughed upon seeing people,
moving their hands and feet,
with their heads attached to the branches.
When a branch was plucked,
the child would die.
It is now in the possession of the king of Dàshí.
Perhaps the sight of the unburnable tree,
see the annotation “burning wood does not die” in the “Ode to Fire.”
How could one expect the return of the soul?
The *Shízhōujì* says:
On Jùkūzhōu, there is a soul-returning tree.
Its root core is cut down,
boiled in a jade cauldron,
and the juice is extracted and simmered,
until it can be formed into pills, named Jīngjīngxiāng, or Zhènlíngwán,
or Fǎnshēngxiāng,
or Quèsǐxiāng.
If a corpse lies on the ground,
smelling its scent brings it back to life.
Bāolì and Kuíhuì,
the *Ěryǎ* says:
Pò,
refers to Bāo.
The annotation states:
Pò refers to trees that grow in clusters, called Bāo.
This is what the *Shījīng* refers to as Yùpò and Bāolì.
It also says:
Bāo refers to sturdy trees,
and Kuíhuì.
The annotation states:
It means trees that do not grow in clusters,
with roots, branches, and nodes twisted and gnarled.
Huì is pronounced as huì,
Bāo is pronounced as bāo.
Fúlóu, Yùpò,
the *Ěryǎ* says:
Huìmù,
refers to Fúlóu.
The annotation states:
It means trees that are diseased, stunted, and bent,
with swollen tumors and no branches.
Yùpò is mentioned above.
Their roots are swollen and knotted,
their branches divided and twisted,
these are all trees of useless lands,
the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
King Huì said:
“I have a large tree,
people call it Chū.
Its trunk is so gnarled and swollen it cannot be measured with a carpenter’s line,
its small branches are so twisted they cannot be measured with a compass or square.
If planted by the roadside,
carpenters would not even glance at it.
Now your words,
grand yet useless,
are similarly rejected by all.”
Zhuāngzǐ said:
“Why not plant it in the land of nothingness,
the vast and barren wilderness,
where you can wander freely and rest beneath it,
and roam idly by its side.”
Thus preserving the fortune of being useless.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Zhuāngzǐ was walking in the mountains,
when he saw a large tree,
with lush branches and leaves,
yet woodcutters stopped beside it and did not take it.
He asked the reason,
and they said:
“It is of no use.”
Zhuāngzǐ said:
“This tree, because of its uselessness, is able to live out its natural lifespan.”
There are also those who delight in the lushness of the Dèng Forest,
see the annotation “abandoned staff heard of by Kuāfù” in the “Ode to the Sun.”
And marvel at the opening of Quèlǐ.
The *Hòuhànshū* says:
Bào Yǒng was the governor of Lǔ Commandery.
At that time, Péng Fēng and Pí Cháng, subordinate commanders of Dǒng Xiàn, each led over a thousand men,
calling themselves “generals” and refusing to surrender.
Shortly after,
the thorns and brambles at Confucius’ Quèlǐ inexplicably cleared themselves,
from the lecture hall all the way to the village gate.
Bào Yǒng found this strange,
and said to his assistant and the magistrate of Lǔ:
“In these critical times, Quèlǐ has opened by itself.
Could it be that the Master wishes the governor to perform the rites,
to help me punish the lawless?”
He then gathered a crowd,
performed the village archery ceremony,
and invited Péng Fēng and others to attend and observe,
intending to capture them there.
Péng Fēng and others plotted against Bào Yǒng,
and brought oxen and wine to feast and reward him,
while secretly carrying weapons.
Bào Yǒng sensed this,
personally fought and killed Péng Fēng and others,
and captured and defeated their followers.
Some use trees to achieve wealth like Héjì,
the *Hànshū* says:
Between Huáiběi, Róngnán, and Héjì,
a thousand Qiū trees are equivalent to a marquis with a thousand households.
Some use trees to commemorate the achievements of Shāyuàn.
The *Hòuzhōushū* says:
During the battle of Shāyuàn,
Qí Shénwǔ fled at night,
pursued to the river,
and was again heavily defeated,
with seventy thousand of his soldiers captured in total,
and the prisoners presented in Cháng’ān.
Upon returning the army to Wèinán,
the soldiers from the various conscripted provinces had just arrived,
so at the battlefield, each soldier was ordered to plant a tree,
to commemorate the military achievement.
Seeing the three pearls at Chìshuǐ,
the *Bówùzhì* says:
The three-pearl tree grows on the banks of Chìshuǐ.
Planting five Zuò trees in the Hàn palace.
The *Xījīngzájì* says:
The Wǔzuò Palace has five Zuò trees,
each so large it takes several arm spans to encircle,
shading several dozen acres.
It is also said that consuming Dìxiū prevents anger,
the *Shānhǎijīng* says:
On Shǎoshì Mountain, there is a tree,
named Dìxiū,
its branches and leaves resemble the poplar but with five forks,
with yellow flowers and black fruit,
consuming it prevents anger.
Eating from Yuánqiū grants immortality.
The *Bówùzhì* says:
On Yuánqiū Mountain, there is an immortality tree,
eating its fruit grants longevity.
Mànqiàn need not worry about its branches breaking or sweating,
the *Dòngmíngjì* says:
In the second year of Tàichū,
Dōngfāng Shuò returned to Hàn from the country of Xīnà,
bringing ten pieces of Fēngshēngmù,
with fruits like fine pearls,
when the wind blows, the branches sound like jade,
hence the name.
When there is military activity, it sounds like metal and leather,
when there is civil activity, it sounds like zithers and lutes.
The emperor gave branches to people,
if the recipient was ill, the branch would sweat,
if dead, the branch would break.
In the past, Lǎo Dān lived during the Zhōu dynasty,
for seven hundred years the branch did not sweat;
Wòquán lived during the time of Yáo,
for three thousand years the branch did not break.
The emperor gave a branch to Shuò,
Shuò said:
“I have seen this branch wither and die three times, only to revive again.
A local saying goes, ‘Before half its lifespan,
the branch does not sweat.’
This tree sweats once every five thousand years,
withers once every ten thousand years.
During the time of Jīnyún,
it grew between the palace eaves.”
Bóqín had already observed the Qiáo and Zǐ trees.
The *Shuōyuàn* says:
Bóqín and Kāng Shū Fēng,
went to court to see King Chéng,
and visited Zhōu Gōng,
but were caned three times in three visits.
Kāng Shū and Bóqín went to see the wise man Shāngzǐ and told him.
Shāngzǐ said:
“Why don’t you two go together to see the southern side of Nánshān!
There is a tree there,
named Qiáo.”
The two went to see it,
and saw the Qiáo tree standing tall, full of fruit, and looking upward.
They returned and told Shāngzǐ,
Shāngzǐ said:
“The Qiáo tree
represents the way of the father.
Why don’t you two go together to see the northern side of Nánshān!
There is a tree there,
named Zǐ.”
The two went to see it,
and saw the Zǐ tree flourishing, full of fruit, and bending downward.
They returned and told Shāngzǐ,
Shāngzǐ said:
“The Zǐ tree
represents the way of the son.
Tomorrow, you two go see Zhōu Gōng,
enter the door and hasten,
ascend the hall and kneel.”
The Duke of Zhōu patted his head,
comforted him, and gave him food,
saying:
"Where did you meet a gentleman?"
The two replied:
"We met Shāngzǐ."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Shāngzǐ is indeed a gentleman!"
Some saw the shadow of a slanting rainbow,
as recorded in the *Dòng Míng Jì*:
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
the Shòufú Língtán was built,
spanning a hundred paces,
with bronze beams and silver embankments raised on all sides.
On the water, trees called "hanging dragons" were planted in rows,
resembling green parasol trees.
They produced crimson dew,
as red as cinnabar.
When the dew dripped onto their leaves,
it fell to the ground and turned into pearls.
Their branches resembled the inverted bodies of dragons,
and they were also called "slanting rainbow trees,"
or "pearl-branch trees."
Some observed auspicious patterns forming characters.
The *Táng Shū* records:
In the twelfth year of the Dàlì era under Emperor Dàizōng,
a man named Guō Yuǎn from Chéngdū Prefecture obtained an auspicious piece of wood,
inscribed with the characters "tiānxià tàipíng" (peace under heaven),
and presented it.
The chief ministers congratulated him, saying:
"The transformative power of supreme virtue
first manifests in plants and trees;
the omen of peace
is thus conveyed through writing.
We humbly request that it be stored in the Imperial Archives
and recorded in the Historiography Institute."
If talents from Chǔ are employed by Jìn,
only the finest wood like qǐ and zǐ is prized.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* records:
Shēngzǐ of Chǔ was sent on a diplomatic mission to Jìn.
Upon his return,
the Prime Minister Zǐmù asked:
"Are the senior officials of Jìn more worthy than those of Chǔ?"
He replied:
"The ministers of Jìn are not as worthy as those of Chǔ,
but their senior officials are indeed worthy—
all are ministerial talents.
Like qǐ and zǐ wood or leather,
they come from Chǔ.
Though Chǔ has the talent,
it is Jìn that truly makes use of it."
Pine
Admire that lofty pine,
Braving this frost and snow.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Confucius said:
"When the cold of heaven arrives,
and frost and snow have descended,
I then know the luxuriance of the pine and cypress."
It is not something that can grow on a small mound.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
On small mounds, there are no pines or cypresses.
It establishes its integrity because of the year's cold.
The *Analects* says:
Only when the year grows cold do we see that the pine and cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
Great is Hé Qiáo, towering and dense.
The *Jìn Shū* says:
Yǔ Yǐ said:
"Hé Qiáo is as dense and towering as a thousand-zhang pine;
though knotty and gnarled with many joints,
when used for a great hall,
it serves as beams and pillars."
See Lǐ Yīng, stern and imposing.
The *Shì Shuō* says:
Lǐ Yuánlǐ is as stern and imposing as the wind beneath tall pines.
But one finds pleasure merely in a single hillock.
The *Fúzǐ* says:
Fúzǐ and Xuánzǐ ascended Mount Tài,
looking down upon a chasm a thousand ren deep,
shaded above by hundred-zhang pines,
feeling serene and majestic, their spirits kingly upon that hillock!
They did not seek glory at the twin palace towers.
The *Xiānshèng Běnjì* says:
Xǔ Yóu wished to observe the emperor's intent,
saying:
"The emperor sits in his splendid hall,
facing the twin towers;
the glory you behold is also attained!"
He said:
"I sit in a splendid hall,
where pines grow densely by the window;
though I face the twin towers,
it is no different from the glory of the Luan-bird circling Kūnlún.
How should I know the means by which to seek glory?"
As for Wò Quán eating its fruit,
the *Lièxiān Zhuàn* says:
Wò Quán ate pine nuts,
and could fly, catching up to a galloping horse.
Fú Shēng consumed its resin.
The *Lièxiān Zhuàn* says:
Fú Shēng, during the time of Tāng, served as Director of Wood,
and often ate pine resin.
Where it grows below, grasses do not thrive.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
Beneath pines and cypresses,
grasses do not thrive.
Where it is on the land, the soil is not fertile.
The *Shuō Yuàn* says:
Zhì Xiāngzǐ built a house of great beauty.
Shì Zhuó said:
"There is a record that says:
'On high mountains and steep sources,
grasses and trees do not grow;
on land where pines and cypresses grow,
the soil is not fertile.'
Now, the timber and earth surpass men;
I fear it will not be secure."
The house was completed for three years,
and then the Zhì clan perished.
Dīng Gù then had a tree grow from his belly.
The *Wú Lù* says:
Dīng Gù dreamed a pine tree grew from his belly,
and said to people:
"The character for pine (松) is 'eighteen duke'."
Eighteen years later, he became a duke,
just as in the dream.
Zhāng Zhàn then had corpses laid out beneath his house.
The *Qí Shū* says:
Zhāng Zhàn liked to plant pines and cypresses before his studio.
People of the time said:
"Zhāng Zhàn has corpses laid out beneath his house."
Admirable was Jiā Yǐn's clever reply.
The *Táng Shū* says:
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn, at age seven, was summoned for an audience as a child prodigy.
The Grand Commandant Zhǎngsūn Wújì and the Minister of Works Lǐ Jì stood talking with him in the court hall.
They teased Jiāyǐn, saying:
"What tree am I leaning against?"
He replied:
"A pine."
Lǐ Jì said:
"This is a locust tree;
why do you say pine?"
Jiāyǐn said:
"Pairing 'wood' (木) with 'duke' (公) makes 'pine' (松)."
Zhǎngsūn Wújì then asked him repeatedly:
"What tree am I leaning against?"
He replied:
"A locust tree."
Wújì said:
"Can you not give a crafty reply?"
Jiāyǐn said:
"Why craft a reply?
I simply take 'ghost' (鬼) paired with 'wood' (木) to make 'locust' (槐)."
Great was the Prince of Péngchéng's composing of poetry.
The *Hòu Wèi Shū* says:
Prince Xié of Péngchéng accompanied the emperor on a visit to Dàidū.
They stopped at the Tóngdī Mountain in Shàngdǎng.
By the roadside were over ten large pine trees.
The emperor, while walking, composed a poem,
and had someone show it to Xié, saying:
"Though I cannot compose a poem within seven paces,
I do not claim it takes long.
You may compose one;
by the time I hear it,
let it be finished."
At that time, Xié was over ten paces from the emperor.
He walked and composed,
and finished before reaching the emperor.
The poem said:
"I ask the pine forest,
how many winters have you passed?
How are the mountains and rivers compared to the past?
The wind and clouds are the same as in antiquity."
The emperor said:
"This poem also reproaches me."
As for enduring through the four seasons unchanged,
the *Lǐ* says:
Just as white bamboo and arrows have their joints,
pines and cypresses have their heartwood;
they endure the four seasons without changing branches or shedding leaves.
Among the hundred trees, they are the elders.
The *Shǐ Jì* says:
Pines and cypresses are the elders of the hundred trees,
and guard the palace gates.
Some were planted beside the imperial highways.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
Jiǎ Shān submitted a memorial saying:
"The Qín built imperial highways,
thickly constructing their sides,
reinforced with metal pilings,
and planted with green pines.
The beauty of the imperial highways
made it so that later generations could not even find a side path to set foot on."
Some were enfeoffed upon Mount Tài.
Yìng Shào's *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
When Qín Shǐhuáng ascended to enfeoff Mount Tài,
he encountered fierce winds and torrential rain,
and relied on holding onto a tree.
He therefore enfeoffed that tree as the "Five Grandee Pines."
The mushroom is named "Flying Node."
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
In pines three thousand years old, there grows within the bark a clustered mushroom shaped like a dragon,
named "Flying Node Mushroom."
The stone is called "Kāngyú."
The *Táng Shū* says:
East of the Púgǔ territory,
one thousand li to the northeast, there is the Kāng River.
Pinewood submerged in water for one or two years turns to stone.
Its color is green,
and it is called Kāngyú stone,
bearing the grain of pine.
Hearing its sound and delighting in it was Hóngjǐng.
The *Liáng Shū* says:
Táo Hóngjǐng particularly loved the sound of wind in pines.
His courtyard was planted entirely with pines.
Hearing their sound,
he joyfully took pleasure in it.
Burning pine knots to read by was Gù Huān.
The *Sòng Shū* says:
Gù Huān, styled Jǐngyí,
loved learning but was poor.
In the evening, he would burn pine knots to read by.
Some transformed into Poria cocos.
The *Xuánzhōng Jì* says:
Pine resin sinks into the earth,
and after a thousand years becomes Poria cocos.
Some compare it to a gentleman.
The *Sūnqīngzǐ* says:
If the year is not cold,
one cannot know the pine and cypress;
if affairs are not difficult,
one cannot know the gentleman.
Mù Mǎn once ascended its stone steps.
The *Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn* says:
The Son of Heaven ascended the stone steps of the tall pines.
Tàisì also dreamed of catalpas.
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
Tàisì dreamed that the catalpas of Zhōu transformed into pines.
Some used it to replace a whisk and wave it.
The *Chén Shū* says:
Zhāng Jī, styled Zhíyán.
The later lord visited the Kāishàn Temple on Zhōng Mountain.
He summoned his attending ministers to sit beneath a pine,
and ordered Jī to expound on principles.
At that time, a yak-tail whisk was not yet brought.
The later lord ordered someone to fetch a pine branch and hand it to Jī,
saying:
"This can replace the whisk."
Some, together with cypress, both perished.
The *Zhǒngmù Jì* says:
The Prince of Dōngpíng returned to his fief,
longing for the capital.
After her passing,
she was buried in Dōngpíng,
and the pines and cypresses atop her grave all leaned westward.
Moreover, Yǔ Sù admired them and composed a eulogy.
Yǔ Sù's "Pine Eulogy" states:
Streams flow, laws fly,
Profound essence sinks and gathers in stillness,
Upright blossoms hold fragrance,
Facing upward, they brush against flying snow.
Cài Fú wrote a rhapsody about them, forming a piece.
"Records of the Two Capitals" states:
Cài Fú had the "Ode to the Reclining Pine,"
which Xuánzōng harmonized with,
and it was carved in stone.
It is not that the root is injured and the tip withers.
"The Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ" states:
A pine a hundred ren tall,
if the root is injured below, the tip withers above.
Thus, it equals the earth and rivals the heavens.
"The Master Who Embraces Simplicity" states:
The reclining-canopy pines of Tiānlíng,
the inverted-growing cypresses of the great valleys,
all such trees
rival the heavens in their height,
and equal the earth in their longevity.
Moreover, it is like Dǎiyú's response regarding the summer altar,
see the "Analects."
Or the analogy of Qí's literature by Liú Tì.
"The Family Instructions of the Yán Clan" states:
In the Qí dynasty, there was a man named Xí Pí,
who despised literature,
and mocked Liú Tì, saying:
"Your writing is like the morning mushroom,
a fleeting amusement,
not of great talent.
How can it compare to my thousand-zhang pine,
which constantly endures wind and frost?"
Liú replied:
"If there is a cold tree,
yet it also blooms with spring flowers,
is that acceptable?"
Xí laughed and said:
"It is acceptable."
Sūn Chuò planted them, and they were pitiable.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World" states:
Sūn Xìnggōng planted a pine tree in front of his study,
and his neighbor said to him:
"The pine tree is not without its lush, pitiable beauty,
but it will never serve as a pillar or beam."
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng sprinkled tears upon it, and it changed color.
"The Master of the Golden Tower" states:
Whenever Emperor Wǔ of Liáng paid homage at the mountain tombs,
the tears he shed
caused the pines to change color.
Zhēn Chēn guarded the grave mound and planted them in rows.
"The Book of the Later Wèi" states:
When Zhēn Chēn's father passed away,
within the grave precincts,
he personally planted pines and cypresses.
In the depths of winter, he carried water and dug earth,
and the village elders pitied him and assisted.
After more than ten years,
the grave mound was complete, and the trees flourished.
Shān Táo observed mourning and personally planted them.
Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jìn" states:
Shān Táo, in his old age, observed mourning for his mother beyond the rites,
and personally planted pines and cypresses.
They are seen both upon the waters of the Qí River,
as the "Book of Songs" states:
The Qí River flows gently,
with cypress oars and pine boats.
And flourish again beside Cúlái.
The "Book of Songs" states:
The pines of Cúlái,
the cypresses of Xīnfǔ.
Note:
Cúlái and Xīnfǔ
are two mountains.
Poets have sung of them,
as they entwine with dodder vines;
the "Book of Songs" states:
The dodder and the creeper vine,
cling to the pines and cypresses.
As mentioned in the "Tribute of Yǔ,"
they are also likened to strange stones.
"The Book of Documents: Tribute of Yǔ" states:
The tribute of Qīngzhōu includes silk, hemp, lead, pines, and strange stones from the valleys of Dài.
Cypress.
Dí Rénjié was appointed as the Dàlǐ Chéng.
At that time, General Quán Shàncái was implicated for cutting down a cypress tree at the Zhāolíng Mausoleum.
Rénjié submitted a memorial reporting his crime and recommending his dismissal.
Emperor Gāozōng was enraged,
and ordered his execution.
Rénjié stepped forward and said:
"The ancients said, 'If someone were to steal a handful of soil from the Chánglíng Mausoleum,
how would Your Majesty punish him?'
Now, Your Majesty wishes to execute a general over a single cypress tree at the Zhāolíng Mausoleum.
What kind of ruler will future generations say Your Majesty was?
Your servant dares not carry out this decree."
The emperor's anger gradually subsided.
Furthermore, Wáng Yàn had an omen of the cypress changing into a paulownia.
The *Qí Shū* states:
Wáng Yàn was a Yuánwài Láng.
The cypress tree in front of his father Pǔ Yào's study suddenly transformed into a paulownia.
Commentators believed that although the paulownia possesses the beauty of attracting phoenixes,
it loses the virtue of enduring the winter.
Yàn indeed later failed to see things through to the end.
Lǐ Chōng had the resolve to personally wield a blade.
The *Chénliú Qíjiù Zhuàn* states:
Lǐ Chōng was in mourning for his father.
There was a thief who came at night to cut down the cypress trees beside the grave mound.
Chōng personally killed him with a blade.
Since chūn wood and gàn wood were presented together as tribute,
the *Shū* states:
The tribute from Jīngzhōu consisted of chūn wood, gàn wood, guā wood, and cypress.
They are also what the wǎngxiàng fears.
The *Fēngsú Tōng* states:
Cypress trees on graves,
and stone tigers at the roadside.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
The Fāngxiàng Shì enters the burial mound to drive away the wǎngxiàng,
because it likes to eat the livers and brains of the deceased.
Since it is not possible to have the Fāngxiàng Shì stand guard at the graveside,
and the wǎngxiàng fears tigers and cypress trees,
therefore cypress trees are planted and stone tigers are erected.
Examining the trees at the mausoleum,
they once served as an auspicious sign for Emperor Xuān.
The *Hàn Shū* states:
During the reign of Emperor Zhāo,
all the withered and fallen cypress trees at the various mausoleums in Cháng'ān stood upright again.
Later, Emperor Zhāo passed away,
and the grandson of Crown Prince Wèi was enthroned.
This was Emperor Xuān.
Floating upon that midstream river,
it also manifests Gōng Jiāng's vow.
The *Shī* states:
"The Cypress Boat,"
is Gōng Jiāng's vow of fidelity.
The heir of Wèi, Gòng Bó, died young.
His wife preserved her chastity.
Her parents wished to force her to remarry,
but she vowed not to consent.
Therefore, she composed this poem:
"Floating is that cypress boat,
Upon that midstream river."
Huái
In ancient times, it was described as having large leaves and being dark,
as stated in the *Erya*:
“Xiāng,
refers to the pagoda tree, which has large leaves and is dark.”
It was also considered the essence of the Lingxīng star.
The *Chunqiu Shuo* says:
“The pagoda tree
is the essence of the Lingxīng star.”
Chú Ní dashed against it in the bedchamber.
The *Zuozhuan* records:
Zhào Xuānzǐ repeatedly remonstrated,
and the duke resented him for it,
so he sent Chú Ní to assassinate him.
Chú Ní went at dawn,
and found the bedchamber door open.
Zhào Xuānzǐ was dressed in full court attire, preparing to attend court.
It was still early,
so he sat and dozed off.
Chú Ní retreated,
sighed, and said:
“He does not forget to be reverent and respectful—
he is the master of the people.
To assassinate the master of the people
is disloyal;
to abandon the ruler’s command
is untrustworthy.
To commit either of these offenses
is worse than death.”
He then dashed against a pagoda tree and died.
Dǒng Shū was bound to one in the courtyard.
The *Guoyu* records:
Dǒng Shū was about to marry into the Fàn family.
Shū Xiàng said to him:
“Why not stop?
You are merely seeking connections.”
Later,
Dǒng Qí complained to Fàn Xiànzǐ, saying:
“He does not respect me.”
Xiànzǐ then seized Dǒng Shū and bound him to a pagoda tree in the courtyard.
Note:
“Fǎng”
means to hang.
Some grow old and catch fire.
The *Huainanzi* says:
“Old pagoda trees catch fire.”
Some were injured, leading to punishments.
The *Yànzǐ Chunqiu* records:
Duke Jǐng of Qí had a beloved pagoda tree.
He issued an order:
“Those who violate the pagoda tree shall be punished;
those who injure it shall be put to death.”
A drunken man injured the pagoda tree,
and was about to be punished.
His daughter, fearful, went to Yànzǐ and said:
“I fear that neighboring states will hear of this
and say that our ruler values the pagoda tree over human life.
Is this acceptable?”
Yànzǐ went in and spoke to the duke,
who then released the three prisoners who had injured the pagoda tree.
It appeared in dreams at Fēngpèi.
The *Sòngshū* records:
Confucius dreamed at night that between three pagoda trees, in the land of Fēngpèi, there was a red aura.
He drove his carriage and saw a grass-gathering child injuring the left foot of a qílín,
and sought firewood to cover it.
It is akin to the brotherhood of oranges and pomelos.
The *Huainanzi* says:
“The pagoda tree and elm join with oranges and pomelos as brothers,
and the Yǒumiáo and Sānwēi become one family.”
As for gathering verdure in the court of litigation,
the *Chunqiu Yuanming Bao* says:
“Plant pagoda trees
and hold court beneath them.”
Note:
“Huái” (pagoda tree) signifies “return” (guī),
meaning that when emotions are revealed, they return
to truth.
It casts shade over the academic market.
The *Huainanzi* says:
“The Huái Market is a place of learning,
planted with green pagoda trees.”
Some fold by day and stretch by night.
The *Erya* says:
“The shǒugōng pagoda tree
has leaves that fold by day and stretch by night.”
Some have rabbit eyes and mouse ears.
The *Huainanzi* says:
“The pagoda tree grows in late spring;
after five days, it resembles rabbit eyes;
after ten days, mouse ears;
and after another ten days, it begins to take shape.”
Some demonstrate the suitability of fertile soil.
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
“In five types of fertile soil,
the pagoda tree thrives.”
Some symbolize the positions of the Three Dukes.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
“Three pagoda trees
mark the positions of the Three Dukes.”
Note:
“Huái” (pagoda tree)
means “to embrace” (huái),
signifying the embrace of people who come.”
Some were planted at the Pìyōng.
The *Sānfǔ Huángtú* records:
“At the Mingtáng Pìyōng,
there were three thousand quarters for scholars.
A market was held there,
with only rows of pagoda trees planted,
where scholars gathered on the first and fifteenth days of the month.
They brought goods from their commanderies and classical texts,
traded with one another,
and engaged in courteous discussions
beneath the pagoda trees.”
Some were planted at the royal gate.
Tàigōng’s *Jīnguì* records:
King Wǔ asked Tàigōng:
“Many spirits come from across the land.
How should we receive them?”
Tàigōng planted a pagoda tree inside the royal gate,
allowing beneficial spirits to enter
and barring harmful ones.”
Immortal recipes use it to nourish the brain.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
“Consuming pagoda tree seeds nourishes the brain,
preventing graying hair and promoting longevity.”
Medical records mention it lightening the body.
The *Běncǎo* says:
“Long-term consumption of pagoda tree fruits lightens the body.”
It was even harvested by the Xuǎn officials.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
“The Xuǎn officials are responsible for harvesting pagoda and sandalwood wood in winter for fire.”
It was used for sacred candles.
The *Běncǎo* says:
“Pagoda trees grow in Hénán,
and can be used to make sacred candles.”
Xiàokuān planted them to mark roads.
The *Hòuzhōushū* records:
Wéi Xiàokuān served as the governor of Yōngzhōu.
Previously, an earthen mound was placed every lǐ along the roadside,
but they often collapsed after rain,
requiring frequent repairs.
When Xiàokuān took office,
he ordered pagoda trees to be planted at the mound sites within his jurisdiction.
This eliminated the need for repairs,
and travelers also gained shade.
Emperor Wén later saw this
and ordered all regions to plant one tree per lǐ along roads,
three trees every ten lǐ,
and five trees every hundred lǐ.”
Jiānwú consumed it to improve eyesight.
The *Liángshū* records:
Yǔ Jiānwú regularly consumed pagoda tree fruits.
Even past the age of ninety,
he could read fine print,
and his hair remained black.”
Furthermore, Gāo Jiǒng did not conform to rows.
The *Suíshū* records:
Gāo Jiǒng, styled Zhāoxuán,
served as the supervisor of Xīndū.
He often conducted affairs while sitting beneath a pagoda tree.
Later, because the trees were not aligned in rows,
officials requested to cut them down.
The emperor specifically ordered them to be spared,
as an example for future generations.”
Zhòngwén often sighed at their swaying.
The *Jìnshū* records:
“At the Grand Marshal’s residence, there was an old pagoda tree.
Yīn Zhòngwén faced it and sighed:
‘This tree sways,
but its vitality is exhausted.’”
Mào composed a rhapsody about the one in Jiǔquán.
The *Liáng Lù* records:
“Initially,
the region west of the Yellow River did not grow catalpa, pagoda, cypress, or lacquer trees.
During Zhāng Jùn’s reign,
they were brought from Qín and Lǒng and planted,
but they all died.
Only a pagoda tree grew in the northwest corner of the Jiǔquán Palace.
Lǐ Xuánshèng composed the ‘Pagoda Tree Rhapsody.’”
They were planted in Cháng’ān and celebrated in song.
The *Jìnshū* records:
“When Fú Jiān usurped the throne,
he ordered pagoda and willow trees to be planted along the roads
from Cháng’ān to all the provinces.
The people sang:
‘On Cháng’ān’s grand avenues,
pagoda and willow trees line the roads.
Below, crimson carriages pass;
above, phoenixes perch.’”
Additionally, there were imperial roads where they were not to be cut down.
The *Tángshū* records:
“During the Zhēnyuán era,
the Ministry of Revenue planned to use the pagoda trees along the roads of the two capitals as firewood
and replace them with saplings.
An official order was issued,
but the deputy magistrate of Wèinán County, Zhāng Zào, submitted a memorandum stating:
‘Where Shào Bó rested,
the trees were not cut;
how much more should the trees along the roads
where the late emperor once traveled not be felled?’”
Then it ceased.
The scholar's tomb often planted.
The "General Principles of the Five Classics" says:
The scholar's tomb plants the sophora tree.
Spreading the deep shade of its lush foliage,
The "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" says:
Planted with green sophoras,
Their deep shade is dense and abundant.
Gathering the lingering white sparrows.
Cáo Zǐjiàn's "Discussion on the Virtue of Wèi" says:
When Emperor Wǔ held the reins of government,
White sparrows gathered on the sophora tree in the courtyard.
This is how the pure filial piety of Shìxióng was manifested.
The "Book of Suí" says:
Niǔ Huí was known for his filial piety.
When he died,
His son Shìxióng again displayed the highest conduct,
Dwelling in a hut beside the tomb,
Carrying earth to form a mound.
In front of their courtyard, there was a sophora tree,
Which was originally very lush and flourishing.
When Shìxióng observed mourning,
The tree then withered and died.
After the mourning period ended and he returned home,
The dead sophora tree revived and flourished again.
Emperor Gāozǔ heard of this,
Sighed at the extreme filial piety of father and son,
Issued an edict to praise and honor them,
And named their residence Lěidé Lǐ.
This also shows the official's expectation of attracting people from afar.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
In the ninth month, the official expects, and its tree is the sophora.
In this month, fortifications and defenses are repaired.
Therefore, planting the sophora tree
Means to attract,
To draw people from near and far.
Willow.
In the past, Huán Wēn, moved by memories, lingered,
clutching a branch with tears welling up,
and said:
"Even trees are like this,
how much more so for humans!"
The Biography of Huán Wēn states:
Wēn campaigned north,
passing through Jīnchéng,
and saw that the willows he had planted when young as the governor of Lángyá had all grown to ten arm-spans in girth.
He sighed and said:
"Even trees are like this,
how can humans endure!"
Thereupon, clutching a branch, he shed tears.
As for praising the beauty of spring moonlit willows in Wáng Gōng,
the History of the Jìn states:
Wáng Gōng, styled Xiàobó,
was of handsome appearance,
and some described him as "fresh and bright like a willow in the spring moonlight."
And appreciating the Línghé willow in Zhāng Xù.
The History of the Qí states:
When Liú Jùnzhī served as governor of Yìzhōu,
he presented several Shu willows,
very tall,
their appearance like silk strands.
Emperor Wǔ planted them before the Tàichāng Línghé Hall,
and once sighed while admiring them:
"These willows, graceful and lovely, resemble Zhāng Xù."
They begin to sprout leaves upon reaching the first month.
The Dàdài Lǐ records:
In the first month, willows sprout.
Note:
Sprouting means
the leaves emerge.
They flourish when they obtain fertile soil.
The Guǎnzǐ states:
The five types of fertile soil are suitable for willows.
They are called ugly branches.
The Ěryǎ states:
Mulberry and willow
have ugly branches.
They are also called solitary shakers.
The Gǔjīn Zhù states:
The poplar has round leaves and weak stems,
also called high flyer,
another name is solitary shaker.
They grow on the left elbow.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
Zhīlí Shū observed at Míngbó Hill and the ruins of Kūnlún.
Suddenly a willow grew on his left elbow.
They gather those chirping cicadas.
The Shī states:
Lush are those willows,
the cicadas chirp incessantly.
Yàfū then gazed arrogantly from the army gate.
The History of the Hàn states:
During Emperor Wén's time, the Xiōngnú invaded,
Zōngzhèng Liú Lǐ stationed at Bàshàng,
Xú Lì stationed at Jímén,
Zhōu Yàfū stationed at Xìliǔ.
The emperor visited Bàshàng and Jímén,
where the army officers all welcomed him.
Later, he went to Xìliǔ,
where the gate of the camp did not open.
The vanguard said:
"The Son of Heaven is about to arrive."
Still it did not open.
The emperor sent word to Yàfū, saying:
"I wish to inspect the troops."
Yàfū then ordered the camp gate opened.
The army officer said:
"The general's rule:
within the army, one must not gallop."
The Son of Heaven then reined in his horse and proceeded slowly,
reaching the central army.
Yàfū then, holding his weapon, bowed and said:
"A man in armor
does not bow;
I request to meet with military etiquette."
The Son of Heaven, moved, leaned on the chariot rail.
After leaving,
his attendants were all astonished.
The emperor said:
"This is a true general.
As for the earlier Jímén and Bàshàng,
they were merely child's play."
Jī Kāng then leisurely worked at his forge.
See the note on "Jī Kāng's forge" in the "Xià Fù."
Lǚ Wèi considered re-flowering as an auspicious sign.
The History of the Táng states:
Lǚ Wèi served as Vice Minister of Rites.
In the Zhōngshū Province, a willow tree flowered again,
and people called it an auspicious willow.
Wèi used it as a topic for a rhapsody,
which the emperor read and disliked.
Xiàoxù considered self-uprooting as an omen.
The History of the Qí states:
Ruǎn Xiàoxù,
at the end of the Jiànwǔ era,
the east gate of the Qīngxī Palace collapsed without cause,
and a great wind uprooted the poplar trees outside the east palace gate.
Someone asked Xiàoxù about it,
and Xiàoxù said:
"Qīngxī is the old residence of the imperial family.
Qí corresponds to the wood phase,
and the east is the wood position.
Now the east gate has collapsed first,
indicating the decline of wood."
There are also Zhílíng and Fèngbó.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
West of Guī Mountain there is a valley,
named Jūnhuàn Valley,
where many trees are willows.
On Fèngbó Mountain, Xióng Mountain, and Zhílíng Mountain, many trees are willows.
On Píngqiū Mountain, there are poplars and willows.
Chēng River and Máo Marsh.
The Ěryǎ states:
Chēng River willow, Máo Marsh willow, and poplar are marsh willows.
Some flourished at Zhǎn Qín's home.
The annotation to the Huáinánzǐ states:
At Zhǎn Qín's home, there was a willow tree.
He personally practiced benevolence and virtue,
hence he was called "Liǔxià Huì."
Another says it is a place name.
Some flourished at Táo Qián's residence.
The History of the Southern Dynasties states:
Beside Táo Qián's residence, there were five willow trees.
He once wrote "Biography of Master Five Willows."
There is also the land of the Wò people.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
In the land of the Wò people, there are white willows.
Beside the Wèn River.
The Shī Shū Yì states:
The Qí River runs beside the Lǔ state's Tài Mountain,
and along the Wèn River, willows grow abundantly by the roadside.
Emperor Jìng was already sung of in rhymes during the Zhōu era.
The History of the Suí states:
At the beginning of the Zhōu, there was a children's rhyme:
"On the white poplar tree head, the golden rooster crows,
there are only maternal uncles, no nephews."
Emperor Jìng was the nephew of the Suí clan.
After abdicating the throne, he died,
and his maternal uncles were powerful and prosperous.
The Yáng clan was also sung of in Tàikāng.
Wáng Yǐn's History of the Jìn states:
At the end of the Tàikāng era,
in the capital Luòyáng, the "Song of Breaking the Willow" circulated.
The song began with laments of the hardships of war,
and ended with events of capture and execution.
At that time, the three Yángs were noble and prosperous but were later exterminated as a clan,
the empress dowager died in seclusion,
fulfilling the omen of breaking the willow.
Jìngzé remembered them at the northern lodge.
The History of the Southern Qí states:
Wáng Jìngzé once served as envoy to Wèi,
and planted willows at the northern lodge.
Later, Vice Director Yú Chángyào returned from a northern mission,
and Jìngzé asked:
"The willows I planted back then, how big are they now?"
Chángyào said:
"Among the northerners, they are regarded as sweet pear trees."
Táo Kǎn recognized them in Wǔchāng.
The History of the Jìn states:
Táo Kǎn had exceptional discernment.
Along the roads of Wǔchāng, willows were planted extensively.
Someone stole one and planted it at home.
Kǎn saw it and recognized it, saying:
"This is the willow from the west gate of Wǔchāng.
Why did you steal it and plant it here?"
The thief was frightened.
Some cast shade in Luósuō.
The History of the Táng states:
The land of Tǔbō was cold and harsh,
with poor and sparse products.
In the Luósuō River region under its jurisdiction, only willows grew,
which people relied on for resources,
and there were no other plants or trees.
Some formed forests in Zhènwǔ.
The History of the Táng states:
Fàn Xīcháo garrisoned Zhènwǔ.
In the Chányú city, there were originally few trees.
Xīcháo purchased willow saplings elsewhere
and ordered soldiers to plant them.
To this day, they have formed forests,
and the residents depend on them.
Where Zhāng and Lù resided together,
the mutual yielding flourished.
The History of the Qí states:
Hé Diǎn was fond of notable things.
Hearing that Lù Huìxiǎo and Zhāng Róng lived in adjacent residences,
with a pond between them,
and two willow trees by the pond,
Diǎn sighed and said:
"This pond is the sweet spring,
and these trees are the mutual yielding."
When Jī and Áng both declined,
the solitary poplar alone flourished.
The History of the Suí states:
Liǔ Jī, styled Kuāngshí.
Initially,
Jī, during the Zhōu, along with his clansman Áng, both held prominent positions.
When Jī and Áng both served in provincial posts,
Yáng Sù, then the Nàyán in power,
took advantage of a banquet hosted by the emperor
to tease Jī, saying:
"Both willows have fallen,
only a lone poplar stands tall."
All present laughed heartily.
As for the song "The Poplars at the East Gate" with its lush foliage,
the *Book of Songs* says:
"The poplars at the east gate,
their leaves are lush and dense."
Or the tender grace of bygone days.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"When I left long ago,
the willows were tender and graceful."
Worrying that Tián Xū was easily uprooted,
the *Supplementary Anecdotes to the Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
King Āi of Wèi appointed Tián Xū as his chancellor.
Huìzǐ said to Xū:
"You are adept at serving those around the king.
Now consider planting a poplar:
lay it sideways, and it will grow;
break it and plant it,
and it will grow again.
But if ten people plant poplars
and one person uproots them,
then no poplar will survive!
Although you have planted yourself firmly with the king,
there are many who wish to remove you—
you are surely in danger!"
Moved by Gù Yuèzhī's premature aging.
The *Shì Shuō* says:
Gù Yuèzhī was the same age as Emperor Jiǎnwén of Jìn.
Yuèzhī's hair turned white early.
The emperor asked:
"Why have you aged before me?"
He replied:
"The willow's delicate form
withers at the approach of autumn;
the pine and cypress's sturdy nature
grows more vigorous in the depths of winter."
There is also the tomb of Nǚwā where trees grew.
The *Táng Shū* says:
During the Qiányuán era,
Guózhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Qíguāng reported:
At Nǚwā's tomb in Wénxiāng County, in the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era, heavy rain darkened the sky,
and the tomb suddenly vanished.
Later, by the riverbank, thunder and wind were heard from the river,
and at dawn, the tomb was seen emerging from the water,
with twin willow trees above
and a massive rock below.
The luxuriance at Gāo Jiǒng's residence.
The *Suí Shū* says:
When the Duke of Bóhǎi, Gāo Jiǒng, was a child,
there was a willow tree in his home,
over a hundred feet tall,
towering like a canopy.
The elders in the village said:
"This household will produce a noble person."
Shoots sprouting as an omen,
the *Yì Jīng* says:
"A withered poplar puts forth shoots;
an old man takes a young wife."
Fencing the garden is criticized.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Breaking willows to fence the garden,
the madman stares wide-eyed."
Note:
The willow
is a weak and fragile tree.
Fán means
a fence.
Breaking it to fence the garden
is of no use.
The "Lush Willow" was satirizing King Yōu.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The Lush Willow"
satirizes King Yōu.
"There is a lush willow,
yet no one rests beneath it."
Characters formed as an auspicious sign for the Hàn emperor.
The *Hàn Shū* says:
A withered willow tree in the Shànglín Park
suddenly revived with branches and leaves,
and insects ate its leaves to form the characters: "Gōngsūn Bìngjǐ ascends."
Suī Mèng interpreted this as a sign of a commoner rising,
and that someone from among the people would receive the mandate.
After Chāngyì was deposed,
Emperor Xuān was enthroned,
whose original name was Bìngjǐ.
Thus, the uses of poplars and willows
are indeed beneficial to the common people.
See the annotation in the "Ode to Arrows": "Gathering rushes from the platform until it is emptied."
Tóng
This excellent tree, the wutong,
The Erya says:
Chèn,
is wú.
Commentary:
It is the present-day wútóng.
It grows on the steep, layered cliffs of Yìyáng.
The Book of Documents says:
The solitary tóng tree of Yìyáng.
Commentary:
On the southern slopes of Mount Yì, tóng trees grow uniquely,
their wood is suitable for making qín and sè.
It contains the wondrous musical pitch within the huángzhōng note,
Zhāng Xié's "Seven Summonses" says:
The tóng tree of the cold mountain,
emerges from the Great Darkness.
It contains the huángzhōng note to produce its trunk,
perched on the verdant peak, it grows in solitude.
It bathes its numinous vitality in the dark rain.
Wèi Míng's "Song of the Fierce Tiger" says:
A pair of tóng trees grows by the empty well,
their branches and leaves naturally intertwine.
A flowing spring waters their roots,
the dark rain moistens their boughs.
Though its seeds can attract nests,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
An empty doorway invites the wind,
the tóng's seeds attract nests.
Commentary:
When a doorway is empty,
the wind delights in entering it.
The seeds of the tóng tree resemble milk,
they attach to the leaves and grow,
birds delight in nesting there.
Yet its wood is difficult to make into crossbows.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The wise have their shortcomings,
therefore tóng wood cannot be used to make crossbows.
Some, imbued with pure essence, are uniquely exceptional,
Wáng Yìzǐ says:
Among trees, there are the fúsāng, wútóng, pine, and cypress,
all receive a pure essence,
making them different from the common kinds.
Some are hollow inside and thus easily damaged.
The Yì Wěi says:
The branches of the tóng are soft and downy, and moreover hollow inside,
difficult to mature, easily damaged,
it must complete its essence before it can flower.
Its down was early heard of in the country of Piào,
The Guǎngzhì says:
In the country of Piào, there is a white tóng wood,
its flowers have white down,
they take this down, soak it, and spin and weave it to make cloth.
Spinning its flowers is further seen in the Huáyáng.
The Huáyáng Guózhi says:
In Yìzhōu, there is wútóng wood,
its flowers are colorful like silk,
people spin them to make cloth,
named huābù.
Again, there are those that grow on high ridges,
from the Shī.
They perch the numinous phoenix,
An ancient poem says:
The wellside wútóng perches the numinous phoenix.
Placed in a jar, clouds arise,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Tóng wood produces clouds.
Commentary says:
Take a ten-dàn jar,
fill it with water,
place a tóng inside it,
cover it,
within three or four days,
vapor like clouds forms.
Laid in a pit, it moves for the imprisoned.
The Lùnhéng says:
Lǐ Zǐcháng, while governing,
wishing to know the circumstances of prisoners,
carved a wútóng tree in the shape of a prisoner,
dug a pit in the ground,
and laid the wooden prisoner inside it.
If the prisoner's crime was just,
the wooden prisoner did not move;
if there was injustice,
the wooden prisoner moved.
It emerged from the essential sincerity of men being transferred to the wooden figure.
Also, like the Lóngmén tree without branches,
Méi Chéng's "Seven Stimuli" says:
The tóng tree of Lóngmén,
is a hundred feet high and has no branches.
The Chuītái tree is a hundred arm-spans around.
The Yóu Míngshān Zhì says:
At Chuītái there is a tall tóng tree,
all are a hundred arm-spans around,
the solitary tóng of Yìyáng is inferior compared to these.
Its leaves account for intercalary months and have a fixed number,
The Dùnjiǎ says:
If the wútóng does not grow, then the Nine Provinces will have anomalies.
Commentary:
