The wútóng is used to know the correct and intercalary months of the sun and moon,
it grows twelve leaves,
one side has six leaves,
counting from the bottom, one leaf represents one month,
if there is an intercalary month, then there are thirteen leaves,
observing which month's leaf is small, one knows which month is intercalary.
If it does not grow, then the Nine Provinces will have a different ruler.
Its flowers bloom at Qīngmíng, responding to the season.
The Lǐ says:
At Qīngmíng, the tóng begins to flower.
Following Zhāoyáo, could it be split?
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Using a giant axe to strike a tóng firewood,
one does not wait for an auspicious time or favorable day to then split it.
Placing a giant axe upon tóng firewood,
yet without the application of human strength,
even if following Zhāoyáo, Xíng, and Dé, it cannot be split,
for it lacks the necessary force.
Nurturing jǐjí thorns is not appropriate.
The Mèngzǐ says:
Suppose there is a gardener,
who abandons his wútóng and jiǎ trees,
and nurtures his jǐjí thorns,
then he is a worthless gardener.
Commentary:
This means discarding the great and choosing the small.
Carving the elegant instrument of Shénnóng and Huángdì,
The Xīnlùn says:
Shénnóng and Huángdì,
carved tóng wood to make qín.
Gathering the tender southeastern branches.
The Fēngsútōng says:
The wútóng grows on the cliffs of Mount Yìyáng,
gathering the tender southeastern branches to make qín,
the sound is very clear and elegant.
There are also those distinguished as zǐ and qī,
The Shī says:
Plant hazels, chestnuts, yī, tóng, zǐ, and qī,
then you may cut them to make qín and sè.
Named róngtóng,
The Erya says:
Róng,
is tóng wood.
Zhuāngzǐ then leans against it and dozes,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
If you externalize your spirit,
and exhaust your essence,
then you lean against a tree and chant,
or lean against a wútóng and doze.
Commentary:
This means being weary and exhausted, hence so.
King Chéng then playfully used it to confer a fief.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
King Chéng and Táng Shū Yú were at leisure in the palace,
he cut a wútóng leaf to make a guī tablet,
and said:
"With this, I confer a fief upon you."
Yú was pleased,
and told the Duke of Zhōu,
the Duke of Zhōu requested to confer the fief upon Yú.
King Chéng said:
"I was just joking with Yú."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Your servant has heard that the Son of Heaven has no jesting words!"
So he conferred a fief upon Shū Yú in Jìn.
It rises from the dark stream, clinging to peril,
Cuī Qí's "Seven Exhortations" says:
There is the wútóng,
growing by the dark stream,
its roots clinging to decaying soil,
perched on danger, born in peril.
Growing in Qí territory, it became a palace.
The Qídì Jì says:
In the city of Qí there is a Wútái,
which is the Wúgōng palace.
Cài Yōng obtained it from beneath the cooking stove,
see the commentary on "Cài Yōng's scorched tail" in the "Qín Fù".
The Prince of Yùzhāng planted it within his residence.
The Qí Shū says:
The Prince of Yùzhāng built a hill at his residence,
planted rows of tóng and bamboo,
named it Tóngshān.
Emperor Wǔ visited it,
set out wine and made merry.
As for employing the worthy, then it grows,
The Ruìyìng Tú says:
When the king appoints and employs the worthy and virtuous,
then the wútóng grows in the eastern wing.
Riding the fire element, it flourishes.
The Lǐ Dǒu Wēiyí says:
When the ruler rides the fire element and reigns,
his governance is equitable,
the wútóng constantly grows.
It perches the yuānchú fledgling from the Southern Sea,
The Zhuāngzǐ says the yuānchú sets off from the Southern Sea and flies to the Northern Sea,
it will not perch except on the wútóng,
it will not eat except on bamboo seeds.
It strikes the stone drum of Línpíng.
See the commentary on "striking stone at Línpíng" in the "Gǔ Fù".
When autumn arrives at Qínchuān,
the King of Wú gazes upon it and is often sorrowful;
The *Shuyi Ji* says:
The Wutong Garden is located in the old state of King Fuchāi of Wú,
also known as the Qinchuān Wú Garden.
The palace is in Jùróng County.
It is said that:
The separate residence of the King of Wú had a forest of catalpas and wutong trees.
An ancient *yuèfǔ* poem says:
"Autumn in the Wú Palace,
the King of Wú is sorrowful"—this refers to it.
When the phoenix came to Ēpáng,
the ruler of Qín planted trees but made a mistake.
The *Qín Jì* says:
Initially,
there was a ballad in Cháng'ān:
"Phoenix, phoenix, alight at Ēpáng."
Fú Jiān then planted tens of thousands of wutong trees in Ēpáng City to await it.
Later, Mùróng Chōng entered Ēpáng City and settled there.
Chōng's
childhood name was Fèng.
Mulberry
One mu of land can feed three trays of silkworms.
Its lushness is seen in Lù Jī's rhapsody.
Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on the Mulberry" says:
In the beginning,
Emperor Shìzǔ Wǔ was the General of the Central Garrison,
and planted a single mulberry tree.
The world passed through three dynasties,
and the years gradually reached three jì.
Its green leaves flourished and grew to over a foot,
its supple branches spread and increased in length.
Regarding finding Yī Yǐn by the waters,
see the note "fell into the village of the hollow mulberry" in the "Rhapsody on Water."
Roaming by the great mound gave birth to Master Ní.
The "Kǒng Yǎn Tú" says:
Kǒngzǐ's mother, Zhēngzài, roamed by the slope of a great mound,
and while sleeping dreamed that the Black Emperor sent an envoy to invite her to go and mate,
saying to her:
"You must give birth in a hollow mulberry."
Upon waking, she felt as if affected,
and gave birth to Qiū in a hollow mulberry.
Note:
"Give birth"
means to produce.
Sometimes interplanted with elm and jujube trees,
the "Suí Shū" says:
During the Héqīng period of Qí, an ordinance was established,
granting each adult male twenty mu of perpetual land as mulberry fields,
among which fifty mulberry trees were to be planted,
three elm trees,
and five jujube trees.
Sometimes used for silk floss and cloth.
The "Qí Shū" says:
The country of Fúsāng is over twenty thousand lǐ east of the Dàhàn country,
its soil abundant with fúsāng trees,
leaves resembling paulownia,
when first sprouting like bamboo shoots,
the people of the country eat them,
the fruit like pears but red.
They spin its bark into cloth,
also making silk floss and paper.
Tribute of fine goods to Qīngzhōu,
the "Shū" says:
From Qīngzhōu, their baskets contained yǎn silk.
Note:
Yǎn mulberry silk,
is used for qín and sè strings.
Its fame spread throughout the Sānfǔ region.
The "Fàn Zǐ Jìrán" says:
Mulberry leaves come from the Sānfǔ region.
Obtaining the remarkable daughter of the King of Qí,
the "Liènǚ Zhuàn" says:
The woman with a tumor from Qí
was a woman from the eastern outskirts of Qí who gathered mulberry leaves,
and had a large tumor on her neck.
When King Mǐn traveled to the eastern outskirts,
all the common people went to watch,
only the woman with the tumor continued gathering mulberry leaves as before.
The king found it strange,
and asked her,
to which she replied:
"I received my parents' instruction to gather mulberry leaves,
I did not receive instruction to watch Your Majesty."
The king said:
"This is a remarkable woman."
He betrothed and welcomed her.
Witnessing the chaste wife of Qiū Hú.
The "Liènǚ Zhuàn" says:
Lǔ Qiū Hú took a wife, and after five days,
went to serve as an official in Chén.
Later, returning home,
before reaching his house,
he saw a beautiful woman by the roadside gathering mulberry leaves.
Qiū Hú was pleased by her,
alighted from his carriage,
and wished to entrust himself to her under the mulberry shade.
The woman continued gathering mulberry leaves without stopping.
Hú said:
"Toiling in the fields is not as good as encountering a good year,
gathering mulberry leaves is not as good as encountering a gentleman.
Now I have gold,
and wish to give it to you, madam."
The woman did not accept it.
Hú then returned home,
his mother called for his wife,
who turned out to be the woman gathering mulberry leaves from before.
She enumerated Hú's offenses,
and threw herself into the river.
As for its branches brushing against the ten suns,
the "Huáinánzǐ" says:
The Fúsāng tree is in Yángzhōu,
where the suns brush against it.
Note:
Where the ten suns emerge,
nine dwell on the lower branches,
one dwells on the upper branch.
Its roots bend down to the triple springs.
The "Xuánzhōng Jì" says:
The tallest thing under heaven is the Fúsāng tree,
it has no branches,
reaching up to the heavens above,
and connecting down to the triple springs below.
Eating its fruit showed the filial piety of Jūn Zhòng.
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
Cài Jūn Zhòng
was from Rǔnán.
During the turmoil of Wáng Mǎng,
people resorted to cannibalism.
Jūn Zhòng collected mulberries in separate containers.
Bandits asked him why,
Jūn Zhòng said:
"The black ones are for my mother,
the red ones I eat myself."
The bandits deemed him righteous,
and gave him two shēng of salt,
which he accepted but did not eat.
Gathering them led to connecting with Páng Tǒng's words.
The "Jīngzhōu Xiānxián Zhuàn" says:
Páng Shìyuán studied under Sīmǎ Dé Cāo as his teacher,
and did not strive for minor fame,
so the masses did not know of him.
Dé Cāo personally gathered mulberry leaves in the rear garden during the silkworm month,
Shìyuán assisted him,
and thus discussed the rise and fall of states with him.
His words were like those of a spirit,
causing them to forget the passing of the day and their hunger.
Disputes led to the conflict of Bēiliáng.
The "Shǐjì" says:
The prince of Wú, Guāng, attacked Chǔ,
capturing Jūcháo and Zhōnglí.
Initially,
a maiden from the Bēiliáng clan of a Chǔ border town
and a woman from a Wú border town quarreled over mulberries.
The two households, angered, destroyed each other,
the magistrates of the two towns heard of it,
became angry and attacked each other,
destroying Wú's border town.
The King of Wú was enraged,
and thus attacked Chǔ.
Yielding showed the virtue of Xì Bó.
The "Qí Shū" says:
The local custom in Xiāngyáng was
for neighbors to plant mulberry trees on the boundary as markers.
Hán Xì Bó, because the mulberry shade encroached on another's land,
moved the boundary marker back several feet.
The neighboring side then encroached on his land,
and Xì Bó repeatedly replanted accordingly.
The neighbor felt ashamed,
and returned the encroached land.
Knowing the heavenly wind, it then withers.
An ancient poem says:
The withered mulberry knows the heavenly wind,
the sea water knows the heavenly cold.
Transforming the Eastern Sea into fields.
The "Shénxiān Zhuàn" says:
Má Gū said to Wáng Fāngpíng:
"I have seen the Eastern Sea become mulberry fields three times."
As for prohibiting the rearing of second-brood silkworms out of concern for damage,
the "Huáinánzǐ" says:
Second-brood silkworms can produce two harvests in a year,
which is not unprofitable.
However, the king's law prohibits it
because it damages the mulberry trees.
Obtaining a dead dragon brings harm.
The "Sānguó Diǎnlüè" says:
A person from Chángguǎng commandery of Qí cut down a withered mulberry tree,
and within it found a dead dragon,
over a foot long.
Those who understood signs believed that Chángguǎng was the original fief of Qí's Tàishàng Huáng,
the Qí house's virtue being wood,
the dragon being the symbol of the ruler,
the wood withered and the dragon dead,
was not an auspicious omen.
The Shǔ ruler's canopy by the side of his dwelling.
The "Shǔ Zhì" says:
On the southeastern corner hedge of the late ruler's dwelling, a mulberry tree grew,
over ten feet tall,
from afar looking lush like a small canopy.
Passersby all marveled that this tree was extraordinary,
saying a noble person would emerge from it.
When the late ruler was young, he played under the tree with the children of his clan and said:
"I will surely ride in a carriage with such a feather canopy."
The Qí ancestor's carriage-canopy tree south of his residence.
The "Qí Shū" says:
Tàizǔ's residence was in Wǔjìn,
south of the residence was a mulberry tree,
shaped like a carriage canopy.
When he was several years old,
he played beneath it,
and his elder cousin Jìngzōng said to him:
"This tree was born for you."
Furthermore, like the "Shī" praising its luxuriance,
the "Shī" says:
Luxuriant are those young mulberries.
The "Yì" records its peril,
the "Yì" says:
Will it perish, will it perish?
It is tied to a clump of mulberry.
Trimming it in the silkworm month,
the "Shī" says:
In the silkworm month, we trim the mulberry.
Holding a deep basket.
The Book of Songs says:
A maiden holds a deep basket,
Seeking tender mulberry leaves.
Already paired in pairs with shared roots,
The Records of the Ten Continents says:
The Fúsāng tree is in the azure sea,
Above it lies the palace of the Celestial Emperor,
Governed by the King of the East.
The tree grows thousands of zhang tall,
Paired in pairs with shared roots,
Leaning and supporting each other,
Hence called Fúsāng.
Immortals eat its fruit,
And their bodies turn golden.
Though the tree is large,
Its fruit resembles the mulberries of the Central Plains,
Sparse and red in color,
Bearing fruit once every nine thousand years,
With an exceptionally fragrant taste.
Also, leaf to leaf they correspond.
Cáo Zhí’s “Song of Beauty” says:
Leaving through the northern gate of Jì,
Gazing afar at the mulberry trees of the Hu lands.
Branch to branch naturally align,
Leaf to leaf naturally correspond.
Some have their left lapels caught,
The Songs of Chǔ says:
Garments, narrow and constrained,
The left sleeve caught on the Fúsāng tree.
The right lapel brushes against Bùzhōu,
The six directions insufficient for free movement.
Note:
Narrow and constrained,
Refers to an unexpansive appearance.
The transformed people wrap themselves,
The Comprehensive Map says:
The transformed people,
After eating mulberry for twenty-seven years,
Transform and wrap themselves,
Grow wings in nine years,
And die in ten years.
Immortals eat them and turn to gold,
See the note above on “paired in pairs with shared roots.”
In late summer, drill it to obtain fire.
The Master Zōu says:
In late summer, take fire from mulberry and paper mulberry.
Also, there is the horse-collar that kills people,
The Materia Medica says:
The white bark of mulberry roots,
Emerging above ground,
Is called horse-collar,
Do not take it,
It is poisonous and kills people.
The crouching snake cures illness.
The Materia Medica says:
Mulberry roots that spread sideways and emerge above ground,
Are called crouching snakes,
They treat heart pain.
Passing by the roadside hut, he gazes intently,
The Songs of Chǔ says:
A maiden by the roadside hut is picking mulberry leaves,
Confucius passes by and gazes intently.
Note:
Roadside hut,
Refers to a guesthouse.
Thinking of Jiāng Yuán treading in the footprints.
The Mysterious Mandate says:
Jiāng Yuán wandered in the Bì Palace,
The ground was Fúsāng,
She trod in the footprints of a giant,
And gave birth to Jì.
Zǐchǎn served as minister of Zhèng and incurred slander,
The Master Hán says:
Zǐchǎn opened fields and planted mulberry trees,
The people of Zhèng slandered and criticized him.
Confucius, from Chén, found contentment.
The Master Xún says:
Confucius went to Chǔ,
Between Chén and Cài,
He went without food for seven days,
And said:
“Those who do not dwell in obscurity do not generate profound thoughts,
Those who do not face adversity do not broaden their aspirations.
How could you know that I have not found my way under the fallen mulberry tree?”
Not only the chancellor of Lángyé,
Used it to make a cup;
Xiè Chéng’s Book of the Later Hàn says:
Gāo Hóng served as chancellor of Lángyé,
His wife and children never entered the official residence,
Using a mulberry cup to hold broth.
There was also a recluse of Chénliú,
Who relied on it to build a house.
Xiè Chéng’s Book of the Later Hàn says:
Shēntú Pán of Chénliú was ashamed that the commandery had no recluses,
So he closed his door to cultivate his will,
Building a thatched hut using a large mulberry tree as its beam.
Peach
Among the many varieties of fruits,
only the peach is truly excellent.
Its color is vibrant and lush,
its blossoms radiant and brilliant.
The *Book of Songs* says:
“The Peach Tree Is Lush and Fair,”
which praises the virtue of the queen and consorts.
The peach tree is lush and fair,
its blossoms radiant and brilliant.
Some believe it can confer immortality and prolong life.
The *Shénnóng Classic* states:
The jade peach,
if consumed, grants eternal life without death.
If taken at the moment of death,
the corpse will remain incorruptible throughout heaven and earth.
Others use it to subdue ghosts and ward off evil.
See the annotation for “painted roosters and reed ropes” in the “Spring Rhapsody.”
Some praise the virtue of the queen and consorts,
as mentioned above.
Some use it to reciprocate the splendor of jade.
The *Book of Songs* says:
“You gave me a wooden peach,
I repay you with fine jade.”
At the Waking of Insects, it flourishes in response to the season.
The *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* states:
During the Waking of Insects,
the hexagram Dà Zhuàng prevails.
On the first nine line,
the peach begins to bloom.
If it does not bloom,
storehouses will suffer many fires.
Farmers rely on it as a reliable indicator of the seasons.
Cuī Shí’s *Monthly Ordinances* says:
In the third month, when peach blossoms are abundant,
farmers observe the timing to plant.
Ascending Yúntái Mountain, one sees peach trees spreading like brocade along the cliffs.
The *Biographies of Immortals* states:
Zhào Shēng, a disciple of Zhāng Líng,
studied under Líng.
Líng and his disciples climbed Yúntái Mountain,
where on a sheer cliff grew a peach tree as thick as an arm.
Líng said:
“Whoever retrieves the peach fruit will be taught the essential Way.”
None of the disciples dared to look.
Shēng leaped from above,
landed precisely on the peach tree,
and returned with his arms full of peaches.
Journeying to Wǔlíng, one sees peach trees lining both banks like spreading rosy clouds.
Táo Qián’s *Record of the Peach Blossom Spring* says:
During the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man from Wǔlíng was fishing
and followed a stream,
forgetting the distance traveled.
Suddenly, he encountered a peach grove lining both banks,
its fragrant blossoms fresh and beautiful,
with fallen petals swirling in profusion.
At the end of the grove was a mountain,
with a small opening in it.
At first, it was extremely narrow,
but after walking four or five steps,
it opened up into a bright, expansive space.
Houses and villages were connected,
with the sounds of chickens and dogs audible to each other.
The clothing of the men and women was entirely like that of outsiders.
Seeing the fisherman,
they were astonished.
They prepared wine and food for him,
explaining that their ancestors had fled the turmoil of the Qín dynasty,
leading their families here,
and thus became cut off from the outside world.
They asked what era it was now,
unaware of the Hàn dynasty,
let alone Wèi or Jìn.
After leaving,
he reported to the prefect,
who sent people to follow him back.
They searched for it,
but became lost and could not find it again.
Jealousy was often heard of in the case of the woman from Wǔyáng.
The *Record of Jealousy* states:
A woman from Wǔyáng married Ruǎn Xuān,
and she was extremely jealous.
There was a peach tree in their home,
its blossoms and leaves radiant and dazzling.
When Xuān admired its beauty,
she immediately flew into a rage,
ordered a maid to fetch a knife and chop down the tree,
destroying its blossoms.
Affection and aversion shifted subtly in the case of Mí Zǐxiá.
The *Hánzǐ* states:
Long ago, Mí Zǐxiá was favored by the ruler of Wèi.
While strolling with the ruler in an orchard,
he ate a peach and found it sweet,
so he offered half to the ruler.
The ruler said:
“How you love me!
You forgot your own mouth and offered it to me.”
Later, when Mí Zǐxiá’s looks faded and the ruler’s favor waned,
he offended the ruler,
who said:
“This man once offered me a half-eaten peach.”
As for carving wood on Suí Mountain,
the *Biographies of Immortals* states:
Gě Yóu enjoyed carving wooden sheep and selling them.
One day, he rode a sheep up Suí Mountain,
and nobles pursued him,
all attaining immortality.
Suí Mountain abounds with peaches,
hence the proverb:
“Obtain a single peach from Suí Mountain,
and even if you do not become immortal,
you will still be considered illustrious.”
Shén Shū used reed ropes.
See the annotation for “painted roosters and reed ropes” in the “Spring Rhapsody.”
Disrespecting superiors was admonished by Wénhóu.
The *New Prefaces* states:
When Wèi Wénhóu visited Jī Jì,
his attendants ate Jī Jì’s peaches,
and Jī Jì stopped them.
Wénhóu said:
“How could Jī Jì merely cherish peaches?
He is teaching me that subordinates must not disrespect their superiors.”
Confucius also spoke of using the humble to cleanse the noble.
The *Hánzǐ* states:
Lǚ Āigōng presented Confucius with peaches and millet.
Confucius first ate the millet and then the peach.
The duke said:
“You used the millet to cleanse the peach.”
Confucius replied:
“Millet
is the foremost of the five grains;
the peach
is the lowest of the six fruits.
A gentleman does not use the noble to cleanse the humble.”
Immortal maidens once fed the two gentlemen.
The *Records of the Hidden and Visible* states:
Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào together entered Tiāntāi Mountain,
became lost and could not return,
and their provisions were exhausted.
They found several peaches on the mountain and ate them,
whereupon they were no longer hungry.
Descending the mountain,
beside a large stream,
they encountered two women of exquisite beauty,
who invited them to their home.
They instructed their maids:
“Although Liú and Ruǎn, the two gentlemen, have just consumed jade-like fruit,
they are still weak and exhausted.
Quickly prepare food for them.”
They stayed for half a year,
then longed for home and returned.
The prime minister of Qí also caused the death of three warriors.
The *Annals of Yànzǐ* states:
Gōngsūn Jiē, Tián Kāiqiáng, and Gǔ Yězǐ served Duke Jǐng,
brave but lacking propriety.
Yànzǐ advised the duke,
presenting them with two peaches,
saying:
“Let the three of you assess your merits and eat accordingly.”
Gōngsūn Jiē and Tián Kāiqiáng first stated their merits,
took the peaches, and rose.
Gǔ Yězǐ then stated his merits,
demanding the other two return the peaches.
The two, ashamed, committed suicide.
Gǔ Yězǐ said:
“It is dishonorable to boast of one’s deeds and act unjustly.”
He also returned his peach,
cut his throat, and died.
Kūnlún is famed for its frost-ripened fruit.
The *Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luòyáng* states:
On Jǐngyáng Mountain in the Hundred-Fruit Garden, there are immortal peaches,
red in color,
translucent throughout,
which ripen only after frost.
They also grow on Kūnlún Mountain,
and are called Queen Mother peaches.
Pángtáng is distinguished for its cold blossoms.
The *Records of Omitted Affairs* states:
Pángtáng Mountain is fifty thousand lǐ from Fúsāng,
beyond the reach of the sun.
The land is cold,
with peaches a thousand arm-spans around,
bearing fruit once every ten thousand years.
Máo and Sī differ in form but share the same name.
The *Eryǎ* states:
Máo
is the winter peach.
Sī peach
is the mountain peach.
Hóu and Bái differ in flavor but are both exquisite.
The *Records of the Jìn Palaces* states:
In the Huálín Peach Garden, there were seven hundred and thirty peach trees,
including three Hóu peaches
and three Bái peaches.
There are also names like Qǐyè and Jīnchéng,
and titles such as Zǐwén and Xiānghé.
The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
The Shànglín Park had Qín peaches, cherry peaches, Xiānghé peaches, Qǐyè peaches, frost peaches, Jīnchéng peaches, and Zǐwén peaches.
Although it is said to be the lowest of the six fruits,
See the note on "Xuě Jiàn heard from the Master" above.
It is indeed the essence of the five woods.
The Diǎn Shù says:
The peach tree,
is the essence of the five woods,
its essence is born at the ghost gate,
controls all ghosts,
therefore, nowadays, peach-wood figures are placed at gates to ward off evil.
Gāo Qiū consumed resin and ascended lightly,
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Lord Gāo Qiū ingested peach resin and attained immortality.
Shī Mén ate blossoms and achieved the Way.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Shī Mén was
a disciple of Xiào Fù.
He could command fire,
and ate peach blossoms.
Xià Kǒng Jiǎ detested him,
killed him, and buried him in the wilderness,
whereupon the mountain trees all burned.
Kǒng Jiǎ prayed,
but before he could return, he died.
There is also the matter of the club of Yì,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Yì died by a peach-wood club.
The fear of Hàn's spirit.
The Méizǐ says:
Wáng Mǎng feared the divine spirit of Hàn Gāozǔ,
so he ordered the Tiger Guard to draw swords and cut down the peach trees at Gāozǔ's temple,
then boiled them and sprinkled the water on the temple roof.
The lushness of the frosty grove in deep winter,
The Shíyí Jì says:
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn, someone presented giant peach trees,
which bloomed under frost,
and ripened only in the height of summer,
so they were planted in the Frosty Grove Garden.
Commonly said to be "mutually encroaching,"
is an error.
The splendor of bean-like fruits in red summer.
The Dàdài Lǐ • Xià Xiǎo Zhèng says:
In the sixth month, peaches are boiled,
to make bean food.
As for the Hàn emperor ceasing to plant them,
The Hàn Wǔ Gùshì says:
The Queen Mother brought out seven peaches,
gave five to the Emperor,
and ate two herself.
The Emperor kept the pits intending to plant them,
but the Mother said:
"These peaches bear fruit once every three thousand years,
and are not to be planted in the mortal realm."
Fāng Shuò secretly stole them.
The Hàn Wǔ Gùshì says:
The Eastern Commandery presented a short man,
the Emperor summoned Dōngfāng Shuò,
Shuò arrived,
and the short man pointed at Shuò and said to the Emperor:
"The Queen Mother plants peaches,
which bear fruit once every three thousand years,
this boy is no good,
he has already stolen them three times."
The fallen plum sighs at being implicated,
see the note on "fallen plums destroyed" in the "Ode to the Well."
The clay figurine pities the floating,
The Shuō Yuàn says:
When Mèng Cháng was about to enter Qín,
a guest admonished him, saying:
"I passed by the Zī River,
and saw a clay figurine speaking with a wooden figurine.
The wooden figurine said to the clay one:
'Now the heavy rain comes,
you will surely be ruined.'
It replied:
'My ruin would merely return me to my true form.
But you are a peach from the eastern garden,
carved into a figurine;
when the floodwaters come,
you will surely float away, drifting aimlessly with no place to stop.'" Mèng Chángjūn then did not go.
The Fán clan competed in magical arts,
The Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
Lady Fán and her husband Liú Gāng both possessed Daoist arts,
each claiming superiority.
In the courtyard were two peach trees,
husband and wife each chanted over one,
and the peaches fought,
the peach chanted by Gāng walked out beyond the fence.
Cài Dàn fabricated tales of immortal travels.
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
Cài Dàn of Wǔyuán entered the mountains and returned,
deceiving his family, saying:
"I reached Kūnlún Mountain,
where there are jade peaches,
luminous, transparent, and hard,
requiring water from the Jade Well to wash them,
then they become soft and edible."
There are also three named varieties,
Pān Yuè's "Xiánjū Fù" says:
Three peaches represent the ranks of Yīnghú.
Their fruit fills ten hú.
The Xuánzhōng Jì says:
Among the great fruits of trees are the peach fruits of Jīshí Mountain,
as large as a ten-hú vessel.
The Tàiqīng soaks blossoms to cure illness,
The Tàiqīng Huìmù Fāng says:
Soak peach blossoms in wine,
drink it to cure all ailments,
and improve complexion.
The Bàopǔ ingests resin to abstain from grains.
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
Peach resin, soaked with mulberry wood charcoal and ingested,
cures all diseases.
Long-term ingestion makes the body luminous,
and enables abstention from grains.
Some chant over it to wash the face,
see the note on "peach blossoms washing the face" in the "Spring Ode."
Some cut open the belly to retrieve it.
The Zhōnglí Yì Biézhuàn says:
The Zhōu Shū states that the Qín historian Zhào Kǎi, out of personal grudge, accused the gardener Wú Qiěshēng of stealing and eating the imperial peaches of the ancestral temple.
Qiěshēng replied:
"I dare not eat them."
The King said:
"Cut open his belly,
and take out the peach."
How could this compare to feasting on green fruits in the western journey,
marking a name on the immortal register.
The Yǐn Xǐ Nèizhuàn says:
Yǐn Xǐ followed Lǎozǐ on a western journey,
visited the Supreme True Queen Mother,
and together ate the fruits of the green peaches.
Lǐ
Ah, the luxuriant plum,
the beauty among fruits.
Immortal pale and divine red,
as the "Fruit Rhapsody" says:
"The immortal plum is pale and the divine plum is red."
It blooms in winter and bears fruit in spring.
The Guangzhi records:
In the gardens of Yè, there is a spring plum,
which blooms in winter and ripens in spring.
Some spread their fragrance like the Huángjiàn,
as the Guangzhi says:
Wheat plums are small and fine,
including the grooved plum, the Huángjiàn plum, the Huángbiǎn plum, and the horse-liver plum.
The sticky plum,
with flesh that clings like sticky rice.
Some boast names like the Qīngqǐ.
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
The Shanglin Park had purple plums and Qīngqǐ plums.
Wǔzǐ uprooted the tree to rebuke stinginess,
as the Book of Jin records:
Hé Qiáo was frugal by nature,
and his family had fine plums.
When the emperor requested some,
he gave no more than a few dozen.
Wáng Wǔzǐ, angered by his stinginess,
led a group of youths with axes to the garden,
ate his fill,
and then cut down the tree before leaving.
Wáng Róng drilled the pits to reveal his pettiness.
The Book of Jin records:
Wáng Róng had fine plums,
which he often sold,
but fearing others might obtain the seeds,
he drilled holes in the pits.
The wonder of the Yùhuá intertwined branches,
as the Book of Tang records:
During the Zhēnguàn era,
plum trees in the Yùhuá Palace grew intertwined,
their branches joining across a stream.
The beauty of Fánglíng's Zhū Zhòng,
as Rèn Fǎng's Records of the Strange notes:
On Dìng Mountain in Fánglíng, there were thirty-six Zhū Zhòng plum trees.
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Life of Leisure" says:
"The forests of Fánglíng hold Zhū Zhòng's plums."
The fresh luxuriance of Ānyáng's Huīzhāng,
as the Records of the Strange notes:
Before the Ānyáng Hall of Emperor Wén of Wei, eight crimson plums descended from heaven.
Eating just one,
he needed no food for several days.
Today, there is a variety called the Ānyáng plum,
large and sweet,
which is descended from those.
The Names of Jin Palaces and Pavilions records:
Before the Huīzhāng Hall, there were fine plums.
The smooth sweetness of Zhōngshān's Dùlíng.
Lù Shìhéng's "Fruit Rhapsody" says:
"The pale plums of Zhōngshān."
The Records of the Strange notes:
In Dùlíng, there are golden plums,
the larger ones called summer plums,
the smaller ones called mouse plums.
Some are named after Yánzǐ,
as the Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
The Shanglin Park had Yānyuān plums,
originating from the State of Lǔ.
Some are recorded in connection with Hán Zhōng.
The Records of the Cavernous Mysteries states:
In the country of Lín, there are jade-leaf plums,
which ripen once every five thousand years.
The immortal Hán Zhōng consumed them,
hence they are also called Hán Zhōng plums.
There are those with a mottled red appearance,
and those known as fruitless.
The Erya says:
Xiū,
the fruitless plum.
Zuò,
the Jiēlǜ plum.
Bó,
the red plum.
Some are sunk in cold water,
as Emperor Wén of Wei wrote in his "Letter to Wú Zhì":
"Floating sweet melons on clear springs,
sinking crimson plums in cold water."
Some are repaid with jade blossoms.
See the Book of Songs.
Biānchūn is seen beyond the borders,
as the Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
Mount Biānchūn abounds with plums.
Yuánqiū is recorded in immortal texts.
The Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Han says:
Among the superior medicines of immortals is the Yuánqiū red plum.
It establishes the noble model of not adjusting one's cap,
as an ancient Yuefu song says:
"A gentleman guards against what has not yet occurred,
and avoids situations of suspicion.
In a melon field, do not bend to tie your shoe;
under a plum tree, do not reach to adjust your cap."
It stirs the beautiful reputation of forming a path,
as Ruǎn Jí's poem says:
"Beneath fine trees, a path forms,
in the eastern garden, peach and plum."
The Book of Han records:
General Lǐ Guǎng,
modest as a rustic,
was not eloquent in speech.
Yet on the day of his death,
all under heaven, whether they knew him or not,
shed tears for him.
A proverb says:
"Peaches and plums do not speak,
yet a path is worn beneath them."
There are also those who consumed dark clouds and attained the Way,
as the Inner Biography of the True Man Wáng Bāo says:
On Mount Wǔyún Dān, there are dark cloud plums;
eating them leads to immortality.
Some are eaten like a vase and emit light.
The Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Han says:
Lǐ Shàojūn told the emperor:
"The plums of Mount Zhōng are as large as vases.
I ate one,
and it produced a wondrous light."
The grub that can be eaten is on the well,
see the annotation "the grub fruit of Wūlíng" in the "Rhapsody on the Well."
The bitter ones left uneaten are by the roadside.
The Book of Jin records:
When Wáng Róng was just seven years old,
he often played with other children by the roadside.
A plum tree had so many fruits that its branches bent,
and the other children rushed to pick them,
but only Róng remained still.
When asked why,
he replied:
"A tree by the roadside with so many fruits
must bear bitter plums."
Upon picking them, it was indeed so.
Bóyáng pointed to it to determine his surname,
as the Biographies of Immortals says:
Lǎozi's mother leaned against a plum tree when giving birth to him.
Lǎozi was born able to speak,
and pointing to the plum tree, he said:
"Let this be my surname."
Sēngrú declined it by not tasting first.
The Book of Qi records:
When Wáng Sēngrú was young,
someone gifted his father winter plums.
His father first offered one to him,
but he refused,
saying:
"Since my father has not yet seen them,
I cannot taste them first."
Such is the beauty of the crimson plum,
crowning the fresh fragrance of all fruits.
Plum.
The Book of Songs says:
“The plums are falling,
only seven left on the tree.”
The Book of Songs says.
As for the sourness of plums and nan trees,
the Erya states:
Plum,
nan tree.
Annotation:
Resembles an apricot, with sour fruit.
It is also an excellent fruit among fruits.
It can be used to freshen the breath,
as the Shiyishu explains:
Plum
is a type of apricot.
Boiled and dried into a paste,
it can be placed in soups or pickles
to be held in the mouth for fragrance.
It is also used in blended soups to achieve harmony.
The Book of Documents, “The Charge to Yue,” says:
If making a blended soup,
you are the salt and plum.
Fàn Wāng could eat them by the full hu measure,
as the Yulin records:
Fàn Wāng was so skilled at eating plums
that he often kept a hu-sized box of them,
and in a short while, he would finish them all.
Sūn Liàng inspected them when soaked in honey.
The Wuli records:
Sūn Liàng was just leaving the Western Garden
and eating raw plums.
He sent a eunuch to the central storehouse to fetch honey to soak the plums.
There was a rat dropping in the honey.
The attendant requested that the matter be handed over to the prison for investigation.
Sūn Liàng said:
“This is easy to determine.”
He ordered the rat dropping to be broken open.
The inside was dry.
Sūn Liàng laughed heartily and said:
“If it had been in the honey for a long time,
the inside should be wet.
Since the inside is dry,
it must have been planted by the eunuch.”
The eunuch then confessed.
One plum’s sourness is not enough for a hundred people,
as the Huainanzi says:
A hundred plums are enough to sour a hundred people,
but one plum is insufficient to sour a hundred people.
Annotation:
This metaphor illustrates that many can accomplish what few cannot,
and a few cannot achieve anything significant.
Yet thirst was quenched for an entire army of three divisions.
The Shishuo records:
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was on a march
and lost his way.
The entire army of three divisions was thirsty.
The emperor ordered:
“Ahead there is a large plum forest,
abundant with fruit,
sweet and sour,
which can quench thirst.”
Upon hearing this, the soldiers all salivated.
The Yuè envoy presented a plum branch to the state of Liáng,
as the Shuoyuan records:
The Yuè envoy Zhū Fā held a plum branch to present to the King of Liáng.
The Liáng minister Hán Zǐ looked at those around him and said:
“How could one present a single plum branch to the ruler of a great state!”
Lù Kǎi sent the spring of Jiāngnán.
The Jingzhou Ji records:
Lù Kǎi and Fàn Yè were close friends.
From Jiāngnán, Lù Kǎi sent a plum branch to Cháng’ān for Fàn Yè,
along with a poem that said:
“Plucking a flower, I meet a courier;
I send it to the man at Lǒngtóu.
In Jiāngnán, there is nothing to offer,
so I present a branch of spring.”
Liǔ Yùn’s archery was so skillful,
as the Nanshi records:
Liǔ Yùn once competed in archery with Lángyá’s Wáng Zhān.
Finding the target too broad,
he set up a plum as the bullseye on the black pearl,
and every shot hit the mark.
Shòuyáng’s makeup was even more novel.
The Songshu records:
Emperor Wǔ’s daughter, Princess Shòuyáng,
on Ren Day, was lying beneath the eaves of Hánzhāng Hall.
A plum blossom fell onto the princess’s forehead,
forming a five-petaled flower,
and would not brush off.
From then on, the plum blossom makeup came into fashion.
Pluck from Líng Mountain or climb the Shànglín Garden,
admire the purple stems or delight in the “same heart.”
The Shanhaijing says:
Líng Mountain has many plum trees.
The Xijing Zaji records:
The Shànglín Garden had red plums, “same heart” plums, purple-stemmed plums, yānzhī plums, beautiful-branch plums, purple-flower plums, and seasonal plums.
Some use them to cook the Hénggōng fish,
as the Shenyi Jing records:
North of the wilderness, there is a stone lake,
a thousand li square,
containing the Hénggōng fish,
which transforms into a human at night.
It cannot be pierced,
nor can it be killed by boiling.
But boiling it with twenty-seven black plums will cook it thoroughly,
and it can cure evil diseases.
Some use them to refine Qǐlǐ’s gold.
The Baopuzi says:
The Qǐlǐ alchemical method:
Take a hundred jīn of lead,
boil it with realgar,
and it all turns to gold.
If too hard,
boil it with lard;
if too soft,
boil it with plums.
The wind of the fifth month signals trust,
as the Fengsu Tong explains:
The fifth month has the “falling plum wind,”
which the Jiāng-Huái region regards as the trustworthy wind.
The rain at the summer solstice is called excessive.
Zhōu Chù’s Fengtu Ji says:
The rain at the summer solstice is called the “yellow plum rain,”
and if it stains clothing, it will ruin and discolor it.
Is it only in Bó Yǔ’s temple
that branches grew, making the affair extraordinary?
The Fengsu Tong says:
In Xià Yǔ’s temple, there was a plum beam,
which suddenly sprouted branches and leaves.
Or perhaps in Sū Dān’s garden,
it healed illnesses with profound efficacy.
The Guiyang Xianxian Zhuan records:
Sū Dān planted medicinal herbs under the plum tree in his rear garden,
which could cure all diseases.
Apricot
Admirable is this patterned apricot.
The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
The Shanglin Park had patterned apricots,
meaning their timber had patterned color.
They received their essence from the Year Star.
The *Canon of Techniques* states:
The apricot tree is
the essence of the Year Star.
It gathers the lush shadows of Líng Mountain.
The *Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
Below Líng Mountain,
its trees are mostly apricots.
It spreads its abundant blossoms in Wèi Commandery.
Lú Yù's *Discourse on Jìzhōu* states:
Wèi Commandery has fine apricots;
its local produce is not without treasures.
Lú Chén recorded the rites of sacrificial offerings.
Lú Chén's *Sacrificial Methods* states:
Summer sacrifices use apricots.
Shī Kuàng divined the signs of abundance and scarcity.
Shī Kuàng's divination states:
If apricots bear much fruit and are not wormy,
the autumn of the coming year will be good.
"Three Mysteries" is its name.
The *Biography of Lady Nányuè* states:
Immortals have "Three Mysteries Purple Apricots."
"Six Petals" is its designation.
The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
The Pénglái apricot in Shanglin Park,
Dūwèi Yútái of the Eastern Sea presented one tree.
Its flowers were variegated with five colors,
had six petals,
and it was said to be what immortals ate.
Tilling the sand, one knows the season for farming.
Fàn Shèngzhī's *Book* states:
When the apricot blossoms are like this,
one can till the white sand.
Blending wheat, one understands the refinement of distinguishing flavors.
The *Xuānyàn Spring and Autumn* states:
Wèi Lún visited me,
and our conversation touched upon flavors.
He praised the late Wèi Palace Attendant Liú Zǐyáng,
who, upon eating a cake, could tell if the salt was raw—
the pinnacle of discerning taste.
I said:
"Shī Kuàng recognized firewood from a worn-out cart,
Yì Yá distinguished between the Zī and Shéng rivers.
Zǐyáng is the master of today;
determining this is hardly difficult!"
Lún then ordered his servant to bring forth parched grain for me to taste.
I tasted it and said:
"It is wheat,
but it has the flavors of apricot, plum, and pear-apple.
These three fruits ripen at different times;
how did you manage to combine them?"
Lún laughed and did not answer.
Later, he told others:
"Shì'ān's discernment surpasses that of Liú.
In my household, the stores are plentiful.
Therefore, when the apricot season approaches,
I blend it with apricot juice;
when the plum and pear-apple season approaches,
I blend it with plum and pear-apple juice,
hence combining the three flavors."
Adrift on the Southern Sea,
it relieved the hunger of boatmen.
The *Records of Strange Things* states:
There is an Apricot Garden Isle in the Southern Sea,
with many apricots.
It is said to be a place where immortals planted apricots.
During the Hàn dynasty,
someone sailing by boat encountered a storm and moored at this isle.
In the fifth and sixth months,
he ate apricots daily,
and thus escaped death.
It is also said there are winter apricots on the isle.
On Niú Mountain during famine,
it served as food for the common people.
Northeast of Sōng Mountain is Niú Mountain,
which has many apricots.
By the fifth month, they turn a luxuriant, brilliant yellow.
Since the central lands fell into chaos,
and the people suffered famine,
they all relied on these to survive.
Everyone ate their fill,
yet the apricots were not exhausted.
As for those that excelled in beauty and embodied elegance,
the *Register of Luòyáng Palaces* states:
In front of the Hánzhāng Hall,
there are four apricot trees.
Those that spread their fame at Xiǎnyáng,
the *Register of Luòyáng Palaces* states:
In front of the Xiǎnyáng Hall,
there are six apricot trees.
By the side of Fàn Lǐ's residence,
the *Geographical Records* state:
Fàn Lǐ's residence is in the middle of a lake.
There are sea apricots,
as large as a fist.
Beside Guāngwǔ's mausoleum.
Zhū Chāoshí's *Letter to His Elder Brother* states:
The apricots by Guāngwǔ's tomb are very fine.
I now send you their pits.
Tribute from the Western Mountains was sent to the land of Wèi.
Wáng Yì's *Rhapsody on Lychees* states:
The land of Wèi sent apricots from the Western Mountains.
They were arrayed at the immortal's shrine in Làixiāng.
The *Records of Strange Things* states:
At the Lǎozǐ shrine in Làixiāng, there are pale-green apricots.
Zhòngní sat beside the black-canopied forest.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
Confucius wandered in the forest of black canopies,
and rested sitting upon the Apricot Altar.
His disciples read books,
sang to stringed accompaniment,
and played the qín.
Dǒng Fèng planted them on the sunny side of Lú Mountain.
The *Records of Xúnyáng* state:
Dǒng Fèng lived on Lú Mountain.
When treating people's illnesses,
he would have those who recovered plant five apricot trees.
They are still called "Master Dǒng's apricots."
Furthermore, there is Zhāng Yuán, who was considered honest for returning them to their owner.
The *Book of the Later Zhōu* states:
Zhāng Yuán
was of an honest and upright character.
His southern neighbor had two apricot trees.
When the apricots ripened,
many fell into Yuán's garden.
Yuán returned them all to the owner.
Mǎ Chàng was fearful of being disrespectful.
The *Táng History* states:
Mǎ Chàng
was the son of Mǎ Suì.
Chàng sent large apricots from his estate as a gift to Dòu Wénchǎng,
and Wénchǎng presented them to Emperor Dézōng.
Dézōng had never seen such before
and was rather suspicious of Chàng.
He ordered a palace envoy to seal the apricot tree.
Chàng, in fear,
offered up his residence,
which was converted into the Fèngchéng Garden.
Some adorned them to make beams.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's *Rhapsody on the Tall Gate Palace* states:
They adorned patterned apricot wood to make beams.
Others followed them to till the soil.
Fàn Shèngzhī's *Book* states:
When apricots first bloom gloriously,
immediately till the light soil and weak soil.
Watch for the apricot blossoms to fall,
then till again,
and immediately harrow it.
This is called one tilling yielding fivefold.
Wáng Yuáncháng's *Essay on Examining Scholars* states:
When apricot blossoms flourish and leaves are abundant,
do not forget to plow and harvest.
The five fertile soils find it suitable for planting.
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
In the five fertile soils,
the suitable tree is the apricot.
In the third month, discern the measure of the fields.
The *Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People* states:
In the third month, when apricot blossoms are abundant,
one can sow fields of white sand and light soil.
It is crowned as a treasure alongside the cherry and cherry plum,
seen in the beautiful rhapsody "Living in Idleness."
Pān Yuè's *Rhapsody on Living in Idleness* states:
Plums, apricots, cherry plums, and cherries—
their blossoms and fruits shine brilliantly.
Pear-apple
Only this white pear-apple,
a treasure among fruits.
It flourishes as the fine fruit of Hǔqiū,
The "Hǔqiū Shān Shū" says:
On three sides of the mountain, there are spring and autumn pear-apples.
It blooms splendidly in the late spring of the Shanglin Park.
See below.
White flowers inspire ballads,
originating from the Heavenly Duke and the Weaving Maiden;
The "Jìn Shū" says:
Emperor Chéng's Empress Dù passed away.
Before this,
women from Sānwú wore white flowers in their hair,
looking from afar like white pear-apples.
A ballad said the Heavenly Duke and the Weaving Maiden had died,
and they wore mourning garments for them.
It was then that the empress passed away.
Dark clouds are presented as offerings,
and further heard of from the Lady of Nányuè.
The "Nányuè Fūrén Zhuàn" says:
The lady's surname was Wèi,
her given name was Huácún.
In the middle of winter, at midnight,
a true man descended.
The lady prepared wine and delicacies in her quiet chamber,
and set out dark clouds and purple pear-apples.
As for Zhāngyè being praised as extraordinary,
the "Guǎng Zhì" says:
Zhāngyè has white pear-apples,
Jiǔquán has red pear-apples.
In the western regions, pear-apples are generally abundant.
Families make them into dried fruit,
storing tens or hundreds of hú,
as accumulated reserves.
Guāzhōu excels in beauty.
Zhāng Zǎi's poem says:
Sānbā's yellow oranges,
Guāzhōu's white pear-apples.
The fruit may be red or white,
Pān Yuè's "Xiánjū Fù" says:
Two pear-apples shine with red and white hues.
Some blossoms are half green and half purple.
The "Xījīng Zájì" says:
The Shanglin Park has purple pear-apples,
with purple blossoms;
green pear-apples,
with green blossoms.
Yáng Yīn paid no heed,
thus earning the name "prodigious child";
The "Sānguó Diǎnlüè" says:
When Yáng Yīn was young,
there was a pear-apple tree at home.
When the fruit fell to the ground,
all the children scrambled for them,
but Yīn alone sat still, ignoring them.
His uncle Yáng Wěi saw this and said to guests:
"This child is serene and composed,
he has my demeanor."
Wáng Xiáng guarded it,
thus fulfilling his filial duty.
The "Xiàozǐ Zhuàn" says:
Wáng Xiáng served his stepmother.
In the courtyard was a pear-apple tree.
When it first bore fruit,
she ordered him to guard it.
Xiáng drove away birds and sparrows by day,
and startled mice at night.
Suddenly, rain came,
and Xiáng embraced the tree until dawn.
His mother saw this and was moved with pity.
Its appearance resembles the flower of the rìjǐ,
Dù Shù's "Dǔ Lùn" says:
The flower of the rìjǐ resembles the pear-apple,
but the pear-apple bears fruit while the rìjǐ is hollow.
The hollow and the real are alike in appearance.
Its name is recorded among the wonders of Yuánqiū.
The "Hànwǔ Gùshì" says:
The emperor grasped the golden essence of Lán Yuán,
and plucked the purple pear-apples of Yuánqiū.
Pān Ní wrote an ode to the clear canal,
Pān Ní's "Dōngwǔ Guān Fù" says:
Sweet melons fly into the Jùn River,
white pear-apples are cast into the clear canal.
Lú Chén established the ritual for summer sacrifices.
Lú Chén's "Jì Fǎ" says:
For summer sacrifices, white pear-apples are used according to the ritual,
and red ones for autumn.
Gathered from the remote lands of Kūnlún,
the "Shíyí Jì" says:
Kūnlún has pear-apples,
which bear green fruit in winter.
Planted in the red earth of Huálín.
The "Jìn Gōnggé Míng" says:
Huálín Garden has four hundred white pear-apple trees.
Those ripening in summer are already fine,
but those maturing in winter are especially precious.
Cáo Zhí's "Xiè Nàizi Biǎo" says:
That evening, a tiger-guard in the palace announced an edict,
bestowing upon us a box of winter pear-apples.
The edict instructed us to eat them warm.
Night is not the usual time for eating,
yet the gift was granted;
pear-apples ripen in summer,
but now it was midwinter.
Things out of season are treasured,
sweetness that delights the palate is profound.
Prepared as offerings for the four true ones,
possessing the fragrant essence of the three mysteries.
The "Nányuè Fūrén Zhuàn" says:
The lady, along with Wáng Zǐqiáo and the four true ones, acted as hosts,
and set out the three mysteries and purple pear-apples.
Date.
The jujube is a fine fruit,
a resource for the people.
Some praise the fruit of the sour jujube,
the *Erya* says:
Èr,
means sour jujube.
The commentary states:
The tree is small and its fruit is sour.
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
Nourish its èr jujube and thorns.
Some speak of the flavor of the short-tasting jujube.
The *Erya* says:
Huánwèi means the rěn jujube.
Commentary:
Huánwèi,
means short flavor.
Some eat the kernel to ward off evil,
the *Liú Gēn Biézhuàn* says:
If one can regularly take the kernel inside the jujube pit,
a hundred evil diseases will not assail again.
Some eat the leaves to stave off hunger.
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* says:
Féng Yīn rebelled,
Dèng Yǔ campaigned against him,
was defeated by Yīn,
reached Gāolíng,
the soldiers were starving,
and all ate jujube leaves.
The Zhòngsī purple fruit,
the *Dàyè Shíyílù* says:
Xìndū presented Zhòngsī jujubes,
four inches long,
purple in color,
with fine patterns,
the pit is plump and flavorful.
The Zhōuwén weak-branched.
Pān Yuè's *Xiánjū Fù* says:
The Zhōuwén weak-branched jujube.
Yànzǐ first spoke of it to Duke Mù of Qín,
the *Yànzǐ Chūnqiū* says:
Duke Jǐng said to Yànzǐ:
"In the midst of the Eastern Sea there is red water,
within it there are jujubes,
that flower but bear no fruit,
why is this?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Long ago, Duke Mù of Qín rode a dragon to govern the world,
he wrapped steamed jujubes in yellow cloth and threw the cloth,
therefore the water is red;
the steamed jujubes,
therefore they flower but bear no fruit."
The Duke said:
"I was asking in jest."
He replied:
"Yīng has heard that for a jesting question,
one gives a jesting answer."
Shàojūn also encountered Ānqī.
The *Shǐjì* says:
Lǐ Shàojūn presented an anti-aging method to the Emperor saying:
"Your subject once roamed upon the sea,
saw Ānqīshēng,
he gave your subject a jujube to eat,
the jujube was as large as a melon."
On the seventh day it is heard of in immortal lore,
the *Hàn Wǔ Nèizhuàn* says:
On the seventh day of the seventh month, the Queen Mother of the West would descend,
and set out for the Emperor jade-gate jujubes.
In the eighth month it is recorded in the *Máoshī*.
The *Shī* says:
In the eighth month we knock down the jujubes,
in the tenth month we reap the rice.
Observe them clustered and abundant,
Pān Yuè's *Shēng Fù* says:
Beneath the jujube tree they cluster,
the red fruits hang plentiful.
How they fall,
turning into withered branches.
Shake them, pick them,
the *Lǐ* says:
For jujubes, say 'shake them'.
The *Erya* says:
For jujubes, say 'pick them'.
The Sānxīng flourishing,
the *Guǎngzhì* says:
The official gardens have the Sānxīng jujube.
The five parks spread profusely.
The *Hánzǐ* says:
Qín suffered famine,
Yìnghóu said to the King:
"The fruits, vegetables, acorns, jujubes, and chestnuts of the five parks are sufficient to keep the people alive,
I request they be distributed."
The abundance of Ānyì and Gǔchéng,
the *Hànshū* says:
A thousand jujube trees in Ānyì are equal to a marquis with a thousand households.
The *Guǎngzhì* says:
The purple jujubes of Gǔchéng in Dōngjùn are two inches long.
The suitability of Xìndū and Liángguó.
The *Guǎngzhì* says:
Xìndū large jujubes,
Liángguó Fūrén jujubes, Tàibái jujubes.
Follow the yáng, ah, the wèixiè,
the *Erya* says:
Zūnyáng means the jujube.
Commentary:
The fruit is small and round,
purple-black in color,
now commonly called the sheep-dropping jujube.
It also says:
Wèixiè,
means the bitter jujube.
The piánbái, ah, the cùzī.
The *Guǎngzhì* says:
Piánbái jujubes, cùzī jujubes,
these two types,
are grown in the official gardens.
Felling the eastern neighbor's tree and dismissing the wife,
the *Hànshū* says:
Wáng Jí's eastern neighbor had a jujube tree whose branches hung into Jí's courtyard,
Jí's wife picked jujubes to give Jí to eat.
Jí then dismissed his wife.
The eastern neighbor, hearing of this, wanted to fell the tree,
the neighbors together stopped him,
and firmly requested Jí to have his wife return.
A local saying went:
"The eastern neighbor has a tree,
Wáng Yáng dismissed his wife;
the eastern neighbor's jujubes remain intact,
the dismissed wife returns again."
Holding a jujube and showing gold to a child.
The *Chūnqiū Fánlù* says:
Hold a jujube and a piece of gold,
and show them to an infant,
the infant will certainly take the jujube and not the gold.
Therefore, among things for people,
the small ones are easily understood.
The immortal child's regard for several decades,
the *Dōngyáng Jì* says:
In Xìn'ān County there was Xuánshì Slope.
During the Jìn dynasty, there was a commoner named Wáng Zhì,
who went to cut wood and reached a stone chamber,
saw four children,
playing the sè and singing,
Zhì therefore stayed,
leaning on his axe handle to listen.
One of the children gave Zhì an object like a jujube pit,
Zhì put it in his mouth and then was no longer hungry.
After a short while,
the children told him to return,
Zhì followed the sound and left,
his axe handle had completely rotted away.
Once he returned home,
Zhì had been away from home for several decades,
relatives and old friends had scattered and perished,
nothing was as it had been in former times.
The three-thousand-year rendezvous with the goddess.
The *Mǎ Míngshēng Biézhuàn* says:
Míngshēng in his youth encountered a goddess,
returned to Dàizōng,
saw Ānqīshēng who said:
"Long ago I roamed with the maiden on the shores of the Western Sea of Ānxī,
ate jujubes of extraordinary beauty,
and suddenly three thousand years have passed."
As for Zēng Xī's fondness for them, never forgetting,
the *Mèngzǐ* says:
Zēng Xī was fond of yáng jujubes,
and Zēngzǐ could not bear to eat them.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked:
"Which is more delicious, minced roast meat or yáng jujubes?"
He said:
"Minced roast meat, of course!"
He said:
"Then why did Zēngzǐ eat minced roast meat?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Minced roast meat is common to all,
yáng jujubes were his alone."
Mèng Jié could hold them in his mouth without eating.
The *Hòu Hànshū* says:
Mèng Jié could hold a jujube kernel in his mouth without eating it,
for up to ten years.
It both supplements the center and aids the qì,
the *Běncǎo* says:
All jujubes are gathered in the ninth month,
dried in the sun,
they supplement the center and benefit the qì.
It also calms the body and increases strength.
The *Shényì Jīng* says:
In the northern wilderness there are jujubes,
their height is five zhàng.
The fruit is six or seven inches long,
eating them can calm the body,
and benefit strength and qì.
The *Dài Lǐ* mentions them as a woman's gift,
the *Lǐ* says:
A woman's gifts are:
dried meat, seasoned dried meat, jujubes, chestnuts.
The *Zhōuguān* sets them as the contents of the sacrificial baskets.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
For the food-offering baskets,
their contents are jujubes.
Some grow in Shí Hǔ's garden,
According to Lù Huì's *Yèzhōng Jì*:
In Shí Hǔ's garden, there were Queen Mother of the West dates,
of exceptionally fine flavor,
with luxuriant, verdant branches and leaves,
that did not wither throughout the four seasons.
They bloomed in the ninth month,
and ripened in the twelfth month.
Some were planted beside the Jǐngyáng Mountain.
According to *Luòyáng Qiélán Jì*:
Jǐngyáng Mountain had a Hundred Fruits Garden,
where each type of fruit formed its own grove,
and each grove had its own hall.
There were Immortal dates five inches long,
with pits as fine as needles,
which ripened only after the frost descended.
Yángjiǎo, Qílián,
According to *Yèzhōng Jì*:
In Shí Hǔ's garden, there were Yángjiǎo (Goat Horn) dates.
*Guǎngzhì*:
There were Qílián dates.
Xìyāo, Jībái.
According to *Ěryǎ*:
Biānyāo dates.
Commentary:
These are Xìyāo (Slender Waist) dates.
Also stated:
Jībái dates.
Commentary:
Nowadays, dates that ripen white.
Some shaded the streets of Zhèng,
According to *Hánzǐ*:
When Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
not a single peach or date shading the streets
was plucked.
Some were abundant in Jìzhōu.
According to *Wèi Zhì*:
Dù Shù submitted a memorial stating:
"Jìzhōu has the largest population,
and also has abundant mulberries and dates,
making it a treasury for the state's requisitions."
Their fame excels as Jīxīn,
According to *Guǎngzhì*:
Dates have names like Jīxīn (Chicken Heart), Gǒuyá (Dog Tooth), Míhóu (Macaque), and Xìyāo (Slender Waist).
Their use is compared to fox fur.
According to *Lǚshì Chūnqiū*:
As for the presence of date and jujube trees,
and the presence of fox fur,
eating the dates from the jujube trees,
wearing robes of fox fur,
the former kings certainly used them,
not because they possessed them themselves, but because they were available.
In summer, they were drilled to obtain fire,
According to *Zōuzǐ*:
In summer, they took fire from dates and apricots.
In spring sacrifices, they were pressed to obtain oil.
According to Lú Chén's *Jìfǎ*:
For spring sacrifices, date oil was used.
There was also the state of Hán Màoguó,
According to *Shuǐjīng*:
The old city of Suānzǎo County
was the ancient state of Hán.
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven established states and named capitals,
sometimes it was based on mountains and forests,
thus Yùzhāng was named for its trees as the capital,
and Suānzǎo (Sour Date) was named for its jujube thorns as the state.
Abundant in Gāotáng,
According to *Shuǐjīng Zhù*:
Beside the Gānzǎo (Sweet Date) Ditch waters in Gāotáng County, there were many date trees,
hence the common name derived from it.
Praising Táo Shuò for maintaining integrity,
According to Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hànshū*:
Táo Shuò of Hénán,
when fellow villagers offered him provisions, he accepted nothing,
but only ate dates and drank water.
Commending Chéng Mò for observing mourning.
According to Cài Yōng's *Zòushì*:
Chéng Mò was fourteen years old,
when his paternal grandfather's younger brother fell ill and passed away,
Mò embraced and lay over his uncle's corpse,
wailing in grief and sorrow.
His maternal uncle, pitying his frail and weak state,
chewed date flesh to feed him,
but Mò, seeing the food, sobbed with emotion,
and could not swallow it.
Planting Yùmén dates in the Shangyuàn,
According to *Xījīng Zájì*:
In the Shanglin Park, there were Yùmén (Jade Gate) dates.
Flourishing on Qí Peak in the northern wilderness.
According to *Shíyí Jì*:
In the shade of Qí Peak at the North Pole,
there were many date trees a hundred xún tall,
their branches and stems all hollow,
the fruit a foot long,
with fine and soft pits,
bearing fruit once every hundred years.
Dù Jī's integrity is worthy of esteem,
According to *Dùshì Xīnshū*:
Dù Jī served as Governor of Hédōng,
General Píng Hǔ Liú Xūn was favored by Tàizǔ,
and his prestige shook the court.
He often asked Jī for large dates,
but Jī refused on other grounds.
Later, when Xūn was executed,
Tàizǔ obtained his correspondence,
and sighed, saying:
"Dù Jī can be said to be 'one who does not flatter the powerful.'"
Sūn Chéng's plot was also commendable.
According to *Dōngguān Hànjì*:
The Palace Attendant Sūn Chéng plotted to kill Jiāng Jīng,
and deceitfully said to Mǎ Guó:
"The Son of Heaven gave me date preserves,
ordering me to accomplish this early."
Then he joined with Guó and others to establish Emperor Shùn.
There is also the name for fruitless ones,
According to *Ěryǎ*:
Xīwúshí dates.
Commentary:
Those that do not bear fruit.
The name Tàibái.
According to *Guǎngzhì*:
The gardens of Liángguó produced Tàibái dates.
Some were fed to horses as preserves,
According to *Shǐjì*:
During the time of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
he had a beloved horse,
which he fed with date preserves.
Some trees were cut to swear an alliance.
According to *Gāoshì Zhuàn*:
Hú Zhāo and Emperor Xuān of Jìn were friends from their commoner days.
A fellow townsman, Zhōu Shì, wanted to kill the Emperor,
Zhāo tried to stop Shì,
but Shì refused.
Zhāo wept to show his sincerity,
and Shì, moved by his intent, desisted.
Zhāo cut a date tree and swore an oath with Shì before parting.
Later, when Zhāo met the Emperor,
he never spoke of it.
The Assistant Administrator distributed them to equalize the troops,
According to *Yīngxióng Jì*:
Kǒng Wénrǎng was attacked by bandits from Dōnglái,
the city was about to fall,
and his Assistant Administrator Zuǒ Chéngzǔ distributed official dates to the fighting men.
The Commandant planted them according to regulations.
According to *Huáinánzǐ*:
In the eleventh month,
the official Commandant
plants date trees.
Spitting them out and dying,
how extreme was Bào Jiāo's scrupulousness;
According to *Fēngsútōng*:
Bào Jiāo farmed for his food,
dug wells for his drink,
and ate dates in the mountains.
Someone said:
"Did you plant these yourself?"
Whereupon he forcibly vomited,
stood withered, and died.
Being called and questioned,
how ingenious was Mànqiàn's technique.
According to *Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn*:
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
the Shanglin Park presented dates,
the Emperor tied the staff he was holding to the railing of the Weiyang Front Hall,
and called to Shuò, saying:
"Chì chì,
xiānshēng lái lái,
xiānshēng, do you know what is in this basket?"
Shuò said:
"The Shanglin Park has presented forty-nine dates."
The Emperor said:
"How do you know?"
Shuò said:
"The one calling Shuò is the Emperor (shàng),
tying the staff to the railing between two pieces of wood (mù),
two 'mù' make a 'lín' (forest),
'lái lái' means 'zǎo' (date),
'chì chì' signifies forty-nine."
The Emperor laughed heartily,
and bestowed ten bolts of silk.
As for blending them with maltose and honey for shared sweetness,
Fù Xuán's *Zǎo Fù* states:
Gleaming white blossoms,
scattered red fruit.
Crisp as frost and snow,
sweet as containing honey.
Placed alongside sour pears,
According to Yìng Shào's *Hàn Guānyí*:
When Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
ascending the altar he saw sour pears and sour dates,
and asked the reason.
The informant said:
"They were placed there by the officials who ascended."
The Emperor said:
"The fēng and shàn sacrifices are grand ceremonies,
occurring once in a thousand years,
why would the officials and scholars act like this?"
The Shanglin Park had offerings from the ministers,
According to *Xījīng Zájì*:
When initially constructing the Shanglin Park,
the various ministers each presented famous fruits,
Many fine names have been created for them,
hence there are the Green Blossom Date and the Red Heart Date.
In cave chambers, they serve as the food of immortals.
The *Biographies of Immortals* states:
Lǐ Yìqí built an earthen cave in a corner of the city,
dwelling within it,
wearing only a single layer of clothing in both winter and summer,
and consuming only wine, dried meat, and dates.
Sometimes he would not emerge for a hundred or two hundred days.
Already grieving over his longing for my brothers,
Fù Xuán’s *Lyrics* say:
Yellow leaves fall from the high branches,
red dates grow from their own shedding.
I do not regret the dates shedding themselves,
but long for my young brothers.
It also laments their growth among thorns.
An ancient poem says:
Sweet melons cling to bitter stems,
fine dates grow on thorny branches.
Ānpíng’s local produce
is not said to lack treasures;
Lú Yù’s *Discourse on Jìzhōu* states:
Ānpíng produces excellent dates,
its local goods are not without treasures.
Fángláng’s burning oil
is also praised as extraordinary.
The *Records of the Hidden and Mysterious* states:
Fángláng’s fine dates come from Mount Fángláng,
which overlooks the azure sea,
and bears fruit once every ten thousand years.
When pressed, they yield oil,
which can be used to light lamps.
Pear
Only the purple pear's moist richness,
The "Yǐn Xǐ Nèi Zhuàn" says:
Lǎozǐ traveled west,
visited the Supreme True Queen Mother of the West,
and together they ate purple pears.
Also, Zuǒ Sī's "Shǔ Dū Fù" says:
Purple pears are moist and rich.
They can relieve vexation and dispel melancholy.
Emperor Wén of Wèi issued an edict stating:
The imperial pears of Zhēndìng,
large as fists,
sweet as honey,
crisp as ice,
can relieve vexation and dispel melancholy.
The Hànhǎi pear endures cold without withering,
The "Xījīng Zá Jì" says:
The Shanglin Garden had Hànhǎi pears,
originating from Hànhǎi,
enduring cold without withering.
The Túshān pear blooms once in a thousand years.
The "Dòng Míng Jì" says:
North of Túshān, there is a pear as large as a dou measure,
purple in color,
blooming once every thousand years,
bearing fruit in winter.
When boiled, it yields a paste;
those who eat it become light-bodied.
It is also called the purple light pear.
Some are admired for their mysterious radiance,
The "Hàn Wǔ Nèi Zhuàn" says:
Among the supreme medicines of the Great One is the mysterious radiance pear.
Some are planted in Qīngtián.
The "Yǒngjiā Jì" says:
The villagers of Qīngtián mostly grow pears,
called official pears.
Cáo Cāo of Shānyáng,
mentioned them in a Wèi memorial;
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"The Shānyáng commandery has fine pears,
I respectfully present two boxes of sweet pears."
Zhāng Gōng's Dàgǔ pears,
are heard of in Jìn writings.
Pān Yuè's "Xián Jū Fù" says:
The pears of Zhāng Gōng's Dàgǔ.
Cultivating them can compare to being enfeoffed as a lord,
The "Hàn Shū" says:
North of Huáiběi, south of Xíngnán,
between the Hé and Jì rivers, if one has a thousand pear trees,
that person is the equal of a marquis with a thousand households.
Eating them can make one an earthbound immortal.
The "Shén Yì Jīng" says:
In the east, there is a tree a hundred zhang tall,
spreading out and supporting itself,
with leaves one zhang long,
six or seven chi wide,
named the pear tree.
Its fruit is three chi in diameter,
when cut open, it is white as silk,
eating it makes one an earthbound immortal.
Zhāng Huá's annotation says:
This is indeed today's pear tree,
only larger.
Savor the sweet crispness of the purple-stemmed pear,
appreciate the fragrant freshness of the pale-stalked pear.
The "Xījīng Zá Jì" says:
The Shanglin Garden had pale-stalked pears and purple-stemmed pears.
As for the excellence of Chángyáng and Zhēndìng,
Fù Xuǎn's "Qī Zhèng" says:
The yellow pears of Héngyáng,
the red tangerines of Wūshān.
Hé Yàn's "Jiǔzhōu Lùn" says:
Ānpíng has fine dates,
Zhēndìng has fine pears.
The flavors of Qúshān and Yùsù.
Zuǒ Sī's "Wú Dū Fù" says:
Among fruits are the pears of Qúshān.
The "Sān Qín Jì" says:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Fánchuān garden,
also named Yùsù,
had large pears as big as five shēng,
which would break upon falling to the ground,
named the melting pear.
Laugh at the Āi family's steamed pears,
The "Shì Shuō" says:
Whenever the Marquis of Nánjùn, Huán, saw someone displeasing,
he would angrily say:
"You've obtained Āi family pears,
would you still steam and eat them?"
An old account says:
In Mòlíng, there was the Āi Zhòng family,
whose pears were very large,
as big as a shēng,
melting upon entering the mouth.
It is said that foolish people could not tell the difference,
and preferred to steam and eat them.
Praise Dào'ān's fair distribution.
The "Shì Shuō" says:
When Dào'ān lectured,
monks often numbered in the hundreds.
Xí Zàochǐ once sent ten pears as a gift,
it happened to be during a lecture,
Dào'ān then personally cut and distributed them among the assembly,
the pears were exhausted and everyone received a share,
with no partiality whatsoever.
In the Xuánpǔ Garden, courtiers composed eulogies,
Wáng Zàn's "Lí Sòng" says:
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
four branches of a pear tree and its central trunk grew together in the Xuánpǔ Garden,
the Crown Prince ordered courtiers to compose eulogies.
On Tàishān, they were placed by all officials.
See the "Zǎo Fù" note on "vinegar pears and others placed together."
Fú Wǔ bit one as a pledge of joint rebellion,
The "Jìn Shū" says:
Fú Shuāng occupied Shàngguī,
Fú Liǔ occupied Púbǎn,
Fú Wǔ occupied Āndìng,
and together they planned to attack Cháng'ān.
Fú Jiān sent an envoy to admonish them,
each bit a pear as a token of faith.
Lǐ Bì had them roasted and was specially bestowed them.
The "Lǐ Yèhóu Zhuàn" says:
Emperor Sùzōng of Táng once summoned his three younger brothers, including Yǐng Wáng, at night,
and they sat together on a felt rug by a floor stove.
At that time, Lǐ Bì had long abstained from grains,
the Emperor personally roasted two pears to bestow upon him.
Diffusing fragrance within Dòngtíng Lake,
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
Within Dòngtíng Lake,
its trees are mostly pear trees.
Planted and entrusted to the Míngguāng Palace.
The "Jìn Gōngquè Míng" says:
Before the Míngguāng Hall, there was one pear tree.
Demanding much and greedy was Xuánmó,
The "Sòng Shū" says:
Wáng Xuánmó campaigned against Huátái,
demanding eight hundred pears from the people for one bolt of cloth.
Taking the small and wise was Kǒng Róng.
The "Wénshì Zhuàn" says:
Kǒng Róng, at four years old,
when eating pears with his elder brothers,
always took the smallest ones.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"I am a small child,
it is proper that I take the small ones."
Again, there are the words of Sòng Wǔ's Xìmǎ,
Emperor Wǔ of Sòng's "Xìmǎ Tái Líhuā Zàn" says:
The fine tree's growth,
upon that mountain's base,
blooms and displays its colors,
untainted by worldly dust.
Wáng Hóng's bestowal by the river.
Wáng Hóng's "Xiè Cì Héshàng Lí Biǎo" says:
I have received the bestowed pears from the riverbank,
their flavor sweet from afar,
each time you deign to bestow them,
I look up, bearing your grace,
bowing down, my reverence increases with shame.
Some are named for green jade,
some are recorded as golden branches.
The "Xījīng Zá Jì" says:
The Shanglin Garden had green jade pears and golden branch pears,
originating from the home of Lángyé's Wáng Yě,
presented by Governor Wáng Táng.
Cuī Yuǎn was compared to a treasure on the mat,
The "Táng Shū" says:
Cuī Yuǎn,
his literary talent was pure and beautiful,
his demeanor stern and dignified,
at that time he was regarded as a "dìngzuò lí,"
meaning a treasure on the mat.
Zhuāng Zhōu praised them as a pleasing taste.
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
Hawthorn, pear, tangerine, pomelo,
their flavors are opposite,
yet all are pleasing to the mouth.
Xiāo Qí transmitted it through prophecies and responses,
The "Guǎng Wǔxíng Jì" says:
During the Tàishǐ era of the deposed Emperor of Sòng,
the melting pear was widely propagated in Jiāngnán.
Previously, there were no such trees,
the common people vied to plant them,
and afterward, the Xiāo clan of Qí received the throne.
Jiè Xiàng entrusted it to the garden official.
The "Shénxiān Zhuàn" says:
Jiè Xiàng claimed to be ill,
the Emperor bestowed a case of fine pears.
At noon, Xiàng died,
and the Emperor buried him.
That same day, in the late afternoon, he arrived at Jiànyè,
and gave the bestowed pears to a garden official to plant.
The official reported the circumstances,
they immediately opened Xiàng's coffin to look,
and found only one talisman.
Some melt like snow in the mouth,
some fall and become water.
Sūn Chǔ's "Qiū Fù" says:
Red tangerines, sweet and fine,
purple pears, sweet and crisp,
The skin does not conceal the broken teeth,
the melting liquid is easier to contain than snow.
Also, Yáng Xuànzhī's "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì" says:
At Bàodé Temple, there is a Hánxiāo pear,
weighing six catties,
when it falls from the tree to the ground,
it completely turns into water.
Therefore, it is said that the pear is the ancestor of all fruits,
how can the hawthorn compare!
The "Sòng Shū" says:
Zhāng Fū's childhood name was Zhā,
his father Shào's childhood name was Lí.
Emperor Wén once jokingly said to him:
"How does Zhā compare to Lí?"
He replied:
"Lí is the ancestor of all fruits,
how dare Zhā compare."
Chestnut.
The Book of Songs says:
"On the hills are the lacquer trees,
in the lowlands are the chestnuts."
Precious products abound in all regions,
The Commentary on the Book of Songs states:
Chestnuts come from various regions,
Zhōu, Qín, Wú, and Yáng are especially abundant,
but only the chestnuts from Yúyáng and Fànyáng are sweet and delicious,
with a lingering taste.
They compare to the wealth of a thousand households.
The Book of Hàn says:
In Yān and Qín, having a thousand chestnut trees
makes one equal to a marquis with a thousand households.
In the Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial, they are placed south of the pickles,
The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial: Funeral Rites for Gentlemen says:
Set the beans to the right of the pickles,
south of the pickles are chestnuts,
east of the chestnuts are dried pork.
In the Rituals of Zhōu, they are used as offerings in bamboo baskets.
The Rites of Zhōu says:
For the food-offering baskets,
the contents are chestnuts.
Thus, there were those who monopolized the price in Nán'ān,
Wáng Bāo's "Contract with a Servant" says:
In Nán'ān, gather chestnuts.
There were also those planted at the Yíluán Palace,
The Records of the Great Enterprise says:
South of the Yíluán Hall in Luòyáng, there is a chestnut forest.
The Shanglin Park had the tribute of Cáo Lóng,
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital says:
The Shanglin Park has Yìyáng chestnuts,
presented by Governor Cáo Lóng.
On Jī Mountain, there is the saying of Yī Yǐn.
The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi says:
Yī Yǐn said:
"Among the finest fruits,
are the oranges of Jiāngpǔ and the chestnuts of Jī Mountain."
Tián Ráo advised using them to treat scholars,
The Garden of Stories says:
Tián Ráo said:
"The pears and chestnuts from the orchard,
the women of the rear palace pluck and pick them,
yet scholars have never tasted even one.
Moreover, wealth
is something the ruler takes lightly;
death,
is something scholars hold in high regard."
Zōng Dù offered them to honor the worthy.
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Hàn says:
Zōng Dù of Yùzhāng was appointed magistrate of Dìnglíng,
a county resident Dù Bóyí was aloof and refused to serve,
Zōng Dù conversed with him,
offering only dates and chestnuts.
Zhōngshān is mentioned in the "Discourse on Jìzhōu,"
Lú Yù's "Discourse on Jìzhōu" says:
Zhōngshān produces fine chestnuts,
its local products are not without treasures.
Sānfǔ is also praised in "Jìrán."
Fàn Zǐ Jìrán says:
Chestnuts come from Sānfǔ.
There are also the abundant chestnuts of Shuòbīn,
Wáng Yì's "Rhapsody on Lychees" says:
Běiyān presents the giant chestnuts of Shuòbīn.
And the fine chestnuts of Gé Mountain.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
Nán Mountain has many chestnuts,
Gé Mountain and Tóng Mountain have trees with many chestnuts.
Those gathered by day were the food of nest-dwellers,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
In ancient times, there were many beasts and few people,
so the people all lived in nests to avoid them,
eating acorns and chestnuts by day,
and resting in trees at night,
hence they were called "the people of the Nest Builder."
Those offered in reverence were the gifts of women.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
A woman's gift should not exceed hazelnuts, chestnuts, dates, or dried meat,
to show reverence.
They also distinguish the varieties of hóu and zhēn,
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital says:
The Shanglin Park has hóu chestnuts and zhēn chestnuts.
They also record the types of lì and ér.
The Ěryǎ says:
Lì,
is ér.
Note:
The tree resembles the húsù but is shorter and smaller,
its fruit is like small chestnuts and can be eaten.
Nowadays, in Jiāngdōng, it is called ér chestnut.
Yìnghóu used them to admonish his lord,
see the note on "five gardens in disarray" in the "Rhapsody on Dates."
Shěn Yuē's enumeration angered the emperor.
The Book of Liáng says:
Shěn Yuē once attended a banquet,
when Yùzhōu presented chestnuts,
measuring an inch and a half in diameter.
Finding them remarkable,
the emperor asked about the number of chestnut-related matters,
and had everyone list what they knew,
Shěn Yuē knew three fewer than the emperor.
After leaving, Shěn Yuē told others:
"This lord hides his shortcomings,
if he hadn't yielded earlier, he would have died of shame."
The emperor, considering his words disrespectful,
wanted to punish him for his offense,
but Xú Miǎn firmly remonstrated and stopped him.
It is also said to harmonize with auspicious signs in famous commanderies,
The Book of Sòng says:
Liú Xiùzhī served as governor of Dānyáng.
Earlier,
Xiùzhī's paternal uncle Mùzhī was in Dānyáng,
and held a feast with his family in the hall.
There was a hole in a pillar,
Mùzhī said to the younger generation:
"Each of you, from a distance, throw a chestnut;
the one whose chestnut enters the hole
will surely obtain this commandery in the future."
Only Xiùzhī's chestnut entered the hole.
They also symbolize repaying a sincere heart to the sovereign.
The Book of Liáng says:
Xiāo Chēn once attended an imperial banquet,
drunk and prostrate,
the emperor threw a date at Chēn.
Chēn then took a chestnut and threw it at the emperor,
hitting his face.
The Imperial Censor was present,
and the emperor, changing expression, said:
"There are people here,
you should not act like this;
do you have an explanation?"
Chēn replied:
"Your Majesty threw a red heart at your servant,
your servant dares to repay it with trembling."
Yán Zūn stood out uniquely among the subjects,
The Biographies of Former Worthies of Kuàijī says:
Emperor Guāngwǔ summoned Yán Zūn to the imperial camp,
when Shǔ commandery presented oranges and chestnuts,
the emperor bestowed them upon the ministers and below,
allowing each to take as many as they could reach by hand.
Only Yán Zūn did not take any,
the emperor asked him why,
Zūn replied:
"A ruler bestows upon his ministers with propriety,
ministers serve their ruler with reverence.
Now, the bestowal lacks a proper host,
so your servant dares not take any."
Wáng Tài stood out among his grandsons.
The Book of Sòng says:
