Wáng Tài was clever and perceptive from a young age.
When he was a few years old,
his grandmother once called the grandsons and nephews to scatter chestnuts on the bed,
all the children scrambled to grab them,
but Tài alone did not take any.
Asked why,
he replied:
"If I do not take any,
I will naturally receive a gift."
His relatives all found this remarkable.
That which makes the people tremble is the Zhōu altar,
see the Analects.
That which brings peace to the household is the eastern gate.
The Hánshī says:
The chestnuts at the eastern gate
bring peace to the household.
Note:
Jìng
means good.
It means under the chestnut tree at the eastern gate, there is a good person.
Some are as large as pears,
the Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wèi says:
In the land of Sānhán,
chestnuts are as large as pears.
Their color matches that of jade.
The Wèi Lüè: The Crown Prince's Letter to Zhōng Yáo says:
The king's letter praises beautiful jade,
red as a rooster's comb,
yellow as steamed chestnuts.
One is called by the term "falling,"
The Elder Dài's Book of Rites says:
In the eighth month, chestnuts fall.
Falling
means descending.
One is named by the term "selecting."
The Book of Rites says:
Chestnuts are called "selected."
Note:
Xuǎn
means to choose.
They are abundant enough to gather magpies,
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Wandering within the fences of Diāolíng,
I saw a strange magpie,
which brushed against my forehead and alighted in a chestnut grove.
Gǎn
means to touch.
Are they insufficient to feed monkeys?
The Lièzǐ says:
In Sòng, there was a man who kept monkeys,
fearing that the monkeys would not obey him,
he first deceived them, saying:
"If I give you acorns,
three in the morning and four in the evening?"
The monkeys all jumped up angrily.
Then, "Four in the morning and three in the evening?"
All the monkeys were pleased.
Sweet
oranges and pomelos,
among the finest,
there is the Húgān of Jiànchūn,
The Shényì Jīng says:
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"Beyond the southeastern wilderness lies Jiànchūn Mountain,
with beautiful sweet trees."
The Gǔjīn Zhù says:
The sweet fruit is shaped like a pomegranate,
called Húgān.
Piled up like the splendor of a bright star,
resplendent as a string of Suí pearls.
Zōng Bǐng's "Gān Sòng" says:
Glorious, excellent fruit,
piled like a bright star.
Southern gold its color,
Suí pearls its form.
Rich in the treasures of Zhījiāng,
praised in the old traditions of Yídū.
The Jīngzhōu Jì says:
Zhījiāng has famous sweet oranges,
Yídū Commandery once had an orange garden,
called Yídū oranges.
Carrying them, one loses the path at Shíchéng,
The Yìyuàn says:
Within the stone city of Guīyì Mountain in Nánkāng, there are oranges, tangerines, pomelos, and citrons.
One may eat the fruit on the spot,
taking as much as one wishes.
But if one tries to take some away,
a great serpent appears,
or one stumbles and loses the path.
Placing them down, one gazes eastward and returns.
The Shùyì Jì says:
In Nánkāng Commandery, there is Dōngwàng Mountain,
on its summit is an orchard,
about four lǐ in circumference,
where all kinds of fruit are planted,
in neat rows,
as if by human effort.
When the oranges ripen,
three men once went there,
ate their fill together,
and also took two with them,
intending to show them to outsiders.
After wandering for half a day,
they became lost and could not return,
when they heard a voice from the air say:
"Release the two oranges, then you may leave."
The one carrying the oranges was terrified,
placed the oranges on the ground,
and in the blink of an eye, the path home appeared.
As for those with flat stems, remarkable indeed,
The Guǎngzhì says:
Some oranges have twenty-one seeds,
there is the Chéngdū flat-stemmed orange,
as large as a shēng.
The yellow rind is extraordinary.
Pān Ānrén's "Shēng Fù" says:
Peel the yellow rind to offer the orange,
pour from the pale porcelain to drink the fine wine.
Zhāng Pán often took them from children,
Xiè Chéng's Hòuhànshū says:
Zhāng Pán, styled Zǐshí,
was the governor of Lújiāng.
The magistrate of Xúnyáng once sent a box of oranges,
his son, seven years old,
took one,
but Pán seized it and gave it to an attendant.
A soldier then privately gave two to the child,
Pán whipped the soldier, saying:
"Why are you bribing my son?"
Sēngzhēn once tasted them in joyful celebration.
The Liángshū says:
Lǚ Sēngzhēn, having achieved great merit,
held a key position of trust,
and was very respectful and cautious.
When on duty in the palace,
even in intense summer heat,
he dared not loosen his clothes.
Each time he attended the imperial seat,
he held his breath and bowed deeply,
never lifting his chopsticks for fruit or food.
Once, after getting drunk, he took an orange to eat,
Emperor Wǔ laughed and said to him:
"You have made great progress today."
In addition to his salary, he was ordered to receive a monthly allowance of one hundred thousand coins.
Plant the "wooden slaves" of Wǔlíng,
The Xiāngyáng Jì says:
Lǐ Héng, styled Shūpíng,
was the governor of Dānyáng.
Héng often wished to manage the household,
but his wife would not listen.
Later, he secretly sent ten men to build a residence on Lóngyáng Isle in Wǔlíng,
planting a thousand orange trees.
On his deathbed, he instructed his son:
"Your mother disliked my managing the household,
hence we are so poor.
In my home region, I have a thousand 'wooden slaves,'
they will not demand food or clothing from you,
but each year yield a bolt of silk,
which will suffice."
When Héng's oranges ripened,
they yielded several thousand bolts of silk annually.
Appoint an official in Lángzhōng to guard them.
A Jìn decree:
Lángzhōng County shall have one official in charge of yellow oranges.
They soothe the thirst of those who long for them,
Zhāng Zǎi's poem says:
Sānbā's yellow oranges,
Guāzhōu's white crabapples.
What the thirsty long for,
inscribed upon sash and belt.
Truly, the essence within the rind.
Guō Pú's "Gān Zàn" says:
Within the rind, oranges and pomelos,
the finest are called sweet.
Zhāng Héng's variety of litchi,
The "Qī Biàn" says:
Litchi and yellow oranges.
Jiǎ Yì's flavor from Xiāngzhōu.
The Xiāngzhōu Jì says:
Within the old great city of the province is Táo Kǎn's temple,
where Jiǎ Yì once planted oranges,
some of which still remain.
In troubled times, they bloom but bear no fruit,
The Tángshū says:
Luófú oranges,
during the Kāiyuán era, were first mountain-planted at Nánlóu Temple.
Later, they were often offered as tribute.
In the years of the emperor's flight to Shǔ and Fèngtiān,
they bore no fruit.
In peaceful times, transplanted, they grow even finer.
The Tángshū says:
During the Tiānbǎo era,
a memorial from the Secretariat reported: "Your servant receives the imperial edict,
hearing that south of the river grows oranges,
north of the river grows trifoliate oranges,
likely because the earth's qi differs,
and the nature of things thus changes.
I have recently planted several orange trees within the palace,
and this autumn they bore one hundred and fifty fruits,
no different from those presented from south of the river and the Shǔ region.
Those plants and trees, devoid of awareness,
how do they flourish and wither with the times!"
Orange
In the month of early winter,
it is then edible.
Held with jade-like hands,
forever adorned with splendor.
Yànzǐ sat in attendance but did not peel it.
The Yànzǐ Chūnqiū states:
Yànzǐ attended the court of Chǔ,
the King of Chǔ offered oranges,
placing a knife beside them,
but Yànzǐ ate them whole without peeling.
The King said:
"Oranges should be peeled."
Yànzǐ replied:
"I have heard that when gifts are presented before a ruler,
melons and peaches are not peeled,
nor are oranges and pomelos peeled.
Now, with no instruction from the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
I dare not peel them.
It is not that I do not know how."
Yán Zūn, when offered a gift, refused to eat it.
See the note on "Yán Zūn differed from his subordinates" in the Lì Fù.
Replacing bitter peaches was already a mistake.
The Chǔ Cí says:
"They cut down oranges and pomelos,
and planted rows of bitter peaches."
Dreaming of yellow-clad men led to further loss.
The Guǎng Wǔxíng Jì states:
Emperor Hòuzhǔ of Chén dreamed of yellow-clad men surrounding the city,
so all the oranges around the city were cut down.
When the Suí army arrived,
everyone, high and low, wore yellow clothing.
As for leaving the warmth of the riverside,
and dwelling in the cold of the northern darkness,
Cáo Zhí's Jú Fù says:
"Planted far across ten thousand miles,
arrayed in the gardens of the Bronze Sparrow Terrace.
Leaving the warmth of the riverside,
dwelling in the clear days of the northern darkness.
Those southern lands, unchanging,
truly find it hard to yield sweet fruit."
Already seen in the note above on "green leaves, white blossoms."
This is indeed what the Bǎiyuè grew weary of.
The Yántiě Lùn states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn pacified Yuè,
turning it into gardens,
and the people all grew weary of oranges and pomelos.
Yet Yáo and Shùn did not eat them often.
The Zhèng Lùn says:
The tribute of oranges and pomelos,
Yáo and Shùn did not regularly taste;
just as the dragon and pheasant patterns,
emperors did not wear as casual attire.
Melon
One can eat over a hundred pieces up to the neck.
The water used for soaking all carries the scent of melons.
There is the insect called the "guardian of the melon,"
as stated in the *Erya*:
"Quán Yúfù guards the melon."
Annotation:
It is the small yellow-armored insect found in melons today.
In sacrifices, there is the principle of offering the upper ring.
The *Book of Rites* says:
"In offering melons, present the upper ring."
Now, admire these lush and abundant ones,
and cherish these continuous and endless ones.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The melons and gourds are lush and abundant."
Also:
"Continuous and endless are the melons and gourds."
They gleam under the morning sun at Qīngmén Gate.
Ruǎn Jí's poem says:
"I once heard of the melons of Dōnglíng,
nearby outside the Qīngmén Gate.
They stretch across the fields, bordering the paths,
with mother and child melons linked together.
Their five colors shine in the morning sun,
and honored guests gather from all sides."
They are washed in the cold spring of the Jade Well.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
Cài Dàn of Wǔyuán
entered the mountains and returned,
deceiving his family by saying:
"I reached Kūnlún,
obtained a jade melon,
and washed it with water from the Jade Well,
after which it softened and became edible."
Sāng Yú cut thorns to aid thieves.
The *Jìn Shū* says:
Sāng Yú was benevolent and virtuous.
His garden was north of his residence,
and when the melons and fruits first ripened,
someone climbed over the wall to steal them.
Yú thought that the garden fence had many thorns and brambles,
and feared the thief might get injured,
so he ordered his servant to clear a path.
When the thief was about to leave with the stolen melons,
he saw the path cleared and smooth,
realized Yú had ordered it cleared,
and returned the stolen melons,
kowtowing to apologize.
Yuánpíng refused water to irrigate his fields.
The *Qí Shū* says:
Guō Yuánpíng made his living by growing melons.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng, there was a great drought,
and the canal no longer allowed boats to pass.
The county magistrate Liú Sēngxiù, pitying his poverty and old age,
released water from the canal for him.
Yuánpíng said:
"Under the vast sky, there is a great drought,
and all the people are suffering.
How can I reduce the water for irrigating fields to allow boats to transport melons!"
So he walked by another route
to Qiántáng to sell his goods.
Praise the elderly Wēng Zhòng who declined gifts.
The *Wú Lù* says:
Yáo Wēng Zhòng once grew melons and vegetables,
tending his garden to support himself.
When people offered him gifts,
he never accepted them.
Admire Shī Yán, who supported himself.
The *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
Shī Yán, styled Jūnzǐ,
was from Pèi.
His family was poor,
and his mother was old.
He often sold his labor to provide for her,
and grew melons to support himself.
As for those renowned as the "Three Mushrooms,"
Jī Hán's "Ode to Sweet Melons" says in its preface:
It is said in the world that among the Three Mushrooms, melons occupy one,
called the "Earth Mushroom."
Their fragrance floats on the Seventh Night.
The *Jīng Chǔ Suì Shí Jì* says:
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
melons and fruits are set out in the courtyard to pray for skill.
If a spider weaves its web on a melon,
it is considered a sign of obtaining skill.
The *Dà Dài Lǐ* marks the season,
as stated in the *Dà Dài Lǐ*:
In the fifth month, melons are tended.
"Tending melons"
refers to the work of cultivating melons.
As for melons,
this is when they are first eaten.
In the eighth month, melons are peeled and stored for the season.
The *Hàn Guān* records the duties.
The *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
The Tàiguān Fruit
Officer, stationed separately outside,
is in charge of melons, vegetables, and edible plants.
On the auspicious day for planting,
in astronomy, there is the Hùguā Star.
It displays patterns in the starry river.
Cuī Shí's *Yuè Lìng* says:
Plant melons on the Wùchén day.
Witness the immortals playing games.
The *Liè Xiān Zhuàn* says:
Fú Lǘ traveled among the shrines along the seashore,
where he saw two immortals gambling with melons in a shrine.
They looked at Lǘ and had him carry several dozen yellow melons,
then told him to close his eyes,
and he ascended to Fāngzhàng Mountain.
Recognize Xú Guāng's illusionary arts.
The *Sōu Shén Jì* says:
During the Wú period, there was Xú Guāng,
who often performed illusionary arts in the markets and neighborhoods.
He asked someone for a melon,
but the owner refused.
So he asked for a slice and planted it.
Soon, the melon grew, spread, and blossomed,
and he picked the fruit to eat it.
He then gave some to the onlookers.
When the seller looked back at what he was selling,
it had all vanished.
Praise the three vines,
as the *Táng Shū* says:
In the summer of the fourth year of Zhēnyuán,
the Right Divine Strategy Army presented an auspicious melon,
with three vines joined into one stem bearing three melons.
Beware of those with two noses.
The *Lóng Yú Hé Tú* says:
Melons with two noses can kill people.
Guarding Kuíqiū without being replaced,
as the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
The Marquis of Qí sent Guǎn Zhìfù to guard Kuíqiū,
and he went at melon season,
saying:
"I will be replaced when the melons come again."
When the guard duty period ended,
no word came from the duke.
He requested to be replaced,
but it was not allowed.
Retiring to Dōnglíng to live in leisure.
The *Shǐ Jì* says:
Shào Píng
was the Marquis of Dōnglíng during the Qín dynasty.
After Qín fell,
he became a commoner,
and being poor,
he grew melons east of Cháng'ān City.
His melons were delicious,
so the world called them "Dōnglíng melons."
Then there are those yellow like golden boxes,
as Fù Xuán's "Ode to Melons" says:
White ones are like plain silk,
black ones like lacquer,
yellow surpassing golden boxes,
green matching emerald hues.
Sweetness surpassing honeycombs,
as Liú Zhēn's "Ode to Melons" says:
Sweet as honeycombs,
cooler than ice tablets.
Rich inside and splendid outside,
as Zhāng Zǎi's "Ode to Melons" says:
Some are dark on the outside and red inside,
displaying purity and containing redness,
with plump skin and splendid exterior,
and green flesh rich inside.
Few segments, much flesh.
Fù Xuán's "Ode to Melons" says:
Fine texture and dense grain,
much flesh and few segments,
exceptionally rich and delicious,
eating them does not cloy.
Flies gathering in the hall,
Táng Wǔ Rúhéng,
styled Tíngshuò,
was a younger cousin of Yuánhéng.
He served as a Secretary in the Secretariat,
while Yuán Zhěn, a Director in the Ministry of Provisions, was in charge of drafting edicts.
Yuán Zhěn advanced through the eunuch Wèi Hóngjiǎn,
obtaining the drafting position without going through the prime minister,
which was despised by public opinion at the time.
During a gathering in the official hall,
a blue fly landed on a melon.
Rúhéng suddenly angrily swatted it away,
saying:
"Where did you just come from,
to gather here?"
Everyone present was stunned.
Foxes hiding beyond the frontier.
The *Sòng Shū* says:
Dù Yù stated:
Guāzhōu
is named for producing large melons.
It is also said to produce fine melons,
hence the name.
As for the large melons,
a fox can enter one,
with its head and tail unseen.
As for calming Zhèng Zhuó's heart,
the *Liáng Shū* says:
Zhèng Zhuó, styled Màozhāo,
He was determined and fond of learning,
often suffering from heart heat due to excessive worry.
When it was the melon season,
he would lie down,
placing a melon on his chest to cool his heart,
then rise and read aloud.
Such was his dedication to his studies.
There is also the complexion of Gāo Yáo.
The "Sūn Qīngzǐ" says:
Gāo Yáo's complexion was like a peeled melon.
Chǔ Yǎ planted them and gave them to others.
The "Dàoxué Zhuàn" says:
Chǔ Yǎ, styled Xuántōng,
lived with others,
often fetching water to sprinkle and sweep,
and in the summer months, he would plant melons,
allowing people to come and take them freely.
Zǐ Liáng provided them to entertain guests.
The "Qí Shū" says:
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng
was skilled at hosting elegant gatherings.
When guests visited in the summer months,
he would serve melon drinks.
There were also offerings for sacrifices in autumn and summer.
Lú Chén's "Jì Fǎ" says:
Summer sacrifices and autumn offerings both used melons.
Different names are given to dié and bó.
The "Ěryǎ" says:
Dié and bó,
their continuation is dié.
Note:
It is commonly called bó guā as dié shào;
the melon vine also bears fruit,
but it is small like a bó.
The divine seed was once seen at Dòng Tái.
The "Huángtíng Nèijīng Zhù" says:
Below Dà Huò Shān, there is Dòng Tái,
the residence of the Lord of Fate.
Within it, there are divine melons;
eating them opens the heart to the profound mysteries.
The crimson fruit was also heard of at Nányuè.
See the note on "xuán yún zài yù" in the "Nài Fù."
I admire Wáng Pí's pure frugality.
The "Hòu Zhōu Shū" says:
Wáng Pí was frugal and straightforward by nature.
Once, a guest was eating melons with Pí,
and the guest peeled the melon, leaving the skin a bit too thick.
Pí was displeased by this.
When the melon skin fell to the ground,
he reached down to the ground,
picked it up, and ate it.
The guest was deeply ashamed.
I lament Shì'ān's lack of learning.
The "Jìn Shū" says:
Huángfǔ Mì was twenty years old,
yet he did not study,
wandering and indulging without restraint.
Whenever he obtained melons or fruits,
he would offer them to his aunt, Rén Shì.
Rén Shì said:
"The 'Xiàojīng' says:
'Even with the nourishment of three sacrificial animals,
one may still be unfilial.'
You are now over twenty years old,
your eyes do not seek instruction,
your heart does not enter the Way,
and you have nothing to comfort me."
She then sighed and wept.
Mì was deeply moved,
changed his ways, and diligently pursued learning.
I have also heard of the forms of the fox-head and woman's-arm melons.
The "Guǎngzhì" says:
There are fox-head melons,
and woman's-arm melons.
There are also names like sheep-shank and tiger-palm melons.
Zhāng Zài's "Guā Fù" says:
Sheep-shank, tiger-palm, cassia-branch, and dense-tube melons.
Bù Zhì worked diligently with his four limbs during the day.
The "Wú Lù" says:
Bù Zhì and Wèi Jīng were friends of the same age,
both supporting themselves by growing melons.
They worked diligently with their four limbs during the day,
and studied the classics at night.
Sòng Jiù irrigated at night at the neighboring pavilion.
Jiǎ Yì's "Xīn Shū" says:
The Liáng official Sòng Jiù served as the magistrate of a border county,
adjacent to Chǔ.
Both pavilions grew melons.
The people of Liáng worked hard and irrigated frequently,
so their melons were excellent;
the people of Chǔ were lazy and irrigated rarely,
so their melons were poor.
The Chǔ magistrate, jealous of the fine melons of Liáng,
secretly damaged them at night,
causing the Liáng melons to wither.
The Liáng pavilion requested its captain
to retaliate by damaging the Chǔ melons,
but Sòng Jiù said:
"This is the way to create enmity and share misfortune."
He ordered people to secretly irrigate the Chǔ melons at night.
When the Chǔ pavilion went in the morning,
the melons had already been irrigated,
and they grew better each day.
Upon investigation,
they found it was the work of the Liáng pavilion.
The Chǔ magistrate was greatly pleased,
reported it to the King of Chǔ,
who was delighted by Liáng's secret concession,
sent heavy gifts in apology,
and formed an alliance with the King of Liáng.
Jiāo Huá was moved by the wonder of the yellow-capped man.
The "Xiàozǐ Zhuàn" says:
Jiāo Huá's father, Wèi, was gravely ill,
and in winter, he longed for melon.
Huá dreamed of a man in a yellow cap,
who said to him:
"I heard your father is ill and longs for melon,
so I bring this to aid his nourishment."
Huá bowed and received it.
Upon waking,
it was in his hand,
extraordinarily fragrant.
His father ate it and recovered from his illness.
Shǐ Léng recorded the omen of the cool palace.
The "Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū" says:
Shǐ Léng, the governor of Tiānshuǐ in Liáng, died suddenly from illness,
but revived after five days,
saying:
"I saw white melons growing all over the Liángguāng Palace."
Later, when the Qín official Liáng Xī destroyed Liáng,
his childhood name was Bái Guā.
I have also heard of repaying with bolts of silk.
The "Liáng Shū" says:
Guō Zǔshēn was pure and frugal,
often wearing old coarse clothes,
using plain wooden tables,
and eating no more than one meat dish.
An old woman once gave him early green melons,
and Zǔshēn repaid her with a bolt of silk.
Wealthy people imitated him with goods and profits.
Zǔshēn flogged them and made an example before the public,
and both court and commoners feared him.
The Weaver Girl presides over them.
The "Xù Hàn Shū" says:
The Herd Boy presides over passes and bridges,
and the Weaver Girl presides over fruits and melons.
Gě Xuán served fresh melons to guests in deep winter.
The "Shénxiān Zhuàn" says:
Gě Xuán served fresh melons to guests in winter.
Sòng Qióng gave melons to his mother in late autumn.
The "Běi Shǐ" says:
Sòng Qióng, styled Pǔxián,
was known for his filial piety.
When his mother was ill,
she once longed for melons in late autumn.
Qióng dreamed of seeing them,
sought them, and indeed found them,
which people of the time found extraordinary.
Yáng Yīn was ridiculed for his speech and appearance.
The "Hòu Wèi Shū" says:
Yáng Yīn oversaw the selection of officials,
often choosing people based on their speech and appearance.
A satirical verse of the time said:
"The Minister selects officials,
like a poor man buying melons,
only picking the big ones."
Hán Língzhēn was moved by the divine wonder morning and evening.
Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Jì" says:
Hán Língzhēn was extremely filial.
When his mother died,
his family was too poor to bury her.
He planted half an acre of melons;
he picked them in the morning,
and by evening, they had grown back,
never diminishing.
The funeral was thus able to be held.
Some fled far away out of fear of death.
The "Gǔwén Suǒyǔ" says:
Initially, Xíng Shǐ Zǐchén said to Duke Jǐng of Sòng:
"From now on, in five sacrifices and five days,
I will die;
after five years, on the fifth month, day Dīnghài,
Wú will perish;
after another five sacrifices, on the eighth month, day Xīnsì,
you, my lord, will pass away."
Xíng Shǐ Zǐchén, on the day of his death,
appeared before Duke Jǐng in the morning,
and died by evening.
Later, Wú perished.
Duke Jǐng was terrified,
remembering Xíng Shǐ Zǐchén's words.
As the day of his death approached,
he fled to the melon garden,
and died there.
He sought and found the insect of himself.
Some were angered by cutting the roots.
The "Jiāyǔ" says:
Zēngzǐ was weeding melons and accidentally cut their roots.
Zēng Xī was enraged,
and struck his back with a large staff.
Zēngzǐ collapsed to the ground,
and after a while, he regained consciousness.
Confucius heard of this,
and told his disciples:
"When Shēn comes, do not let him in."
Zēngzǐ sent someone to ask Confucius,
and Confucius said:
"When Shùn served Gǔsǒu,
if it was a small rod, he would wait,
if it was a big staff, he would flee.
Shēn offered himself to await violent anger,
if he had died,
he would have trapped his father in unrighteousness,
what could be more unfilial than this?"
Not eating, he sighed at Zhòngní,
as recorded in the *Analects*.
To quench thirst, he once shared with Qí Wǔ.
The *Book of Qí* says:
Emperor Wǔ and Dào Huī once followed Sòng Míng to shoot pheasants in the countryside,
thirsty and tired,
Huī obtained a green melon,
and shared it with the emperor, cutting it in half to eat.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he promoted Huī three times to the positions of Minister of Education and Left Chief of the Imperial Secretariat,
recalling the old times.
Great is the sweet delicacy of Dōngyě,
Fù Xuán's *Ode to Melons* says:
Nurtured by human effort,
cultivated by the six qi,
though the sweetness of the fox-head melon is delightful,
it is not as marvelous as the greatness of Dōngyě.
What harm is there in the bitter stem?
An ancient poem says:
Sweet melons embrace bitter stems,
beautiful dates grow thorny branches.
Beside the thorns, there are knives,
greedy people still harm themselves.
Dragon
The dragon is the essence of divine spirits,
as the Ruì Yìng Tú states:
The yellow dragon
is the essence of divine spirits,
the foremost of the four numinous creatures.
It can be hidden or manifest.
The Shuō Wén says:
The dragon,
the foremost of scaled creatures,
can be hidden or manifest,
can be small or large,
can be short or long,
ascends to heaven at the spring equinox,
and enters the abyss at the autumn equinox.
Its blood is sometimes dark and yellow,
as the Yì states:
Dragons battle in the wild,
their blood dark and yellow.
Its form is sometimes like a silkworm or caterpillar.
The Guǎn Zǐ says:
The dragon, adorned with five colors, roams;
thus, when the spirit wishes to be small, it is like a silkworm or caterpillar;
when it wishes to be large, it encompasses heaven and earth;
when it wishes to ascend, it soars through the clouds;
when it wishes to sink, it hides in springs.
Swords transformed at Yánjīn,
see the annotation in "Sword Rhapsody": "Léi Huàn obtained the precious sword from Fēngchéng."
Saliva stored in the Xià court.
The Shǐ Jì states:
During the decline of the Xià dynasty,
two divine dragons descended at the court of the Xià emperor and said:
"We
are the two rulers of Bāo."
The Xià emperor divined whether to kill them, drive them away, or keep them,
but none was auspicious.
He requested their saliva and stored it,
which was auspicious.
Thus, he laid out offerings and prayed to them,
and the dragons departed, leaving their saliva in a box.
When the Xià perished,
this vessel was passed to the Yīn.
When the Yīn perished,
it was passed to the Zhōu.
None dared to open it.
When King Lì opened it to look,
the saliva flowed into the court.
The king ordered women to strip and shout at it.
The saliva transformed into a dark turtle,
and a young girl from the rear palace, having just lost her baby teeth, encountered it.
She became pregnant without a husband and gave birth,
then, in fear, abandoned the child.
During King Xuān's time,
a ballad said: "Mulberry bows and quivers of arrowweed
will truly destroy the Zhōu state."
A couple selling these items
were seized by the king's men.
They fled on the road,
saw the demon child,
took her in,
and fled to Bāo.
A man of Bāo, having committed a crime,
presented the abandoned girl to the king to redeem himself.
This was Bāo Sì,
whom King Yōu loved,
ultimately leading to the fall of Zhōu.
Zhāng Huá once discerned it in a gift of pickled fish,
as the Jìn Shū states:
Lù Jī once gave Zhāng Huá pickled fish as a gift.
At the time, guests filled the seats.
Huá opened the container
and immediately said:
"This is dragon meat."
The crowd did not believe him.
Huá said:
"Try washing it with bitter wine,
and something unusual will surely happen."
Soon, a five-colored light arose.
Jī later asked the fish supplier,
who indeed said:
"Under a pile of thatch in the garden, I found a white fish
with an extraordinary appearance.
I made it into pickled fish,
and it was exceptionally delicious,
so I offered it to you."
Emperor Hé also heard of it through a gift of soup.
The Shù Yì Jì states:
In the first year of the Zhānghé era of the Hàn dynasty, during heavy rain,
a blue dragon fell into the palace.
The emperor ordered it cooked,
and gave each minister a cup of dragon soup.
Thus, Lǐ Yóu's "Seven Commands" says:
"Flavors combined with dragon soup."
Congratulated Lǚ Guāng at Qiūcí,
as the Jìn Shū states:
Lǚ Guāng attacked Qiūcí.
One night outside the southern camp, there was a black object,
like a broken bank,
swaying with head and horns,
its eyes shining like lightning.
By dawn, it had vanished.
At the spot, traces of scales were faintly visible on the ground.
Guāng sighed and said:
"It is a black dragon."
Dù Jìn said:
"The dragon is an image of the great man's beneficial appearance.
General, exert yourself
to achieve great celebration."
Guāng showed a pleased expression.
Carried Wú Měng at Gōngtíng,
as the Yùzhāng Jì states:
Wú Měng, implicated in Guō Pú's affair, was arrested.
He boarded a boat heading south,
instructing the boatman not to open the door.
The boatman heard sounds like tree branches under the boat,
peeked to see,
and saw two dragons carrying the boat.
In one night, they reached Gōngtíng Lake.
Known as the Rain Master,
as the Bào Pǔ Zǐ states:
In the mountains on chén days,
those called Rain Masters
are dragons.
Also called aquatic creatures.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
The dragon
is an aquatic creature.
Since water officials were abandoned,
dragons are not captured alive.
Sinking wood gave birth at Āiláo,
as the Hòu Hàn Shū states:
The Āiláo barbarians:
Their ancestor, a woman fishing in the water,
touched sinking wood and became pregnant,
giving birth to ten sons.
The sinking wood transformed into a dragon,
emerging from the water.
Nine sons fled in fright,
but one did not leave.
He sat with his back to the dragon,
and the dragon licked him.
Later, the other sons made him the lord of Āiláo.
Floating water was also heard of with Sù Fú.
The Jìn Shū states:
Féng Bá's younger brother Sù Fú, along with his cousin Wàn Ní and other youths, was playing by the water's edge
when a golden dragon floated up from the water.
Sù Fú asked Wàn Ní:
"Do you see anything?"
Wàn Ní and the others all said:
"We see nothing."
Then he took the dragon and showed it to them,
and all considered it an extraordinary auspicious sign.
Thus, nine-colored dragons pulled the Queen Mother's chariot,
as the Hàn Wǔ Nèi Zhuàn states:
The Queen Mother rode a purple cloud carriage,
pulled by nine-colored striped dragons.
Five-colored dragons bore Emperor Shùn's chart,
as the Hé Tú states:
When Shùn ascended the throne as Grand Commandant,
he and the Three Dukes observed the river.
A yellow dragon with five colors
bore a chart forth,
placing it before Shùn.
It had a yellow jade case,
white jade cover,
golden cords,
yellow mushroom mud,
inscribed: "Huángdì's seal."
Stranded at Héjīn, exposing its gills,
as the Sān Qín Jì states:
Héjīn is also called Lóngmén.
Traces of the Giant Spirit remain,
nine hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān,
with hanging waters below.
Note:
Turtles, fish, and the like cannot stop the river and sea.
Large fish gather below the gate by the thousands but cannot ascend;
those that ascend become dragons.
Thus it is said:
"Exposing gills at Lóngmén,
hanging ears under the carriage shaft."
Descended at Jīngshān, hanging its beard.
See the annotation in "Dǐng Rhapsody": "Casting at Jīngshān."
Praise Dǒng Fù for taming them,
as the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Cài Mò replied to Duke Xiàn of Wèi:
"In ancient times, dragons were kept,
so there were the Dragon-Keepers and Dragon-Drivers.
Long ago, Liào Shū'ān had a descendant named Dǒng Fù,
who truly loved dragons,
could seek their desires and feed them accordingly.
Many dragons came to him,
and he tamed and kept them,
serving Emperor Shùn.
The emperor granted him the surname Dǒng,
and the clan name Huànlóng.
Thus, the house of Emperor Shùn had dragon-keepers for generations."
Mock Zhū Pēng for learning to slaughter them.
The Zhuāng Zǐ states:
Zhū Pēngmàn learned to slaughter dragons from Zhīlí Yì,
exhausting his family's wealth of a thousand gold.
After three years of training, he became skilled,
yet his craft found no use.
He lingered in Huán Wēn’s studio—
the *Jìn Shū* says:
Initially,
Huán Wēn built a studio in Nánzhōu,
covering it entirely with paintings of dragons,
and named it the “Coiling Dragon Studio.”
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
Liú Yì campaigned against Xuán,
and Xuán died in the studio,
after which Yì occupied it.
Yì’s childhood name was Pánlóng (Coiling Dragon).
He dwelt in the thatched hut of Nányáng.
The *Sānguó Zhì* says:
Xú Shù said to the Former Sovereign:
“Zhūgě Kǒngmíng
is a reclining dragon.”
Also, in Liàng’s “Memorial on Sending Out the Troops,” it says:
“Your subject plowed the fields in Nányáng,
and the Late Emperor thrice visited your subject in his thatched hut.”
Then there was the appearance at Jiàngjiāo—
the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
A dragon appeared at Jiàngjiāo.
Xiànzǐ asked Cài Mò:
“I have heard that
among creatures, none is wiser than the dragon,
because it cannot be captured alive;
they call it wise—
is this true?”
He replied:
“It is actually humans who are not wise,
not that the dragon is truly wise.”
Prayers were offered at Fǔkǒu—
the *Jìn Shū* says:
During Shí Hǔ’s time,
from the first month until the sixth month, there was no rain.
Fótú Chéng went to the Fǔkǒu shrine,
kowtowed and exposed himself to the sun,
and that very day two white dragons descended at the shrine,
whereupon rain fell across a thousand *lǐ*.
It bore boats for Xià Yǔ—
see the annotation “Yellow Dragon Moved Yǔ” in the “Rhapsody on Boats.”
It raised its head to aid the Suí army—
the *Chén Shū* says:
When the Suí army crossed the river,
after Jīngzhōu’s Lǚ Sù was defeated,
a separate commander, Liào Shìchǒng, led a large vessel pretending to surrender,
intending to burn the Suí warships
and fight a decisive battle to the death.
At that time, five yellow dragons, each over ten *zhàng* long,
raised their heads in succession,
and flowed eastward with the current.
Great winds and waves arose,
clouds and mist darkened the sky,
and the Chén troops were terrified.
Unaware, they set themselves on fire.
As for Chéngguāng driving them in the Southern Sea—
the *Bówù Zhì* says:
When the virtue of Xià was at its peak,
two dragons descended.
Yǔ had Fàn Chéngguāng drive them
to travel beyond the borders.
After completing the circuit, they returned to the Southern Sea.
Passing by Fángfēng,
two ministers of Fángfēng, because of the execution at Túshān,
saw Yǔ’s envoy,
became angry and shot at them.
There was sudden thunder, wind, and rain,
and the two dragons ascended and left.
The two ministers, terrified,
pierced their own hearts with blades and died.
Yǔ pitied them,
pulled out the blades, and treated them with herbs of immortality,
thus creating the people with pierced chests.
There was a ballad about Fú Shēng east of Luò—
the *Jìn Shū* says:
At the beginning of Fú Shēng’s reign,
a ballad in Cháng’ān said:
“The great fish of the Eastern Sea transforms into a dragon;
men become kings, women become lords.
Ask where it is—east of Luò City.”
At that time, Fú Jiān was the Dragon-Soaring General,
and his residence was east of Luòmén.
Later, it indeed came true.
A warning about danger under the chin—
the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
By the river, there was a poor family that relied on weaving reeds for a living.
Their son dove into the deep,
obtained a pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold,
and brought it back to his father.
The father said:
“Bring a stone to smash it!
A pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold
must lie in the ninefold depths of the abyss,
under the chin of the Black Dragon.
That you could obtain the pearl
must mean you encountered it while it slept.
If the Black Dragon had awakened,
what would have been left of you!”
Praise for borrowing reputation among men—
the *Jìn Shū* says:
Sòng Xiān, styled Lìng’ài,
had lofty principles
and lived in seclusion on the Southern Mountain of Jiǔquán.
The governor, Mǎ Jí, visited him,
but Xiān refused to see him.
Jí sighed and said:
“His name can be heard, but his person cannot be seen;
his virtue can be admired, but his form cannot be glimpsed.
I know the master is a dragon among men.”
Some shed their horns to show auspiciousness—
Cuī Hóng’s *Qián Yān Lù* says:
A black dragon and a white dragon appeared at Lóngshān.
Mùróng Huàng personally led his officials to observe the dragons.
Staying over two hundred paces away,
they offered a grand sacrifice,
and the two dragons frolicked, shed their horns, and left.
Huàng named his new palace the Hé Lóng Palace (Harmonious Dragon Palace).
Some dragged their tails to foretell misfortune—
the *Sòng Shū* says:
Xú Xiànzhī once passed through the mountains
and saw a black dragon over ten *zhàng* long,
with a head bearing horns,
its front two legs fully formed,
but no hind legs,
dragging its tail as it moved.
Later, when Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
Xiànzhī ultimately met a violent end.
They rely on five-colored flowers for food—
the *Kuòdì Tú* says:
At Lóngchí Mountain,
high on all four sides,
there is a pool in the center,
seven hundred *lǐ* square,
where many dragons dwell.
There are many five-colored flower trees,
which the dragons eat.
It is four thousand *lǐ* from Kuàijī.
They gather four snakes to follow them—
the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
When Jìn Wén returned to his state,
Jièzǐ Tuī refused to accept a reward
and composed a poem himself:
“There was a dragon in flight,
circling all under heaven.
Five snakes followed it,
serving as its support.
The dragon returned to its homeland,
and found its proper place.
Four snakes followed it,
and received its dew and rain.
One snake was ashamed,
and died in the wilds.”
He posted the poem on the palace gate
and hid beneath the mountain.
Wéngōng heard of it and said:
“Alas!
This must be Jièzǐ Tuī.”
Hánzǐ feared the danger of the reverse scales—
the *Hánzǐ* says:
The dragon, as a creature, can be tamed and ridden;
yet under its throat are reverse scales a foot across.
If you touch them, it will surely kill you.
A ruler also has them.
If a persuader can avoid touching the ruler’s reverse scales,
he is close to success.
Mò Dí avoided slaughter due to his black color—
the *Mòzǐ* says:
Mòzǐ went north to Qí
and met a diviner.
The diviner said:
“The Emperor will today slaughter a black dragon in the north.
Your complexion is black,
so you should not go north.”
Mòzǐ did not listen,
went north to the Zī River,
but failed to cross and returned.
They ranked Huà Xīn as the head—
the *Wèi Zhì* says:
Huà Xīn, Bǐng Yuán, and Guǎn Níng were three friends,
called “one dragon.”
Xīn was the head,
Yuán the belly,
and Níng the tail.
They startled Yègōng, causing him to lose his spirit—
the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Yègōng Zǐgāo loved dragons so much
that the carvings and patterns throughout his house all depicted dragons.
Then a heavenly dragon heard of it and descended,
peeking its head through the window
and dragging its tail in the hall.
When Yègōng saw it,
he lost his spirit.
Thus, Yègōng did not truly love dragons;
he loved what resembled dragons but was not real.
When hidden, it is not to be used—
the *Yì* says:
The hidden dragon: do not use it.
The yang is below.
When it appears, it rides the moment,
as the Book of Changes says:
"The dragon appears in the field;
it is beneficial to see the great man."
It rides the six dragons at the proper time
to drive across the heavens.
Its scales formed characters,
as the River Chart says:
A yellow dragon emerged from the Luò River,
approached Yú Shùn,
and the characters on its scales and armor were complete.
Shùn ordered them to be copied,
and when the copying was finished,
the dragon departed.
Its fat was also used as lamp oil.
As the Records of Omissions says:
On Fāngzhàng Mountain,
also known as Luánzhì Mountain,
to the east there is a dragon ground,
a thousand li square.
There was a dragon
whose skin and bones formed mountains and hills,
and whose fat and blood flowed like water.
During the time of King Zhāo of Yān, dragon fat was used as lamp oil,
clear and pure as water,
its flames glowing in five colors.
Hū Zǐxiān rode it and ascended lightly,
as the Biographies of Immortals says:
There was one called Hū Zǐxiān,
a diviner in Hànzhōng,
who lived over a hundred years.
Before departing, he called to the old woman who ran a tavern:
"Prepare quickly,
I shall go with you."
That night, an immortal arrived holding two straw dogs and called for Zǐxiān.
Zǐxiān took one and gave it to the old woman,
and they turned out to be dragons.
They rode them up to Huáyīn Mountain.
Later, he often shouted from the mountain:
"Zǐxiān and the tavern matron are here!"
Ān Gōng rode one and ascended.
See the note in "Rhapsody on Fire" for "scattering Táo Ān's smelting."
And then there is ascending to the dark clouds,
as the Huainanzi says:
When Bó Yǔ dug wells, dragons ascended to the dark clouds,
for wisdom increased while virtue diminished.
They are born in accumulated waters,
as Master Xún says:
When earth accumulates to form mountains,
wind and rain arise there;
when water accumulates to form rivers,
jiāo dragons are born there.
A black one was seen at Wèi River,
as the Records of the Three Qín says:
Lóngshǒu Mountain is sixty li long,
its head entering the Wèi River,
its tail reaching Fán River.
It is said that in ancient times, a black dragon
emerged from the south of the mountain
to drink from the Wèi.
The path it traveled formed an earthen mountain,
hence the name.
A yellow one was reported at Chéngjì.
The Book of Han says:
In the early Hàn dynasty,
Zhāng Cāng held that Hàn possessed the virtue of water.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
Gōngsūn Chén argued that Hàn possessed the virtue of earth,
and a yellow dragon should appear.
In the fifteenth year,
a yellow dragon appeared at Chéngjì.
The emperor issued an edict summoning Chén to be an erudite.
The eight refers to the Xún family,
as the Book of the Later Han says:
Xún Shù had eight sons:
Jiǎn, Gǔn, Jìng, Shòu, Wāng, Shuǎng, Sù, and Zhuān.
People of the time called them the "Eight Dragons."
The six refers to the Biàn family.
The Book of Jin says:
The Biàn family had six dragons,
among whom Xuánrén was matchless.
Xuánrén
was the courtesy name of Cuì.
Liú Lěi served Kǒng Jiǎ,
as recorded in the Zuozhuan:
During Emperor Shùn's time, there were dragon breeders.
By the time of Kǒng Jiǎ of the Xià dynasty,
the emperor bestowed upon him riding dragons,
two from the Hé River and two from the Hàn River,
each pair male and female.
Liú Lěi learned to tame dragons from the dragon breeders
and served Kǒng Jiǎ,
able to feed them.
The Xià sovereign praised him,
granting him the clan name "Yùlóng" (Dragon Driver).
He replaced the descendants of Shǐwéi.
When one female dragon died,
he made it into paste and fed it to the Xià sovereign.
The Xià sovereign enjoyed it,
but later demanded more.
Fearing punishment, Liú Lěi fled to Lǔ County.
Zhòngní could not fathom Lǎozi.
As the Zhuangzi says:
When Confucius met Lǎo Dān,
he returned
and did not speak for three days.
His disciples asked him why,
and Confucius said:
"Now I have seen a dragon.
The dragon coalesces to form a body,
scatters to become patterns,
rides upon the clouds and mists,
and is nourished by yīn and yáng."
There are also those that rise to heaven upon the clear wind,
as the Comprehensive Hexagram Divinations of the Changes says:
At the beginning of summer,
the clear wind arrives and dragons ascend to heaven.
They gaze upon layered clouds and leap into the abyss.
As the Huainanzi says:
When a tiger roars, the valley wind arrives;
when a dragon rises, the auspicious clouds gather.
The Book of Changes says:
"Or leaping in the abyss."
His countenance was called Gāozǔ's,
as the Records of the Grand Historian says:
Hàn Gāozǔ had a prominent nose and a dragon countenance.
Note:
Countenance
refers to the forehead and brow.
His drunken state startled Chén Xuān.
As the Book of Chén says:
When Emperor Xuān was first in Jiānglíng,
the army commander Lǐ Zǒng was an old acquaintance of the emperor.
Once the emperor was drunk at night,
and fell asleep with the lamp lit.
Zǒng happened to go out,
but soon returned
and saw that the emperor was a great dragon.
He fled in fright to another room.
Again, it is heard that in the palace ponds they are kept as domestic animals,
as the Rites says:
When turtles and dragons are in the palace ponds,
and dragons are kept as domestic animals,
then fish and sturgeons do not flee.
Note:
Fleeing
means hiding away.
They are associated with gold and jade, manifesting auspicious signs.
As the Rites Containing Cultural Elegance says:
Dragon horses, gold, and jade
are auspicious signs for emperors and kings.
Poisoning fish can sometimes bring rain,
as the Records of Strange Things from the Southern Provinces says:
In the Dān Abyss of Jiāozhōu, there is a divine dragon.
Whenever there is a drought,
the local people place ruì grass in the upper stream of the abyss,
causing many fish to die.
The dragon becomes angry,
and immediately heavy rain falls.
To attack bandits, one must wait for the dragon to sleep.
As the Book of Liáng says:
When Lù Fǎhé resisted Rèn Yuē,
they reached Ānnán and entered Chìtíng Lake.
Fǎhé rode a light boat,
unarmored,
and sailed down the stream.
He went to within one li of Yuē's army before turning back.
He said to his officers and soldiers:
"Their dragon is asleep and unmoving,
while our army's dragon is quite vigorous.
If we wait until tomorrow to attack,
we can defeat the bandits without harming our guests."
As for when it emerged from the armory and Liú Yì did not congratulate,
see the note in "Rhapsody on the Well" for "heard in the Jìn era of the dragon's appearance."
When it appeared at Línpíng, Wúliàng did not watch,
as the Book of Táng says:
Chǔ Wúliàng was orphaned and poor in his youth.
He lived near Línpíng Lake.
Once, dragons fought in the lake,
and the entire neighborhood went to watch.
Wúliàng was thirteen at the time,
and continued reading calmly without moving.
Later, he mastered the Three Rites and the Records of the Grand Historian.
Zhāng Jùn, disliking it, cast a copper dragon,
as the Records of the Western River says:
Zhāng Jùn built the Qiānguāng Hall.
After its completion,
five dragons appeared in the pond during the day,
remaining for a while before vanishing,
and the water turned green.
Jùn then cast a copper dragon to suppress them,
but Jùn ultimately did not prevail over this hall.
Tàihào used them to mark offices.
As the Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
Tàihào Páoxīshì,
whose surname was Fēng,
had the auspicious sign of a brilliant dragon,
so he used dragons to mark offices.
Again, it is heard that they are born in great marshes,
see the note in "Rhapsody on the Snake" for "produced in deep mountains by Shū Hǔ."
The rising of auspicious clouds,
as seen in the Commentary says:
When the striped tiger roars, valley winds arise;
when the responding dragon chants, auspicious clouds gather.
Some leap forth from the land,
as the Yīnfú Jīng says:
When heaven unleashes its killing mechanism,
dragons and snakes rise from the land.
Others hibernate to preserve themselves.
The Yì Jīng says:
The hibernation of dragons and snakes
is to preserve themselves.
There is also Zǐmíng who was released,
as the Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Língyáng Zǐmíng enjoyed fishing,
and once caught a white dragon.
Zǐmíng removed the hook,
bowed in thanks, and released it.
Decades later, he caught a white fish,
inside whose belly was a text.
It taught Zǐmíng to take certain herbs,
so he ascended Huángshān to gather five mineral pastes and stone lungs to ingest.
After three years,
the white dragon came to welcome him,
and he dwelled on Língyáng Mountain for over a century.
Féng Sūn was raised.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Qílóng Míng found dragon offspring in a pond,
resembling geckos,
over ten of them.
He built a thatched hut to guard and raise them.
When the dragons grew large,
they gradually departed.
Later, one day,
Qílóng said:
"I am the grandson of Féng Bóchāng.
All people within a hundred lǐ of this place will die."
By the eighth month, when the waters rose,
the dead numbered in the tens of thousands.
Since it is a constellation of the east,
the Xīng Jīng says:
The seven eastern constellations form the Azure Dragon.
It is also called the chief of scaled creatures.
The Jiāyǔ says:
There are three hundred sixty scaled creatures,
and the dragon is their chief.
In Léizé, Táo Kǎn obtained a shuttle,
as the Yì Yuàn says:
Táo Kǎn once fished in Léizé,
and found a weaving shuttle,
which he hung on the wall upon returning.
After a while,
during a thunderstorm,
the shuttle transformed into a red dragon,
which leaped from the house and flew away.
In Gěbēi, Fèi Chángfáng threw his staff.
See the note on "threw into Gěbēi and swiftly transformed" in the "Staff Rhapsody."
Transforming into a fish, it was endangered in Qīnglíng,
as the Shuō Yuàn says:
The King of Wú wished to drink with the common people.
Wǔ Zǐxū admonished:
"It is not permissible.
In the past, a white dragon descended into the Qīnglíng Abyss,
transformed into a fish,
and the fisherman Yùqiě shot it in the eye.
The white dragon appealed to the Celestial Emperor,
who said:
'At that time,
what form had you taken?'
The white dragon replied:
'I descended into the Qīnglíng Abyss,
transformed into a fish.'
The Celestial Emperor said:
'Fish are what men shoot;
what crime has Yùqiě committed?'
That white dragon
is a prized creature of the Celestial Emperor;
Yùqiě
is a lowly subject of the state of Sòng.
Had the white dragon not transformed,
Yùqiě would not have shot it.
Now, abandoning the position of a ruler of ten thousand chariots
to drink with commoners,
I fear there may be the peril of Yùqiě."
The king then desisted.
As a monster, it was once paired with Wǎngxiàng.
The Guóyǔ says:
The water monster is called the dragon Wǎngxiàng.
Carving heard of Zōu Shì,
as the Shǐ Jì says:
Yǎn discourses on heaven,
Shì carves dragons,
Kūn roasts the axle grease pot.
Yǎn is Zōu Yǎn.
Shì is Zōu Shì.
Kūn is Chúnyú Kūn.
Displaying beauty, Jī Kāng.
The Jìn Shū says:
Though Jī Kāng's form was like earth and wood,
he had the markings of a dragon and the grace of a phoenix,
a natural heavenly quality.
Some, when soaked, revived,
as the Bié Zhuàn of Fótú Chéng says:
During Shí Lè's time, there was a drought.
At Shíjǐng Gāng, a dead dragon was dug up,
over a chǐ long.
Soaked with water,
after a long while, it revived.
Chanted over and sacrificed to,
the dragon soared into the sky,
and immediately heavy rain fell.
Hence, Shíjǐng was named Lónggāng.
Others, when blown upon, then grew.
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
Western magicians skilled in divine incantations would stand by a deep pool,
perform Yǔ steps and blow breath,
and a dragon would emerge afloat.
When first emerging, it was over ten zhàng long.
Then the magician would blow again;
with each blow, the dragon would shrink,
until only a few cùn long.
The magician would then pick it up and place it in a pot.
Sometimes there were four or five dragons,
kept with a little water,
the pot mouth sealed.
When the magician heard of a place with drought,
he would take the dragon there to sell it,
one dragon worth several tens of jīn of gold.
The whole state would gather funds to hire him.
Once payment was complete,
he would open the pot and release one dragon into a deep pool.
Then, performing Yǔ steps and blowing again,
with each blow, one would emerge,
growing to several tens of zhàng long.
In a moment, clouds and rain would gather from all directions.
Displaying divine transformations in three pools,
the Hòu Wèi Shū says:
In Bōzhìguó, there are three pools.
Tradition says the large pool has a dragon king,
the next a dragon wife,
the smallest dragon offspring.
People must offer sacrifices to pass,
otherwise they often encounter wind and thunder.
Adorned with patterns and colors of the five directions,
the Táng Shū says:
During the Dàhé era of Emperor Wénzōng,
five dragons gathered in Mìzhōu,
arriving in sequence,
the colors of the five directions all present.
Not to be harmed by nets,
the Rénwù Zhì says:
Divine dragons do not dwell in waters with nets;
phoenixes do not soar in lands with snares.
How could ants and insects injure them?
The Chǔ Cí says:
When a divine dragon loses water and dwells on land,
it is cut down by ants and insects.
Seeing but not seeking,
already heard from Zǐchǎn;
the Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
In Zhèng, there was a great flood.
Dragons fought outside the Shímén Gate at the Wěi Abyss.
The people requested a sacrifice.
Zǐchǎn did not permit it, saying:
"When we fight,
dragons do not watch us;
when dragons fight,
why should we alone watch them?
We have no need of dragons,
nor dragons of us."
So it ceased.
Needled and then carried away,
further recorded of Shī Huáng.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Mǎ Shīhuáng
was the Yellow Emperor's horse doctor.
A sick dragon hung its ears down,
mouth agape.
Shīhuáng needled its lips,
gave it licorice decoction to drink, and it recovered.
Later, one morning, it carried him away.
Snake
Vipers flourish densely,
The Chǔcí says:
Vipers flourish densely,
and giant foxes roam for a thousand miles.
Riding clouds and mist, they wander as spirits.
The Ěryǎ says:
Téng,
is the téng snake.
A note states:
It is a type of dragon,
capable of summoning clouds and mist and wandering within them.
The Shènzǐ says:
The téng snake wanders in mist,
the dragon rides on clouds.
Some, severed, can reconnect,
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Divine snakes can be severed and reconnect,
but they cannot prevent others from severing them.
Some hibernate to preserve themselves.
See the Yìjīng.
Springs have the peculiarity of the Fāngqú,
see the note on "the soil of Bīn produces green snakes" in the "Shuǐ Fù".
Pearls possess the treasure of Túyún.
The Dòngmíng Jì says:
Snake pearls come from the country of Túyún,
where green spirit snakes produce pearls,
their color and luster white like fine jade.
Huà Tuó treated it and the illness was cured,
The Hòuhànshū says:
Huà Tuó was once traveling on the road,
when he saw a man suffering from a blocked throat,
so he told him:
"At the roadside vendor's shop ahead, they have very sour pickled scallions,
you can take three shēng of their juice and drink it,
the illness will naturally go away."
The man did as Huà Tuó said,
and immediately vomited a snake,
and the illness was thus cured.
Xuán Sú purged it and the illness ended.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Xuán Sú was
a medicine seller in the capital market,
treating all kinds of illnesses.
The King of Héjiān was ill,
bought and took his medicine,
and purged over ten snakes.
Leaving a basket already disturbed the common households,
The Tángshū says:
During the Yuánhé era,
the minor envoys of the Five Workshops would often gather in groups at shops selling wine and food,
indulging freely in eating and drinking,
and when about to leave,
they would leave a basket of snakes.
Admonishing the owner, they would say:
"We use these snakes to procure offerings,
you must feed the birds and sparrows well,
do not let them go hungry or thirsty."
Only after the owner bribed and apologized to them
would they consent to take them away.
Chasing a rat, they then arose among the armored soldiers.
The Tángshū says:
Tàizōng was stationed at Bǎibì,
and often wished to spy on the enemy,
sending troops secretly on distant raids,
with cavalry scattered in all directions.
Tàizōng and one armored soldier ascended a hillock and fell asleep,
suddenly enemy troops converged from all sides like clouds,
and they were unaware of it.
It happened that a snake was chasing a rat,
the rat bumped into the armored soldier,
who woke with a start,
and hurriedly reported to Tàizōng.
They both mounted their horses,
galloped over a hundred paces,
were overtaken by the enemy,
Tàizōng shot his great-feathered arrow at them,
killing their valiant general,
and the enemy cavalry then retreated.
Coiling on the tent, and Měngxùn turned his army around,
The Jìnshū says:
Jǔqú Měngxùn attacked Hàomén,
when a snake coiled in front of his tent.
Měngxùn laughed and said:
"The one in front is a téng snake,
Heaven's will desires that I turn the army back to first secure Jiǔquán."
He burned his siege equipment and returned.
Coiling around a pillar, and the Yáng Palace initiated sacrifices.
The Sōushén Jì says:
In the first year of Lǔ Dìnggōng,
there were nine snakes coiling around a pillar.
Divination held it as an omen that the temple of the ninth generation would not receive sacrifices.
Thus the Yáng Palace was established.
Again, like fighting at the Zhèng gate and Duke Lì entered,
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
An inner snake and an outer snake fought at the southern gate of Zhèng,
the inner snake died.
Six years later, Duke Lì entered.
Emerging from the Quán Palace and Shēng Jiāng died.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
A snake emerged from the Quán Palace,
in the number of the former rulers,
in autumn, the eighth month, on the day xīnwèi,
Shēng Jiāng passed away.
The Quán Terrace was destroyed.
Note:
From Lǔ Bóqín to Duke Xī, seventeen rulers.
Dǒng Fèng killed it in Jìnxīng,
The Guǎngzhōu Jì says:
On the roadside of Jìnxīng Commandery, five or six lǐ away, there was a creature,
a hundred arm-spans in girth,
tens of zhàng in length.
Travelers who went to look at it,
would go and not return,
for years it was like this,
and many people were lost.
Dǒng Fèng, coming from Jiāozhōu, passed by this ridge,
saw it and was greatly alarmed, saying:
"This is a snake."
He halted the travelers,
applied talismans and commands,
and went to look after a night had passed,
the snake was already dead.
Those beside him said:
"White bones piled up into a mountain."
Wú Měng killed it in Yùzhāng.
The Yùzhāng Jì says:
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
there was a great snake over ten zhàng long blocking the road,
when people passed by,
it would always use its breath to suck them in and seize them,
having already devoured hundreds.
The Daoist Wú Měng went with several disciples,
intending to kill the snake,
but the snake hid in a deep burrow and refused to come out.
Wú Měng sent a talisman to Dù Gōng of Nánchāng,
and the snake then emerged from its burrow,
its head raised several zhàng high,
Wú Měng climbed along its tail onto its back,
pressed the snake's head to the ground with his foot,
and his disciples behind killed it with an axe.
Although repaying kindness to Suí Hóu,
The Sōushén Jì says:
Suí Hóu was traveling,
when he saw a great snake injured,
and thus treated and saved it.
Afterwards, the snake held a pearl in its mouth to repay him.
Or being exorcised by Shòuguāng.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Shòuguāng Hóu was
a man of the Hàn Zhāngdì era,
capable of exorcising all kinds of ghosts and demons.
There was a woman made ill by a demon,
Hóu exorcised and captured a great snake,
and the woman thus became well.
Also, there was a great tree,
people who stopped beneath it would die,
and birds passing over it would also die.
Hóu exorcised the tree,
the tree withered in summer,
and there was a snake seven or eight zhàng long,
hanging from the tree, dead.
If warned by it and rectifying governance,
The Jiǎ Yì Shū says:
Duke Wén of Jìn went out hunting,
his vanguard returned and said:
"Ahead there is a great snake,
as tall as a dike,
lying across the road."
Duke Wén said:
"Turn the chariots around and return."
His charioteer said:
"Your servant has heard that auspicious omens should be welcomed,
and inauspicious ones should be confronted.
Now ahead there is an inauspicious omen,
I request to attack it."
The Duke said:
"That will not do.
I have heard that if the Son of Heaven has a bad dream, he cultivates the Way;
if a feudal lord has a bad dream, he rectifies governance;
if a high minister has a bad dream, he cultivates his person.
Now if I have committed faults,
then Heaven warns me with an inauspicious omen.
To attack it
is to defy Heaven's command."
So he returned to fast and lodge in vigil,
and made offerings at the temple.
He withdrew and rectified his governance.
After three days,
he dreamed that Heaven punished the snake, saying:
"How dare you block the path of a sage ruler!"
Duke Wén awoke,
sent someone to look,
and the snake had already rotted like fish.
How could encountering it be inauspicious?
The Shuōyuàn says:
Duke Jǐng of Qí was hunting,
going up the mountain he saw a tiger,
going down to the marsh he saw a snake.
He asked Yànzǐ:
"Is this not inauspicious?"
Thus, he drank wine.
Now, having already defeated Wèi,
if you shift your troops to attack Qí,
it would be like adding legs to a snake."
Zhāoyáng realized his point,
and withdrew his army.
A snake coiling around a wheel foretold disaster for Shēnshēng.
The Xīnxù states:
Crown Prince Shēnshēng arrived at Língtái,
and a snake coiled around the left wheel of his chariot.
The charioteer said:
"Quickly obtain an auspicious sign for the state."
The crown prince then did not return,
but fell upon his sword and died.
The deep mountains gave birth to Shūhǔ.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Shūxiàng's mother was jealous of Shūhǔ's mother's beauty and would not allow her to serve.
Her sons all advised their mother.
Their mother said:
"In deep mountains and great marshes,
truly are born dragons and snakes.
That beauty of hers—
I fear she will give birth to dragons and snakes to bring calamity upon you.
Why should I cherish her?"
She sent her to attend in the bedchamber,
and she gave birth to Shūhǔ.
Thus, the Yángshé clan met with disaster.
Obtaining a strand of hair at Zhāolíng.
The Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn states:
Pèigōng lost his imperial mother in Huángxiāng.
When the realm was pacified,
he sent an envoy with a catalpa coffin to summon her spirit from the desolate wilderness.
At that time, a red snake was in the water,
and of its own accord washed and entered the catalpa coffin.
At the place where it bathed, there was a strand of hair left behind,
hence her posthumous title was Lady Zhāolíng.
Fù Zǎi died and received offerings.
The Chén Shū states:
In the final years of the Later Lord's reign,
the Palace Library Director Fù Zǎi submitted a memorial remonstrating.
The Later Lord forced him to take his own life.
Afterwards, there was a vicious snake that climbed onto the roof,
came to the spirit couch,
and positioned itself to receive sacrificial offerings,
leaving and returning again,
for over a hundred days.
At times, there was a sound of snapping fingers,
and soon after, Chén perished.
Dù Yù became drunk and transformed his form.
The Jìn Shū states:
Dù Yù was previously in Jīngzhōu,
and due to a banquet, lay drunk in his study.
People outside heard the sound of vomiting,
and secretly peeped through the door,
seeing a large snake,
hanging its head and vomiting.
Those who heard of it found it strange.
Observe how moving from a dried-up marsh can have a divine aspect.
The Hánzǐ states:
Chīyí Zǐpí served Tián Chéngzǐ.
Chéngzǐ left Qí,
fleeing to Yān,
and Chīyí Zǐpí carried the travel pass and followed.
Upon reaching Wàngyì,
he said:
"Have you not heard of the snake in the dried-up marsh?
The marsh dried up,
and they were about to move.
A small snake said:
'If a large snake travels and a small snake follows it,
people will think it is merely a snake traveling,
and someone will surely kill you.
You would do better to carry me in your mouth as we travel.
People will surely think I am a spirit.'
So they carried each other and crossed the public road.
People all avoided them.
Now, you are handsome and I am ugly.
If you act as my distinguished guest,
you are a lord of a thousand chariots;
if you act as my envoy,
you are a minister of ten thousand chariots.
It would be better for you to be my retainer."
Thus, Chéngzǐ carried the travel pass and followed him.
Upon reaching the inn,
the innkeeper received them with great respect.
Using Chángshān as a metaphor to discuss military formation.
The Sūnzǐ states:
One skilled at using troops is like Shuàirán.
Shuàirán
is the snake of Chángshān.
Strike its head and the tail arrives;
strike its tail and the head arrives;
strike its middle and both head and tail arrive.
Transforming Lǐ Mì's belt.
The Suí Shū states:
At the end of the Dàyè era,
Zhái Ràng once saw Lǐ Mì's robe on a rack,
and its belt transformed into a red snake.
Ràng found it strange in his heart,
and was ultimately killed by Mì.
Seeing Féng Gǔn's ribbon box.
The Fēngsú Tōng states:
Chariot and Horse General Féng Gǔn,
when first an Imperial Counselor,
opened his ribbon box,
and there were two red snakes.
Xǔ Xiàn divined and said:
"After three years, you will become a border general,
taking the east as your name.
After five years, you will become the Great General Who Conquers the East."
This is the venomous sting that severs the hand—
alas, how fearsome it is!
The Qián Hàn Shū states:
If a viper bites the hand,
a brave man cuts off the wrist.
Turtle
The divine turtle manifests its substance,
Truly the scattered essence of Yáoguāng.
The *Yùn Dǒu Shū* states:
The Yáoguāng star scatters to become turtles.
It bears the eight trigrams of the *Hé Tú*,
The *Hé Tú* says:
Heaven gave Yǔ the book from the Luò River,
Meaning a divine turtle carried the patterns arrayed on its back and emerged.
It marks the four numinous creatures of the *Classic of Rites*.
The *Rites* say:
The qilin, phoenix, turtle, and dragon
Are called the four numinous creatures.
Some harmonize with the qi of water and fire,
Some manifest the names of mountains and marshes.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
First, the divine turtle,
Second, the numinous turtle,
Third, the snapping turtle,
Fourth, the treasure turtle,
Fifth, the patterned turtle,
Sixth, the divination turtle,
Seventh, the mountain turtle,
Eighth, the marsh turtle,
Ninth, the water turtle,
Tenth, the fire turtle.
Fǎhé had it dug up and drew on the ground.
The *Sānguó Diǎnlüè* states:
Liáng’s Lù Fǎhé arrived north of Xiāngyáng city under a large tree,
Drew a square two feet on the ground,
Ordered his disciples to dig there,
And obtained a turtle
Five inches long.
Tapping it with his staff, he said:
"You have wished to leave this place for hundreds of years.
Had you not met me,
How could you have seen the light of day?"
He bestowed upon it the Three Refugees,
And the turtle then went into the grass and left.
Zhāng Yí relied on it to build a city.
The *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
In the thirteenth year of Qín King Huì,
Zhāng Yí and Sīmǎ Cuò conquered Shǔ.
Yí accordingly built a city,
But the city eventually collapsed and fell into ruin.
Later, a large turtle
Emerging from Yán,
Circled and walked about.
They then built along the path the turtle walked,
And it was completed.
Prepared as a delicacy, it is thus offered.
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
The turtle officer offers turtles and clams in spring,
And turtles and fish in autumn.
Following the seasonal ordinances, it is thus presented.
The *Rites‧Yuèlìng* states:
In the ninth month, slay the jiao-dragon and take the tuó-crocodile,
Present the turtle and take the yuán-turtle.
Some presented an auspicious sign to Wèi Wén.
The *Wèilüè* states:
During Emperor Wén’s time,
A divine turtle emerged from the Língzhī Pond.
Some repaid virtue to Máo Bǎo.
The *Sōushén Xùjì* states:
Máo Bǎo was traveling by the river
And saw an old fisherman catch a white turtle.
Bǎo ransomed it and released it.
Later, he was defeated in battle at Zhūchéng,
Threw himself into the river,
And something carried him,
Gradually bringing him to shore.
Looking at it,
It was the white turtle he had released before,
Its shell about four feet long.
When the turtle reached midstream,
It still looked back at Bǎo.
As currency, it sufficed for use in trade.
The *Qián Hànshū* states:
Wáng Mǎng, because the character "Liú" contained "gold" and "knife,"
Abolished the cuòdāo, qìdāo, and wǔzhū coins,
Creating items of gold, silver, turtle, cowrie, coin, and cloth,
Named "treasure currency."
Altogether, there were six types of coin currency,
One type of gold currency,
Two types of silver currency,
Four types of turtle treasure,
Five types of cowrie currency,
Ten types of cloth currency.
Five materials, six names, twenty-eight types.
It guides the qi, truly suitable for aging and decline.
The *Shǐjì‧Guīcè Zhuàn* states:
People by the river often kept turtles, feeding them,
As they could guide and induce qi,
Beneficial for aiding decline and nurturing the aged.
As for the "Black-robed Inspector,"
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
The turtle is also named Black-robed Inspector,
Also named Yuánxù.
The "Dark-clothed Grandee."
Sūn Huì’s *Ode to the Turtle* states:
There is a dark-clothed grandee,
Clad in black embroidered robes.
Riding a rumbling covered carriage,
Driving through clouds and mist, soaring freely.
It caused decay and ruin for Yuánxùn.
See the annotation "Calamity of the Withered Mulberry" in the *Ode to the Tree*.
It fell into the net of Yúqiě.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
Sòng Yuánjūn dreamed at midnight of a man with disheveled hair peering through the side gate,
Saying:
"I come from the abyss of Zǎilù.
I was on my way as an envoy of the Qīngjiāng to the dwelling of Hé Bó,
When the fisherman Yúqiě caught me."
Yuánjūn awoke,
Summoned a dream interpreter to divine it,
Who said:
"This is a divine turtle."
The next day,
Yúqiě came to court.
The lord said:
"What have you caught while fishing?"
He replied:
"In my net, I caught a white turtle,
Five feet in circumference."
The lord said:
"Present your turtle."
When the turtle arrived,
They cut it open to use for divination,
Seventy-two drillings without a single miscalculation.
As for its lifespan distinguishing divine and numinous,
Rén Fǎng’s *Shùyìjì* states:
A turtle grows hair at one thousand years,
At five thousand years of age it is called a divine turtle,
At ten thousand years of age it is called a numinous turtle.
Its form distinguishes prone and supine.
The *Ěryǎ* states:
Among turtles,
The prone ones are numinous,
The supine ones are xiè.
Truly it is the treasure of the Son of Heaven.
The *Rites* say:
Those with green-black borders
Are the treasure turtles of the Son of Heaven.
Hence it is called the chief of armored creatures.
The *Dàdài Lǐ* states:
There are three hundred sixty armored creatures,
And the divine turtle is their chief.
Some dwell within fine forests,
The *Shǐjì‧Guīcè Zhuàn* states:
There is a divine turtle in the fine forests south of the river.
Fine forests are those where
Beasts have no tigers or wolves,
Birds have no owls or harpies,
Grasses have no poisonous stings,
Wildfires do not reach,
Axes and hatchets do not come near.
These are fine forests.
The turtle dwells within them.
Some coil atop curled ears.
The *Bówùzhì* states:
A turtle of three thousand years coils atop curled ears.
Yarrow of one thousand years has three hundred stalks.
Sharing the same root in age,
Thus they know fortune and misfortune.
It bears the name of a timely lord.
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
In the mountains, on sì days,
That which is called the timely lord
Is the turtle.
Its patterns form the image of arrayed stars.
The *Lǐtǒng* states:
The image of the divine turtle:
Above, round, modeling heaven;
Below, square, modeling earth;
Its back has a disc modeling hills and mountains;
Dark patterns interweave
To form the arrayed stars;
Its movements correspond to the four seasons;
It clarifies fortune and misfortune,
Speaking not, yet trustworthy.
Imitating it, one may achieve soaring flight.
The *Bówùzhì* states:
A person traveling fell into a deep ravine,
With no way out,
Starving and near death.
He saw many turtles and snakes around,
Morning and evening stretching their necks toward the east.
The person then prostrated and learned from them,
And thereafter was no longer hungry.
His body became exceptionally light and agile,
Able to climb the rocky bank.
After several years,
He tried to straighten his body and raise his arms,
And then soared out of the ravine,
Immediately able to return home.
His complexion was joyful and radiant,
Rather more clever and wise than before.
Returning to eat grains
And savor flavors,
Within over a hundred days, he returned to his original state.
Practicing its methods, one can naturally guide and nurture oneself.
The Baopuzi says:
Xiè Jiǎn in his youth was out hunting,
when he fell into an empty tomb.
He saw a large turtle there,
repeatedly turning around,
facing no fixed direction,
opening its mouth to swallow qi,
sometimes bowing, sometimes looking up.
Jiǎn realized the turtle could guide and lead [qi],
so he tried following what the turtle did,
and consequently was no longer hungry,
ultimately able to swallow qi and abstain from grains.
There is also the case of seeing celestial patterns in the Southern Han.
The Star Classic says:
The Celestial Turtle is a five-star constellation in the Southern Han.
And the transmission of tadpole script from Yuècháng.
The Record of Strange Things says:
In the age of Táng Yáo,
the state of Yuècháng presented a thousand-year-old divine turtle,
over three feet square,
with writing on its back,
all in tadpole script,
recording events since the beginning of creation.
This was recorded to create a turtle calendar.
Fú Tāo, describing the emperor's merits and virtues in an inscription, said:
"The writing of the barbarian script and the turtle calendar."
The divination at Luò was auspicious for settlement,
The Book of Documents says:
The divination at Luò was auspicious for settlement.
Divination by turtle shell is considered superior to divination by stalks.
The Zuozhuan says:
When Duke Xiàn of Jìn was about to take Lí Jī as his consort,
he performed turtle shell divination,
which was inauspicious;
he performed milfoil stalk divination,
which was auspicious.
The diviner said:
"Stalk divination is short, turtle divination is long;
it is better to follow the long."
In Yáo's time, there were red patterns and vermilion characters,
The Waiting for the Book says:
Yáo sank a jade disc into the Luò River,
a dark turtle emerged from the water bearing a text on its back,
with red patterns and vermilion characters,
which halted at the altar grounds;
when a jade disc was sunk into the [Yellow] River,
a black turtle emerged with red-patterned inscriptions.
In the Zhōu dynasty, it was pure green with a bluish glow.
The Waiting for the Book says:
When the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent for seven years,
establishing rituals and creating music,
King Chéng observed at the Luò River.
After the ceremony of sinking the jade disc was completed,
the king withdrew.
There was a dark turtle, pure green with a bluish glow,
its carapace arranged with writing,
which climbed up onto the altar,
its red patterns forming characters,
which the Duke of Zhōu transcribed.
There is also the case of observing writing on the flank,
The Records of the Grand Historian, Treatise on Turtles and Milfoil says:
A divine turtle nested upon a fragrant lotus.
The writing on its left flank said: "The jiǎzǐ cycle repeats its brilliance;
he who obtains me, a commoner, will become a ruler;
possessing land and governance,
a feudal lord who obtains me will become an emperor."
There is also the case of propping up a bed,
The Records of the Grand Historian, Treatise on Turtles and Milfoil says:
An old man in the south used a turtle to prop up his bed leg.
After more than twenty years,
when the old man died,
they moved the bed,
and the turtle was still able to circulate qi and guide [its breath].
How could it wish to have its belly carved open?
The Zhuangzi says:
Confucius said:
"A divine turtle was able to appear in a dream to Lord Yuán,
yet it could not avoid the net of Yú Qiē;
it could be divined upon seventy-two times without a single miscalculation,
yet it could not escape the calamity of having its belly carved open."
It only wishes to drag its tail [in the mud].
The Zhuangzi says:
Zhuangzi was fishing at the Pú River.
The King of Chǔ sent a senior official first to announce to him,
saying:
"I wish to entrust the affairs of my state to you!"
Zhuangzi, holding his fishing pole, did not look back,
and said:
"I have heard that in Chǔ there is a divine turtle,
dead for three thousand years already.
It is wrapped in cloth, placed in a bamboo box, and stored in the ancestral temple.
This turtle—
would it prefer to be dead, leaving its bones to be honored?
Or would it prefer to be alive, dragging its tail in the mud?
I will drag my tail in the mud."
The 'ten pairs' [of turtle shells] are already seen in Fúxī's Classic of Changes,
The Classic of Changes says:
Sometimes it is augmented by a turtle worth ten pairs [of shells].
The 'six chambers' are further heard of in the Rites of Zhōu.
The Rites of Zhōu says:
The Turtle Officer is in charge of the six kinds of turtles,
each having its own name and characteristics.
The celestial turtle is called the 'spirit kind',
the earthly turtle is called the 'unraveling kind',
the eastern turtle is called the 'fruit kind',
the western turtle is called the 'thunder kind',
the southern turtle is called the 'hunting kind',
the northern turtle is called the 'yielding kind'.
Each is distinguished
according to the color of its region and its bodily form.
Generally, turtles are captured in autumn,
and prepared in spring.
Each according to its kind
is placed into the turtle chamber.
The commentary states:
'Kind' [shǔ]
means they are not all the same.
The celestial turtle is black,
the earthly turtle is yellow,
the eastern [turtle] is green,
the western [turtle] is white,
the southern [turtle] is red,
the northern [turtle] is black.
These are their colors.
A turtle that looks down is the 'spirit' [kind],
one that looks up is the 'unraveling' [kind],
one whose front is covered is the 'fruit' [kind],
one whose rear is covered is the 'hunting' [kind],
one that leans left is the 'thunder' [kind],
one that leans right is the 'yielding' [kind].
These are their bodily forms.
The six kinds of turtles each have a separate chamber.
There are also accounts transmitted about turtles among clumps of milfoil,
The Baopuzi says:
A thousand-year-old turtle
possesses all five colors.
It understands human speech.
Sometimes it floats upon lotus leaves,
sometimes it is beneath clumps of milfoil.
There are also records of the anomaly of the green-haired [turtle].
The Book of Southern Qí says:
During the Yǒngmíng era,
someone presented one green-haired divine turtle.
Also, it is heard that the large Ruò [turtle] has three legs,
and the Jūnshān [turtle] has six eyes.
The Erya says:
A soft-shelled turtle with three legs
is called 'néng'.
A turtle with three legs
is called 'bēn'.
Commentary:
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
Cóng Mountain has many three-legged soft-shelled turtles,
Dàruò Mountain has many three-legged turtles.
The Records of Yìxīng says:
Below the temple on Jūn Mountain there is a pond,
in which there is a three-legged, six-eyed turtle.
Also, during the Tiānshēng era of the Táng,
Jiāngzhōu presented a turtle with six eyes.
Kǒng Yú was once enlightened by a look back,
The Later Records of Worthies from Kuàijī says:
Kǒng Yú, styled Kāngjìng,
once traveled to the Yúbù post station in Wúxīng.
He saw someone had caged a turtle by the roadside,
so Yú bought it and released it into the stream.
When the turtle reached the water,
it turned its head back to look at Yú.
Later, when he was enfeoffed at this post station,
and the seal was cast three times,
the [turtle-shaped knob on the] seal each time looked left.
Yú understood,
and thereupon took it and wore it.
Huáng Ān frequently saw it raise its head.
The Records of Penetrating the Obscure says:
Huáng Ān regularly consumed cinnabar,
so his whole body was red.
He sat upon a large divine turtle,
and said:
"When Fúxī first created nets and snares,
he gave this turtle to me.
This creature fears the light of the sun and moon,
