and raises its head once every two thousand years.
I have sat upon this turtle
through five instances of it raising its head."
When he walked, he carried the turtle and moved,
and people in the world called Huáng Ān 'Ten Thousand Years'.
Alas, the Lóugōu [turtle] did not deceive,
The Zuozhuan says:
Zāng Zhāobó went to Jìn.
Zāng Huì stole his precious turtle named Lóugōu,
and used it to divine whether [Zhāobó] was truthful or deceitful.
The divination indicated deceit was auspicious.
So [Huì] went to Jìn.
Zhāobó asked about family matters,
and [Huì] answered everything.
But concerning [Zhāobó's] wife and his younger brother Shūsūn,
he asked repeatedly,
but [Huì] did not answer.
Zhāobó returned,
and stayed outside to observe them.
None of these were present.
Later, they were seized outside the middle gate of the Jì family.
Jì Píngzǐ was furious,
and said:
"Why have you entered my gate with soldiers?"
The Jì and Zāng families were at odds.
When Zhāo Bó followed the Duke and fled to Qí,
Píngzǐ established Zāng Huì.
Huì said:
"The hunchback did not deceive me."
He laughed at the ephemeral mayfly's worries.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The tortoise lives for three thousand years,
while the mayfly does not exceed three days.
For a mayfly to worry about the tortoise's means of nurturing life,
people will surely laugh at it.
Zāng Wén performed one divination and was praised for its excellence.
The Jiāyǔ says:
Confucius asked Qīdiāo Féngzǐ:
"Regarding Shì Wénzhòng,
Wǔzhòng, and Rúzǐ Róng,
which of these three great officers is the most worthy?"
He replied:
"The Zāng family possesses a guardian tortoise for divination.
Wénzhòng performed one divination in three years,
Wǔzhòng performed two divinations in three years,
and Rúzǐ Róng performed three divinations in three years.
From this, Féng discerned their character.
As for whether the three are worthy or not,
I dare not claim to know."
Confucius said:
"A true gentleman,
this son of the Qīdiāo family!
When he speaks of others' virtues,
he is subtle yet clear;
when he speaks of others' faults,
he is gentle yet distinct.
If wisdom cannot reach it,
and clarity cannot perceive it,
who can be like him?"
Wǔzhòng could offer requests and devise strategies.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
Zāng Wǔzhòng sent word from Zhū to Zāng Jiǎ,
and also presented a great tortoise shell,
saying:
"My offense does not extend to cutting off sacrifices to you.
I present this great tortoise shell with my request;
it may be acceptable."
Then there are the eight winds and nine provinces,
the Southern Dipper and Northern Ladle.
The Shǐjì·Guīcè Zhuàn says:
First, the Northern Ladle tortoise;
second, the Southern Dipper tortoise;
third, the Five Stars tortoise;
fourth, the Eight Winds tortoise;
fifth, the Twenty-Eight Mansions tortoise;
sixth, the Sun and Moon tortoise;
seventh, the Nine Provinces tortoise;
eighth, the Jade tortoise.
Residing in the Kǎn trigram, embodying the Lí trigram.
Lǐ Yóng's "Ode to the Tortoise" says:
Its substance corresponds to the Lí trigram,
its position is fixed in the Kǎn trigram's abode.
I despise those who crave greedily,
and honor my spiritual talisman.
Floating on the Luò River,
seeing the weft texts,
penetrating secret teachings,
comprehending profound mysteries.
With a snake's head and a dragon's neck.
The Shuōyuàn says:
The spiritual tortoise is five-colored like jade,
its back facing yin, its belly facing yang,
its arched top resembling heaven,
its flat bottom modeling earth,
its movements responding to the four seasons,
with a snake's head and a dragon's neck,
its left eye symbolizing the sun,
its right eye symbolizing the moon,
knowing the numbers of survival, demise, fortune, and misfortune.
Sometimes it communicates dreams to Gāo Lǔ.
The Qiányān Lù says:
At the end of Fú Jiān's reign,
a man from Gāolíng dug a well and found a tortoise,
three chǐ in size,
with patterns on its back resembling the Eight Trigrams.
Jiān ordered the Grand Diviner to dig a pond to raise it,
feeding it millet.
When it died,
its bones were stored in the ancestral temple.
That night,
the temple attendant Gāo Lǔ dreamed the tortoise said to him:
"I originally came from the south of the Yangtze River,
but encountered untimely misfortune,
and perished in the Qín court."
He also dreamed someone said to Lǔ:
"The tortoise lived for three thousand six hundred years before its end.
Its end must herald ominous rise,
an omen of a state's downfall."
Not long after, Jiān was defeated.
Sometimes it manifests auspicious signs to Empress Zhāng.
The Chén Shū says: Emperor Wǔ's Empress Zhāng's mother once met a Daoist priest,
who gave her a small tortoise,
colorful with five hues,
saying:
"In three years, there will be a sign."
When the time came,
the Empress was born,
with purple light illuminating the room,
and the tortoise was nowhere to be found.
As for the front covering resembling fruit,
and the left inclination being unlike,
the Ěryǎ says:
The tortoise that lowers its head is divine,
the one that raises its head is exhausted,
the front covering resembles fruit,
the rear covering resembles hunting,
the left inclination is unlike,
the right inclination is not as.
Note:
Lowering its head while walking,
raising its head while walking,
front covering means the front shell is long,
rear covering means the rear shell is long,
left inclination means the head leans left while walking, indicating left-side feeding,
right inclination means the head leans right while walking, indicating right-side feeding.
Ní,
pronounced ní.
How could it be like the ox's hoof or pig's skull?
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The ox's hoof and pig's skull are also bones,
yet people do not scorch them for divination.
They must ask the tortoise about fortune and misfortune
because it has endured for ages.
One must see it scorched inside and patterned outside.
The Guóyǔ says:
Clothing is
the pattern of the heart,
like the tortoise:
scorch its inside, and patterns will appear outside.
It bore the chart for Fúxī.
The Gǔshǐ Kǎo says:
In Fúxī's time, a spiritual tortoise bore the Hé Tú on its back,
which is the Eight Trigrams.
Praising King Níng for leaving it behind.
The Shū says:
King Níng left me the great treasure tortoise.
Note:
King Níng
is King Wén.
Only the tribute from Jiǔjiāng,
truly the great treasure of Yángzhōu.
The Shū says:
Jiǔjiāng presented as tribute the great tortoise.
Fish
"Fish caught in the weir,
catfish and carp,"
"The nobleman has wine,
abundant and delicious,"
as for "The bream's tail turns red,
the royal house is like a blaze."
All are from the *Book of Songs*.
Some recall perch upon autumn's arrival.
*Shì Shuō* states:
Zhāng Hàn, styled Jìyīng,
served as an assistant to Prince Qí Jiǒng.
In Luòyáng, seeing the autumn wind rise,
he thought of the water shield soup and perch sashimi from Wúzhōng.
He then ordered his carriage and returned home.
Soon after, Prince Qí was defeated,
and people of the time considered him perceptive of opportunity.
Some offer sturgeon in spring.
*Lǐ Jì* states:
In late spring, sturgeon are offered at the ancestral temple.
So large it fills a cart.
*Kǒng Cóng Zǐ* states:
A man from Wèi was fishing in the river
and caught a giant fish,
so large it filled a cart.
He said:
"I lowered bait for a bream,
but the giant fish passed by without a glance;
then I used half a piglet,
and it swallowed it."
Zǐsīzǐ said:
"Alas!
The giant fish died from greed for bait,
just as scholars die from greed for emolument."
Heard of a fish a thousand *lǐ* wide.
*Liè Zǐ* states:
North of the eight cords lies the dark sea,
where fish are a thousand *lǐ* wide,
their length proportionate.
Then there was Emperor Zhāo's cultivation in Kūnmíng.
*Sān Fǔ Gù Shì* states:
Emperor Wǔ built the Kūnmíng Pool for naval training.
Later, Emperor Zhāo raised fish in the pool
to supply the imperial mausoleums and sacrifices,
with the surplus sold in Cháng'ān market,
making fish cheap.
Rèn Zǐ crouched in Kuàijī.
*Zhuāng Zǐ* states:
Master Rèn crouched in Kuàijī fishing in the Eastern Sea,
and after a year, a giant fish took his bait.
When Master Rèn caught this fish,
from east of the Zhè River
to north of Cāngwú,
all were sated by this fish.
Disdained the insufficiency of the imperial carriage officer.
*Wèi Zhì* states:
Emperor Wén campaigned east against Wú,
while Empress Wéndé Guō remained in Qiáo.
At that time, her cousin, the imperial carriage commandant Guō Biǎo, wanted to dam water to catch fish.
The Empress said:
"What the imperial carriage lacks now,
is it really these fish?"
Praised Xián Zhāng for declining.
*Yàn Zǐ Chūn Qiū* states:
Duke Jǐng shot at a target,
and only one person in the hall praised him.
Xián Zhāng entered,
and the Duke said:
"Since I lost Yàn Zǐ,
I have not heard criticism of my faults."
Zhāng said:
"I have heard that if the ruler likes something,
the ministers follow;
if the ruler craves something,
the ministers provide it.
The inchworm turns yellow when eating yellow,
and green when eating green.
Could it be that you, my lord, have been fed flattering words?"
The Duke said:
"Well said."
He awarded Xián Zhāng fifty carts of fish.
Xián Zhāng returned home,
with fish carts blocking the road.
Zhāng patted his servant and said:
"Those who praised earlier,
all desired these fish."
He firmly declined and did not accept.
Bestowed a fine name upon Kǒng Lǐ.
*Fēng Sú Tōng* states:
When Bóyú was born,
someone happened to gift Confucius a fish.
Delighted, he considered it auspicious,
thus named him Lǐ,
styled Bóyú.
Offered surplus fish to Zhòngní.
*Jiā Yǔ* states:
When Confucius traveled to Chǔ,
a fisherman offered him fish,
but Confucius declined.
The fisherman said:
"The weather is hot, and the market is far.
I have nowhere to sell it,
and if I discard it in the dirt,
it would be better to offer it to a nobleman."
Confucius bowed twice and accepted,
then swept the ground and offered it in sacrifice.
Táo Zhū raised them and became wealthy.
Táo Zhūgōng's *Yǎng Yú Jīng* states:
King Wēi invited Zhūgōng
and asked:
"Your family has accumulated billions in gold,
what method did you use?"
Zhūgōng said:
"There are five methods for livelihood:
aquatic husbandry is the first.
Aquatic husbandry means raising fish.
Use six *mǔ* of land for a pond,
with nine islets in the pond.
Then seek twenty female carp, three feet long and with roe,
and four male carp,
and release them into the pond on the first *gēng* day of the second month.
The reason for raising carp is
they do not eat each other, grow easily, and are valuable."
Lóng Yáng discarded them and grieved.
*Zhàn Guó Cè* states:
The King of Wèi and Lord Lóng Yáng were fishing together on a boat.
Lord Lóng Yáng caught over ten fish and shed tears,
saying:
"When I first caught fish,
I was very pleased;
but later, when I caught larger ones,
I wanted to discard the earlier catches.
Now, despite my unworthiness,
I am favored to attend to your pillow and mat.
Within the four seas,
there are many beauties.
Hearing that I have gained your favor,
they will surely lift their skirts and hasten here.
You, my king, will then regard me as I regarded the discarded fish."
The king then ordered within his borders: "Anyone daring to speak of beauties will be executed along with their clan."
Worry lies in leaving the deep pool.
*Lǎo Zǐ* states:
Fish cannot leave the deep pool;
the sharp tools of the state
cannot be shown to others.
Joy should be among the water plants.
See the *Book of Songs*.
Form corresponds to Bǐng and Dīng.
*Ěr Yǎ* states:
A fish's skull is called Dīng,
its intestines are called Yǐ,
and its tail is called Bǐng.
Used to refer to fresh and dried fish.
*Zhōu Lǐ* states:
The fish officer manages the distinction between fresh and dried fish
to supply the king's meals.
Note:
Fresh
means raw.
Dried
means cured.
Fresh is pronounced xiān,
dried is pronounced gǎo.
Sùshā excelled at fishing.
*Lǔ Lián Zǐ* states:
In ancient times, the skilled fisherman Sùshā Xízǐ
could make fish appear on mountains,
but even then,
Sùshā could not catch a single fish.
Sùshā was not ignorant of fishing methods;
it was because mountains are not where fish live.
Zhān Hé could fish skillfully.
*Huái Nán Zǐ* states:
Lord Zhān could catch a thousand-year-old carp.
Verified trust extends even to pigs and fish.
*Yì Jīng‧Zhōng Fú* states:
Trust extends to pigs and fish.
Praised for filling the spiritual pond.
*Book of Songs* states:
The king is at the spiritual pond,
where fish leap abundantly.
Some have forms like swords.
*Ěr Yǎ* states:
Liè,
is the sheath knife.
Note:
This is today's jì fish,
also called the sword fish.
Priced more valuable than cattle and sheep.
*Luòyáng Qié Lán Jì* states:
A saying in the capital goes:
"Carp and bream from Yī and Luò,
are more valuable than cattle and sheep."
Transformed into the spring of Shūgū.
See the "Water Rhapsody" note on "Shūgū's spiritual transformation."
Returned to the storehouse of Qīngtián.
*Yǒng Jiā Jì* states:
In winter, the water of Qīngtián Stream is as warm as soup,
and many fish gather there,
called the fish storehouse.
Some fish in Wèi,
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Tàigōng Wàng sought to serve Zhōu Xībó by fishing.
Xībó was hunting
and encountered Tàigōng on the north bank of the Wèi River.
He took him in his carriage and returned with him.
Some observed fishing at Táng.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Lord Yǐn of Lǔ was about to go to Táng to observe the fishermen.
Zāng Xībó remonstrated, saying:
"If a thing is not sufficient for discussing great affairs,
and its material is not sufficient for preparing implements,
then the ruler should not engage with it.
The products of mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
are matters for petty officials and menials,
the duties of minor functionaries—
these are not what the ruler should concern himself with."
The lord said:
"I shall merely inspect the territory."
He then went
and had fish displayed for his observation.
Xībó pleaded illness and did not accompany him.
Pulling three and hauling two,
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Western Campaign" says:
"Piercing gills and grasping tails,
pulling three and hauling two.
Separating threads and dividing tips."
Zhāng Héng's "Seven Arguments" says:
"The zūn fish of Gǒngluò,
cut to make delicacies,
dividing tips and separating threads,
fine and tangled like mosquito legs.
Their night flight once startled the wényáo fish;
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Three Capitals" says:
"The wényáo fish flies at night and touches the lines."
Their dwelling on land also startled the lónglǐ fish.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"The lónglǐ fish
dwells on land,
its shape resembling a carp."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"The lónglǐ fish has a single horn."
Apocryphal texts record the tiger carrying fish;
the Yùndǒushū states:
"When the four quarters are troubled and disturbed,
and the common people lose favor,
a tiger carries a fish."
Seasonal ordinances mark the otter's sacrifice.
The Book of Rites says:
"On the day of the Rain Water solar term,
the otter sacrifices fish."
There is also the tale of Jiāng Shī's pair of carp.
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
Jiāng Shī was extremely filial by nature.
His mother often drank water from the Jiāng River.
His son went to fetch water and drowned.
Fearing his mother would find out,
he deceitfully said:
"He has gone to study."
Soon, a spring gushed forth beside their house,
producing a pair of carp daily.
And Yáng Zhèn's three zhàn fish.
The Book of the Later Han states:
Yáng Zhèn was a guest in Hú,
and did not respond to invitations from the commandery and prefecture.
A stork carried three zhàn fish in its beak and flew to gather before the lecture hall.
The chief lecturer took the fish and presented them, saying:
"The zhàn fish
is a symbol of the attire of ministers and high officials.
The number three
corresponds to the Three Terraces constellation.
From this, sir, you shall rise."
Some buy them and eat vegetables instead;
the Shīshū states:
"The xù fish resembles the fáng but has a large head;
it is an unappetizing fish.
Hence the local saying goes:
'Buying fish and getting xù,
is不如不如 eating vegetables.'"
In Xúzhōu it is called lián.
Some obtain them and forget the trap.
See the Zhuāngzǐ.
Leaping into King Wǔ's boat,
see the annotation "The white fish auspicious for Zhōu" in the "Rhapsody on Boats."
Entering Zhòngyù's boat.
The Book of Jin states:
Xià Tǒng, styled Zhòngyù.
His mother was ill,
so he went to Luòyáng to buy medicine.
It happened to be the third day of the third month,
when the nobles and officials of Luòyáng and below all gathered at the floating bridge.
Tǒng paid them no heed.
Grand Commandant Jiǎ Chōng, finding this strange, asked him:
"You dwell by the seashore;
are you skilled in water performances?"
He replied:
"I am."
He then took the rudder and oar,
turning and maneuvering in midstream.
Thereupon, wind and waves arose, startling all,
and soon eight or nine white fish leapt into his boat.
The onlookers were all terrified.
Qín Gāo first appeared at the Zhuō River.
The Biographies of Immortals states:
Qín Gāo served as a retainer to King Kāng of Sòng, skilled in playing the zither,
and practiced the arts of Juān and Péng.
Later he took his leave
and entered the Zhuō River to fetch a dragon's offspring.
He arranged with his disciples to fast and purify themselves,
and set up a shrine by the water.
Indeed, he came riding a red carp,
emerged from the shrine,
stayed for a month, and then re-entered the water.
Wù Guāng finally returned to the Lú River.
The Fúzǐ states:
Wù Guāng threw himself into the Lú River,
and the Earl of the Lú River sent him off with a red carp.
The one who obtained the spiritual talisman was Juānzǐ.
The Biographies of Immortals states:
Juānzǐ was a man of Qí
who fished in the rivers and marshes
and obtained a talisman from inside a carp.
He secluded himself on Dàng Mountain
and could summon wind and rain.
The one who entrusted a cinnabar letter was Gě Xuán.
The Biographies of Divine Immortals states:
Gě Xuán saw a man selling a large fish
and said to him:
"I trouble you to temporarily take this fish to the Earl of the River."
He then placed a cinnabar-inscribed paper into the fish's mouth.
After a short while,
the fish returned, leaping onto the bank,
with a letter in bluish-black,
like a tree leaf.
Zhuāng Zhōu compared it to borrowing grain.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
Zhuāng Zhōu's family was poor,
so he went to borrow grain from the Marquis of Jiānhé.
The marquis said:
"I am about to receive tax revenue from my fief;
I shall lend you three hundred pieces of gold then. Is that acceptable?"
Zhuāng Zhōu angrily said:
"When I came yesterday,
I heard someone in the road calling me.
Looking into a rut, I saw a crucian carp there.
It said:
'I am a wave official of the Eastern Sea.
Do you, sir, perhaps have a peck or a dou of water to keep me alive?'
I said:
'Very well.
I shall travel south to persuade the kings of Wú and Yuè
to stir up the waters of the Western River and welcome you. Is that acceptable?'
The crucian carp said:
'When you speak thus, you might as well go early to the dried fish market to look for me.'"
Chúnyú laughed at it in the field blessing.
The Shuōyuàn states:
Chǔ was about to attack Qí,
so the King of Qí sent Chúnyú Kūn to seek aid from Zhào,
bearing a hundred catties of gold
and ten teams of four horses each.
Kūn said:
"My neighbor prayed for his fields,
offering a box of rice and a crucian carp, and prayed:
'May my low, waterlogged fields yield a hundred cartloads of grain.'
I laughed at him for offering so little
yet asking for so much."
The king then increased the gifts to gold and white jade,
and a hundred teams of four horses each.
The shàn resembles a snake.
The Hánzǐ states:
"The shàn resembles a snake,
yet fishermen catch shàn but fear snakes.
Where profit lies,
all become like Bēn and Yù."
The xí fish is said to have wings.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"From Zhuōguāng Mountain
flows the Xiāo River.
There are many xíxí fish there,
resembling magpies but with ten wings.
They can ward off fire."
Chén Xiāo gave it away to a thief.
The Book of the Later Han states:
Chén Xiāo of Kuàijī,
when young, was catching fish by the water outside the city walls.
Someone stole his catch.
Xiāo saw him and hid in the grass,
then pursued him and gave him the fish.
The thief was ashamed and would not accept it.
From then on, no one stole his fish again.
Wáng Hóng presented them to relatives and acquaintances.
The Book of Sòng states:
Wáng Hóngzhī was fond of fishing by nature.
On the Shàngyú River there was a place called Sānshítóu.
Hóngzhī often cast his line there.
Passersby did not recognize him.
Someone asked:
"Does the fisherman sell the fish he catches?"
Hóngzhī replied:
"He does not catch them,
and even if he did, he would not sell them."
In the evening,
he would carry fish into the city of Shàngyú,
passing by the gates of relatives and old friends,
and leave one or two fish at each gate before departing.
The Línyì fish soaring through the clouds,
the *Record of the Kingdom of Línyì* states:
"The flying fish has wings like a cicada,
it dives and swims at the bottom of the sea,
and when it flies, it soars above the clouds."
The stone-carved fish of Kūnmíng.
The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
"At Kūnmíng Pond, stone fish were carved,
and whenever there was thunder and rain,
the fish would roar,
with their fins and tails moving."
During the Hàn dynasty, prayers for rain
often proved effective.
Entering the Yǔyuān and transforming suddenly,
the *Records of Omitted Matters* states:
"Gǔn of the Xià dynasty failed in his efforts to control the waters,
and was submerged in the Yǔ River,
transforming into a black fish,
a thousand feet in size.
Later, he died,
and his body lay across the rivers and seas.
In later generations, the character for 'black' was combined with the character for 'fish,'
forming the character 'Gǔn.'"
Disliking Wǔchāng and refusing to eat its fish.
The *Records of Wú* states:
"During Sūn Quán's time, there was a desire to move the capital from Jiànyè to Wǔchāng.
The people of Jiànyè sang a ballad:
'Better to drink the water of Jiànyè,
than to eat the fish of Wǔchāng.
Better to return to Jiànyè and die,
than to settle in Wǔchāng.'"
Qǐfú bought them and released them all,
the *Book of Suí* states:
"Qǐfú Huì served as the governor of Tán and Guì,
where the customs were frivolous and fickle.
Huì personally practiced simplicity to rectify this,
and the customs greatly improved.
Once, he saw people catching fish with nets,
and he bought the fish with silk and released them."
The character '簺' is pronounced 'sài.'
Wáng Gù prayed over them but caught none.
The *Book of Liáng* states:
"Wáng Gù once visited Wèi as an envoy,
and was feasted at Kūnmíng Pond.
The people of Wèi, knowing that southerners were fond of fish,
set up many nets.
Gù chanted Buddhist prayers over them,
and not a single scale was caught."
Explaining the governance of Shànfù in a brief account,
the *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Jìzǐ governed Shànfù for three years,
and Wūmǎ Qī, wearing coarse clothes,
changed his appearance,
and went to observe the transformation.
At night, he saw a fisherman catch a fish and release it.
Wūmǎ Qī asked him,
saying:
'All those who fish
do so to catch fish.
Now you release it,
why is that?'
The fisherman replied:
'Jìzǐ does not wish people to take small fish.
What I caught was a small fish,
so I released it.'
Wūmǎ Qī returned and reported to Confucius, saying:
'Jìzǐ's virtue has reached its peak.'"
Note:
Jìzǐ
is Zǐjiàn.
Presenting a large fish reveals Wáng Gōng's virtue.
The *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
"Chén Fān served as a legal officer in the commandery.
During the morning audience with the governor Wáng Gōng,
a guest presented a white fish to Gōng.
Gōng said:
'Yǔnán actually has such fish?'
Fān said:
'The fish is large due to Your Excellency's virtue.'"
It is also heard that Xiè Yǔn summoned carp,
the *Continued Records of Searching for the Supernatural* states:
"Xiè Yǔn returned from Wǔdāng Mountain,
and while seated with Huán Xuānwǔ,
someone mentioned that Zuǒ Yuánfàng had summoned perch for Lord Cáo.
Yǔn then said:
'This can be done.'
He requested a large jar filled with water,
and threw a talisman written in vermilion into the water.
Soon, two carp appeared, flapping their fins in the water."
Zuǒ Cí transformed perch,
the *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
"Zuǒ Cí, styled Yuánfàng,
was once seated with Cáo Cāo.
Cáo said:
'It is a pity there are no perch from the Wúsōng River!'
Cí then requested a copper basin filled with water,
and fished in the basin with a bamboo rod.
In a moment, he pulled out a perch.
Cáo said:
'One fish is not enough.'
So he cast the line again,
and pulled out another,
both over three feet long.
Cáo had them sliced before him."
Zhuān Zhū presented roasted fish,
the *Jīnlóuzǐ* states:
"Zhuān Zhū wanted to assassinate King Liáo of Wú,
so he learned to roast fish,
and the fragrance could be smelled for miles.
Liáo requested roasted fish,
and Zhuān Zhū hid a knife inside the fish's belly."
Chén Shèng placed a message,
the *Book of Hàn* states:
"Chén Shèng raised a great plan,
and wanted to awe the soldiers.
So he wrote in vermilion 'Chén Shèng will be king' and placed it inside the belly of a fish caught in a net.
When the soldiers bought the fish,
they saw the message and were greatly astonished."
Entering the boat, he knew in advance that they would lay down their armor,
the *Records of the Former Liáng* states:
"The governor of Jīnchéng, Hú Xù, rebelled,
and Zhāng Guǐ sent the commander Zōng Yì and the administrator Línghú Liú to attack him.
While crossing the river in midstream,
a white fish entered the boat.
Liú said:
'Fish,
a scaled creature,
means the enemy will surely lay down their armor and surrender to us.'
Xù indeed requested to surrender."
If there is an inscription, it is compared to bearing a chart.
The *Book of Táng* states:
"During the Kāiyuán era,
a fish was caught in Qúzhōu,
bearing an inscription,
and it was presented.
The attendant Péi Guāngtíng and others memorialized:
'Fish and dragons produce charts,
which emerge from the Hé and Luò rivers.
Compared to those prosperous times,
this is insignificant.'"
Zhōu Fā was once said to be fond of salted fish,
the *Discourses of the States* states:
"The crown prince of King Wén of Zhōu, Fā, was fond of salted fish.
Tàigōng wrote a commentary for him, saying:
'Salted fish is not offered in sacrificial vessels;
how can something improper be used to nourish the crown prince!'"
Hàn Chè once heard of obtaining pearls,
see the annotation in the *Ode to Pearls*: "Hàn Wǔ dreamed of Kūnmíng."
Already finding contentment by the Háo bridge,
the *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ were strolling on the bridge over the Háo River.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'The minnows swim about so freely;
this is the happiness of fish.'
Huìzǐ said:
'You are not a fish;
how do you know the happiness of fish?'
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'You are not me;
how do you know that I do not know the happiness of fish?'"
Also forgetting each other in the rivers and lakes.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"When the spring dries up,
the fish are left on the land,
moistening each other with their breath,
and wetting each other with their saliva,
but it is better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes."
A single piece is called the king's leftover,
a pair is called the side-by-side eyes.
The *Records of the Investigation of Things* states:
"The King of Wú had leftover sliced fish from his meal,
which he threw into the river.
It transformed into a fish,
named 'the King of Wú's leftover sliced fish.'"
Zuǒ Sī's *Ode to the Three Capitals* states:
"A pair are the side-by-side eyes,
a single piece is the king's leftover."
Sometimes the eyes fall and become pearls,
Cáo Pí's *Ode to Watching the Tides* states:
"Divine whales come and go,
riding the waves and leaping with scales;
spraying mist that gathers,
exhaling water to form a ford.
Their bones become islands in ruins,
their eyes fall as bright moon pearls."
Sometimes the oil is burned to make candles.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"In the tomb of Qín Shǐhuáng, fish oil was used as lamp candles."
Offering sacrifices and receiving a response was Zhōu Píng,
the *Records of the Strange* states:
"In Guānzhōng, there is a golden fish deity."
It is said that during the time of King Píng of Zhōu,
when there was no rain for a hundred days,
they sacrificed to this deity,
and suddenly a spring gushed forth,
with fish leaping and rain falling.
To demonstrate integrity, Yáng Xù hung up a fish.
The Book of the Later Hàn states:
Yáng Xù was fond of eating raw fish.
When he served as the Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
the Assistant Prefect, Hóu Jiǎn, presented him with a carp.
Yáng Xù accepted it but hung it up.
A year later, Hóu Jiǎn sent another one.
Yáng Xù then took out the dried fish he had hung up to show him,
thus discouraging his intentions.
Crucian carp is particularly suitable for summer.
The Classic of Divine Marvels states:
In the southeastern sea, there is a warm lake,
where crucian carp live.
Eating them is suitable for summer and helps avoid wind and cold.
The shū fish can dispel worries.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
In the waters of Zǐhú at Dài Mountain,
there are many shū fish.
They resemble chickens with red feathers,
having three tails, six feet, and four heads.
Their sound is like that of a magpie,
and eating them cures worries.
The Illustrated Eulogy states:
Disturbing harmony and harming peace,
nothing is more painful than worry.
The Book of Songs praises the daylily,
while the Classic of Mountains and Seas mentions the shū fish.
Long heard of is the whale that traverses the sea.
Mù Xuánxū’s Rhapsody on the Sea states:
Among fish, there is the whale that crosses the sea,
soaring alone in solitude.
Its giant scales pierce the clouds,
and its massive fins reach the sky.
Its head forms a mountain,
and its flowing fat becomes an abyss.
Greatly recorded is the fish that swallows boats.
Pān Yuè’s Rhapsody on the Sea states:
Among fish, there are whales that swallow boats.
Jiǎ Yì’s Lament for Qū Yuán states:
How can those ordinary muddy ditches
accommodate the giant fish that swallows boats?
Some take seven days to encounter its tail.
The Records of the Mysterious Realm states:
In the Eastern Sea, there is a giant fish.
Those sailing the sea
encounter its head on the first day,
and its tail on the seventh day.
Some weigh one jīn but number a thousand heads.
The Extensive Records states:
In Wǔyáng, there are small fish
as large as needles,
called “a thousand heads per jīn.”
The people of Shǔ use them to make sauce.
Fortunately, by channeling water, fish can be attracted.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
To attract fish, one must first channel water;
to attract birds, one must first plant trees.
When water accumulates, fish gather;
when trees flourish, birds assemble.
Do not dry up valleys to seek fish.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
If the ruler seeks timber,
his ministers will devastate the forests;
if the ruler seeks fish,
his ministers will dry up the valleys.
There is also the bream from the Liáng River.
Lù Jī’s Commentary on the Book of Songs states:
The bream
is a delicious fish,
and the bream from the Liáng River is especially plump and tasty.
Thus, the local saying goes:
“Live by the Liáng River for its bream.”
And the crucian carp from Dòngtíng Lake.
Liú Shào’s Seven Glories states:
The crucian carp from Dòngtíng Lake comes from the Jiāng and Mín Rivers,
with red bellies, green heads, red tails, and blue scales.
It responded to Wáng Xiáng’s ice-breaking.
The Book of Jìn states:
Wáng Xiáng was extremely filial.
He lost his mother early,
and his stepmother, Lady Zhū, was unkind,
often slandering him,
causing him to lose his father’s affection.
When his stepmother fell ill,
he never loosened his clothes,
and personally tasted all medicines.
His stepmother desired fresh fish,
but the weather was bitterly cold and the water frozen.
He removed his clothes and was about to break the ice to seek fish
when the ice suddenly cracked on its own,
and two carp leaped out.
He took them and returned home.
It moved Cài Zhòng to dwell by the grave.
The Biographies of Former Worthies states:
Cài Jūnzhòng was extremely filial.
When his mother passed away,
he lived by her grave.
Four divine fish from heaven appeared before the grave as an offering.
The state of Chǔ was enlightened and thus governed well.
The New Prefaces states:
A man from Chǔ presented fish to the king,
saying:
“Today, I caught fish while fishing,
but I cannot eat them all,
nor can I sell them,
and it would be a pity to discard them,
so I have come to present them to you.”
The attendants said:
“How crude his words are!”
The King of Chǔ replied:
“You do not understand that this fisherman is a benevolent man.
I have heard that when granaries overflow with grain,
the state still has starving people;
when the palace is filled with secluded women,
the common people have many unmarried men;
when surplus wealth is stored in the treasury,
the realm is filled with impoverished people.
All of these are failures of governance.
Thus, while the kitchen has fatty meat
and the stables have well-fed horses,
the people bear the signs of hunger.
The fisherman understands this,
and he is using this to admonish me.”
Thereupon, he dispatched officials to relieve widowers and widows.
Thus, the fisherman presented surplus fish,
and the state of Chǔ benefited from it.
The King of Yuè raised fish and prospered.
The Annals of Wú and Yuè states:
When the King of Yuè resided in Kuàijī,
Fàn Lǐ and others said:
“In the mountains of Kuàijī, there are two fish ponds, one upper and one lower.
The waters contain the flow of three rivers and four waterways,
and the vastness of nine streams and six valleys.
The upper pond is suitable for the king,
and the lower pond is suitable for the people and officials.
If fish are raised for three years,
the profits can amount to tens of millions,
and the state of Yuè will become wealthy and prosperous.”
There is also the story of Wáng Yán’s filial piety.
The Book of Jìn states:
Wáng Yán was extremely filial.
His stepmother, Lady Bǔ, once desired fresh fish in the depths of winter.
She ordered Wáng Yán to find some, but he could not,
so she beat him until he bled.
Wáng Yán went to the Fén River, knocked on the ice, and wept.
Suddenly, a fish five chǐ long
leaped out onto the ice.
Wáng Yán took it and presented it to his mother.
Lady Bǔ ate it,
and it lasted for days without being consumed.
Thereupon, she realized her mistake
and treated Wáng Yán as her own son.
It supported Lù Zhèng’s care for his mother.
The History of the Northern Dynasties states:
Lù Zhèng was extremely filial.
His mother was from Wú
and loved fish.
In the north, fish were scarce,
and though Lù Zhèng sought them,
he often struggled to find any.
Later, a spring suddenly emerged in his residence,
producing an endless supply of fish,
which he used to provide meals for his mother.
People of the time thus called the spring “Filial Piety Spring.”
When medicine is placed inside, the fish plays in boiling water.
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity states:
Take a pellet of arsenic and place it in the mouth of a live fish,
then throw it into boiling oil along with another fish without medicine.
Under intense heat,
the fish without medicine will cook quickly and become edible,
while the one with medicine will float and play, splashing about without dying.
When its blood is smeared, one can walk on water.
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity states:
In Dānyáng’s Dān River, there are dān fish.
Ten days before the summer solstice,
watch for them at night.
If the fish float by the water’s edge at night, they emit a red glow.
Cut them and take their blood to smear on your feet,
and you can walk on water.
As for those that spout water to form clouds,
Wáng Zǐnián’s Records of Omissions states:
Yíngzhōu is also called Húnzhōu
or Huánzhōu.
Beside the isle lies a deep abyss,
a thousand lǐ wide,
where a fish dwells.
It is a thousand zhàng long,
with brilliantly colored scales,
a horn on its nose,
and often frolics in groups.
If someone gazes from afar,
they may see multicolored clouds above the water.
Approaching them,
they find it is this fish spouting water to form clouds.
It exhales breath to create wind.
The "Lǐngnán Yìwù Zhì" states:
In the southern regions, there are giant fish,
whose voices are like thunder,
whose breath is like wind,
and whose frothy saliva becomes mist.
Jiè Xiàng once fished for them in front of the palace hall.
The "Shénnǚ Zhuàn" records:
Jiè Xiàng and the King of Wú discussed that the mullet was the finest fish.
He then dug a square pit in front of the hall,
filled it with water drawn from a well,
and sought a hook to bait and catch it.
In a short while, he caught a fish,
and the king had it sliced for raw eating.
Wáng Sù cooked it into a soup in Luòyáng.
The "Luòyáng Jì" states:
When Wáng Sù first entered the state,
he did not eat mutton or dairy products like yogurt,
but often ate crucian carp soup.
Sometimes they can be subdued by ants and mole crickets.
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
A fish large enough to swallow a boat,
if it is tossed ashore and loses the water,
can be subdued by ants and mole crickets.
Thus, birds never tire of flying high,
and fish and turtles never tire of dwelling deep.
How could they be accommodated in a puddle left by an ox's hoof?
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
In a puddle left by an ox's hoof,
there is no room for sturgeon or giant perch.
They emerge from the Bǐng Cave and enter the water.
The "Shuǐ Jīng" states:
The Bǐng Cave produces the jiā fish,
which typically emerges in the second month
and returns in the tenth month.
Water springs from the cave, cascading down in a suspended stream.
The fish pass from beneath the cave into the water.
The cave entrance faces the direction of Bǐng (south-southeast),
hence it is called the Bǐng Cave.
They cross the Yǔmén and transform into dragons.
The "Shuǐ Jīng" states:
Sturgeon and carp emerge from the Gǒng Cave.
In the third month, they ascend and cross the Dragon Gate.
Those that succeed become dragons;
those that fail return with bruised foreheads.
Sometimes the principle does not extend to guests.
The "Yì Jīng" states:
If one wraps a fish,
the principle does not extend to guests.
Sometimes the merit is praised as being without Yǔ.
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
Master Liú said:
"How magnificent were the achievements of Yǔ!
His brilliant virtue reached far and wide.
Without Yǔ,
would we not all be fish?"
One must make the bait fragrant.
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
Those who catch cicadas by torchlight strive to make their fire bright;
those who fish strive to make their bait fragrant.
Thus, fish come before the sacrificial stand.
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
On the sacrificial stand, raw fish comes first;
in the sacrificial vessel, millet soup comes first.
These are not determined by what pleases the eyes and ears,
nor by what suits the mouth and stomach.
Yet the ancient kings valued them,
placing the fundamental before the trivial.
There are instances where they were shot and bled.
The "Sān Qí Jì" states:
The First Emperor offered sacrifices at Qīngchéng Mountain.
He built a stone city extending thirty lǐ into the sea,
and shot fish there.
The water turned the color of blood for several lǐ,
and it remains so to this day.
There are also those that fly high and ride the rain.
The "Línhǎi Yìwù Zhì" states:
The yuān fish resembles a kite,
the yàn fish resembles a swallow.
During overcast or rainy weather, both can fly over a zhàng high.
Then there are the golden minced condiment and jade-like sliced raw fish.
The "Dàyè Shíyí Lù" states:
In the sixth year,
Wú Commandery presented dried sliced perch from Sōngjiāng.
The flesh was white as snow
and not fishy.
This is what is called the golden minced condiment and jade-like sliced raw fish,
a delicacy of the southeast.
Green perch and azure scales.
See the note above on "the crucian carp of Dòngtíng."
There was the fondness for carrying water in boxes.
The "Suí Shū" states:
Yú Xiàorén had a luxurious nature.
He often used camels to carry boxes filled with water,
raising fish to supply himself.
There was the benevolence of halting the net for nursing fish.
The "Táng Shū" states:
Tàizōng observed fishing at the Western Palace.
Seeing fish leaping,
he asked the reason.
The fisherman said:
"These fish are nursing."
Thereupon, he stopped and removed the net.
We also hear of Dù Xiào placing fish in a bamboo tube to send home.
Xiāo Guǎng's "Xiàozǐ Zhuàn" states:
Dù Xiào from Bā Commandery was on duty in Chéngdū.
His mother enjoyed eating live fish.
Xiào obtained live, fresh fish while in office,
cut a bamboo tube, placed two fish inside, and sank it in the water,
saying:
"My mother will surely get these fish."
His wife went to the islet,
retrieved them, and presented them to his mother.
Zhāng Zhāo wove nets to provide meals.
The "Jìn Shū" states:
Zhāng Zhāo, styled Démíng,
was filial from a young age.
His father, Hàn, often suffered from diabetes
and craved live fish.
Zhāo personally wove nets to catch fish
to provide for his father morning and evening.
Wú Yǐn suspected his intentions.
The "Jìn Shū" states:
When Wú Yǐnzhī was the Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
his attendants presented fish to him,
each time picking out the bones and keeping only the flesh.
Yǐnzhī sensed their intention,
punished them, and dismissed them.
Gōngyí declined the competitive offerings.
The "Hánzǐ" states:
Gōngyí Xiū served as Prime Minister of Lǔ and loved fish.
The entire state competed to buy fish and offer them to him.
Gōngyízǐ did not accept them, saying:
"Precisely because I love fish,
I do not accept them."
The manifestation of twin horns in Yuánhǎi.
The "Jìn Shū" states:
Liú Bào, the Zuǒxiánwáng of the Five Tribes and Chányú,
had a wife named Hūyán.
During the Jiāpíng era of Wèi,
she prayed for a child at the Dragon Gate.
Suddenly, a large fish appeared,
with two horns on its head.
It raised its fins, flashed its scales, and came to the sacrificial site,
lingering for a long time before leaving.
The shamans and sorcerers all found it extraordinary,
saying:
"This is an auspicious sign."
That night, she dreamed that the fish she had seen during the day transformed into a person.
In its left hand, it held an object
about the size of half a chicken egg,
radiant and extraordinary.
It handed it to Hūyán, saying:
"This is the essence of the sun.
Consume it, and you will bear a noble son."
She awoke and told Bào,
who said:
"An auspicious omen."
Thirteen months later, she gave birth to Yuánhǎi.
The transformation of Yángqiáo for Zǐjiàn.
The "Shuō Yuàn" states:
Yáng Shū said to Zǐjiàn:
"I was of lowly status in my youth
and did not know the art of governing the people.
There are two principles of fishing:
Those that throw themselves at the line and bait, swallowing them upon encounter,
are the yángqiáo fish.
As fish, they are thin and not delicious.
Those that seem present yet absent,
seeming to bite yet not biting,
are the bream.
As fish, they are rich in flavor."
Zǐjiàn said:
"Well said."
When a whale dies, a comet appears.
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
When qílín fight, solar and lunar eclipses occur;
when a whale dies, a comet appears.
When the crocodiles left, the people of Cháo were free from calamity.
The "Táng Shū" states:
Hán Yù served as the Prefect of Cháo Prefecture.
He inquired about the sufferings of the officials and people,
and they all said:
"In the marsh west of the prefecture, there are crocodiles.
They emerge and transform,
devouring nearly all the people's livestock."
Yù went to inspect the area.
He ordered his assistant, Qín Jì, to roast a pig and a sheep and throw them into the marsh,
praying:
"Now, Cháo Prefecture has the great sea to its south.
From the largest whales and rocs
to the smallest shrimp and crabs,
all are accommodated.
Now I make a pact with the crocodiles:
If you do not leave within seven days,
then this prefect will select skilled and strong men,
wielding powerful bows and poisoned arrows,
to deal with you crocodiles!"
On the evening of the incantation,
a violent storm and thunder arose from the marsh.
After several days,
The marsh waters completely dried up,
and they moved to a spot sixty li west of the old marsh.
From then on, the people of Cháozhōu had no trouble with crocodiles.
If the farmland could be cultivated,
the *Lǐngbiǎo Lùyì* says:
In the mountain fields of Xīnzhōu, Lóngzhōu, and other prefectures,
they select a flat, uncultivated area,
and use hoes and spades to open it into paddy fields.
Awaiting the spring rain,
they store water in the mounds,
then first buy grass carp roe and scatter it in the fields.
After one or two years,
the fish grow large,
and eat all the grass roots.
This both creates cultivated land
and yields profit from the fish,
and when planting rice,
there are no barnyard grasses.
This is indeed the superior method for the common people.
Why gaze enviously at the river?
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
Gazing enviously at fish by the river
is not as good as returning home to weave a net.
As for Línyì transforming iron,
see the annotation "Fàn Wén's swordfish transformation" in the *Shān Fù*.
Flowing abysses produce jade fish,
The *Hàn Wǔ Nèizhuàn* says:
The Queen Mother said:
"Among the superior medicines of the immortals are the flowing abyss jade fish."
The lazy wife is ashamed to hear of the & - ; species,
The *Yìwù Jì* says:
The shrimp has four legs,
yet bears the name of fish,
its head and tail resemble & - ;,
and it walks with a staggering gait.
It grows in mountain streams, entering and leaving deep pits,
with light atop its head,
spouting streams against the wind.
It is said to be a lazy wife who, resenting diligence, threw herself in.
The Water Lord is fearsome in human form.
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
The Water Lord looks like a person riding a horse,
with many fish guiding and following.
It is named Yú Bó,
and appears during great floods.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, someone saw it by the riverbank.
Both the man and the horse had scales and armor,
like a large carp,
only the hands and feet were different.
The eyes and nose were no different from a human's.
After gazing at the person for a long while, it entered the water and vanished.
Having received the letter, one adds to the meal,
An ancient poem says:
A guest came from afar,
and left me a pair of carp.
Calling my child to cook the carp,
inside was a foot-long plain silk letter.
I knelt long to read the plain letter—
what was the intent within the letter?
Above it said "add to your meals,"
below it said "endless longing."
It also communicates through dreams and prolongs life.
The *Liáng Shū* says:
Liú Zhīhēng, Grand Administrator of Nánjùn, once dreamed of two men surnamed Lǐ
who came to him begging for their lives.
He did not understand it.
The next day, in mid-summer,
someone presented him with two live carp.
Zhīhēng said:
"This is what moved me in the dream."
He released them.
He then dreamed they came to thank him, saying:
"We shall cause you to have extended years."
To cook them, one must avoid frequent stirring,
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
Governing a large state is like cooking a small fish.
Annotation:
When cooking a small fish,
one must not stir it;
when governing a large state,
one must not cause vexation.
Vexation causes the people to toil;
stirring causes the fish to fall apart.
To achieve it, one dislikes its extreme clarity.
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Response to a Guest's Objection" says:
When water is extremely clear, there are no fish;
when people are extremely discerning, they have no followers.
Taking from marshes warns against draining them,
The *Shuōyuàn* says:
Draining a marsh to catch fish
does not mean one cannot get fish,
but that next year there will be no fish to catch.
Examining the abyss detests clarity.
The *Shǐjì* says:
Wú King Liú Bì feigned illness and did not attend court.
The Emperor questioned the Wú envoy,
and the envoy replied:
"To see clearly the fish in the abyss
is inauspicious."
The Son of Heaven therefore bestowed upon the King of Wú a small table and a staff,
indicating old age,
and he did not have to attend court.
This is sufficient to verify human affairs
and establish the principles of statecraft.
How could it merely be reciting the "Jiǔ Yù" from the *Máo Shī*?
The *Shī* says:
The fish of the nine-bagged net
are zūn and fáng.
Or observing the single star in astronomy.
The *Xīngjīng* says:
There is one star, Tiānyú,
behind the Tail constellation in the River.
When this star is bright, large fish emerge from the sea.
Creatures
Even the tiniest insects, in their simple movements,
all gather in groups and live together.
Observing the autumn chirping of crickets,
an ancient poem says:
"The cricket awaits autumn to chirp,
the mayfly emerges in the shade."
Awaiting the fluttering wings of the "shā jī" (a type of insect).
See the Book of Songs.
The annotation states:
"In the sixth month, the shā jī's wings mature and it flutters them."
The "yī wēi" (a type of insect) is indoors,
the "xiāo shāo" (a type of spider) is at the door.
Book of Songs.
The annotation states:
"The yī wēi resembles millet,
the xiāo shāo has long legs;
this occurs when there is no one in the house."
Some guard melons to feed,
see the "Melon Rhapsody" annotation: "There is a guard, the yù fù."
Some gnaw on mulberry trees as borers.
The Ěryǎ says:
"Shàng gnaws mulberry."
Annotation:
"Gnaws mulberry trees,
bores holes into them."
Shàng,
pronounced shì ràng qiē.
Admire the five colors of the "láng tiáo" (a type of cicada),
the Ěryǎ says:
"Tiáo,
láng."
Annotation:
The Xià Xiǎo Zhèng says:
"Láng tiáo,
possesses all five colors."
Pity the five abilities of the "shí shǔ" (a type of rodent).
The Shuōwén says:
"Shí,
is the five-skill rodent:
it can fly but not beyond the room,
it can climb but not to the top of trees,
it can swim but not across water,
it can burrow but not conceal itself,
it can run but not outpace humans."
"Yāo yāo" the grass insects,
"tì tì" the hill grasshoppers.
The Book of Songs says.
The "yín yú" (silverfish) delights in clothing and books,
the Ěryǎ says:
"Yín,
is the white fish."
Annotation:
"An insect in clothing and books,
also called bǐng yú."
Yín is pronounced yín.
The "qí cáo" (grub) moves in dung and soil.
The Ěryǎ says:
"Féi,
is qí cáo." Annotation states:
"It lives in dung and soil."
Then there is the earthworm, which has no heart,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
"Those that feed on water are good swimmers and can endure cold,
those that feed on soil have no heart and lack wisdom."
Annotation:
"Those that feed on water are like turtles and fish,
those that feed on soil are like earthworms."
Bees and scorpions are venomous,
see the "Bee Rhapsody" annotation: "Being venomous, how can one not be prepared?"
Fireflies emerge from rotten grass,
the Lǐjì says:
"Rotten grass transforms into fireflies."
The "xiē" (wood-boring insect) is born from decayed wood.
The Ěryǎ says:
"Qiú qí,
is xiē."
Annotation:
"It lives in wood,
now commonly called xiē,
though it varies by location."
Imitate the spider in spinning webs,
the Dìwáng Shìjì says:
"Tāng went out and saw someone setting nets,
descended from his carriage,
ordered three sides of the net to be removed and one side left,
and further instructed him,
praying:
'In the past, spiders spun webs,
now humans learn to weave them.
Those who wish to go left, go left;
those who wish to go right, go right;
those who wish to go high, go high;
those who wish to go low, go low;
I will take only those who defy fate.'"
Pity the flying moth rushing toward the candle flame.
The Sòng Shū says:
"Emperor Shǎo lacked virtue,
Fù Liàng inwardly harbored worry and fear,
and was on duty in the palace.
Observing a night moth flying toward a candle,
he composed the poem 'Gǎn Wù' (Reflections on Things),
to convey his feelings."
Emperor Tàizōng swallowed locusts to avert disaster,
the Táng Shū says:
"During the Zhēnguàn era,
locusts plagued several counties in Zhōngnán.
Emperor Tàizōng went to the garden,
saw the locusts,
picked up several and prayed to them:
'If the people have faults,
they lie with me alone.
If you have spirits,
only devour me,
do not harm the people.'
He was about to swallow them.
Attending ministers feared he would fall ill,
and hurriedly advised against it.
Emperor Tàizōng said:
'What I hope for is to transfer the disaster;
why should I avoid illness for my own person?'
He then swallowed them.
From then on, the locusts caused no disaster."
King Chǔ ate a leech and received blessings.
The Jiǎ Yì Shū says:
"King Huì of Chǔ ate cold pickles and found a leech,
so he hastily swallowed it,
and developed an abdominal illness, unable to eat.
The Prime Minister entered to inquire about his illness,
and the King said:
'I ate pickles and found a leech.
If I do not punish the offense,
the law would be abandoned and authority not upheld;
if I reprimand and execute,
I fear all the food supervisors would die,
so I swallowed it.'
The Prime Minister said:
'The Way of Heaven shows no favoritism,
it only assists the virtuous.
The King has humane virtue,
the illness will not harm you.'
The King indeed recovered from his illness."
Zhuāng Zhōu dreamed of being a butterfly,
the Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Once, Zhōu dreamed he was a butterfly,
fluttering joyfully as a butterfly.
Suddenly he awoke,
and was startled to find himself Zhōu.
Did Zhōu dream he was a butterfly,
or did the butterfly dream it was Zhōu?"
Wǔzǐ stored fireflies in a bag.
The Xù Jìnyáng Qiū says:
"Chē Yìn, styled Wǔzǐ,
was fond of learning and never tired of it,
but his family was poor and often lacked oil for lamps.
In summer, he would put dozens of fireflies in a gauze bag,
to continue studying day and night."
The snail's horns battle between the Mán and Chù tribes,
the Zhuāngzǐ says:
"There was a state on the left horn of a snail,
called the Chù clan;
a state on the right horn of a snail,
called the Mán clan.
They fought over territory,
leaving tens of thousands of corpses,
and pursued the defeated for fifteen days before returning."
Mosquito eyelashes gather the jiāo míng.
The Lièzǐ says:
"On the riverbanks, tiny insects are born,
called jiāo míng.
They fly in swarms and gather on mosquito eyelashes."
Some have front claws and rear spurs,
the Huáinánzǐ says:
"All blood-and-qi creatures,
bearing teeth and horns,
with front claws and rear spurs:
those with horns butt,
those with teeth bite,
those with venom sting,
those with hooves kick.
They play when happy,
harm each other when angry—
this is their natural disposition."
Some chirp with their chests or with their legs.
The Zhōulǐ says:
"Those that chirp with their mouths,
those that chirp from the side,
those that chirp with their wings,
those that chirp with their legs,
those that chirp with their chests—
these are called the small insect category."
The annotation states:
"Chirping with the mouth—
belongs to the jīng liè type;
chirping from the side—
belongs to the tiáo ní type;
chirping with wings—
belongs to the fā huáng type;
chirping with legs—
belongs to the gōng xū moving-leg type;
chirping with the chest—
They belong to the category of crawling creatures.
Some have legs, some are legless.
The *Erya* says:
Those with legs are called *chóng* (insects),
while those without legs are called *zhì* (legless worms).
Some crawl in winding paths, others move sideways.
The *Rites of Zhōu* says:
Those with exoskeletons,
those with endoskeletons,
those that move backward,
those that move sideways,
those that move in lines,
and those that move in winding paths.
Annotations:
Those with exoskeletons
belong to the turtle family;
those with endoskeletons,
to the soft-shelled turtle family;
those that move backward,
to the earthworm and similar creatures;
those that move sideways,
to the crab family;
those that move in lines,
to the fish family;
those that move in winding paths,
to the snake family.
They are only seen sealing their burrows.
The *Book of Rites* says:
In mid-autumn, hibernating insects seal their burrows.
How could they be spoken to about ice?
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
A frog in a well cannot be spoken to about the sea—
it is confined by its dwelling.
A summer insect cannot be spoken to about ice—
it is bound by the season.
As for the giant earthworm being an auspicious sign,
the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
During the time of Huángdì, a giant earthworm appeared.
The earth's energy was dominant,
hence its yellow color.
Gāo Yòu's annotation:
Yǐn
refers to the earthworm.
The mole cricket signifying good fortune,
the *Hétú* says:
When Huángdì rose to power, a giant mole cricket appeared.
Also, Liú Xiàng's *Biélù* says:
Zōu Yǎn stated that during Huángdì's reign, with earth as the ruling virtue,
there were mole crickets as large as oxen.
Mosquitoes gathering can create a thunderous sound.
The *Hànshū* says:
Zhōngshān Jìngwáng said:
"When many blow, they can move mountains;
when mosquitoes gather, they can create thunder."
The gadfly flies by attaching itself to a swift horse.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
The gadfly, with the swift horse, can travel a thousand *lǐ* without flying,
and without provisions, it does not hunger.
The scorpion stings people with its tail.
The *Shī Yìshū* states.
The "hanging maiden" spins silk and hangs itself.
The *Erya* says:
Xiǎn
refers to the "hanging maiden."
Annotation:
It delights in hanging itself to death.
The *Yì Yuàn* says:
The "hanging maiden" spins silk and hangs itself.
In the past, Qí's Dōngguō Jiāng, after causing chaos in Cuī Zhù's household,
Qìng Fēng killed her two sons,
and Jiāng also hanged herself.
Folklore says this woman transformed into a "hanging maiden."
Also, it is said that ants learn by constant practice.
See the annotation "shí shù zì zī" in the *Ant Fu*.
The inchworm seeks to stretch.
The *Yìjīng* says.
Entering Empress Mǎ's dream,
the *Dōngguān Hànjì* says:
In the Yǒngpíng era, officials proposed establishing the Chángqiū Palace,
but the emperor had not yet spoken.
The empress dowager said:
"Noble Lady Mǎ's virtue surpasses all in the rear palace."
Thus, she ascended to the highest honor.
A few days prior,
she dreamed of tens of thousands of small flying insects
attaching to her body and burrowing into her skin,
then flying away again.
They gathered on Wáng Zé's body.
The *Qí Shū* says:
When Wáng Jìngzé was young, hunting in the grass,
insects like black beans gathered on his body.
When plucked off, they bled,
and Jìngzé found this disturbing.
A diviner said:
"This is an auspicious sign of being enfeoffed as a marquis."
Jìngzé was pleased,
so he left the capital to prove himself.
The ephemera's attire is elegant,
the locust's wings are numerous.
Both are seen in the *Book of Songs*.
It is also said that the centipede has a hundred legs.
The *Bówùzhì* says:
The centipede,
also called the hundred-legged worm,
when cut in half, its head and tail each move independently.
The hornworm is multicolored.
The *Guǎngzhì* says:
There are multicolored hornworms.
The fragrant locust tree hornworm is multicolored,
while those with horns are very foul-smelling.
The dung beetle rolls dung balls.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
The wisdom of the dung beetle
lies in rolling dung balls.
The centipede delights in eating small snakes.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Humans eat domesticated animals,
deer eat grass,
centipedes delight in eating small snakes—
who in the world knows the true taste?
Annotation:
Dài
refers to small snakes.
Centipedes delight in eating their eyes.
There is also the short fox, which spits sand to shoot shadows.
Lù Jī's *Shī Yì* says:
Yù,
the short fox,
also called the shadow-shooter,
resembles a turtle with three legs.
If it shoots a person's shadow, it can kill them.
When southerners wish to enter water,
they first throw tiles or stones into the water
to muddy it,
lest the creature spit sand at them.
The mantis raises its arms to block a chariot.
The *Hánshī Wàizhuàn* says:
When Duke Zhuāng of Qí went hunting,
a mantis raised its legs as if to fight his chariot wheel.
He asked his charioteer:
"What insect is this?"
The reply was:
"This is a mantis.
As an insect, it knows only to advance, not retreat,
and underestimates its strength, lightly engaging the enemy."
The duke said:
"This is the bravest insect in the world."
He turned his chariot to avoid it,
and brave men came to serve him.
Smearing green coins to bring back money,
see the annotation "jí cǐ qīng fú" in the *Coin Fu*.
Burying dragonflies to transform into pearls.
See the annotation "mái qīng líng yú dì zhōng" in the *Pearl Fu*.
Speaking of the Way, one feels ashamed before the vinegar fly.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
When Confucius heard Lǎodān's words,
he came out and said to Yán Huí:
"As for the Way,
am I not like a vinegar fly?"
Annotation:
Refers to the midge.
In governing, one is compared to the gourd wasp.
The *Book of Rites* says:
Governing
is like the gourd wasp.
Annotation:
Pú lú,
refers to the gourd wasp,
which carries mulberry insects to raise as its own offspring.
Such is the vast variety of these species—
how could they all be listed one by one?
Cicada
Ah, the tiny insect of the Qí maiden,
also breathes and roams in play.
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
Niú Xiǎng asked Dǒng Zhòngshū:
"Why is the cicada called the Qí maiden?"
He replied:
"Long ago, the Queen of Qí resented the king and died,
her corpse transformed into a cicada,
climbed a tree in the courtyard and chirped shrilly,
hence called the Qí maiden."
Riding the cool breeze, it flutters and soars,
responding to the white dew with its singing cry.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
In early autumn, the cool breeze arrives,
white dew descends,
and the cold cicada sings.
Though small and feeble, lacking strength,
the *Yuánshén Qì* says:
The cicada lacks strength,
therefore it does not eat.
Yet it bears patterns and has tassels.
The *Lǐ* says:
The silkworm spins, yet the crab has a frame;
the wasp wears a crown, yet the cicada has tassels;
when an adult's elder brother dies, Zǐgāo wears mourning for him.
I admire Wáng Chōng for not catching them,
the *Lùnhéng* says:
Wáng Chōng as a child,
did not recklessly mingle with peers,
nor did he cover sparrows or catch cicadas.
I understand Shàorú's dampened clothes.
See the note in the *Lù Fù*: "Shàorú borrowed words about catching sparrows."
I sigh at Shāng Tāng, using it as a metaphor,
the *Shī* says:
Alas, you Yīn Shāng,
like the cicada, like the small cicada.
Note:
Tiáo,
is the cicada.
Táng,
is the small cicada.
It darts among elm and sandalwood, suddenly flying.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
The Péng bird's wings are like clouds hanging from the sky,
soaring on the whirlwind up ninety thousand li.
The cicada and the turtledove laugh at it, saying:
"We rise abruptly and fly,
darting among elm and sandalwood to rest,
why go ninety thousand li to the south?"
It lacks the distant knowledge of snow,
the *Yántiě Lùn* says:
Not believing because one has not seen,
is like the cicada not knowing snow.
It merely sucks dew to sustain itself.
Cáo Dàjiā's *Chán Fù* says:
It sucks clear dew in the crimson garden,
raising itself on high branches to groom its wings.
I revere the glorious radiance of the imperial court,
shining brightly upon leopard and sable.
Zhū Yì was astonished by the extraordinary feathered cap,
see the note in the *Guān Fù*: "The flying cicada delights in Zhū Yì."
Hé Jǐ prided himself on the wonder of the painted fan.
See the note in the *Shàn Fù*: "Hé Jǐ's fondness for cicadas and sparrows."
Though it has no mouth, it can sing,
and though it does not eat, it does not hunger.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
The snake lacks feet yet moves,
the fish lacks ears yet hears,
the cicada lacks a mouth yet sings.
It does not eat,
see the note above on "lacking strength."
Some catch it with skill,
the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
Zhòngní saw a hunchback catching cicadas,
as if picking them up.
Zhòngní said:
"Skillful indeed,
is there a way?"
He replied:
"I have a way.
In five or six months, stacking two pellets without dropping them,
then misses are rare;
stacking three without dropping them,
then misses are one in ten;
stacking five without dropping them,
it is like picking them up.
I position my body,
like a stump or a stake;
I hold my arm,
like the branch of a withered tree.
Though heaven and earth and the myriad things are many,
I am aware only of the cicada's wings.
I do not turn or shift,
not letting the myriad things distract me from the cicada's wings,
how could I not succeed!"
Some glue them without missing.
Fù Xián's *Zhān Chán Fù* says:
The cherry tree provides much shade,
its fruits ripen early,
planted before the hall,
in the height of summer, I stroll leisurely beneath it.
A cicada sings,
I look up and see it,
so I order it glued and caught,
to amuse the children.
Upon reflection, when the cicada delights in this tree,
it does not know the glue is coming;
just as humans delight in wealth and honor,
and do not anticipate the arrival of calamity.
It foretells omens of ministers' negligence and strange rumors,
the *Zhōushū* says:
Five days after the summer solstice,
the cicada begins to sing;
if it does not sing,
high ministers will be negligent.
On the day of the beginning of autumn,
the cold cicada sings;
if it does not,
ministers will not strive diligently.
The *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* says:
In the top line of the Gòu hexagram, the cicada begins to sing;
if it does not sing,
the state will have many strange rumors.
It embodies the form of purity, emptiness, and awareness of change.
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
Diāochán is Hú attire.
Diāo,
is chosen for its patterned fur without being flashy,
outwardly soft and yielding,
inwardly strong and firm.
Chán,
is chosen for its purity, emptiness, and awareness of changing times.
Those in position have refinement but do not flaunt it,
have martial prowess but do not show it,
cultivating purity and emptiness within,
acting in awareness of the times.
It sings without missing the season,
grasping the nodes of midsummer and late autumn;
the *Lǐ* says:
In the month of midsummer,
the cicada begins to sing;
in the month of late autumn,
the cold cicada sings.
When it gleams and is caught,
it is due to the method of bright fire and shaking the tree.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
Those who glean cicadas must make their fire bright,
and shake the tree;
if the fire is not bright,
even shaking the tree is useless.
If a person has bright virtue,
then all under heaven will turn to him,
just as cicadas turn to bright fire.
Bees
As for the minute insect known as the fēng,
The Erya states:
Fēng,
is the chǒu yú.
There are distinctions between earth and wood varieties.
The Erya states:
Earth fēng and wood fēng.
They are called mēng wēng,
and also called yōu shuì.
The Fāngyán states:
Fēng,
in the regions of Yān and Zhào are called mēng wēng,
or called yōu shuì.
The large ones that have honey
are called hú fēng.
Yōu shuì,
pronounced yōu shuì.
During the harmonious spring when they breed,
if one smears a vessel with wax and honey,
and if a few bees can be captured,
then the entire swarm will all arrive.
The Bówùzhì states:
In distant mountains where beeswax and honey are found,
they use wood to make vessels,
open a small hole,
and smear the vessel with beeswax and honey,
coating it thoroughly inside and out.
In spring when the bees are about to breed,
they capture two or three and place them in the vessel.
The bees fly away,
then soon bring companions back.
Day by day they gradually increase,
and eventually settle in the vessel.
When they attached to Jiǎ Méng's carriage,
it indeed foreshadowed his execution;
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū states:
Yán Fēng of Yùzhāng, styled Ménghóu,
served as the Registrar.
The Grand Administrator Jiǎ Méng raised troops
intending to attack Wáng Mǎng.
Flying bees attached to the crossbar of Méng's carriage.
Fēng advised against it,
considering it an inauspicious omen.
Méng did not listen,
and was indeed killed.
When they gathered on Yuán's boat,
news of defeat soon followed.
Wáng Yǐn's Jìnshū states:
Grand Commandant Táo Kǎn recommended Cāngcáo Cānjūn Yuán Qiān as Grand Administrator of Gāoliáng.
Before reaching within a hundred lǐ,
bees covered the sun and descended onto Qiān's boat in the inlet.
He then received an urgent document from the commandery,
stating bandits intended to attack the vulnerable commandery.
Qiān wished to hasten there.
The next morning he advanced southwest,
but suddenly encountered a great wind with flying sand,
heaven and earth darkened and merged,
he could not return to the inlet,
and thus perished at sea.
They dangle their stingers and always intend to sting,
The Xiàojīng Yuán Shénqì states:
Bees and scorpions dangle their stingers.
Being poisonous, how can one be unprepared?
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
The Zhū people sent out an army.
The Duke despised Zhū,
and prepared no defenses against them.
Zāng Wénzhòng said:
"No state is too small,
to be taken lightly.
My lord, do not say Zhū is small.
Bees and scorpions have poison,
how much more a state!"
Their cells cannot accommodate a swan's egg,
The Huáinánzǐ states:
A bee's cell cannot hold a swan's egg.
Their nests resemble bells strikingly.
The Jiāngbiǎo Lù Yì states:
In the Xuān-Shè region, bees build nests in mountain forests,
as large as huge bells.
They use smoke to disperse the queen bee,
then take them.
One nest yields several dǒu of bee larvae.
They select those without fully developed wings and legs,
stir-fry them with salt and fermented milk, dry them in the sun,
send them to the capital Luòyáng,
as local tribute.
Some gather on cliffs and are collected,
The Bówùzhì states:
Remote mountain commanderies produce beeswax and honey.
The beeswax and honey are all attached to sheer cliffs and stone walls,
inaccessible by climbing.
Only by descending from the mountaintop in a suspended basket
can one obtain them.
The bees then leave and do not return.
The remaining nests and wax attached to the rock
are pecked by birds smaller than sparrows,
flocking by the thousands.
By winter, they are all consumed,
and the places look as if polished and washed.
Come spring, the bees all return to the washed spots,
and build nests as before.
This happens year after year,
initially without any error or disorder.
People also each claim their flat spots,
calling them wax strongholds.
The birds are called líng què,
but catching them is ultimately impossible.
Some devour field seedlings and cause calamity.
The Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn states:
In the thirty-eighth year of King Zhāo of Qín,
the Shàngjùn commandery suffered a great famine,
as bees devoured the field seedlings.
They build their dwellings beside Féng Mountain,
The Shānhǎijīng states:
Píngféng Mountain has a spirit resembling a human,
with two heads,
named Jiāo Chóng,
the chief of bān insects,
and indeed the dwelling of honey.
Guō Pú's annotation states:
Jiāo is the chief of the bān insects.
The dwelling is where bees reside.
Mì is also a name for bees.
Bān pronounced bān.
They pursued bandits in the land of Jiàn'ān.
The Xuānyànjì states:
In the first year of Yuánjiā,
over a hundred mountain bandits in Jiàn'ān commandery
suddenly attacked the commandery seat,
plundering the people's assets, sons, and daughters.
They then entered a Buddhist temple,
searching for treasures.
Previously, all the ritual offerings
were separately sealed in one room.
When the bandits broke the door,
suddenly tens of thousands of bees
emerged from the clothing chests,
stinging them simultaneously.
The bandits' bodies and heads swelled painfully,
their eyes swollen shut.
They abandoned all their plunder
and fled.
Some recorded the form of the slender-waisted wasp,
The Bówùzhì states:
The slender-waisted wasp is among those without a queen.
It takes mulberry caterpillars or mole cricket eggs, embraces them, and makes them its own offspring.
The Shī states:
"The míng líng has young,
the guǒ luǒ carries them away."
Some marveled at the strangeness of the gourd-like ones.
The Chǔcí states:
Red ants like elephants,
black bees like gourds.
Armies should be warned beforehand,
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
If troops on the march suddenly encounter swarms of flying bees or gadflies,
especially if honeybees are numerous,
prepare for hidden ambushing bandits.
One's bosom and sleeves can be startled unexpectedly.
The Jìnshū states:
Zōu Zhàn said to Emperor Wǔ:
"When a fierce beast is in the field,
taking up a spear and going out,
any ordinary man can do it.
But if bees or scorpions arise in one's bosom or sleeves,
even a brave man is startled and alarmed,
because it is unexpected."
Some were killed by burning Húsū,
see the annotation for "Then hills have hard metal for rims" in the Chē Fù.
Some painted on banners and flags as auspicious signs.
see the annotation for "Auspiciously heard gathered bees" in the Zhōu Fù.
Spitting from the mouth as a trick,
what divinity did the immortal guest possess?
The Bié Zhuàn of Gě Xiāngōng states:
Immortal Gě was dining with a guest.
The guest said:
"I must ask the Master to perform a marvelous trick."
Before the meal was finished,
the Immortal spat out the rice from his mouth,
which all turned into flying bees filling the room.
Some gathered on the guest's body,
causing everyone to tremble with awe,
but none stung.
After a while,
the Immortal opened his mouth wide,
the bees flew into it,
and all turned back into rice.
Attaching them to clothing to incite slander,
what crime did Bóqí commit?
The Liènǚ Zhuàn states:
Yǐn Jìfǔ's son Bóqí was extremely filial.
His stepmother took bees, removed their venom,
and tied them to his clothes.
Bóqí approached,
wanting to remove them.
His mother then cried out loudly:
"Bóqí is pulling at me!"
Jìfǔ became suspicious of him.
Bóqí took his own life.
Ant
If it resembles the shape of railings, trellises, towers, and terraces,
it is called the "Ant Palace."
In the past, someone saw tens of thousands of large ants gathered together,
all of them golden in color.
They dug into the ground until they reached a spring,
and there they found this stone.
It originates from the ruins of Kūnlún.
The "Shānhǎijīng" says:
Zhūyǐ,
its appearance resembles an ant.
Guō Pú said:
Yǐ,
refers to pífú (large ants).
It is located in the ruins of Kūnlún.
Piercing flesh with the tip of a lance,
see the annotation above on "the strange incident of Tāng Wò Huán Qiān."
Observing fish in an inkstone.
The "Zuǎnyìjì" says:
There was a man named Xú Xuánzhī
who was reading at night
when he suddenly saw hundreds of warriors ascending onto his bed,
hunting freely on a flower-patterned carpet.
He also saw hundreds of people climbing onto his desk,
carrying fishing nets and tools,
fishing in the inkstone,
and catching hundreds or thousands of fish.
The next day, he dug and found an ant nest,
which he completely burned.
The astonishing sight of ants as large as elephants,
Sòng Yù's "Zhāohún" says:
O soul, O soul, return!
The south is not a place to linger.
Red ants are like elephants,
and black ants are like pots.
Hearing the sound of fighting oxen without any emptiness.
The "Shìshuō" says:
Yīn Zhòngkān's father suffered from a deficiency-induced palpitation,
and when he heard ants moving under his bed,
he said it was the sound of oxen fighting.
Collapsing a thousand-zhàng-long dike,
the "Hánzǐ" says:
A thousand-zhàng-long dike can collapse due to the burrows of ants.
Forming knots at the four corners of a funeral carriage.
The "Lǐ" says:
At the funeral of Zǐ Zhāng,
Gōngmíng Yí composed the eulogy.
The red silk covering,
had ant knots at its four corners.
Annotation:
The four corners of the painted silk covering
were patterned like ants crawling,
intertwined with each other.
Selecting elegant and beautiful phrases,
we have already heard from Guō Pú;
Guō Pú's "Pífú Fù" says:
Adorning the funeral carriage of the Yīn people,
intertwined at the four corners;
aiding Duke Huán of Qí's exhausted army,
by the high anthills east of the mountains.
Sensing the budding yang to move stealthily,
knowing to seal the nest when rain approaches.
Such is the ignorance of this insect,
yet it shows foresight akin to wisdom.
Delighting in tranquil and leisurely thoughts,
we further see from Yìng Qú.
Yìng Qú's "Letter to Cáo Zhāobó" says:
The empty city is vast and desolate,
what one hears is the mournful wind,
what one sees are birds and sparrows.
In the past, Minister Chén served as a county magistrate,
and wherever he was, it was tranquil and secluded.
Sitting alone in melancholy thought,
he relied on wandering ants to amuse his mind.
Comparing it to the present,
I know it was not an exaggeration.
